Strange or bad design decisions abound in this game including but not limited to the following:
General Subjective
- Terribly boring single player/co-op missions (essential for progression and receiving gear)
- Movement skills are clunky (feels as if you have 200 or so ping at all times)
- Guns feel clunky and inaccurate even when they should be hitting
- Damage and TTK seems way too low
- Cluttered UI
General Objective
- Friendly minions Body block, which would be okay, but you can't jump over the large camp summons and they can box you out of a retreat)
- Relating to the point above, the two MOBA maps are designed around tiny chokepoints
- Non exsistant match making (lvl 1-10's get matched versus lvl 60-100's almost every game)
- Single player/ co-op mobs are bullet sponges and were clearly not balanced for Melee or AOE characters (most require headshots only to kill in under 30 seconds)
- After the first objective (tower) is killed, creeps turn into superminions causing the winning team to snowball too hard
- Miko's ability to sprint while healing
- Marquis and Toby Exploit for Overgrowth still not fixed (can snipe the enemy objective from their own base)
- Marquis view model bug (can peek over cover and shoot safely, head cannot be seen or shot)
- Deande's clone has same color health bar, (for teammates) making it hard for your own team to tell which is which
- Enemy name plates bug out for characters like Pheobe, making them almost invisible unless you're looking at the minimap (mostly a problem with screen clutter and FOV)
FOV
- Poor FOV for most characters (affects melee mostly)
- Poor View models for most characters (severely affects melee)
- Unnecessary screen shake on melee characters like Kelvin (making them nausiating to play)
- Pheobe's basic attacks flash on screen (only for her), making them hard to stomach for an entire match (seizure inducing)
Hilarious
-FOV - The community responds to these FOV issues by suggesting melee has to look at their mini map rather than their screen while fighting in order to see/kill enemies.

- This game is a clear step back in quality and polish from Gearbox's previous games (Borderlands 2 and Pre-Sequel) in almost every aspect: Character design, level design, enemy variety, character builds, player gearing, weapon and view models, FOV, Gun and movement feel, Story and writing, and single player/ co-op campaign.

Battleborn is an FPS-MOBA crossbreed in the emergent 'Hero Shooter' genre by Gearbox, creators of such awesomeness as Borderlands and the original Counterstrike and producers of such utter steaming cow dung as Aliens: Colonial Marines (An outsourced botch job by Timegate Studios that they had to remake in six months from the ground up that was most definitely their fault. This game almost made me swear off buying from Gearbox again due to Randy Pitchford's attitude afterwards.) and Duke Nukem Forever. (Abandoned Vaporware from 3D Realms that 2K bought from them and gave to Gearbox to complete- not their fault.).
So first things first, I wasn't interested in this game in the beginning, I saw it at the Playstation Experience and sortof went 'meh' because the truth is, I normally hate MOBAs. I never got into Smite, don't enjoy the gameplay of League of Legends, DOTA 2 and Heroes of Newerth and so as soon as I see the term 'FPSMOBA' being applied, I rolled my eyes.
Then the Open Beta happened and I learned that actually, this game has a PVE story element similar to Borderlands. 'Cool.' I gave it a go and played 'The Voids Edge' first and didn't get off to a great start as our wolf sentry, affectionately known as 'Wolfie' that we were tasked with protecting died halfway through my first game. Damn...
Then I played 'The Algorithm' and was introduced to two of my favourite Battleborn characters...Geoff and ISIC.
I'm not going to spoil the level, but suffice it to say that it was the most fun level of a game that I've played all year and the dialogue was *EXCELLENT* and I was hooked, but cautious...I didn't know how many story missions there'd be and how much of the weight of the game would be on the Multiplayer, which I never thought in a million years that I'd enjoy.
So, I was going to uninstall the Beta and call it a day after completing the two available story missions during that test...when I just said 'f*** it' and loaded into a PVP queue for Incursion.
My god was I ever wrong, I loved the PVP even more than the PVE!! :D
'Incursion' is a semi-traditional MOBA mode where you push creepwaves (Known as 'Minions' in true Gearbox fashion) up to a Robot Sentry (Which act as this game's towers) in order to get past it and attack the enemy's main base. There are mercenaries that spawn periodically that you can also fight to recruit them into joining your minions as well as turrets, accellerator-points and a spawnable 'Elite Minion' that can be built and recruited using 'shards' the games currency. Games can last up to 30 minutes.
I was hooked completely from there on in and went to clock in over 40 hours during Open Beta. There was another mode available to me during that time, which was; 'Meltdown.' An unorthodox take on the MOBA formula, Meltdown sees you defending and attacking across two lanes. The object of this mode is to escort your minions into 'grinders' (Which are actually the gaming maw of a crazed and psychotic 'Magnus' AI called MINREC.) in order to stave off MINREC's wrath and ensure that he doiesn't murder your whole team. This mode is much more directly about battlefield control and working out when is appropriate to attack and disengage. Again, games of this type can last up to 30 minutes.
Throughout my time with this game, I found the dialogue to be funny and generally well written, the plot is basic and does just enough to keep you engaged and interested (Though may hamper future titles if this is to become a series.) the gameplay is fluid and there are many diverse hero types each with a role they can play and wiggle room to adapt them to your playstyle through a 10 level skill system called the 'Helix System.' Playing a tank, but want more damage? Well, there's usually a skill for that. Playing an attacker, but there's no healer on the team? Why not spec into Life leech? I find the system to be pretty cool at this point.
I'm not normally a fan of melee in a first person shooter and this I confess is my biggest problem with the game as it's easy for enemies to move erratically and bunnyhop out of your melee range unless you can somehow stunlock them into place and this is definitely an area I hope that improves over time.
There's also a Control Point multiplayer mode too which is great for trying new heroes and having a quick game, clocking at just 10 minutes!
So, having bought the Deluxe Edition of this game, I've got to say I'm having no regrets. Sure, there are some balance issues and exploits at present, but the game has only been out two weeks so-far and we haven't had our first major patch as of yet. Gearbox are active on their forum and a little less on the Reddit about the development of patches and content and they often ask for our feedback and input. The story mode missions can get a little bit samey, but there's enough there for some good replay value and rewards for playing that you can take into PVP in the form of 'Gear Items' that you can activate also using shards.
All in all, I think Battleborn is a surprisingly excellent game with a fresh sense of humour and launched surprisingly smoothly considering how modern Multiplayer launches tend to go. (The Division & Diablo III come to mind immediately.) If you like Team Fortress 2 or Monday Night Combat but would like a splash of DOTA or League in there for good measure, I'd recommend giving this game a go. I love it, I've clocked in over 100 hours (Beta included) with it so far and it'll be with me for a long, long time to come.
Now, well over a year after release, unfortunately this game's fate is sealed. The game made a transition a few months ago towards a Free to Play model and unfortunately never recovered the many players that it lost after launch to titans like Overwatch and PUBG. That said, I'll always look back over my time with this game with fond memories and now that all of the story content has been released, I can safely say that at the extremely low prices this game now sells at, you'd be mad not to pick up a copy just to play through the PVE missions and enjoy the wacky characters, fun dialogue and non-linear storytelling (There's about 3 - 5 different ways a story will play out as well as tonnes of objectives that change each time you play.)
Battleborn is a very good video game that is a victim of its publisher (2K do not make good decisions with games like this- just ask Evolve and the latest NBA game with it's faux-freemium economy to improve your player in a full-priced 'Fee-to-Pay' game.) and of being released just before one of the most successful videogames of all time, Overwatch. We only have so-much time to devote to games and unfortunately, alot of people dropped this very quickly. I myself have stopped playing both, but I did get well over 120 hours out of this game across BETA and launch and am overall very happy with it.
Never die Battleborn...never die. :'(

I've never played an FMV game before, although I have heard of their prevalence back in the day. So I'll be talking about it as a newcomer to the genre with a considerably smaller pair of nostalgia goggles than some others.
The atmosphere is pretty good. The screen glare, the CRT-monitor style works pretty well to give you that 90s movies' sense of searching through really old archived VCR videos. On the monitor, there is a bit of reflection off the lights in the background which flicker sometimes (and is brilliantly used as an element of the plot).
As for the story, holy crap. The game starts off with the database search program open, with "murder" typed in. There are only five clips, but they summarize the story and create a motivation just using the five clips, as well as giving you "keywords" to search to continue the game. For a game that supposedly feels open and lets you search any clips, it's beautifully paced. Everything was planned and orchestrated wonderfully. When you learn an important detail about her life, you can feel the game go "this is exactly how I planned it". The dialogue itself is really well done, considering that keywords needed to be planned out in advance to give the player just enough to motivate them.
There are definitely moments that send a chill down your spine as you start to realize her motivations, her childhood and start to piece together how it all came to be. And the story itself is really unique.
But as fantastic I say this game is, there are some issues with the way the story is told. The non-linearity makes it great when you find a piece of evidence and you follow that trail to the inevitable plot twist, but it's not that great when around a quarter to half of all clips you visit initially make no sense until you obtain the context around them. But by the time you get the context, you've either lost that clip or that clip contains absolutely no useful information at that point. The non-linearity doesn't help replayability either. The game's great when you're eagerly following a plot thread, scribbling down keywords to search later, but an absolute pain in the♥♥♥♥♥when you revisit it two days later and have no idea where to start.
If there is any chance of patching this game, I'd have the game automatically place a found clip in some sort of filmstrip timeline thingy, so I could quickly remember and catch-up on the story or find out where a clip belongs in the narrative.
My recommendation: buy it when it's less than $5 and sit down and play through the whole thing in a three-hour stretch.

Her story is an indie game from Sam Barlow the designer for Silent Hill Shattered memories and sees you navigate an old computer database trying to find out information on an old murder case from 1994. The database is a mess and without the ability to view the whole interview you must instead search for clips by searching for words that appear in the transcripts.
For example if choosing a term such as "Speeding" or "witness" appears in the transcript of one or more clips in the database, they are shown to you for viewing. You can only see 5 clips at a time so this encourages you to search for more obscure terms as you try and unravel the mystery of the murder of Simon and the interview of his wife.
What really drew me in to the game was how well it really made me feel like I was doing genuine detective work. There is no tutorial or guidance you are merely looking at a computer terminal knowing you need to solve the case of a murder. Not for years have I used a scrap of paper to write down notes as I progressed through the game and this approach to “Her Story” was fantastically nostalgic.
The game relies on you as a player’s interest to drive the narrative forward. Even though I am a notorious “cut scene skipper” I was so engrossed in the world of the game at no point did I skip any of the sequences. Had this game appeared on the SEGA CD 20 years ago this would have been a killer app we would still be talking about today.
The time setting of the game is perfect. The dubious operating system with references to pop culture from time such as Amstrad computers, “You’ve been Framed” and Ceefax. 1994 is also a time that many of this game’s target audience will remember but that is not to say that younger gamers will lose all points of reference. The video clips have been perfectly designed to look old. I spoke to Sam at a press event a few months ago and he told me how making the clips (that were filmed on a HD camera) look like ♥♥♥♥♥♥ VHS from the 90s was one of the harder tasks.
The game is not perfect however. It took me about an hour and a half to solve the murder and probably another hour to find most of the spares clips. There is also a very obvious cheat you can do in order to make the game show you everything without trying although I did not pick up on this until after the end credits. My biggest issue however was the game’s apparent lack of a real ending. At a certain point when the game feels you have seen enough to piece together the story a very out of place MSN style chat menu appears that simply asks you “Do you know what happened?” At this point you do not have to actually explain anything you simply say “yes” and the game ends. I would have defiantly preferred something a little more interactive and satisfying that essentially a popup menu asking me if I had had enough.
Her Story is something different and a game that I would 100% recommend to any fan of detective dramas or anyone looking for something a bit unusual. Her Story is the best FMV game ever made and one that you should definitely add to your collection.

Because you have to work together its very fun and tactical, especially if you play with friends. The best thing is, that it only costs 20 bucks. The only contract thing I have is, that the upgrade stuff isn't explain very good (you have to press tab while in the game, and choose the class you want to upgrade in the next level up). The graphics aren't exactly crisis, but they look good (in my opinion). Finally I can only say, if you are tired of all these military FPS or just want to experience something unique in FPS or love movies like heat or the town or just want to play a great game, then go and buy payday.

I have to admit that I've played the original flash game N way back when I went to school and loved it, but wasn't able enough to finish most of the game.

Then some time later, N+ was released for the PSP and NDS, sadly locking me out as a sworn PC gamer.
Now recently, N++ came to my attention as it appeared on my Steam store page.
Even though I have high standards for a new N game released on PC, it didn't disappoint me in any way and impressed me by maintaining its original vector graphics look which I think was lost on the handheld N+ version.
The level design is fantastic (and includes most, if not all of the previous titles), the soundtrack just as good and it has timeless looking vector graphics with loads of unlockable colour schemes.
I would absolutely recommend this to any fan of platformer games, but would tell them to try the free original N first to see if they can handle the difficulty.

Psychonauts is the action-adventure-platformer cult classic game that unfortunately didn't get the recognition it deserved when it was released(like many doublefine games to be honest) it's charming, creative, and fun. The game is about exploration and you travel in an astral plane into diffrent minds and this leads to so many creative worlds (as everyones mind is diffrent and chaotic in some way) and you develop new powers as you progress. You will levitate, move objects(with your mind),set things on fire and so much more, they are so much fun to use that I spent a few hours playing and seeing what I could find using them. The platforming is very high quality and was a joy going through, with many clever sections that are humorous and engaging.The dialogue is very well writen and is usually very funny, and the characters are all very well defined and feel real.
The sound design is good overall but a few hiccups with the SFX(a small delay when you hit something) nothing major. Speaking of which, the combat is pretty bad. It's not broken or anything, but it never felt satisfying. On the plus side it's not really a focus in the game as it's more about puzzles or exploring. I have heard some talk about a difficulty spike at the end and it does have one, but I didn't find it too sharp. Also it's a bit on the shorter side but this is a world I want to go back to again. You are a young man called Faust. Your life is boring, your job is just decent enough to pay the bills and nothing exciting is going on. That is, until you met someone who can give you the chance to change your life at the cost of your soul.
Soul Gambler is a very short game that plays like a comic book/graphic novel. As you advance in the story you will have new ways of increasing or decreasing your soul. You can buy an easy way out from some dull activities or you can put yourself in a better situation at the cost of a little percentage of your soul. It may be possible for you to meet your soulmate, getting in a fight or witness the loss of someone you may know. It will all be depending on the choices you make.
There’s isn’t much more to be said about Soul Gambler. You can finish the game in about one hour and there’s some replay value if you want to see a different ending or make different decisions through the chapters. I purchased Soul Gambler at the 2015 Steam Summer Sale and it was well worth the price I paid for.
The music is relaxing and quite simple, same as the gameplay elements as you just need to click in order for the conversations to proceed as well making your choices when they appear. If you just want a quick game to play for a couple of hours with no difficulty attached at all I recommend giving Soul Gambler a fair chance.

I really wanted to recommend this game, but i can't. I'll talk first about the good stuff: the story, the choices you can make, and the art. Miasmata is a game that will test your perseverance and patience. Initially, this came across as a tedious and boring - I wasn't crazy about the game after spending thirty minutes in it, so I put it down and played other games.
Eventually, I came back to give it another try.
After 9.1 hours of play, I can safely say that this game surprised me, and I didn't expect to enjoy it as much as I did. Exploring the island in search of remedies for Robert Hughes' ailments was astonishingly fun and rewarding; although, this game remains one that had room for improvement.
:
- Fantastic exploration
- Learning curve that makes succeeding that much more rewarding
- Beautiful environment (most of the time)
- Unexpectedly strong sense of isolation and survival
- Very realistic
- Beautiful music (during the few instances that you are able to hear it)
- Touching plot
-
:
- Very awkward animations
- Bizarre physics when falling down hills (falling down hills is not advised)
- Lack of sound effects during synthesis
- Pretty buggy (the two devs acknowledged that after five years developing Miasmata, they were exhausted and stopped fixing bugs)
- Some mechanics may only be learned the hard way (either never explained or poorly explained)
All in all, I will reiterate that I was surprised by how much I enjoyed Miasmata. I needed some time to warm up to it, but once I gave it that luxury, I became immersed in the world and my surroundings. The astonishing sense of isolation and survival kept me on my toes and kept me efficient throughout my in-game experience. It was a rewarding endeavor, and I would recommend this game as long as you are willing to give it the time it deserves.

Goethe's Faust reconceived and redesigned as a visual novel. The story is actually quite good and the replayability is high, due to a number of meaningful choices that affect the game flow and ending. For some reason, the story is much more immersive than most visual novels out there.

As a literature major and a fan of the old German folktale, I can safely declare that this game basically made my day. Games that reinterpret classic books usually end up being tedious and ruin the original work.
, on the other hand, is a beautiful modernization with an elegant subtext of its own.
Our main character, Faust, is easy to empathize with. He is a young adult stuck in the dreary routine of everyday life: bored and jaded - until an old crone makes him an offer he cannot refuse... He is given the opportunity to sell pieces of his soul to rearrange the reality according to his own whims. We make some choices and live through their consequences while trying to discover the actual price of our new found powers.
The display is quite basic; with hand-drawn art and thrilling soundtrack. The story is incredibly well put, with consistent references to the actual tale and a well weaved world of its own. The narration is easy to follow and sets an air of mystery and the thrill of the unknown successfully. As a visual novel, it presents actual replayability and several different endings to discover based on your choices.
As a surprising side note the price of the game hits ridiculously low from time to time, it is a welcome addition to anyone's library. You shouldn't think twice before grabbing it. As a modern interpretation of the classical Faustus tale, this visual novel is a marvelous little gem for the ones that enjoy a mystical story.

A really nice, relaxing game. You explore and chart an island, find ingredients, craft potions with them and try not to get eaten by a mysterious creature that lives on the island. Your ultimate goal is to find the correct ingredients to create a cure for a plague that has infected humanity, including you.
At first this may sound like a typical survival horror game, but it is not. You will hardly ever see the creature and if you do it's relatively easy to escape or hide. The potions you craft aren't really needed either as the creature is the only enemy in the game and all you need to stay alive is water (which you can find almost everywhere) and a bed (which is also easy to find since there are huts and tents from a previous expedition scattered across the island). So why is it fun you may ask. Simply because the island looks beautiful and is fun to explore, the cartography game mechanic is wonderfully implemented and moving your character around is fun and different as well - since he's infected with a disease he is quite hard to control (in a positive way) and if you don't pay attention he'll fall down a ledge or pass out.
If you're looking for an action game or a (survival) horror game look elsewhere. If you like a relaxing game where you slowly explore an island and discover what happened to the scientific expedition that arrived there before you then Miasmata is definitely worth playing.

- Stean Acheivments and trading Cards
- Low Price
- The Artwork for the game was pleasent enough to enjoy.
Cons:
- Too few Hidden-Object puzzles.
- No fast travel which I've come to expect from Jet Dogs games of this type.
- Poor instructions on Non-hidden-object puzzles.
- Lots of back tracking
- While the story was easy to follow it was pretty poorly written.

Overall I have to give this game a lower score than most of their games and would rate it at about a 5 out of 10, It isn't terrible but it just isn't very satisfying as a hidden-object game. If you really need something to play for cheap get it otherwise pick up a better one.

The Monster Inside, a game described as a “noir style audio-visual novella”, created by studio Random Seed Game, the indie game developer from Easter Iowa behind TIMEframe and Lacuna Passage, right off the bat lets you know that it will be a spectacular game from the vibe it gives you the second the title appears.
The Monster Inside follows the story of a man called Jack, an ex-police officer and struggling detective troubled by nightmares, rough nights and a mystery brought to him at his office by a young woman named Lilly. Right from the start, the game put me into a sort of trance with its enigmatic music (written by Clark Aboud) and it’s absolutely gorgeous style of visuals. Although a short game divided into short seven chapters, The Monster Inside ultimately is indeed an audio-visual novella rather than the detective game I sort of which it could have been, not due to a lack in the game itself, but rather because by the end of its 10 to 15 minutes of “gameplay”, I wanted to know more, more about the characters, about the story, its universe, I wanted to continue experiencing whatever feeling I was feeling, curiosity. Although short and limited, the game does offer you some gameplay/interaction through conversations and choosing what to reply or ask at times, whatever animation they decided to put in some scenes added a little something that felt just perfect, and I (sadly) clicked and read my way through the game and its story quickly, fascinated, curious, until I had reached its end.
10/10 - There’s not that much that I can add without giving some portion of the story away. But what I can say is that I highly recommend The Monster Inside. It is a quick read, a quick but fantastic experience with a little something-something I expected due to its striking visuals. I could feel that it was going to be something nice, and it was just that and some more. I can only hope that Random Seed Game gives us more of these types of game, perhaps a sequel for The Monster Inside, perhaps a series of similarly styled short audio-visual novella. A woman can only hope.
P.S: The 4 tracks of the game are available on soundcloud so make sure to check these out because the music was so very lovely.

I've got mixed feelings about this game.
The way the story was told was indeed very cool and innovative, and I can see this general concept being used for much larger stories and games. And the story itself was also pretty well-written and was really interesting to unravel. The acting was pretty cool, and the more of the story you understand, the more you notice little things that slowly start to make way more sense.
So if you're open for something new, this is going to make you pretty happy. It has this "not actually a game"-vibe, similar to "Gone Home" or the likes, and the gameplay is kept to a minimum, but still, I did feel involved and it did feel I'm not just watching a show, I was really actively piecing together a story.
I'm a little unhappy about how short and simple it all seems when you're done. When I read all the reviews about people going "oooooooh I'm gonna need pen and paper for this one!" I got pretty excited for something really complex, but once you're through, you could sum it up in about 3 sentences.
Also, it has absolutely no replay value, but that's a given with story-focussed games like this one.
So in general, I'm relatively happy with this game, and would say it was worth the 5€ for the general experience, but it was an even shorter experience than it had to be, really. This whole concept and piecing-together mechanic could make up for pretty big games and complex stories, and that is what I would really love to see.

Yes, there will be a lot of watching footage, but I found it interesting the way that your perceived viewpoint could radically alter depending on what footage you watched, and the order you viewed it.

Battleborn, despite how it may look at first glance, is anything but a simple game. For its game modes, we have:
- The PvE story missions where each level plays like its own raid dungeon. The content in each mission can range from escorts to tower defense. Every main boss (and even mini-bosses) of each level has their own mechanics that easily differentiate them from each other. The dialogue you listen to is (subjectively) humorous and provides a lighthearted feel to otherwise dire mission objectives. The story is great for those who enjoy gathering a group of friends to run dungeons with for either the fun of it or for the chance of obtaining awesome loot.
- The PvP Meltdown mode where you escort minions down two seperate lanes to incinerators where they meeth their doom in order to appease a whacked-out recycling AI that believes its a volcano. The first team to reach 500 points wins. Coordination and map awareness are two huge assets to have in these matches. There are turrets, accelerators, supply stations that restore health, and giant minions that reward more points that can all be built by pay with the shards collected throughout the map to help your team gain an advantage over your opponents.
- The PvP Incursion mode. Perhaps to most MOBA-like mode in the game. You're once again guiding minions. However, rather than to their doom, you're bringing them to the enemy sentries—who can kill you easily without minions around—in order to bring their shields down to destroy them. In addition to the buildables found in Meldown, there are also Thrall mercenary camps where you can defeat said Thralls and then contract them to aid your team. Also, there is only one lane in this mode, giving it the feeling of playing a rather chaotic match of tug-o-war. Victory goes to the first team that can take down both sentries.
- The PvP Capture mode. Probably the most simple mode there is in this game. Lends itself well to those who don't have much time to play and are looking for a quick jolt of fun. In this game mode, you fight over three points that give your team points the longer they are held. First team to 1000 points wins. Contrary to the other two PvP modes, there are no minions to be found. There are, however, some Varelsi PvE enemies that appear at each corner of the map that are minding their own business, open to be killed for the sake of gaining extra experience in order to give you or your allies an edge in the constant team fights you'll find yourselves in.
On top of that, each of the 25 characters (5 more on the way at the time of this writing) feel incredibly unique both in gameplay and personality. There's a lot of interaction between characters you can hear during the PvP modes that just enhance the lore behind each of them. A nihilistic AI in an ornate death robot, a narcissistic bird with a rocket launcher, an adorable penguin in a mech suit, a heavy machine gunner with an outrageously huge body and and a tiny head, the list goes on for the amount of sheer creativity on display here. The voice acting is also a wonderous display in and of itself.
If you're looking for variety and a fun game to play with friends (or a game that can help you find new friends), this may be more to your liking. So long as you have a penchant for following objectives rather than following a Team Deathmatch mindset, that is.
Also, despite both being Hero Shooters, Battleborn and Overwatch play almost nothing alike. Feel free to get either both or whichever one scratches your itch best.

I loved this game when I saw the first ads for it on Steam, it looked like incredible fun.
As Larian Studios made me a fan of their games with earlier releases when this went on sale I bought it.
That is where the fun ended.
With close to a quarter century of RTS games under my belt (Yep, Herzog Zwei was that long ago) this one just doesn't work. You fire it up and lose. Then you lower the dificulty and lose again. Then you are at lowest difficulty and after your generals lose every battle the game is quickly over. The game allows you to reload to your last save, saying the game didn't end horribly but that just lets you send you general to lose bad again and again and again.
Why not take my dragon in and run the battle myself? That is how the game plays out. Defend you capital every turn. Same map again and again and again. You make enough money (7 gold) each turn to buy 2 of the cheapest units or 1 of the next level up. Better units than that you will never afford. each turn the AI snuffs them with its endless firehose of units and you start again.
With my limited time playing the game there is nothing that makes me want to waste any more of my time playing it. I have close to 400 Steam games to beat so a casual play through is good to see if I want to paly again at a higher difficulty. Here a casual play through (easiest mode) is a short game that ends in loss before the game really gets to develop towards anything you see in the ads.
The easiest mode (casual) feels like playing Total Annihilation at max difficulty against 9 allied enemies... only when you tried that you had been playing TA for ages. Here it starts out at that level on the stratigic map; RTS map wise you will just loop the same "defend your capital" battle forever. It feels like the game made the mistake of setting difficutly to what their devs and game testers though was appropriate after thousands of hours of play. Fail you way to victory is never fun. Having a game with only one specific rush move to start or you lose.. also not fun.

I have to submit a mixed review, simply because, as a strategy game this is flawed. There are no "comeback" moments where you and your ragtag group defeat a much larger army due to precision positioning and tactics, there is simply too many mechanics working against situations like this, situations that are possible in just about every other strategy game. There is no worker or scout unit available at your citadel, so if you do run out of units and only have the one building, you have lost even if it is on the other side of the map and you are in dragon mode, fighting fiercely, because you can not really 'gain ground' from that scenario, even if the enemy stops making units just to laugh at you. There is also 'defecting' meaning if you are holed up in a corner of a map the enemy can simply bleed out your manpower and overwelm you with endless numbers. This is a strategy game that can not be played defensively by any means, and by limiting how you can play like that is in my opinion against the open ended potential of strategy games. The characters are interesting and the setting is lovely, and this game would be incredibly fun, if the RTS portion was not so bland, with handful of "rock paper scissors" units, and the encouragement to spam. This is just my opinion, and I havent sunk that much time into this game at all and maybe it is just that I am not in the proper mood to play this game but as it stands now, this is a great story and ambitious game, that falls flat because of a bad foundation. Ill be looking for mods to fix the strategy portion now, in the hopes that this game can live up to its name.
I do not regret my purchase because I got it from the Humble Bundle, I just hope my attitude towards this game changes.

The whole idea of selling parts of your soul for certain choices seems pretty pointless. It's a high-micro RTS! It's a global resource-management sim! It's a political sim! It's all of them, and more!
Just none of them very -well-.
Ultimately, Dragon Commander is not a terrible game. It's solid, I guess, but I think the best word to use to describe it would be 'Shallow'. Each of the parts of the game is simplistic and fairly easy to master, and there are no 'Long-lasting ramifications' to worry about, for the most part.
The RTS is shallow, although you will need some fairly decent micro-managing skills until you can research the big guns and then simply laugh at everything for the second half of the game. Most often, using the 'Dragon form' involved phasing in, firing off two or three abilities, and phasing back out. Alternately, you can auto-resolve battles, which can easily result in you steamrolling across a continent since having a moderate numbers advantage usually causes the auto-resolve to declare you won with no losses against a force 60% your size.
The resource management sim is shallow. You have two resources - gold and research. The victorious solution is always 'Expand quickly'. Research is trivial, I finish researching everything in the game before the end of the second act of this three-act game. At least on Normal difficulty, the AI isn't really good at mounting offensives, and will spread their units too thin unless you make choke points for them, allowing you to funnel your gold here and there to expand very quickly and thus get even MORE gold and drown them in units.
The touted 'Political choice' was shallow. Choosing a princess consists of clicking on four women, hearing a voice clip from each, and then making your call. Most of the things the council asks you to arbitrate are also oddly modern - for example, being asked by the money-grubbing dwarf to supress research showing that 'Smoke-sticks' are bad for you, because that research could hurt smoke-stick sales and be bad for the economy. And ultimately, choose whatever you want, because the result either way will be something like "-3% income for 5 turns" or "+1% population in all areas" or something largely ignorable. And as far as I can tell, not a single one has any affect on the ending.
All things considered, the thing that bugs me the most about this game is that the only part of the game that REALLY feels like it matters is the Risk-style board game. You could basically ignore everything else and auto-resolve almost every fight and win.You'd then get roughly the same ending as you would if you had not done that... So what's the point of all that other stuff?
Honestly, I have no idea.

this game is an absolute GEM!
plus it is surely in my top 10 games of the last decade.
this game is not just an RTS. in fact, if you dislike traditional PC-RTS games you could still love Dragon Commander:
the mix of RTS, a map of the whole world where you wage the full-scale civil war, the RPG talking elements including the "make-decisions-for-your-empire" choices, 3rd-person-dragon-action, a tiny bit of enomomy and research all blend together perfect. and not to forget the ultimate "good-or-bad" decisions that not only affect an empire but also the immediate people around you! The answers you give will influence how your wife will become. Or the ultimate personal hapiness of some of your generals.
i kinda was reminded of the early sid meiers "pirates!" game  which blended so many different genres so well together. Dragon Commander does the same.
and if you do not like one of those mentioned elements before, you always have options to ignore those you dont like!
Dont like the story part? Then play the mode without story.
Dont like researching? Just start a game and give yourself enough tech-points to unlock everything in the beginning.
Dont like the RTS part? Then let the battles be fought by the AI. This "autoresolve" works great and very balanced in this game, which is quite unique. I found that the Campaign Map rules seem to work quite similar to the rules of the "Axis and Allies" or "Conquest of Nerath" board games, so you can get much joy out of them if you are a fan of such a thing without touching the RTS part at all.
What makes this game great:
one reason why the mix is working that perfectly is an intriguing story and some very funny writing for the characters. this funny writing also comes into play for the political choices.
i really got immersed in the story, and this is also down to the fact with all the possibilities of marriages that you have.
the replayability of this game is biiiig. normally i dont touch a game again nowadays.... i am too much a veteran for that, and being grown up takes its toll on gaming time and stuff, but after finishing the campaign here, i immediatly started a second one and i cant wait to this time be a bit more "evil", maybe even sacrifice my wife.
i had it on my radar since release but now finally bought it and i am glad i did.
i salute the developers!

When I first  tried this game for a few hours, I didn't like it. I thought the graphics were poor, the repetition of tasks irksome,   the fact that  my characters hands remained bloody however many times I  drank from water pools was ( and still is) annoying,  and the tension of trying to find somewhere to rest before dark or before the beast got me was  ever-present on  each new journey. Well... I have  restarted the game several times and, you could say, got used to it now, so my view point has amended. For one thing, I have discovered that the beast can be hidden from, if you are in the right terrain. He is not very bright, or maybe just short-sighted, as just hiding behind a rock near the waters edge works, so I feel there is more of a chance of survival once I hear that heart-beat. The limitation on how many  plant-species you can hold, and how many can be stored is another area of challenge, and I am getting desperate to find a successful match of two plants. All I have is 'one of each' in respect of mental acuity, strength,  agent y possibility, etc and all my six parking bays are full - and I need to  create some more  health boosters as well, so life is not easy! That is the point of the game, I suspect. If it were a breeze we would have lost interest and gone elsewhere before the map was half covered - and I haven't even covered a third of it yet. So, now I recommend it. Look past the minor irritants, try and keep one step ahead of dragon-creature ( why do some call it Milo I wonder?) keep looking for the right plants, and surviving WILL get easier sooner  or later... I hope..

Another supernaturally-themed detective thriller. Given that my last review was for Adam Wolfe, I wouldn't blame you for thinking I'm on some sort of binge here...but it's all just coincidence yer honour, I swear. And while this is definitely the inferior of the two, it's also the more inexpensive of the two (i.e. free!), so I'm gonna go easy on it. But only this one time. Capeesh?
There's three main things people tend to expect from "visual novels". The first is a nice visual style, and this game most certainly has that (with nice sound design and dandy music, to boot). The second is a good story, and while there's the hint of something potentially noteworthy here, it's all too brief and half-baked to carry much weight (the narrative feels like it wraps up just as it starts to get going).
Thirdly, and perhaps most importantly if one were to classify this as a "game", there's the issue of player agency...of which there is extraordinarily little in this title. I even re-played the first half to see if different "choices" had much bearing on proceedings: they didn't. Just seven linear chapters and one ending, unless I'm mistaken; a theory which seems borne out by the fact that you can get 100% Achievements just by playing the game through once (so there is THAT, if you're the Achievement-hunting type).
As a brief and only mildly interactive "experience", it's alright. A long way from amazing, but perfectly alright. Especially for free. No, scrap that: ONLY for free. I'd be hesitant to recommend this for even zero dollars and ninety-nine cents, the minimum RRP of any game asking money on Steam. It's much closer to an impressive proof-of-concept than anything truly tangible or greatly worthy of your time.
(Curiously enough, I see that the same devs were responsible for another game on Steam called TIMEframe. If you're looking for a similarly short yet somehow much "deeper" experience than this - and are willing to part with at least a little dough in order to achieve such ends - you'd be better served looking that-a-way. It packs a much, much bigger punch than this one does.)
That said, and I'll say it again...this IS free. So while there's not a whole hell of a lot to recommend, there also ain't a whole hell of a lot to be hating on. There's definitely worse ways to waste fifteen minutes of your time, should you find yourself at a bit of a loose end.
Verdict: 6.5/10.

This game is amazing. The only other game I can really compare it to is Analogue: A Hate Story--except Her Story uses video instead of text logs, and you have only your own search strings to guide you through the database.
The story is well-written and haunting, and told in a completely unique way. The game's themes and questions are closely interwoven with your path through the database, even with the most innocuous aspects of the computer interface itself. It's hard to stop mulling over the missing gaps in the interviews and in Hannah's story that will never be filled. The game's fragmented and disordered narrative keeps you from ever getting a sense of completeness, even as you start to piece together the heart of the mystery.
The subtly flickering screen and the pacing of discovering revelations about the story all make this the perfect game to play alone in the dark. Staying up to solve this mystery with my husband late at night, I still got persistent chills.
My only complaint about the game is that the mechanisms controlling your paths through the database can, inevitably, be detected with time. You become tempted to game the system if you can. Then, the first time you finish the game, there's information in the credits that will help you find the remaining available videos. But gathering the last missing pieces this way felt much less exciting.
However, I think that was the whole point--that tantalizing block of videos we didn't manage to access until finishing the game didn't actually reveal anything else about the story. The only information we have is all here. You'll just remain haunted by it long after closing the game: mulling over your remaining questions, trying to piece together the answers.

Overall: Okay, but I did not like it
Likes:
- Manages to capture a sense of investigation and discovery through fragmented, nonlinear storytelling
- The concept is pretty clever and original
Dislikes:
- The acting and writing are bad, like something you would find in a low-budget made-for-TV movie
- The big reveal is implausible, even laughable
- It seems very difficult to find some of the videos naturally.  Fortunately, they aren't needed for the story.
- Short -- I pieced together most of the story in less than 2.5 hours
- Very little replayability (which is to be expected from this kind of game)
Fascinating experiment, and well worth your time.  You want to go into this one knowing as little as possible, but it's a great mystery to unravel.
A unique twist on the mystery genre where you're piecing the clues together by unlocking responses to questions.  Well acted to boot.
I'm sorry to say, this game had promise, but it's just boring and I can't recommend this game to anyone.

This is a game made for Serial-bingers and anyone who has ever sacrificed a night to Wikipedia's Search Term Gods bouncing from one search term to another. That is literally the only mechanic in the game. Being limited to the first 5 entries is sometimes frustrating, but it's also the game's way of preventing you from just cheesing common terms, so I can't begrudge it too much. Besides, the difficulty means that finally stumbling upon a "hidden" video will fill you with unbearably satisfied smugness.
Something to know going into this game is that you'll probably conclude or discover the "twist"/"solution" very early. That, however, is largely inconsequential; this game isn't a who dunnit, or even a how dunnit: it's a why dunnit. This is a game not just about truth, but context. While I understand why some people were dissatisfied, I think it's quite an enjoyable detective game for those interested in teasing out motive over means.
Though you'll be asked to accept an absurd premise (I think my literal response was "lol wut") the game saves itself by absolutely committing to it. It commits to this fantastic situation with such vigor that you're willing to swallow this huge impossibility to savor the thousand tiny truths. That's because, at its heart, this is a fairy tale wrapped in the trappings of true crime.  Stories, especially fairy tales, are a motif that arise many times.
From a narrative standpoint this game is fascinating. There's only one storyline, but the way it's uncovered will be unique to the player and what train of thought they choose to follow. While the starting clips do provide the groundwork, the game actually avoids putting you on rails. Clips contextualize and re-contextualize other comments or actions, and you may find yourself going back to the same ones several times once you know what you're looking for. There are actually a number of smaller things you can choose to track or ignore that aren't really "relevant" to anything but feeding your own aspirations of cleverness. Personally my aspirations never turn down a meal, so I got a lot of mileage out of it. There are multiple layers and, both frustratingly and gratifyingly, questions that are never answered.
While I did enjoy the search-term mechanic, filling in the Database Checker does become a bit of a grind-quest at the end.  However, if you complete the game once you are given something to help with this, so if you're a completionist you do have recourse besides taking a hammer to your laptop.
I'd be lying if I said there wasn't one section that made me want to put my fist through the screen, and it's tied directly to the search mechanic. By the end of 6 hours or so I'd hit a stretch of 10 files or so that seemed completely inaccessible, forever taunting me with their forbidden promises. I finally used the end-game tool to find them, and without wishing to spoil the rationale behind their inaccessibility was absolutely infuriating. Logical, but infuriating.
TL;DR: Some fiddly annoyances related to the mechanic, but a genuinely interesting method of storytelling and an engaging experience for anyone who likes the feeling of accomplishment that comes from research and detail. Best (and plausibly) done in one sitting, and does not require 100% completion to feel satisfying. Interesting story, but don't wait for the inevitable Youtube videos splicing together the interviews in chronological order -- the experience of personal discovery really is what makes it exceptional.
And seriously, guys, it's like $6.00. I've spent more than that on a drink, and Her Story didn't serve me a glass half full of ice.

Her Story is not really a game, and if you come in expecting gameplay (of any sort), you will likely be disappointed. But it is an excellent and interesting experience, one that is worth the price of admission. I think it's great to see something different being offered, and hope that this game inspires more like it -- hopefully more with a bit of gameplay and challenge weaved into a narrative.

Her Story is a throwback to the full motion video games of the 1990s and an experiment in narrative game design. You are an investigator trying to piece together what happened based on video fragments from police interviews. The game's sole mechanic is a database which you use by searching for words said in over 200 video clips. How you interpret the story is up to you and "the truth" turns out to be not as simple as it seems when several twists emerge. The narrative is presented in a completely non-linear fashion (although you can attempt to put the videos in chronological order) and it doesn't have a clear-cut ending. If a straightforward story is what you want then you may not find it here. The game left me thinking even after having seen all of the footage.

I hadn't been surprised by a game the way I just was by Her Story in a long, long time.
It has a brilliant game mechanic: you play as a detective utilising an old police terminal, and you can search for videos related to a ten years old case.
At first, you've only got one keyword ("murder"), but examining the resulting videos you discover more themes and words that you can then use to find more videos, that you can examine to find more keywords, etc etc.
As the story unfolds (in a totally non-linear way as there's no exact order you'll find the clips in) you start piecing together the events behind it, feeling like a real detective.
The writing is absolutely stellar. As you discover more and more elements, videos that were perviously uninteresting take on a whole new meaning, and little meaningless details start coming together to form a wide picture.
An absolute gem of a game, from the writer and designer of one of the best games of the previous generation. (Silent Hill Shattered Memories).

I played this game when I was a kid. It was difficult for me at first, but doable. Playing this game brought back nostalgia. However, you know what many people say: The nostalgia glasses hide the actual game. This game as of right now is reminiscent of the Xbox Classic that I'm used to. However, there are issues that I wish were addressed, if not at least allowed to mod by the modding community. I'll start with the positives, then go with the negatives.
Positives:
+The game is fun. It's turn based, and has a great storyline. What Star Wars game doesn't?
+The game requires actual skill to do some things in the game, while other parts require luck. Fortunately, it's more of the former rather than the latter.
+It's alright in terms of stability. I've only had it fail on me once since I got it.
+Nostalgic. It's a good game for its age.
Negatives:
-When you take off the nostalgia glasses, it shows how the game is very clunky in mechanics. You can get stuck running in place because of your NPC allies.
-The choices are painfully obvious. Want to be on the light side? The choices that sound like you aren't being a jerk will be the way. Want to be on the dark side? Choose the choices that always end up in killing, and always choose the choices "that always have exclamation marks!".
-The game is heavily unoptimized. Every single cutscene I go through, the game cuts out on itself and then I have to reboot. Sometimes this doesn't help especially in the ship firing scenes.
-The save system is mediocre in this day and age. Quick Save doesn't work well, and honestly, you can just save it manually, and it's much faster.
Overall, I would personally recommend this game. It may be a bit biased because of my nostalgia, but I am willing to overlook the negatives because the gameplay mechanics (while clunky) are mechanics that I personally like. What I would love to see is this game to receive the same treatment as KOTOR 2, another game that I grew up playing. Bug fixes, optimization, achievements, mod support, the works.

Battleborn, despite how it may look at first glance, is anything but a simple game. For its game modes, we have:
- The PvE story missions where each level plays like its own raid dungeon. The content in each mission can range from escorts to tower defense. Every main boss (and even mini-bosses) of each level has their own mechanics that easily differentiate them from each other. The dialogue you listen to is (subjectively) humorous and provides a lighthearted feel to otherwise dire mission objectives. The story is great for those who enjoy gathering a group of friends to run dungeons with for either the fun of it or for the chance of obtaining awesome loot.
- The PvP Meltdown mode where you escort minions down two seperate lanes to incinerators where they meeth their doom in order to appease a whacked-out recycling AI that believes its a volcano. The first team to reach 500 points wins. Coordination and map awareness are two huge assets to have in these matches. There are turrets, accelerators, supply stations that restore health, and giant minions that reward more points that can all be built by pay with the shards collected throughout the map to help your team gain an advantage over your opponents.
- The PvP Incursion mode. Perhaps to most MOBA-like mode in the game. You're once again guiding minions. However, rather than to their doom, you're bringing them to the enemy sentries—who can kill you easily without minions around—in order to bring their shields down to destroy them. In addition to the buildables found in Meldown, there are also Thrall mercenary camps where you can defeat said Thralls and then contract them to aid your team. Also, there is only one lane in this mode, giving it the feeling of playing a rather chaotic match of tug-o-war. Victory goes to the first team that can take down both sentries.
- The PvP Capture mode. Probably the most simple mode there is in this game. Lends itself well to those who don't have much time to play and are looking for a quick jolt of fun. In this game mode, you fight over three points that give your team points the longer they are held. First team to 1000 points wins. Contrary to the other two PvP modes, there are no minions to be found. There are, however, some Varelsi PvE enemies that appear at each corner of the map that are minding their own business, open to be killed for the sake of gaining extra experience in order to give you or your allies an edge in the constant team fights you'll find yourselves in.
On top of that, each of the 25 characters (5 more on the way at the time of this writing) feel incredibly unique both in gameplay and personality. There's a lot of interaction between characters you can hear during the PvP modes that just enhance the lore behind each of them. A nihilistic AI in an ornate death robot, a narcissistic bird with a rocket launcher, an adorable penguin in a mech suit, a heavy machine gunner with an outrageously huge body and and a tiny head, the list goes on for the amount of sheer creativity on display here. The voice acting is also a wonderous display in and of itself.
If you're looking for variety and a fun game to play with friends (or a game that can help you find new friends), this may be more to your liking. So long as you have a penchant for following objectives rather than following a Team Deathmatch mindset, that is.
Also, despite both being Hero Shooters, Battleborn and Overwatch play almost nothing alike. Feel free to get either both or whichever one scratches your itch best.

Fun, wacky, and a very enjoyable MOBA-FPS hybrid.   Reminds me much of the really awesome Demigod...but without the main issues that Demigod had.  Matches are rather quick to join, less than a few minutes easily (in the US/NA region, that is).
Heroes level up in each game mode via killing minions, upgrading ally stations, or killing enemy heroes.   Changes it up so that heroes don't just play the same every time (unless upgrading the same every time).
Gear  builds help add depth to the game.  They're not unlocked automatically, but instead require the same shards that players use to purchase station upgrades with.  So either upgrading yourself or your team is another level of strategy to the matchs.
As previously said: wacky.  The heroes have some very crazy taunts to apply at any time during the match, though especially useful when just after killing an enemy.   They all have some witty banter that interacts with the home base, the other ally/enemy players, and overall match.   When an Oscar Mike is facing another Oscar Mike on the other team, for example, he starts to mention his "evil clone" running around.  And of course when he kills him, the quips mention it too.    This all leads to much personality to the game.
Sure some of the negatives are there.   The game is in need for balancing for some of the heroes as well as maps (Marquise on Overgrowth).  These are acknowledged by the developers and will be fixed sooner rather than later.   Unlocking heroes is kind of an issue with some players who want everything up front. It's different, it's interesting, it's disappointing.
Fighting as a dragon is about as awesome as you might expect, and takes longer to get tired than you might think, especially if you set yourself a good range of skills. You have limited army control in this mode, so can at least fight with a thrash of units under you, radiant in the healing, damage-boosting auras you emit.
But you can basically forget trying to play the RTS as designed, because someone put this on top of a Starcraft-y set of units with lots of manually-triggered abilities. You might occasionally switch your artillery in and out of deployed mode, or tell your tanks to use their short-range sonic burst attack, but not much more unless you forego being a dragon. And then I have to ask why you are playing a game whose main defining feature is that you are a dragon.
One reason possibly being for the challenge (and inevitable achievement). The dragon is basically like spawning with a Supreme Commander Experimental right at the start. You can assert almost total control of any one point on the map. It's rare for an RTS battle to last more than a few minutes, and if you lose it's because you just got overwhelmed by the AI's ability to multitask harder, or bit off such a ridiculously one-sided starting position that you got rushed while the dragon was in its first-minute cooldown.
On the strategic layer, you can only fight personally once per turn, and the rest is up to autoresolves, possibly modified by generals and cards. There's some depth here, especially in picking which fight you want to be your certain win, but nothing to get ecstatic about. Units are almost too mobile, especially naval ones which loop around the map, for territorial control to mean much more than "keep units on every tile". An offensive force headed by your dragon self can steamroll forward so much more effectively than any other that there's limited utility to fighting on multiple fronts.
The diplomatic side is basically brilliant. Characters are well-written and well-voiced, although the fact that every choice is binary is oft irritating; there's quite often no room for moderation or nuance. You probably won't want to put up with the actual *war* part of the game long enough to play it through enough times to see everything, and savescumming a bit just to see branches not taken is confounded by several turns' worth of delays between action and consequences. Turns padded by war.
The ending is flat as a pancake, however. You capture the last key territory, everyone says well done in turn, title screen.
And the multiplayer side? Ridiculously crippled. Pick from one of three predefined dragon loadouts (despite loadout-building being a key fun part of the singleplayer), four players per map tops, no AI dragons, only armies. (It's not much of a spoiler to get the disappointment out of the way and say that nothing of the sort shows up to peturb the mix in the campaign, either. There is no climactic final battle here, just another identikit skirmish.)
Get it in a sale, enjoy the council going at each-other's throats, and divebombing down onto massed enemy forces to unleash a huge firestorm amongst them before swooping around to gather your own army and charging forward into the enemy base with a bellowing roar. The ambience is great. Just expect by the final chapter to be looking at the strategic map with a weary, tired eye that just wants to autoresolve but knows the Imperial Army will blow a 70% chance and get driven back, and occasionally wishing your conversations didn't feel so railroaded.

Fantastically entertaining blend of strategy and political RPG.
The writing and voice acting went way above my expectations, easily AAA quality. Most people will find the dialogue excessively wordy, but it's pretty rare to ever hear that comment about a game. Dialogue choices do impact the game, and I made multiple save points so that I could go back and explore the other outcomes. The game very frequently forces you to make the best choice out of several bad choices, and tries to really punch you in the morals at every opportunity. It leans heavily on real-world allegory, and reminds me a lot like being in a commanding role on Deep Space 9 or Babylon 5, but in a fantasy/steampunk setting.
The rest of the game is fairly standard turn-based overmap strategy, and real-time tactical combat. The overmap game is very simple, although you'll feel burned by some of the "rules" in your first playthrough - the map expands and resets your assets, which can leave you in awkward positions at the start of the next story phase. The tactical combat is generic, however the dragon-mode spices things up. I found myself frustrated at all the limitations on the dragon game mechanics, especially since it's one of the most unique (and heavily advertised) features of the game.
Overall I recommend the game to any RTS, RPG, or moral dilemma fan. This game has left me dreaming of a perfect world where the Divinity RPG/story components are married with the solid strategy of a game like StarCraft II.

That acceleration curve still seems weird to me. It's unique, I've never seen a game do anything quite like it, but there might be a reason for that. Enemies having the same effect makes it hard to predict where they'll be when your shots arrive, until you memorize their patterns. It makes some enemies and bosses difficult or really, really slow to deal with until you get more weapon options... which are RNG dependent.  I've got more problems with it, but I'm having a hard time expressing it well, and it's probably an intentional design?
Suggestions!
I notice that I wind up with so much money that it's pretty ridiculous, at least at the prices I'm seeing so far- without trying for money I can already afford something like 100 of the most expensive part I have available. Maybe supplement the random part drops with an option to pay to unlock parts in case the randomizer feels stingy? A black market shop, or funding spies, something like that.
Instead of the shop button on the design screen, I would have gone with the game letting you place pieces after you ran out of inventory, and making you pay the cost before it would save the changes. Just have a running total appear over the save button.
Another handy thing would be a secondary fire button, and the ability to set weapons to one or the other button when designing. Slow firing weapons like beams might be nice to have on a separate control than my quicker firing guns. I could see this being difficult to implement on top of the existing functionality, and I'm not sure how much of a difference it makes overall, or maybe that was a design decision? Just a thought.

Miasmata is a game that redefines what you might picture as a game. It's almost not a game, in some ways; the punishing sicknesses you can get wandering around the island, the analysis of different flora to cure the aforementioned afflictions, and the use of your surroundings and triangulation to determine your position on the map...all of these things are something a person would do in the given circumstances. As a huge fan of first person games, I really enjoy the fact that the arms and hands are put to realistic use as well, and how immersive and well thought out the environment is. It surprises me still to imagine two people working on something of this scope. It has its little quirks, and some of the kinks in the fabric haven't quite been worked out just yet, but if you're looking for something that isn't your run of the mill first person shooter or puzzler, this game is definitely worth checking out.

Despite the enormous glut of platformers out there, you’ll find few as essential to the genre as the N series. Now over twelve years old, N boiled down the platformer genre to its barest essentials and then cranked up the difficulty that could be offered through those mechanics. We’re two generations removed from the original Flash release, and N++ contains all the content, concepts, and challenge you would expect from an evolution of the series. Assuming you can hang with the precipitous difficulty curve, there’s an absurd amount to discover about the game even for fans of N and N+.
You’re a ninja, which is a pretty good plot hook in and of itself. There’s no story offered aside from you loving gold and you needing to escape… wherever the hell you are. This translates into single-screen levels with an exit door and a switch that opens said door. All you have to do is hit the switch and get out before time runs out, and collecting gold helps bump your timer back up. Complicating matters are a vast array of explosives, lasers, drones, clones, zappers, and other traps between you, the gold, and the exit. The further you get into the game the more you’ll need to cheat death as you sprint and wall-jump your way from one level to the next.
It’s a challenge platformer, one that prides itself on giving you simple, solid mechanics and pressing you to master them completely. You have no attacks or special moves, just a brisk run, a floaty jump, and the ability to cling to and leap from walls. Everything in your way kills you instantly with just a touch, even walls and ceilings if you get your momentum up high enough. The controls are impossibly tight so you have full command of your ninja in weaving through minefields and springing from narrow ledges, and they even hide a few clever mechanics like being able to reach high ascent speeds through quick wall jumps or getting extra air from leaping perpendicularly from inclines.
There’s always going to be a frustration factor with instant death platformers but N++ handles this aspect with an expert level of wisdom. Respawns are near-instant, and with levels being only one screen large there’s a general limit on how long they can be. However, levels are grouped together in sets of five that must be beaten in a single sitting. You can always quit a level if it’s too hard and come back to it later but sets must be started from the beginning, so if you’re stuck on the last of the five there’s a very real pressure on you to power through it. Late in the game this subtle goading is used to great effect in sets that have multiple problem levels, keeping you chipping away at the latter ones just because the former ones were such a pain.
The levels themselves are exquisite works of minimalist art, living squarely in that space of clean lines and smooth animations that REZ, Lumines, and EDGE occupy. Most have some resemblance or pattern or meaning in their structure, supported by clever titles always shown in the lower right corner. You’ll also unlock color schemes as you play, allowing you to change the simple grays to vibrant mixes of every hue imaginable. Some even introduce their own challenges by making certain traps blend together, but can certainly be avoided in favor of more practical, high-contrast palettes.
With such a simple gameplay concept it’s the traps that give this one life, and it’s also the traps that fans of N and N+ will be most concerned with. Most of the design is based around mines, explodey things that will kill you instantly. Levels often have these dotted along walls, laid in patches on floors, protruding from corners, and assembled into aesthetically-pleasing clusters all to threaten you with death if you flub a wall jump. N++ introduces a major new mechanic here with inactive mines that arm after touching them once. This allows for entirely new styles of levels where you have to choose your paths carefully lest you render them impossibly lethal for the return trip.
While mines will be your primary nemesis, there are plenty more ways to end your very swift and mobile life. Electrified drones and seekers will trace walls or home in on you to kill you with a touch. Turrets of all types, machine gun, laser, and the dreaded homing missile, will track you if you dare poke your head out of cover. Moving platforms, one-way floors, trap doors, and powerful springs can all help or hinder your progress depending on how they’re used. A few notable additions here include accelerators that boost your momentum when you pass them, used to launch you over gaps or crush you against walls. Then there are the clones, ominous swirls that form into copies of you that follow your moves exactly and kill you if they catch up to you. The new additions for this version in particular are used to set up some very clever and unique challenges, keeping the game fresh even for long-time veterans of the series.
Rounding out this solid offering is the fact that it is absurdly huge in scope. There are, and I’m not making this up, over 1500 single-player levels to complete. Sets of levels are arranged in a huge grid with the top row unlocked, and beating one of those sets unlocks the set below it which gives some much-needed flexibility in level selection. Then if you beat a set of five sets it becomes unlocked in Hardcore mode, where your retries are limited and tied to your timer. You’ve also got hundreds of Co-op and Race levels for local multiplayer, and then the vast oceans of user-created levels to choose from. All this makes N++ not just the definitive entry in the N series but one of the definitive challenge platformers in the genre. Near-flawless mechanics, clever level design, and massive amounts of content make it a must-have for any fan of platformers.

Tattletail is a relatively short, but fun horror game.  The basic premise is maybe you're a bit too eager for your Christmas gift.  So you go ahead and peak a few days early - it's a Fur... +Great atmosphere, keeps you on the edge of your seat

+Keeps you wondering about the world and the backstory behind Tattletail
+The jumpscare's sound isn't boosted +50db above every other sound in the game (this was my main problem with FNaF)
+Text effects are flashy and appealing to the eye, along with other smooth and quick animations that add to the urgency of some situations
+Voices and other sounds are great in keeping you in the world
+I had no idea how much of an impact making sound had until day 3
Cons:
-Mechanics of Mama are difficult to understand (this one has been made a lot better with the gift update)
-I spent like 2 hours trying to see if there was any way for me to get past the fence gate in the back (there wasn't)
Overall, very enjoyable horror game; atmosphere was good, effects were smooth, tattletail was lovable, and the best part was being scared of the jumpscare instead of being scared of the earbursting sound that came with it. Really hope the devs keep updating this one and let us in Tattletail's world.
