It’s another one of those games where I have an ambivalent stance towards, which isn’t entirely unusual for me. Especially concerning critically acclaimed games. Psychonauts tends to be lauded like few other games, so you can understand that I feel somewhat underwhelmed with what I encountered now.
That’s not to say that there’s nothing to like here, quite the contrary. The setting, themes, art direction, story, writing and humor are fantastic here. It’s a unique idea that provides the player with tons of variety, starting with the great cast of characters and their unique quirks down to the different visual and gameplay themes of the various levels. And it certainly captures and amplifies the humor that Schafer and his crew already employed during their time at LucasArts and thus means that it’s one of those rare games that’s actually funny on purpose.
However, the inexperience of working in genres other than adventure games is quite apparent here. For one, the platforming isn’t all that satisfying, especially in cases where the game fails to detect that you’re within reach of a ledge but stubbornly refuses to let Raz engage with it. The same is true for the combat that feels fairly underdeveloped. What irked me personally the most was the lack of health pick-ups. I know that you can buy healing items at the store, but it’s just a pointless waste of time whenever you’re in a level and you have to exit it just to restock on supplies. They could’ve just axed the currency collecting entirely and given the player more health drops instead.
Speaking of collecting, here’s an aspect that didn’t work so well. Collecting cards and figments in order to increase your rank is for the most part a totally brainless activity, because there’s not a lot of challenge to these bits and as such the entire progression system feels perfunctory. It would’ve made much more sense to just introduce new abilities during the levels where they are a requirement, like most other games do. Because doing it this way means that a lot of the time your character’s abilities don’t see much use. Take for example clairvoyance: After you’re done with the Milkman level, you’ll never need it again. Sure, you can use it to look through the eyes of other characters and gain some insight into who they are, but that’s all window dressing that never materializes into something concrete.
The side-quests are similarly underutilized, where you’re forced to collect a variety of objects without being given a lot of justification for why it’s useful to the player. Which is why I also haven’t completed a single one of them.
Again, all in all the game is a mixed bag, where the phenomenal themes, characters and art are at odds with the lackluster gameplay experience. Here’s hoping that they’ll fix it in the sequel, which I’m interested in seeing. The way the game is structured around a summer camp certainly suits itself to a sequel that takes place in the rest of this world. Because I’d be interested in seeing what they do with the world design in general, given that these psychic phenomena seem to be rather common.

PLEASE NOTE
This is a generally good review, however I am not recommending it for the following reasons:
- Poor Matchmaking
- Inability to report potentially toxic players
- Once a player leaves/is disconnected from a game, you are permanantly short a player leaving for an unenjoyable experience
While not a bad game, it's multiplayer seems lacking.  I am NOT referring to the lack of maps/characters.  The in game "plan" has stated that more are in the works.  I'm referring to the fact that the above flaws are in other games.  Just about every MOBA-esque game has some form of proper weighted matchmaking, not allowing full 5 man premades to go up against a full squad of randoms just because a couple of people grouped up.  Same could be applied to the reporting system, as it regulates the level of salt and vitriol in the community.  The ability to add players mid match was done by this game's predecessor, Monday Night Combat.  The joining players would simply get a credit/xp boost accordingly to the time into the match.
Given these downsides, If the most egregous error of matchmaking was fixed, potentially with the adding of people. I would whole heartedly recommend this game.  If fixed while I am active in it's community, I will edit the review to reflect.
The Positives include:
- A phenomenal campaign, fully voice acted, quirky sense of humor, and decently written.
- Rock solid net code, making a smooth experience.
- Good in game voice comms, along with text chat, making it easy to communicate with your group.
- Good lore for each character that you unlock while playing each character
While the PvP is horrendous with the community/matchmaking, the single player shines out, like the last star! It's funny challenging, and provides significant rewards with the credits and unboxing.  I consider this game decently bought if it was slightly cheaper ($40-$50) for the singleplayer/co-op alone.  For those who like a good cheesy story and great characters, pick it up, maybe on sale, if only for the chuckles and laughs you will get from characters responses in the story to their lore and voice clips.  I will continue to jump on for the single player, just to learn the lore of all these characters.  Sadly a fair portion of these challenges are linked to the multiplayer. I suppose I could try to use bots for that, but those games feel almost grindy.
TL;DR
Multiplayer matchmaking = Crap, Single player and lore = Awesome

Whoever designed the RTS evidently either hasn't played one from the last decade, or seriously decided to kick it old-school: it's all rock-paper-scissors unit-smashing blobfests that actually expects you to micro when all you can really do is mash queue buttons and ctrl-a everyone into the fray.  So that leaves the dragon part, except that you should be microing your units instead, and the diplomacy, which has some interesting writing.  Even though the mechanics of DC are different, the game reminds me off another "mash it together and hope it sticks" game, Space Rangers.  Lots of promise on the surface, grey tasteless mush underneath.

Tries to mash together several different gameplay styles, but ultimately all feel very shallow. The RTS part has little variety as all sides have mirrored units. As the dragon, too few of the skills are useful and it's difficult to utilize your units.
For the strategy section, the luck of the cards you get has far too much influence. Hint: Have lots of Mercenary cards.
And for the political, you get to make 2D political choices (With moral brow-beating by the writers) with a diverse cast such as: The Sexual stereotypes! Obvious lesbian and the man-hater. The Religious stereotypes! Religion-hating scientist and♥♥♥♥♥♥condoning zealot. The Political stereotypes! The greedy capitalist who loves to tax himself and the high-horse liberal. And the Social stereotypes! Sheltered girl and business-only lawyer lady.  The most original characters in the game are the bigot who's totally open about it and the engineer who almost worships technology.

Divinity: Dragon Commander is a real-time strategy game for people who generally don't enjoy (or, like me, are simply not very good at) RTS games.  Conscious of criticisms that D:DC lacks certain features or innovations appurtenant to the RTS genre (read: "It's not Starcraft, uuggghh"), I gave this a go and have thus far found the game varied, delightful, and eminently playable.
At its core, D:DC features three different games rolled into one.  The first is the core RTS game, wherein you fly a great big dragon with a jetpack while occasionally micromanaging troops.  The game permits letting the dragon carry a battle, because frankly I've won battles where my dudes otherwise got overrun.  I'm certain hardcore RTS gamers would balk at this as a crutch, but for a far more casual player like myself I count it as a feature.  Flying a dragon around helicopter-d*icking enemy units is just awesome, and it allows me enjoy a game that I would otherwise find needlessly frustrating.
The second game is the "Risk" element, which is a grand strategy overland map that tracks conquests and strategic movements.  On this map, the player manages income, research, and movement of troops over the map.  With adequate planning and maneuvering, you can let your NPC generals auto-resolve battles with a probability slider indicating the likelihood of success.  Alternately, you can take a skirmish into the RTS game, which is especially helpful for swinging unlikely battles to your favor by way of your dragon stomping all over enemy units.  The game is usually won or lost on this portion of the game, though I suppose players who are generally good at RTS games will quickly master the strategic map.
The third game is a political simulator.  As an upstart monarch, it is necessary to occasionally tend to civic matters.  The player's decisions on a wide variety of issues, from trade policy and conscription to women's suffrage and gay marriage.  Your decisions affect the allegiances of constituent races, which are loosely analogous to real-life political interest groups.  The elves are leftist environmentalists.  The dwarves are laissez-faire capitalists.  The lizardfolk are libertarian republicans.  The imps are mad scientists and sociopaths.  And the undead are religious conservatives.  One can either balance issues in order to keep everyone relatively happy, or forsake certain interest groups in favor of others.
In all the game is varied, fluid, and fun.  I picked this up on sale, and in retrospect this is a game that I would have paid full price for at launch.  I can definitely see myself playing the heck out of Divinity: Dragon Commander in the days to come.

CONS:

The first game I've played start-to-finish in a while, J.U.L.I.A.: Among the Stars is a fantastic story and puzzle game. You take on the role of Rachel Manners, an astrobiologist who left Earth to explore a nearby star system that was emitting an artificial signal. You awake to alarms and your ship's computer, JULIA, informing you that a meteor storm has cause significant damage to the ship.
This opening sequence introduces you to two of the three primary characters and the interfaces and puzzles you'll encounter. JULIA is the exploration ship's artificial intelligence. She wakes you from your cryoslumber to inform you of an on-board emergency. The ship has encountered a meteor storm and there are fires, gases and electrical issues that need to be addressed.
After the initial danger has passed, JULIA informs you that you are the only surviving member of the expedition. Additionally, some of her memory has been corrupted and she is unable to access or reconstruct the events preceding your awakening. JULIA identifies your position and identifies a mobile laboratory on the nearby planet. She introduces MOBOT, a reconnaissance robot, that you can use to explore the planet and the lab.
You continue to explore the star system, create upgrades for MOBOT, discover the fate of your expedition members and solve many puzzles. All of these add up to an enjoyable experience that I finished in about eight hours. While some of the story is telegraphed and on trope, the characters, pacing, environments and music are fantastic.
J.U.L.I.A.: Among the Stars isn't the best game out there, but it is a terrific experience. I picked it up on a Steam sale and would recommend you do the same. A capable protagonist, balanced supporting cast, compelling mystery, and interesting gameplay makes this a highly recommended game.

J.U.L.I.A follows astrobiologist Rachel Manners, who is awoken from cryo-sleep by the ship's Intelligent Unit following a disaster which can only be fixed with the help of human hands. Rachel then finds out that she is alone. With revelations and mysteries which soon occur regarding the disappearance of the rest of her crew, Rachel must explore the solar system to uncover what exactly happened.
If you love space, puzzles, and a decent storyline, then I highly recommend giving this game a try.
The game sees you explore multiple planets where underwater, snow, and jungle environments are but a few places where you must work out what happened to the crew. The puzzles are really varied and provide a fun challenge, and the datapad hacking/researching was a particuarly engaging way of uncovering the mysteries. As the story progressed (no spoilers don't worry!) the twist was surprising and completely unexpected, all of which led the player to a either/or type choice right at the end!

I found J.U.L.I.A. to overall be an enjoyable point an click sci-fi adventure.  Being from an indie developer, some of the 3D characters and animations look like they come from a slighly older game, but I don't have a problem with that.  The story was interesting and kept me coming back to finish things off.  For the most part, the puzzles can be finished without cheating.  Some of the puzzles end up just being sessions of trail and error, which I'm not a big fan of, so that detracted from things a bit.  There was a decent variety of puzzles throughout the game, so it didn't get overly repetative.  I believe my play time from start to end was around 10 hours, which included some minimal bumbling around.  If you're a fan of point and click adventures from the 2000's, this should make you feel right at home.
Despite feeling a bit awkward technically, this game presents an interesting storyline.

JULIA Among the Stars is an excellent game. Its a point and click style game, but the pointing and clicking never gets old! The story is also great. Manners wakes up to an empty ship, and you play the game trying to figure out what happened to the rest of the crew. There is also JULIA, the ship AI, and MOBOT, the loveable robot that you control while exploring the different planets.
I liked that there was a button that would tell you all the clickable objects in the area. Very helpful. Every planet was gorgeous and looked different from the rest. I liked the voices of JULIA and MOBOT, but Manner's voice sounded too much like she was another AI rather than a human.
However, there was a massive game altering bug I encountered. Well, before I mention it, I will say that the developers clearly had a specific order in mind of the planets you visit. Once you leave the first planet and can travel to others, you can travel to any one you want but really there is a "best" option. I noticed this in the beginning and tried to mimic this order based on the direction the plot was going.
Well, I just happened to stumble on an achievement that talks about a hidden planet. Assuming that this was just an added secret to the game, I went and found it. I shortly realized that I accidentally skipped a nice chunk of the game, because all of a sudden the game was ending. If the developers had a sequence of planets that they based the game's story on, do the players a favor and block the player from accessing planets ahead in the sequence!
I did end up going back and playing through the parts I missed, but it wasn't the same.
The game was good, but it would have been great had I played it in the right order.
Also, there are no jump scares.

You know... It saddens me to have to say this, but I really didn't like this game very much, and I love open-world games like this.
Here's a tip for the programmers: If you want a game that is to go toe to toe with the Elder Scrolls franchise, it would be wise to actually make a game with gender selection in your character creation and have combat that actually... I don't know.... is good.
The first problem I have that I will list is a small nitpick, but still a problem in my eyes. The character creation. I understand the hero of the story is canonically male, but so is the Champion of Cyrodiil from Oblivion, but Oblivion still lets you play a character that is female. I don't know if this was just a design choice or if Two Worlds was just TopWare/Reality Pump's first RPG, but.... Why can I only have a male character? That completely limits your role-playing. Why do the siblings HAVE to be brother and sister? Why can't it be two sisters? If you want to make a game that is about playing the way you want like a Bethesda RPG, then allowing the player to have a male OR female character would be a good start.
Second is the combat. Particularly the archery part of combat. WHY CAN I NOT STRAFE WHEN USING A BOW? It makes archery almost completely useless and pointless. Hell, I've died multiple times on easy enemies because I tried to strafe like in any Elder Scrolls game to establish distance, but instead ran away, cancelling my bow attack. Melee combat unless you get a good enough weapon is pointless. The only thing that isn't barely functional in this game when it comes to combat is magic. When I buit the hero as a mage, the dude was nearly untouchable.
Third, the atrocious animation, dialogue exchanges and the awful voice acting. "The.Orcs.Having.Religion? ...Bah...!" Why does it sound like the voice actors were having an off-day and why use King James English so awkwardly? There is a fine art to using the language of medieval speech. The lip-synching is very much off, making the first Godzilla look like Star Wars in terms of mouth movement to the sound of the actor's voice. It also is like the game can't decide if the protagonist is fully voiced or a silent protagonist. When you choose a dialogue option for speech, he doesn't say anything. Yet any other time, he's chatting. Hell, he even gives some bad one-liners when in combat. "Pathetic." Or when you come back after dying. "I live again." (Or... sorry, that should be,) "I.Live.Again."
Fourth, for an open-world RPG meant to put Oblivion to shame, the world is actually rather small comparatively.
Five, the fact that the game just.... expects you to know all this stuff and who this Aziraal or Aazhizha or whoever, without the slightest hint of an explanation, leaving me like, "Okay, and I should care about any of this.... why....?" A bit of depth into the lore of the game's universe would have been nice. Or the game also could have told you that the woman you're off to save was your sister earlier than when you get the note telling you that your sister is alive and well.
Six, the story barely makes any sense and feels like a knock-off of the Final Fantasy franchise.
On the plus side, the game looks.... pretty good and the armor designs at times are pretty cool. The soundtrack is decent from time to time.
My point being.... If you're a fan of games like the Elder Scrolls, there are better games out there than Two Worlds. and the sad part is, the game's not absolutely horrible, it's just..... Mediocre.

Warfare plain and simple.
For the more serious RTS player.
No base building.
Limited Ammo, Supplies, and Units.
Attrition is as much a part of the game as Attack and Defence.
RECON will be more important than almost all modern warfare RTS's.
Wonderful detail and views when you zoom in.
None of the strange time/distance dilation that you get when you play RUSE (from console),
where the units appear to travel too fast and be of unusual scale compared to landscape when close up.
Watch from above or zoom right down to ground level, it's all scaled well!
Zooming in on the field is easy is quick and easy in free-cam or a nice solid chase-cam; swing the cam around from one you're locked in on and simply zoom to another vehicle or point with a quick mouse wheel roll.
TONS of units, many nations, all available to put in your deck from the get go,
none of the "unit unlocking" required from the earlier Wargame version.
Great Multiplayer. Co-ordination is key. Enough units and map space to play a specific roll for your team if you wish.
One of the few RTS's I've played where Air units behave like Air units.
Limtied time in the air, they cover large areas when flying in a holding pattern, and need to be used wisely. Breaking off and getting them out of combat is just as important as getting them in. You will not be swarming the air with great numbers, in fact you'll be using them in tight pairsto double up aroll or to work in multiroll tandem. You'll find yourself cheering when a small group of fighters makes a great little sortie over enemy space just barely making it out alive as your cluster bombs and napalm lay waste to an enemy position. And tense when you watch an air-to-air battle take place over the front line and it gets down to the wire.
There is a good chance at first you will lose a lot at first. It can be very tough while learning the details.
. Keep your eyes hidden everywhere on the field, and destroy thier RECON as much as possible.
.
This is not a game of just "swarming" with units. You'll need to use the terrain, overlap your defence and attack units. And figure out where to hide all the recon you'll need. This RTS feels far more like a good warfare sim, instead of just another generic RTS. Definately for the serious RTS'er who's looking for a good modern warfare based game. PLus you'll be nicely rewarded with some great imagery!
the visually cinematic moments you could want when you put a plan into action. And with the SAVE REPLAY option you can go back and watch the enitre battle with a free cam and no HUD for the most clear spectating of your strategy and tactics at work.
If you know that some losses are part of winning then this will be for you. If you like to zoom in and watch the action, this is for you. If you like to see action in RTS's not just "representations" of it, this is for you.

It’s another one of those games where I have an ambivalent stance towards, which isn’t entirely unusual for me. Especially concerning critically acclaimed games. Psychonauts tends to be lauded like few other games, so you can understand that I feel somewhat underwhelmed with what I encountered now.
That’s not to say that there’s nothing to like here, quite the contrary. The setting, themes, art direction, story, writing and humor are fantastic here. It’s a unique idea that provides the player with tons of variety, starting with the great cast of characters and their unique quirks down to the different visual and gameplay themes of the various levels. And it certainly captures and amplifies the humor that Schafer and his crew already employed during their time at LucasArts and thus means that it’s one of those rare games that’s actually funny on purpose.
However, the inexperience of working in genres other than adventure games is quite apparent here. For one, the platforming isn’t all that satisfying, especially in cases where the game fails to detect that you’re within reach of a ledge but stubbornly refuses to let Raz engage with it. The same is true for the combat that feels fairly underdeveloped. What irked me personally the most was the lack of health pick-ups. I know that you can buy healing items at the store, but it’s just a pointless waste of time whenever you’re in a level and you have to exit it just to restock on supplies. They could’ve just axed the currency collecting entirely and given the player more health drops instead.
Speaking of collecting, here’s an aspect that didn’t work so well. Collecting cards and figments in order to increase your rank is for the most part a totally brainless activity, because there’s not a lot of challenge to these bits and as such the entire progression system feels perfunctory. It would’ve made much more sense to just introduce new abilities during the levels where they are a requirement, like most other games do. Because doing it this way means that a lot of the time your character’s abilities don’t see much use. Take for example clairvoyance: After you’re done with the Milkman level, you’ll never need it again. Sure, you can use it to look through the eyes of other characters and gain some insight into who they are, but that’s all window dressing that never materializes into something concrete.
The side-quests are similarly underutilized, where you’re forced to collect a variety of objects without being given a lot of justification for why it’s useful to the player. Which is why I also haven’t completed a single one of them.
Again, all in all the game is a mixed bag, where the phenomenal themes, characters and art are at odds with the lackluster gameplay experience. Here’s hoping that they’ll fix it in the sequel, which I’m interested in seeing. The way the game is structured around a summer camp certainly suits itself to a sequel that takes place in the rest of this world. Because I’d be interested in seeing what they do with the world design in general, given that these psychic phenomena seem to be rather common.

A new take on storytelling, stripping away any hand-holding, allowing you to go through the story at any point and pleasantly, at your own pace. Trying to focus solely on only the investigation probably takes away from the experience, because that's hunting for clues. With the set up of the search bar, you have a very nice overlooked element that no one is going to go through the game similarly because you have the freedom to ask anything pertinent to the case. Unfortunately, with that said, some people catch onto key words more quickly than others, offsetting the balance of hours of searching. That breaks the illusion of being in the game, which atmosphere is a good part of keeping you entralled. The supposed twist is not original, but I can forgive it because it's executed well, both by writer and actress, and only once you know enough about the woman, you do see the multiple layers of the story. As it turns out, the woman seems to hog all the spotlight while the reason why she is being questioned takes a seat beside her, which could be another point that detours less story-focused players.
It took me about 3 hours to earn the ending, but I pushed forward, wanting to learn everything I could. Keeping a pen and paper handy was good, because especially in the beginning, you have many things to search for, so it's certainly handy to keep around, but if not, there are tags you can add to the video, in case you don't have any lying around. I greatly enjoyed this and thought it earned it's money's worth. I am satisfied that it fulfilled my “$1 per hour of game play” rule and the great story Sam Barlow penned for all of us. Viva Seifert, who played the woman, did a very good job conveying the frustration, tiredness and solemn tone.
I frankly think it's a good buy, because I've have very few games give me a similar experience, making me so excited to hunt down the truth and every facet of detail to 'Her Story'. For $6, I might give it a pass for the great content, but if you can get it on sale or, like me, you try to get every achievement, it's a nice addition to your game library.

The monster inside is  a visual audio novella by Random Seed Games. They did a good job expressing good writing, and good visuals. However I do feel this novella lacked in context despite it's amazing story.
Firstly the context, it does not tell you anything about the world or what cretures there are. You don't even know much about the main charecter. In the story there is much mystery as to what the world is or who the charecters are.
The rest of the story was honest and drives you through. The constant mystery combined with suspense and a plot twist keep the reader intrested. One such devolpment are the mystery scenes. These are where the reader can interact with points to learn more about what happend and the story behind it. However, there are only two points and the scene itself feels very short for what information is given.
In terms of visuals, the visuals went perfectly along with the story and the music was timed just right. It made the novella  feel like a Sherlock Holmes film. It all ties in to the mystery and suspense of the novella.
In conclution I do reccomend this novella for it's suspense and mystery. However, I would have prefered more context as to the world it is built in. After all, the story revolved around beasts the reader may no nothing about.
Final verdict: 7/10

Miasmata excels in creating a haunting atmosphere that is at once peaceful and tense.  I enjoyed exploring the island and learning the unique cartography system while keeping one ear out for the quickening heartbeat that signalled the creature's presence.  The paranoia of the creature's sudden and inevitable appearance kept me moving from save point to save point obsessively for fear I'd lose any progress I'd made in acquiring plant samples or additions to my map.  Overall Miasmata is an interesting mystery to solve with unforgiving physics (don't try to slide down the side of a cliff for a shortcut!) set against a beautiful yet dangerous backdrop.

The unique real-world pacing of the game may be a tough pill to swallow, but if you can open your mind to feel the reality of isolation and being completely vulnerable while also being dependent of your environment, then be ready for a fullfilling and engaging experience.
Being marooned and sick with the plague you will go through periods of frustration feeling helpless navigativing the island just trying to survive to the next day.  Though discovering new areas, clues to the mystery of the island, and finding new species of flora that will help you maintain your health are all satisfying moments that keep you moving forward.
Your worst enemy is most likely the danger of clumsily navigating steep cliffs or potentially drowing when caught in deep water, yet the silent presence of a single creature stalking you is never to far behind; adding a great sense of tension to the experience.  Also not keeping up your health with rest, medicines, and water, is a sure way to a quick demise.
The feeling of helplessness being caught lost in the dead of night, waiting for morning to come.  Running and hiding from the island's lone predator while avoiding tumbling off a cliff and not dropping the much needed plant you just found, all wilst keeping your bearings on the nearest safe-haven.  These are some of the intense moments this unique survival game will deliver to you.
The lack of way-points, weapons, and a traditional HUD, having to brutaly survey your map manually , and "realisic" way the character reacts and moves through movement may drive some gamers away.  But the sum of these parts, I feel, make for a completely unique and refreshing experience.
Not without its flaws, but def one of my personal favorites of the year.  No guns-a-blazing, no special super-human abilities, no fellow travelers to help you here; just your wits and knowledge of the land will get you through this non-linear, challenging game of survival.

Arguably one of the worst RPGs I have ever played and I'll explain why.
Yes, I'm basing it on only 2 hours of playtime. I know that it takes more than that to judge an RPG but holy hell it's unplayable. I'm not calling unplayable because it only has 4:3 support. I'm not calling it unplayable because of bugs, I'm not calling it uplayable because of the graphics, I'm calling it unplayable because of the gameplay and writing.
The main quest has poor writing. What really ticked me off is the quest to get the Sith Armor so you can visit a certain area. You'd think you could just knock out some trooper and take his armor, or buy it from a black market merchant, or loot it off a corpse or something. No.  The writers decide that there should be one option. That one option is to talk to a female sith officer who complains that she's lonely because she's a sith officer. Because you exchanged like 4 lines of dialogue with her, she decides to invite you to a party where she painfully points out that OH WE'RE GOING TO GET SO WASTED AFTER, WE WONT HAVE TIME TO REPORT TO BASE AND PUT OUR ARMOR AWAY HAHA.
The game has poor gameplay. Combat is just awful and I want to avoid it completely. I don't know what to call it other than "queue based combat", I've never seen anything quite like it in an game. It's a mix between turn based combat and real time combat where you queue up orders.  This works for some fights but enemies tend to move around sometimes causing your characterto follow them into an area where enemies can kill you easier because you're character is programmed to always be in range of attacks.
Overall, it's a generally painful experience for someone who likes RPGs but doesn't love them.

A new take on storytelling, stripping away any hand-holding, allowing you to go through the story at any point and pleasantly, at your own pace. Trying to focus solely on only the investigation probably takes away from the experience, because that's hunting for clues. With the set up of the search bar, you have a very nice overlooked element that no one is going to go through the game similarly because you have the freedom to ask anything pertinent to the case. Unfortunately, with that said, some people catch onto key words more quickly than others, offsetting the balance of hours of searching. That breaks the illusion of being in the game, which atmosphere is a good part of keeping you entralled. The supposed twist is not original, but I can forgive it because it's executed well, both by writer and actress, and only once you know enough about the woman, you do see the multiple layers of the story. As it turns out, the woman seems to hog all the spotlight while the reason why she is being questioned takes a seat beside her, which could be another point that detours less story-focused players.
It took me about 3 hours to earn the ending, but I pushed forward, wanting to learn everything I could. Keeping a pen and paper handy was good, because especially in the beginning, you have many things to search for, so it's certainly handy to keep around, but if not, there are tags you can add to the video, in case you don't have any lying around. I greatly enjoyed this and thought it earned it's money's worth. I am satisfied that it fulfilled my “$1 per hour of game play” rule and the great story Sam Barlow penned for all of us. Viva Seifert, who played the woman, did a very good job conveying the frustration, tiredness and solemn tone.
I frankly think it's a good buy, because I've have very few games give me a similar experience, making me so excited to hunt down the truth and every facet of detail to 'Her Story'. For $6, I might give it a pass for the great content, but if you can get it on sale or, like me, you try to get every achievement, it's a nice addition to your game library.

I have always been a fan of good storytelling in any medium, whether it is a video game, movie, or even a song. Adventure games and RPG games interests me the most because of its stories. Her Story is one of those games with a good story to tell. A woman is interviewed seven times by the police about her husband and we play as someone who is searching through an old database of these videos. For people who likes their game to be more fast paced, this is definitely not for them. The gameplay only revolves around typing key words to find videos of this woman's interview. Since we will be typing the key word ourselves, the videos will be shown at random regardless of chronology based on the key word we enter. We will form the story ourselves by making sense of all the videos (of which there are literally hundreds) and connecting the story in our heads. This game works best if you keep a pen and paper next to you to write all the possible key words to try. The experience is very nice and a throwback to old school adventure games.
The feeling of playing this game reminded me of playing Gone Home and Analogue a Hate Story/Hate Plus, especially Analogue a Hate Story and its sequel. In Analogue you're also required to read all of the text in an abandoned spaceship. The feeling of watching a story unfold is also reminiscent of Gone Home. The twist of Her Story is not that surprising and you'll probably figure it out within the first one or two hours of playing, but that is not the point. Watching the story unfolds and piercing together all the clues is what makes this game. The acting of the actress is also really really good. In summary, this is a good game with a good story and a unique way of playing that I really really liked. The story and twist is not as good as Analogue a Hate Story, but overall Her Story is worth your time, especially since it didn't take very long to finish.

It's your typical 'Lets go rescue/save someone from evil' theme that has been used frequently.
The storyline in Dracula's Legacy, it sort of radiates a little bit of 'cheesy B-rated movie feel,' similar to Sinister City. But Dracula's Legacy fair a bit better than Sinister City in gameplay wise.
There isn't much can be said about the game's visuals asides from that they're okay. Pretty much the same thing can be said about the game's audio. The audio can be adjusted in the game's option menu.
There are two different game difficulty modes to choose from: Easy and Advanced.
There are sixteen different achievements to be earned from the game. Each of these achievements has certain requirements that needs to be completed before they can be obtained. The achievements are rewarded after exiting the game.
The inventory panel doesn't have an option to have it lock in place. But it does slides up and down.
All of the hidden object scenes consists of traditional word lists. Some of them do require little or no interaction.
Most of the puzzles in the game are rather simple and easy to solve without much difficulty for some.
There are total of five different trading cards. You only get the three of those cards from the game. There are several ways to get the rest of the trading card: Purchased from Steam's Market; Trade with friends; Booster Packs and it's Booster Pack Creator.
Final thoughts, there's a bit of plot holes in the storyline, which breeds a bit of confusion in the player's mind. As it was mentioned before Dracula's Legacy fair a bit better than Sinister City in gameplay wise. But there isn't much of replayability nor its' story rememberable. I would recommend this game but not at full price.

What is Battleborn?
Battleborn is a mix of many different gamemodes, both PvE (So co-op with your friends or strangers), or PvP (so the classic team death match, capture the flag and such).
However, it also offers a more MOBA approach as seen in SMITE or Paragon - the Incursion mode, where you lane your minions to the enemy's sentry.
Alot of people like to compare Battleborn with Overwatch, but they are mostly clueless Blizzard drones, so don't sweat it - they are completely different games with two very different focal points.
If you like SMITE, Paladins or Paragon, you should feel right at home with Battleborn. The first patch is just about to be released at this time of writing, along with the first new Battleborn outside of the 25 you get in the base game.

The biggest problem with video games nowadays is that the breathing noises are really unrealistic. Miasmata aimed to fix that, and I think in Hindi, Miasmata means "HEAVY BREATHING SIMULATOR 2K9" so it is a really fitting title. The basic premise is that you're washed up on an island and you have to find a cure for your fever and also your long term illness. The fever makes everything blurry and you're really weak as well and you can die from drowning and fatigue which is really exciting because I can empathise with the main character. The graphics are great and there's a load of suspense, it's also reaaaally easy to get lost on the island. Yesterday I ran out of breath climbing some stairs and I can see now why this game is so realistic and great.

An exploration/crafting type game that has been surprizingly engaging for me. It has a feeling of exploration and survival horror blended into wonderful environments. Quite the amazing piece of work for two people, I am impressed.
Miasmata does a good job of putting the player in a life-or-death survival feeling... and the ability to find resources and slowly make better and better medicines gives you a sense of continued progress.
The main issue I have is the control and smoothness of play.  The game runs well, but the character itself is very hard to manuever, and handling objects is equally hard. Fortunately, these are not game breaking problems.
In the end, Miasmata is a quality experience that seems like a mediocure game at first glance, but is truely a hidden gem.
Interesting exploration, simple surviving system, interesting movement system (yes, it can be interesting) makes traveling difficult sometimes. Bad optimisation.

This, I feel, is the most important part and the best reason for playing this game. The looks, your movements, the sounds, the story and the mechanics all work together to make this an interesting and immersive experience. You feel that the character, you, isn't doing well, that you're often exhausted and have to fight both the exotic environment as well as your illness. You huff and puff at any exertion, thirst and untreated fevers impair your vision and coordination, falls will often disorient you and even finding out just where you are is something of a chore. Day-to-day survival is work here, giving you a sense of vulnerability, compounded by the fear of the Creature.
I'll give each of these a closer look below.
This is a very good-looking game, most of the time. There are a few graphic oddnesses, like the arms and hands that, while important and immersive can't help looking a little awkward at times. Texture pop-in and the sometimes very 'grainy' water are easily forgivable sins, seeing that most everything else works very well. Special mention should be made of the day and night cycle. Not only do dawns and sunsets look fantastic, as do the rays of sunlight filtered through the trees, they also actually work. Looking toward a brighter light, like the sun or a torch, will make dark areas even darker and more difficult to navigate. Nights are very dark indeed, there being nothing more than the moon and stars to light your way. Your lighter is a decent emergency light and burning twigs or a torch will properly light up your immediate area, helping you find your way to some sort of shelter.
I suspect that many will find moving around in this game to be an awkward business, much unlike the fluid movements in other First Person games. Moving forwards is generally fine but try any looking-left-while-strafing-right to look around while moving or a very quick turn and you're in for a surprise. It would seem that Robert can't run sideways as fast as he can run forwards. This shouldn't be the shock it is, since most people can't. You also have momentum to contend with - running downhill can be a very bad idea and may easily run you right over a ledge into a nasty fall. Climbing hills is a slow to laborious process which is further influenced by your current state. Thirst and fever will make you weaker and slower, making progress more difficult.
If all this sounds awkward and off-putting, you can rest assured that there are good and design-conscious reasons behind every seeming impediment.
The soundscape of Miasmata is fairly minimal but well implemented. There are near-constant ambient noises, such as wind, rustles, trickling or rushing water, bird-calls, crashing waves or rain, but next to no score. There's music in the game, to be sure, but it's held back to mark certain locations or the odd special moment.  Your footfalls have their own sounds, in keeping with whatever surface you're on, which is a nice touch. Loose rocks and crackling twigs could have a few more samples though, being a bit repetetive.
A brief look at some of the different ways things are done in the game.
are "synthesized" in the labs around the Island, using one or two plants for each new type. Each plant first has to be found and examined. How to do this is clearly explained in the first few notes you find and works well. The process does get repetetive but the animations can be interrupted. A few more different animations would be nice to have. Notes scattered around the island will tell you where to look for crucial elements and thus give you a good incentive to travel all over the place.
is a large and important feature in the game. You have precious little idea of where you are, most of the time, since you have to 'draw' the map on your own. This is accomplished by triangulating your current position, using your compass and known landmarks. Distant and unknown landmarks can be triangulated by moving between two known positions and marking them on the map. Much like in real life. Well implemented, with a chance of a minor 'exploit' as a handy shortcut.
does flow here, as shown by your watch and the well made day/night-cycle. This gives you a sense of urgency, since being caught out after dark has the very real consequense of easily losing your way to that shelter and bed. Unfortunately, the sense of urgency is diminished by the fact that you don't see a definite progression of your illness, that you can stay alive on water and medicine indefinitely.
is a somewhat mysterious and certainly threatening presence on the island. It can turn up at nearly any time and will likely send chills down your spine as you hear the sudden thump of your own heartbeat, reminding you of your precarious situation. There are techniques and medicinal boosts that can help you avoid being found, which is a good thing, seeing as you're in no shape to fight this beast. Well done, overall, but it does occasionally get stuck in a loop, which can be annoying.
I intentionally left this for last, since it's in the manual and of litte importance. When starting the game, you're placed in the shoes of Robert Hughes, a plague-stricken scientist, stranded on an unknown island, in search of a cure. Precisely why a name is mentioned is something of a mystery, since the who of you is of utter insignificance to anything that happens in the game. (Here the developers missed a chance to involve female players a little more.) The more imortant words are 'stranded', made evident by your bloody hands and the wrecked boat beside you and 'plague-stricken', as you'll notice shortly.
Fever, thirst, brutally murdered scientists, mysterious messages, baffling notes, helpful discoveries, rain, darkness, swamps, glorious sunsets, coluorful fungi and more plants than you can shake a burning twig at will help and hinder and baffle you on your journey.
Your goal, ultimately, is to find the cure and escape this island. The cure is to be found among the rich flora of the island, which you will research, annotate and cook up various medicines from. Some will just be a temporary stay of your recurring fevers and some will give you more lasting effects. To help your progress, you'll find the notes of the expedition scattered around in their huts and tents.
Escaping the island, alive, will not be easy.
There are some missed opportunities for exposition and deepening the story, such as conspiracies or cover-ups that are just hinted at, the obvious mystery of the murders which could be better developed and the odd and disconcerting Creature.
All in all, I found this to be a very rewarding exerience. I thoroughly enjoyed the lush environments of the island, the often beautiful vistas opening up in front of me as I clear the crest of a hill, the deep dark of the nights and the heart-pounding fear of being found by the Creature. I even liked the work of mapping my progress around the island, since it added both realism and a feeling of accomplishment set against the helplessness of being lost.
Kudos and a hearty 'Well done!' to the brothers of IonFX.

Some people have found the unrestricted wilderness exploration and cartography irritating or the beast too hard to handle. They collect a couple of plants and seem to get frustrated or bored. It's as if these people have become so used to a synthetic gamer's world where conflict is handed to you on a platter in spoon-fed form that when you come upon a game presenting a real life situation with actual bush crashing and navigation skills, even provided with countless prominent features such as the fire pillars and Easter Island heads on every high hill, you can't handle it. This is an interesting survival/adventure game.  Exploring the island was kind of neat.  Trying to find all the landmarks and get the entire map to show up is a bit of a challenge on its own.  There's a few buildings scattered around that you'll run into here and there that also have notes in them to give you an idea of what happened since you're all alone and don't have any idea what you're doing there.  I also liked collecting the various plants to craft painkillers and other drugs.  It almost made me wish there were more things to collect and craft than there are.
My biggest complaint is a possible small spoiler, so I'll hide that next.
The next small thing is when night falls and you don't have a light source, you're pretty much screwed.  It's completely black and you mostly end up literally rolling down hills on your face and/or falling into the water where you're likely to drown.  You learn real quick not to try going out at night without a torch in hand and another one nearby to take its place.
Overall I found this to be an enjoyable game in spite of the complaints I have above.  It's worth a play through if you like exploring the unknown.

This is one of the best real time strategy games that I have had the pleasure of playing. And when I say the best I'm comparing it to other icons in strategy gaming such as Command and Conquer and Age of Empires. However, after several hours of playing this game I can tell you that the learning curve is terribly steep. Either you know how to play it or you don’t, it’s that simple. One of the best bits of War Game: Airland Battle is the attention to detail throughout the game. Ironically when I first discovered this franchise I brushed it of as some games made in the early 2000s and not worth my time. But the graphics alone are good enough to invest into this. It takes a huge map and that is nice on its own and lets you zoom in to ground level to see the grass waving in the field. It’s amazing, and totally blew my first theory out of the water. Also they don’t just send your troops out with infinite ammo. Instead you have to pay attention to supplying your troops if you want to win, and I appreciate those details.
Still there are some other minor issues with the game play. One of them is that its way to easy to spot infantry. I don’t think that a tank is going to spot a platoon of infantry laying prone in a field with waist high grass from 2000 meters. I just can’t see that happening in actuality. Another issue with the game is a bit too accurate with military units. Most people have no idea about the names or functions of most military hard wear. It was difficult for me the first times that I played and I study up on military history for the heck of it, just to give you an idea how tough it is to wrap your head around it. This game is full of it, which adds to the learning curve that is already insane. And that’s just with NATO, when you get to the PACT your just about ready to give up. Don’t do that. Keep working at it and one day you will find that you understand, and that’s a great feeling.
After continually suffering defeats one day I managed to do something good. It was a simple action, all that I did was move some infantry into the path of the enemy thus halting their advance, but it was good. In the biggest reason this game is so good is because it is challenging and difficult, but it makes the little victories all the sweeter. So if you are looking for a game that is both fun and challenging invest in this. Trust me, it will be worth it.

This isn't an RTS. This is a battlefield simulator.
Let me paint a scenario for you: My defensive line has crumpled under the weight of a zerg of T34s and T55s. A detachment of marines, aided by an M1A1 Abrams tank, are stranded in a city near the middle of the map. At my last and final command point, lays a thin line of M1 Abrams, three to be exact, 2 M113 APCs armed with Vulcan Miniguns, and a cluster of Chapperall SAM sites. My deploy points are numerous, but I have exhausted nearly all my units. My air force is a team of 2 resupply chinooks, 4 Apache helicopters, a Huey command vehicle, an F117 Nighthawk, an F111 Ardvark (armed with cluster bombs), and an F18C.
I had very little in terms of options. I could spawn a couple of recon HMMWVs, but they are only armed with M134 miniguns, useless against armor. I strengthen my line with them, and peer over the rest of my available units. 6 Blackhaws filled with Delta Force infantry, 2 Blackhawks with Ranger recon units, and a Kiowa recon chopper. I deploy my last hope towards the edge of the map. My goal is to cut off the enemy's air passage, their home base. If I do this, It could serve a vital blow to the enemy and would permit my bombers to hunt and kill the remaining command vehicles, which, without, they will lose the match.
My recon units land nearby, with my delta units following a safe distance back. Their FOB is spotted, along with their artillery and a SAM site. My delta force lines up in a bush, waiting for a strike from the F117 on the SAM so that my ardvark could carpet bomb the area. Just then, my recon unit discovers an armor column of nearly 20 BTRs. The F117 drops it's bomb, and the carpet bombing commences. Half the column dies, the other half engages my delta force. My units quickly disperse into the woods, where it is easier to defend against armor. Just then, their command vehicle lights up, in the same patch of woods as my delta force. Suddenly, the air passage becomes neutral. I rush in my command huey.
After an arduous fight, my delta team secures the forest and the surrounding area. There is a hill to the south that has around 90 footsoldiers, as my resupply chinook discovered while attempting to resupply delta. I use the word attempt for a reason. The footsoldiers are mostly just infantry, but there are two AA groups embedded, making an air attack impossible. My recon unit by now has scouted the entire north end of the map, coming across the straggling infantry, easily erasing them. I then push my scout Kiowa north of my original base, my current final stand. The armor seems to have vanished towards the hill, so I moved my previously stranded marines just north of the Kiowa, essentially blockading the enemy onto a small, but very dangerous hill.
The problem was that there were only 2 ways to get onto the hill with vehicles, and there were 15 or so T55s, supported by 30 or so BTRs, along with 90 footsoldiers. At the time, my units had not discovered a collection of 5 T72s, 4 jeeps with Konkurs AT mounted, and 2 Tunguska AAA that were also on that hill. The north enterance was blocked by my delta force, but they couldn't advance because they were in the open while the footsoldiers on the hill were in the cover of dense trees. The marines and Abrams tanks to the south couldn't advance because the T55s were embedded and outnumbered the Abrams 3-1.
My Kiowa reveals all of the previously unkown enemy positions before getting destroyed by a tunguska. I call in my F117 and demolish the tunguska. One less threat. I have my Ardvarks carpet bomb the forest twice. By the amount of points I earned, I could reasonably guess I did some major damage. Now was my time to shine. The Marines, backed by the Abrams, pushed over the hill, supported by Apaches. Just when all the fire was directed at them, my delta force came in from behind. The marines and Abrams were demolished, the entire front nearly eradicated. Before they could pull back, they lost all but 1 tank and 3 marines. My Delta, on the other hand, evicerated the enemy. Their footsoldiers were gone. One T55 remained. 2 BTRs. I pushed up my marines one last time, and my delta force followed suit. The hill, bloody as it was, became ours.
Puzzled, I scouted the hill. The enemy must have moved the command vehicle in the chaos. It was nowhere to be found. Just then, the air corridor that my delta previously liberated turned red, meaning they recaptured the base. Bad news. By this point, the enemy barely had any units left to command as well. They did have jets, though. Two Mig25s streaked above, and circled for a pass on the remnants of my units. I looked at the air corridor. The only place he/she could really put the command vehicle, where it was not in the open, was a very small patch of trees. Through a desperate strike, I carpet bombed the forest. Just as my bombs touched down, the screen froze. Then, just as the screen faded, I saw a vehicle explode in the woods. The last enemy command vehicle was eliminated.
"Minor Victory", it was called. It didn't seem minor. My forces were zerged almost into obliteration. Then, from a stroke of pure luck, a strategic placement of special forces turned the tide of the battle, which helped un-strand the remnants of my fighting force, which gave themselves in order to secure a hill the enemy used as their last bastion. Then, from another hail mary, my bombers managed to hit a needle in a haystack. That was total victory, in my opinion.
It's a game where you can easily get attached to units, and get frustrated and angry over their loss. You can go from a massive armor column staring you in the face to a DIY scrapyard, all because a teammate decided to throw some artillery your way. It's a game decided not on what you have, but how you use it.
If that description of a recent battle of mine doesn't interest you, then this game isn't for you. If you were enthralled by each and every word and intruiged by the strategy involved, buy this game. It won't dissapoint.

In Turbo Dismount, all you do is pick a course, pick a character, pose, vehicle, and maybe some obstacles, and see how far into the course you can make it without total destruction. It's a very fun, little, simple game. Some of the poses that the characters do on certain vehicles are just hilarious, like, the one wrecking ball pose. Nary is a generous runner made by dedicated guy. You have to dodge the obstacles by jumping as well as killing your enemies with the directional arrows ! It can takes some time to get used to the jumping mechanic (the game works well but you have to be rigorous with your inputs, wait for the character to land before pressing the button again and don't hesitate to maintain the jump button to gain some height). You have to get through 6 levels with various abilities (jump, double-jump, dash and gravity switch). The game offers a lot of different modifiers that you have to unlock, tweaking or changing the rules of the game. If you are into runners or challenging games, you could try this one, it's advantegeously priced, you'll have some hours of playtime (and I hope fun) and if you stumble against a glitch or an inconvenience, Khud0 (the developer) will gladly help you out. Recommended :)

Just finished this game for the 1st time after seeing that it was $2.99 on the Steam Holiday sale, & it's by far one of my top 5 RPG games of all time.
Pros:
I love how vast the Star Wars KOTOR universe is (especially for such an old game) & how the player can steer the game in any direction that they choose since there are so many ways the game can be played.
Also, the character customization is great & the story is very solid & immersive. If you're a fan of Star Wars & love RPG-type games such as the Witcher series, then I highly recommend this game.
Cons:
In my opinion, the ending/s of the game was a little weak. It was very short, abrupt, & unsatisfying after playing through such a deep & immersive story to say the least.
Also, once you finish the story, you can no longer free roam. Instead it takes you back to the main menu where your only options are to reload previous saves or start a new game. I wasn't a fan of this since I spent so much time upgrading my character & making him look cool just to find out that you literallty can't do anything with him after completing the story.
Still an amazing game though! Highly recommend.

This game really is a Diamond in the rough or perhaps it's a rough surrounded by Diamonds, at any rate this game is great fun and a giant step away from your typical RPG experience. It wreaks of originality and has a style of it's own and isn't afraid to flaunt it.
This game caught a lot of flak due to how it strives for originality in it's own obscure way. People complained about the voice acting, but really, I feel these people just struggled to digest an approach totally foreign and new to the genre and this conflicted with their usual expectations of what an RPG should be, but Two worlds broke the mold and I can appreciate that.
The style, characters and atmosphere in Antaloor gives you an immediate feeling of a strange yet authentic medieval culture. People talk strangely to one another, but the more time you spend in Antaloor, the less strange it becomes and begins to feel genuine and relatable. Sure there are some awkward dialogues and the VA can be a little hit-and-miss, but overall it's laden with intrinsic value and thoroughly enjoyable.
Even the combat is strange, strangely enjoyable though. Combat feels impactful and organic, albeit a little clunky. There's a good balance of combat techniques you can use, with a good mix of Archery, Melee and magic. Archery mechanics are done quite well and you'll often find yourself trying to snipe tough enemies or pull them towards you in a more orchestrated attack.
But one of the more interesting aspects of Two worlds, at least to me, is how gear actually stacks! Essentially, instead of finding one rare or unique armor or weapon, you are able to find multiples of the same type and combine it into your original piece making it's stats ever more powerful Muahahahahah! So once you've found something nice, it quickly becomes an obsession to track down more items of the same type- but don't be fooled! It must be the exact same "breed" of item. You will find many different versions of items but to "stack" they need to be of the same family, i think this is reflected by a number as well as the aesthetic of the item.
Lastly, this game is a loot-♥♥♥♥♥'s wet dream. You'll be constantly on the hunt for more items to help you grow in power, but as discussed above. not in the traditional way and you'll also be on the hunt for a Steed capable of hauling your massive collection of weapons and armors around and spend countless hours deciding which stuff to keep and which to sell. Speaking of selling, this game is also a Merchants wet dream and I surprised myself at how much time I spent traveling to strange new towns with a glimmer of hope in my eye that the traders there would have yet another piece I could stack together.
There's probably a lot more I could say about this game, but that could take all day and I want to play games! It also probably goes without saying that my Steam hours played does not represent my actual play time in this game.
Two worlds is a bit rough around the edges, but there's more than enough goodness to compensate. Good for at least a few hundred hours, I recommend it!

In a world of FNaF games where Anamatronics are always the big threat coming to kill you...being a kid running from a deadly toy screamed "CHILDHOOD MEMORIES!" I felt it was a great concept for a horror game. Onto how it handles, the audio is done well, the music stings kept me on edge the entirety of the first level, and the atmosphere is all there. For a $5 game, I felt it was totally worth the money.
I'm only on the third night, and so far I haven't felt like gimmicky scares are everywhere which is what I was afraid of. I don't know if it was just me, but I survived the first and second night no problem...which is good. With FNaF (yeah, going to keep comparing the two even though they aren't alike at all) you get killed for reasons you don't understand. I'm very happy to announce at the moment I haven't experienced death for the sake of random death. The game is actively teaching me mechanics while keeping me on edge. If you'd like to see how the game runs, how the game sounds, and how the game plays, here is my experience for the first two nights.
I believe Night 3 is where stuff is going to really start cooking and I can't wait to play some more.

Checkpointing is frequent enough until the final night, but honestly I was more stressed trying to find all the eggs than by any of the objectives in the game, and it took me about 90 minutes to finish the game with all the eggs collected (still missing 2 cheevos but pretty well completed).
In smaller details, the house is unfinished with walls that don't properly connect to other walls, the lighting is weird and objects seem to have a lot of lighting underneath them even in total darkness, and sound is the same through floors and walls.
The hardest part here is saying what I would do differently.  I think the main issue is that I don't know why I'm carrying the Tattletail doll around my house at night other than that's what I need to do to progress the plot.  The game has given me no real reason to be invested up.  The final act was kinda cool but it came out of nowhere and I feel like it could have done with some leadup.  As it stands, the game feels like a collection of bad horror game tropes slapped together with a couple fun characters.

I'm almost an hour into Tattletail. So far, it's an incredibly charming, well-made game. The gameplay loop is incredibly fun, and genuinely scary. It's definitely a game that really shines when you make a point to play it late at night, with all the lights off. Sure, there are jump scares in there, but for me it'd be totally wrong to dismiss this game as relying on cheap scares in order to punish you. There's a lot more nuance and soul to the game. You can really tell that it's creator has poured a lot of love into it.
The overall aesthetic and feel of the game, I expect will be incredibly polarising. I really liked Tattletail's unique style, and I think they got the distorted/lofi/VHS glitch thing down perfectly. People who like this sort of thing, generally love it. Others won't really resonate with it, and that's absolutely fine. I get the impression that the low price point will help make this game accessible to people who wouldn't usually play this sort of game. It's definitely worth picking up if you're looking for a charming, strange and genuinely scary game to spend a dark evening alone (or with friends) with.

Not a terrible game/visual novel, but it leaves a lot to be desired. On the graphics side things look quite good in screenshots, however actually playing the game is a little less impressive, as you are just clicking through static comic book panels. There is almost nothing in terms of animation or transitions and it ends up lacking a lot of dynamics. There is also not much in terms of sound effects, just background music. So the whole atmosphere feels a little flatter then it should.
On the interface side, the lack of visual novel typical dialog-skip function for replay is an annoying omission, as it makes replays rather painful. Even quickly clicking through dialogs isn't possible, as there is a minimum of time a dialog has to be on screen before you can click it away. The rest of the interface is ok, but there just isn't much you can do in the game, most of the time you just click to move on to the next dialog.
As for the story, it feels quite weak and just way to short to leave much of an impression. The whole game takes just a little over 30min for a single playthrough, which doesn't really leave much time to introduce characters properly or let things unfold. You just end up jumping between locations and talking to people and none of it feels like organic exploration. You are just hopping around between plot points without agency. The choices you have in the game also feel pretty meaningless as the story stays mostly the same.
Overall it's an alright game when you can find it for cheap in a bundle or something, but it just feels way to underdeveloped for a full game, even by indie standards.
