INTRODUCTION
Turbo dismount is a game I've put a lot of time into. The graphics are great, the possibilities are nearly infinite, and the workshop has thousands of levels. If you want to get the game, yet you are still slightly skeptical, here's my review on Turbo Dismount.
STORY
Oh, story. Yeah, this game has none! The most a completionist can do is play all the pre-made levels and get all the achievements, which will still take around 20-30 hours. The point of Turbo dismount is to mess around with what you got. I've (so far) put around 27 hours into the game and I still can't get enough of the game.
FEATURES
The game comes with some levels to mess around in, but you can always download levels from the steam workshop if you get tired of those levels. You can choose several vehicles, which are all unique in their own way. There's a Tricycle, Fire truck, Wrecking ball, Skateboard, Sports car, etc. If you are wondering, you can choose different characters that can pose and be customized. One of my friends had fun putting the face of Donald Trump on his character, then he would do whatever he wanted to. For poses, there's tons of them, exclusive to each character. Yes, you can do a Miley Cyrus pose on the wrecking ball, and you can do poses on the Wastelander (Inspired by the Mad Max films) that are related to the movies. There's also obstacles you can place down such as a speed boost pad and ramps.
GAMEPLAY
After choosing your character, vehicle, pose, and obstacles, you have to hold down [SPACE BAR] to adjust speed. It's a frustrating task because if you release it at the wrong time, you can go really slow, or way to fast for you to comprehend.  I can still use turbo pads to go fast though, because I usually want to go fast. Characters can have their bones broken, dismembered, twisted the opposite direction, etc, and makes the game more interesting. The physics engine is not realistic though. Once I was using a skateboard and my head got blown off from a wooden paddle when I was only going around a smooth 20 mph ( around 32 kph for foreigners).
AUDIO
The SFX is clear and more realistic than the physics engine. The sounds bones crushing and muscles tearing is what gets me. I probably wouldn't have laughed at this game if SFX and the music weren't there. The music is a jazzy rhythm, and makes the game seem like an overly-edited fail compalation that you can control.
PLAYABILITY
The game has barely any glitches, and recieves laughs from anybody who watches it or plays it. It has the perfect blend of humor and control of paths that I like. This is a must play when my friends come over, and we end up putting 1 or 2 hours of into it everytime. We can laugh at the insanity that happens before our eyes when our character gets blown up by a mine and afterwords mauled by a snow plow. If your mind is thinking "Why would you laugh at that, ONLY SADISTIC MINDFREAKS WOULD LAUGH AT THAT!", well I have a claim. Your so called "character" is a test dummy, and the game is only a simulation. Also you would be calling Jacksepticeye, Markiplier, Pewdiepie, Kwebblelkop, Ssunde, Ihascupquake, and DanTDM sadistic mindfreaks ( If you don't know who they are, look them up on a trusty site I call Youtube).
SUM UP:DO I RECCOMEND THIS GAME?
I reccomend this game to a certain crowd. If you are easlily offended, than no. Despite a couple cons, it's definitely the most fun I've had destroyng stuff on my PC (Just Cause 3 is on my XBOX One, so I'm specifying to PC), and is no doubt, a "kinetic tragedy"(that's the games slogan)
My rating? 8.25 out of 10. You can play it with friends, family, yourself, and can see what sort of crazy things the community has done because I forgot to mention that you can upload gifs

It was quite an enjoyable game. We play as Rachel, a scientist waking up as the only person alive on a spaceship after many years spent in cryosleep. To discover what happend to the expeditions crew, she is helped by Julia, an amnesic human-shaped AI computer, and Mobot, an exploration AI robot. The different planets of an unknown solar system can be explored. I quite loved the space exploration atmosphere. A reference to 2001: a space odyssee is made especially on one of the planet. One can freely explore, find and collect objects and alien samples, analyze them, hack passwords, assemble components parts... Diverse puzzles are encountered on the way. The least to say is that puzzles difficulty goes from extremely easy to easy, which was frustrating sometimes...
I quite liked the beautiful graphics and the imagination brought in the game to describe alien life forms. The game tries to make you feel like a scientist, but still with a simple approach that maybe make this game more befitting to children.
There is one huge mistake in the game one cannot miss. The developpers might have confounded Nitrogen with Hydrogen or another explosive gas, if this could be corrected.
So, anyway, I might write a better review later, but if you enjoy beautiful visuals, freely exploring places, collecting objects, reading, an AI good sens of humor (Mobot) and dont mind too easy but very diverse puzzles, then you wont be disappointed by this game.

I wasn't sure what to expect when i picked JULIA up. I've always liked exploration and adventure games so I figured I would give it a shot.  I was actually pleasantly surprised.  There are some annoyances from a technical point of view (fixed resolution video comprises most of the gameplay, which is fine if your screen is exactly 720p or 1080p, not so super fine if not)  But overall from the very first moments, the story won me over.
I do confess as a systems engineer, the opening scenes where the character laments she is not a systems engineer, had me sort of privately cracking up and going 'never fear, your player will save you!' but in the end the overall story is quite intriguing and carrys you well through the exploration and puzzle focused gameplay.
I really did care for the agency/plight of Rachel (the protagonist) and uncovering the mystery of how she got into her current situation (and what happened to the rest of the crew) is very satisfying.
While some of the 'mini game' systems were mildly annoying/repetitive, overall the game hasd enough of them of sufficient novelty/quality that any annoyances you have with any one or two of them shouldn't detract from the overall experience at all, and the main exploration gameplay is done very well and engagingly.
Once or twice i felt somewhat at a loss as to how to progress, but re-tracing some steps usually stumbled me back on track.
In the end, this is a worthy sci-fi take on a myst like exploration game and I do reccomend it to anyone who likes more relaxed discovery/mystery games.

Amazing RTS game set in the most unstable era of mankind: The Cold War.
The game features 4 campaigns, playing as each side of the conflict for 2 campaigns each.
There is also a massive multiplayer element to the game, with 10v10 brawls.
Alright, so lets see what i gathered:
Pros
- Amazing graphic detail, even at lower settings
- I never witnessed any bugs whatsoever, everything played as it should
- 10v10 online (you NEED to try this!)
- Massive customisable 'decks' which represent the force you command, pick to be a specialised force or a generalised force before battle
- Never got boring, the AI would always play unpredictably and aggressively
- unlike some other strategy games, like the C&C series; the games would last about 20 minutes depending on player count, as opposed to the paltry 5 to 10 minutes max offered by C&C
- Unlike other strategies, rushing is the worst early battle option, allowing for a more realistic strategy experience
However, i am not very good at this game at all, so my opinion may be slightly biased for my side.
Cons
- I dont hate the micro managing features, however they can get irritating while trying to organise a massive push, you have to regularly supply all units with fuel, ammunition, and spare parts/repairs, id rather either be the resupply guy or the combat guy
- Dont expect a friendly welcome. upon the realisation they have a 'noob' on their team, many will take the opportunity to guess and mock your apparent junk size, your age, and if you get where this is going... generally noob unfriendly playerbase
- There are alot of trolls on this game, who will park artillery units near you base and leech fuel and ammo en masse, leaving you with none
- The AI sometimes fails to use variety, and will use only one type of unit, either all tanks, or all helicopters sometimes
And i guess thats my review guys, look forward to seeing you on the field.

Tattletail is a basic survival horror game with gameplay elements from Slender but with a furby wannabe that demands to be taken care of.  That right you need to make sure Tattletail is fully charged, feed and brushed at all times.  Otherwise, you'll die. Because in certain nights a monster will hunt you down and kill you, either you get too close or look at it for too long.  Instead of collecting pages from Slender, you get different objectives for each 5 nights of Christmas in order to progress the bare-minimum story its telling.  There's not much of a story to tell for this game, since the lore is kinda non existent and the outcome of the game finale is pretty laughable at best and overall predictable.  In fact, I had a good laugh at how bad this game gets, but once the artificial difficulty comes in, I get disappointed.  Good thing there's checkpoints utterwise this would've been a torture to play through.  You also have to be aware of the sound you make if you sprint or shake that glowing flashlight.  Which the monster can shut off your flashlight instantly if seen.  Keep in mind, the Tattletail will make so much noise that you have to make sure he is calmed so you don't get killed a lot, which it will happen if you fail to take care of the Tattletail.  This is why he must be feed, brushed, recharged at all times in order to keep him happy and hopefully staying alive throughout this rather mediocre game.  Some aspect of the game are kinda immersion breaking like why does a toy need to eat?  Unless it all just in the kid head or something...  And why does the kid jump so good?  Unless he was secretly trained by Mario himself (Jumping pretty useless in this game btw).  Music is uninteresting but that didn't matter to me since I was already bored of this rather shallow repetitve horror game.
Overall, this game is only fun for children.  It much more fun to watch them scream in terror than playing this meh of a game.  It got good ideas but its not very well executed.  Horror Fans, including me deserve better.

MY GAMEPLAY OF THIS COOL GAME!!!:
TattleTail is a refreshing take on the FP Horror games that include scary cute things that go f$%#kin nuts after dark!!!
The atmosphere helps create an early 90's VHS vibe of pure creepiness & makes you feel just like a kid sneaking around the house in the middle of the night while the rents' are in their xanax comas. After playing for about an hour, I can truly say it is very entertaining & keeps me interested in seeing the end result!
The Sound is what makes this game scary & is done very well. The jumpscares aren't bad, but if you like creepy atmosphere's & great sound in horror games, you surely will not be dissapointed!

The Cons to this game are that maybe the "alert ringing" when Tattletail is scared or hungry can be quite piercing, so if you are wearing headphones, you may need to turn the sound down a little. The other con would be the jumpscare. It could use a quicker animation with some other screen filters that can elevate the dread the rest of the atmosphere already provides.
All in all, cool & very entertaining while also being super affordable. Thanks!!!

This game is not for everyone. It was made by two people, and it is therefore a little rough around the edges. The graphics are by no means bad, but they are certainly not AAA-quality. The two brothers who made the game designed the engine as well (which is kind of impressive), but they clearly were not able to optimize it to run as well as some better-known game engines, so you may not get quite the frame rate you expect, and you will see lab equipment pop-in when you approach a campsite. There are a few other things that are imperfect as well.
All that said, THIS GAME IS AMAZING! The strange thing about this game is that I had imagined a game remarkably similar to Miasmata, but never expected it to actually exist. When I saw it on Greenlight, I was surprised that such a game finally existed. When I played it, I was quite satisfied.
This is a true survival game: stand still long enough, and you will die from lack of water/fever/creature attack. Exploring the island, making your own map by triangulation, finding plants to make medicine, finding notes and journal entries that help you figure out what's going on, and hiding from that creature add up to a great survival experience. The movement system of the game is also great. It more effectively simulates illness than any other game I have seen. If you go down too steep a slope, or go down too fast, you'll slip, eventually going head over heels. You have to carefully manage your momentum by holding back while going down a slope, or examining the terrain to find a safe path down or around. This both avoids the usual video game problem of being able to run around everything in a way that would not work in real life, and the problem of walking becoming boring; your illness makes walking a game challenge. As a final note, I love the UI, more accurately, the lack of UI, in this game. Your character carries an actual journal and map that you use in real time.

“Her Story” is easily one of the most engrossing experiences I’ve had in recent memory. There are two things to keep in mind, however, before purchasing:
1. This is not so much a “game” as it is a non-linear story. It unfolds at whatever pace you choose, in any order that you choose. Those looking for a straightforward narrative, or even one that provides definitive closure, should probably look elsewhere or (even better) approach “Her Story” with an open mind. There is no way to “win.” There is no “congratulations” screen. You simply unearth the truth as best you can and ruminate on what you piece together.
2. The interaction is kept to a minimum (perfectly, in my opinion). There are no puzzles to solve or enemies to beat. This is purely an exercise in using your own deduction and observation to advance a narrative.
Having said all of that, half of the fun of “Her Story” lies in piecing together the chain of events that led up to the videos you are watching, and then comparing your version of events to others. Everyone has the potential to see the same clips—there are no branching stories here—but the writing is solid enough to allow for multiple interpretations of the same events and statements. Even within the initial play-through, clips can take on new meanings depending on which pieces of information have been uncovered by the player.
“Her Story” is absolutely worth your time and money and has the potential to be my top game of 2015. Finally, Viva Seifert deserves immense praise—her performance is easily one of the best I’ve seen all year, in any medium.
Brilliant writing. Brilliant performance. Brilliant game.

Turbo dismount has a simple concept. Crash.
Ok let me get straight in. Turbo dismount is a game where a rag doll is put in a car, and then the car crashes. The immense variety of everything in this game may make this review a bit tedious, but bear with me.
Let's touch on the gameplay. You dismount your vehicle by holding down a button on the screen that says "dismount", and you release it when it fills up to your liking. The more filled the button is, the faster your viechles will go.
Now that we've done that, let's talk about the vehicles. The amount of cars and other things to ride is pretty huge, and each vehicle has different acceleration, speed and weight. Because of how many there are, we can't cover them all, but I'll try to cover a good variety. The squealer is the fastest vehicle in the game, and basically resembles a F1 racing car, it's downside is that it is not very durable, and will sometimes fall apart because of how fast it is going. The red hot engine is a fire truck with a crane arm on top, and most dummies can sit in this. This vehicle, along with the wrecking ball and the bulldozer, is the strongest viechle in the game, and only has a few breaking points, the downside of this vehicle and the other two I just touched on, is that they are not very fast. The last vehicle I'll look at is the boss throne, which is a swivel chair. That's all it is. Along with the tricycle and skateboard, these vehicles are quite slow, and because of how small they are, don't break.
Now we've looked at a few of the vehicles, let's touch on the characters. Each character is different in size, has a different name, and has different poses. Mr. Dismount is the main character, and Ms. Dismount is basically a female version of Mr. Dismount. Mr. Ego has a big head and looks depressed most of the time, Mr. Heft is a chubby man who has some more daring poses, Mr. Reach is a skinny guy with long limbs, Ms. Bumblebee is a big bummed woman, and  finally, Ms. Diva is a fat model. These characters can even be customized from the main menu to have a picture on where their face should be, or make a bobble head, which is hard to explain, just look it up. The vehicle can also be customized to have a logo on them.
Now, we look at the levels. Each level is different from the rest, and because there are some many, I can only cover a few. Hit the fan is a level where you start on a road, and drive into a big area full of wind turbines, and by adding a ramp at the start, you can literally hit the fan. Space program is an interesting level. It's basically a huge vertical wall that you can try to drive a car up. Can you get to the top? Lets keep going is a level that is a rocky cliff. Have fun! The last level I will touch on is Run DMZ. It's a road that is surrounded my a minefield. You can drive into it! There is also a huge steam community for this game, and there are tons more workshop levels for you to download!
The final thing I need to touch on is the obstacles. These can be placed in levels and moved around, and add a lot of variety to your crashes. Some include; road bumps, mines, traffic cones, bowling pins, ramps, boost pads, brake pads, roadblocks, breakable brick walls, invincible mega walls and an oilslick.
Did you make it this far? If you didn't I don't blame you, but if you like endless replayability, lots of laughs, and exploding dummies, you WILL love this game.
My final rating is... 9/10

Battleborn is a unique first person shooter. The easy thing to do is say it is just a MOBA or a wannabe Overwatch, but really it is its own game and if you ever get to spend any time playing it you quickly realize this. The sad thing is the price tag which makes it hard to really find this out, because the only way to find out what Battleborn truly is is to play it.
I'll try to describe it best I can in these categories: Story/Characters, Gameplay
There's also a note on game Updates and the devs at the bottom because others here are spreading misinfo.
Story/Characters:
I consider this to be a big part of the Gearbox experience ever since vanilla Borderlands 2 or the Zombie Island of Dr Ned in Borderlands 1.
It features the awesome writing talents that made me fall in love with the characters of Borderlands. All the characters' personalities in Battleborn are just as unique and memorable as the ones in Borderlands and many of them have the potential to become great memes of CL4-TP/Crap-Trap or Buttstalion tier.
Some of the dialogue of the levels may be repetitive, but a majority of the time the different sequences of the levels feature randomized voice over combinations of the different characters in order to make each playthrough unique, and even the right characters in the right location seem to change the narrative of the story mission entirely (such as El Dragon being played in the first mission).
The story itself sounds kind of serious, being about the end of the universe and all, but the universe doesn't seem to take itself too seriously as many of the previously mentioned random voice lines are quick comical. If you were a fan of Borderlands 2's humor and laughed through many of missions of that game, then this sense of humor is very familiar to you. It's very much like the first few minutes of gameplay with Jack's Buttstalion monologue.
The characters are so unique and in variety that it is easy to develope a favoritism for one or find one with the right set of characteristics or tropes to entertain you. My favorite character in the game is ISIC, who is basically a demented version of Clippy except he is a skull and not a paper clip. His personality and voice lines are so humorous and fun to me that I decided to learn and main him just because he was so entertaining. The devs have done a great job fleshing out each character.
PVP/PVE Gameplay:
PVE:
On a similar note to the last one made in the previous section: The characters' gameplays are so unique that you can find many different styles of gameplay in this game and choose the one that suits you best. Each character from there has more playstyles within the Helixes (skill tree each character has). You will likely find a character you find both highly entertaining to listen to as well as play.
I honestly didn't like ISIC's gameplay a lot at first, but after I got the hang of it was the perfect combination of PB&J, except rather it was Personality and Playstyle.
The PVE gameplay experience of the story mode is very much like short, quick bursts of a Borderlands game. You are matched with hordes of enemies that are pretty challenging at first, but after you get the hang of the game (which could be instantly) then they can become rather easy to plow through in Normal Difficulty. The game also features and Advanced mode where it takes considerably more strategy than just plowing through the levels. Both Normal and Advanced have Hardcore options removing extra lives, but allowing teammates to rez you potentially. The more allies in a match the more difficult a mission can be, and depending on the objective of the level it may be easier just to solo it.
Some of the story levels do get repetitivem and there are only 8 of them. They are really fun for several playthroughs however and the many variations of narrations and NPC lines I mentioned earlier make it very worthwhile to do.
Some of the funner and more fleshed out missions can feel like their own gamemodes, that can be compared to the challenge of player vs player combat.
Battleborn's PVE provides two things that HELP YOU IN PVP that the other competitors of Battleborn, who lack PVE, might not:
PVE modes provide a convenient and challenging way to try new characters you have just unlocked. That why you do not have to rush blindly into a PVP match to figure out how a character works and feels before trying yourself against other players.
PVE provides a decent break in between PVP matches if you start to tilt. It can be a great stress reliever to go around capping thralls and robots for a bit until you've blown off all your steam.
The PVP:
There are a lot of good complaints about PVP, but there are also a lot of bad ones.
The queue is very... primitive? It doesn't seem to have any regard for player levels and I am not sure what queue time will be for you but it looks like it differs from region to region. I (from America) do not have any trouble finding a group. It does not take 30 minutes. The longest I've ever waited was 4-5 minutes tops.
The server population is definitely at question, but this is of course definitely reliant on how many people buy the game in the first place. I saw complaints in other reviews that this is a reason you shouldn't buy the game. That is just bullsh**. If you are afraid to buy the game because there might not be anyone else buying the game, then someone has to break this line first and just buy the game.
The gamemodes are OK. They definitely aren't wildly unique or anything:
There's Incursion which is the reason people call this a MOBA genre game. It playes exactly like a typical MoBA match, but with just one lane instead of three. This creates a lot of problems such as bottlenecking in some cases as 10 people are squished into a lane. Some of the matches can feel a little cramped from this. It seems to borrow from the Merc camps you see in MOBAs such as Heroes of the Storm, as you can recruit hefty minions to help make big pushes. You can purchase and upgrade sorts of mini-towers to help defend as well (these are in each gamemode).
Meltdown is a race to see who can get the most of their units across the map as quickly as possible and destroy as many of the enemy's as they can in a sort of Real Time game of Checkers I guess. It is really fun despite my bad joke in the last sentence. The levels are far larger than Incursion's levels and also feature more lanes and side-objectives. There are no merc camps here, but there are more large minions you can buy in your base to help push.
Point Capture is a gamemode straight out of TF2. It plays very similarly, but there are towers to buy and upgrade here in order to get a stronger grip on the locations being contested.
All gamemodes whether PVE or PVP make use of the items you collect from PVE or PVP to augment your characters and the Shards used to buy them. Shards are sort of like Gold in a traditional MOBA, but they are mostly gained from map environment. You have to use them to unlock your items, but you can also use them to buy minions or towers/upgrades for your base that provide very good experience. Much like in a MOBA you want more experience/levels than your enemies so you have to make a decision: Do I want more general but maybe weaker passive bonuses from items or faster levels for characters' ability-specific bonuses? It's sort of a neat way to balance items so that anyone with any quality items can play PVP without having to have good items to unlock (because honestly the base upgrades are WAAAAAY better investments).
Devs/Updates: A lot of the actual problems with battleborn are being discussed frequently on the official forums. The devs are talking with players and are open to SUGGESTIONS for improvements. This is a new genre for them and they are willing to learn. They are even getting tips from Riot games and Hi Rez apparently (who enjoyed thegame). You should Battleborn a chance

[having just posted that I could never really get into Myst, even though I am a fan of the adventure game genre and was actually an active player back when it was first released...]
speaking of games that are kind of like Myst but that i actually really enjoyed... JULIA: Among the Stars wins my award for "most logical puzzles ever" in a point-n-click adventure game. They're also fairly easy, which doesn't hurt when you're a time-limited gamer who's starting to lose his mental edge, like me. The best things about the game are its elements that challenge you to reconstruct the stories of what happened to the interstellar expedition that you were a part of, and the recent and ancient history of the system you have discovered. It's a quasi-realistic detective simulation in that aspect, as you must use an interactive mind-map tool to create timelines that make sense of all the evidence you collect. Its other strength is the variety of puzzles... apart from the password "hacking" minigame and the circuit-schematic puzzles that are used for creating upgrades, I can't think of any puzzle types that you actually do more than once-- pretty much every scenario is its own kind of challenge. I also particularly like the notion that you are just sitting up in a spaceship by yourself, sending a remote probe to do all your "adventuring" and not able to actually interact with things yourself. It makes a lot of the limitations inherent to the genre make sense.
[yet another note... i did not pay full price for this game, but however I got it (a bundle of some sort, or more likely a deep discount during a seasonal salew) I was happy with the value proposition. Most importantly, i found it worth the TIME i spend playing it (and having my young kids watch me play it, which is a huge boost to the value in my opinion)]

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PvE:
So, first of all, the beta was by no means representative for this product:
Enemies are in full 'Gearbox mode' again. That means they are bulletspongy as f*ck and just melt through the objectives you have to defend. Without any chance at defending them as they ignore you most of the time and stright beeline in for the kill. That means that a mission that went well for about an hour can just be failed in a few minutes and you go home with nothing.
Apart from that the level design is just really bad.
For f*cks sake, you can't even choose a level, there is just a random selection of 3 levels on standard difficulty to vote on. Which is the stupidest idea as you need to grind arbitrary achievements to unlock some heroes - like get a silver rating on all coop missions.
So, what are you gonna do when you just have a single mission left? Right, randomly join and disconnect on games, mess with all the other players queuing just to eventuelly get the one you need. If your mates don't decide to vote for the other ones that is.
The best part is that it even then sometimes decides to put you in a party on your own. Great fun.
And the worst part is that the platform is there. You can play specific missions on different difficulties in Private Game Mode. But you got to go solo or with friends as there is no queueing there. I don't know who thought that this would be a great idea.
Also they force you to watch a unskippable 10 min cartoon intro with bad rap music (and I usually listen to rap so I know what I'm talking about) before you can even play the game.
Plus there is bugs and unfixed problems everywhere. Examples:
One boss got stuck and wouldn't drop its invulnerability shield.
In a defend section, enemies would just stand where they spawned and shoot at the objective - out of reach for the players to kill them.

Benedict, a humanoid bird with a rocket launcher, is being played as a melee character, because his slow moving rockets are easy to evade but fired right into the enemies faces hits them guaranteed (but not Benedict himself as he is immun to his own damage). Thorn, a bow and arrow sniper, is similarly bad. Due to her high health, incredible single shot damage, high mobility and AoE slows she just jumps into you without any chance of escape for enemies.
But why bother balancing / fixing a deadborn game when you only have to cash in on the preorders and Season pass. They apparently didn't even bother to test AMD compatibility.

It is a simple puzzle game with a poor interface. Attached to it is a blurb which described the original motivation along with a variety of research organisation and game company branding.
This is a very good example of why the current system of funding and evaluating academic projects needs reform. It might originally have been good idea. However, it has all the hallmarks of being a multidisciplinary project where many months were spent trying to do something more sophisticated but the programmers and academics failed to understand each other. Rather than abandon it, the team probably had to produce a “deliverable” outcome, which is this very poor game, for the research council in a short timeline. They probably secretly hope nobody will ever actually play it.

If you really want to understand how inequalities develop in game form play a roguelike like BOI or FTL. While they may be a small number of brilliant players who can regularly complete the game. They will be vastly outnumbered by people who received good items drops and lucked their way to victory, but still claim to be gaming geniuses.

Jacob tries to unite gameplay with a sociologic message: Starting difficulty is randomly picked to match the real-life "starting difficulty" of financially/socially/educationally weak people.
Long review short: Without the message, the educational part, Jacob would have been a easy puzzle game. Are you into easy puzzle games? Give it a try. It's not that bad.
You get some time to pick randomly arranged ladder pieces, build a ladder and climb it. If you don't manage to get to the end of your construction by the end of the countdown, the part of the ladder you didn't reach will disappear. One such action (pick, build, climb) is a turn, and you have several turns to get as high up as possible.
Pros:
It's free
Once you figure it out, it's not that hard
Sound is okay
Visuals could be better, but could be worse, too
Cons:
No tutorial
Once you figure it out, it's no longer challenging
No replay-value
Overall it's not a remarkable game
The sociologic message is projected right into your face, however you don't feel it in your heart while playing
The prologue deserves its own paragraph
The prologue consists of a giant wall of text on a yellow background, explaining the idea behind Jacob (social injustice, privilege, the relation between wealth and more wealth, what kind of studies you can look up if this topic interests you...) It's basically a bunch of information and numbers. I'm fine with that. But why does it have to scroll down on it's own?
I tried to scroll up because I wanted to reread something. Tried to scroll down because I'm a fast reader. Takes an eternity to scroll two lines up or down.
You can click it away anytime. But if you want people to read your sociologic message and view your game from a sociologic point of view, let them scroll through the text on their own.
Also, why is this game called Jacob? Is it a wordplay based on Jacob's ladders?  Or is it because poverty could happen to anyone, even to guys called Jacob? Or is it empirically proven that Jacobs are poorer than the average Michael? That's the real mystery here.

There are some pacing problems to the game over all. When the game is teaching you about itself, you're not really in any danger to speak of. Multiple nights go by without the possibility of a failstate. There are clearly delineated sections where you can't die. In some cases, this is a good thing. It gives you an intermission and a moment to breathe, and it's not like Five Nights where you constantly feel like you're on the verge of a heart attack.
However, I feel like it ramps up from this into its final challenge way too fast. If you're a chickenshit like me and not stopping to figure out how the monster's systems work (and why would you, you're supposed to avoid it), you're hosed. It's a ninety degree brick wall of a difficulty spike. Furthermore, the final level drops most of the systems the game had been working with (that is, you don't carry Tattletail around) and becomes much more Slender-esque, a challenge of finding a series of objects in an enclosed space with the monster constantly teleporting around you. And then you die. You die a lot. And then you see the jumpscare game over screen. A lot. And then gradually the horror wears off as you feel your way around for a strategy to find those damn candles and shut up those Furby knock-offs and their "no more Mama", creeping around in the basement with your flashlight off and hoping shaking it on again won't summon the beast. It's more slog than fun, because the candle placement is randomized, too. The last level is a pretty big let down, but the Tattletails in their little Satanic circle like we'd always joked about in elementary school kept me playing because I was honestly kind of intrigued to see what would happen next. That's the power of a good concept.
Having a jumpscare stinger ending is really cheap though. Come on, guys, really?
I can't say I regretted the two hours I spent playing through it in exchange for my five dollars and I hope this concept can be improved upon. It's certainly unique, which is what drew me to the game in the first place. But I don't think calling it "storydriven" is totally accurate and the constantly escalating stinger ambiance music wears thin after awhile, though where sound design is concerned I will applaud the devs for not using a horrible screaming noise every single time you die. It's charming enough and it will probably rekindle my deepseated childhood fear of basements. Thanks for that one, guys.

I'm not sure why I purchased Her Story. When I saw the screenshots at the front of my Discovery Queue, I thought it was a film and was prepared to remove it with prejudice. I was surprised to discover that it was a game, although it had FMV, which is often more frustrating than nostalgic. Still, it was a detective game made by the creator of a Silent Hill game, so why not give it a try?
I loaded the game up, and was immediately confused. The focus on interrogation had reminded me of LA Noire, so I expected to be playing a game where the object was to determine a subject's guilt or innocence, whether they were lying or being truthful. This was not the game I found. In truth, it was something more like Papers, Please or Please Don't Touch Anything -- a game where you repeat the same action, with slight variations, over and over to try and dig up new results.
What results is a story unfolding in a mosaic style, determined as much by the player as by the director. This is a fascinating piece of fiction, a game that left me every bit as unsettled as a Silent Hill game, but for completely different reasons. I won't spoil any of the details, but I will say this is a tremendous game with a solid amount of replayability.

I was a bit suspicious about this game, because the description was just vague enough that I thought it might be another Gone Home, where the description sort of teases with the idea that it might be about something interesting but then ends up just being a poor quality romance story. And there is a heavy romance influence in this game, but there's also an actual story to it as well. The gameplay is very simple, essentially boiling down to just watching small clips of a series of interviews with a woman and searching important words from the clips in the database to find more clips, which there are a lot of. There's no real deducting or pointing out suspects; you just keep finding videos and eventually the story becomes clear and then it ends. It's extremely easy to "sequence break" by accident and find a clip of the end of the interviews that sort of spoils the mystery aspect, but the rest of the clips are still interesting to see how the story got to that point. Overall there really isn't much to the game, and while I normally don't agree with people kneejerkingly calling story-based games "movies" it's hard to deny that this essentially is one (though it's told in a unique format), but the story is interesting, so if you want to pay $5 to watch a movie then this isn't a terrible way to do that.

Her Story consists entirely of entering key word searches into a database and watching short video clips (often < 30 seconds). The "mystery" exists only because of the arbitrary restriction imposed by the database--you have to find clips by searching rather than simply browsing them in chronological order.  Eventually the game will cue you when it feels you have watched enough of the clips to grasp the entire story. For me this was after a little more than an hour, though I got the gist of the story after about 30 minutes or so.
This is not a detective game, it's an exercise in fractured narrative.  I'm not sure why so many reviewers have pointed out a need for pen and paper, it makes as much sense as watching something like Eternal Sunshine with pen and paper. Narrative games are fine, but the story in this one is quite absurd and many of the clips are poorly acted/written/just nonsensical (e.g. the song, so "on the nose" and completely inappropriate given the context). I hit on the main twist about 15 minutes in and spent the next hour expecting a counter-twist because the initial twist was so ridiculous.
Over all it's entertaining until you realize there's actually nothing to it, and it won't last you more than 2 hours.
edit: This review seems to have become a lightning rod of sorts. I didn't write this because I'm some anti-"SJW" alpha-wannabe caveman, I just thought the game was bad. Mostly because of poor writing and acting. I love narrative games--if you want to play a really great one with a female protagonist play Life is Strange.

What do you expect from this game? Because if you are looking for a good RTS and turn based gameplay, Divinity Dragon Commander isn't the game that's going to scratch that itch for you, even though it employs those mechanics. But if you are looking for a conceptually interesting game, with emphasis on story, character and choices, then I dare say that Divinity Dragon Commander might be worth checking out, if and only if, you are willing to be patient with it and accept the shortcomings of the action phases, meaning the RTS battles.
Divinity Dragon Commander is divided in three parts of gameplay: story and political decisions, turn based Risk-like movement troops on a military map and real-time strategy confrontation during which you can control a dragon. The three phases of the game influence each other in a delightful way: the political decision you make have an impact on all the areas of the map, and the level of bonuses you get from them, depending on the faction to which each county belongs. For example, if you are popular with the elves, your elven controlled regions will grant you more money and will also be more easy to defend. At the same time, it will be harder for the enemy to hold on to those elvish districts. Obviously, should you be less popular, those bonus would become penalties, making the game actually very difficult, even in the RTS sequences of the game, where the number of recruits, and thus units you can build, is tied to your popularity.
But on that point, it needs to be said that the whole game is pretty difficult if you don't know its workings. The learning curve is all over the place. The game doesn't explain the consequence of your political decisions and the nefarious effects of a popularity of zero percent with one or more factions. Worse, going against the wishes of the undead faction, which is blessed by the gods, actually gives you a penalty during automatic battle resolutions, which is bound to happen sooner or later since you can only manage one battle per turn personally. This battle penalty can go pretty high as I found out, up to -26% apparently. I wouldn't necessarily recommend that particular experience. The RTS phases are a lot easier if you compromise you political stance and try to accommodate most of the factions, at least some of the time.
The problems during the battles do not only spring from what the game doesn't establish in mechanics, but also from balancing issues. At the start of the game, you can choose from three dragons, but the differences aren't obvious: the mage-like dragon has more health and better mobility but deals the least amount of damage, whereas the biggest, fastest dragon has the best damage output, but the less health and mobility. The starting skills of each dragon are also different, but since you can unlock every talent for every dragon, it's really a none issue. The problem is that the mage-dragon deals so little damage, that it takes ages to kill anything while the enemy has no problem pummelling that particular dragon to death. Sure, in multilayer, it might make a difference, but for the story campaign, I see no point in going down that road.
Also, on the turn based map, it is possible to build local improvements which in turn grant you cards that you can play before a battle to improve your odds of winning, or granting temporary bonuses to counties. But, from all the dozens and dozens of different cards it is possible to get, very clearly the tavern, which grants you mercenaries, is the best way to go. All of a sudden, you can attack an enemy, one unit against ten, and then just summon a whole army of mercenaries to take care of things.
Besides these balancing issues, there is also the fact that it is possible to carry over gold between acts. There are three acts in the game, and while you are limited in what you can take with you between act I and II, there is no limit between what it is possible to import to act III. While the game puts an emphasis on rushing down opponents, it is well worth waiting a dozen turns at the end of each act to maximise the treasure, the research trees and the cards, stacking up on mercenary ones. The worst part is, winning or, at least for me, enjoying the game, seems to require using these exploits to gain the upper hand against the IA and avoiding most of the dreadful RTS sequences.
Because there is no way around it, those sequences aren't well made. That they are functional is about the only good thing I can say about them. The RTS aspects of it are rather simplistic, and the tactics are seldom more developed than surviving, building a large army and dumping it on the enemy. The fact that it is possible to play as a dragon during those phases is refreshing, and it is nice to fly over the battlefield, helping you troops and raining down fire on your enemies. But this makes it almost impossible to control you troops, managing your army, buildings, etc. So it is constantly necessary to switch back and forth between dragon and RTS controls.
As a balancing issue, -again!-, the speed of the game is a huge problem. It is possible to determine how fast, or slow, the RTS portion of the game can run. This means that everything can happen either twice as fast, or only at fifty percent of the speed. Here is the kicker: the dragon you control isn't influence by the change in pace, meaning that he still moves and attacks at the same speed, regardless of the speed of the enemies. This is completely broken since it means that enemies can dish out twice as much damage to you on higher speed, but only fifty percent on the lowest speed, which makes it also much more easier to dodge. So turning the speed to “slowest” during the RTS section is almost a vital necessity.
But if, on paper, one third of the game is worth rushing through, the rest of it must be that much better, to compensate, right?
From the start, Divinity Dragon Commander pulled me in: the introduction sequence, and it's music, set a refreshing tone for me, as well as the first contact with the generals under your command. The personality, characterisation and style really shines through during those moment. It is the most polished part of the game and the effort shows.
The characters feel almost larger than life, straight out of a play, going through individual arcs with their quirks and personal demons, down one path or another, depending on your guidance. The voice acting is just perfect, I couldn't even think of one thing to improve on in that regard. It hits every mark! The dialogue made me think, it made me laugh, it completely mesmerized me. There is so much personality here, even in the background of the scenes where you make decision (like the amazing skeletal barmaid).
The opinion of the player is asked constantly over subject which are sometimes trivial and funny, or very serious. It is sad to only have two options as choices, no matter the subject, but it does make things more straightforward. Although, you would be surprised how often the obvious choice isn't always the right one. I liked it a lot, but I suppose it requires a certain interest in political issues, if only to catch the jokes, the nudges and the parodies represented here.
I was also very surprised by some of the different issues you get, depending on what you decided earlier. Turning down the imp faction looking to build a giant bomb will result in them coming back with a super soldier project, whereas agreeing in the first place, will only ask more and more of you in the search for the “biggest and badest explosion ever”. Each faction (of which there are five), each general (four in this case) and each queen (again, four) has one of these quests with a lot of multiple branching.
Still, although I enjoyed my time with Divinity Dragon Commander, I cannot justify its full price tag, for what content I liked amounted to not even half of what the game had to offer.

You should, without any question, buy this game. (Especially if you enjoy Mass Effect.) If you have concerns about getting it to run, there is a lot of support out there and there is almost always some fix out there for everyone. I tried everything to no avail until finally I found a suggestion in a buried thread to do the following:
1) Go to the game folder. Steam>steamapps>common>swkotor>swkotor.ini
2) Under "[Graphics Options]", change "FullScreen=1" to "FullScreen=0". Then, add a line that says, "AllowWindowedMode=1".
3) File>Save.
4) Run the game. Hopefully it'll work. It did for me after changing only these things. Save often. Mine still crashes, especially during movies. But reloading it allows it to get through the movie. If you don't like it windowed, you can change it to fullscreen once the game opens without causing it to crash by minimizing the game, re-maximizing it, and then dragging the window to the top of your screen.
Happy playing!

===
===
GRAPHICS: 8 / 10
Honestly, for being a game from 2007, graphics are very good. Textures are mostly detailed, there is AA, FOV, good particle effects, well done enemies... models of people are kinda deformed sometimes, but the game more than makes up, on this side at least, with very well done armors, weapons and environments.
SOUND: 6 / 10
Well, the sound design is average, no shame and no glory. The main theme music deserves a mention because it's very good, then the in-game ambience and sounds are average.
GAMEPLAY: 3 / 10
The gameplay part of this title is really flawed by major problems. I will just say this here and then focus on detail later in the review.
LONGEVITY: 9 / 10
If you are a completitionist, to find everything the huge world has to offer will take you a very long time. There are a myriad of quests and secret dungeons to discover, no doubt about this.
===
- Very large world to explore, there are really a lot of dungeons and places to discover, cities to visit and stuff to loot in said places.
- Great variety of weapons, armors, crafting materials and accessories, there are around 250 different sets of armor and something around 150 different weapons, which is not bad at all.
- Complex and rewarding alchemy system: combine the elements you find from nature or defeated enemies to create custom potions with effects based on what you put in them. Even combine potions with each other to create more powerful ones.
- Decent number of spells and character skills
- Good variety of enemies: undeads, wild animals, constructs, demons, golems, dragons, and more
- Cities are quite crowded and you can enter almost all buildings, plus there are many vendors and skill trainers around
===
- Horse travel is crippled by major problems, and is the only way to explore undiscovered areas quickly. Horses have bugged pathfinding, will get stuck randomly, are very clunky and will stay where you left them in the world. The problem with this last thing is that the Call Horse command does not work if you are farther than around 50 metres from your horse.
- The world may be huge but is really empty. Most of the time exploring, it will just feel like travelling in a demo map with some trees, rocks and some props. The world does not feel alive and linked together as it should be, but instead feels like dungeons and cities put inside a vast nothingess with no interest apart the occasional wild animal or alchemy herb. Very limited interactivity and dynamicity of environment in the overall game world.
- NPCs in the cities are always the same 5-6 models, it will happen to see the same NPC models over and over very quicly, even groups of them being just plain clones. All NPCs will answer the same 3-4 default questions and have nothing characterizing them apart from few main quest characters, all the rest is just a bunch of generic placeholders just there to trade or give quests. Immersion and RP experience is really downgraded because of this.
- Externally, cities are all the same, big dark brown stone walls, doesn't matter if the city is Nanic, Human or whatever other race. Zero characterization of racial buildings in this aspect.
- Enemy AI is rudimental and will just follow the player to attack him, ranged enemies will run away if a melee player gets too close. enemies lack any semblance of coordination or group support actions such as ie. mages healing fighters and similar. Huge mobs of enemies can be carried around indefinitely. Enemies will just attack the player on sight without any role-playing interacion or eventual faction alliegances, there are allies by default and enemies by default, no grey in the middle, and that's it.
- Zero role-playing decisions player-side. Each dialogue is scripted and apart from general questions about some characters or the world, there is no reallly matter of choice in anything, just accept or decline an assignment, with no depth in choices or branching of events during any quest.
- Combat system is clunky and just underwhelming: melee characters will just have to swing a weapon until low on HP, drink all the potions they want and just keep spamming attacks until everyone is dead. Ranged classes can just run away from the enemy, then stop, aim, fire, and then run away again before the enemy can target them. Potions can be spammed so challenge is zero because as long as you have money to buy potions you are good.
- Economy is broken: you can pick up all the stuff an enemy has on him, then when you are full of stuff go to a city and sell everything for massive amounts of money even from early game. You also can go and travel to a high level area, go to a random merchant, and buy crystals / potions / rings / anything with no level restriction of 20 levels ahead of you and just use them right there. Merchants will also havfe unlimited money and buy everything, always.
- There is a skill to get bonus damage against enemies riding horses. But in the game there is no enemy ridiing a horse. There just isn't. I put this just to get you an idea of how half-finished this game really is.
===
- Alchemy is completely game breaking: ingredients can be combined to make potions, but also different potions with the SAME effects can be stacked. Example, you make 5 potions, all of them give you a Bonus to Strenght attribute, right, but all of them have a different name and a slight difference in the bonus, example: they give +10,+11,+12,+13 and +14 Strenght. Well you can drink ALL of them together and get ALL of the bonuses TOGETHER, for a total, in the example, of +60 Strenght, this applies to any potion you can imagine. Basically, when the game gets hard, just drink all the potions you have created and become a demi-god for a short time, kill anything, and done.
- Weapon upgrading is aswell completely game breaking: you can stack an unlimite damount of upgrade crystals (which grant a % of bonus damage based on the element they are) on a weapon, so if you have like 50 upgrade crystals, which can be found easily or created with alchemy, you can put all of them on a weapon, getting a +10% damage bonus 50 TIMES. So that weapon will become just ridiculous.
- Healing shrines ruin combat: in the world there are many, TOO many healing shrines, which will give the player a very high health regen over time. They are on many roads and even inside dungeons. fact is, you can make enemis follow you and stay inside a healing shrine to fight, so you will have health regen and be near invincible, but enemies will not have the bonuss and so your fight will be really easy. Same thing goes for Mana shrines if you are a mage, same principle but with mana, so unlimited power.
- Inexplicable random stuttering inside cities or in crowded combats, even on recent computer system, this is a result of bad optimization on the overall game engine both graphical and coding-wise.
- Main quest and side missions are just anonymous, uninvolving, poorly written and underwhelming, sketched, half finished, poorly refined.
===
Some aspects of Two Worlds are well done, almost too much well done, like the incredible number of weapons and armor, or the variety of enemies, or the principle upon the alchemy system is based,. But, as i explained, a lot of other aspects have been butchered with poor realization, badly thought out balance and gamaplay implementation, or just left there half finished.
This is a game with GREAT potential, which has been released unfinished like a lot of today's Early Access games, because in the end this is an early access game, an alpha, a demonstration of the potential this game COULD achieve if it was finished fully.

So I've not been much of a lover of MOBAs, or PvP FPS's, and I wasn't keen on the Overwatch beta, but I thought I'd give this game a whirl, because if I ended up hating it, I could just get a refund, right? And it interested me from the stuff I watched on Youtube.
Well I'm glad I gave this game a shot. Every element is fun. The pacing is great in the story mode (which you can play with randoms), the levelling mid-match is really cool, because you can tech your character how it suits the specific situation. The unlocks are pretty steady, the loot is interesting. And the graphics are awesome.
I mean, I suck at this game, but I have a lot of fun.
The game is BorderLands at its core, and a well executed FPS-only MOBA.

Overall I have been loving this game. It's so much fun to grab some buddies and go to town with it. Great sleeper hit.
PROS:
- Great multiplayer both Co-Op and PvP.
- Characters have great personality and all play and feel different.
- Overall the balance is pretty good save for a few minor things.
- Tons of progression to keep you busy, something a lot of other hero shooters forgot to add.
- LOOT.
- Rath is voiced by the same person who voiced Vegeta.
- Matchmaking is usually pretty quick. I find games within 15-30 seconds usually. I think router settings have a lot to do with people having issues.
- Balanced gear by making you have to activate it mid match with shards.
- Relatively loyal/helpful playerbase.
- ISIC
-Loads of replayability.
CONS:
- Matchmaking is a little unbalanced in terms of the average level of both teams. That said level past 3 does not really provide an inherent advantage, just more options.
- Currently unable to queue for advanced missions via public matching. (Might be for the best though some of them are tough)
- Inability to directly pick which mission you want to play unless you set up your own match with people you have invited.
- They really could have done more marketing.
- Campaign is a touch short.
A majority of issues for the game can be solved with either having a group of friends to play with. (If you don't I'm sure you can post on a forum to find people) Or figuring out how to fix things on your end.
Overall the game has been very enjoyable I'd rate it a solid. 8/10 with some QoL changes and future content patches it could be an easy 10/10

Without going into the eventual comparison to that other game, Battleborn is a game that tries different things but suffers from an identity crisis. The FPS elements are a nice touch, but with the bright colors and all the action going on, things can get a little hectic. While some people are ok with this, it seems to me that it triest to focus the game with FPS elements (explosions, guns, grenades, etc.,) while it also tries to push the MOBA element into this, further pushing away that PVP element while also keeping it present. Three game modes exist, and your teammates are almost incompetent enough that they will sometimes follow the objective. They want a PVP mode, they chase down the enemies, and ultimately get 10+ kills. 10+ kills is great...for another game. Sure, they can rack up the kill count, but the minions are the most important targets in this game, ultimately they are ignored by your teammates in favor of chasing down the enemy. Communication within your team is almost non-existent, and I say almost because in the rare occasions that I eventually get a reply from someone, the communication stops there. I say, if you have friends, use them and communicate, cooperate, coordinate. If you are going to play this alone, good luck in finding competent teamates. This game has a Borderlands look without the charm the series presents. 2.5/5

FPS as in you simply pick a range character and guns blazing away.
Hack and slash is playing as a melee character fighting at frontline.

Battleborn, albeitly has a slowstart. You might have to play the game, around 10~30hrs to get most characters to unlock.
After that, the game has some difficulty curve new players might have to get around:
Example like your playstyles vs some characters, the gear difference from your opponents in pvp modes, gear's optimisation for maximum impact/to compete and many more.
Battleborn is a interesting game, chaotic and fun at the same time. Just like Borderlands 1/2, from gearbox that is also known for.
Although story mode can be short and repetitive, expect future DLCs and contents that will surely quench the playerbase's thirst for more.

This game is a blast to play. While it's not Borderlands or a traditional MOBA, the game blends in the two in such a way to provide players with a fun online experience. The game features a variety of modes and offers both PVE and PVP, with gear and progress shared between the two. I don't play a lot of PVE but I don't feel impaired or inferior when I go play PVP.
The PVP of Battleborn is complex and full of depth typical to what the other MOBAs offer. This is its defining characteristic and makes me love Battleborn more than the more simplistic and repetitive tug-of-war type gameplay in Overwatch. Sadly, the complexity and somewhat high learning curve means that players who are new to the MOBA genre will require a lot of learning in order to become somewhat proficient in Battleborn's two longer PVP game modes. Playing the game solo can also provide an unstable mix of fun, as your performance is heavily reliant on your teammates you get from matchmaking. But if the stars align, the fun and competitiveness that this game provides exceeds anything Overwatch provides. There is lane pushing, capturing neutral camps, picking up extra shards (income), leveling up ingame, developing and building gear loadouts.

Great concept, poor execution.
First off, I'll start with what I liked about the game.
Mapping is pretty cool, the idea of using triangulation to uncover the map and mark yourself/landmarks is awesome and works fairly well.
The island is large, there is tons to explore, and the game lets you do just that if you want.
Night time is dark, and you can easily get lost if you don't have a light.
The idea of finding, identifying, and mixing different flora of the island together to make different tonics/medicines is nice.
The slightly bad.
Map at night. If you're not holding anything, then you pull out your lighter at night to view the map. But if you're holding anything before pulling it out (including a torch) the map ends up being a useless black square in the dark. Requiring you to drop your torch and have it roll away every time you want to look at the map.
Weapons. Why give me knives/axes if they're completely useless?
The "Creature". I played this game for 5 hours and only saw the "creature" once. It found me when I was out in the open and had nowhere to hide, so I just kept watching it while walking backwards towards the closest hut. It never attacked me, just followed a few feet away the enire time. Once I reached the hut it wandered off, never to be seen again.
The bad.
Your character controls like a 400 pound blob wearing bowling shoes. Once you get the slightest bit of momentum going, it's really hard to stop. This had me constantly running off cliffs and falling down hills that I should've been able to stop infront of. Any slight incline and you will either start sliding or just start running down it. This makes exploring extremely frustrating at times.
While I have stopped playing out of frustration, I may pick it up again at a later date to see if they've updated it at all. I really do love the idea of this game, and could probably have forgiven a majority of the flaws, but the controls ruined the experience for me. They drove me absolutely insane and were the sole reason I stopped playing the game. It's unfortunate, but I just can't reccomend this game because of the controls.

Given all the different genres mashed up into this game: real time strategy, strategic board game, and conversation driven political sim, I was ready to forgive this game for each portion being weaker than any dedicated single genre title.
Even then this game falls short. I got it on sale for $25 and still feel ripped off. $10 would be the max.
The strategic board and RTS are shoddy and awful (again, I went into this not expecting it to be the next Starcraft). They wouldn't even be good as free flash games.
So that leaves the conversational political sim. The political support you get for different decisions ends up not mattering. The support you get from each race only affects battle you manually resolve (maximum of one battle per turn) and even then it only affects your max army size which is never a limiting factor.
So you're left with only reading the conversations for the dialog. This is probably the strongest area of the game, but not enough to justify the whole thing. The voice acting is uniformly excellent (surprising, giving how they skimped on the gameplay portions), and some of the characters are entertaining.
But then the cracks start showing. All the political decisions are based on current political topics, but they don't even bother throwing on a layer of clever satire so it all comes off as preachy and break the immersion (would a general involved in a world wide war of genocide really care about coming out of the closet?). Heck, I'm a donating, card carrying member of the ACLU and even I found this game to be simplistic leftist preaching. Some the political views the game preaches are downright disturbing. The "good" path has you encouraging vigilante murder of people with backwards bigoted opinions, and eliminating due process fair trials for anyone accused of♥♥♥♥♥♥ It feels like the game was written by Tumblr users eager to shred the bill of rights in the name of a twisted form of social justice.
In the end, the only redeeming aspects of the game are some of the conversations. I recommend you save your money and your time (the RTS and strategic gameplay is really really awful) and just go watch all the conversations up on Youtube.

I'll keep this short. This game tries a lot of things at once. It tries to be a turn-based grand strategy, it tries to be an RTS, it tries to be a political RPG. One of these is merely average, one is decent, one is glorious.
Merely average are RTS battles. While the addition of being a dragon, the rest of it is a basic spamfest of cheap units in huge quantities. It does require tactics, but most fights work in the ways of rock-paper-scissors, so it ends up in making a blob of compositions and throwing it at the enemy. If you make a good use of the Dragon, the battle will be over in a few minutes, but because AI can control multiple things at once (army, capturing buildings, abilities) and production, you'll get outspammed eventually and the battle will drag on. However, you can only enter one RTS battle each turn. My biggest issue with the (singleplayer) RTS component is that when you bring a huge army to a battle, you start with only a fraction of it, while your enemy starts with every units. An easy win become a very hard battle where you are outnumbered 10 to 1.
Decent is the grand strategy component. It's quite simple, but it's competent and works well. The layout of maps makes you use strategies and calculate your moves carefully. I found it very enjoyable. What is weird is that you have 4 generals, but you can use them only once per turn, even though you use only one of them. Where do the other 3 run off to?
However the RPG and politics are where the game excels. You can visit your ship and go to various parts of it, and talk to characters and crewmen, much like in Starcraft 2. And there is not a single uninteresting or 2D character. Same with political decisions brought to you by the council of 5 races. Each decision doesn't have a black or white answer, and each councilor makes sense when explaining his position on the issue. Strangely enough, the Lizards are the most liberal and open-minded. However, my issue here is that all decisions are absolute. There is no way to find a middle ground. For example, one of the decisions was to create a republic instead of monarchy, and while I wanted to do it, other councilors made convincing arguments how the population is just not ready and educated enough. Someone wanted me to fire half my male officers and replace them with women, and I couldn't invite women to the ranks, I could only fire these guys or tell that person to back off. However, this is a minor issue.
Long story short. Dragon Commander was a highly enjoyable title. It has issues, quite a few, but overall, it's a very good game that has amazing amounts of character. There is much more depth than I descirbed. The design is awesome as well, steampunk-ish combined with technosorcerery. You don't see that often.

Game has a lot of Decision making involved to the point you almost forget its a RTS. Which is a good thing since the RTS part gets kinda boring after a dozen battles, there is a auto resolve which makes it a little faster, since all sides have mirror units not much uniqueness to the battles save for the fact you can summon your dragon form and fly across the battlefield burning all your enemys almost single handedly which is generally fun.
A good game to get if you like bickering politicians, rowdy generals, and a Dragon with a jetpack!
Worth getting but recommend waiting for a sale.

This game mixes many different game types into one epic package. It has three main game types, A risk-like board game, an RTS/third person shooter game, and a political simulator.
The battle board will be familiar to anyone who has played risk. The player moves units turn based and can choose to join a battle to aid the troops. This part is well executed and integrates well with the ability to upgrade and research new units.
When in a battle the RTS gameplay takes over. The controls take a little getting used to in the rts mode. The ability to transform into a dragon and change the tide of the battle is what really sets this game apart. It is so unique and refreshing and it give a whole new responsibility for the player to use skills.
The political simulator is decent. It is lacking in some depth, but what it is lacking is easily made up in the rest of the game. The choices are yes and no and are somewhat predictable. However juggling the outcomes and viewpoints of the races was very fun in my opinion.
If you follow the story line, it is easy to stay interested. The gameplay can get a little repetitive though. Luckily there are things that can keep it interesting such as the strategy cards.
Overall I would give this game an 8/10 because it is so unique and refreshing to use your brain to follow the different possible outcomes.

This game isn't very friendly towards newcomers to the genre. It feels like an experiment for veterans, who know what they do. Yet, as a new player, I feel this game to be very enjoyable. Graphically my style of games, an amazing soundtrack, very diverse gameplay and well done animation.
The only thing that made me go meh, is the concept of the story. It's basic, cliche even. Yet, I can forgive the devs for it since it works perfectly for the core idea of the game. And it doesn't throw a billion new words at you. Phew!

You are a dragon with an army, an airship, and the latest in cutting-edge gnomish steampunk rocket pack technology strapped to your scaly back. Go nuts.
A compelling combination of Risk-style turn-based strategy, traditional realtime strategy, and story-driven political simulator, Larian Studios crafted this chimera of an idea into a quirky but ultimately impressive game. While the RTS elements are a little light, what really sold this game for me is the dynamic, well-written NPCs that the eponymous Dragon Commander interacts with in between trips to the battle map. Your airship is visually gorgeous, the AI is relatively challenging, and there's even online multiplayer, provided that's your cup of tea.
Pros:
-- Excelent writing and dialogue. (I can't stress this enough; it's the best I've ever seen in a game.)
-- Awesome environmental art.
-- Solid AI.
-- Very reasonably priced.
-- You're a dragon.
Cons:
-- RTS element is a little underdeveloped.
-- Some players may have issues with the political decisions presented to them. If you're not a hardcore crazy conservative, you shouldn't have a problem, though.
(Note: A significant portion of my playtime for this game was in the pre-release beta that was offered through Steam.)

While I do have a few gripes with Dragon Commander, I'd be lying if I didn't say it was a blast.  Fantastic voice acting, meaningful moral choices that...actually aren't totally black and white, and an interesting bit of RTS and table top strategy, with a Dragon wearing a jetpack mixed in for good measure, make this a mess that shouldn't work...but it does.  IT DOES WORK!  This game is glorious for any fans of strategy.
My major gripes are with the rather blah main story, you'll get most of your story fix from just interacting with your crew and friends than the "plot" as it were, some moral choices and characters that ARE as stupid and pointless as they seem, a lack of differentiation between the hero and enemy on the field of battle, and generally being a pain to actually get going...it took me three days to make it work on my laptop.
That being said, once this game gets rolling, it is supremely fun.  I've found myself thinking "Just five more minutes" on this until I've spent an hour longer than I wanted to playing.  Highly recommended, in spite of my gripes.

This game is a blast to play. While it's not Borderlands or a traditional MOBA, the game blends in the two in such a way to provide players with a fun online experience. The game features a variety of modes and offers both PVE and PVP, with gear and progress shared between the two. I don't play a lot of PVE but I don't feel impaired or inferior when I go play PVP.
The PVP of Battleborn is complex and full of depth typical to what the other MOBAs offer. This is its defining characteristic and makes me love Battleborn more than the more simplistic and repetitive tug-of-war type gameplay in Overwatch. Sadly, the complexity and somewhat high learning curve means that players who are new to the MOBA genre will require a lot of learning in order to become somewhat proficient in Battleborn's two longer PVP game modes. Playing the game solo can also provide an unstable mix of fun, as your performance is heavily reliant on your teammates you get from matchmaking. But if the stars align, the fun and competitiveness that this game provides exceeds anything Overwatch provides. There is lane pushing, capturing neutral camps, picking up extra shards (income), leveling up ingame, developing and building gear loadouts.

A very simple yet incredibly detailed survival game centered around exploration and cartography rather than hunting and gathering.
You wake up as a man who has crashed onto a deserted island, only to immediately find abandoned huts and makeshift laboratories riddled with research notes and corpses, all of which is directly related to a plague that has ravaged the fictional home country of the island's former inhabitants experiencing a nationalist take-over.
The player-character is apparently infected with this same plague and begins the game incredibly weak and fragile, not being able to swim for any length of time, only able to sprint for a few seconds, and easily able to slip and fall down hills and slopes, weakening the character until they die.
The goal of the game is to explore the island, collect as many notes and maps as you can, and eventually find many medicial plants that will allow you to synthesize the cure for the plague. Along the way you will find notes for other medicines and stimulants that allow you to temoporarily and eventually permanently swim, run faster and for longer periods, and climb steeper hills and control yourself better to avoid slipping or falling.
Most of the games mechanics are simple, but they are used effectively and everything comes together very naturally.
The game requires good situational awareness and memory in order to track your own location and avoid getting lost, though there is a map and a triangulation mechanic that allows you to use landmarks to fill it in. There is a dehydration mechanic, so being able to find safe sources of water is important, as becoming dehydrated will cause you to periodcally lose some control of your character, making it easier to slip and fall when climbing, as well as accelerating the rate at which you develop a fever and start to lose health.
You keep a journal that keeps record of all the plants you find and study, as well as a collection of the various medicines you'll create with them. Creating medicines is very simple, only requiring you to collect one or two plants and then combining them by placing them on a lab table. You can hold one of each type of medicine, as well as stock up to six plants of any type in a storage bin that carries between labs.
Other than simply picking plants, there isn't much interaction with the environment, as the few objects you can pick up aren't particularly useful. There is a strange creature that can stalk and attack you randomly as you explore the island, but there is no way to damage it, forcing you to run, hide, or escape to terrain it can't cross. Simply running as fast and far as you can is the easiest way to escape it, though there is a light stealth mechanic where you can sense the creature and know when it can see you when you create one of the permanent medicines.
Though it might not be terribly pretty, and there are some long load times and technical hiccups, the sheer scope and level of detail in the environment and the tension throughout the game is nothing short of brilliant, and being a fan of survival games in general, it's great to see one that has unique gameplay. For a project between only two people it is truly impressive and a great experience.
