8/10 fun when playing levels that focus on being solved
0/10 to 2/10 when playing levels that try to be action levels
Overall 6/10, but would recommend because mostly well done.
To explain:
-around 220 levels
-gather keys in them to unlock access to further areas and rarely stars to do the same
-a little story around the game which is nice
-mechanics are based on eating stuff to transform the character, causing changed functionalities and jumping (sticks to top / bottom of walls) with environment and enemies also contributing to the mechanics
-the game autosaves once a level is entered / completed and when you exit the game
Issues:
-switching fullscreen and windowed after some time of playing crashes the game as well as alt-tabbing after some time of playing
The good:
Levels that are fun to solve by focussing on their "figure it out" part instead of stressing the player.
R-button for reloading the level or the most recent checkpoint works fast and well whenever needed.
Nice animations and design.
The bad:
Levels that try to put pressure on the player with tight timings, sudden things appearing, manipulations of other kinds that cause disadvantages on the user's side (camera not showing the other part of the level until almost entering it / vision manipulation / very low time to react), levels that require precise, almost pixel-accurate movement to not die, often causing a frustration loop of being stuck in repetitive, annoying tasks of such kind and often also lacking a save point where it matters. Thankfully such levels are only a few but they are superiorly annoying and drag the game down as the boss fights are of such kind.
Mixed feeling on that one in terms of recommending it. It's mostly good to very good but the bad parts drag it down.
One thing should've been explained: What "secrets" are and how they work because they aren't actually "secrets" like hidden things. It's more that such "?"-marked levels, if solved correctly, enable the player to finish them while still being transformed, allowing to use the transformed bonus outside the level, in the world. This way access to furthr areas can be unlocked.
Room for improvement:
1) The game would be much better if it had a button that, while pressed, would increase game speed by a modificator. The blocks doing that for enemy movement only aren't always there where needed.
2) Sometimes I'd also like a grid displayed to know when falling like a whole screen of distance whether or not I'll hit the spot I want to hit and whenever I'm already touching the next grid, eventually touching a bomb block when jumping then.
3) 3 rows of usable quicksaves would also be nice instead of checkpoint-like saves as those can't be re-used, just swapped and most often aren't there when and where needed the most.
4) An interact button would've been a better choice when there are signs, screens, info blocks and even jars instead of often using that accidently and unintended just by passing by.
5) I bought this game for it's "figure it out" part, not for having a jump'n run game. There are other games more dedicated to this that are actually fun that way. This one is not. It's just a frustration loop with it's bad, action-like levels, where the player is forced to do perfectly x times in a row before being allowed to save and progress or just progress. It's also not okay to force situations that will always 100% kill the player if not having the knowledge of the level and situation in advance.
6) For boss fights: Stop the game while anyone talks so that there's time to read ! Also let the player use the interact button or some other non-accidently pressed button to scroll through the dialogue or skip it.
Hint: There's a gate with a ?-icon in the underground area early on that, if trying to enter asks whether or not it should open the Hoggy1 levels in your browser. Decline. Otherwise hundreds of tabs may flood your browser (don't know why they did it that way instead of a single downloadable file with level selection) and due to the mentioned fullscreen / windowed mode / alt-tab crash issue after some time of playing your game might also crash.

My feelings about this game are mitigated. The first thing is that, if you are looking for a "choose your own aventure" type of game/VN, then this is really a bad one for you, because the game is not making any effort to let you identify yourself as the main character. It doesn't give you the amount of choices and freedom to feel & empathize with your character.
On the other hand... the game do tell an interesting story. The lack of choices and freedom are somewhat justified and understandable once we finish the game and get the "moral of the story". However, it is sad that the story is not more developed, and lots of potential are unexploited...

Well, there have been quite a few well documented issues with this game that persisted for way too long, such as the white screen loading issue. I am happy to report that this has finally been addressed with what I believe was a new programming team if I understand things correctly.
Anyway, I was pleased to finally be able to play this game, and it was actually quite enjoyable, so in this case, it was well worth the wait. It's an interactive novel presented in comic book fashion, with the page frames and such. The artwork is quality. You would expect to see this published by a larger comic company if it was in paper form due to the excellent artwork and coloring. The story was also well written and engaging, and in fact, there seem to be many variations on how this tale can play out, so it carries a choose your own adventure style to it as well. You start out with some very basic RPG options which impact your choices later. There aren't upgrades or anything....whatever you choose is what you stick with, although your choices may end up adjusting some of the stats as part of the story.
There are some issues with the actual script itself, such as poor sentence structure at certain points (much like my writing here in this review, lol). It seems like English may not have been the original language for this script, and the translation was solid with just a few blemishes. Anyway, nothing major, but you will notice it when you read through the text.
The OST was quite nice, and appropriate to the theme of the game as well.
All told, I think I give this game an 8 out of 10 surprisingly, and I would encourage people to read the more recent reviews when making a determination as to whether or not you might purchase this game, as the technical issues that caused a lot of the negative reviews have been solved at this point.

Tattletail is a really thoughtfully put together short-form game, that manages to bring some genuinely new ideas to indie horror games in both the gameplay and the theme.
The game very quickly layers various flavours of disquiet and unease by combining 90's nostalgia (for Christmas and toys), with the distinctive VHS glitches of that decade. It's a very effective starting place that steadily spirals into chaotic horror as you progress.
The gameplay, like the best in the horror genre, forces you to do the very things you don't want to do, in order to survive. Shaking the flashlight gives you light, which you want, but makes noise, which you really don't want. Figuring out the patterns of the danger that you face can sometimes feel like a bit of a trial & error process, but learning how to survive, when to run, when to hide, when to perform a necessary action, is part of the fun and the challenge.
The climactic scene, which I wouldn't dream of spoiling, is a lovely combination of all of what makes the game quite special. Indie horror games can sometimes feel cheap, but this one feels rich. Tattletail is satisfying, like a good short-story is satisfying.

Null Vector is a 80's arcade simulator where you try to move a little cube to different. It's like Asteroids got a makeover and it's so boring. You basically move around in a room shooting stuff. Gameplay-wise, this is a controller game. You move your triangle with the left controller stick and aim-shoot with the right controller stick. Kill all enemies to complete a zone. You have lives and if you get hit an enemy, you lose a life. If you lose all your lives, it's game over. You can collect crystals and trade them in to heal any damage you receive and vice versa. You can also use the crystals to buy ships parts, upgrade ship parts, permanently weld them to the ship, find secret locations, etc.
Conclusion, skip this game. It's like Asteroids in a room with the ability to move and shoot. Sure there are walls and different enemies but the core of the game is moving around and avoiding objects.

There is a very strong core game here and this games hits its 80s arcade theme pretty dead on, but I have a few small niggles with it (as the game is still being finalised these may become irrelevant).
There are a couple of fringe retro "features" that could be improved or trimmed without upsetting the 80s motif IMO.
1. the cryptic/impartial description of the ships' status. I want to know exactly what ship parts I already have, Why not just give this basic information?
2. a description of items would be nice. What do nanobots do, for example? Retro games generally had instruction manuals, as this doesn't it should pick up the shortfall with a little description (granted this is redundant for most items thus far).
3. the points system is obsolete. Noone has cared about points in games for the last 30+ years, if they ever did, and its not clear even how points are gained. The game should be more clear about user performance, giving the user a clearer idea of what they can improve. I know that contradicts the arcade motif, but in my opinion in recreations of older products,  one should ideally extract only whats good, and be mindful of sensible modern improvements. This may make for a marginally less authentic product, but a higher quality one.
Finally, this feels like a game targetting a hardcore audience, but isn't really that difficult. I hadn't even mastered the controls (I was constantly getting my wires crossed between moving the ship and shooting, and mostly only kept to 4 directions instead of 8), and still beat the game quite comfortably, just by upgrading the right way (basically stacking up attacks and slaughtering everything on screen).
Obviously game length is not a current strong point, though with permadeath there is an inherent soft limit.
Finally controller support is a must.

You love the classic 3D platformers like Crash Bandicoot / Spyro.
I can easily see why Psychonauts is a cult classic. It has all the familiar hallmarks of the great action/adventure platformers of the PlayStation era. The levels, in particular, are superb - many as unique and memorable as the other. Where they take place in various denizen's minds, it allows for some exceptional design choices; whether it's uncovering conspiracies in a paranoid individual, hunting down the source of self-doubt in a theatrical production or playing your part in an oversized board game. They are, in terms of their creativity, without peer.
Contrary to how the game might appear, the psychic aspect isn't overly convoluted but graciously fits into the routine powers we're probably used to: Ranged attacks, jump boost, invisibility, shield... and setting stuff on fire. That one's fun. It's playful and creative, but ultimately feels familiar; which I feel works greatly in its favour, especially as I was hesitant at whether the concept would get too far up its own backside.
And don't let the weird-looking characters put you off either. The voice acting and scripts are very well-crafted to create a surprisingly likeable cast, even if a bit stereotypical (c'mon... it's an American Summer Camp. What do you expect?) Raz himself is pleasantly likeable and well-mannered. Not bad when most other 12 year olds are screaming at you over Call of Duty. The FMV's have aged terribly, but the in-game graphics are surprisingly decent for 2005 and scale well to larger screens; a rarity for most ports.
The humour's also cracking, with some excellent laughs and one-liners to be had. The in-game comic strips are, in particular, outstanding; a remarkably clever way of giving backstory with nothing more than a handful of beautifully drawn panels. Some funny, others surprisingly moving. The vast array of collectables to hunt down are addictive and create the wonderfully familiar "how do I get up
?" puzzles most good platformers have tucked away.
The only problem I have, however, is that the game feels like it loses puff about halfway through. After some nice twists and turns with the question of "goodness, I wonder whose minds I have left to explore?" You receive the answer in the form of "oh hey, help these unrelated NPC's you haven't met before get over their problems in order to proceed". Don't get me wrong, the level designs are great but it felt like the story suddenly fell dead from that point.
The last level also blows. The design is (perhaps intentionally) unpleasant, and the difficulty is suddenly cranked up with tight races and "ha! You suck! Go back to the start" checkpoints. Challenging, but frustrating too. That and the crass "oh and how they laughed" ending definitely left a mixed aftertaste - akin to following up an opera with an armpit-fart for its encore.
Disappointing but, at the very least, didn't derail the rest of the enjoyment. The finale aside, this is an utterly superb game to be had. Very well executed and should be a welcome sight to those who loved the 3D platformers of old.

Hey everyone,
First of all, not it's not Overwatch but who cares?
The game is awesome! Stop comparing it to Overwatch!
Overwatch is extremely different.
Let's get to Battleborn.
Ok, first off, Battleborn is a MOBA (in first-person) which is a pretty good concept, if you ask me.
There are 25 available free heroes to unlock and play.
The heroes are sorted into 5 different fractions. (Eldrid, Jennerit, Rouge, UPR and LLC)
You get "gear" through playing story and leveling which you can buy with shards(the currency in Battleborn), which gives you extra attack speed, attack damage, etc.
You can level your heroes which unlocks mutations (modifications for skills)  and skins.
When you start playing Battleborn you got 1 Loadout where you can put up to 3 gear items in.
The multiplayer is extremely intense most of the time, if you play it the right way.
With the right way I mean playing objective, trying to win and not going only for kills.
There are three multiplayer modes at the moment.
1. Capture (Standard domination with 2 maps to play on and 3 flags to capture and to collect 1000 points to win  the game).
2. Incursion (There are 2 robots you need to destroy together with your team and you have to defend you own robots from the enemy team through building sentry towers and other defensive machines)
3. Meltdown (In Incursion you need to push all your minions through the map so they can destroy two machines on also 2 maps)
There are challenges you can do to level up faster, unlock skins, get credits (currency for the marketplace) or unlock gear.
The story mode is alright.
In the story mode you get to know most of the heroes of the game, which I would recommend to play first.
Currently there are 8 missions to play.
You can choose any heroes you want to play in story mode.
So,
I hope you guys now understand that it's not like Overwatch but a really good game, maybe it's not for everyone but it's great for people who want to try something new.
Have a great day,

All the skins (except promo ones), all the heroes and their advanced abilities, all the taunts, and all the missions, are all unlocked during play. It's weird having to unlock the DLC like one had to do back in classic games like Golden Eye, it's also a pleasant change.
It was over fine tuned and meta'd before release, giving it a feel like it is simple, but there is more to it than that. The game can feel too simple because many elements used in the PvP side of the game, feel like they were slapped together in a modular fashion for the PvE story games. Saying that, the story does have unique elements to it that are not in PvP.
At first I wasn't impressed with the game, as the PvP should have a warning that there are items that drop randomly in PvE that you might want to earn and equip before entering PvP. They make a massive difference, and not even the people I met early in thr community brought this up, maybe they could of had more wins and more fun if they actually helped people. The ques outside of the busy period take ages to fill up, and even then you will probably have to que for Incursion (the MOBA mode), when at times the Capture mode or Meltdown modes would make a pleasant change. Some heroes are easy to play and be thrust straight in to PvP, while others need to be farmed up a bit in PvE before they get their advanced Helix unclocks before they become viable. They should not of pushed the whole Borderlands success, I was expecting a very borderlands style game, this is somewhere between a more comical Borderlands and a living breathign Anime, even they main wolf droid thing looks like it was ripped from ghost in the shell. The lack of cell is a pleasant change from Borderlands, making it feel very kiddy, but has swearing and some adult themes spread through it that make you go "wat tha".
Lack of popualtion, and some people doing some killer metas that made it seemingly unnoticed through play testing are it's only faults. I love Gearbox. I love the style, feel, and character of their games, and Battleborn is no exception. The story mode is amazing, fun, challenging and altogether worth 2/3 the price of the game. The multiplayer is unbalanced, and heroes unlocked at higher levels are significantly more difficult to deal with using the starting set of heroes. This is important, because the matchmaking is absolutely terrible. This game WILL match a team of level 12 and under players against level 80 and 90 players, and it will do it frequently. Map design is in my opinion excellent, and it's completely wasted by the fact that a drastically out-levelled team will never see most of it. The helix progression system is cool and adds a nice customizability, but again, many players will get rolled by the ridiculous matchmaking before getting past level 7 in any given match. The multiplayer subtracts $10 from the game from these flaws, making this $60 game worth about $30 in my very generous estimation.
I want to recommend this game, and I want to love this game. If I never play another multiplayer match, I might come to that conclusion, but seeing as it's fully half the game's content, that time is not now. Wait for a 50% off sale, or a massive rebalancing and matchmaking fix from Gearbox. It's not worth the salt.

I didn't really know what to expect from this game as I mainly bought it due to the dearth of 'traditional' sci-fi adventure games, and I was quite positively surprised - in fact I ended up playing it through in a little over two days because I wanted to see how the story would go. :3 Despite having certain weaknesses and the plot fizzling out towards the end (perhaps due to rush?), it's still a solid Myst-like adventure which makes use of its space exploration mystery delightfully.
Pros :
The atmosphere is great practically all the way to the end, and there's a definite feeling of mystery while you can explore everything in peace.
Enough discussions to make the game world not feel abandoned, but not so much that you'd be drowned in characters to meet.
The puzzles aren't terribly difficult and are generally logical, and the game eschews pixel hunt by pointing out anything which can be examined or taken. There also aren't any timed puzzles or dying from trying different things (sans one exception).
Graphics look neat and aren't very taxing as they are mainly static screens with effects, which means you can make do with a fairly lightweight computer.
Cons :
There's no easy or central way to review all the information you get during the game, especially discussions, which makes the plot somewhat hard to keep track of at times since you have to remember everything by yourself unless you want to move around to re-read everything.
The setting starts to fizzle towards the end as the final portions themselves are barely explained and the game mostly concerns itself in fully revealing information you can already infer during the rest of the game, after which you're very swiftly whisked to the end. Thus the last part feels rather disconnected from the rest.
Few puzzles take a good deal of time simply because they are based on trial-and-error and have to be reset every time you fail.

Also, the puzzles seem to come together organically and make rational sense, but none overstays its welcome, which was nice.

Each world was different, sometimes using a different interface or method. Point and clicks can get really repetitive or cyclical, but this game is a great stab at breaking the pattern.

Everything from filling out a map of the island using landmarks to seeking for medicinal herbs and freshwater for survival, Miasmata is a rich, peaceful romp on a game where you're marooned on a deserted island, slowly dying from a debilitating disease you have to make a cure for, and strange horrors await you in the depths of the forests.

Probably one of the best games I've played so far this year.  It's strong in both its exploration and horror elements.
Exploration involves triangulating your position with respect to known landmarks, which is much more realistic than simply revealing the map as you travel.  In Miasmata, you make the map as you triangulate!
The horror elements in the game involve The Creature.  I won't give too much about him away, though, since I don't want to spoil it.

I love to have the freedom to explore in games and that's where Miasmata delivers. It's actually the entire game. You wake up on a beach and have to roam the landscape, searching for botanical ingredients to a plague cure and piecing together the story of a group of researchers who recently occupied the area.
The really great bit to the game is how a handful of minor obstacles shape the experience. Your character starts the game sick, so he's not able to run for long without getting winded, climb steep slopes, or swim more the a few feet in deep water. If you try to push him harder, he'll just get sicker. When he starts to run a fever, he needs medicine or bedrest or it gets slowly worse until he collapses. When you're not as sick, it's still very easy to get lost. There's a map, but you have to update it by triangulating your location from known landmarks. On top of all that, there's a mysterious creature on the island that occasionally harrasses you. All the obstacles are pretty easy to overcome or avoid, but when you make one mistake, it usually snowballs, culminating in a frenzied attempt to get to safety.
The story is very minimal and based mostly on found notes, but it's just enough to add to the mood while letting the experience be your own. Miasmata has a very lonely beauty to it and few limits that seem artificial.  Almost the entire experience is just you stumbling through the woods, but it still manages to be compelling.

Also, the game penalizes you for being awake all day (a neat  thing that few games do), with moments of exhaustion, which can be remedied by (strangely enough) sleeping!
I'd like to see a sequel.

Jacob is a game about social inequality. Your only goal is to climb higher and higher into the sky using random ladder parts while dodging clouds that represent oppression, society, and higher social classes.
No, I'm not kidding.
By the time you sit through the lecture on social classes (The game give you a quick rundown of "gameplay mechanics" in the form of a list. Sources cited, of course.) you'll realize that the only thing that this "game" has accomplished is to highlight the fallacy of the ideas within and the inability of the developer to successfully convey their ideas.
Here is a section of the opening message:

There isn't very much gameplay and could use more instruction, but what it is supposed to mean is that people are born in circumstances with very little privileges (ladder piece), and other people in the world are born with a ton of privileges (the pieces that go straight up).
I don't think this game was meant to be very fun or have good gameplay in any way, but I think it is more of a social experiment to help people to see what it is like to like in third-world countries where they have to make-do with what they have. By playing this game, it shows you that people in third-world countries don't get very high up on the leaderboard, whearas people with more privilege can go farther and higher up on the ladder and leaderboard.
Thats it.
P.S. My name is Jacob too, and the reference is supposed to be Jacob's ladder.

You love the classic 3D platformers like Crash Bandicoot / Spyro.
I can easily see why Psychonauts is a cult classic. It has all the familiar hallmarks of the great action/adventure platformers of the PlayStation era. The levels, in particular, are superb - many as unique and memorable as the other. Where they take place in various denizen's minds, it allows for some exceptional design choices; whether it's uncovering conspiracies in a paranoid individual, hunting down the source of self-doubt in a theatrical production or playing your part in an oversized board game. They are, in terms of their creativity, without peer.
Contrary to how the game might appear, the psychic aspect isn't overly convoluted but graciously fits into the routine powers we're probably used to: Ranged attacks, jump boost, invisibility, shield... and setting stuff on fire. That one's fun. It's playful and creative, but ultimately feels familiar; which I feel works greatly in its favour, especially as I was hesitant at whether the concept would get too far up its own backside.
And don't let the weird-looking characters put you off either. The voice acting and scripts are very well-crafted to create a surprisingly likeable cast, even if a bit stereotypical (c'mon... it's an American Summer Camp. What do you expect?) Raz himself is pleasantly likeable and well-mannered. Not bad when most other 12 year olds are screaming at you over Call of Duty. The FMV's have aged terribly, but the in-game graphics are surprisingly decent for 2005 and scale well to larger screens; a rarity for most ports.
The humour's also cracking, with some excellent laughs and one-liners to be had. The in-game comic strips are, in particular, outstanding; a remarkably clever way of giving backstory with nothing more than a handful of beautifully drawn panels. Some funny, others surprisingly moving. The vast array of collectables to hunt down are addictive and create the wonderfully familiar "how do I get up
?" puzzles most good platformers have tucked away.
The only problem I have, however, is that the game feels like it loses puff about halfway through. After some nice twists and turns with the question of "goodness, I wonder whose minds I have left to explore?" You receive the answer in the form of "oh hey, help these unrelated NPC's you haven't met before get over their problems in order to proceed". Don't get me wrong, the level designs are great but it felt like the story suddenly fell dead from that point.
The last level also blows. The design is (perhaps intentionally) unpleasant, and the difficulty is suddenly cranked up with tight races and "ha! You suck! Go back to the start" checkpoints. Challenging, but frustrating too. That and the crass "oh and how they laughed" ending definitely left a mixed aftertaste - akin to following up an opera with an armpit-fart for its encore.
Disappointing but, at the very least, didn't derail the rest of the enjoyment. The finale aside, this is an utterly superb game to be had. Very well executed and should be a welcome sight to those who loved the 3D platformers of old.

Psychonauts may be 12 years old now at the time of writing this review but it encompasses everything that made me fall in love with computergames as a 7 year old child. It's a cultclassic that received far too little praise from the consumer when it was launched, despite excellent reviews by many gaming journalists.
From the artwork to the voice acting this game is a work of pure love for gaming as a medium and a hobby. It has a wonderful mix of RPG-lite, platforming and third person action gaming elements that make for a thoroughly enjoyable and constantly challenging experience from start to finish as you venture into the minds of the people you meet and try to fix what is broken inside.
Marred only by a somewhat frustrating final level (Oh Meat Circus you know I detest you) and graphics which by today's standards are a tad outdated this game is still withstanding the test of time with the component that really matters: solid gamplay and a sheer sense of fun and surprise waiting around every corner.
As such it represents something that any proper computergame developer should aspire to: Making a wholy original and imaginative game that is already an instant classic upon release.
Peronally speaking, I can't wait for the sequel to be released.
All time classic nostalgia trip, dated but still holds up in my opinion to this day.

If you're playing this game for the story, the cartoon cutscenes are nice and the humor is... alright, I guess.  It felt too breezy and unengaging, but that oculd be chalked up to opinion.
Now, if you want to play this game for the PVP content:
Don't
The matchmaking will throw you into games with people who are 60 levels higher than you, which wouldn't be a problem if not for the biggest, most glaring problem - equipment.  The boosts that equipment give you are insane, and the higher level you are, the better access you have to better equipment.  That in itself would be fine if the game had any proper matchmaking, but it doesn't.  So people with very good equipment are getting matched up against newbies who have very little to work with.  Not only are there these items, but the game locks you into certain playstyles for the characters until you level them up, putting you at another disadvantage against players who have played longer than you.  All in all, this game is severely gimped by items and leveling, which should have no place in a PVP competitive game that this tries to be.

It pains me to give this game a thumbs down, since the basic mechanics of the game are very good. But its flaws just utterly hinder any enjoyment you can get from this game.
Let's start with what the game does well. You have 25 characters which all have their unique twist and don't just feel like a reskin of the same 3-4 characters. You have melee, sniper, support, healer, skirmisher, flying characters, high DPS, defenders, tanks and all kinds of in between characters to this.  Discovering all the different characters is quite a lot of fun, The PvP, when well matched, is one of the most entertaining ones I have seen due to the wide variety of characters. There's also the voice acting. Hey it's Gearbox, you expect great voice acting, you get awesome voice acting. Hearing a german aristocrat say "I declare war on all liberal arts major" is just awesome.
Now for what the game does not so well. The PvE, while pretty fun, is just 8 maps of defend the checkpoint against the same 3-4 enemies. It's miles off from what Borderlands was. I personally don't think this is much of an issue, because it's still quite amusing to kill hordes of enemies and it's a great way to discover how a character play mechanics work. However, some people, understandably, find this off-putting especially for a Gearbox release.
Finally for the major flaws of the game. This is what, sadly, destroys all the work the developers put into character building: the matchmaking. It has 3 major issues.
1. The algorithm is god awful. You get matched in with ANYONE. This means level 8 gets matched with level 76. I know level doesn't directly affect your character, but come on, some who player 300+ hours matched against someone who just bought the game is extremely unfair. I played over 30 hours and more than 80% of the time I'm getting my♥♥♥♥♥kicked by people who have been playing the game since the alpha.
2. The lack of player population. Well this is in part due to the first point. It's also been extremely poorly marketed. I bought the game at launch and after 1 week the waiting time is around 10 minutes during peak play time and 15-30 minutes in off time.
3. If someone disconects duing matchmaking; tough luck you know play 4 v 5. And if you rage quit, well ♥♥♥♥ you got to wait 30 minutes as a godam penalty now. If you want to stop getting analy♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in the game you need to covince 3 out of the 5 players to surrender and let me tell, some people would rather give up their first born than surrender a game where you are 200 points behind.
So when you buy the game, here's what you have to look up to: spend 20 minutes waiting for a game where you will be matched against some one who has already invested 200 hours in this. After a good 10 minutes of getting your faced bashed like there is no tomorrow, you will ask for surrender just to get hit by a wall of "Just learn how to play". You will think, this was only one bad experience so you will try again. After sinking 20-30 hours into this game, you will realize you spent more time waiting to play or respawn then actually playing the game and just give up.
Thing is, the base game is awesome. It's just not ready to be played. I feel like Gearbox just released as fast as possible to try to beat Overwatch. However, by doing so, they actually killed the game. I highly doubt there will be anyone left playing this game after Overwatch comes out.

After having this game back in the heady days of the Xbox 360 I spotted it on sale and thought I would give it another whirl.
I'll start with the bad points:
- Combat becomes quickly repetitive
- Insane difficulty curve in new areas, but strangely coupled with a resurrection mechanic which removes challenge from the game
- Graphics are poor, even for the time period it was produced, gameplay is actually better than the cutscenes!
- You will often see several of the same character model in an area
- Voice acting is terrible, filled with medieval words such as "Mayhap, perchance, T'would" etc, with about 10 different voice actors ("Oblivionitis")
- Main plot is a non-starter for me, I had completely forgotten what it even was after a few hours
- Multiplayer is completely broken, don't even bother
- Many buildings are just *there* as artwork on the landscapes
- Horse combat is lauded up in this game, but riding a horse is about as easy as flying a helicopter when its attempting to lift a merry-go-round with an elephant on one side
Phew.
Okay, onto the good stuff:
- The game world is HUGE
- Many towns/settlements in the game, and they actually feel populated with lots of NPCs milling around
- There are hundreds of side quests to complete, not just simple fetch or kill quests but lots of different types, including assassinations in which you can double cross the original quest giver
- Multiple clans/houses to gain respect with (or gain a bad reputation with)
- Probably thousands of armour/clothing combinations
- The weapon/armour upgrade system makes alot of sense and is easy to use
- Magic system is simple to use yet deep, with power up cards and multiple schools of magic available
- The soundtrack isnt half bad either
- THE VOICE ACTING IS SO BAD ITS HYSTERICALLY FUNNY

The Monster Inside is a short story driven experience.
I honestly cannot suggest this game for the following reasons.
The game is very short. This usually wouldn't be a problem, but the lack of playtime leaves the game and story feeling half baked. The game moves at a break neck pace killing off people who you know nothing about in order to build up to a quickly resolved climax.
The writing is cliched and uninteresting. This game has the staple noir tropes, but doesn't do anything with them that you haven't seen before. It also uses same tired similes you'd see in other uninspired noir games. The Monster Inside seems to take it's inspiration from the tropes and cliches of the genre rather than the films themselves.
Being a big fan of noir this game just reminded me of how great the writing in film noir is and how badly this game misses the mark
The fantasy part of the game is apparent from the beginning, and the twist that comes with it is uninspired and predictable.
The graphics and music are noirish and probably the best parts of the game, but they can't save the story or the writing.
Overall the game tries to create a film noir experience that just really doesn't deliver.

The monster itself isn't very scary...but when you can't defend yourself against it at all and you're so close to finding a new drug, that's scary on its own.
Every new plant I found and researched was like a small achievement deserving a jump for joy, whether it was a simple antibiotic, a temporary boost to my stats, a part of a permanent change to my stats, or one of the key plants needed for the ultimate cure. What's bad about it is that there are alot of slippery slopes...literally. Due to the fact that you're traversing this seemingly empty island by foot with a increasingly degrading disease, a small slip could send you tumbling down a small hill, making your sickness worse and on top of dropping all flora you were currently holding. Though they can be found around the area of the fall, if night is quickly approaching, the creature is on the hunt, or whatever reason, chances are you'll have to trek back and pick more up, you clutz. Also, the view of the island is breathtaking, but the characters graphics, which consist of two arms, are glitchy and underdeveloped. You'll see what i mean when you see it.
Start the game and you quickly realized that you are undeniably SCREWED. Finish the game, and feel like a champion for rising above such an imposing challenge.

I wouldn't advertise this as an addictive puzzle game, as it's certainly not addictive. The game suffers not only because of its gameplay but lack of general presentation. Everything just looks and feels pretty cheap and cramped together.

The central thought behind the game is interesting but the game itself is really quite shallow. I recommend this game to people who love puzzles and to people who enjoy a good story.

(Disclaimer: Typed this on November 20th, 2017, so around three weeks after Update #2.)
"What if the contestant from Smash TV hijacked the ship from Asteroids and crashed it into an retro arcade game that stole some of the excess neon from Farcry Blood Dragon?"
That's pretty much Null Vector in a nutshell. A very much retro-styled twinstick shooter in which your ship and weapon can be upgraded with various stacking power-ups. Like in many retro games, the task you're given is simple: survive six randomly generated floors and, if you get far enough, fight against the boss at the end. Or go down in a blaze of glory.
Even in its relatively barebones and early access state (which, at the moment is currently at the crazy price of nothing!), Null Vector does precisely what the blurb on the Steam store page says it does; give you a rogue-lite experience that, reminiscent of the arcades, lends itself quite nicely to being one of those "pick up and play" experiences that you can play in short bursts without having to tax yourself.
Other than dodging bullets (and the enemies firing them!), there isn't too much focus needed. And, sometimes, that's what you want in a gaming experience. Don't feel up to shaving down your lap times in a sim-racer or countering the opposing team's strategies in an FPS? That's what twinsticks are for. Blast little polygonal enemies into bits: The Game.
Sure, right now, I've got a shade over two hours of accumulated game time but, in those a hundred and twenty-odd minutes, I must've chalked up a dozen attempts and only managed to kill the boss once. If you make it that far, it really doesn't take that long to get to the end; a really condensed and fun experience, if that's what you're into.
One last thing: Is there any better weapon combo than Piercing Ricochet Rockets? :P

A fun little rogue-lite shaping up to be a solid game. There's a lot of potential here, and if you enjoy the genre, this is a nice distraction. Still a bit bare bones, but for a f2p early access game, easily worth the download.

Writing a review because I enjoyed this game a lot. GET IT NOW AND PLAY IT!
Pros:
-can customize your ship to match your playstyle (some upgrades better than others imo)
-difficult but very satisfying to play
-music is bomb + retro arcade style creates such a cool vibe
The game is fairly short but not easy; it's addicting and keeps you coming back. All the combinations for your ship, the music, and the experience of dodging bullets and emerging victorious are exciting! It's fun trying out different equips for your ship imo.. had 4 bots with me at one point and hid behind a wall as they took care of some waves haha.
Some things I noticed that may help you:
-rockets seem to be easier to use than lasers in my experience. You need to be more precise with lasers because they shoot instantaneously and are thin, while rockets have that slight traveling distance and what feels like a bigger hit box.
-do not get multi shot with lasers if you suck at the above^ IT'S WORSE.
-upgrading damage also increases your weapon size (bigger rockets/bigger lasers)
-there seems to be a cap/limit on fire rate at a certain point ? (equipping two slots of fire rate) not sure but there probably is one for all enhancements.
-It's one or the other with lasers/rockets. Be careful on what you permanently keep because you can't change it afterwards.
-lasers + ricochet? not such a good idea unless you're good at aiming at angles. Lasers + ricochet + multi shot is better.
-if using the keyboard to play, you can not only move diagonally (holding down two buttons simultaneously) but can also shoot diagonally (same thing)
My tips on beating the boss:
-rockets
-HIGH fire rate
-damage/pierce
My first failed attempt was with lasers, ricochet, and multi shot (possibly also high-ish fire rate). Other than that epic disco look and the feel of firing a laser, Lasers < Rocket imo. I had some laser and rocket bots with me, which was helpful but unecessary. Shields are always great. Got those for safety so I could take some hits and still win, but if you're good at dodging shots, it's not necessary. The times I won were when I had those listed above and ricochet, which was DEVASTATING. Wiped the boss pretty easily. Ricochet is awesome, but I think what's key are those above.
Oops, long review. TL;DR GET THE GAME!
Have fun and good luck!

Let me tell you a story.
When I was a kid, back in the days when Steve Jobs was still alive, when I only barely understood where babies came from, when I read books about Forestclan and Firestar, when the only video game I actually physically owned was Myst, there were flash games. These were, mostly, the only games that you could share or show to other people. And among your Fancy Pants Man and Run, there was N. One little ninja VS a seemingly impossible number of levels, fueled by gold and a passion for juking rockets.
I played the eff out of it. And then, in time, I came to the edge of my abilities. The limits to my perseverence. Eventually, I stopped, but not before enjoying it half to death. There were a few other times, in later years, when I came back to it on a memory trip, downloaded it off the webpage, and kept a tally of deaths as I strived for 100% completion. But again, I eventually became overwhelmed by life and such.
And now N++ is here. Faster. Simpler. Bigger and, I will say, better. And now, with tunes. It is the essential N experience, and I am so happy it exists. I can feel myself entering that platforming Zen as I work my way though, a rock garden full of mines and golden flowers. And I continue to be reminded:
Simple does not mean Easy. Hard does not mean the opposite of Fun.

With Star Wars Episode VII's recent release, and this game being on sale, it prompted me to write a
review of Knights of the Old Rebublic (KOTOR).
I played KOTOR on a friend's XBOX in 2009-2010, and even by then, it was quite dated. Despite that, this still became one of my favorite games of all time. Don't discount it due to its age; it aged well.
You'll like KOTOR if you like RPGs with dialog choices (Dragon Age). It has dialog and combat rules derived from Dungeons and Dragons (yes, the iconic tabletop game), so your ability to attack/defend/persuade/pick locks/etc is based on your attributes and "dice" rolls. I often hear KOTOR compared to Baldur's Gate in this respect.
KOTOR takes place 4000 years before the movies. Through the choices you make, your character will align more with the light or dark side, affecting choices and story down the line. It is easy to become immersed in this rich world.
If you are a Star Wars fan or an RPG fan, then you owe it to yourself to play this. It's one of the best RPGs of all time, and it truly enriches that galaxy far, far away.

Dragon Commander is an interesting mishmash of several game genres, all mixed together to make an awesome game. It's one part turn-based strategy, one part real-time strategy, and one part role-playing game. Though each section is generally weaker than other games dedicated to that genre, Dragon Commander is greater than the sum of it's parts, and for the most part, it succeeds.
The strategy map is invocative of Risk or Total War, but even simpler. Create units in your war factories, move them to enemy territory, go to the RTS map. You can also build gold mines to make more money (Important), academies to make more science, taverns for mercernary cards, and other buildings. On this map, you can use cards to grant yourself an advantage, be it sabotaging enemy units or territories, or boosting your own. The ones I've found most useful are mercernary cards: free units for one battle. Comes in handy when the AI sneaks up on you, or you need that extra edge. You don't have to fight every battle that comes your way; in fact, you can't. You can only go to the RTS map once a turn. Other battles are resolved by autoresolving, but you can nominate a general to lead your troops for one battle a turn. Science is a bit of a dead weight later on, and it's easy to max out, especially if you stall. It's not too complex, but not overly simple.
That leads into the weakest part of the game: the RTS segment. Now, I'm far from an expert on RTS games, but the segment simply falls short. Micromanaging your units, which is crucial in the late game, is damn near impossible, and is when you're in dragon mode. They all generally look the same, so good luck picking them out of a crowd. As for dragon mode, it's the best part of the segment, though not without it's faults. It's impossible to micromanage your units in the mode, since you can't target them directly. The AI never suffers from this; they're extremely competant at micro, even on the easier settings. The AI isn't too bright, even on the harder modes. They really do just spam the counter of your current army, and later on, figure out spamming Warlocks is the best way to go. The RTS segment, in the end, is just average. Which is a far cry from what I expected.
The game's strength, however, is in it's RPG segment. During your stay on the Raven, you can talk to your generals, councilors, and even get a waifu of your own. All of these characters have their own story, and your decisions in them can help you on the strategy map. Overall, the voice acting is superb, the characterization is enjoyable, and the dialogue is well-written. Though it is written quite strangly sometimes, as if it's meant to be read, not spoken. But I think that adds to the game's charm, I mean, this is fantasy, after all. The addition of a choice of a wife (It's an arranged marriage, so you have to pick one) is a nice novelty, though I wish their stories lasted a bit longer. Would've helped with the characterization. Even in the ending, you can't talk to your wife, which really threw me for a loop. In-story, she's out looking for a place for your castle, but I get the feeling they didn't have enough time to implement scenes for them. They didn't have enough time for an imp princess, after all. But the more important part of this is the throne room, where you decide Yea or Nay to your councilors' proposals. They introduced modern politics into a fantasy game, and did it well. You'll be deciding government health care, democracy, gay marriage, everything. Even the less important issues, like nudism. Each of the five races represent a stance in the political spectrum, from the reactionary undead to the libertine elves. Each case is well-represented, and they pulled it off very well. The only problem is that everything is binary; you either say yes or no. Though it's better than good or evil, I would've liked to seen some third choices. Regardless, I love the RPG segment the most. In fact, if they want to make a spinoff where it's nothing but the RPG segment, improved and expanded, I'd buy it day of release!
In the end, Dragon Commander is a great game, though with it's flaws. I highly recommend it, even to someone skeptical. Buy it, try it, you won't be disappointed.

I wasn't sure what to expect from this game, but I was pleasantly surprised.
The game is a mix of turn based and real time strategy. There's a strategic map with territories to capture and resources to manage, and each turn the player earns resources that they can use to purchase new units and tech. The units can be moved around the strategic map to claim territory, and when a battle breaks out, the player is taken to an RTS map to play out the battle, with their initial position being stronger or weaker depending on a number of factors, like the units they had present on the strategic map, their approval among the population of the region, and how long they've held the territory (if defending). The player is also able to earn (or buy) a selection of 'cards' that can be played on territories or before battles to swing the odds in their favor - things like hiring mercenaries for the duration of the battle, imposing penalties on enemy units, buffing their own units, or causing effects on the strategic map like altered population or extra gold earned.
The single player campaign features 3 chapters, each consisting of a separate strategic map to conquer, but in addition, the player is frequently brought matters of state to address, or approached about the personal affairs of the generals in their army or other crewmembers of The Raven, an airship from the player commands. While I generally find this sort of thing to be rather tedious in similar games, I actually enjoyed it quite a bit in Dragon Commander. The issues are interesting and varied, and have consequences regardless of what side the player takes, so there doesn't feel like there's a clear 'right' and 'wrong' side to take in any issue. The characters have personality and it's quite easy to start caring about them - I'd say the character development is better than most RTS / TBS games.
The real gimmick (from which the game derives its name) is that during the RTS battles, the player is able to transform into a dragon and fly around the battlefield killing things or assisting their own units. Research points can be spent (during the strategic phase) to gain additional abilities for your dragon form, such as massive fireballs, damage reducing shields, or stealth detection. Since, as a dragon, the player can fly very quickly around the map and generally rain death upon most units, it ends up playing a much more active role than the 'commander' unit in most RTS games (Supreme Commander, for instance), and it's quite satisfying to tear around the battlefield dishing out destruction. Otherwise completely unwinnable battles can be won by deploying some of the potent dragon abilities at key points.
Overall, Dragon Commander is a fun game with a few gimmicks to set it apart from otherwise similar titles, and if you're a fan of RTS / TBS games, it's worth picking up.

As a huge fan of Burnout ("he says as he's barely played Point of Impact"), the prospect of a standalone crash mode game had me pretty excited from Danger Zone's trailer. I hate to be the kind of guy to suck up to developers (because as we all know there's a very thin line between having reasonable standards and no standards at all), but the way I see it, Danger Zone is a game that is exactly as advertised. You crash into things, and only crash into things - no racing or career mode in sight.
Now, what if I told you that despite this game not being Burnout 7, this game does a pretty
job of recreating the fun of crash mode from the now-deceased franchise, all with the added benefit of fairly-improved graphics (minus that horrific anti-aliasing option). Not only are the controls mirrored to a T, but the camera angles, OCD-inducing replayablity, and suprisingly-detailed sound design (why those folks at Criterion and Three Fields have always insisted on gear-shifting sounds in their arcade racers I have no idea) make for a pretty genuine Burnout-esque expirience.
That being said, I cannot stress enough that this is
the full Burnout package. Aside from the fact that it's "only" crash mode, there's a very limited selection of cars (so limited, in fact, you have no choice in which car the level gives), the car handling can be iffy as heck, and there's no early-2000s rock or DJ Not-omica to adorn the distant ambience of the menus. Another thing that's evidently a DealBreaker for some people is that the crashes presented in-game aren't "real", but "virtual crash tests". I myself like my racing games with a dash of postmodernism, but for those who'd rather feel like they are "actually" causing millions in insurance and government costs, Danger Zone won't make you feel quite like the gridlock-terrorist that Burnout does.
In closing, I like to think that Danger Zone is the ghost of Criterion Games (no not THAT Ghost) apologizing profusely for the lack of a crash mode in Burnout Paradise. Let's hope it leads to greater things to come from Three Fields Entertainment.

== Story ==
Miasmata's storyline is not very complicated and easy to grasp, while at the same time being deep. With deep I mean there are a lot of notes scattered around the island that can give a greater depth to the story, if you care to read them.
You are a scientist, stricken by plague and on hunt for a cure. You are washed up on a mysterious island, Eden. Eden is home to the plants and fungi that are nevessary ingredients of the sought-after cure. On this island you find yourself alone, with empty camps and a few dead bodies around the island. Or are you really alone?
== Gameplay ==
Miasmata is a free roaming exploration-centered survival-game. It is free roaming and exploration-centered as you are dropped on a mysterious island with no clear objectives. You must find your own way around the island, and exploring it is very much a part of doing so.
It doesn't have a very heavy emphasis on the "survival"-part, as the only things you must do in order to stay alive is drink water, stay out of deep water and not fall off cliffs or slip into the hands of a hungry creature.
Most of the gameplay boils down to five things:
- Trying to triangulate your position and reveal new portions of the (fairly large) map.
- Picking flowers
- Drinking water
- Trying to navigate up or down a steep hill
- Running (as means of travel or trying to avoid a threat)
That being said, it may sound very basic and boring. Well IT IS NOT. I found it very satisfying to explore the map, trying to find a new camp or new objects I can triangulate. Once I found a new camp I got a tickly feeling in my entire body. Finding a new flowers and bringing it back to the base while hoping that it is of some use to you gives you a feeling that other games rarely can give.
== Graphics ==
Miasmata is made by a two-man team and the engine that powers the game is made by just the two of them. With this in mind, Miasmata could be a worse-looking game. Sure, it doesn't look like an AAA-title like Battlefield, and the animations are a bit wonky. But what do you expect?
It does succeed in giving the game a very cozy and atmospheric feeling, which is core in a game like this. Never did I once during the game (except for maybe the first minutes) feel that "This game could really use some better graphics".
== Summary ==
Miasmata may have some weird movement from time to time, the graphics aren't the best, and you would hope that a scientist could carry more than three flowers at the same time.
But what it lacks in those parts, and some other parts aswell, it makes more than well up for in the other parts. Exploration is fun and extremly satisfying, especially when you find a new camp that has important notes or when you find a new fungi that is part of the cure. Triangulating your position in order to reveal parts of the map is hard but rewarding, something that many games are missing.

Battleborn has been one of the few games that has made me swap my daily list of games. All this due to the fact that the characters in the game are one of the most unique characters you'll ever encounter in a MOBA. They all have awesome abilities which vary your gameplay during the PVP and in addition to those - those abilities also have these so-called Helix Upgrades.
The Helix upgrades are acquired through character rank. At a certain rank you unlock a new helix upgrade which alters your abilities in one way or another.
This makes the character you currently love to play even more interesting. Then there's also the epic gear which you unlock by doing challenges (Achievements basically) which also have their ways of altering your abilities.
The gameplay naturally doesn't boil down to only what the characters can do. There are three different pvp modes, each with 2 maps, then there's the campaign which is 9 maps if you include the intro.
The PVP in this game at first appears hectic, chaotic and hard to decipher. But the moment you start to get the hang of it, the moment it all becomes clear (and trust me it will) the pvp can be one of the most intense fights you've had in a game in a long while. The clutch gameplay you do with your teammates as you combine your efforts to push through the enemy lines gives you a feeling of satisfaction that closely resembles other MOBAS. Then there's also the fact that everything you do, every ability you use - you have to aim it, resulting in it being even more satisfactory once you do.
But to speak more of the PVP maps themselves.
In PVP you have three gamemodes, all which have 2 maps each. The gamemodes are
Capture - Capture the point sort of gameplay. Example, Battlefield Conquest but on a smaller scale.
Incursion - The "Moba" Mode so to say. But this work a tad different. In this gamemode there are two sentries that in represents towers in a moba. The only thing is that on a MOBA there are 3 lanes, in incursion there can be less than that. The sentry is a huge robot unit with an overshield which you must destroy before you can damage the sentry itself. The sentry also attacks back, giving you a more difficult time to down it. In order to be able to remove the shield quickly (It has protection against backdooring you see) you must escort your minions to it, who will in turn disable the shield for you. In order to do this you cannot only rely on your small minions, but have to either kill neutral minions (Which are at the outskirts) to "hire" them, or buy a bigger minion. You can buy minions with shards which you collect on the battlefield.
Meltdown - Meltdown is a gamemode in which you must escort your minions into a grinder which the enemy has. THe minions follow a designated pathway which leads into the grinder. After 250 minions the grinders move further up, making it more difficult for the attackers to press on, but easier for the defenders to defend, and once they reach their 250th mark, they get the same odds, giving you a good way for a comeback if neccessary.
These three gamemodes have been an incredible joy for me. Due to fact that every character feels like playing a new game (Due to the skilltree being vast and having a possibility to get upgraded), as well as the gamemodes themselves have been very fun to play.
Then there's the Campaign.
Throughout this review my thought proccess was that I had nothing but positive remarks about this game, but that was until I started thinking about the campaign. The game has two missions which are an incredible joy to play. They feel so well executed, so well made and feel like they're packed with action. These two missions are the Algorithm and the Voids Edge. They both start of with you mowing your way to the boss, with an epic midboss (or it is epic om the Algorithm), followed by an endgame boss which is beautifully presented and really fun to play.
These two set the standard for me for when I wanted to play further on... But oh boy was I ready to get disappointed. After this you got to play the Renegade, which was nothing sort of ... Hordemode upon hordemode. I will say this. I hate. Hordemode.
Then you've got The Archive. Much like the Void's Edge you have to escort a sentry. Only difference is that on the Voids Edge, that sentry could fight, protect and heal itself. This one however cannot! And it moves INCREDIBLY slow, resulting in some moments being nothing but complete silence due to that the sentry has not yet reached the designated scripted area for the enemies to spawn.
Then there's the Sentinel. This is one of the better levels with an awesome level desing, but the bosses and dungeon creeps in it are SO DAMN BORING! You get to this new area and fight the usual thrall, varelsi and stuff. But then you get introduced to a new sort of enemy. A rocky-thing! Awesome! And the boss? ... The same rocky thing except bigger. The final boss, i.e the sentinel? The same rocky thing except even slightly bigger. And the worst part? All of these bosses have the same tactic as the smaller minions. So... yeah, a mission that had the same potential as the Algorithm to be epic, but simply didn't utilize that possibility.
The Experiment. Hordemode the map.
The Saboteur. Hordemode the freaking map.
The Heliophage. It's just... yeah, Hordemode the map. Except slightly changed. You go to this crystal which you have to defend against hordes of enemies.
Honestly, I have to admit that I got a sour taste in my mouth after having to get to play epic levels such as the Algorithm and The Voids edge on the beta. They were one of the bigger benefactors to my choice of pre-purchasing battleborn. I wanted more epic levels like that, but I sure as heck didn't get them.
But, final verdict is still to purchase this game.
The PVP makes up a huge deal for it and makes the game worthwhile. While the campaign is definitely lackluster, and honestly SHOULDN'T BE... GEARBOX... It's still entertaining enough to chop off a few hours in your gametime. The PVP and characters is where this game shines. The pvp is packed with tactics and twich-reflexed gameplay (seeing as everything has to be aimed), while the character progression system makes you feel as if you're properly investing yourself into a character, which of course is boosted by the fact that you're unlocking helixes and lore for the character.

Let me tell you a story.
When I was a kid, back in the days when Steve Jobs was still alive, when I only barely understood where babies came from, when I read books about Forestclan and Firestar, when the only video game I actually physically owned was Myst, there were flash games. These were, mostly, the only games that you could share or show to other people. And among your Fancy Pants Man and Run, there was N. One little ninja VS a seemingly impossible number of levels, fueled by gold and a passion for juking rockets.
I played the eff out of it. And then, in time, I came to the edge of my abilities. The limits to my perseverence. Eventually, I stopped, but not before enjoying it half to death. There were a few other times, in later years, when I came back to it on a memory trip, downloaded it off the webpage, and kept a tally of deaths as I strived for 100% completion. But again, I eventually became overwhelmed by life and such.
And now N++ is here. Faster. Simpler. Bigger and, I will say, better. And now, with tunes. It is the essential N experience, and I am so happy it exists. I can feel myself entering that platforming Zen as I work my way though, a rock garden full of mines and golden flowers. And I continue to be reminded:
Simple does not mean Easy. Hard does not mean the opposite of Fun.

I have never heard of the Divinity series before but after this game, I believe I'm going to try my hand out on more of them. I just bought the Divinity Anthology and I am currently waiting for it to come in the mail. Divinity: Dragon Commander was enjoyable. This is the first time I've ever seen a strategy game like this. It has included all of my faviorte elements of games I enjoyed today, such as Mass Effect, Risk, the Total War series, and put them together into one big pot. The RTS battles were a bit difficult though, even on casual. With the enemy troops constantly zerg rushing, camera controls being awful, and with not the best computer out there, I found the RTS battles extremely difficult, so I avoided them during the campaign part of the game. The controls in RTS will probably take some time getting use to, especially for new players playing RTS games for the first time. Just using the turtorial alone to get a feel of the game isn't enough, you'll need to pratice a bit with skirmish battles., that and the tutorial is very lacking. I wish they included much more useful tips in it.
Playing as a dragon with a jet pack is really fun in the RTS battles, my only complaint is how difficult it is to handle your troops and micro manage as a dragon. Not to mention selecting them is a bit difficult. I died quite a few times when I attempting to get the hang of things. The dragon can be a life savor though if you're inexperience. Overall, I enjoyed the Risk like board in the campaign mode, and I really enjoyed the politics and how it affected your army, gold, and troop morale. I attempted to play the game as a good character and it was difficult having to pick the higher road when in return you had to sacrifice resources. Sometimes, the high road can hit you badly with its outcomes. This is perhaps the first time I've seen a stratagey game with rpg elements, I really enjoyed the different characters and their personalities. It's important to interact with your generals as much as you can, seeing as finishing their stories will improve your chances on the battle field. I didn't realize unil the end of Act II that your actions can affect the personality changes in your generals, and that there is more than one ending for them, and the princessess that you can marry which makes the replay value in this game high, seeing as the choices you make can lead to different outcomes. With the Imperial pack, there is a chart/diagram that can show you the different outcomes for each character, not to mention some behind the scene stuff, concept rp, and a dlc.
I highly recommend this game for others; this is something refreshing in the strategy genre. There were a few things that I had quirks about, like the rewarding for zerg rushing, how insanely powerful your dragon can become when maxed out and control issues, but overall, I believe the good parts of the game out weigh the bad part. I wouldn't give it a ten out of ten, but it's a lovely game to have in your library. Hopefully, the other Divinity games will be too. For certain, I'll have to make a guide and indepth review for this game in the future.

J.U.L.I.A.: Among the Stars is quite an excellent game. I'm actually surprised myself how much I enjoyed the game. Many point and clicks I have played the past few years have been a little flat or seem to drag on. J.U.L.I.A. however, did not.
The Good:
The game has a large variety of puzzles so it's not overly repetative and on top of that, they aren't too easy either. In order to solve everything you're going to have to actually learn the game itself. ----The puzzles often times can only be solved if you've payed attention or following the story.
The game has a night atmosphere and very pleasing on the eyes as well as ambient which is always a plus to me.
There's a lot of depth to the story in superficial details and even some humorous references as well.
The Bad:
A few times the voice acting seemed a bit flat or static, however as two of the protagonists are robots it didn't really bother me and sometimes almost seemed to do more good than harm with the characters.
The Ugly (Indifferent):
There were a few parts I predicted, but overall you couldn't guess what was going to come next and each new event peaked my interest quite a bit. Even the parts I could guess, the journey to that point was quite interesting.
Some animations or parts seemed to take a little longer than necessary, but this is really a minor detail as it doesn't take away from the gameplay or story.
Overall: The game to me is quite comparable to some of the Myst series. If you enjoy Myst or a good puzzle point & click with some interesting sci-fi/unique worlds  I'd say try picking up this game.  $20 might be a bit much for some people, but I don't think it's that bad, and if you can get it on sale and enjoy point and click puzzles (That aren't too easy or dragging) I'd get it.

This is a bad game, don't buy it.
Your character controls like a drunk, stumbling all over the place and incapable of ascending a gentle slope at faster than crawling pace.  The game crashes when leaving the ESC menu.  There are a ton of cases where the wrong models are used during plant analysis.  The achievements are glitched to hell.
You are in more danger of dying from tumbling down perfectly climbable inclines than you are of getting killed by the 'creature'.  Speaking of the creature, I met it once after playing for a couple hours.  You get a warning that it's nearby via a loud heartbeat.  There's no indication of what direction it's in, and if you see it out of cover it will see you.  However it doesn't really move very fast so if you just run away you're fine.  Despite what the store page says, it doesn't really track you- it just randomly spawns near you.  So, just run in practically any direction and you're fine until it randomly spawns near you again.  Pointless.  Oh and if it hits you, you die instantly.
The landmark system sounds clever except for the fact that trees and inclines seem to be placed specifically so that you can't see landmarks most of the time.  Also there seem to be no sanity checks involved.  You can walk like 10 feet for a second triangulation to verify where distant landmarks are, and can use landmarks that are in line with you to verify your own position.  There's no minimum angle between landmarks or minimum distance between triangulations.
Health is represented solely by how sick you are.  So, falling down a cliff gives you a fever, rather than bruises.  There's food on the island but you can't eat any of it because it's all half-rotten fruit.  You can supposedly drink from any non-saltwater source, but I already found a river that I couldn't drink from.
This game is a MESS.

Cashing in on people's memory of the Burnout games.
After about 15 minutes, you have pretty much seen all the game has, and it's not fun unless your main purpose is to perfect a level and beat other player's scores.  There is no fun in crashing, and it does not feel like a sandbox of explosions.
To me this feels nothing like the Crash levels in Burnout.   The levels make me feel claustrophobic.  They are in large concrete rooms with a low ceiling.  I don't feel free to play around and crash things, I feel hemmed in and restricted.  The actual gameplay is the same.  There are "Score Multiplier" powerups you MUST pick up if you even want to get to the next level, and you do.  You want to get to the next level so you do not have to play the level you are on.  The cars seem to only have 2 states, Driving straight, or blowing up, and contrary to the screenshots, the explosions are not great.
There are trucks with a lot of propane tanks on them.  You would think that the propane tanks explode.  They are Red, they are Propane tank shaped, and this is a video game.  They don’t...  They just fly around the same way a crate would.
There may be explosion physics, but almost no actual car/driving physics.  Some levels you have to drive in-between cars going the same direction as you, a light tap may divert them a little, but not how cars would react, and anything more than a light tap and they explode.  There is almost no deformation of cars at all.
The camera is poor.  It is hard to see any cool explosions because it always stays rather close in on the car.
tldr: Even for the price, this is forgettable and makes me regret spending the money(And I spend quite a lot of money on steam).

An accessible free-to-play arcade title that leaves much to be had but is nonetheless fun at its core.
For the sake of the dreaded game comparisons, if you combine the aesthetics of the retro-arcade-favorite Tempest with a Geometry Wars that’s taken some time off its steroids, you get Null Vector.
Late 80’s-inspired visuals and rock synth create the atmospheric vibe of a day at the arcade clad with tucked-in shirts, rimmed glasses and sweaty determination. In Null Vector, you traverse procedurally generated, grid-layered rooms fighting off opposing geometries.
While gliding across these random battles, the triangular protagonist can apply various, yet limited upgrades to its ship – often coming across wielding stations that permanently attach these improvements, allocating space for newer items.
At face value, the game’s fast-paced, reactive environment makes for a re-playable title; dying just short of completing a floor when you’ve completely upgraded your ship fuels motivation to beat the game in one fell swoop.
However, this is also part of a larger problem: the game is too damn short now. Other than its difficulty, there’s a lacking incentive to replay the game once you’ve beaten it.
Though, this shortcoming shouldn’t be rapped on too much; what is clearly a F2P title has much room to grow and expand its level. Overall, I’d give it a go for the sake of lost nostalgia for the stellar 80’s atmosphere.

N is a very tight, movement based platformer game. It offers a huge variety of levels on very different skill levels, varying from a casual experience to hardcore grinds to finish one.
First thing I've noticed after launching the game were modes, you have a standard singleplayer platformer experience, but that's not it. There's also a CO-OP mode and race mode. The co-op mode is self explanatory, you plug another controller in, and play along a friend, the level design in those is pretty good, you often need both players to survive, and even if not they're really helpful to have around. The race mode is a bit weird, and I didn't have the chance to get into it fully at least yet, so there's not much I can say about it, but there's plenty of levels in it too.
The main part though, is definitely the singleplayer experience, where you have 3 tabs full of levels as of now (Ultimate Edition) and also intro levels tab. There are a lot of levels starting At A and ending on E all having 20 episodes consisting of 5 stages each. Then after you finish all those you get to move along to X row which is basically an expert challenge. I personally dislike the idea behind the episodes, as you have to beat all 5 during one playthrough to get the progress done, because when you beat one the level progress doesn't save, and you have to start an episode over, but that's a minor flaw.
The game is also movement based. It takes a while to get used to the "slide-y" movement, but it's actually very tight, and feels good, not being floppy whatsoever. There are coins scattered throughout all the levels, and the ninja collects them to get some more time for finishing the episode, but those can often be skipped without paying much attention to, because there's usually plenty of time. You can also try to collect them all, as it's often fun to go through an alternate route to gather some, and they provide a pretty tough additional challenge, though I suggest going for them after beating an episode, as you can only access a particular level after beating said episode.
The graphics and music fit together very well. The minimalistic artstyle goes along greatly with this soundtrack. The electronic beats make a great "background noise". There are also plenty of themes to play around with, as you unlock them by beating episodes. Only thing I wish was added would be a theme editor, as I don't think it'd be hard to implement and some of the themes are just straight up bad(For example light blue menu with lighter blue text).
To sum it up, there are some things I have issues with, such as boring waiting game levels with tough parts near the end that basically test the limits of your patience, and the episodic nature of the world hub which doesn't allow for easy quitting, but overall, the game is very good, the movement feels amazing, the physics feel very good once you get used to them and the soundtrack is great.
