Battleborn is a pretty good game overall. Really enjoyable gameplay, a lot of characters to play; most of them being quite fun to play too, and a fairly enjoyable story mode. Interesting Lore system, allowing you to unlock an item unique to the character, as well as a title, once all of them have been completed. It also reminds me of Borderlands a lot, thank you Gearbox.
I personally enjoy the gamemode Incursion the most, as I feel it is a lot more team-based, whereas Meltdown basically just requires you to kill the enemy minions. Someone like benedict can just sit at the back, kill the minions, and try to pick off a few kills. I haven't played too much of capture, but it seems like it could be okay.
I played this in the open beta, and the two maps that were available then, (Overgrowth for Incursion and Paradise for Meltdown), are essentially the two only enjoyable maps, and are the only two that are somewhat well optimised.
A few problems I have with Incursion is that a Marquis can easily snipe the sentry's shield and take it down while completely out of harms way. This has been an issue for a long time and should've been resolved by now. As well as this, he can easily headglitch on Overgrowth to the point where you can't even see any of him, but he can get easy headshots on you.
Another issue I have with the game in general. but more so with Overgrowth as I play this the most, is the collision. Both the environmental collision and the mob/player collision is awful. I'll find myself turning to run away from an enemy, only to have the two thrall mercenaries we just recruited to be blocking the entire pathway.
Also, there's Galilea. What were you thinking when you designed this character? Invulnerability, a shield that blocks a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of damage, and massive damage reduction as well as lifesteal. I can imagine this on a character that is meant to simply sponge attacks and let their team go in, but she does so much damage that she can literally 1v5 late game given they know what they are doing. Rath is also quite dumb, he just knocks you up, ults, and you can't do anything.
Also, your matchmaking sucks. I often find myself put on a team with level 5-10s against level 80s. Good job.
Despite all this complaining, I do really enjoy this game, and plan on playing it further. It is usually a really enjoyable experience, especially when with friends. This game needs a lot more polishing done to it, as a lot of things feel very half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥or incomplete, but I would by no means call it a bad game.

I would wait. Two to six months from now, this game will either be dead from lack of players and/or not being Overwatch, or barely surviving because Gearbox came to their senses and made it free to play. Either way, you're better off waiting. It's not a bad game, but it's not a particularly good game either. The character designs range from interesting to idiotic, but all of them are utterly uninspired in terms of functionality, the combat is flat and two dimensional compared to any game with a decent map designer, and it needs *at least* four times as many multiplayer maps as it has currently to even reach the minimum variety requirements of a shooter. Are you the parent of someone who worked on Battleborn? If the answer is no, then I promise you, there is nothing here you need to rush to see.
The Hero Shooter/MOBA Shooter is going to be a wildly oversaturated genre by the end of 2016, and Battleborn is not going to be one of the winners of the inevitable battle royale that will ensue. Not with a $60 price tag, and not in anything like its current state.
*** If you find this review short, or less than comprehensive, it's because of my continuing efforts to refine game reviews for the modern era. As gamers, we need to move forward. Imagine if every time a movie critic reviewed a romantic comedy, they started by explaining what a romantic comedy was in the first place. It would be both moronic and excruciating. Yet, that's exactly how most video game reviews are still written.
My goal is to only tell you the things you might not know already, or to offer a perspective you might not have considered. In a world saturated with screenshots and let's play videos you don't need me, or anyone else, to explain Battleborn (or any game) from the ground up. No more than you need someone to explain what a science fiction movie is before you watch Star Wars.

At the time of this review, I've put in a little over 8 hours into the game and have acquired 22/31 STEAM achievements.
You play as Rachel Manners, an astrobiologist that has been awoken from cryosleep to save the probe ship.  Upon your salvaging of the ship, you learn of the terrible fate that some of your crew met on a planet in the solar system you are orbiting.  Through travel to other planets and moons, upgrading the mobile robot that you send to these worlds, and analyzing data/evidence, you are to use reasoning to draw conclusions and understand the order of events as they happened and to work with a discovered sentient race.
I have to say that I thoroughly enjoyed this game.  It's not very often that I'm ensnared to the point of trying to get a game finished as quickly as possible so that I can see a story progress.  The story is gratifying and progresses quite nicely.
For the most part, this game is a 'Point-and-click' discovery/puzzle' type.  You are on various worlds that aren't entirely habitable by the human animal, so the probe Mobot is sent in your stead.  There is plenty of material present in each of the worlds and the help screens for the puzzles are informative and do not lend to giving away the answer.
That being said, if you want to finish the game for the sake of finishing it, I am sure there are guides that enable you to breeze through the puzzles.  However, I found the puzzles refreshing and interesting.  The situational placement of them throughout the game is done well and parallels real life puzzles that you may face if you were that character.
The visuals are wonderful with segments of cutscenes throughout.  The different worlds are stunning and I appluad those designers.
I find that this game is highly underrated and flies under the radar more than it should.  Absolutely stunning.  I'll be playing through again so as to find other things I may have missed.

This game is very engaging, even though the 'gameplay' is pretty barebones. The story is deeply layered - every once in a while you come across a plot point that sheds everything you've seen in a new light. It quickly becomes much more than a simple murder mystery. Some of it is cliche, sure, but the sense of voyeurism and the rollercoaster ride of trust and empathy that the story puts you through is well worth the trip.
Bring a notepad and a pencil, because you'll need to take a ton of notes to piece this game together - especially if you're going for 100% completion! Investigating seemingly unimportant things can lead you down some wild rabbit holes. You'll look back on the experience as a masterpiece in storytelling and editing.

After a few hours I got a solid sense of this womans life and the events that have taken place, but I know I can't trust her. Now I need to piece it all together and figure out where the lies are. I have no idea how this will end (as in, can I get a victory screen? can I solve this case and "win"?) but at some point I'm going to make a decision. I'm going to be the detective and the judge.
The tale is deep and very well written. Within the short clips of video offered (and there must be at least a hundred of them) I get a bunch of leads to chase and each one gives me more of the story, more of her personality, and still leaves me with empty spaces that I want to fill. It gets darker as I go, the words of the dialogue so well chosen that following the leads slowly unravels the story with excellent pacing. It's hard to describe how impressive this is as interactive fiction.

I'm usually intrigued but very disappointed with games that proclaim strong story via unconventional means. I hated
and didn't much care for
. On the other hand, I adored
. For me, the story had better be damn good (which DE and TVoEC were not) and the game mechanics should either be fluid (not true in DE) or worth the trouble (not true in TVoEC).
is fluid and simple, but built around an intriguing premise: Figure out what the heck is going on, based on the interviews with this woman after her husband goes missing. It's confusing and sometimes frustrating, but ultimately worth it. The story is thoughtful and satisfying, and the gameplay is very very basic.
This last part is very important. As Brian Upton explained on a recent episode of the podcast
, figuring out a complicated game is a kind of story decoding in itself. As a result, piecing together a complicated story at the same time is aggravating, because "it's hard to play two games at once".
does a superb job of dodging this trap by making the gameplay as simple as possible. The focus is entirely on the story, as it should be, and the game is much better for it.
My one complaint is the unsatisfying finish. I can't explain without giving spoilers, but suffice it to say that I wanted something a little more concrete and/or rewarding when I got done. (I felt the same way when I finished
.)
Maybe this is just an unfair expectation from standard video game structures, but as Brent Knowles (lead designer for
) said: "When I invest a hundred hours into a game, I need to walk away feeling like a hero." (The corollary for me is that when I invest three hours into a game, I need to walk away feeling satisfied.)
Still, I recommend this strongly, and proclaim it to be a rare example of unusual game mechanics combined with intriguing story done right.

Miasmata is a First-Person Survival Game with a strong focus on discovery and exploration.
You are a criminal (forgot the name, sorry about that), who gets banished on an island. You also are sick and have to find different plants and fungi to create a cure and then escape the island. But you are not alone. A creature follows you across the island and tries to kill you. Will you survive to find a cure ?
Miasmata has the same combat mechanics as popular horror-games like Amnesia and Outlast. There are none. The only thing you can do during creature encounters is run and hide, which creates a tension and you sometimes almost go mental, because the creature is pretty deadly and hard to escape from. But honestly, I am a bit disappointed by the creatures AI and the spawning points. Sometimes you run away from the beast, just to encounter it a couple hundred meters further again, this time infront of you. Or one time it spawned on a small island at the beach and was unable to swim, so it could just look at it without any danger. I would not call such cases bugs, but they brake the illusion of a superior enemy and quickly show the mechanics behind it.
Still, the fact, that creature encounters are quite rare at times and your hearth starts to beat, when the creature is near, builds tention and you got a good chance to escape.
But 98 % there is gameplay without fleeing from the creature. In this time you have to find plants with which you can create different kinds of medicines. With those, you can cure injuries (which can kill you after some time), can boost your stamina, strench, perception and ultimately cure your illness, which makes you a pretty weak human being. Without any boosts of medicine, your swimming and sprintingrange are very limited and noticing your worst enemy is up to you. But collecting and finding plants to create medicine is necessary and ultimately the goal of the game.
Finding very specific plants for specific cures can be very difficulte. The main problem besides surviving is orientation. You have to draw your own map through triangulation. You do this with markpoint, represented through statues, buildings, ruins, and pillars, which you find scattered over the map. Whenever you can see two such points, you draw your surroundings. This can be pretty difficulte and forgetting to draw your map can get you lost pretty quickly. The fact, that you do not see your position on the map without boosting your perception, makes it even more difficulte.
From time to time, you find mappieces in huts, which sometimes show you the location on your map, sometimes just hint at it. Finding specific plants can be really annoying, but also rewarding, when you finally get your piece of the cure or another boost to run faster or longer.
Graphicaly, the game is mediocre at best, aiming at a realistic graphic style. But honestly, it never bothered me, the landscape looks nice, little bunnies run away from you, butterflies and birds fly around, you hear the wind blowing. Everything is very athmospheric and the graphics fit. There are games out there with way better graphics, but look also way ugglier.
Verdict: Miasmata is a very athmospheric survival game. It builds a feeling of loneliness, in a cheerfull world, while being hunted by a fearsome creature. The survival aspects could be done better and finding plants can be ridiculous and getting lost is daily business. But despite these flaws, Miasmata is a solid game, which deserves your playtime.
It's really well done for what it is. More people should buy it!

If you love filling in blank spaces on a map, scavenger-hunting map icons, humping the spacebar to climb hills... this is your game.
It won't dazzle you with a lot of different mechanics, but what it does provide is unique. As far as I (suburban dude) can tell, it's an eye-opening wilderness hiking simulator, where you experientially learn how it's a seriously bad idea to set off on a trip without lots of daylight, a clear goal, a good map, and plenty of water.
To be clear: the game doesn't lecture you about survival and navigation. Instead you get certain reflexes drilled into you after you stay out too late, run out of daylight, get lost and dehydrated, fall down a hill, stumble into a lake and drown. Since you can only save your game at certain locations, well, drowning after a day-long expedition is bad.
The orienteering and cartography mechanics are just plain neat (and well-described elsewhere). The game provides a layer of goals and some mysterious opposition to deal with, but those aspects just add context to the exploration. It's nicely atmospheric and very zen at times. And occasionally scary.
Keep in mind that this is an "indie game by 2 guys", but more often than not it's a better-designed package than you might expect from that. It's still a niche-audience thing, but outstanding if you're in that audience.

An accessible free-to-play arcade title that leaves much to be had but is nonetheless fun at its core.
For the sake of the dreaded game comparisons, if you combine the aesthetics of the retro-arcade-favorite Tempest with a Geometry Wars that’s taken some time off its steroids, you get Null Vector.
Late 80’s-inspired visuals and rock synth create the atmospheric vibe of a day at the arcade clad with tucked-in shirts, rimmed glasses and sweaty determination. In Null Vector, you traverse procedurally generated, grid-layered rooms fighting off opposing geometries.
While gliding across these random battles, the triangular protagonist can apply various, yet limited upgrades to its ship – often coming across wielding stations that permanently attach these improvements, allocating space for newer items.
At face value, the game’s fast-paced, reactive environment makes for a re-playable title; dying just short of completing a floor when you’ve completely upgraded your ship fuels motivation to beat the game in one fell swoop.
However, this is also part of a larger problem: the game is too damn short now. Other than its difficulty, there’s a lacking incentive to replay the game once you’ve beaten it.
Though, this shortcoming shouldn’t be rapped on too much; what is clearly a F2P title has much room to grow and expand its level. Overall, I’d give it a go for the sake of lost nostalgia for the stellar 80’s atmosphere.

Null Vector is a callback to older, simpler times in Video Games. With a visual style reminiscent of Tron and gameplay similar to Asteroids, it definitely succeeds. When you first enter Null Vector's world, you will be welcomed with an arcade machine, reminding you that it's all a game. But when you begin playing, you get absorbed by your desire to succeed.
The mechanics of Null Vector are finely tuned to allow tight control over the player-character, leaving each consecutive defeat at the fault of the player alone. But unlike other rogue-likes, you can return to your point of death quickly as you get better with each run. Eventually you find yourself cruising through rooms with little-to-no damage each time, and then become faced with an even bigger challenge.
The boss really ties everything together. The first time you encounter it, you will likely die. The second time, you will die again. This addendum forces you to think about every hit you take and every item you grab. Are you being efficient enough? Will you have enough potential to defeat the boss? How much room for error can you have? Without the boss, this element would be completely missed.

I would wait. Two to six months from now, this game will either be dead from lack of players and/or not being Overwatch, or barely surviving because Gearbox came to their senses and made it free to play. Either way, you're better off waiting. It's not a bad game, but it's not a particularly good game either. The character designs range from interesting to idiotic, but all of them are utterly uninspired in terms of functionality, the combat is flat and two dimensional compared to any game with a decent map designer, and it needs *at least* four times as many multiplayer maps as it has currently to even reach the minimum variety requirements of a shooter. Are you the parent of someone who worked on Battleborn? If the answer is no, then I promise you, there is nothing here you need to rush to see.
The Hero Shooter/MOBA Shooter is going to be a wildly oversaturated genre by the end of 2016, and Battleborn is not going to be one of the winners of the inevitable battle royale that will ensue. Not with a $60 price tag, and not in anything like its current state.
*** If you find this review short, or less than comprehensive, it's because of my continuing efforts to refine game reviews for the modern era. As gamers, we need to move forward. Imagine if every time a movie critic reviewed a romantic comedy, they started by explaining what a romantic comedy was in the first place. It would be both moronic and excruciating. Yet, that's exactly how most video game reviews are still written.
My goal is to only tell you the things you might not know already, or to offer a perspective you might not have considered. In a world saturated with screenshots and let's play videos you don't need me, or anyone else, to explain Battleborn (or any game) from the ground up. No more than you need someone to explain what a science fiction movie is before you watch Star Wars.

This is a situation where I really wish there was a neutral button. I personally adore the game. I find the characters charming and love working through their lore and running missions and the pvp to try and uncover new bits of dialog and story. They're all so entertaining for me and unique that I've only found roughly a handful I can't get the hang of out of the 25 released.
However the pvp matchmaking is horrendous. I could get a match in at most five minutes the first few days after launch, but now I can sit in a queue for a solid half an hour playing a different game on my second monitor and finally give up. That's terrible for a game just released, with the devs insisting on always on play and the fact that versus bots does not count toward any of the unlocks that are supposed to keep players interested and invested.
The game launched with 25 characters, eight story missions that can be played out of order, but still tell a cohesive narrative, three separate pvp maps and hundreds of lines of dialog and unlockables if you're into the characters. Plus they intend to give away the next five characters and dlc a handful of new misssions, taunts and costume variations.
Despite all that I still don't think it justifies the $60.00 flat base cost. The matchmaking it truly atrocious, the always online is frustrating and causes a ton of lag and I really do feel like the game needs to offer that fine balance between running a story mission and then queuing for a match or two and with the matchmaking situation as it currently stands I find myself getting more frustrated and simply turning off the game.
That's unacceptable in a title that released roughly two weeks ago.
I've definitely gotten my money's worth based solely on playtime, of which I'd say about 100 hours or so were actually playing and 30 hours of waiting in queues. But for me personally those 30 wasted hours have cropped up in the last few days and that's a disturbing trend that needs to be reversed.
Seriously just let the versus bot matches count for lore/challenge unlocks. The vast majority of things gotten are titles, costume color variants and taunts. The only thing that's really 'game changing' would be once you've mastered a character you get a personalized piece of equipment with two generic abilities and one specifically tailored toward that character. Really even getting to unlock the characters via bot matches isn't an advantage or disadvantage. I'm a mediocre pvp'er at best and outside of taking twice as many actual hours versus people with co-ordination and a sense of direction, I unlocked everyone through leveling up my command level.
As of the time of writing this review I've only now finished my first run of all the base game missions. I've still got several characters that need to be unlocked under challenges by actually completing various objectives, even though I've had everyone unlocked for days now purely from simply enjoying the hell out of the game.
Seriously though, they need to fix the matchmaking and/or offer alternatives. The game isn't nearly as much fun when you can't get into the multiplayer maps and you don't want to run one of the very few, fairly challenging on the lowest difficulty (I'm a filthy casual though) that can take between 30 and 90 minutes to complete solo versus a pvp map that has a 30 minute timer.
If they can get some quality of life fixes in then I do recommend the game if you like that Borderlands style humor. The universe they've created is IMHO entertaining, colorful and just a ton of fun and considering how many generic brown shooters have been flooding the market for years, that alone is such a wonderful change. If they can't get those quality of life changes in before the playerbase gives up on them then I'd wait for a giant sale and group buy the game and turn it into a party challenge or something.
Regardless I don't think they offered enough stability and content for a base $60 price tag. With the matchmaking challenges the game feels like it's already showing sagging seams. Everything needs to work for the full smorgasboard effect, if one side is broken, it's hard to stay invested or interested because grinding what you can manage to solo starts to feel like a chore. If they'd priced it at $40.00 and the $20.00 season pass I think that would have been more than passable provided everything was working correctly.
Since there is no middle road I'm giving the game a tentative thumbs up simply because I truly love the universe and characters, but I really hope the devs can pull it together. I'd like to see more content and characters.

I do love this game, while it can be infuriating at times, if you can contest against decent skill level enemies and know when to use the surrender button when the game is pear-shaped. I tend to do decent in most pvp games and I loved the campaign. Even though the campaign can be walking sim, there's always challenging modes, and the longest walking sim I had was in The Archives when I lost track of the objective and had to find my way to it.
With the three different types of progression in this game it's very satisfying to try and get all three. Leveling the characters actually do something in and out of game, allowing for well-balanced trees suited to how a person plays versus what the best choice is. Sometimes it's quick to decide which side of the tree you pick for the level, and other times you need to decide "Okay, so I'm Mike, Crowd control, or higher DPS." and it might change depending on where you are in the match, what match you're in, and how the teams are stacked together.
If you're on the pacific coast, you'll find that prime time matches you with a group who's determined to wreck your day every 1 in 6 ish games. In my opinion, far too common, but when the average opinion of MOBA is to be the biggest♥♥♥♥♥♥and victory is the only thing that matters I feel it's a lot better than, say, LoL without matchmaking.
From my 26.6 hours, there are two people I've seen in nearly every game, and a couple that are commonly switched around. This would be fine, but one of the two gets really lopsided as they level. In a group (I've beaten a couple that were just in for the fun) the lopsided hero tends to get favored for player kills, sometimes even leaving one at low health for their lopsided just to get the kill risking the hero getting away. The best thing to do when that happens is RUN! Don't stick around, your health is low Teleport to base using B or whatever you have it bound to.
The campaign is short, but makes up for it by offering three to four different types of dialogue. Sometimes even adding character specific dialogue on top of it. The downside is that there are three different types of mission, kill guy, cap and defend point until told to move, and escort. These aren't at all tedious unless you're trying for a challenge run (and I don't mean difficulty increases) they offer various types of boosts to try and distract you from what's going on by offering challenges. The challenges tend to be given when it's about to get hectic as a means of trying to alter the combat by making you focus down specific enemies, going out of your way to collect things, or by making you make♥♥♥♥♥♥explode! The bosses all try their best to have unique stages, and effects. Though you may fight a couple of bosses multiple times due to story reasons.
My only gripe is the community, they're either ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, or non-responsive for the most part. I've only had one group that's actively taken the time to communicate with me. I can't tell if this is because the tutorials don't go out of their way to tell you to talk, or the people playing don't give enough ♥♥♥♥♥. If you like the complex mind games that go with MOBAs and hard characters(because of skills rather than stats) then this game will allow you to get about an hour for $3. I would recommend it to some of my friends who enjoy this type of game, but for anyone who is looking for a game that will be easy for newcomers to just hop in and enjoy, this isn't it.

Even on sale this was a waste of money.
DC is obivously geared toward the impacts (political/strategic) of your decisions.  Decisions that are most readily made through dialogue.  The dialogue is smooth and the voice acting is very well done, but the game seems to skimp on the unavoidable RTS function in order to emphasize the 'consequence of decision' mechanisms.  This makes the combat feel very casual and inconsequential.
Maybe this sounds like the game for you? Well..
For better or for worse, I'm a gamer that thrives on story development, seeing the consequences of my decisions, affecting the game world, and thereby tailoring my experience as I desire.  So.. what am I complaining about?  I should love DC!  ..what I don't care for is a scripted experience that offers the illusion of choice.. Particularly when that type of functionality is the obvious focus of the title.  Unfortunately, this is about all that Dragon Commander offers.
The problems that arise which require the use of the dialogue functions, the political issues offered up for consideration, and most importantly, the black and white decisions you are forced to choose between, (let me emphasize "forced,"  as not making a decision is akin to selecting a predetermined default) all serve a political agenda.  This game is a kind of "righting the wrongs" of the world, setting the great (perceived) injustices of our time straight and then scolding/punishing the player who would dare to take an opposing point of view.. with dragons..
In short;  if you're a large government minded, radical feminist, who moonlights as an LGBT advocate.  DC is for you.
The rest of us are better off steering clear, there's just not much else going on here.

While I love the concept of Dragon Commander, the game is obviously rushed and the writing is the most cliche thing I've ever read.
The game play is passable. A nice mashup of total war and dawn of war, but after that? It all goes down hill.
The characters are almost universally 2 dimensional. Once you've spoken to them once or twice, you know immediately how they'll react to any given situation without even having to talk to them. They're purly defined by their sterotypes. The bigotted lizard is always bigotted, the sexist ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ general is always a sexist ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, the icequeen manhating general is always an icequeen manhater and that's the only thing that ♥♥♥♥ing defines her decisions. It's infuriating. The two most believable characters from the 1st chapter are the ♥♥♥♥♥♥vixen' general, and the Imp Ambassador. While both are probably meant to come off as 'lol random!' they actually come off as believable because they have reasons for their beliefs and decisions that are above and beyond simple sterotypes. I mean, come on. A character has to be VERY badly written when the mad scientist character and the token wildcat female party member are less formulaic than said character is.
Also the stuff in anachronystic. A lot of the political decisions make NO sense in context. There's a world war going on. While some of these decisions would make sense when you own more than one country, or even more than one province, when you're just trying to get a foot hold, making a call on gay marriage, for example, is simply not what people are going to be concerned with, at least not on the highest levels of government. Your ambassadors are going to be more worried about the impacts of war on their populations, refugee populations, criminal♥♥♥♥♥♥ Getting the FOUNDATION of your new empire running would take precedence. Establishing public order, getting laws established, all of those things.
Finally, the game shows some obviously lazy programming, art, and UI managment. THe game resets the difficulty to normal between games rather than switching it, so you need to check on the difficulty every time you reopen Dragon Commander. The Undead are literally skeleton textures pasted onto humanoid body skeltons and polygons, so that you have bones and jaws moving as if they were made of flesh and muscle, not solid calcified bone.
I -really- wanted to like Divinity: Dragon Commander. It was SUCH a cool concept. But it failed so badly in execution on the small things, such as writing and art, that I'm having a hard time suspending my disbelief. Every time the dwarf acts like a neo-con ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ over incredibly stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥during a time of ♥♥♥♥ing war, every time the undead is an intollerant ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, every time the elf is a hippie even when it would probably cost the lives of his own dudes. All of it just takes me out of the experience.
They also could have used a more robust system of imperial politicing. Allowing us to have multiple choices, accepting proposals in part or in full, or even tacking on things to it. Making compromises and settling the thing fully. Not just a simple yay-nay system, with all of the decisions inevitably being 'are you liberal or conservative!'
What if I don't want to deport convicts? What if I want to send them to Imp war foundries to help the war effort? What if I want to have limited conscription or at the very least incentivise joining the war effort rather than just ripping people out of their houses and homes?
There was so much potential in Dragon Commander. And it feels wasted on this subpar, rushed game.

The Monster Inside is a short visual novel made in noir style.
In the game you play as a detective Jack (I’m not surprised he’s named like this), so you're going to investigate crime scenes (three) searching for clues (two in each scene). But keep it in mind The Monster Inside is more a narrative than а game.
The plot is interesting (no spoilers) and text is well written. Moreover in this game fitting grammar is like fitting shoes. Sadly the game is so short that you can complete it less than one hour.
The noir atmosphere is excellent.
Music is nice and matches the atmosphere of the game. It's not something I'd listen to on my own time (it's simple and not a lot of variety), but I didn't feel like turning it off while playing the game.
The Monster Inside is one of those games that falls into the quirky category of "for its price it's pretty good." The game is free so I recommend it especially for those who like noir detective stories.

This game is going to stay with me a long time. The story is compelling, well written and well acted, and the atmosphere evoked by the subject and the interface is second to none.
Some parts of the game are clunky, obscure and frustrating - but I'd argue this adds to the experience. Your tools are imperfect, just like your eventual understanding of what happened and why. You're struggling to dredge up a fragmentary story which is obscured by the interview format, the complex relationships between characters and the inability to sequentially access clips. This is important - you're never going to be 100% certain. You only need to prove to yourself that you made your best effort to understand the stories, actions and motivations of people you only really know from a set of 20 year old video clips.
Play for as long as you like but your mind will be turning over what you learned - or what you thought you learned - for a long time afterwards. Highly recommended.

Let me preface this by stating that this is not a game for everyone. The gameplay is entirely focused around the use of a search engine to enable the player to watch videos (in full FMV glory). There is no real way to lose, nor is there any clear objective. Instead, the player is left to figure out what is happening on their own, with only their keyboard and a database of videos. The story is entirely non-linear, and allows the player to chart their own path through the narrative. You watch a clip, you form an opinion. You watch another clip, and that previous opinion is completely changed. The path I found through the story involved plenty of twists and turns, shattering my preconcieved notions, and ultimately creating a memorable experience. Your path could be a linear telling (though it would be very unlikely) or it could be nonlinear string of nonsequiters. Forming the plot is the experience, so make sure you avoid spoilers, though do know that the story is well-written and captivating. It will probably leave lingering questions, and that's ok.
Besides the story itself, The acting by Viva Seifert is great, and not just for an FMV game. The aesthetic is simple, but effective, emulating a late 90's, early 2000's computer. The sparse soundtrack is effective when it plays, and as effective when it doesn't. If you are looking for a unique, intriguing, and effective use of experimental storytelling in gaming, then look no further. Her Story is more than worth the $6 asking price, and should be played by anyone with an open mind.

This game gets my highest recommendation for fans of adventure games.
The premis is quite simple: You are awoken from cryogenic suspension because the ship you were on suffered severe damage from a meteroid storm. Once the crisis has calmed down enough to talk to the main computer, you learn you are last crew member on the ship. So where did the other crew members go? And why aren't you with them?
This sets up a sci-fi mystery. Opions will vary, but I found the story engaging -- nay, gripping. Puzzles were overall on the easy side but got challenging toward the end. Some people will be annoyed by frequent cutscenes, but I enjoyed them and they tend to be very short for atmosphere.
No game is perfect -- for me JULIA has a bit of an on-rails feeling to it -- which is ironic since you can pick any of several planets to explore. But once you are there, each planet has relatively few locations [auto-mapped maze excepted], and within a location the puzzles and locked doors and such mean it is rare for you to be working on more than one issue at a time. I also knew enough physics that I had to correct a few of the things I was told --- the most egregious being told that an atmosphere with high concentrations of nitrogen was explosive.
Overall this ranks as one of my very favorite adventure games -- very surprising since I had never heard of the company before. Grab it if you like adventure games and/or spooky sci-fi and/or narrative-heavy games.

I have mixed feelings about this game:
The Pros:
- Gorgeous aesthetics ( graphics and music ).
- Superb voice acting by Rachel. Very good voice acting by J.U.L.I.A. and Mobot.
- I did enjoy the initial sleuthing; trying to figure out what happened to the crew. I enjoyed hacking into datapads, to read diary entries. I really liked the jigsaw puzzle ( scrambled memories ) and cypher puzzle at the end.
- I liked the fact that you could play it hidden-object style or click on a magnifier, which would show you all the hotspots ( I dislike hidden object games ).
- I did find the alien sloth's plight emotionally moving. I was saddened and depressed a few times.
The Cons:
- Poor pacing of the story. You figure out the end of the game after the first mission ( maybe an hour into the game ). Then there's a reveal at the end of the game, which isn't a reveal at all, since I have seen this plotline done before, in books and a few famous sci fi movies. I was waiting the entire length of the game, for an explanation as to the crew's demise? ( similar to watching a movie, where 10 minutes in, the premise is uncovered, yet you have to wait 1 hour and 50 minutes for an explanation as to why?)
- I found the "translate the alien language"  puzzle and most puzzles thereafter simplistic and tedious. The help file for the alien translation was incomprehensible to me, so I had to use Steam community hub / walkthroughs for an explanation as to what I was expected to do ). I put it down to a Czech-English translation problem.  From that point on, I was never entirely sure if the puzzle was being explained poorly, if I needed a precursor item for the puzzle ( like in the stone blocks manipulation puzzle ) or if I was just bad at the puzzle ( I hardly play point and click adventures ).
- The puzzles were fairly basic. I disliked having to regurgitate the story back into the form of a puzzle. At the end, there is a full on cypher decryption ( the puzzle unevenness was mind boggling - my eyes popped out of my head ).
- Taking scientific samples becomes tedious because nothing interesting happens.
- J.U.L.I.A. becomes antogonistic and annoying, just for the sake of being antagonistic and annoying.
- I don't think that the science crew acted like actual scientists, so I had a hard time believing the diary entries towards the end of the game. The strange behaviours, of a space-faring expedition, just seemed implausible.
- The endings... one of them was OK, the other was just illlogical, implausible and poorly thought out.

This game is nothing graphically, but the level design and music are where it shines. The level design is perfect at inducing a sense of flow along with the music. Without having to collect the gold pieces or to beat levels quickly or to beat levels in a gauntlet without dying, it's an easy game for people who want to play it casually. Collecting the gold often forces a player to carefully balance their movement with two or more mechanics at once, and it's implemented brilliantly. For example, many levels require you to carefully balance on blocks that move with your weight as a laser homes in on you. Each level has a sense of motif, and challenge feels well-rewarded. Plenty of times a challenge ahead of me seemed tough, but not impossible, and the game has lulled me into spending 30+ minutes on specific levels to prove myself.

Miasmata is a curious game I completed over the course of a week or so, having watched a fair number of the playthrough videos by Mesh of Mack & Mesh fame on youtube.  It seemed like the perfect game for my mood at the time, nothing too heavy or intense, no fiddly controls to figure out or the wonderful task of re-binding keys due to being left-handed!  And what a game it turned out to be.
For the most part an island exploration simulator, where you wander through valleys, over mountaintops and into dense jungle, Miasmata can be a theraputic, calming experience.  Aside from the task of having to locate and synthesize a number of plants into drugs to cure your character of an unknown plague (admittedly not a relaxing expeience for the guy you're playing), there are no constant swarms of enemies charging towards you or restrictive timeframe placed upon your actions, besides the passing of day into night.
Of course this changes to a degree a certain number of days into the game, when another 'element' is added to the experience, which certainly got my blood pumping on a few occasions!  Having a beast roaming the island with you adds an air of menace to proceedings, as you learn to be stealthier, sneakier or downright panicky in order to esacape its clutches when you cross paths.
In truth, the beast is only a small part of the joy of Miasmata, as I gained the most pleasure from simply roaming over the terrain, triangulating my way across the map in search of the next hut, piece of vital information, or important plant for examination.  If you have a powerful enough system, the island is a wonder to behold, if somewhat sparse if you are used to running into streams of characters to interact with.
I couldn't recommend this game highly enough, for the time I invested into it.  Buy it when it's on a Steam sale like I did and enjoy :)

For a game by just two developers Miasmata is really impressive. It's quite atmospheric, with the lighting and water effects in particular setting the tone, and the sound effects and music are solid.  It feels good to have no HUD and to be flicking through your journals for info instead of menus and holding up your compass instead of following a quest marker. What really sets this game apart is your character's fragility; you can't edge around and up steep hills like in Elder Scrolls games and such, and charging downhill will just cause you to trip and fall. It's a slow-paced game that mostly involves running from place to place, gathering ingredients and charting the island.
However, it's all very rough around the edges. The graphics, particularly the textures, are very dated in places. The inventory system (your left hand) is slow, limited and frustrating. Don't expect combat- you can swing a knife around but it won't achieve anything other than looking bad. Ultimately, Miasmata still feels like a demo for a real game, or a sample project, but it's a very promising one. I'd love to see more from these guys- maybe not a polished Miasmata, but a similar adventure game with much higher production values.

Battleborn has got to be one of the most unique and enjoyable games I have played in years. I was looking for a new game to play and happened to see the beta for Battleborn was live. I downloaded and proceeded to enter the multiplayer. My first few games I was clueless as to what the objective was in multiplayer and it took me a few matches to learn how to play. But finally settling on Thorn as a character I enjoyed I managed to put in nearly 40 hours over the next 4 days that the beta was active. I haven't had this much fun with a multiplayer game since Halo 3 and can definitely recommend Battleborn.
Pros:
-Unique FPS/Moba Hybrid multiplayer
-25 Unique Battleborn to choose from (with 5 more FREE characters on the way and depending on how the game is doing Gearbox is hoping to release more)
-No microtransactions
-Currently 3 different game modes to choose from:
1.Meltdown- My favorite of the three because of the similarities with Dota and the MOBA feel of the game mode (teamfights, strategy, ganks, and more than one lane that needs to be controlled). Most importantly all characters can be viable depending on your team composition.
2.Incursion- Technically the actual "moba" game mode, however, due to there only being one lane it turns into a stalemate 5v5 in the middle that can get rather boring. Unfortunately this mode suffers from some of the cast just not being viable when compared to the few Battleborn who excel in this mode.
3.Capture- I personally have only played a few games but definitely felt like the most shallow and in my opinion boring game mode. The objective is basically domination from Call of Duty where you need to hold on to capture points in order to earn points to win. This mode benefits from having short matches so if you just want to hop on and play a game for 15 minutes and kill other players than this mode if for you.
-More game modes are coming soon (free)
-More maps are coming soon (free)
-DLC will be coming out that will introduce some new campaign levels and bosses to fight but will not affect PVP multiplayer besides a few exclusive skins
-Gearbox humor
- Dev's listen to the community and interact frequently on reddit when ideas or fixes are proposed
- Fairly quick turn around when bugs are reported (however, this part is a con, patches for the PC are held back until the patches go through the verification process for consoles so we have to wait a couple weeks for the bug fixes to actually be released thanks to Sony/Microsoft)
Cons:
-Visual clutter can take some time to get used to
-Lack of PVP tutorial can make it difficult to know what is happening (I recommend starting with incursion as it is the easiest mode to get started with)
-In each game mode there is a 30 second video clip explaining the basics of the game mode but at this point you'll likely be playing with people who have already put 10-20 hours in and have a decent idea of how to play the game so this 30 second video is not quite enough
-I found the campaign to be somewhat boring because I prefer compelling stories or open RPG's to missions and raids
-However, if your coming from an MMO background the Raid missions are likely to be right up your alley if you just want
to do a quick boss fight with some friends without having to grind out hundreds of hours to get a decent level and gear
Overall an excellent game with just a few flaws. The community is small but up until this weekend was growing slowly but surely(alot of players are waiting for the patch that will fix the biggest issues with the game right now). Unlike most MOBA's the community is also quite friendly, in my close to 170 hours I have encountered only 1 toxic player in the last 2 weeks.
8.5/10

Battleborn is an FPS from Gearbox Studios (Borderlands series) that attempts to merge the MOBA/Dotalike genre in with FPS mechanics, sort of like how Borderlands was an attempt to blend ARPG + FPS. I really want to like this game to be honest with you as I actually think the idea of a MOBA+FPS is pretty cool as someone who has been a competitive FPS player and loves DotA. That said Battleborn misses the mark in so many ways it is unbelievable.
First, the campaign. The campaign is a series of 8 missions + a tutorial mission, the 8 core missions each take about 15-25 minutes to complete and are filled to the brim with your usual Borderlands-esque humor and little in the way of an actual story or actual characters beyond "bad guy trying to destroy the universe" and archetypes that are used strictly to tell jokes. This is going to be a hit or a miss for you depending on if you find Borderlands 1+2+Pre-Sequel funny or not. Personally it struck the same chord for me, which was most of the jokes missing really hard but a few of them being amazing - but not worth the price of admission alone. These story missions have a few problems, one being that their gameplay is just jerry rigged versions of all the MP modes and not much happens other than killing thousands of enemies with bad jokes interlaced in-between, but perhaps worse is that it feels like the Single Player suffers from the constraints of the Multiplayer's mechanics which I will go into in a bit. Even worse, the Season Pass content that isn't strictly cosmetic is only 5 Single Player missions which for the price of the Season Pass is absurd since getting characters is easy and the cosmetics - if the cosmetics already in the game are anything to go by - won't be super impressive.
Before I rattle off the mechanics in this game and my problems with them, I will tl;dr it for you right now: Battleborn fails to perform as a MOBA or as an FPS very well and it feels like Gearbox had no clear idea of what to do with the game. This is a structure composed of a couple gems and mostly a lot of garbage glued together poorly, essentially.
: I'll be the relatively unique voice in the wind and say that I'm okay with gear in an FPS. I am not okay with how Gear works in this game, as it misses the mark of any equivalent in a MOBA or an FPS. The gear grind itself isn't too bad I guess other than the unique PvE legendaries you have to farm for in PvE, but the biggest problem with gear is that 90% of it is inconsequential and 10% of it is utterly game changing and a lot of the 10% is the stuff you have to farm in PvE or do lore challenges to earn, with the only real exceptions being the 0 shard cost common gear you can get in packs easily. They should have done more of a system like DotA - 3 gear slots still if they want, but you don't have to grind to unlock the RNG gear, instead it's set stats and
.
: The structures are a bit weird because they don't work like MOBAs in any mode and is a weird Tower Defense type feel instead which feels kind of out of place but I don't mind it too terribly much. I wish there was more diversity in what we can build on each spot in MP, which is what you'd expect because in most of the SP build spots you actually get to choose 3 options for each spot. In MP you only get 1 option. Minions handle fine, and are actually one of the better things done in this game as you can shoot specific parts of them to crit or expose more crit spots.
: The Helix system is essentially like Talents or Perks in other games and is one of the few systems I think is near perfect. Sure, it needs balancing - like all launch games - but for the most part it is a great system with one exception:
: Here comes the big problem with the game which is mostly how the game feels. Take a character like Benedict who is your usual Rocket Launcher type character...he feels completely wrong. His rockets feel floaty, his flying feels wrong, his hovering feels weird...it just doesn't feel right and this is true for every FPS parallel character in the game. Even a character like Ghalt who uses a shotgun and a hook feels so much worse than Roadhog in Overwatch who is the same archetype. The movement feels great, but the way guns & abilities feel is just "off" in a way I don't even understand how they are off. It just doesn't feel as smooth as a triple AAA FPS. At the very least, unlocking all of the characters is easy but it better be for a 60$ game.
: In MP there is 3 game modes, one is basically Conquest from Battlefield, one is a single lane MOBA mode, and the other is a mode with 2 lanes where you have to help push minions into parts of the enemy's territory. Each mode only has 2 maps for a total of 6 maps which gets really repetitive because this game is not as deep as say, DOTA, which can get away with only one. There really needs to be more maps and Gearbox does have 3 more on the way, but it's going to be too little too late at that point.
: So, the combat in this game doesn't really feel like an FPS and definitely feels like a subpar MOBA in that almost no one can solo any other character and instead combat comes off as this weird pseudo-chess like game where you're trying to get people into a position where you can combo stuff with other people on your team to take them out by chaining CC etc and trying to avoid positions where that happens to you. It's unique, and I actually don't mind it, but I think it is going to miss the mark for most people because this is not a very lethal game on your own. That said, when you pair certain characters with other characters (coughcoughGalilea&Miko/Rayna) you can turn into a god who destroys everything in your wake. While I like it due to its uniqueness, this is just another feature that doesn't live up to the hype of either a MOBA or an FPS to me.
: The matchmaking is not good, but the population is not good either which is a big problem for good matchmaking. You will get into a lot of rolls, I can say that at Command Rank like 22 or so I've experienced 3 good close games. That is kinda absurd, but it's hard to blame the matchmaking with how small the population is and when the population is split between 4 queues.
: This gets its own section because it is the dumbest mechanic in any multiplayer game. So if you get knocked up by an ability an enemy can get right underneath you and balance you on their head to keep them stunned forever. This is absurd and for quite a few characters is essentially a pseudo-stun and makes certain melee characters who can knock people up really strong since their whole gameplan revolves around knocking you up and then balancing you on their head while they melee you to death.
: Battleborn is a game that I have to say is just mismanaged or does not have a clear enough vision. I would normally say it was released too soon except the game was delayed like twice already. It doesn't do Singleplayer or MOBA or FPS very well, and the way it is currently setup just feels unsatisfying. There is already aimbots on the PC version and people commonly use exploits to win as well as leave with no punishment for either. People who surrender at the slightest loss in momentum are common and most of your games won't go to the end. The content for every mode is light. The population is already near death, only having ~7k users on at prime US time on a weekend, and that's 7k users split between 4 queues.
I can not in good conscience recommend anyone buy this game for 60$. Battleborn could be a great game eventually, but it'll probably be too little too late for it at this rate.

This games takes a moderately decent hack-n-slash RPG series and turns it into the video game equivilent of District 9.  It's at least 5 different genres smashed into one game, and somehow comes out the other side better for it.
The bulk of the game plays like Risk, but where you can choose to manually resolve battles in a Dawn of War style RTS.  They also tie in the original RPG series by allowing you to spawn yourself as a dragon on the battlefield during the RTS segments, which can be very effective if done at the right times.  Also, your dragon has a jetpack now.  On top of that, you get empire management between rounds, where you have to make choices to keep your generals and the ambassadors of the 5 races of the world happy and supporting you.  And choosing how to spend your research points to upgrade units and/or your dragon form.
In the end, I picked up the game because I liked previous Divinity games and I was intrigued, but I ended up with a surprisingly good hybrid that has almost nothing to do with the series it's based on except for the setting.

Having said that, Psychonauts is an absolutely fantastic game, and you should go buy it and play it right now. There are levels in this game that will make you smile and laugh. And there are levels that you will remember until your dying day. Not because they were hard, but because of the character and absolute GENIUS of the design. I'm talking about Lungfishopolis. I'm talking about The Milkman Conspiracy. I'm talking about Black Velvetopia. I'm talking about Waterloo World.
You have not played Psychonauts yet, so you don't understand what I mean. But you will if you buy this game. And you should buy this game. It's not perfect, but the good parts are so DAMN good that it doesn't matter. It is genuinely better than it has any right to be.
Also, this game was a AAA, $60 release, about a decade ago. So you are getting a fantastic game at an insane discount. Did you buy this game then? no? well, then, you might be part of why it didn't do as well as it should have. Relieve your guilt by playing one of the best games ever made, Psychonauts, right now.

You're struggling to dredge up a fragmentary story which is obscured by the interview format, the complex relationships between characters and the inability to sequentially access clips. Let me preface this by stating that this is not a game for everyone. The gameplay is entirely focused around the use of a search engine to enable the player to watch videos (in full FMV glory). There is no real way to lose, nor is there any clear objective. Instead, the player is left to figure out what is happening on their own, with only their keyboard and a database of videos. The story is entirely non-linear, and allows the player to chart their own path through the narrative. You watch a clip, you form an opinion. You watch another clip, and that previous opinion is completely changed. The path I found through the story involved plenty of twists and turns, shattering my preconcieved notions, and ultimately creating a memorable experience. Your path could be a linear telling (though it would be very unlikely) or it could be nonlinear string of nonsequiters. Forming the plot is the experience, so make sure you avoid spoilers, though do know that the story is well-written and captivating. It will probably leave lingering questions, and that's ok.
Besides the story itself, The acting by Viva Seifert is great, and not just for an FMV game. The aesthetic is simple, but effective, emulating a late 90's, early 2000's computer. The sparse soundtrack is effective when it plays, and as effective when it doesn't. If you are looking for a unique, intriguing, and effective use of experimental storytelling in gaming, then look no further. Her Story is more than worth the $6 asking price, and should be played by anyone with an open mind.

That was the sound I made when I beat the final level of Danger Zone and realized I had seen everything this game had to offer. By the way, I'm being generous when I call this a game; it's a tech demo, more so than Dangerous Golf. At least that game had some pretty scenery to look at, but this game's environment is more drab than gridlock on a Friday afternoon on the way home from work.
Danger Zone is the latest game from Three Fields Entertainment, an indie studio founded by the original founders from Criterion. Based on that statement alone, it was only a matter of time before they would make something like Burnout, if you don't count Dangerous Golf that is. Regardless, Danger Zone has its occasional moments. The one car you get steers decent enough, traffic checking (returning from Burnout: Revenge) feel good enough to get the job done, and seeing the wreck you caused afterwards via slow flyby does bring back some nice memories.
Danger Zone takes place over 20 levels as you smash your way through cars and grab cash tokens to up your score. Simple stuff really, but here's my number one problem with Danger Zone: The cash tokens. See, in Burnout 3: Takedown, all the pickups
were visible from the start and order wasn't important so you could crash through a level however you wanted to. In Danger Zone, you have to grab all 3 bronze tokens and the 2 silver ones before the last gold token appears, similar to Dangerous Golf. Also, you have to grab them in order, bronze then silver and finally gold, otherwise you lose out on an extra $2.5 million added to your crash total. This system is pointless and only encourages frustration as you try and figure out the EXACT ROUTE the developers want you to take instead of FINDING or MAKING the best route on your own. However you feel about it in Dangerous Golf, it doesn't feel right here and removes what made the Crash Mode in Burnout so special in the first place.
Speaking of special, what happened to the scenery? I get being on a tight budget and all because they're a small dev team, but the little things would have gone a long way to make this one stand out. A building here, a light pole there...where are all the light poles? They can put toll booths in one level, but no light poles? These highways have no proper barriers or anything other than makeshift ones in one level; they're literally just floating road that cause a fail state if you fall off. The 'tunnels' also feel out of place with the open sides in some levels, but road underneath. Is it a tunnel or not? I get that it's because this is all part of a virtual training simulation aesthetic, but that aesthetic robs this game of any life in my opinion. Setting this in the arctic would have been better; not many trees there either but at least it isn't in some underground bunker where you can't even see a sky.
All of that about the scenery feels like nitpicking as I'm typing this out
, but it's not. Danger Zone is from people that were behind Burnout and it can have some nice nostalgic moments, but it has none of the heart, the soul, or to be quite honest, the fun. The scenery and virtual presentation are pretty boring and nothing out of the ordinary. The Grand Slam cash token bonus, along with only having one drivable car, strips away any experimentation and forces you down one route where rigid execution matters more than style or substance. Also, let's be honest: Crash Mode, while fun to play, was always a side mode compared to the racing. It didn't need to be its own game.
If you're like me and played Burnout almost non-stop back in 2004 and 2005, you'll see everything here and get all the achievements in under 2 hours. In and of itself, the length isn't really that bad, but when the game is so monotonous, it feels too similar well before that runtime is over. It's obvious that the focus here was on the explosions and particle effects, as the cars don't even get banged up that much, they just get some scratches on their crash test paint jobs. Here's a good question:
Danger Zone may give you some nostalgia while it lasts, but the Grand Slam cash bonus (required if you want the best scores, which why wouldn't you?), the one car, and the stale scenery won't make you want to come back. This game, and in my opinion this studio, needs a major creative boost, which no update to this can fix as far as I'm concerned. I'm not mad that I played Danger Zone; I'm just disappointed.
If you want something similar, get
instead; it's not so much a game as much as a crash sandbox, but it has multiple vehicles, Steam Workshop support for custom levels, and is also made by an indie studio that managed to churn all that out in a game that costs less than this one does, and it's received multiple free content updates since its 2014 release. Also, the cars and ragdolls actually break apart, and the audio and visual presentation is top notch. Buy that instead.
Speaking of presentation, a game called
doesn't even have
in it, or any music AT ALL. Even Dangerous Golf had a theme song. Skip this one.

Remember when EA didn't suck massive dongs and completely abandoned a strong racing franchise in favor of an arguably weaker one that EA forced the devs to make games for before canning them and throwing them on the new Battlefront games? Those were the days when the Burnout franchise reigned supreme as the ultimate destruction racer. Even from its first iteration back on the PS2 we were introduced to a high octane smash fest of aggresive racing and traffic dodging. However, the pinnacle wouldn't be reached until 2002 when Burnout 2: Point of Impact introduced a series of minigames involving smashing a car into heavy traffic to cause a chain reaction of carnage. This formula wouldn't be perfected until Burnout 3: Takedown when the mode took a more arcadey approach allowing you as the user to control the flying remains of a destroyed vehicle into even more traffic to cause a bigger wreck. Oh yeah, there was also racing too.
After the last good Burnout game, Burnout Revenge, came a successor called Burnout Paradise that pretty much sucked all the "success" out of the very thing it was trying to be. While the removal of a structured circuit race was replaced with an open world point A to point B system the biggest insult was the removal of Burnout's Crash Mode in favor of a mode called Showtime which allowed users to, at any point, spin their car out of control and start smashing into traffic endlessly until they ran out of momentum from hitting traffic. It sucked because it never really showcased all the destruction you were causing until at the end when it somewhat showed you the aftermath during the scoreboard. The best thing about Burnout's original Crash Mode was that each level was structured uniquely outside the confines of the tracks already in the game allowing the developers to create some really wild scenarios for you to crash your car into. The game also highlighted whenever some poor unsuspecting victim hit the brakes too late and skidded into a tanker causing him to explode.
Fans of the Burnout franchise have been left without a crash mode successor for 12 years. TWELVE. YEARS. And don't even get me started on that joke of game development called Burnout Crash! That is not Crash Mode. It was a sad excuse for a Crash Mode successor.
So come the other day when I'm just lazing around and hear about this trailer for a Burnout Crash Mode successor and to my surprise upon watching the trailer I find out it was released 4 days ago. I quickly refunded Tokyo 42 because that game was such a disappointment and put my money towards this instead and, man, I sure feel quite the opposite!
It's no surprise that this game is pretty much exactly identical to that of Burnout's original crash mode. The handling, driving physics, the floaty destruction physics, behaviors of the NPCs, the after-touch explosion system, the camera focusing on the points of impact, etc are all included in this game and that's because Three Fields Entertainment is a company founded by Ex-Criterion founders who worked on the original set of Burnout titles. The moment I picked up the controller and smashed into the first scenario I was blasted by a whirlwind of nostalgia and felt the relief of a 12 year old itch finally being scratched. There was nothing more satisfying than seeing everything familiar with the game that I loved playing over and over so many odd years ago and it is special to see that they kept all the charm of Crash Mode in this spiritual successor.
Now, obviously, there are a few things that are different this time around. The first and most obvious is the aesthetic of the game. Everything is done inside of a crash test simulation complex. I don't know if this was for budget reasons to keep the cost down but don't expect a wild change of scenery through the levels like we experienced with some of the real-world reimagings found in Burnout 3 and Revenge. It pretty much all looks the same, but they at least put forth the effort to make the facility and simulation rooms look and feel genuine with flashing lights, large metal doors, and rooms that "code" themselves into existence. Every vehicle, including yours, has a crash test logo on it as well and every letter features a bright sign that displays some sort of text. None of these have only gotten a small chuckle out of me but it's nice that it's there.
The biggest changes are two additions they added to the levels themselves. Crash Mode in Burnout was pretty simplistic in its mechanics. You have a car, you try to drive into traffic and rack up as much of a combo as you can get from the pile up. The more cars piled up, the bigger multiplayer you recieved and the more collateral you collected. You could also build up a meter called "Crashbreaker" which allowed you to blow up your vehicle and, for a few seconds, fly it around and toss it into traffic you may have missed or otherwise can't get to without making use of the mechanic. Danger Zone features these same mechanics as well, however Crashbreaker is now referred to as Smashbreaker and you only get one of them after meeting the minimum requirement during the first point of impact. The only way you can get more Smashbreaker is to control your first Smashbreaker into a collectible Smashbreaker icon located on the map. Its a weird design choice as it makes the crashes you cause feel less dynamic. Its like you have to follow a path set by the developers in order to obtain the high score which sorta of dampens the beauty of experimentation from its predecessor and turns it into a challenge and competition with the inclusion of the leaderboard. They do also include money pick ups as well for extra points, and collecting all of them reveals a secret cash pick up that rewards you with $5 million in points. That being said though it doesn't really diminish from the fun and nostalgia the game has to offer but I would have liked if this wasn't included.
Along with that there are bigger changes. The multiplier system only comes into affect after initiating a Smashbreaker and it will only count cars you either destroy with the radius of the explosion and other cars you knock into while you're flying around. They also included out of bounds areas on the map which will cause a game over if you fall into it and give you bonus points if you throw an NPC into it. This becomes a game of balancing because you obviously get the most points from causing pile ups but if you throw all the vehicles off the map with your Smashbreaker you lose creating an obstacle for other NPCs to crash into yet you need to use your Smashbreaker in order to obtain a higher multiplier for the pile up collisions. Timing is crucial in obtaining the most points you can possibly get and following the route you need to for that mad-mad money is difficult as your car only bounces when rolling on its sides and bouncing off of other traffic. It will refuse to move while it's grinding on the chasis. This can make for some frustrating moments as one poorly timed collision after using a Smashbreaker can send you away from another Smashbreaker you desperately need to keep the chain going.
The most disappointing thing however is the lack of any other vehicles for you to drive. You are only given this midsize 4 door sedan that sounds like it has the engine of a Ford Mustang. Obviously the maps are tailored around this one specific car, but I would have liked if they played around with a variety of different vehicle classes. Again, it's probably due to budget constraints as they are a small team that's self-publishing on Steam, but aside from that this is pretty much the Crash Mode that veteran Burnout fans have been craving for over a decade now. It's definitely worth the asking price of $12.99 and, hopefully, with some good sales we'll finally see a real Burnout successor. I highly recommend it to fans and to newcomers alike.

For my previously semi-unhelpful views on Airport Madness 3D, head here:
The Madness begins again! A 2nd volume of 8 fantastic airports to play with, crash aircraft and get frustrated over. Then play them again and again and again! Because you're not actually frustrated with the game, but with yourself for failing hard!
In the first Volume the original 4 airports that came with Volume 1 were pretty good. As the game developed 4 more were added over time, showing a marked improvement in quality with each new airport release. Volume 2 alone is a collection of airports that showcases how much Big Fat Simulations has improved over that original volume. The airports are more detailed, more complex, and compared to the original airports, some here are huge!
If you're new to Airport Madness 3D, I will reiterate, this is an Arcade game based on time mangement and ever increasing levels of multitasking. So I recommend starting with Volume 1. The airports in Volume 2 are no pushover to beat..
Hong Kong is a good starter, but is very heavy traffic, finding gaps are easier, but queues will quickly arise.
London & Nepal will test your time management skills to the limit. Every inch counts on a Single Runway where air traffic will be coming at you head on as you try to move aircraft back the way they came.
Chicago is the jewel in the crown with 8 runways to keep track of and aircraft coming and going on each. Multitasking better be your strong point. Crashes are a certainty, the very definition of Madness!
Also, more 'feature' content will be coming in the future too at no additional cost. This isn't just more airports at a price (which the developer deserves to be paid for).. There are planned features such as emergencies, night time play and more! So this is a game worth investing in as the developer is always adding new stuff through updates and patches.
So whilst Volume 2 may be more of the same gameplay, this is by no means bad at all.. The series goes from strength to strength, and Volume 2 offers the best Airport Madness experience to date!
I love it! Plain and simple... Here's to another 75+ hours of fantastic fun!

Bought this game on impulse when it was a flash sale, and I'm very glad I did.
It's part RTS, part RISK, part empire sim, and it manages to mesh together fairly well. You're a half-dragon, seeking to retake your dead father's kingdom from your siblings from a floating ship known as "The Raven." On board your ship, you'll meet with councilors from each of the five races in the game besides humans (dwarves, elves, lizards, imps, undead) to make political decisions to run your exapnding empire. You'll also be tasked with moving your armies around on a Risk-style map, playing cards earned through gameplay to help your forces and hinder your enemy's. Finally, when armies meet on the map, you'll have to command your forces in battle in simplified RTS combat, with the gimmick of being able to transform into a dragon to turn the tide of battle in your favor.
The best part of the game is making political decisions to run your empire, and the consequences those decisions entail. Will you implement national healthcare? Deport foreign criminals simply because they're foreign? These are typically not easy decisions to make, as they all have pros and cons. It does get a bit limited--you can only make "yes" or "no" answers to everything. But it's still a very interesing commentary on modern politics. If you're unable to compromise your own views, for example, to keep the other races satisfied, it'll be more difficult for you to raise forces in regions dominated by that race.
The RISK style map is basically what you expect. You maneuover your armies around, taking territories and attempting to outsmart the AI- which, so far for me, hasn't been terribly difficult. You can build one building in each territory, from a selection of around 7 or 8. These range from war factories to recruit units with to Wizard Towers that generate cards to give you an advantage in battle.
When you confront another army on the map, you can choose to lead your forces into battle, or one of your generals. The RTS-combat is very simple-- there are only around 4 buildings you can build, and one type of resource- recuits. Your main goal is to capture a Recruit plot outside your starting base. If you do this, you'll quickly be able to outproduce your enemy and it won't be long before you overwhelm them. At first, these battles are fun, but they grow repetitive, and you'll find yourself wishing you could skip them entirely. You can, of course, if you elect to have your generals fight for you, Total War- autoresolve style. Unfortunately, this can lead to lost battles that you would otherwise win.
The RTS-part's main gimmick- transforming into a dragon-- is fun at first, and creates an interesting mechanic in RTS battles. You can't quene up units while in dragon form, so if you stay transformed too long, you may find yourself out of allied troops to fight with and the battle may turn against you. At the same time, the dragon is powerful and can turn a losing battle into a winning one. Most times, though, the nature of the RTS battles renders the dragon a utility unit. To win, you'll need to outproduce your enemy, and if you're doing that, the battle will quickly snowball in your favor anyways.
Divinity: Dragon Commander is a fantastic game. The RTS portion is unfortunately a little weak and gets in the way of the game's more fun empire managing and political decision making, but I would still highly recommend it to strategy enthusiasts.

For starters:  this is not a game by most standard definitions.  It can even be argued Gone Home is more of a game than Her Story.  You interact with an emulated desktop and type words into a search toolbar to access interrogation videos in an evidence database.
However, the storytelling method is beyond compelling.  You stumble upon facts and details out of order, but the struggle to flesh out the meat and potatoes of the plot due to the nature of the system in place will keep you searching for every single video.
If you manage to get every video "unlocked" in under two hours, I implore you to not troll the refund system and hang on to it.  The dev deserves to be compensated for such an intriguing platform, and this is yet another title I wish I had thought of doing first because the novelty is really fresh.
Sidenote:  it gets annoying at times, but do not disable the screen glare.  You need it for certain visual effects that appear from time to time and it helps keep things creepy.
