The time is January 2008. Yung destro has received a PSP from a Bagel Bites™ instant win competition (Yes, really).
His first game... Burnout Revenge. I had never had a chance to play it, or Burnout 3 on PS2 when they came out, and I decided to try it.
And god, damn... What a game. I'm sure this game made my grades go down. Burnout revenge is probably one of my favorite racing games of all time, the only thing that satisfied my lust for car crashing glory even a little bit as much as this game did was Full Auto for the Xbox 360. Anyway, Burnout was Forza/Gran Turismo on meth. Instead of following the rules and not breaking real driving policies, the drivers basically give no damns. However, while Burnout Revenge had a long single player racing mode, there was a side mode that was pretty fun, and addicting as all hell. It was called Crash Mode. I 100%'d crash mode, got the firetruck, and all that stuff. Really, if you haven't played Burnout Revenge, DO IT!
Anyway, this isn't a review for Burnout Revenge, but you need to know all of this to understand where i'm coming from. I've waited for a game like Burnout Revenge for YEARS. Nothing compares. Burnout Paradise is pretty good, but it's not really the same. I see it as more of an open world game, which is cool, but I like Revenge much better. Danger Zone is a successor to burnout, since it's been dead in the water since 2008. They tried to cashout on crash mode with a phone style arcade game in 2011, and they succeeded in♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥the fanbase off.
Danger Zone is... well, the gameplay is there. I love the explosions and how basically they took crash mode and made it a game. The thing is... I don't know that anyone really ever asked for this. I would LOVE a new burnout, or even a new burnout-inspired game or successor, and if it had crash mode, HELL YES. That is a $60 game I would pay for. But the crash mode here is very bare bones for a full game. My first big disappointment was the fact that there is no city. There isn't any buildings, it's basically just a generic Aperture Science™ style chamber with a grid floor that if you fall through, you lose. And the music... There is none! I understand that this is not AAA development, you can't get licenced tracks like some of the great soundtracks the burnout games have, but no music at all? Another thing is how badly they make you depend on the pickups. Why are there so many money drops that you NEED, and why is the pileup the objective of the game when that isn't how crash mode plays????
The game is short, I unfortunately lost motivation to continue once I reched the middle of tier 2. I am not going to refund it, because I want to support this developer. They mean well, but there isn't substance, nothing that keeps me coming back. Where is the option to use a ambulance? Or a fire truck, or a bus? You guys just took the barebones original crash mode and put it out. There's just not much they can do with it, it should have been paired with the racing of classic burnout. If this was the first build of a Early Access game, I would probably be in love. But the fact that it's the full game, even for $12, isn't satisfying. If the developer decides to flesh the game out more, i'll probably come back, but I am definitely disappointed.
If you haven't yet, pick up a PSP/PS2 emulator, and take your pick of Burnout Games. You already know my reccomendation. I continue my search for the perfect Burnout Revenge successor...

I loved the Crash mode on Burnout 3 Takedown and Revenge, it was always my favourite game mode as it was so addictive and made you chase after that unbeatable score. Over 10 years later, and it makes a glorius return, made by the same people behind the Burnout series. It's very similar to Burnout 3's version in which you had to collect the bonus pickups and extra crashbreakers. The score multipliers are gone, but instead replaced by "Grand Slam" in which if you collect all of the pickup's you can smashbreak your way to collect the golden bonus coin. This can add several million to your score.
Unreal Engine 4 powers the game and even moderatly modern hardware should have no problem running this at full HD resolution.
It is quite short, and all the levels are inside this large warehouse type building so the environment gets a bit "samey". But the gameplay is there so Three Fields at least have given us an insight as to what sort of "full game" they have in mind.
I would love to see an expanded follow-up title, but even if they added a "level generator", different types of veichles and a multiplayer mode as DLC I'd buy it!

It's OK.
It has potential.
I worry that this was meant as a guinea pig/testing game, and it kinda sounds like the dev is thinking if this sells well, they will simply make and sell another game, instead of adding to this game.
And that would be a shame.
There is potential here, but this is a 2-3 hour play at most. One car, pretty terrible setting (the metal and darkness actually hurt my eyes to play for more than 30 minutes at a time) and the crashes are unspectacular compared to the predecessor, Burnout.
Therefore, although it is an OK game, due to how Steam allow you to either say yea or nay, I kinda have to say nay. It's not a rip-off at $12.99, but it is not quite enough game for that price, either.

I really wanted to like this. I love crash mode, I still wish that mobile game (Burnout Crash) made it to more platforms too. I thought, this series has been around for over a decade, surely they will put that experience and knowledge to good use, even if they don't have much money. They'll improve on the excellent foundation that's already there.
Well for starters, they somehow took crash mode and turned crashing/pile-ups into not only NOT the primary goal, but an obstacle to it. Sure, Burnout 3 had money pickups but they were just a little bonus. Here, the pickups will make or break your score, which you will lose a significant chunk of if you miss even ONE of them or collect them in the wrong order. Where previously I'd be smiling at that giant pile-up I created, now I'm cursing at it for blocking my path to the next Smashbreaker (Crashbreaker) pickup.
Which brings me to the Smashbreaker/Aftertouch system. Instead of being able to retrigger it by continuing to accrue new wrecks, now it will trigger ONCE and after that you have to try to collect Smashbreaker pickups to trigger it again. Your car didn't roll properly? Got clipped by the corner of a bus? Now you're stuck and have to retry the whole crash again. While for the most part the physics are ok, your own car can only maintain speed properly if it rolls end-over-end, something you have very little control over (think Showtime from Paradise except with more accurate physics and no helpers). Not only that, the car will stick to the ground if it lands right-side up (despite losing its wheels in the initial crash) and destroy any momentum/flipping you built up with your Smashbreaker jump.
Essentially Danger Zone is a 3-D platformer about limited jumping, where your success often depends on the physics being nice to you. It could improve down the line with fixes/additions but right now it's an exercise in frustration.
Other things to note (as of this review, obviously they could change later):
- Camera control; you only get it after your car becomes a wreck, and only on the horizontal axis. Yes, this does become a problem when trying to see pickups you're above.
- No restart button, no rebinding of any kind
- It is a graphically nice game, especially the light sources. Thanks UE4.

Exploration and the sense of loneliness. Miasmata's huge open world is full of atmosphere and mystery. You will get lost and you will die unless you find a cure. Great game. Beware what lies in the woods.

Back when Myst first came out, there was a Fox Trot cartoon in which Jason hacked up a version of Myst that was exactly the same as the original, except that velociraptors were chasing the player. That's a pretty good description of Miasmata.
Exploration is the driving mechanic of the game, and in this respect, the island of Eden is a paradise. Every part of the island is unique, with hills, rivers, swamps, ancient ruins, and dense foliage of many kinds. The lighting and water effects are very impressive. At the same time, Eden's beauty is tempered by its dangers. Fatigue, sickness, and the terror of being stalked are conveyed in an organic and immersive fashion, which makes them all the scarier.
Miasmata is a beautiful sandbox experience. I also found it very frightening, at times. Perhaps not everyone will find it as scary as I did, but anyone who loves exploring will find it very engaging.

This is not an action game: there is no combat although there is an animal on the island which will kill you if you fail to hide from it.
This is a game of exploration: you are stranded on an island, suffering from a plague.  The cure is on this Island although those that made it are all dead.  You explore the island, mapping it as you go, searching for the plants required to create the cure (as well as the scientists notes with regards as to which plants you actually require).  In your diseased state you are weak.  A slight fall, dehydration or lack of sleep will lead to a fever...left untreated the fever will kill you.  You can use various plants around the island to synthesise drugs to combat the fever or to increase your strenght, endurance and awareness.
In this game it is the environment which is your enemy: the island is a mountainous, jungle environment full of steap slopes: in Miasmata your body has momentum and navigating all of those hills becomes a matter of life or death.  You will slide, trip and fall but it all feels very natural.
I loved this game: the island setting is well realised...the sounds of the environment are very well done, while the lighting is fantastic.
The game was made by two people, with an engine they built specifically for the purpose.  There are rough patches to the graphics but I can honestly say that I never noticed them unless I went looking for them.
I highly recommend it, but it may not be to everyone's taste.
A truly freeform horror game, where using your map and landmarks can mean the difference between finding a safe shelter for the night or wandering a forest in the pitch dark.

A very immersive game, with a focus on survival and exploration. Your time will be spent hiking through dense jungle, over ancient ruins and across rocky shores while researching various flowering plants and fungi to manufacture a cure for a debilitating plague which is slowly killing you.  This game features a unique mapping system which allows you to chart your location based on landmarks that you've identified which I think is fantastic, and the UI is very minimal, allowing you to focus more on your surroundings than on numbers and gauges. Meanwhile, the mystery of what happened to the other researchers on the island is there to confound you, and beware, for you are being hunted.

Miasmata is an exploration, survival, horror game. (In that order of significance) If you enjoy getting lost in Minecraft and finding your way back to your known area, you'll enjoy this game. I'd say its a mix of Minecraft exploration (without dynamic environments or mining, but some crafting), the "LOST" like island mystery, and some Dear Esther visuals and minimal action gameplay.  It also has some Myst elements to it, without the awkward puzzles. There is a cartography element where you need to reference two familiar landmarks (statues etc) to locate yourself and surrounding on the map, and do this with a 3rd new landmark from two different locations to make the new landmark a familiar one. There is a threat on the island, but its hasnt been a big issue for me yet. But my big gripe is the physics of slopes, basically your character struggles to climb even a 5 degree slope, and you can easily fall. Basically it feels like you're wearing roller skates in the wilderness. Also, you have a sickness that constantly requires medicine, so going in water and falling, makes you get sick a lot faster. Good mechanic I guess to keep people from just swiming everywhere. There are also a lot of impassible terrain to get around. So if you're into exploration and mystery, this might be a game for you. But not so much there on the action end, but there are some good survival elements, which can be intense, as you race to make more medicine to survive. One bummer is you only get 1 save slot per game. But all round its something different and fun for those into exploration.

Also, there are a few technical glitches here and there that can detract from the immersiveness of the game. The game feels a bit rushed as well, as you have a knife that doesn't kill anything and animals that run around that you can't eat. Despite the technical issues and some missing features, I really like this game.
Also, the giant panthers are very friendly and love to play fetch.

Incredible game. You may think the style is extremy simple and you know what, you're right! Its simple yet its so charming, you get tons of different palletes to choose from, different colors for your ninja and some accessories, the customization here for the levels alone is pretty damn solid that there's bound to be one that interests pretty much everyone, in general they have rather contrasting colors to have the level stand out. I think if it wasn't for such a simple artstyle, the developers not have as much content in the game, its a good compromise in my opinion.
Controls are solid, I mean SOLID. It has a floaty feeling yet has finesse and precision. You feel like you have complete control over when your character starts and stops both up and down and left and right, I have yet to find a game that manages to balance it out as well as this one does. The momentum mechanic works really well, your character feels like it has force applied to it when you run and jump, jumping off of walls and gaining speed. Its so satisfiying!
The amount of content you get for this game is absurd, I've already put 5 hours into it and I haven't even scratched the surface of what this game has to offer. It does not descriminate, whatever way you choose to play is here. Want to speedrun? Got it, collect them all for that completionist side of you? Right here! Want to take it nice and steady, go at at reasonable pace and not care about speedrunning or collecting? The game has you covered, in fact the time it gives to complete a level is generous, I have not once found myself even when I was taking my sweet sweet time to fail a level because the timer ran out. The developers promise 100+ hours and so far I believe them on that, even just completing the solo mode itself will take you I'd say a solid 20-30 hours if you don't touch the rest of the content or collect anything and just rush through it, you've already got more than what you paid for. Heck I remember when we paid 60 dollars for triple A games for 8 hours. 8 HOURS!
Besides the solo mode as I mentioned it also has hardcore which is basically your time attack mode in which you try to complete a level as fat as possible, you're given a reasonable starting time and from there it stacks if you collect the orange squares. Feeling brave? Do hardcore without going for the orange squares and that right there will be an extra challenge.
THEN, you also have the level creator, yes I am not done yet. You've got thousands upon thousands of user made levels, granted some of them aren't up to snuff with the content the devs provided, it further expands the playability of this game beyond what you'd imagine for a 15 dollar game.
Have I mentioned the soundtrack yet? No? Well I must!!! The soundtrack is absolutly superb, its a combination of electronic with slow relaxed drum and base tones with some occasional chillstep, it is incredible, it really goes hand in hand with the gameplay.
Don't miss this game! I nearly gave it a pass because I thought it was going to be a rather bland experience yet everytime I jump in, I feel so compelled to sink hours of my life into it. Like a tube of pringles, once you start you won't stop. ;)

Divinity: Dragon Commander is an interesting game.  It's part RTS, part empire sim, part card game, and all these mechanics play well together.  That being said, the game's core content seems to be the combat system which is engaging as the novelty of being a dragon with a jet pack doesn't fade quickly. The scenarios are rather unispired though and I found myself skipping many battles later in the game.  Aside from that, the only flaw I can say the game has is a far too heavy handed approach of introducing real world political topics into the game.  Issues such as same sex marriage, universal healthcare, etc, all show up in the game with all the subtlety of a sledgehammer.  There's some designer bias in these topics but, for the most part, each decision is given as having pros and cons.   Ultimately the decision-making at these junctures are a bit jarring from the fantasy aesthitic the rest of the game presents and I can't help but feel the game would be better off without, or with at least more fantasy inspired controversy.   All-in-all the game is great fun and beautiful to look at but mediocre combat scenarios and blatently obvious political topic insertions hold the game back.

RPG, strategy, RTS, and dragons! This game combined a lot of elements that I love into a game I couldn't wait to buy, one of the few I've ever preordered. I quite enjoyed Larian's Divinity II and thus had faith that they'd do well with this game as well, and they lived up to expectations. Once you finish the campaign you can make a custom one that avoids the cutscenes and seperate acts, making for a lot of replayability so you can explore the many political decisions set before you. The strategic overview is simple but funtions quite well, the units on said overview map coming with you into the RTS battles in contested territories. The RTS component itself is much simpler than most as it comprises a single resource, recruits, that is shared amoung all the players. Controlling more Citadels means you get a larger portion of this pool, and should a battle exhaust this resource it comes down to who can manage what they got from the pool better. Of course my personal favourite part of the game is entering the battle yourself as a dragon, and if played well you can significantly change the flow of battle, often strong enough to strafe around and destroy smaller groups of units. You have limited RTS control in dragon form however, and may have to exit dragon mode to execute further commands, though transitioning back and forth is quite fluid.

PAYDAY: The Heist is a first person shooter that allows players to embark on a spectacular and intense experience of a career criminal.
The 6 original heists (First World Bank, Heat Street, Panic Room, Green Bridge, Diamond Heist and Slaughterhouse) provide a variety of approaches to achieve the best payday, including blasting the way through a downtown bank vault, managing hostages in an armored car hijacking and even a midnight infiltration of a high-security facility.
This game challenges the player with dynamic environments and adaptive enemy tactics, which means that the scenarios will never be repeated, forcing the player to adapt to different situations every single time.
The game features an amazing 4 players cooperative experience, and teamwork is essential to ensure the plan's success.
The gameplay is good, the graphics are great in my opinion and the soundtrack is superb, although the AI could be improved.
The released content provides 3 amazing new heists (Undercover, Counterfeit and No Mercy) and plenty of fun.
I highly recommend PAYDAY: The Heist along with the Wolfpack DLC.

Okay, so this game is weird. Yet, I think it's a good kind of weird.
Is it a moba? Not really.
Is it a co-op first person shooter? Not really.
Is it an fps rpg? Not really.
Don't start playing this game expecting it to be any one of these, cause you might be dissapointed if you do.
In reality, Battleborn is all of those things and then a little more, all wrapped together in some package like a giant mystery burrito which when you bite in to it you don't really know what your tasting. Yet it works, it honestly all works. The game is lots of fun and the characters are all pretty diverse and all tend to have a unique playstyle with advantages/disadvantages to playing them. Each character also tends to counter a different character ala a classic class based game. The helix system and the little bit of customization each character is offered helps to expand them just a little bit, with the helix system being the highlight of this. Allowing you to select which skills you want each time you play a match, as your level will always start at 1 at the beginning of any match. The underlying gear system also adds a little bit of loot variety ala borderlands and it allows more tweaking of the characters through permanent gear you can activate after reaching enough currency in a match. The story mode is kinda meh and leaves a bit to be desired, but the dialog is enjoyable at times. Not quite off the wall as borderlands but still made me chuckle a couple times. The missions don't really flow together well, so you don't really know the order of things. Yet they are still enjoyable experiences to play through especially with others. Multiplayer is this game's strength though. From the moba style game mode to just the standard domination game mode, all are enjoyable. Making plays against others or pushing with your team is great. Even just one on one fights between different heros is enjoyablel to see how the they affect and counter each other. Gearbox wanted to do something different with this game and they deffiantly did that and it all tends to work. It's weird, but it works.

Never played this game before, but picked it up on a steam sale. Decided to play it before the new movie came out. Spent 4 hours slogging through fetch quests and stilted dialogue on the 1st planet, Taris. Got bored, started reading up to see when the game was going to get better. Some fans reported spending 15-20 hours on Taris on their first playthrough. Ugh. Not wanting to make a part time job of this, I downloaded and installed the mod that lets you skip Taris entirely.
Started a new game. First dialogue prompt lets you skip Taris. Excellent. A series of video clips play, then you get dumped into a sequence where you, not-luke-skywalker, in your not-the-millenium-falcon ship, are fighting off not-TIE-fighters. Which would have been fine, except that the mouse controls are glitched/broken for this minigame, and you're forced to use WASD controls for precision aiming. On top of that, your ship has shields made of kleenex, and if you fail, you're dumped back to the main menu and forced to reroll a new character, because you never got a chance to save the game. Whee.
So I cranked up the mouse sensitivity before trying again, hoping that would fix the issue. Nope. Manage to squeeze through barely with the keyboard controls. Get to Dantooine, and all the Jedi business. Okay, cool, game starts now, right? Well after a series of incredibly stilted sequences and the most blatant of Mary Sue training montages, you're finally ready to... take a multiple choice quiz. Based on some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t terminology you have to go running around to your fellow padawans and crib off their notes to be able to pass. Screw that noise.
I've spent 5 hours in-game, on top of about 3 hours troubleshooting installation and graphics. And at no point did this game open up and become interesting. I'm not complaining about the turn-based combat. That's fine. But the dialogue and story is painfully slow, and the gameplay seems to careen between holding my hand and punching me in the face. I don't understand the nostalgia for this game. It must get really good towards the end, because the first 5+ hours are a goddamn chore. But I'm really not interested in putting in the time investment needed to get there. Like I said before, I'm not interested in taking on a part-time job, especially not one where I'm working for free (and paying the game creators besides). A game should be fun from the beginning, and the story should be interesting from the beginning, and the characters should be interesting... from the beginning. Unless you're a masochist, you will find nothing here to keep you interested.
Don't waste any money on this turd. Without nostalgia goggles, there's nothing worth seeing.

It's basically Burnout 3's crash mode reimagined and it's worth every penny. Any Burnout is better than no Burnout if done right.

Unfortunately. No.
This is a pet project piggy-backing off the success of the teams earlier Burnout games when Criterion did them, great you might think! However, although seemingly fun for the first half an hour or so, a pattern of issues and shortcomings come to light.
So what does it do right? Well...It scratches an itch, but not for long, and for £9.99 I even feel like it is too much to pay. What else...it's crash mode done on a budget, which for a DEMO is great, however for a release it's hard to justify.
Here are the problems, and IMHO these for me, kill the feeling of wanting to play more. It feels half baked. Sound effects are severely lacking for some of the more intimate clunks, crashes, wheel spins, skids, crack and explosions. There is little to no ambience, or sense of scale in the audio work so this make it fall short. Car sound is average, it teases at sounding very very good when it's revving but alas it's just a bog standard V8 sample. Physics, very very on rails and floaty, virtually no sense of weight or impact to the cars, everything feels like it hits with similar force, driving is overly grippy but not in that classic slidey burnout way, in a new way that feels "arcade machine" as arcade racer. Graphically, very very bland, ugly even (for an UE4 title, never thought i'd say the word) as it's just very flat, even explosions and fire does not look UE4 quality. The damage effects are burnout 3 at best and non existent at worst. Only scraps and scrapes with the odd panels, no deformation from Burnout: Paradise or other details. The lighting is actually rather nice, but it's the models, meshes and texture work that doesn't complete it.
Gamplay wise, 20 levels, 1 car (plus a police skin with siren for all Plat medals, which is quite a let down) can be beaten in about 90 minutes or in my case, I got far enough before getting bored. And boring, it simply is. It's far to much about getting the linked medal combos to get the case injection boost to your crash score, than it is about actual skill in where, how, and when you throw your car into the traffic and crash breakers. Burnout 3/4 were not like this, you could easily get huge scores without getting the medals but this seems far to forced into make you play each level a very set way to even just manage to get a Gold, never mind a Platinum medal.
Thoroughly let down by this game, Dangerous Golf was at least prettier but Danger Zone suffers from the "little done little shown" ethic of games design. I want them to make a true spiritual successor to Burnout, not this what can only be described as a low key tech demo. So I can not recommend this game which is a shame IMHO.

The developers behind Danger Zone know exactly what their public wants, but it’s been tough for them to satisfy that want so far. Their first release was Dangerous Golf, a spin on Burnout‘s Crash Mode that had a rough launch and a patch that was seen as too little too late by many. After that, they took a VR tinged side trip with Lethal VR, producing a functional but unimpressive shooting gallery that didn’t stand up among the countless other entries into that genre. Now, Three Fields Entertainment is back one more time with a more direct version of Crash Mode. Danger Zone brings back the cars and the crashsmashbreakers, but it ultimately ends up offering nothing but a tantalizing glimpse at one possible future.

This is quite possibly my all time favorite game.  I've now bought it for myself 3 different times (Once on xbox, once in disk form for the PC, and once on steam), and even gifted several copies on Reddit.  It is astoundingly deep, and has some neat stacking mechanics that I thoroughly enjoyed.  However, since I don't want someone reading this review, getting the game and going in blind, I don't want to sugarcoat it.  The first 30 minutes are miserable.  Maybe even the first couple hours.  It has possibly the worst first impression of any game I've ever played.  The animations aren't particularly smooth, giving it a pretty cheap feeling, the graphics aren't great, even for 2009 (though the scale is huge), the voice acting is atrocious, and there are parts of the game that they get incredibly wrong that seem like simple mechanics (Horse Riding and Archery) - and yet, if you give it a few hours, I think it's brilliance shines through, and would hook anyone that likes the genre.
There are tons of different environments - You've got your standard medieval knights, forests, swamps, caves and dungeons.  There's a Samurai land with giant starship troopers like bugs.  Creepy cults and necromancy.  Desert nomad lands, and dune like worms.  Cities are massive, and you can go in almost every house, with worthwhile loot in most of them.  You can create permanent stat gain potions to a ridiculous degree allowing anyone that wants to become a demigod to do so.  Finding extra copies of the same spell don't just become useless inventory items, each new copy you find stacks on previous ones making them stronger, in fact you can do the same with items in the game.  You could go around killing the easiest enemies in the game, stacking hundreds of their clubs, and have a decent weapon for a while just from that.  Speaking of items, the sheer amount of them is crazy.  Where there might be 20 unique weapons in Skyrim there are hundreds in this game, and hundreds of armor items as well.  You can look like a samurai warrior, a monk, an evil wizard or a menacing black knight.
I have never found a game like this (even the sequel in my opinion, while fun, pales in comparison), it is really incredible, you just have to struggle through a bit of muck before it will shine, but I can guarantee if you wade through it, it's a game you wont forget.

The gaming:

It is an touching game if you take your time and just do what you would do by having the same choices and chances as the main character has. The contra-side:
As charming as the game is, you will need to run through the game again, having the knowledge you haven't had before and that is making your choices become more or less incorrect to what you would do usually. Therefore you are only trying to break your own destiny. You are desperately searching for the best outcome and I bet you will make it all worse.
My thought:
This game is art and not really gaming. The clicking of up to 4 possible answers/reactions on any given moment will change your personal outcome and represent how miserable your life is. It is deep, hard and true.
So:
As I said before, I like games like this. The almost everlasting run for the best possible ending on the other hand turns games like this into an mountain you can never climb up on to see what would happen by the change of every single choise. This was a solid game and worth the $5.09 I paid for it.
+ Solid story
+ Solid acting
+ Good thematic cohesion
+ Good atmosphere
- Main reveal comes a little too easily and is not terribly original
- Very simplistic gameplay
- Little replay value.
Bottom line: You should be able to tell by the trailers and description whether this is a genre you would like and, if it is, you will enjoy this game.
Extended Review:
The writing is good, better than many games, but it doesn't quite reach literary heights. I feel too often video game players are so quick to elevate game stories just because they're so often looked down on and that causes some exaggeration. It was a good story with some flaws. Telling a story completely through one-sided dialogue has its limits for how invested I become. The big reveal of the story is hardly original and borders on being a trope. Plus, it felt like I came to understand the main truth a little too quickly and easily. Some red herrings or other characters might have prolonged the mystery.
That said, there was a lot of skill in having the various parts relate to each other and tie in thematically. As I was going over the files a second time, I could see how certain phrases and events reveals a slice into the truth. This web was artfully woven in its completeness and cohesion.
The acting was well done for the most part but it really seemed like there should have been more emotion present at times, especially when certain people's fate becomes clear. The dialogue was well done overall but at times felt like it was trying a little too hard to be natural. Still, a good performance by the actress.
There truly is not much of a game. You simply query for words and unlock videos and watch them. The fun is understanding the mystery and the layers of that mystery. It would have been nice if there were documents or pictures that you could have viewed as well, to give a fuller experience (and it could have provided some misdirection to keep the mystery going).
While the database query system is a bit of a conceit, it does make it so that players will have much different experiences based on what they view and when they view it. I definitely appreciate that. Of course, there really is not much replayability, especially if you've viewed all the videos.
It was a relatively easy game to get 100% achievements on, which is nice. You can see my 100% achievement guide
if interested.

This isn't a game where you're trying to win, this is a game where you're trying to find out the truth. I got sweep up in finding more pieces to the story and learning about what I can about this woman's life and the mystery surrounding it that i didn't even notice how long I've been playing it.
This game isn't going to be for everyone since it is pretty much punching in words into a search engine and watching videos out of order. You're not solving a crime so much as you're trying to understand why and how things happened through her interviews. The story is a bit of soap opera plot but the way its presented and how the player goes about unrevealing the order of events makes you want to dig deeper for more clips.
If I do have some complaints, its that if you're a completionist, finding the smaller clips once you've pretty much watched all the bigger, more narritive clips can be tedious. There is also isn't an option once you've found all the clips to watch an edit of all of them in order (unless I missed finding that option.) Also, unless I missed something, we don't learn what happened to her after these interviews.
Overall, if you're someone who loves stories in video games and are open to new forms of interactive narratives, I would recommend this game.

Her Story is a game where you watch snippets of video, ranging from a few seconds to a couple of minutes each, of a woman being interrogated by the police regarding the murder of her husband.
Your job is to piece together the story.  You do this by searching for key words, which will then pop up new, unwatched videos.  The more videos you watch, the more clues you get as to what to search for, but also as to what happened in the story.
The videos are not in any order, although each one does have a date and a time stamp, so it is possible to piece them together chronologically if you wish.
There are well over 200 videos in all.  The beauty of this game is that no person will play it exactly the same way as anyone else.  Each person will watch the videos in a different order, but ultimately will get a clear picture as to what happened so long as they find enough videos and think about what they've learned.
I can't stress enough the brilliance of this game design.  Sam Barlow really set the bar high for what a thinking man's game can be.  Once you start to learn some of the twists in the plot you'll be glued to the screen, trying to unearth that next video that will shed more light on what's going on.
To top it all off, there are a couple of different theories on what the story is actually about, it's up to you as the player to decide for yourself which one is actually true.
Viva Seiffert, the actress, is amazing, and the music is perfect.  This is absolutely a must-have game.  No one's ever done anything quite like it.

Her Story is an interesting game. Well, less of a game and more of an experience. Well, less of an experience and more of a movie.
Basically, you're given this large database of videos you can watch that were recorded during multiple interviews with the main character. The order in which you watch them is determined basically by what you want to see first. If you type in a word, then every video where the main character says that word pops up.
So some videos appear to just be filler, but most of them contribute some sort of info to the plot. So the helpful ones give you more terms to search to get more information.
I think I had a little more than 50% of the videos discovered when I "beat" the game. I use that term loosely because the story is very vague, and largely up to the player's interpretation. However I will admit that there are some bits of the story that you can learn very early on that get endlessly repeated.
It's not a game without its flaws. It doesn't really have you solving any puzzles (other than piecing together the story). There's no information you technically need to "beat" the game, you just type "yes" and then "yes" and you're done. Also it's become a bit tedious to find every single video, which is a task easier said than done, considering there are 272 videos.
However I will ultimately recommend Her Story because, well, it's never been done before. It may not be the best new experience ever but I'd be damned to say I didn't find it interesting. I definitely believe that this is also something worth experiencing on your own, because the odds of someone having the exact same playthrough as you are incredibly slim.

Her Story is a crime story where you are challenged to figure out what happened. You are sitting at an old computer with a search program that access a series of recorded interviews. All of them are of her and you become a detective, trying to piece together her story from this short video segments.
The trick is that you can't access these in order. They are sorted by keywords. This makes the game feel something like the great text adventure games of old. From the segments you watch you have to figure out what you want to search for next. So in this case everyone's game will play out differently.
While I got to an ending of sorts after a couple of hours, I know there are a lot of segments I haven't seen. I plan on spending more time with the game, refining my investigative technique, and therefore seeing much of what I've missed. One thing in particular is nagging at the back of my mind that I particularly want to reach a resolution on.
If you only want to play games with a lot of action, you probably already know Her Story isn't for you. But if you a looking for a game where story is important and you enjoy the challenge of connecting the dots, I recommend you pick up Her Story. For $6 it's a great deal, only made better by the current 10% discount.

First of all, something important: This game is NOT Overwatch. Many people compare it to Overwatch, and honestly, I don't blame them. The marketingcampaign pretty much only showed the colourfull characters and nothing about the actual gamemodes, so let me explain them for you.
In terms of gameplay, the game reminds me a little bit of smite, you level your character, get equipment and improve your overall stats. The equipment itself, you can get out of packs you buy in the game for ingame currency(no real money transactions at the current point in time)
The game has a campaign, consisting of 8 levels, each of them lasting for about an hour. While the humor is decently funny(if you like the boarderlands-style of humor) and the very first mission is really awesome, most of the other ones are just waves of mobs you have to shoot before they destroy some thing you have to protect(often you only have to destroy the hordes, but that is pretty much the same but with less risk).
The meat of the game though, is the PvP, consisting of 3 modes, each of them featuring 2 maps.
Capture: You have to controll 3 points, generationg points for your team until you finally win.
Incursion: the most MOBA-like of the modes, where both teams fight in a single lane to destroy 2 sentrys in the enemy base, errecting towers along the way and capturing neutral merccamps while waves of creeps try to push through the lane.
Meltdown: This mode consists of 2 lanes, where you have to push the minions through, so they can sacrifice themselfs in the enemy base, generating points for your team.
The pros of the game:
-Meltdown and Incursion are pretty unique modes
-There is a wide variety of diverse characters
- although it is sometimes repetative, I find the humor of the game to be overall amusing
The cons:
-The game sometimes has random framedrops and starts to stutter for no apparent reason, most of the time you can only fix it by restarting
-There are WAY to many colourfull effects all over the place, making it hard to see stuff, ESPECIALLY with meleecharacters
-As if it weren't hard enough to see, the weaponmodels are really big, and even at max FOV, block big parts of your screen
-Many of the characters are really imbalanced at the current state in the game
-Not only, do you have to unlock the equipment for the characters, many of their abilitys are locked as well and you can only unlock them by individually leveling every single character over many games(it can take you over 10 games to get all of your unlockable abilitys on a single character!!!)
-You have to unlock every individual character, at this point in time, with around 50 hours of gametime, I am still missing 2 characters and it will take me around 5 more hours at least to unlock them
-unitcolission is a gigantic problem in this game, many times you get stuck on creeps, other players, random scenery and so on, and thanks to the limited cameraperspective you don't even see what you are stuck on! worst of all, if you ever get thrown in the air, it is really easy to get juggled, rendering you unable to do anything, since every time you land on some creep or player on your way down, it stops your fallingspeed for a moment, most of the time you will be dead before you hit the ground again.
-in the Incursionmode, snipers can destroy the first of the 2 sentrys without even going to the enemy base or pushing creepewaves there! The problem already existed during the open beta and was reported, and it is still around, 2 weeks after release!!!
I would love to be able to recommend this game to you, belive me, I really do... But I simply can't. There are way to many problems, and the obnoxious unlocksystem(you have to unlock the characters, their abilitys AND their items) already put you at a disadvantage if you were to start now, let alone, in a month or 2!
If you consider getting this game, I recommend getting it now, because I am pretty sure, 2-3 months down the line, most of the people still playing the game will not only be experienced pros, but they will also have unlocked everything and just stomp you for hours and hours.
It's a shame, but that's how it is...

I cam into this game expecting a decent, space-based adventure with a relatively engaging story and some puzzle elements.
I got all of that, and so much more.
J:AtS starts you off on a ship with a vaguely creepy AI, and soon enough you're remotely piloting a robot through space, exploring a mystery spanning an entire solar system. The beginning gives you a sense that there's something off with the whole situation, and the revelations along the way are more than enough to keep you engaged in the story to see it through. The story starts off small and expands itself to encompass multiple species, planets, and a series of events that took place over many years.
Then we get to the puzzles. I consider myself a reasonably intelligent person when it comes to solving puzzles, but there were times in the story I was basically forced to consult a third party guide to continue at all. There are a few puzzles that require you to sort of half-solve them before realizing you don't have what you need yet, and need to explore another planet and solve other puzzles first. This wouldn't be an issue if there was much of any direction as far as where you need to go immediately after you leave the first planet. There was also a point at which I had to re-solve a puzzle that I had already solved. I would assume that it was a bug, but it was still rather frustrating. Some of the late-game puzzles are just plain aggravating, including one that fully resets whenever you make a mistake, even if you've mostly completed it. The biggest issue is that the game gives you very limited clues on what you actually need to do to solve many of these puzzles.
To be fair, the majority of these issues are encompassed entirely in a small number of puzzles, and the majority of them are quite intuitive and interesting.
Overall, the game was very solid and I would recommend it, especially considering that the majority of the development was handled by two people. Two people managed to create a more interesting and engaging experience than many AAA development teams, and that is something that should always be applauded. From what I ascertained in the end credits, many names in the game were the people that supported the game on IndieGoGo, and adding something like that in is always a cool way to acknowledge those who supported you.

A somewhat strange but unique and interesting space adventure.
The female A.I. of the starship you - astrobiologist Rachel Manners with a voice and face - are on awakes you from cryo-jail to help her repair the ship's systems after it was hit by meteors from the planet it had been orbiting. All alone on the ship you wonder what happened to the other crew members, soon realizing that you had been in cryo for 60 years. With the tech, logistic and even moral support of the ship's A.I. "JULIA" you make out to trace back the steps of the long dead crew as their expeditions had left them behind on the various planets and moons in the apparently fictional solar system you are in, far away from earth and with seemingly no immediate way back, staying yourself in orbit while exploring the planets' surfaces, caverns, canyons, jungles, deserts and waters through the eyes of another A.I. companion, a mecha drone named "MOBOT", who is voiced as well.
J.U.L.I.A. is a hidden item adventure game but offering the convenience of a button to highlight things in the world you can interact with. It doesn't have classic adventure puzzling and item combination work (you don't have a visible inventory to begin with) but consists mostly of exploration, of collecting and analyzing samples from the planets and of codeworking and puzzle-like minigames that vary from planet to planet and technology to technology you handle. I remember at least one time-based challenge but it wasn't too hard. There is rather little handholding; there is a mission log that states your basic goals and that memorizes some passwords, but these are brief one-liners that really only give you a very basic idea about what to do. There were some puzzles/minigames where I couldn't see the solutions all-too-soon which is why I looked up a walkthrough a few times. The mechanics of the puzzles aren't complicated by nature, but it's sometimes tricky to get into them and actually "see" the solution. But if you do it can feel quite rewarding.
Soon you'll have to fly between planets back and forth in the search for items and connections of events that happened across the solar system, eventually discovering things like betrayal, suffering, crimes and questions that transpire human existence. I was never annoyed by the back and forth - I thought it was well made and greatly immersive. You'll actually want to understand what happened in the solar system and what led to the de-facto failure of your crew's research mission that was apparently meant to be vital to the far-away Earth, becoming something of a space Sherlock Holmes. These events can feel confusing at times, especially since a significant part of them is expressed through text logs of former crew members scattered across the planets. But there are even optional "puzzles" that are basically only there to help you understand the series of events.
I sometimes felt like a helpless observer of long past events and can imagine that this feeling was very much intended for this is what Rachel Manners would probably feel if she was real. There are JULIA and MOBOT, but even with the first having a great voice actress and showing sometimes more empathy than Rachel herself regarding the effects the expeditions had in the solar system and the latter cracking a joke or being sarcastic despite having claimed to have no "emotional" code or whatever - in the end they are not human and Rachel still pretty much all alone. This is why this game can be pretty scary in some ways too: Supported by some eerie music and primal or coldly minimalistic sounds you see a lot of things, yet you can often only suggest and imagine how the actual events were back then and how your colleagues each found their own, sometimes cruel demise among the rubble of their once bold mission, far away from anything that could ever be related to as a "home" or place of warmth. And even then you may still wonder if there is something lurking here and there ready to take you (or MOBOT, as he takes all the punches aimed for you) apart and whether there is a way to undo certain wrongs and show that humans aren't that bad after all.
The great immersion is helped by what feels like a good amount of scientific knick-knack. You can analyze all sorts of planet samples, but from what I got you don't actually have to do that with too many items. But you can, if you want, and not only get some achievements as an aspiring astrobiologist yourself through that but also some actual nice explanations. Your spaceship has rather detailed interfaces too even though you don't actually use much of it (anymore - the original game from 2012 or so apparently had you use more of the ship's systems). But it's there, it looks cool and it helps the feeling.
A tiny complaint: The text logs of the crew members sometimes felt too "casual" for my taste. Doctors, scientific guys and I believe even military types using emotes when texting each other, while being far away from home on a serious mission with more or less severe and increasingly dangerous problems at hand? I don't know about that.

As pumped as I was to get this game, I can't help but feel like I should have done more research.  This game looks incredible at a glance, combining real time strategy with third person shooting action with a dragon (not enough games let play as dragons like that IMO) and all this complimented by the political decisions you have to make between each match.  So much to do, and yet none of it is as deep or thought provoking as you may think.
On the plus side of things, the graphics and the voice and conversations of this game are pretty good.  While some of the unit designs seem uninspired, all the characters aboard the Raven (the hub you go to between turns) all have intersting designs.  Futhermore, these characters you converse with have their own distinct personalities and are generally enjoyable to listen too.  The political banters these guys  get into often reflects current real world problems, and getting to have your say in them can be fun.  However, the decisions you make are always either "yes" or "no".  This may work for some things, but other times I didn't like the all or nothing approach this game presented to me.  Overall though, this was still my favorite part, as it was fun to see their reactions.
Unfortunately what you may consider to be the main part of the game, the RTS and turn based map sections are lacking.  On the map, too much comes down to sheer luck.  Whether it's what cards you get, which you can use to boost your advantage or cripple an enemy in some fashion, or just moving into the wrong place at the wrong time, there is just too much that can change in one turn.  Sure many strategy games are like this, but in this one it feels more like luck instead of skill.  In battle, the real time strategy elements are hardly even there.  It is difficult or sometimes even impossible to try to micro, and the macro only consists of taking over building plots and building one of a very limited number of buildings (only five different ones all things considered) and keeping them from being taken over.  It just feels like a tug-of-war.  The only fun thing is playing as the dragon, although I found that to be repetitive after a while as it was so much easier to sabatoge the enemy's attempts at expanding than it was to fight with my units as the designers probably hoped you would.
Overall, this isn't a terrible game.  Though it has some good points, they aren't enough to overcome the badones.  I would certainly not recommend this at full price.  Even at 50% off, you may not get your money's worth, as much of the value of this game comes from playing it repeatedly and making different political decisions, but it's hard to go through all of those conversations a second time.  This game is worth a look ONLY if you are looking for a strategy game that tries some things different.  Otherwise, there isn't much here to warrant your attention.

Dragon Commander throws so many game styles and systems together that it is a little overwhelming at the start. It takes an hour or two to wrap ones head around it all. The balance of the game deteriorates the further you get into it as I found on my play-through on Normal difficulty.  It was still a very fun experience because you continuously master all of the systems and use them to utterly destroy your opponents.
Everyone has been touting the game's characters and the political decisions you make based on their proposals. This is by far the best part of the game. Decision making is interesting because it often rewards you even if you thought there could have been severe detriments to your empire. Great writing and voice acting overall.
The real time strategy (rts) portion of this game has a learning curve. If you have ever played an rts that relies on heavy hotkey usage like Starcraft, you should be able to master it very quickly. The best part of the rts is playing as the dragon and gaining advantages on the AI by using it to pick off units or obliterate groups with the end game abilities. There are a lot of unit abilities you can use to gain advantages as well. Two that I recommend are the warlock meteor and the trooper's spoils of war.
The one main problem with the rts portion of the game is that if you have a greater than 60%+ chance to win, the battle boils down to selecting all of your units and attacking the enemy base right at the start. At that point I just started using the Auto-Resolve system whereby the Generals conduct battles automatically similar to the board game RISK. Unlike RISK, though, I've never had a significantly larger force lose because of dice rolls...Maps where you have 50% or less chance of winning actually take some strategy to beat, but the AI has flaws in its behavior that are exploitable, especially with the dragon. If you have less than 20% chance to win, then you might as well retreat and come back at a later turn.
Overall it is a good thing that the game lets you skip useless or tedious battles.

In Miasmata, the player explores an island in search of plants, to craft a cure for a disease. The game is almost entirely non combat, which may put off some gamers. You will be attacked by a creature at various times, but its best to just run away and hide. You can also be injured by falling down hills, and will die if you don't heal fast enough. Other threats include thirst, sleep deprivation and drowning. Crafting plants can restore health and provide buffs. I loved how much freedom the player is given. Miasmata is a lesson for AAA developers about how to create an open world without waypoint markers, and still guide the player to quest locations in an intelligent way. There are lots of clues to find such as maps and journal fragments, which point you in the right direction. If you're willing to overlook some minor flaws such as graphical glitches and menu presentation, this is a really nice, intelligent game, and easily worth the indie game purchase price.

Miasmata is a tough game to recommend.  It's not that the game is particularly bad or anything (I think it's a great experience honestly), but it's one of those games that is so unique that it will most likely polarize people.
Miasmata is a game of survival and exploration.  You wake up on the shores of an uncharted island stricken with a plague.  Your primary goal is to cure it, and you do this by collecting plants, researching them, and discovering their properties.  This is what you'll spend most of the game doing, aside from dealing with the occasional run in with the creature that roams the isle.  The game is highly immersive.  It pulls you in with a strong sense of place.
The only major issues with this game comes from the technical side.  There are lots of graphical glitches here and there (the pop in is particularly bad at some points), and the framerate occasionally dips (at least on my laptop it did).  Considering the game was designed entirely by two brothers, I can actually look past most of these issues.
If you want a gaming experience like nothing you've played before, I would highly recommend this game.  If you are not the patient type, I would caution you on this one.  This is definitely a game that rewards patient exploration, and if that's your thing, then you are in for a treat.

Miasmata is a great idea with a somewhat flawed execution.
You're a scientist on an island looking for a cure. To find this cure you have to find plants and create potions, while triangulating landmarks to create your own map of the island.
The island is huge and you're free to go wherever you want, as long as you can keep yourself alive. You have to be careful that you don't dehydrate, drown, get killed by a creature (I haven't encountered it myself yet) or that you take your medicine in time.
The game is played from a first person perspective, which actually works quite alright, but walking and running (and especially stopping/slowing down) can be awkward and clumsy. It tries to be realistic by slowing down your character when climbing up the hills or speeding up when you're heading downwards. Most of the times it seems random and I've lost count of how many times I've fallen.
You're also allowed to carry a maximum of 3 different plants at the same time, and you can't carry more than one of the same plant. So most of the times you have to make multiple trips. However, there are cabins scattered across the island. These cabins allow you to transfer your plants between any of them, which helps, but limiting the amount of plants you can carry is still a bit frustrating. On the other hand, it does create a certain tension so I guess there's something to be said for it. Especially traveling when it's dark is not recommended, because it can get pitchblack without any torches. And then there's this creature I keep hearing about...
So, I'm having some mixed emotions here. I guess I shall be taking my journal and compass, and enter the world once more to see if my opinion changes for the better... or for the worse.

Gone is the "star" system in WG:EE, so every unit is unlocked right away. This kinda kills the purpose of singleplayer a bit, though you can still play that for funs. The campaign this time around is not a mission-by-mission thing, but a strategic map game where you move units and have them fight over territories in relatively short battles. Can be fun, but also a little repetitive. It can also be a bit unforgiving if you mess up, but anyone who played the first game knows that already.
So basically this is a multiplayer game with some singleplayer stuff. Your choice of whether or not you get this depends upon how interested you are in multiplayer, because that's the core of this game.

All I ask of any game is that it does what it sets out to do and does it well enough to be fun. That's why I can thumb up hidden object games and super bare-bones indie titles, because I don't expect every game to be Invisible, Inc. or The Talos Principle. This is one of those rare times when that's not enough, however. Time Gentlemen, Please! and Ben There, Dan That! certainly do what they set out to do and do it competently, but the bargain-basement mechanics and severely dated humor sets them too far back to recommend in this day and age.
Ben There, Dan That! (the first game in the series, despite the pack name) follows the adventures of Ben and Dan as they quest to get their broken television working. This gets them sucked up into an alien spaceship full of portals to alternate dimensions, where they must assemble the items they need to return home. Once they do, an even more ridiculous set of events ties the conclusion into the opening of Time Gentlemen, Please! where Ben and Dan rule the world. A characteristically bone-headed decision on their part annihilates humanity, and they have to ♥♥♥♥ up the timestream even worse to set it all right again.
It's a hell of an adventure that could have been pretty engaging, had it been handled better. Right away, the games make some painfully amateur mistakes to hook the player by starting right in the middle of an adventure, explaining virtually nothing, and then segueing directly into their dumb TV woes. At no point are you going to get a compelling reason to care about their misadventures, partly because this setup is so weak and partly because it only serves to propel all their jokes. It's a parody game through and through, but one you've doubtless seen before at this point. There are the jokes about looting homes for items, about grabbing useless items because they'll be needed, and every other bit of point-and-click metahumor that Sam and Max did better.
The puzzling at least does its job, but only barely. Each area or dimension you end up in has an unspoken objective, usually to get the random item that unlocks the next area. With a limited number of scenes and items to interact with, you're likely to stumble upon the puzzle solutions before you even realize there are puzzles present. That's exactly what happened to me in the dimension where America took over England, I just clicked a few funny lines with the pub-goers and clicked the items present, and that was all it took. Despite having old-school commands for look and use and talk and items and use your partner Dan, all you need to do is grab the right items and talk to the right people and you're golden the whole way through.
I think what really pushed this one over the line from passable to intolerable was the art style. We're talking MSPaint here, all the way down to the animations which are pretty much two frames each. Ben and Dan gyrate around like a pair of demented cactuars and everyone else is barely alive, usually just with blinking eyes or wiggling fingers. The plain landscapes certainly make it easy to find the few items there are but foul up the dialogue something fierce. They went with the LucasArts-style floating colored text but without the chunky pixels or intelligent color choices, the outlines of backgrounds and letters blend together into a nasty, eye-straining mess.
I'm sure these two titles would have found more favor eight years ago, when adventure games were still sort-of-but-not-really dead and metahumor hadn't been beaten even deader by Borderlands. But even then I can't say I would have enjoyed them because they make so many little mistakes that add up to big headaches. More than that, though, there's nothing of substance to help you power through other than some awfully belabored jokes. I can tolerate a rough or even bad game for awhile but I have little patience for parodies that are not on point, and these two lost the point long, long ago.

Time Gentlemen, Please! and Ben There, Dan That! Special Edition Double Pack Review - Raymond KT
Summary: What’s worse than finding out that your future evil selves have set about a series of events that wipes out all human life on the planet? Going back in time to fix things with half a mind on preventing coathangers from ever being invented, and accidentally setting up an alternate-universe Hitler with an unstoppable army of dinosaur clones instead, that’s what! Whoopsie! [Zombie Cow Studios]
British. Humor. Lots and lots of British humor. In a nutshell, that is the way Time Gentlemen, Please! can be explained. The game has relatively simple graphics and color schemes, and the music is also simplistic and not overwhelming in the slightest bit. The music actually doesn’t have much to overwhelm, because all of the dialogue must be read for yourself, so no clashing of the voices and music here! However, you must sift through many jokes in just about every dialogue session to read what you really need. Now, I don’t mind British humor one bit, but when you beat a dead cat so much that you can’t recognize that little ball of fur anymore as it blows away in the wind, that’s a bit much.
This game is sure to delight some old-school gamers out there. But not my cup of tea

is a very run of the mill, very mediocre, slowly paced racing game set in the 1950's. And it's overpriced. But in the interest of full disclosure I paid $1.49USD on Bundlestars and used the key activation.
The game has some semi-wonky physics that adhere to the laws of inertia ten fold. It's very slow to get going and even more difficult to get something to stop moving or to go in a different direction. I get that the cars were heavier back then and the engines weaker but it may be taken to bit too far here. But again, at a lower entry point I wouldn't expect much more. They aren't terribly bad physics that can't be overcome through adaptation and it's nothing that improving the cars can't make feel a lot better. However, the E-brake will make the game become an uncontrollable ridge racer offshoot so don't use it unless you have no other choice.
There is a slowly paced progression in career mode (which is the only mode). Very few cars to choose from. However, there are quite a few options to customize those cars cosmetically in regards to bumpers, wheels and paintjobs. You can upgrade performance here as well though all the stats are described as percentages making comparisons between the cars specs impossible without testing them yourself.
The career mode is broken into what are essentially rival races. You have a set number of tasks to complete before each rival race is unlocked. For example, 3 clean overtakes, win 2 races with different cars or stay in the slipstream for some duration (drafting in otherwords). And it goes on this way. There are some style points very reminiscent of something like kudos from PGR or something that made your nitro charge faster in Burnout for driving into oncoming traffic or having near misses and it does make use of a turbocharger function that effectively acts as a nitro.

Motorama is hands-down one of the literal worst racing games that I have ever played. And it's all because of the physics engine it uses. Every little input, the game percieves as 100x stronger, giving out the feeling that the road is at all times made of damn solid ice. Please keep in mind that you are given 2 car choices at the beginning and I took the one with
Your car will always, somehow, end up spinning on the road. Oh, and when you try to turn the wheel and get back into the race? You do another spin. That forces you to restart the race and play it over and over and over until you learn to do millimetric movements of the controller's bumper.
Also, I encountered a lot of bugs in just 30 minutes of playing. Apparently sometimes when I press forward, the game thinks I pressed reverse. I tried it on both keyboard and controller, to make sure it was not an external input fault. Guess what: it wasn't. That and a lot of clipping through texture, visual bugs, the npcs you are racing against can pass through the cars in the trafic like ghosts while you have to avoid them.
TL;DR: Physics engine is the worst, you can't complete a single race because the road will seem like it's made out of ice. Also, the game itself is a buggy mess. Don't buy, under any circumstance.
UPDATE: After writing this review, before uninstalling the game I just HAD to create a new category in my library, titled "Never to play again". This game is the "proud", first, and as of now, only member of this category.

I had the pleasure of having this game gifted to me, and I appreciate being able to play through this interative visual novel. I completed the game in one sitting, which took a little less than an hour.
If you like reading, interactive visual novels, and decision trees, then you will really enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are fantastic, the are is very well-done and each scene contains a lot of detail. The music and sounds (ambient background noise) is also great, however, I noticed that the game's audio looping could use some work (it is very obvious when the tracks are starting over again). Note that I like to dj/mix in my spare time, so I particularly look out for this in videogames if it's obvious enough. The music changes with the scenery, and during "Dark World" scenes - which can occur and conclude very quickly - the music will react accordingly; this aspect of the game is very well-done.
The controls are very simple, you are just clicking on dialogue/decision options with your mouse. The learning curve is minimal, and the concept/theme of the game is explained to your very close to the beginning of gameplay.
Your character is offered a "pact" that will allow him to barter off percentages of his soul for wishes. The percentage of the soul to be used as payment is determined by how critical the wish is to your character. For example, making your bus show up early costs 3% of your soul, while discovering the answer to ancient questions will require 200% of your soul (otherwise impossible). You are given many opportunities to use trade parts of your soul for wishes, and finding out all the possibilities adds to the replayability of the game.
Granted, most of the decision trees have few long-term consequences; however, there are multiple endings, and obtaining each one depends on your precise decisions during key moments in the game. The game is fairly linear, but the journey - especially your first playthrough - can be very enjoyable if you like story-driven games and interactive fiction. After one or two playthroughs, you will be able to just breeze through most of the game by repeatedly clicking your mouse until you reach the crtitical decision points in the game.
You are given "skill" points to distribute in the beginning of the game, and your score for each skill (athletics/health, social/manipulation, intelligence, and charisma) will influence some of the encounters and outcomes in the game.
There are achievements for the 100% completion junkies, and this requires multiple playthroughs. Since you ALWAYS have to start from a fresh game after reaching the end (you cannot just save near the end of the game and keep loading to view different endings), Achieving 100% can take at least an extra hour on top of your total playtime.
If you are interested in the theme of using your soul as a bartering tool, visual novels, and text-heavy gameplay, then you should give Soul Gambler a try.
Recommend!

Soul Gambler is a choose your own adventure type visual novel. You start the game by choosing to put points in four categories: Strength, Persuasion, Charisma and Intelligence. Basic gameplay involves choosing from a list of dialogue or actions. Stat checks during the story will often allow you to make special choices that will affect the game.
I've only completed 1 playthrough as of writing this review, which took about 30 minutes. There are a variety of achievements to earn which show that your choices will have some effect on the outcome. This game was entertaining enough that I want to play through differently just to see how it changes.
The graphics are well drawn and nice to look at. The sound is a little boring and doesn't add much to the gameplay. The writing kept me interested throughout, and made me want to give it another play.
The big downside is the length. The playthrough took about 30 minutes, and I imagine another playthrough would be shorter since I could skip through a lot of the repetitive dialogue. Looking at the list of achievements, there don't appear to be enough endings to require more than 2-3 playthroughs. So, about 90 minutes of gameplay is all you will get out of this. It's fun while it lasts, but definitely think about your budget when making the purchase. Whatever 90 minutes of entertainment is worth to you, that's how much I'd spend.
I recommend this game, but do keep it mind the short length. I got it in a bundle so did not spend much, and did enjoy my time with it.

Her Story is a crime story where you are challenged to figure out what happened. You are sitting at an old computer with a search program that access a series of recorded interviews. All of them are of her and you become a detective, trying to piece together her story from this short video segments.
The trick is that you can't access these in order. They are sorted by keywords. This makes the game feel something like the great text adventure games of old. From the segments you watch you have to figure out what you want to search for next. So in this case everyone's game will play out differently.
While I got to an ending of sorts after a couple of hours, I know there are a lot of segments I haven't seen. I plan on spending more time with the game, refining my investigative technique, and therefore seeing much of what I've missed. One thing in particular is nagging at the back of my mind that I particularly want to reach a resolution on.
If you only want to play games with a lot of action, you probably already know Her Story isn't for you. But if you a looking for a game where story is important and you enjoy the challenge of connecting the dots, I recommend you pick up Her Story. For $6 it's a great deal, only made better by the current 10% discount.

The acting in all those videos make this game worth more than $5. Amazing direction by Sam Barlowe, astonishing acting by [placeholder for the actress' name, I don't it have in my mind now], and the twisted yet believable story make Her Story one of the best detective, FMV game on the market.
Also a big +1 for making me use pen and paper again for a video game. It's possible to write all my notes in some word document but the excitement of filling up 2 sides of an A4 paper with theories and keywords is hard to find these days.

This is the first Steam review I've written, but I felt compelled to do so after finishing this outstanding game just now.
As the store page description states, the gameplay consists of you being presented with a PC screen accurately designed to look like a CRT monitor from the late 90s or early 2000s. You're given limited access to a police database that contains lots of short video clips (varying in length from 5 seconds to nearly 3 minutes) of a woman being interviewed by the police. The authentic appearance and audio of the videos are just as spot-on as the CRT monitor.
You begin by typing search terms into the search field. If that word is spoken in any of the videos, those videos will display as your search results. You then watch the videos – thankfully an eye icon is displayed on any video that you have not viewed – and listen/read the subtitles. As you watch more videos, you gain ideas for more search terms, which gives you access to more videos, and so on.
My immediate reaction when finishing: Holy s--t, this game! It's so good! It grabbed very quickly, and sunk its hooks further in the more I played, due to me continuing to receive what I can imagine are dopamine hits in my brain as I slowly unravel and realize things.
Obviously, I'm avoiding spoilers, but I can't recommend this innovative game enough. Maybe it's the "high" that I'm still on because I just finished it, but Her Story currently has a very good chance of my personal GOTY. It's that good, that innovative, that gripping, and that impactful.

I'm not huge on FMV games but I love a good mystery.  The premise of this game intrigued me and for 5 bucks I decided to give it a try.  I am so glad I did.  You are given access to police archives of an interview with a woman whose husband was murdered in the 1990's.  Each video clip offers hints at other possible keywords to search for in the database to unlock more videos.  You ultimately have to put together the puzzle of a sort of "whodunit" and solve the mystery.  The clips add twists and turns and a few even little puzzles to solve within the video itself.  It doesn't take that long to unlock the whole thing, a few hours total, but well worth the time and effort.
I finished the game wanting more, in a good way.  You know how when you finish an amazing book and you're left there like "Wow, this was so good, why did this have to end?"  That's how I feel here.  And frankly, I would totally read a book series just based on this few hour long video game.  That's how good it was.
If you like mysteries, don't hesitate.  This game is amazing!
