***THIS GAME REQUIRES INTERNET EXPLORER 10 AND UP***
I believe the developers should make this note much larger rather then just in the additional notes section of requirements. If you don't have it installed the game gets stuck on the loading bar.
I also feel it is important to go into this game knowing what to expect of it. This game is actually an interactive novel with multiple endings and choices to be made. It is by no means up to the length and high standard of Cinders, but that is why the price is lower.
The game offers a nice amount of options that will send you in different story sections. The endings are rather similar, but are different enough to spark curiousity for another play through or two. You may want to read the achievements section just to give you an aim of how to get to them. The attributes in the game matter more then you might expect. You have to pass certain checks in order to get certain dialogue. If you don't have a certain amount of intelligence you might fail a check that requires it.
The different sections of dialogue you can run into if you play your attributes/choices/dialogue options right will lead you to interesting little easter egg things before the end of the game such as ending up in the hospital or on the run from the cops. These are the areas the game truly shines. The multiple endings are interesting, but not as fun as these side routes that lead to them.
All in all I got this game for a buck before it got greenlit from indie gala and it has been well worth it. I'm not sure if it is worth the full $5 steam price, but it would for sure be worth $2.50

Imaginative is a term we, as people, use to describe all sorts of great works in all art forms. However, few games have had the astounding right to be called imaginative. Yet Psychonauts, with its charm, witty humor, brilliantly engaging characters, and wholly incredible worlds is certainly one of them.
Psychonauts comes from the mind of Tim Schafer, as the box art proclaims, and it shows in spades. Infamous in the gaming community for his charming and quirky adventure games from his times spent at Lucasarts, Schafer was a master at the genre. But when the time came for Schafer to found his own company, Double Fine, he made his grand overture to the masses with a 3-D action adventure platformer, Psychonauts, a massive departure from what fans have come to expect from him.
But you know all that, what matters is the game, and the game is utterly brilliant. It follows a very character driven plot cut up between sections of platforming. Psychonauts follows this sure trend for a long time, with the exception of one area, the asylum. The asylum halts the story to spend time on 4 entire levels which to some may be unexpected and a bit of an annoyance. However, I saw this as a welcome roadblock as it gave me the time to explore the wonderfully damaged minds of the inmates...which sounds rather dark when you think about it too much. That's actually the main gimmick of Psychonauts. As you may or may not know, exploring the inner mindscapes of the people who surround you is the central premise of the game. The concept alone is good, but what pushes the game past normality is the characters, writing, stupifying mindscapes and well-crafted psychic abilities you discover on your journey.
These, in tangent with the main hub world (that I'll explain later), are the main attractions of Psychonauts. First, the characters and writing are top notch. Every character from the lovable nutty mentor to Raz, the psychic boy whom you control, to the smallest 5-minute appearances like the suave Mr. Pokeylope the turtle. These characters are held together by masterful Schafer-style writing that makes me laugh at every turn. The gameplay side has Raz collecting a variety of collectibles which tend to lead to increasing your rank. Your rank dictates what psychic abilities you can collect and upgrade, however, some powers are in the minds of others and help expand upon the gameplay. This became another main driving force behind my urge to keep playing. I wanted to see what cool psychic power I would receive next, and I was never disappointed. Although, even the writing, characters, and psychic abilities wouldn't matter if the levels were not fun, which they are. They involve jumping into the minds of others to help solve their problems by fighting their demons and sorting emotional baggage, literally. These levels are not only tons of fun to play because of varying gameplay elements and very interesting concepts like becoming a Godzilla-like monster and destroying a city made up of fish people, but they also act as a platform for the characters and writing to leap off. The characters are often expanded upon by exploring the depths of their minds and it can offer some really witty and clever writing. All these things and more offer a true gem of a game.
However, it isn't perfect. It houses some major problems. The biggest all-encompassing issue being the pacing of the story and gameplay. The game is divided into two halves, one which is basically a long tutorial including about 4 levels, and a pure brain exploration half which features few things to do other than progress through about 6 other levels. It creates an annoying sucker punch as well everything you've come to expect from the game is just stripped away. The brilliance is still there including the things I mentioned earlier but a lot of other good bits are completely hacked off. For instance, your main hub world is a psychic summer camp, one I quite like. It has charm, lots to explore, great character interactions, and an overall atmospherically poetic setting. I loved it yet when the second half hits, the camp becomes barren without characters, atmosphere, thanks to it being perpetually nighttime, and nothing to do. It is very bothersome. This also affects the story. See, as you explore the first half of the game you come to expect that there are a few things wrong with this camp, and you begin to feel adventurous like you're ready to take it on, but all of the sudden the game turns to night and all that freedom, adventure, and mystery the game had just kinda is explained. It feels like if you were in an escape room that successfully managed rather than scaring you to make you intrigued in the story of the room, but half way through the attendant entered and just toured the room with you. It felt annoying and rather brought on as the entire pacing split happens very impromptu.
There are a number of other issues with the game, like only ok music, fairly easy boss battles and some forced portions like requiring an item that costs what Bill Gates is worth, but the worst of it all is the final level in the game. It is the masterstroke of all critics of the game when people praise it, the Meat Circus, that, ironically, has a hilarious name for being an infuriating level. First and personally the most annoying thing to me is the fact that it is an escort mission. Just hearing that might make your boner deflate like seeing your grandmother but it gets worse. It's not the Resident Evil 4 type of escort mission where you can stuff your escourtee in a nearby trashcan and be fine. No, it's the opposite. You serve a small child that, without spoilers, you'd pretty much be doing the exact opposite of saving if this were any other situation. To top it off he has a high pitched ear grading voice and never shuts up. Oh, and he's perpetually in danger with a health bar shorter than your temper while playing this section. Plus, you have little control over him he is dumb and can't stay put which leads to the type of migraines that turn your vision red. And that's just one part! It also has an enormous climax of difficulty that will suck your life bar up like a smoothie, that the game drinks while laying upon your defeated husk of a body that it now uses as a lawn chair. It feels insulting, especially because all of this is not why I hate this level despite it having a number of more problems I can't even mention, the worst problem is that it has no clever design. With minimal writing, no reason to collect anything, no new powers and pseudo-timers to propel your platforming love into k-mart's value bin where you throw your copy of this game. However, this all culminates at the very end of the level with a set of alright boss fights (3 with the same guy), and a pretty good end with all the heart and wonder of the rest of the game.
Yet even with the breadth of issues this game has I find myself loving it. The pros heavily outweigh the cons in such a way that I can't recommend it more. All of the good parts are well worth the low price tag and it rests on my list of favorite games of all time. But don't let me over hype it, buy the game and see for yourself, maybe it will be the game that changes your life, or maybe you'll just not find it that fun. Yet still, there's only one way to find out. Buy it.
For those who skipped to the end:
BUY IT. DON'T HESITATE, IT'S GREAT!

I was very impressed with this game overall. It starts out pretty rough at least partly by design, as being thrown into an unfamiliar setting and being so physically weak that you can barely move around and get easily lost are all part of the character. However, as you play the game you will learn how to get around more easily with the cartography mechanics, creating the right drugs to get you out of tough situations, and just as a result of internalizing the game's systems. Each time you create a shot that returns some of your physical abiltiies to normal the regular paths become easier to traverse and more difficult places become reachable. By the end of the game, you can get around so easily that it's hard to remember how rough it was at the beginning. Overall, the experience is very satisfying and I throughly recommend the game to anyone with the patience to get through the slower and tougher parts early on.

Two Worlds is a game I had originally heard of, but never played until about a year ago. I didn't keep up with the hype and the marketing for this game, and it was because of a YouTuber called ProJared and his review of this game that I bought it, mainly to see if it was as bad as he said it was. And - surprise, surprise - he was right.
Two Worlds, according to ProJared's Review (be prepared to see ProJared's name come up a LOT in this "review"), was going to put another game - The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion - to shame. Needless to say, it didn't even come close to matching Oblivion in anything. And I'm going to prove it.
The game starts off with the Main Character and his twin sister, Kira, riding through the rain. Kira is injured, and falls off the horse. Here is where one of the many problems of Two Worlds starts to show. First off, the voice acting. It's God-awful. Every single voice actor - well, with an exception or two - is bad. Every line of speech is forced, no emotion is in the dialogue and even worse, the text in the game looks like it was written by someone trying to emulate Shakespeare.
The story for this game is simple. As the Main Character goes to look for a shelter that he and Kira can stay in for the night to keep out of the rain, Kira gets kidnapped. About six months later, in the first village you're in (I don't remember what it was called, just more proof of how bad this game is) you recieve a letter telling you that your sister is alive. After reading the letter, the village elder gives you your first quest, the traditional cliché quest at the beginning of most RPGs out there: clear a cave of monsters. You do that, you come out of the cave which is really a temple, and when you're through with that task, some guy from the first village tells you that some "hard warriors" have come looking for you. After that, you find the man who kidnapped your sister - Gandohar - and he tells you to go and meet his master Reist in the Goat's Cave. You meet Reist, and he tells you to go and talk to Gandohar. Refresh my memory, why did I need to go in there again? Anyways, speaking with Gandohar reveals that he "claims" that he wants to help Kira, and to do that, he needs you to go and collect four treasures representing the four elements: Fire, Wind, Water, and Earth. There's also a fifth piece that binds them together just like that ring from Lord of the Rings. And apparently, only the Main Character and Kira can touch the key and nobody else can, similar to the Vampire Killer whip from the Castlevania franchise. That's really all I can say about the story, because I pretty much quit playing after that.
Gameplay: The gameplay is somewhat similar to Oblivion, but they somehow managed to screw that up. When you're fighting anything in this game, and I mean anything, it all basically amounts to a button masher swinging wildly at everything around you, and I mean everything. There's no surefire way to be sure that you're hitting something other than the blood that shoots out of enemies, and the punch sound that accompanies trying to hit something with a steel blade that clearly is there to cause bruises rather than draw blood, but whatever.
The graphics here are a mixed bag. The character models and everything look awful, to the point where they would barely pass as PS2 graphics, and they're animated so poorly. The lip-synching is also terrible, which makes Godzilla movies look masterful. However, and this is what I mean by the graphics being a mixed bag, is that not everything looks terrible, the enviroments are kind of nice. I can admit that.
The music sounds like your typical midieval sword & sorcery-style RPG, with light tunes when exploring, heavy tunes when in danger, things like that.
All in all, I have to say that it's a damn shame this game didn't quite live up to the hype, because it shows great potential that could have easily put The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion to shame, but they let their ambitions and a clichéd story along with awful gameplay get in the way of it all. Also, the voice acting was really disappointing as well. Still, hopefully they learned their lesson with this game and made Two Worlds II MUCH better, but I'll be going into it expecting the worst.

behaves terribly on the surface. This map is also likely resourcce intensive for the game engine, and the car wanders left and right continuously . STOP AND READ THIS BEFORE YOU BUY THIS GAME!!! This is a description of Battleborn's fatal flaws. This game is a lot of fun, but this information is IMPORTANT if you wish to make an informed purchase decision. VOTE THIS REVIEW UP to spread the word!
Firstly, the 5v5 PvP will matchmake your team with people who are all normally around your level. I'm level 12 at the moment. This means that my team will all be around levels 1-20ish. However, the awful matchmaking will put you against an opposing team of players who all could be Lvl40 and higher! There is a 30 minute penalty for exiting an unbalanced game, so you're forced to waste your time being completely obliterated by people who have played for 200+ hours, and are far more experience than your team is. I've played 6 matches in a row which are like this, this problem is very recurring.
Secondly Matchmaking is the worst of any game I have ever played. If you live in Australia, you can only exclusively play on AU servers; so before 12pm, and after 2AM, you will not find ANY matches as everyone playing is asleep. IF there are people playing, it can take sometimes a minimum of 15 minutes to find a game, as people exiting matchmaking will repeatedly reset an already lengthy matchmaking. There shouldn't be so few people playing this so close to launch, so if Gearbox doesn't patch their matchmaking, this game will most likely be dead within a month.
On a side note, the game only has two maps per PvP mode, so that may be worth considering, as Incursion, the game's most popular mode, only has one map people ever vote to play on. This is probably where you will be wanting to spend most of your time, however Gearbox desperately needs to release some more maps before players get burnt out with the lack of selection.
Battleborn is otherwise a really solid and entertaining game. It hurts me to not recommend it in its currents state. Do some research to check whether these issues have been patched before purchase. I would have waited a few weeks had the reviews I read and watched mentioned what I described, however the matchmaking is probably much better in America where the majority of the reviewers probably played the game.
Anyway, I love this game otherwise. Thanks for taking the time to read. Best of luck with the game everyone!!

It's challenging platformer and it may seem hard at first, but it gets better, when you improve, but also harder levels will come and some maps in later rows was really hard even for me (I completed all N-reality and Nv2 metanet levels)
Story is really simple: It's you (ninja) in a room full of enemies and your only goal is to get door key and get to door to continue your adventure in next level. You can either play through official episodes, where you need to complete 5 levels in a row to unlock next episode, or you can play user-created levels, which are in all forms of difficulty/playability.
Official metanet levels are very good and mostly with fine difficulty. Thanks metanet software for making this game, as I said I'm a long time fan of N the way of the ninja series. Probably only things I don't like much are that some levels are too hard  to get all gold for me, but I know it's supposed to be challenge. And when rocket crashes near you, you suddenly don't see anything and can easily make a mistake.
If you liked any older N game version, get N++ for sure, you won't regret it. And if you never played game like this before, try it too, it has simple old school graphics, but there is great amount of content for that price and lot of options, how to play the game. Divinity: Dragon Commander makes an attempt to mix action, RTS, RPG, and a politics, and does somethings brillinatly right and others horribly wrong.  Your father, the Emperor of Rivellon, has been murdered, and his kingdom is split between the children that tried to usurp his throne. It is now up to the illigitimate child, of both dragon and man, to defeat the children, unite the lands, and claim the throne.
The story it's self is quite well-written and humorous, mixing serious matters and a light-hearted undertone. The political part is by far the most excellent part of the game, forcing you to hear your advisors side, as well as forging your own opinion. This also parodies current world matters, such as gay marriage, women rights, arranged marraige and so on.The action comes into play when in the middle of a battle, you can turn the tide by switching into a dragon, The RPG elements allow custimization of your dragon as well as its abilities, and your own armies and bonuses to them.
However the most under developed part is the RTS part, very close to the StarCraft style. The game encourages "Zerg Rush" style gameplay because otherwise your battles will last forever and never end, and will mostly end in a lack of workers to make more units. In conclusion Dragon Commander could be so much more, by immensely improving on it's RTS elements, and eliminating the "Zerg Rush" need to win.
If you like Board Games, RTS, Political simulators, or even action games, I encourage you to try it. If your not good at RTS, just let the computer do it for you. You won't regret it.

Divinity: Dragon Commander is of a unique sort. It's one part Real-Time-Strategy, one part RISK, one part RPG, and one part action game. This all sounds like a recipe for a messy disaster does it not? In most other cases, it would be, however, Divinity: Dragon Commander manages to pull off a good chunk of it's intended goals and then some, to create one of the more unique experiences of the year.
The story begins by declaring that you are the son of the now deceased king who once ruled over the land of Rivellon. Now it is your fate that you must now compete with your brothers and sisters for the empty throne.
Roughly 50% of the game is spent on your ship talking to your advisers and upgrading yourself and your forces. This is the stronger of the two halves of the game because it is here that the excellent writing is put on display. There is a colorful cast of characters to interact with and there are a ton fun and interesting choices to make as a ruler that directly impact the Strategy portion of the game.
The other 50% of your game time belongs to the Strategy side of the game. This half sadly, is the weaker younger brother to the RPG elements I mentioned earlier, but it is by no means bad. Most of your movements will be made on a RISK-style campaign map as you claim territory from your siblings. Here you can play various cards to help you or hinder your foes in the battles to come. It's a little shallow overall, but it is very snappy and it's all very well-presented.
The RTS sections are fast-paced and entertaining to play for one major reason and one of this game's main selling points: The Dragon Form. At any point in the battle, provided you have a enough resources, you can transform into a dragon and take direct control of it to support your forces and rain death upon the enemy. This form is wildly entertaining and it does a good job of making you feel powerful. It almost makes you forget the lack of unit variety between the factions, as there is technically only one army in the game. However, in the quick and brutal multi-player, the introduction of player-controlled dragons really spices things up and can lead to some really interesting experiences.
So overall, Divinity: Dragon Commander is a very unique experience. It is also a very good one, not perfect, but considering the ambition present in this project, it turned out very well for Larian Studios. It shows a lot of ambition in a genre that is otherwise starting to hit a period of stagnation, and that alone is to be commended.

A good game...  Just one that is so strong in one part... And so weak in another two.... I find it difficult to recommend.. I think some will really love this game, and others will bounce off it. I am somewhere inbetween... And after 8 hours, I just felt like I'd had my fill.
There are three parts to this game, the RTS battles where you can take the form a dragon to rain down fiery terror on your enemies while commanding your forces about and building a base... the strategy map where you move your forces around in a turn based environment, very much like the board game RISK.. and the part of the game that I call the Emperor simulator.
For me, the RTS part of the game is the weakest, and ultimately what made me run out of steam and stop playing. I spent most of my time in RTS battles and to be fair they are half decent. The graphics are competent, the AI is good on Normal difficulty and although the units all kinda look the same they are varied in their functions and what they can do. You have land, sea and air units and coupled with the ability to change into a Dragon to help out a crucial time or go on a daring raid to destroy a key building is fun!    ....... For a while.
It just becomes stale, at least in my opinion. Granted, I am not an extreme RTS player so maybe I don't have the grizzled veteran stripes that would see me through, but I have finished a few in my time. World in Conflict, a few C&C games, Starcraft 2, Dawn of War.. and similar games... so I feel qualified enough to say that the RTS element of Dragon Commander stops being fun and ends up repetitive and at times... a grind.
Fighting so many similar battles, often on similar maps, repeating similar tactics over and over eventually erodes the fun for me and facing X amount more hours of it isn't something I relish. Most of the time selecting all your units and pointing them to the enemy base tends to work as a tactic, as long as you time it right.
The strategy map is half decent, knowing where to spend your turn by turn income and when to commit your forces is crucial to success... and that part is engaging. No real complaints .. or specific praise about the map. It is clean, functional.. and works. So.. good!
By far the best bit of the game however is playing Emperor. In between battles and troop deployments you will move around your command ship (a big airship powered by a demon) and speak with your generals, learn what makes them tick, settle disputes and do your best to people manage your commanders who are all very different and clearly have different ways of thinking and fighting. You'll also need to manage to needs of the people... in the form of approving or rejecting policies your council proposes.
Things like a national health service, conscription, gay marriage and censorship of the media. The choices you make have direct influences on the war, impacting finances, morale and available troops.
On top of that you also pick a princess to marry from one of the 5 races (I think) in the game, each have their own story arc, wants and needs and of course who you pick and what happens with them throughout the course of your game influence your standing with that particular race and how the others view you also.
It is well voice acted throughout, the characters are well written and they are animated to be full of life and colour. It was a real pleasant surprise!
I feel like I am just scratching the surface on this part of the game, but this facet of Dragon Commander is great... and for me..if they could of attached it to a more fulfilling game... like... well... I'm not sure.. .perhaps a fantasy kingdom manager in the mould of Anno 1404 or something? Rather than this repetitive RTS game... then I think this will have been a classic for me.
Thumbs up ... because it isn't a bad game... however whether you'll fall in love with it or not... is difficult to say.

Remember Age of Mythology? Yeah, it's been that long since there's been an RTS game of such quality. Divinity: Dragon Commander reaches awfully close to these borders of my personal most favourite RTS game. Combine this with a huge Risk-like Grand Strategy mode and there, it hit the spot. I am not (read: try not to be) overly biased due to the fact that this game allows you to turn into a DRAGON, aiding your troops by supporting, attacking and even commanding unit production, direction and spawning at the very same time.
Honestly, I do like the complicated RTS games nowadays. Think of Civ V and so on. However, such games attempt to cram complex mechanics, charts and resources all into one complicated game mode. This can work out really well, but the power in Dragon Commander's RTS mode lies not in its complexity. More like its simplicity.
In total, there are but 13 units that can be created, balancing each other out quite reasonably, and each having the possibility of being upgraded thrice. One main resource, a population cap, building sites and some natural obstacles. Although this may sound quite basic (which it is), the actual gameplay proves to be very interesting and many different strategies apply. Plus, the Dragon is a massive gamechanger. Dragon mode can either save your life or ruin it because of improper microing while being one. 3 Dragons with their own abilities fight for the additional variety.
Not only does the simply epic Dragon mode, a USP that's been praised to the heavens, contribute to the most valuable aspects of the game; the strategy mode (which is basically RISK combined with cards and special abilities) and especially the single player campaign also make this game as epic as it is.
In single player, not only do you have to fight your enemies in strategy mode as well as RTS mode, but the entire storyline around Dragon Commander demands that you will take on the right to make important political, moral and economical decisions that have direct impact on gameplay factors such as research, currency, abilities, luck, popularity etc. There are always races disagreeing with you. After all, being the emperor of a world housing undead, elves, imps, dwarves and lizards is bound to cause conflicts that will always have adverse and beneficial effects at the same time. Now it is up to you to keep the balance right. Give it a try, it's not as easy as you may think.
In conclusion, I'd say that Dragon Commander is a surprisingly effective game regarding gameplay and mechanics, sadly quite underpopulated on multiplayer ends. Narrative-wise, the game is very immersive and allows for quite the suspension of disbelief. The characters in singleplayer (like our ultimate posh friend general Edmund) as well as the models and environment in the entire game look astonishing for its genre. Not that much lag issues in multiplayer, and if there are people online it's quite fun to challenge each other. With a blend of RTS and TBS/Grand Strategy, and the addition of your personal touch of Dragon, invoking challenging and innovative strategy gameplay, I'd most definitely say it is worth acquiring this game. It is expensive, I give you that, but it's most certainly not a disappointment. In fact, it's quite the gem.

This game deserves a lot of praise.
The mixture of RPG elements on-board an RTS style game works very well. The UI doesn't feel over encumbered, without limiting your control over the game. Tutorials are short, sweet and easy to get the hang of. The ability to control your army while offering it assistance as the titler Dragon Commander is a great feature. His Third Person Gameplay doesn't feel tacked on in any way either, it feels like a proper solid element in it's own right.
On top of that all of that, the management of the factions ambassadors gives even more depth. There is a large amount of varied, interesting characters to meet, greet and discuss with on your command ship. They don't feel forced, and can sometimes be a joy to interact with. I get a lot of pleasure having a large battle, then coming back to sort out a trade agreement or some such with the ambassadors only adds to my enjoyment.
I'd highly recommend this to anyone fond of Management/RTS games. However, if you want to play it mainly for the Dragon, Management or the pure RTS Gameplay, you have to take into account that each is only a part of this game. You will have to do all three; manage your Empire, as well as your army, upgrades and your Dragon form.
The last thing I will say is; if you want this game I have another suggestion. Buy the boxed version new! I bought it when it first came out, cheaper then any digital download version I saw. The box itself is a very nicely put together thing with a lot of detail, no slap dash cheap boxing. The main thing about it though is the box copy comes with both Steam and GOG versions of the game. The Disk is the steam version, but there is also a Redeem code for a full digital version of the game for GOG. I gave it to a friend as a gift, perhaps you could too?

First impressions:
I've played the game for about 35 minutes so far. Out of the four games I looked at today it was easily the most fun.
(optional let's play footage)
The game look's pretty good. When it says graphic novel it really means it. There doesn't seem to any animation at all. I like it. The gameplay relies heavily on the dialogue which have to read.
Starting off you actually get to choose the protagonist's attributes i.e. level of physical strength, intelligence, charisma and so on. These determine the success of certain actions e.g. you need adequate strength to fend off a brute or good charisma to get information from characters. As the game progresses you are presented with various situations where you are tempted to sell your soul in exchange to manipulate reality in a way that benefits you. You start with 100% soul and the price for changing reality is offered as a percentage usually 10%.
I like how can you customize the attributes of your character. You can't make them all high. I think it adds to the variety of gameplay and potentially the replayability of the game. You can be a physically weak person who is adapt at manipulating people or someone who is average in most areas but really tough (this is what I chose). Not being very charismatic I sucked at convincing people to provide information to assist with an investigation but because of my strength I was able to fend off a thug. The game is all about making choices, do I sell my soul for this or that, do I skip a day at work to or track someone down, do I cooperate with this person. Your life seems to be manipulated those who want you sell your soul in order to tempt you to do so. For example after refusing to sell your soul you conveniently fall very ill and come close to dying. You are offered to be healed in exchange for a fraction of your soul. However if you continue to refuse you eventually make a full recovery mysteriously. I stubbornly refused to sell any of my soul at all. The way some offers are made to you kind are sort of reminiscent of receiving phone calls from telemarketers 'for just 10% of your soul you can turn your boss into a camel' lol. I enjoyed just saying no to every offer. I really felt engaged in the narrative. You don't who to trust, who is really good or whether someone apparently trustworthy really has ulterior motives.
So far I would definitely recommend this game. One of the things I liked most about it was that no matter what you always seem to have the option to stubbornly refuse to sell any of your soul. I was even able to not skip going to work and agreeing to work late at a job which my character hated and thought was completely boring. So basically I played a stubborn boring character lol

two worlds has become one of my favorite games ever, and no one is more surprised than me. first of all, I didn't start playing fantasy rpgs until a few years ago, they always looked too generic and boring, plus I really hated everything, and I mean
, about the two worlds demo. but thankfully I gave it another shot and had a ton of fun playing it.
it's not a perfect game by any means, but also very far from the trainwreck a lot of reviews make it out to be. the graphics still hold up, the viewing distance is really amazing, you can see stuff in the distance from really far away (yet grass seems to grow under your feet, which is one of the very few complaints I have). the music's great too and the voice acting falls into the so-bad-it's-hilarious category. it was grating at first but became entertaining soon, the over the top usage of 'olde english', the protagonist's sarcastic remarks and taunts like 'say hello to death!' or 'they look like my in-laws'.
some of the mechanics are pretty interesting too: you can use a bunch of active skills during combat (after you learned them from trainers) and there's a jump back button, which is essential against bigger but slower enemies. there are horses, but I found them only useful as inventory extentions, just park them next to a teleport and you're good. riding on the road is actually fine, but as soon as you go off-road, it's hell. you can probably get the hang of it eventually, but with a generous amount of static teleports and your personal teleport stones you don't really need a mount to get around. sprinting would've been nice though, even if you run faster with your weapons put away.
speaking of weapons and gear, you can combine multiple copies of the same items to make them more powerful, which is great, and also makes inventory management easier. there's a crazy amount of loot in the game though, with a lot of variety in everything, so multiple trips to merchants will be necessary to grab and sell everything. I wouldn't have minded a third inventory screen, actually.
there's also magic and bows (no need to worry about arrows) and I'd say combat is good enough, you can mix things up, though it can get a bit hectic because aggroing an enemy usually mobilizes their friends as well. but most importantly (for me anyway), the game doesn't have respawning enemies (there's a ghost mechanic though that's explained in the game, but it's only troublesome in the beginning) nor level scaling, which can make for one-hit deaths early on if you run into something far above your level.
the alchemy system is pretty good too, you can make temporary and permanent potions and gems from almost everything, plants, monster drops, minerals, and they really make a difference. if you're into exploring and hoarding, you can become so powerful that almost everything will die in a few hits. this might be a problem for some, but you don't have to make potions, obviously, and you don't have to kill every wolf you run into for even more xp. that's what I did though: I can't remember the last game where I wanted to explore absolutely everything and where exploration was so relaxing even with literally thousands of enemies around. I'm not one for farming and grinding, but I killed them all (more than 10.000) while I was at it. I wouldn't say the game world is especially unique, though later on you'll run into some weird creatures and unsettling environments.
there are a lot of quests, some of them are pretty basic, some are more involved, and sometimes you have to make a decision, you can't complete everything (though it's possible to have max reputation with all the factions at the same time until you anger them). the main story is nothing to write home about, your sister's missing, go find her, oh, and save the world in the meantime, will you? the game shines in the sidequest department though. there are a few funny ones, some are touching, and they can have unforeseen consequences. you think you're done and did the right thing, but when you go back to the village or npc later, you'll find you actually made things worse. I loved these.
I could go on for days about the game but I'm sure these reviews have a character limit, so I'll stop before I get too much into it. long story short, if you're looking for an open-world fantasy rpg you probably haven't played, check this one out. if you want to do everything, it'll keep you busy for more than 100 hours (or you can just concentrate on questing and be done a lot faster).

I bought this game on a whim a couple of days ago, and I do not regret it. Point-and-click games have interested me a while; with the low-pace focus on deep exploration and story and lack of cheap action for instant and shallow gratification most games use. But at the same time I've been offput by some experiences demanding rediculous puzzles (like go there, get that pipe, go to a place you haven't been for 5 hours and somehow know to talk to that guy, then solve an impossible puzzle and then get some story).
While I used a guide when stuck on a few puzzles, generally it was pretty clear what to do and it was mostly short, fun puzzles that didn't slow down the narrative too much.
The story itself, was mostly well written and had some minor surprises here and there, but most of all it was just captivating, without being fantastic. The single thing I miss most in video games in general is good story-telling, and even super-classics like FFVII or Chrono Trigger didn't really leave a mark on me. Games that are praised for its story-telling can seldom even get close to competing for truly great works of cinema or literature. I really enjoy my share of Mass Effect or Deus Ex: HR but the narrative and story in those has serious problems and I think many games gets exaggerated praise for story just because the competition is so lacking.
While J.U.L.I.A. certainly is no masterpiece, it was still an engrossing experience exploring the world and learning more about the expedition and its crew, the ecosystem of the solar system, and the overall story of the game. The visuals helped create a sense of a fascinating world, while mystery was always part of the experience. The writing was'nt always great, a problem of most games, but I would still say the story and narrative is better than most games out there, even those who pride themselves on storytelling. This game is rather shallow compared to works in other art-forms though. The fact that the protagonist is female doesn't really matter to the game in meaningful ways and I think that's fine, but I gotta say it's refreshing to not always play a Nathan Drake-like white guy hero. Rachel is not extremely interesting, but IMO; her situation is. She is very alone deep in the galaxy, but has company of two (to each other) rather different AI:s/robots.
If you do buy the game, I suggest playing it in a couple of days like I did, in solitude and maybe with headphones for immersion. I think this is such a game that you lose interest in if you play for short amounts of time and far between. Took me 10 hours in maybe 3 or 4 sessions, and the length of the game seemed perfect to me. Not to short, but certainly not too long. The full price tag seems reasonable, but don't think twice about getting this on a sale!

This game is the most philisophical and thought provoking game of our age. It's deep allegorical nature will leave you pondering your own life. It is a perfect reflection of our mundane day to day lives as ordinary humans.
You see the levels in this game are meant to symbolize life in the way that they are long, arduous, confusing, and pretty much look the same the whole way through.
The zombies, a horrible plague of undending monsters spewing out from all directions and all angles, they represent out insecurities constantly follwing us and attacking us sometimes trapping us and preventing progression.
The guns you use to mow down the endless waves of zombies represent hope and self-confidence as they are the tools you use to destroy your insecurities gaining the ability to push through life,
The other players in the game all mindlessly running around as well trying to their own thing and figure out what's going, they represent society. As you stumble your way through broken and confused harassed by your insecurities you see other people stumbling through as well. You look at them and think "What are they doing? Are they stupid? Maybe they have the right idea, what am I doing? Am I stupid? Should I do what they're doing? What's going on?"
The goal of the game is to try and figure out how to progress through the level while killing as many zombies as possible. While the goal of life is to try and figure out how to progress and achieve your dreams while fighting off your doubts and insecurities. The game shows that with some hope, some help, and a little bit of stumbling around that anything is possible.

An interactive story game where you're not in control of the events, but instead are trying to piece them together. You're presented with a very spartan, pseudo Windows 3.1 interface that accepts only keyword queries. The database you're searching through is a collection of old police interrogation tape snippets covering a single case and a single woman. If your keyword is mentioned in a snippet, you can watch it.
All the archived clips are quite short, ranging from five seconds to just over a minute. A name or a thing mentioned in one part leads to another, that one to yet another and so on. This is quite an intriguing (and challenging) way to tell a story, and I have to say that I throroughly enjoyed chasing the tiniest of hints while slowly coming into a realization about the big picture.
Talking about the story itself isn't really fruitful since everyone should experience it on their own and in their own way. Suffice to say that the tale is satisfying enough, although not any kind of an instant classic or the best thing ever. I personally found the story even a bit implausible by the end when everything clicked into place, but not overtly so.
Overall, a story well worth experiencing, told in a way that has rarely, if ever, been seen before.

I have really enjoyed playing this game. Just got the 100% completion on it. I highly recommend this game if you like puzzles and story-heavy games. The non-linear story means that you need to pay attention to what is going on, and WHEN it went on.
What this game does well:
- The actor. Since gameplay is searching for and watching videos, she has to sell the story. And she does it well. In fact, after certain plot points were revealed to me, I really liked going back to review old videos and piece together things I may have missed at the beginning.
- The videos themselves. The videos really do look like they were recorded in the 90s. The subtitles are those dark yellow ones you used to see on TV back in the day, too. The videos remind me of the days when games had FMVs, like The 7th Guest.
- The computer. Aside from the database, you can interact with everything else on the computer desktop.  There's glare on the computer screen (and other assorted graphics that I won't discuss) that really make you feel like you're looking at the screen itself, not just the desktop. You can turn that glare off if you'd like, but imo it loses some of the immersion that way.
- The music! Oh, it gave me chills in places. After certain videos, different music will play. It startled me at first, but I think that in a game where interactivity is limited, anything extra to engage the player does a world of difference.
- The story. I don't want to give any spoilers, and of course the nature of the game means that some players will figure it out more quickly than others. By the first hour in the game, I had gotten the major pieces figured oaut. I guess it took getting around half of the videos unlocked. Getting 75% was pretty easy too, but I started running into dead ends after that. I will say that after a certain point, the game alerts you that you've found enough information to consider the game "finished", and at that point you can trigger an ending sequence and credits. (If you go back to play later, your completion rate is still there.)
- It's not pretentious. There are a lot of art games that disregard "traditional" gameplay and sometimes that can alienate players. There is no fail state in this game. There is a score in that the game tracks your completion rate, and there is a win/completion state. But the game presents its gameplay and story clearly and plainly.

Look, I haven't played this game much on Steam, but I have on...um...another platform. I've played it for close to 100 hours.
There are a few negative reviews that raise some concerns. I'm going to boil them down to a few words and respond.
Too hard: yes, the game is difficult, especially later on. That's the point. Like Super Meat Boy or other similar platformers, the game is easy-ish early on while you become comfortable with the controls and learn what all of the traps do. If you persist into the late game, you are going to die a lot, and you will spend absurd amounts of time on individual levels. But holy crap does it feel good to complete those levels.
Repetitive, difficulty doesn't rise enough, physics feel wrong: these criticisms are decently fair, although I don't think the game is repetitive. This game has a LOT of levels, so getting to the most difficult levels will take some time. As for the physics: either you like them or you don't. The way it works is very deliberate, and it came to eventually feel great for me.
Free similar flash games out there: I don't typically browse around the free available flash games out there, but as I noted above, there is an absurd amount of content in this game. And once you start getting into some of the hidden things, you'll really come to appreciate the level design. Everything is incredibly well-designed - you'll notice how perfectly places some traps are, which are meant to make you pay attention when you're trying to get through a level.
I can't sing the praises of the game highly enough.

I usually stick to writing only positive reviews but when I saw the price of this game I had to do this. I like racing games, and I like old cars. Looking at the screenshots this game looked appealing to me and I immediately wanted to revive the nostalgic experience I had with games like Street Rod back in the day. Street race for money and then upgrade and customize your car, sounds great.
Luckily this game was in bundle so I at least don't feel ripped off but I'm writing this for people who might think about buying this for 17,99€ (or whatever equivalent) or even anything more than 2-3 bucks.
There's so much wrong with this game I don't know where to start...
I won every race in this game within 3 hours. The content in this game is simple math. There's around 10 cars, 5 race tracks and 8 racing modes, which sounds like a good variety factor but it's not... you go forward, you win, you crash, you lose. Career mode is build of 5 events, each containing 5 races. That's it. I finished whole game with the very first car I upgraded becase it was best (yea). Customization is very limited. Basically contains 2 categories: performance and visual upgrades. Visual upgrades are kinda nice but you won't care about them. You will save money for performance upgrades and cars and then you will finish the game and propably upgrade visually just for the achievement. Other than this Career mode there's nothing else to do. There's no multiplayer. No challenges. No other playmodes. No difficulty setting. No nothing... Thankfully. Why? Let's get to the next point...
I don't know if I am even capable of describing how horribly this game handles. Controls are simply laggy and unresponsive. Thankfully you just go straight forward most of the time. Sometimes you had to slow down not so you won't crash while turning which would transform your car into unhandleable mess. The very first car is only one that handles "not so bad" when it's fully upgraded... the "better" cars goes crazy during turns and some even starts slipping just because they go fast. Even AI has constant problems handling the cars. I'm not even kidding, it's hillarious. Propably only positive thing I came upon while playing. But I digress. The so-called Career Mode is basically this: you find first race you're able to win, you repeat it for cash, buy upgrades until you're superior and win just because you go faster. Colission model is a joke as well as physics, there's no destruction model, no weather changes or any other features you might be used to in racing games. Instead of features, there are bugs.
On Steam, this is propably closest you can get to infamous Big Rigs: Over the Road Racing. It's not nearly as bad but as I said... I haven't been able to buy racing game on Steam that would be even remotely broken as this one. Your opponents go through the traffic (you don't), you can't disable music in menu (you can but after every race it's on again), you go trough trees, controls sometimes don't work and stuff like that... my favorite was when I started a Knockout race which starts with animation of you and your car setting off. But instead of going forward, the animation made me go backwards which resulted of me going reverse and giving my opponents headstart.
I don't care about graphics and talking about how this game looks would be beating a dead horse. I can say that some of the screenshots on Store page with the sunlight effects looks edited because the game don't look appealing like that in reality. The visuals are not awful. They're functional (no graphic settings btw. ... was this a mobile phone game?) but it just doesn't matter at all because everything else is horribly done.
I wouldn't recommend this to anybody unless you're achievement hunter in which case optimal price would be 2$. Price tag of 17,99€ for this is an insult to Steam users.
I prefer to play Bad Rats than this. I guess I don't have to say anything more.

Tough to rate this one based on a sole recommended or not recommended choice. After some tought i wouldnt recommend the game.
While dragon commander tries to implement an interestening gameplay, which makes incredibly fun to get into the first rounds, soon afterwards you are annoyed by the always repeating same rts gameplay.
Dragon commander is a mix from real time strategy,  a turn based gameplay where you send out, build new troops and upgrade equipment, and a political simulator. The most fun probably is the politcal simulator where you roleplay as a king and have to make decisions about political dilemmas that a race confronts you with. Those are usually applyable to modern problems in some way like brutal board games, smoking etc. Each race is displayed as a hardcore stereotype of a poltical point of view, elves are hippies, undeads are very religious and so on.The thing is that you can only choose yes or no to a dilemma and cant find any way of compromise that favor or dislikes slightly everyone but not as hard as saying yes or no. Having some kind of money system would have improved so you could have chosen to use money for some problems that instead could have been used for more troops. Also the decisions dont have much influence except how much troops you can recruit where the other races life.
The graphics are beatiful. The artstyle is pretty good and unique. The characters really feel realistic, make good moving gestures and the atmosphere on the commander ship is top notch. The Maps and units in the rts part are also good to look at , but lack a bit of the detail.
You can also marry a princess from each faction except the imps ,sadly, and turn her points of view away. Like making the elven princess dont care about animals anymore etc. This story aspect is probably the best of the whole game in my opinion. I wish that there would be more roleplay aspects you can do in this area since you basically can only hear her story and make a couple of decisions that always end in kinda 3 ways. Having events politcally and/or with your wife would have improved the story and decision making.
The rts system is okay. Its not really awesome but not completely broken. Only mayor flaw is the lack of variety. Not only in gameplay wise, but in therms of maps, there are no battles inside cities, as an example. You can random out the fight luckily, but only if you have better/more troops otherwise its very risky. After some time the battles get repetetive and that is the thing i really dislikes about the game. The battles arent that fun to make me want them to do over and over again, and having not a much variety of maps also hurts the gameplay. But i have to admit that the steampunk troops look cool and there is a variety of troops.
The game is very short. A campaign takes you around 6 hours i would say. A little bit more or less depending on you. First playtrough is very fun but the game never randomizes anything, like the map, therefore every playtrough is only different based on your wife and politcal decisions.
6.5/10 Game really is promising but lacks replay value due the repetetive fighting gameplay. Some kind of money system for the economic stabillity, infrastucture, and so on, would have improved the strategic factor of the game and i really wish i could have done more with my wife.

In short terms: Interstellar like story with chick with british accent (instead of MM) but with much less Nolan and black holes.
In longer terms: It is a nice sci-fi adventure based on classic p'n'c mechanics with the touch of some modern beautiful visuals and a good atmosphere.
Enter the space shoes and thoughts of biologist Rachel Manners, (accompanied by some well mannered A.I.'s) the only living survivor of expedition that went horibly wrong. What happend light years from our home and why was she only one kept alive is a mystery. Help her uncover the truth.
Like in almost every other point and click game out there, gameplay is based mostly on clicking on almost static images, looking for clues and so on. There is some backward storytelling through a lot of dialogues, but the best part of the game is story itself and there is a constant feeling that drives you forward to reveal the next tiny piece of the greater picture. Slow paced story revealing is great but once you finish it, everything is revealed and replay value drops basicaly to zero. And if you belong to the group of people that don't like to read or listen too much then this game is not for you. As you go along be prepare for some riddles and some peculiar puzzles but don't worry, they are not Broken Sword level.
Game lenght is fair enough. If you take your time there is 11-12 hours but if you hurry you can finish it under 7 or 8. The price on the other hand is somewhat high and I would suggest to buy this on action sales - but let's be fair - it is a indie game mady by two people and for what it's has to offer, it is a great game.
To wrap it up I would definitely recommend this but to p'n'c and sci-fi genre lovers only.

So... what type of game is this?
Two genres come to mind: point-and-click and find-the-hidden-object...
The game actually tends more to the former:
- There's an interesting story (even if I didn't agree with some of the narrative towards the end - but hey that's part of what stories are supposed to be about, right?);
- There is a lot of puzzle-solving (after some hidden-object hunting).
- The game gives you a couple of choices that influence the outcome of the game (although not mind-bendingly)
Overall I enjoyed the game - there's a LOT of polish on here (which is something I respect and look for in games). And from what I could tell from the credits, the majority of the game was created by two guys... So respect :)
Buy this game if:
- You like first-person adventure games (like I said, there is a hint of find-the-hidden-object in there, but you'll definitely forgive it).
- You like polished productions (cutscenes/graphics, interface, voice-acting, design) - its got a really nice Sci-Fi vibe.
There's not much replay value obviously, but I'll definitely recommend this game for 9-10 hours of interesting entertainment :)

Overall: 75%
Pros:
- At its best moments a truly enjoyable game, with suspense and the excitement of exploration
- A variety of puzzles - not repetitive; figuring out what the puzzle is about is half the fun.
- The story is not breathtakingly original, but mostly OK.
- Voice acting is above average (although some may find the voices themselves a bit annoying).
- Visually pleasing, in an oldschool way
Cons:
- UI is sometimes disturbingly counterintuitive (works differently than what you'd expect - the jigsaw puzzle, arrgh!) or too complicated (when there is only one kind of action that a mouse click can perform on a given object, why bother with a context menu? I'm looking at you, laser beacon!) The permanent UI is overcomplicated and it is sometimes tedious to find the information you are looking for or the next task you are supposed to do.
- Sometimes too many things happen at once (you are supposed to listen to the conversation AND read the analysis results at the same time - and when the conversation is over, both disappear automatically).
- Parts of the story feel just shoveled together without much thought or effort - given the sci-fi setting, I was particularly put off by nosense talk about strange "energies" and unheard of chemical elements. Hey, writing good sci-fi is not easy. That's what the "sci" part is for...
- The level of "handholding" is uneven: sometimes the game feels just pushing you through the steps (when you'd rather do something different) or instantly offer a vital clue to the puzzle you haven't had a chance to understand yet - and sometimes you are just left to jump from planet to planed because you don't realize where does the story continue.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Look, I haven't played this game much on Steam, but I have on...um...another platform. I've played it for close to 100 hours.
There are a few negative reviews that raise some concerns. I'm going to boil them down to a few words and respond.
Too hard: yes, the game is difficult, especially later on. That's the point. Like Super Meat Boy or other similar platformers, the game is easy-ish early on while you become comfortable with the controls and learn what all of the traps do. If you persist into the late game, you are going to die a lot, and you will spend absurd amounts of time on individual levels. But holy crap does it feel good to complete those levels.
Repetitive, difficulty doesn't rise enough, physics feel wrong: these criticisms are decently fair, although I don't think the game is repetitive. This game has a LOT of levels, so getting to the most difficult levels will take some time. As for the physics: either you like them or you don't. The way it works is very deliberate, and it came to eventually feel great for me.
Free similar flash games out there: I don't typically browse around the free available flash games out there, but as I noted above, there is an absurd amount of content in this game. And once you start getting into some of the hidden things, you'll really come to appreciate the level design. Everything is incredibly well-designed - you'll notice how perfectly places some traps are, which are meant to make you pay attention when you're trying to get through a level.
I can't sing the praises of the game highly enough.

The developer Sam Barlow said LA Noire didn't make him feel much like a detective, Phoenix Wright did a better job but still was too rigid for his taste. So he made this game.
It is a non linear detective murder mystery in which you try to understand a case that lies 20 years in the past.
Your tool of investigation is a computer with a database of tapes, FMV clips of an actress interviewed by the police.
All are a couple of seconds long and indexed (and searcheable) by keywords and phrases.
So if our mysterious lady said the word "murder" in one of the tapes and you type it into your searchfield, you'll find up to 5 videos in which she said that word. You can look for the word "the" and get 5 hits, this is a bit weird to me but in the end it can be helpful if you're stuck or out of keywords to search for.
After a couple of minutes I was starting to write down notes via pen and paper and found myself already pretty deep in the mystery.
And that is how you play the whole game.
The actress Viva Seifert delivers a great and deep performance. Sometimes you watch a clip and think: 'Hmm, this is weird...', and 2 hours later, with new information at hand, you realize that the thing you thought was weird now totally makes sense. It's just an odd experience, and I liked that.
Let's be honest, the human brain wants to order and structure everything it gets it's "hands" on and that's exactly what makes the game apealing.
That and that little bit of voyeurism we all have inside us and can safely endulge in here.
The games big quality (nonlinearity) can also be it's downfall: If you're searching for certain words that might spoil the whole mystery for you in the first 20 minutes you won't get as much out of the rest of the clips.
I knew a little too much for my own good in the first half an hour, I feel. But it was still fun until the end.
How do you end a game like this, I asked myself. Well, pretty organic, mostly like you played it.
It all works in a way and I enjoyed it but it has it's flaws and it's probably not for everyone.
The writing and the acting made it work for me and even if I'm not super happy with the final conclusion I had concerning the case, the way of getting there was really fun!

N++ is an amazing platformer game. Fans of Super Meat Boy and the like will enjoy its hard difficulty and the insane amount of levels the game has to offer (2,360 of them, as a matter of fact,
). The physics can take a bit of getting used to, as N++ feels a little floatier than Super Meat Boy and other platformers, but gameplay is very fluid  overall. The pacing varies from level to level, ranging from careful and methodical planning to "run-as-fast-as-you-freaking-can", and resetting a level from the inevitable death or two (hundred) is almost instant. The art style is very crisp and not too busy for the eyes, and the range of colors that you unlock as you progress through the game give you something different to look at, which helps in changing things up and keeping the game looking fresh.
To top it off, the soundtrack is perfect for a game like N++. The soundtrack is an assortment of ambient IDM-style tracks which all manage to pull off the difficult task of giving the game atmosphere while not being distracting at the same time. Also, as mentioned above, there are user-created levels for those looking for a challenge or something new. N++ also has a cooperative mode and a competitive racing mode (local only).
For fans of the previous N games, this game is a no-brainer. This game is a must-have for fans of difficult platformer games. I highly recommend this game. 10/10

You have to give some of yourself to this game, but it will give you so much in return. It's as deep and as hard as you want it to be. There has never been a platformer with more rewarding physics.

A couple things to be aware of:
- The userlevel community is great! It's easy to just totally not notice behind the innocuous-looking "Browse" menu item, but making levels, playing new levels as they come in, and competing on the weekly featured levels are where I spend easily half my time with the game. Don't miss it!
- If you care about high scores, which is a great thing to do, make sure you turn on the "submit level scores" option so you don't lose your level runs when you do full episodes. It's kind of a historical accident that it defaults to off. Hopefully this will be fixed in the next update.
- Race mode and Coop are *really good*. There's no online multiplayer, so you'll have to find someone to play with, but they are good enough that some hardcore players have literally flown internationally to play with each other :D
- Come hang out with us in the public discord! There's a level of the day for high scoring, userlevel contests, frequent streams by high level players, and general discussion and friendliness.

I was on the fence with this game.
I played the first N+ for hours and absolutely loved it. Now that I've played this game for quite some time I will try to point out the main differences that I see and feel in the game as quickly as possible.
Controls:
-Jumping is inconsistent at times
-Games seems more slippery(ie sliding into bombs when trying to stop)
-Good news is you can jump on pointy geometry now
Objects:
-Missiles have a tighter turn radius, which was just annoying in my opinion
-Bombs are bigger and have a active/inactive state to them
-Bouncy Blocks are WAY different from the first game. Different point at which to jump to get maximum lift
Hit detection: This part I think is what frustrated me the most, apart from the controls not being consistent. I found that the top of your character is not really the top of your character.  It's almost as if your head doesn't count as part of your body. This is nice for some levels, but more frustrating than it is helpful.  You can no longer graze a switch with the top of your head and have it activate. Your movements need to be more explicit when hitting time and switches.
Collecting Time: I found myself never needing to go after time which made the game easier than I was hoping. I can only remember 1 time when I NEEDED to get some time or I wasn't going to complete the level. Most of the challenging parts of the levels you can skip because they involve collecting time that your really don't need.  The only reason to go for it is to get higher on the leader board.
The developer did include the legacy levels from the first game in this one which I have to commend.
Overall it's not a bad game, its just different from the first game in ways that are frustrating more than challenging and fun.
I would recommend you buy this game on sale if you want a challenging platformer.

Been playing this for about an hour and a half and I have to say I'm really impressed. Her Story is a throwback to the old FMV games that were made back in the 90s, only this time it isn't♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's actually surprisingly great. The purpose is to try and find out - by going through archive footage of numerous police interviews with a woman that took place two decades earlier - what happened to her missing husband. This is done through keyword searching, so it's best to play this with a pen and paper handy as a video will throw up another clue or word that could be vital in your investigation.
As an exercise in non-linear storytelling Her Story is incredibly well written and a huge amount of thought has clearly gone into not just the dialogue and plotting, but also into the length of the videos. Some of them can be as short as 3-4 seconds and at first viewing seem absolutely redundant. As you delve further into the archives, however, they can take on a whole new meaning. The actress who plays the subject of these interviews deserves huge credit for her work here, her performance only truly reveals its brilliance the further you progress and you begin to notice her intonation, mannerisms and overall demeanour are all absolutely perfect.
If you're after something truly different, interesting and original then look no further. Her Story is a little gem of a game. Recommended.

What I have been doing so far is to write down the key incidences, items, characters on a notebook, marked with the clip number, time, and her dress color.
The game provides such a seemingly simple but brilliantly creative way of telling stories. Compared to other detective-like games, it is definitely unqiue and challenging in its own league. Additionally, decent time-related graphic design, extra mini game, beautiful protagonist. I have limited academic background in game studies at this point, but to me this game could be one of the special cases for studies in the narrative games domain and video game storytelling.

Motorama is 'classic racing' game in a 1950's theme with the same single
piece of music playing throughout; over and over again.  There has been some graphical bugs in the form of cars or terrain flickering, or drivers floating in the air, and even unsee-able maps that render the game unplayable at times.
You earn rewards as you play the game, and there are a decent amount of
car selections and upgrade performance options, but the cost of purchasing
performance upgrades plus the cost of purchasing new vehicles does not balance
with the cash awards for winning in races.  This leads to a lot of grinding just
to get enough money to buy upgrades (which are necessary), to progress forward.
There is also a lot of selection for cosmetic upgrades for those that like to
pimp out their vehicles.
Overall I found that if you didn't establish a big lead in the first 20
seconds of gameplay, you have little to no chance of winning.  If you are leading
the race, your competitors magically catch up in the one straight segment of road
despite you holding a significant lead throughout the rest of the track.  Hitting
a wall or going off road most of the time guarantees a loss, which makes the game more restrictive than enjoyable.
The different types of missions are done very well.  The racing element
is pretty decent and is somewhat enjoyable, and I wanted to like this game.  The more I played, the more I found the bugs,
the annoying UI, the grinding and the discrepancy in balance throughout gameplay
makes this game not one I would recommend.

After reading most of the reviews i decided to give this a try and found out that it wasn't so bad as mentioned.  If you are a person who is picky about the gameplay, AI intelligence, etc... then i would admit that this would probably make you want to play another game rather than spend time playing it.
However, If you are just looking for a game to explore an open world type of RPG and can create your own adventures without playing a linear story, then i would definitely recommend this as i had a fun time myself just doing what i wanted.

I would recommend it for open world adventurers (who would just like to have fun whilst fighting unknown dangers) and first timers who are new to open world RPG games just so they can have a taste of what it's like. As a guy named Ben in real life, I connected with these games on a personal level. These games perfectly simulate the average everyday life of anyone who is named Ben (and also Dan, but it's not nearly as immersive of an experience with him). That being said, these are the most entertaining point-and-click games I have ever played and there is plenty to enjoy in both of these games even if your name isn't Ben or Dan.
10/10 would Ben again.

Ben There, Dan That is a lot of things.
It's ugly, truthfully. It's crude (in many senses of the word), definitely. It's locked into a tiny resolution, puzzlingly. It's paying homage to its roots, certainly. It's poking fun at pop culture and specific events, absolutely. It's short, unfortunately.
If you can get past the presentation and all its warts, and you have a bit of a warped sense of humour, you'll probably find more than a fair share of chuckles (or at least smiles) within this game.
I do stress that it is s a love letter to classic adventure games, right down to the occasionally frustrating puzzles. Know the genre, and know this game. If you don't like point and clickers, and all that they stand for, you'd best pass.
-----

The games are available for dirt cheap, but adventure game fans should find value even at full price. I certainly did.

Been playing this for about an hour and a half and I have to say I'm really impressed. Her Story is a throwback to the old FMV games that were made back in the 90s, only this time it isn't♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's actually surprisingly great. The purpose is to try and find out - by going through archive footage of numerous police interviews with a woman that took place two decades earlier - what happened to her missing husband. This is done through keyword searching, so it's best to play this with a pen and paper handy as a video will throw up another clue or word that could be vital in your investigation.
As an exercise in non-linear storytelling Her Story is incredibly well written and a huge amount of thought has clearly gone into not just the dialogue and plotting, but also into the length of the videos. Some of them can be as short as 3-4 seconds and at first viewing seem absolutely redundant. As you delve further into the archives, however, they can take on a whole new meaning. The actress who plays the subject of these interviews deserves huge credit for her work here, her performance only truly reveals its brilliance the further you progress and you begin to notice her intonation, mannerisms and overall demeanour are all absolutely perfect.
If you're after something truly different, interesting and original then look no further. Her Story is a little gem of a game. Recommended.

Ok, I have to review this game after only 1.7h played time. Because this game is a, as the description said, groundbreaking narrative game.
It's maybe a bit spoiler but the main aim of the game is to figure out what her story is. And this only way of achieve this goal is to view all her video clips and put together those narrative jigsaws. However, the challenge is, the only way of selecting your target video clips is via entering searching keywords, which are also the things you shall figure out yourselves. Kindly the developers offered the feature of saving clips, which, however, is not barely enough either. What I have been doing so far is to write down the key incidences, items, characters on a notebook, marked with the clip number, time, and her dress color.
The game provides such a seemingly simple but brilliantly creative way of telling stories. Compared to other detective-like games, it is definitely unqiue and challenging in its own league. Additionally, decent time-related graphic design, extra mini game, beautiful protagonist. I have limited academic background in game studies at this point, but to me this game could be one of the special cases for studies in the narrative games domain and video game storytelling.
RECOMMEND.

This is a fantastic game, and one of the best Star Wars games ever released.  The level system has skills and feats, and your attributes affect those in ways that are very similar to D&D.  This is not a bad thing, however, as the playstyle feels natural and easy to understand, and thus leveling up becomes a fun experience rather than a chore.  The story and companions are well written at every level, and the game could not have been better executed.  Side quests are abundant and engrossing, and sometimes there are random little alcoves to explore just for the fun of it.
The only real shortcoming is the complete duality of the moral system.  You're either a nice guy or a jerk, with nothing in between.  Still, this doesn't take away from the enjoyment of the game itself.  It'll take roughly 40 hours to complete one playthrough if you do most of the side quests, and multiple playthroughs offer different experiences.  There's no reason not to buy this game.
HK-47 deserves a special mention as the single best supporting character in any game I've played.  If you haven't experienced KOTOR with HK-47 in your active party at all times, go back and play it again.  Meatbag.
