First of all, I really liked the beta's. I played them quite a lot and enjoyed the game. I didn't preorder it but bought it at launch.
Positive:
- Gearbox vibe. If you're familiar with Borderlands, you'll feel right at home
- A lot of cool different characters with some really cool abilities.
- Game seems balanced (if both teams pick balanced combo's that is: tank - support - (ranged) assassin - DPS)
- graphics are cool (if you like the style. I do). It might get clusterfukkie, but that's just something you need to get used to
Negative:
- matchmaking (or total lack thereof). The game will without issue let you start a match 4v5. It will match level 72 players with level 2 noobs. Great fun garanteed! You either roflstomp the enemy team or get steamrolled yourself. I can count the really close games I had with one, perhaps two fingers (admittedly, I only played around 10-15 matches or so)
- Ridiculous lack of content: 2 (two) meltdown maps. This must be a joke. Plus, nobody wants to play that second map anyway, so you end up with that same map you've been playing since beta.
- Characters are locked behind progress walls. I don't like this idea. I want to try out the support characters. Now I need to grind boring other characters I don't want to play in the first place to unlock these.
- Story mode: so-so. Lot's of shooting, yeah. But why, what is the story? Jokes are 'meh' at best (not on the same level as Borderlands). You can clearly tell this has been added in a rush.
- Gear loadout: why is it so damn difficult to build an intuitive way of managing your gear? I'm clicking, double-clicking left and right, but it's always a chore to move gear in and out of your loadouts. Also, when I select a character and his loadout, am I really supposed to learn by heart what every item does? You can only see it's icon in the character select screen.
- Please order the battleborn by their role. At this point, the game is new and a lot of people (including me) don't fully know all battleborn's role. It might help if you'd put all tanks together, all DPS characters together, and so on...
- the need to grind for better loot. Ugh.
Conclusion:
This game could have been a real hit, but I fear Gearbox just wanted to cram too much into one game and they ended up with a game that's only average at best. The story mode is mediocre. The multiplayer lacks content (basically just one mode and map that everybody plays). They just shot themselves in the foot with this game I fear. But hey, sales figures will probably be good, so we can expect a Battleborn 2 in a couple of years. I do hope they focus on the one thing this game really needs: good content.

Ben There, Dan That and Time Gentlemen, Please! are two typical indie point & click adventure games that try to bring back the atmosphere of the old wacky LucasArts titles with a large dose of British humour. And it’s not just a gut feeling: the games are full of references and easter eggs about titles such as Sam & Max, Full Throttle, Day of the Tentacle and all other loved classics.
The first game was originally released as a freeware, and like most of the freeware adventure games, it’s more of a showcase of the writing and game design capabilities of the two creators, not a full game. Still, the story works in its own completely absurd way, the places you visit are designed well, and the puzzles are sometimes hard, but not too difficult. And it’s one of the few adventure games where item usage does not equal the main protagonist robbing every person blind, the items come from very logical sources. (Well, mostly.)
The sequel was made as a commercial game and the developers really wanted to give as much as they got. And the problem is that they gave too much. The story takes a very drastic turn in Time Gentlemen, Please, and in the end it becomes too convoluted even for the writers. The puzzles start as quite challenging and I the end they reach almost impossible levels. In the meanwhile the trademark absurd humour start to fade slowly to give room to the increasingly complex plot.
But the game has saving graces, and mostly in the main ideas behind the different time periods, where the developers constructed the most far-fetched, zaniest alternative timelines you can see outside of Doctor Who. And all of those are featured in Day of the Tentacle-like four-dimensional puzzles of course.
To sum it up, these games – particularly the first one – are excellent for those who love British humour and still hold a special place in their hearts for the LucasArts adventure library. And if you like a good challenge in brain-twisting puzzles, then all the better.
But if you don’t like games where some puzzles remind you of Gabriel Knight 3, or absurd humour is not your cup of tea (or pint of ale), then you will find very little enjoyment in these two.

I'm sure that many of those interested in buying this game were convinced to do so after watching a number of YouTube personalities♥♥♥♥♥♥themselves laughing. I was the same way at one point. Take my advice: just watch those videos some more. They're way more fun than the actual game.
The objective of Turbo Dismount is to orchestrate vehicular accidents that cause as much damage as possible to your vehicle and the hapless mannequin forced into this dilemma. You have at your disposal various maps, vehicles, obstacles to litter the course with, and poses for your mannequin. If you've seen any of the aforementioned YouTube videos, you're no doubt aware of the sort of destruction that can ensue. This would be all fine and dandy if it actually felt like the player had any real control over the outcomes of these crashes.
Accelerating the vehicle consists of holding down a button and releasing it at the moment when a meter is at the desired level. Because of how obscenely quickly the meter fills up and then empties again, precise timing is nearly impossible. This is compunded by the vehicles' tendency to do whatever they want to, such as letting up on the gas when you want them to speed up, vice versa. Many of the obstacles frequently fail to produce an intended effect, and sometimes fail to produce any effect at all. Even in levels that involve other traffic, those other vehicles appear in random order and speed by so quickly that it's nigh impossible to properly time a collision.
The physics engine is capable, but unpredictable. A satisfying crash can have vehicle and body parts being strewn about and colliding with each other in amusing ways, but these moments are scarce thanks to the physics' refusal to behave consistently. It's also frustrating how your ragdolling mannequin often struggles to maintain its pose, or even stay attached to the vehicle, in order to have it hit something in a desired manner.
All of these frustrations combine to form an experience that is usually comprised of restarting a level over and over and over again to get a desired result. When a beautiful catastrophe does happen, it tends to feel less like the results of the player's planning and effort, and more like the result of unintentional happenstance. Even if the player learns the mechanics and nuances well enough to consistently create satisfying crashes, what's left at that point is just a shallow, one-note time waster. Ragdoll crashes car. Ragdoll goes ragdolling. Oh, how the lolz are killing me.
Turbo Dismount is a one-trick pony that ♥♥♥♥s up its one trick nine times out of ten. It may be worth getting if you have some easily amused eight-year-old children in your home who are in need of a distraction. Maybe you're into the sort of boring Sunday afternoon that's reminiscent of tossing about Legos in a feeble effort to create imaginary explosions. Otherwise, don't bother.

Hyper Knights can be summed as a simplified 2D version of the Mount and Blade games. It is a game which puts you in the command of an army and yourself as the badass king who leads them. The gameplay loop of Hyper Knights is pretty simplistic, most of the enemies you face can be killed by two button prompts: X or C. Some enemies can be killed by three same button prompts or a mix of the two.
You can also use space for Dashing and F to heal yourself or perform a combo when your combo meter has filled up. The enemies also tend to be only of two types: melee and ranged.
You can also command your troops to fight alongside you in the battles to take over enemy fortresses. While the initial premise does not seem that interesting,
Hyper Knights provides enough large scale battles on a small platform to remain fun for sometime without getting overly repetitive. While you are not busy fighting in the real time battles, you can manage your troops and your controlled regions and castles. The castles you control can be given troops to increase their protection or troops can be withdrawn to help you in your various raids.
When you attack an enemy castle, it shows you the amount of soldiers present in it which helps you decide in attacking or abandoning the raid. In such a case, you can either kill a few roamers which will help you upgrade as well as decrease the enemy castle’s strength.
The real fun of Hyper Knights starts when you join a friendly knights battle or vice versa. From here you will witness hundreds of mini soldiers clashing against each other while you make your way through the battlefields like this game wants you to be. Since killing enemy soldiers is really easy, it gives you the sense of a king without being too overwhelming.
You can only do this sort of badassery only while you are surrounded by your troops though as going Rambo against a squadron of enemy troops will make you fodder for the archers. When you die, you are given a proper quick time event with which you can resurrect yourself on the battlefield while failing to do so will respawn you way back to the starting point while your soldiers get slaughtered without their leader.
Hyper Knights does well to keep things balanced and it keeps turning up the difficulty so that you never get too overpowered but even then, there is very little depth to the game. Take down the scale of the battles and nearly every battle you fight is the same in regards to the gameplay.
The only difference between fighting roamers and castles is that you have to destroy a few buildings while you are raiding an enemy fortress. Let me correct myself there, your soldiers have to destroy a few buildings as you don’t have the ability to destroy the said buildings.
Regardless of the power you use there is no way your sword does damage to a structure where your soldiers take their own slow time to destroy the buildings. These structures also provide no benefit to the enemies as till the time the gates are closed the enemy remains trapped inside. They don’t fire from the top or anything, they just stand there while your soldiers bash away at the gates.
Another point to be noted is that since you require soldiers to destroy buildings and there are a few stages where buildings need to be destroyed to gain a victory, if you do not have a soldier left at the end of such a stage there is no way but to replay it all over again. It becomes quite stale after some time and there is no real incentive to keep playing as the story is very negligible.
Personally, I did not like the way Hyper Knights present itself. While my first impressions of Hyper Knights were average, it reuses many assets that it quickly becomes tiresome to the eyes. Even though some of the large scale battles manage to stand out, the bland maps and clunky unit movements make visuals a less impressive package than it could have been.
Similar to its play style, the soundtrack of Hyper Knights feels like a miniature version of epic sound designs. It is smooth and soothing with light hints of war sound design mixed in subtly. The problem though is the fact that Hyper Knights use the same soundtrack everywhere and like the rest of the game, it also slowly grows boring to hear to.
Hyper Knights is an enjoyable albeit repetitive romp through miniature army clashes. It has the ability to make you sit down and play it for a few short bursts and that should mostly be what you should be expecting at its price of admission but a lack of depth and the fact that every battle feels the same makes it a loose its steam before it should.

First of all, I really liked the beta's. I played them quite a lot and enjoyed the game. I didn't preorder it but bought it at launch.
Positive:
- Gearbox vibe. If you're familiar with Borderlands, you'll feel right at home
- A lot of cool different characters with some really cool abilities.
- Game seems balanced (if both teams pick balanced combo's that is: tank - support - (ranged) assassin - DPS)
- graphics are cool (if you like the style. I do). It might get clusterfukkie, but that's just something you need to get used to
Negative:
- matchmaking (or total lack thereof). The game will without issue let you start a match 4v5. It will match level 72 players with level 2 noobs. Great fun garanteed! You either roflstomp the enemy team or get steamrolled yourself. I can count the really close games I had with one, perhaps two fingers (admittedly, I only played around 10-15 matches or so)
- Ridiculous lack of content: 2 (two) meltdown maps. This must be a joke. Plus, nobody wants to play that second map anyway, so you end up with that same map you've been playing since beta.
- Characters are locked behind progress walls. I don't like this idea. I want to try out the support characters. Now I need to grind boring other characters I don't want to play in the first place to unlock these.
- Story mode: so-so. Lot's of shooting, yeah. But why, what is the story? Jokes are 'meh' at best (not on the same level as Borderlands). You can clearly tell this has been added in a rush.
- Gear loadout: why is it so damn difficult to build an intuitive way of managing your gear? I'm clicking, double-clicking left and right, but it's always a chore to move gear in and out of your loadouts. Also, when I select a character and his loadout, am I really supposed to learn by heart what every item does? You can only see it's icon in the character select screen.
- Please order the battleborn by their role. At this point, the game is new and a lot of people (including me) don't fully know all battleborn's role. It might help if you'd put all tanks together, all DPS characters together, and so on...
- the need to grind for better loot. Ugh.
Conclusion:
This game could have been a real hit, but I fear Gearbox just wanted to cram too much into one game and they ended up with a game that's only average at best. The story mode is mediocre. The multiplayer lacks content (basically just one mode and map that everybody plays). They just shot themselves in the foot with this game I fear. But hey, sales figures will probably be good, so we can expect a Battleborn 2 in a couple of years. I do hope they focus on the one thing this game really needs: good content.

This is an amazing game. Although it has some flaws, it's really fun to play. I know that pretty much everything that can be said about this game has already been said, but I decided to make a list anyway
-Great story. If no one has spoiled it for you yet, hurry buy and play this game. There are some great twists that are even better if you don't know they're coming.
-Cool looking combat animations
-Pause system works great
-Lots of choice. Many different things you do will affect the rest of the game, may it be short term or long term, the affects are there.
-Weapon customization. Not the best on most weapons or armour, but I find upgrading and changing your lightsaber makes it feel a bit more... Personal.
-There are a max of 9 companions, but (like I touched on above) certain choices can lead to never getting certain companions. Again, this makes it more fun, as your actions matter.
-Really feels like a Star Wars game. Although Bioware later went on to make Mass Effect, this will always have that charm of being in the universe we all know and love.
-Great level up/skill tree system. Every couple of levels, you get to choose a new "feat" for your character (and with a Jedi, you also get a new force power). So basically no two playthroughs are the same (assuming you aren't trying for the exact same skill tree everytime). You can make every character whatever you want them to be. Although most are kinda "suggested" to be a certain way, you can make them something completely different. Want someone to be a melee fighter? Upgrade their Strength, Defence, and choose a bunch of melee related skills. Want them to be a gunner? Upgrade the traits for that (I can't remember the exact names) and upgrade skills that make you more accurate, more gun abilities, and upgrade which gun type you want to be good at. Besides weaponry, you can also specialize in computers (hacking), demolitions (mine disarming/recovering), security (lockpicking), stealth (sneaking without anyone noticing you), and a few more. Most of them are very useful, with a couple exceptions. Awareness is almost completely useless I think. Unless there's some hidden use for it I don't know of, you only use it like twice when getting attacked by Madalorians, and even then it's not really necessary. I also only used Stealth like once, but I'm sure it could be useful if you actually set your mind to finding ways to use it.
-Not the biggest amount of sidequests, but this game has quality of quantity. There's only a couple quests that have one stage, where you do something, come back, and get a reward. The rest of them are in my opinion quite interesting, especially all the sidequests related to your companions and their backstories.
-Lots of different planets to explore, most being fairly large.
-It can be VERY annoying to actually get it working. If you know what you're looking for, it might not take long, but there's quite a lot of things that I tried to make it not crash on start up. Eventually I think I just took off some things in the settings and was able to make it work, but it really shouldn't be an issue in the first place. I should be able to play the game with tall grass and soft shadows on if I want them!
-The graphics haven't aged very well. The art style itself is nice, but so many times I'm looking at what could be a beautiful scene and thought, wow, this game would look amazing, if the pixels just weren't so visible. This doesn't take away from the gameplay at all, but I really think this game would look gorgeous in HD, and that really makes me sad.
-The boss fight is maybe a bit TOO hard. This is more of a nitpick, but there is a very large difficulty curve between the last stage (a fun challange), the second last boss (a bit more of a challenge), and the final boss (just insane). I don't want to spoil the ending for you, but I think in trying to make a climactic ending, they went a bit too far. The story leading up to that was insane, and I really wanted to see how it would end. But then 10 seconds into the boss "your entire party has been killed, returning to main menu." Oh ok, well let's try agai- "you party has been killed". Well maybe another go. "killed". You see what I'm getting at here? There were a few times in the game that I died a lot, but at least it fealt hopeful. But this boss' stats were just so much higher than your own, it was hard to feel  any hope. In the end I had to resort to more uhh, "unconventional means" to win. (No not cheating.) I liked the whole boss fight atmosphere, and the level design, but I would have enoyed it more if it's defence and attack stats weren't so insane.
...or maybe I just wasn't prepared enough. If you're like me though and you were cought off guard, you're gonna have a bad time.
-Your companions that follow you don't exactly follow you all the time. This seems to happen more often when you get a speed boost, and one or both companions with you either don't recieve it, or just stand still.
All in all this is a great game with a few flaws. If it were to have an HD remake or something though, I think it could be a nearly perfect game, as the combat, atmosphere, and story are all there and brilliant. Definitely recommed this game to any Star Wars or RPG fan.

This game is fine, but it isn't very polished. It feels like a budget game by one or two people, and it makes a lot of rookie mistakes in its design. Everything is very basic, but doesn't feel very stable. Enemy AI is very simple, always firing where you are instead of where you're going. Most fights just boil down to repetitive kiting.
Nothing is explained or discoverable. There aren't any tutorials or controlled settings for you to learn how to play, you're just dropped in and expected to figure it out without any signposting. This wouldn't be a big issue in some games, but because of how hectic the fights are, you don't get a chance to absorb information or experiment. When you inevitably die to something that blended in to the chaos fired by an enemy that blended in to the background, the screen presents you with the option to "restart" or "quit". "Restart" sends you back to the main menu. "Quit" closes the game.
I could go on for hours on the tiny mistakes the game makes all over the place, but overall the game isn't objectively bad. A lot of the problems could be fixed relatively easily. Regardless, I still can't recommend this game considering how many other games on steam are essentially the same game with a hell of a lot more polish.
The soundtrack is nice, though.

Paranautical Activity is truly something special. I remember back when the game was in early access and how the developers were pretty much neglecting their fanbase. I think it took them like 8 months to fix a couple of bugs yet everyone was in shock that the game wasn't abandoned. Now, I haven't really followed the controversy surrounding the game since I'm not interested in developer drama but I am glad that the current developers are actually putting effort into it.
The game itself, to me personally, is nothing more than a nice time waster. Kind of like The Binding of Isaac, you play in randomly generated levels with rooms you must clear in order to advance to the next floor. What differentiates it from other so-called "time wasters", however, is the pure adrenaline you get from fighting multiple enemies or hugh mungus bosses. Even though I haven't played many rogue likes (mostly because I'm not a fan of the genre), I think this game is a great introduction. Your reflexes and coordination will be put to the test, along with your sense of direction in the sometimes overwhelmingly confusing levels. The voxel graphics are nice to look at for what they are though the level design is pretty bland and not memorable in the slightest.
I'd personally recommend the game if you find it on sale. I see a lot of people saying Ziguratt is better and even though I haven't played it, they seem like two entirely different games. While there are certainly better games than this one, I think you will have a good time with Paranautical Activity.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Man, I want to love this game SO badly. It does almost everything right: It has a twitch element and a variety of obstacles to overcome, plus a level editor. The graphics are cute, the palette is colorful, the design element is clever...even the menu is fun! However, the one thing that kills the game for me is that %#$! timer. It's ridiculously fast in parts, and gets my blood pressure elevated far more than any other platformer I've played (including that ubiquitous poster-child for rage quitting, Super Meat Boy). In short: It makes a beautifully designed game more frustrating than enjoyable. The only way to succeed is to fail, and try again. And fail. And try again.
If there were a way to increase the timer by percentages for a more customizable experience, so that the game would appeal to more players, I'd recommend it to everyone. If there were a "puzzle mode" (ie; no timer) I'd recommend it to everyone. Unfortunately, neither of those options exist, and so I have to hang my head in sorrow over the thought of something that could have been more than just a niche experience. It breaks my heart a little bit because the amount of time, love, and care that has gone into its creation is so obvious. I really want to enjoy it. I really want
to enjoy it.
Even with the included Workshop support (which I was really looking forward to using), I cannot recommend this game with the only mode being "fail until you succeed."
EDIT: After playing a bit longer, I've noticed some wonkiness with the hit boxes: They aren't accurate. On the early "saw" level, I completed it by bouncing around like a jackrabbit, including several bounces in the middle of the green poison water that should have killed me but didn't. On the next level, I did a slide-into-jump that accidentally placed me right in front of a dart trap; I should have died instantly, but said darts passed right through me. Conversely, there have been several times where I was merely close to a trap (without contact), yet died anyway. There is a market for difficult games (and, as I've said earlier, I don't mind them) but the controls and hit boxes have to be precise.
This game is pretty fun, and looks really beautiful. Get it!

Video:
Plot/Overview:  Kill things with simple combos, raise armies, hire other knights to do your bidding, then conquer the world.  The loop is simple, fight the enemy army with your's and win the day!
Menus:  The menus are pretty cut and dry as the game isn't really graphics intensive.  You have your resolution options that go up to 4k, full screen toggle, vsync, AA, the option to turn off the gaming running when alt tabbed, language options and the friends names, which will be knights you can hire or fight against while playing.
There is also Twitch integration which allows your viewers to give you extra gold and experience and name knights after them.
You have seperate sliders for sound and music, as well as a master slider.
All the controls are rebindable from the options menu.
The game supports Steam Workshop integration for armor and weapon sets.
Music/Sound:  The music fits the game, it has a nice mediviel sound to it and the sound effects, while generic suit the game well.
Gameplay:  This is the meat and potatoes of this game, it's a simple gameplay loop of raise armies, fight other armies, raid villages, siege castles, and face other knights in fast-paced combo combat where each unit type requires different combos to take down.  While you can use special abilities to heal or wreak havok on your opponents.  And this is where the game to me becomes monotous and boring as it's the same loop, but you have more knights and you have more combos and skills.
The AI does their own thing and you have limited control of your army, using the map to tell where troops to go, but beyond that, no other control.
Controls:  A controller is strongly reccomended for this game.  And as mentioned above, all the controls are rebindable for your own comfort.
TLDR
Pros:
Simple and addictve gameplay.
Rebindable Keys.
Neutral:
Twitch Integration
Music/Sound
Cons:
Gameplay becomes repetitve.
The game turns in to a grind.
Everything is a QTE
Enemy Knights can become a chore as they focus you.
Limited control over the AI.

Honestly the game is kind of interesting, but not really worth the price.
The graphics were nice, and the atmosphere was great, but the world still felt blocky, so adding more static objects or something to make it feel real and not square would be awesome. The walking felt really slow, but considering the first part of the game is set in a small area, it makes some sense if they want the game to play a tad longer, but even the running was barely faster than that and felt way too slow for a game. The puzzles I played were pretty bland, lack-luckster, and had been done countless times since the 90's, nothing really special there, although I didn't get the full experience as the game keeps crashing when loading the 2nd area. Sound effects were great, but the lack of music made it awkward. No, not tense, or suspensful. Awkward, and kind of distracting from the whole atmostphere.
The writing seems bland, un-motivated, and very simplistic. It's kind of obvious they were going off of nothing here, which isn't inherently bad, but it really didn't have anything special going for it. Bland "puzzles", bland writing, no music, and decent at best graphics didn't really give this game much to stand on.
Honestly, not a bad game at all, the devs are off to a good start, but it doesn't seem polished yet. I can't say it doesn't feel complete, as I didn't get a chance to finish the game, but the part I HAVE played, the beginning, wasn't very polished, and the beginning is where you want the majority of your polish, since it's the first thing the player gets to experience for your game, and will form A LOT of assumtions and expectations for the rest of your game, so it's important to set that tone and atmosphere correctly, but who knows? Maybe it has better puzzles once you beat the beginning in 10 minutes!
Overall has the potential to be a cool game, but right no it's not worth the money unless it's you have some extra steam-cash laying around. I think the developers have potential, FOR SURE! They just need to work on polishing their skills a little more and maybe communicating with others in their field to gather opinions and playtesters to REALLY polish the game and make it a solid $20 experience rather than a half-baked $4 one. Maybe do some more research as to the deep, intricate analysis of video games. Games aren't as simple as just making them, there is A LOT of thought that must go into all aspects of games, and that's something I personally find enjoyable to educate myself about, and is a necessity for any budding game-developer. Good luck to the devs and their future endeavours, and if you decide to buy the game, I hope you can actually load all parts of it!
EDIT: As a side note, there are no options in the game either. No brightness, no volume, no resolution, nothing. Just "New Game", "Load Game", and "Exit". Don't expect anything else.

I'm not a big fan of roguelikes, and I'm not very good at them.  This game has a lot of good things going for it, but fell just short of being great.  If you're a fan of roguelike fps games, then it's worth a try.   However, be aware that the learning curve may be steep.  There's no single starting character that is well balanced for someone new to the game.
Pros
-Great music.  The music may be the best part, imo.  I don't know if I'd call it dubstep, as the outline has.
-The voxel artwork is interesting, and the bosses are all pretty great in their own ways.
-The Seafarers Guide pdf is useful and the mini documentary is interesting. (To find it, right click your game and click properties, then click the "local files" tab and "browse local files")
-I believe a lot of thought was put into the pickups and weapons and effects and differentiating objects from each other.
Cons
-There's no well balanced character for a begginning player to pick up the game quickly with.
-It's not obvious what pickups do.  The seafarers guide will tell you, and google might.
-A lot of pickups can be detrimental to gameplay, and those seem to be the items I get most.  For example, I seem to get a lot of slow down items when I'm the tank until I move too slow to get out of the way of anything.
-When there are a lot of particles on the screen it can be hard to tell what's going on (this may just be an unavoidable side effect of bullet hell shooters)
-The menus can feel a little cheap.  I can't put my finger on why exactly.  But they're menus, so they don't really matter.  They are the introduction to the game.  Also,  the Unity frontloader always feels kind of amateur(cookie cutter) to me. Moving the controller options and video options into the main game menu and dropping the frontloader would have remedied that.  Again, it really has no effect on gameplay, so it's not a big deal to me.
-On my machine, in OSX, there seems to be some issues with music lagging and possibly other kinds of lag.  An fps counter would be nice, so I could know for sure.  This could just be my machine, or just OSX.  I don't know.
-The controversy surrounding this game is highly disconcerting.  I hope those at fault learned the right lessons from the experience, and that everyone involved was compensated fairly for their efforts.
Games are hard as hell to make, and overall I feel like this was a really good effort.  Without the controversy, and with some incremental improvements, I feel like this game could have gone much further, and been a lot more successful.

To be completely honest...it's really disappointing but I keep playing it anyway.  I put most of my time in the cooperative mission.  They're fun for a bit, but still very repetitive.
Pros:
*Good mechanics; controls feel great
*Art style
*Story missions (not the narrative itself; that sucks.  The missions are comparable to Destiny strikes but more repetitive)

Cons:
*If someone drops out (they will) they aren't replaced - even if it's during character selection.  It would be nice if they would patch this.
*Matchmaking - it matches you up with people around your level, but you'll be pit against a team of high levels.
*Optimization: for the visuals that are in this game, it does NOT run well.  I mean it runs almost acceptably, but what you see on the screen doesn't justify the power you have to have to crank it up.  It's silly.

Создателям в рамках одной игры пожалуй удалось совместить несовместимое. Игра реалистична и боевые действия показаны очень правдоподобно, при этом управление очень простое и интуитивно понятное. Бои очень захватывающие и динамичные, но при этом вы успеваете не только всем войскам раздать приказы, но и просчитать все на пару ходов вперед как в шахматах.
Что вообще из себя представляет игра? В игре показаны битвы между блоком НАТО и ОВД в сеттинге 1975-1990 годов.
В игре обширнейший парк техники - порядка 900 юнитов. Здесь есть все: и разные виды пехоты, и броневики, и артиллерия, и танки, и вертолеты, и самолеты, и система ПВО, есть даже огнеметные танки. Например из танков есть и Т-34-85, и Т-55 разных модификаций, разные Т62, Т-64, Т-72, Т80 - всего не перечислить. А самое главное ключевые особенности техники показаны очень правдоподобно! Техника в игре обладает теми же сильными и слабыми сторонами, что и в реале.
Второе что безумно радует - техника СССР великолепна. Это не мальчики для битья как в других играх, это грозные и страшные машины. Т-80У - самый грозный и страшный танк в игре, Су-25Т способен нанести непоправимый урон вражеской бронетехнике, ЗСУ Бук - быстро приземлит любой, даже самый совершенный НАТОовский самолет.
Но я увлекся :)
Чем еще хороша игра? Она как шахматы! Тут надо думать и просчитывать все наперед. Если вы все тщательно продумали и действуете грамотно вы разобьете любого противника, даже если у вас меньше войск, даже если у него техника лучше - это радует.
В игре есть несчетное множество тактических решений и все они работают при грамотной реализации - все приносит свои плоды.
Отдельного разговора заслуживает создание армии. Тут также все сбалансировано. Игрок может взять в бой не так уж много моделей бронетехники и чем совершенней техника - тем меньше ее можно взять. Это приводит к тому, что нет однозначно выигрышного сетапа армии, а также к тому, что вы еще неоднократно вернетесь к редактированию своей армии. Это очень хорошо.
P.S. Напоследок совет. Не играйте в сингл - против вас будет компьютер (да, он играет также отлично, но все же это не живой человек). Лучше найдите еще одного единомышленника (а лучше 3 или даже четырех), созвонитесь по Скайпу и идите в мультиплеерные бои в одной команде. Столько позитивных эмоций вы не получите ни в одной другой игре!

I also myself, am a zombie slaying addict and adore the zombie modes they have in store as well as different normal modes.
Yes i agree it is a bit of a Pay To Win, but you can still outskill people with the standard guns.
Anyway, Here are my Pros and Cons.
Pros:
- Great feel and gameplay , just like old Cs
-Good weapon system, and daily login rewards (same guns but you get them for free for a day - few days)
-Good zombie and normal modes with different maps to play on!
-Different, and cool weapons you get from crafting or decoders!
Cons:
-Alot of people do pay on this game (from having alot of nicer weapons, i have spent a little money on this game to make this an honest review.) But fortunatley you dont really need nicer guns for pvp (like classic or deathmatch, team deathmatch etc.) Thats just based on skill, really.
-Not as many english speakers anymore on the N. American servers like when the game released in 2014. But still fun to shoot and kill or rack up zombies and farm.
Well, that wraps up my review. Overall i very highly recommend this game.

Gonna mix these because they go hand-in-hand. There are only sounds for certain things in the game. The Bug Princess is finally widely available in the USA. Mushihimesama is one of Cave's most beautiful shooters and the culmination of a decade in developing the craft that is a modern shooter. Significant level of detail is given to enemy placement and movement, as well as bullet speed and patterns.
Quality Cave shooters are more like a well choreographed dances and Mushihimesama is maybe the pinnacle of Cave's efforts without relying heavily on fan service or tropes. The artwork and character sprites are absolutely gorgeous. The game comes with many options, monitor rotations, an arranged mode, and a 1.5 update.
This is a great shmup for the casual crowd, and Cave recognized that their games were becoming increasingly esoteric and pigeonholed for a very specific type of fan of the genre.  They decided to break away from genre tropes in the setting and art style, also reconsidering the way the player interacts with the game and bullet patterns.

This is an excellent vertical bullet hell shoot em' up (shmup).
Everything in this game just feels right. Of course, I haven't gotten to the TLB, but so far so good.
The modes are quite diverse, with different feeling in each one. The  Novice mode is a nice addition to newcomers, although it will feel boring after a dive to the Original's Maniac mode, but it it a good place to get your first ever 1 credit clear before moving on to greater challenges.
Even though there are massive amount of bullets and you'll die a lot, it never gets frustrating. It doesn't even feel unfair, because controls are fluid and every mistake is yours alone. No invisible bullet syndrome here. And after a while of dying in the barrage of bullets you'll get better and it's very exhilarating to successfully dodge waves of bullets that might have seemed impossible before. I notice that my vocal cords produce funny sounds under pressure: different grunts and yells and laughs while dodging the impossible.
The main difference in Mushihimesama and other shmups is the beautiful, fantasy-like setting. Flying around surrounded by the lush greenery and colourful landscapes while butchering thousands of equally colourful and interesting bug creatures is really ...relaxing (?) in way. I think this is where the charm of Mushihimesama is. Most shmups are usually in a military setting or in space, so this is a welcome change of scenery.
There are cool features like leaderboards for Score Attack mode and the option to watch other peoples replays to get better or uploading your own. There's even a training mode for all modes excluding novice (it doesn't need it anyway) for you to train specific levels with different settings.
For newcomers to the game or genre, I suggest to try all the different modes of Normal before going to novice. Then laugh while the enemy falls before you before being able to do anything. Then get bored and go back to Normal Maniac to have some adrenaline-induced fun. (insert creepy yet somewhat satisfied but still craving smiley) Watch videos because they teach a lot. And don't get discouraged by inevitable losses or the intimidating barrage of bullets. Everything is surprisingly manageable with proper conditioning. And I still haven't been able to pass the third stage without continues in the original game. But I know I will.

I have never really played a game like this before.  It is quite difficult, and on one of the levels I played through and died about 30 times in a row before I figured out what I was doing wrong.  At first I found myself wishing for a tutorial, but then I realized that figuring it out on my own made me feel like I had really accomplished something.  You know, sort of like when you don't understand some math homework, but then suddenly the answer dawns on you.
Since I have young game players in the house, and also because I prefer not to watch bloody and gory animations, I truly appreciate that the developer included a 'no gore' option to make the game family friendly.  It's always a positive when gamers are given a choice, and it shows that the developer is willing to put work into the game to make it accessible to everyone.

Death traps, close calls, and puzzles that will make you shout at your screen welcome to InfiniTrap: Ohio Jack and The Cup Of Eternity! You are greeted with a treasure hungry protagonist named Ohio Jack who is on a mission to acquire the Cup of Eternity from Culsus deadly lair. She plays along with your search and grants you the power to revive as long as you keep playing the “game”. The puzzles are simple at first but gradually get tougher with the time limit playing a big factor and you will find yourself dying not once, not twice, but thirty times! The 2D graphics are simple and fun with a standard color palette for exploration in ruins. The music is nothing spectacular but charming in a way to make you think and eager to go to the next level. I found myself loving the levels and progressing to get closer to that cup, even though I died the death animations are amazing. I did find  a couple of problems with the levels such as for one of them where you’re surrounded by zombies and you have no idea where the end is and to me that level is based on luck. A puzzle game should be based on strategic thinking, a optional minimap can easily solve this problem and make some of the levels like that more successful in being stealthy. Another problem I found were the traps…well the one really where you could not even tell it was a trap, I know the idea of a trap is surprising but this one was not obvious…the floor is somewhat cracked if you look really close at it. I know there are limitations for 2D graphics but players are going to get frustrated if they can’t tell what traps look like in the game. I did take a look at the level editor and it took some tinkering but I understand how the triggers, setting enemies, and emitters work, but play testing and seeing the custom map in game did not work for me, I’m hoping the issue will be resolved as soon as possible! Overall I enjoyed the levels I played and would definitely recommend it to anyone who wants to play a fun exploration puzzle game. Onwards to your journey!
I also made a Let's Play video if you want to check it out of the first 12 levels!

I've only played "Ben There, Dan That!" so far and I can say that it was worth every minute. The humor was outstanding with lots of references to P&C classics, the game doesn't take itself seriously at all and doesn't hesitate to break the 4th wall, which is a good thing in my opinion. Gameplay-wise it's very Lucasartsy, no verbs or anything but you cycle through actions and click. There is a rudimentary inventory and you can combine objects.
After playing through the game though it's clear that it was meant more as an homage and a parody than an actual game. The puzzles are very easy and while the art has a unique identity, the music and sound FX can certainly be improved. Voice overs would have been welcome but the game plays fine without them.
All in all a very solid B+ and a must for any P&C veteran

A fun, quirky, goofy point and click romp throughout alternate dimensions. First, the gameplay: your controls are the usual point-and-click fare, no surprises. You have an inventory of objects you find along the way that you use to accomplish specific goals- and almost any of these objects can interact with one another, either to make something useful, or to get a remark from Dan about how stupid the combination you just tried is. There's trees and subtrees and subsubtrees of interactive dialogue with characters you meet along the way. You may also interect with literally everything in your environment, too. Basically if you can see it, the developers wrote an action for it.
Style is very cartoony, but fun. Don't be looking for top-end graphics here, it's quite choppy! I personally feel like this just adds to the silly, goofy feel. Character design is pretty standard for Dan and Ben, but some other characters you meet are pretty funky looking.
The game constantly makes one-liners or jokes. It's very tongue-in-cheek, and they break the 4th wall all the time. I promise some of these things will literally have you laughing out loud at least once. Funny dialogue, funny situations, funny level designs... the whole game is one giant cheesy gag and it's fantastic.
The one con Ihave to say against this game is it's length. It was over far too quickly and left me wanting more. Luckily there is...
A continuation of the first game with even more exploration, interactivity, and fleshed out story arc. Much longer than BTDT, too. Everything good about the first game is in here too, but better. Some of the puzzles are *really* hard in this game, miles beyond anything in  the first. They also added a time element that involves crisscrossing timelines and seeing alternate versions of people and places.
Two thumbs up. Buy it. For an even sweeter deal, get it on sale. You won't regret it.

If this was the only dungeon-crawling procedurally-genrated permadeath FPS I've ever played, I'd probably recommend it. It has a strong style going for it—I admire that—but it just feels a bit mediocre, especially when compared to other games of this genre.
The gameplay is really basic: murder bad things with weapons, run & jump & dodge, enhance your character with power-ups, and progress forward. This is all just fine, but there's not much that makes it stand out here, just like this paragraph!
I understand the logistics in building the enviroments as cubes of equal size, but the designs within are so unimaginitive: too much symmetry and open space. There are a few areas that utilized space in all three axes quite well, but they are rather sparse.

The voxel graphics and lighting are my favourite aspects of this game. The enemies are neato, and I especially love the minotaurs... woof, so sexy!
I do like this game, but I don't recommend it because there's more fulfilling ways to spend time and money.

A fun roguelike shooter with pixelated graphics. Not the best in its genre, but fun nonetheless.
In Paranautical Activity, you have a few classes to pick and they differ in speed, damage, fire rate, health and starting weapons. After picking your character, you'll be traversing through randomly generated rooms, defeating enemies on the way, collecting money and using said money to buy upgrades when you come to a room with items for sale. At the end of each level, you'll fight a boss before progressing to the next level.
The main issue with the game is that it can be very confusing at times. As a roguelike game, it's expected that the game won't hold your hand and a lot of trial-and-error will be involved, but even then the game does little to tell you what each item does. The game could certainly benefit with being at least slightly more descriptive.
Another issue is that because rooms look mostly the same and enemies repeat themselves a lot as well, the game can become quite repetitive.
In comparison to games like Tower of Guns or Ziggurat, it doesn't stand out, but it's still recommended for those who enjoy roguelike shooters.

Gearbox has been a favorite developer of mine for some time, but I never heard of this game until a friend told me about the first trailer which should have been a bad sign. For some reason this game was under-marketed with a failure to advertise the game properly and that is somewhat factoring into the low number of players. However, it is a decent game but in my opinion I don't enjoy playing this game. Some of these cons and pros may be opinionated and others will be plain fact.
One thing I like overall is the progression which allows you to unlock more characters and just have a goal. Characters are great and have humorous moments and dialogue like Oscar Mike who is my personal favorite
One major issue is that this game has a horrible memory leak which causes major stuttering and frame drops from long sessions of playing without resets to the game (Easy fix, so it is not put as a con to anything really). The game is somewhat taxing at higher visual settings.
And I know this game is not Overwatch and I will not compare it to eachother, but it is somewhat obvious that this will end up being a competitor of Overwatch. Overwatch is also a leading factor in the reason why the player count is so low as the game was released very close to an Open Beta of Overwatch which saw drastic differences in the player count, which is rather sad when people won't give Battleborn a try in any method such as Steam Share, borrowing a copy, etc.
(Going to the community hub will tell you how many players are currently playing the game: HIghest I have seen is 6000 players at once)
Now for the main piece:
It is an okay game, but honestly it begins to feel like a generic fps with rpg elements like Destiny. When viewed as an FPS with RPG and MOBA aspects it is unique. I just happen to dislike this combination of game styles I guess and don't see the MOBA aspects unless playing Incursion.
The moba aspects make it competetive and the several different characters allow for different tactics and uses. However, because it is a moba there is no drop-out and drop-in gamemodes and the matches will range from 30 minutes to an hour. With that comes perks as the game requires communication and strategy to excel, so this is both a pro and con it its own way.
The gear system is refreshing, but really is a dumbed down item shop that you have to customize before games. As a result of being unable to customize on the fly, it hinders the customization as you cannot change gear depending on the situation like in Dota or League of Legends.
The game is funny sometimes with obvious points of humor, but in some cases takes itself too seriously and you see a drastic drop in jokes throughout the campaign with stale moments. The multiplayer has some occasionally funny dialogue as well and I wouldn't expect much humor from that aspect of the game.
The multiplayer is actually fun when you know what is happening while action is occuring. It is not fun to watch members of your team begin to leave when you begin to lose the match though.
Especially with the low amount of players currently which admittedly has a really nice community. I almost enjoy the fact that there is no META yet and it allows you to experiment and mess around without getting yelled at and berated by insults questioning your mental capacity.

Case #8 is a horror adventure game that makes you play as a character in a deep underground prision. The game involves some puzzles to complete in order to progress, I feel like this game has a lot of potential but for the time being it still has it's crashes here and there whlist your playing through the game.
When you think of a typical horror game you might think of complicated puzzles that make the game string along a bit more and make your playtime on that game a bit more than you would of liked. Although, Case #8 has very simple and easy puzzles that you can get through fairly quickly. The hardest part about the game would be finding the correct equipment in the game in order to finish a puzzle. Even then though, thanks to the graphics it kind of stands out what you can interact with and where the tools could possibly be. This really helps the game as it does not try to make you have a longer playtime on the game from the difficult puzzles that are in most horror games. But would you would expect in a horror game would be, well, scares throughout the game to keep you on edge. But, unfortunatly there really aren't any scares at all which lets the game down slightly. There are no jumpscares, which are the most cheap and common, nothing that will really make you terrified or keep you on edge. There is no tutorial for the game to tell you what each of the controls are, maybe even a screen at the beginning of the game with the controls would've been nice. It's not exactly hard to figure out how to move and interact with objects and stuff.
For the graphics that are in this game, there's nothing that really seems to be good or to be a very high quality. Some of the walls look a bit bad, and since the game basically uses the same walls over and over you will have ti put up with it throught the game. The lighting of the game seems to be well done, as most of the lights are very dim which is what you would expect from a horror game. This really creates a nice atmospheric feel that there isn't any power through this prison and that there is obviously something out there to get you like in most horror games.
On the other hand, the sound effects of this game are very good. Each of the sound effects are very well designed, such as the doors opening when you unlock them and your footsteps when you are obviously walking. All the sounds that are produced are of a very high quality, and definatly makes you feel as if you are in the game and such.
+ Very atmospheric
+ Nice sounds effects
+ The lighting is very nice
+ Good price
+ Trading Cards
- The graphics are a bit off for the quality
- There are no scares
Case #8 isn't much of a scary game, which is a little disappointing for such a horror game that really sets up a tense atmosphere. The lighting is very nice, really seems like there is hardly any power to the areas, and the sound effects of the game are reallly good quality that also sets the atmosphere. For the price that the game is asking for, it's a nice horror game, just not many scares throughout the game to keep you on the edge.

Myst is now 24 years old. It's the product of a simpler time. I didn't expect to enjoy it as much as I did, but having just finished the main game in two days, I think it still holds up well compared to some of the latest walking simulators out there.
The story is simple, but the otherworldly music, the haunting writing, and the surreal worlds of Myst give it a glorious mystery that mesmerized me from the moment I picked up a book in Atrus' library. The voice-acting is actually quite fitting; Sirrus and Achenar are disturbing to interact with, while Atrus projects this Jedi-like air of enigmatic wisdom.
I was surprised by the lushness of the graphics. Most roleplaying games struggle to have textures half as good as the ones I saw here. Granted, Myst's worlds are tiny in comparison to modern games; the whole of Myst would fit into the Presidium from Mass Effect, or Michael's mansion in GTA V. But it's a beautiful game regardless.
I played realMyst with classic Myst controls, and they still work just fine. You won't get more than 50% of the achievements without the new free movement controls, but that wasn't important for me. While some of the puzzles, particularly the auditory ones in the Selenitic Age, are illogical and difficult to understand, most of them are interesting or fun once you figure out the trick behind them. And many of the clues for solving them are available from the beginning of the game, you just need to put them all together.
realMyst: Masterpiece Edition successfully updates a gaming classic, and is a great buy for players looking to relive the early 90s.

As a die-hard gamer, I can remember waiting in line to play the table top coin op PONG, then Asteroids, then Space Invaders.  After Commodore 64 came out, the dream of being able to game at home became a possibility, but no one could foresee to what extent until MYST was released in 1993.  The Millers opened the flood gates to the gaming world we virtually live in today. The high definition of graphics and soundtracks heightened your senses as you immersed into the story of surreal expectations (and this was BEFORE surround sound and VR).  MYST set the pace for gamers and then raised the bar for other developers to follow. The game never grew old, but its OS did which is the only reason I stopped playing it -- it was no longer compatible with my gear.  I'm proud to say that it was Myst that brought me to Steam; the little engine that could steampower me back into the world of MYST. Since then, I've purchased all the Cyan bundles, Quern, and several other "casual" "puzzle" "adventurer" solo-playing games. I am digging it. Wasn't disappointed with the quality then, am not now nor ever will be thanks to the developers of a definite classic.

Additionally Mushihimesama seems to be best of those releases on Steam.
Instead of shooting enemies, the gameplay comes much to dodging and situation analysis (here I can dodge there, now I can dodge there and shoot that one, now I blank and panic and use bomb). Little by little player's situation analysis skills develop and panic-bombing can be saved later in the game.
The pace of the game is very high and player needs to be constantly push his/her consentration and sit on the edge of the seat. Mushihimesama kind of reminds me from the good old times (I never actually experienced) when computers had names, joystics were the thing and video games came much to constantly retrying that seemingly infinite (actually 20 min long) game myriad of times, which can be surprisingly fun :)

Such a long mystery! It took over 20 years to reach the end(ings) of
. I started playing it at a friend's house when I was 15, both of us agonizing over the puzzles and clues in an age before the balm of Gamefaqs and Youtube tutorials. Now, thanks to the magic of retro gaming remastered reboots, I finished
and can exhale a breath more than two decades old.
"Atrus! I finally get it!"
In 1995, the first time I landed on Myst island, the game had already been out for a couple of years and blown away fans and critics, generated a host of clones, and provided the seven-person team of Cyan, Inc. enough capital to make four sequels. Every time a new sequel dropped, I'd cringe. "SO wanna buy that, but I never finished the first one. Arrgh!"
Having watched all the endings, 100-percented all the achievements, and found all the Easter Eggs, I can move on. I can play those sequels and call up my high school friend to gloat: "Spoiler! I know which brother to rescue!" (I don't think he ever finished it; the dude was the king of rage-quitting before it was a thing.)
So how does the game compare to the original? Awesomely!
is unquestionably prettier, sharper, less buggy, easier to navigate, and more fun to play than the original. It's even oodles better than the 2002 remastered version...or that Nintendo DS one...or that IOS mess. The free-roam option takes full advantage of the Unity engine as do the water and sky.
How does it compare to modern Walking Simulators and Adventure games? Not so good. It's important to remember that
set a benchmark in gaming and storytelling that greatly improved the quality of PC games for decades, but it has indeed been bested several times since the 90s. All those games, though, have a bit of
within them and it's fun to meet the grandpappy of them all.
Hands down, I loved it! Enjoyable, lore-filled, nostalgic, historic, and a great world to visit and revisit, Myst has something to offer today's puzzle-solving adventurer.

This game is incredible. I basically grew up with it--we had it on CD-ROM when I was a kid, and my parents tell me they played it through together when they were first married, before internet walkthroughs. For a game with no dialogue and very little required reading, there is a lot of lore behind it and it is wonderful to just explore the different ages.
On the first playthrough, the puzzles can be pretty difficult. They're pretty complex, but I think if you keep at it they can eventually be figured out without turning to the internet. I think it has some replay value, even though you have to wait a while so the puzzle solutions aren't fresh, because a big part of the experience is exploring the ages.
The game itself is pretty short. I know the basic ideas behind most of the puzzles, and it took me about two hours to finish.
If you want a shortish game for the exploring rather than the action, and you like to do a bit of reading to get at the lore (some of the books in the library are readable) then this game is fantastic.

Mushihimesama is a game that I went back and forth over buying for quite some time.  I'd heard stories of CAVE's arcade shmups (especially DoDonPachi, Espgaluda, and Ketsui) for years, but had never actually had the opportunity to play any of them.  Upon seeing Mushihimesama on Steam I was excited, but after watching the trailer I decided to hold off on it.  I'm not sure exactly what it was about the trailer, but it failed to sell me the game.  I'm sure the rumors I heard that it wasn't a very good port didn't help matters either.  Eventually I decided to pick it up anyway, and I'm really glad that I did.  Perhaps you shouldn't always judge a game by its trailer.
Although I've never played any of their other games, it's my understanding that Mushihimesama plays similarly to other CAVE games.  Your “ship” in this game is actually the main character Reco riding on a golden beetle named Kiniro.  Reco's hitbox is tiny, which is good, because saying, “there are a lot of bullets to avoid” would be a massive understatement.  CAVE certainly lives up to their reputation.  Depending on the difficulty setting, the enemy bugs will fire an astounding number of bullets, sometimes filling the majority of the screen.
Fortunately for beginners, there are quite a few different ways to adjust the difficulty.  The game has three different modes: novice, normal, and arrange.  Novice and normal are further broken down into original, maniac, and ultra.  Arrange doesn't have any additional difficulty options but features a different soundtrack, maximum attack power and options, auto-bombing on hit, and different enemy locations.  In addition to normal modes of play there is also a rather robust training mode where you can practice specific stages.  There really is a difficulty mode here for everyone here.
There are three different attack modes to choose from when you start the game.  The difference between the three deals with the movement speed of Reco/Kiniro and the spread of your attack (narrow to wide).  All of the attack modes have the ability to perform a concentrated fire attack which heavily slows your speed.  This is particularly useful for precise movement when navigating through bullet dense areas.  There are also two modes for options: trace and formation.  The attack mode and option mode can be changed by collecting the corresponding power up during the game.  In addition to weapons and options, Reco also has screen clearing bombs at her disposal which are very useful for getting out of sticky situations.
As far as the rumors of Mushihimesama being a bad port, it's difficult for me to judge as I never played the original arcade release.  The game looks and sounds great.  The only issue I experienced was a single crash in almost twenty hours of gameplay.  Perhaps It should be noted that you can stretch the screen so it reaches the top and bottom of your monitor.  I didn't realize this at first and spent some time playing with the default settings.  As far as I can remember all the previous shmups I've played stretch it out by default.
Mushihimesama is a lot of fun, and I've ended up spending a lot more time playing it than I thought I would.  It's the sort of game that validates the phrase, “practice makes perfect.”  You can play casually through the game in about 30 minutes or you can spend countless hours trying to clear each difficulty mode without using a continue.  This is a game that I would definitely recommend.  I hope more CAVE games are brought to Steam in the future.

Originally released for Arcade in 2004 and later ported to other systems such as PS2 and Xbox 360, Mushihimesama is a shoot 'em up (shmup) game belonging to a sub-genre called danmaku aka bullet hell developed by japanese company Cave which is one of the experts in producing this type of game. For those not familiar with danmakus, I usually define as a type of shmup characterized by gameplay fast, intense and frantic with the enemies "urinating" bullets all the time, defying dexterity and motor skills of the player who often have millimetric spaces to dodge the bullets and hit your enemies. Mushihimesama has excellent quality with top gameplay, great music, excellent controls and a particular thing that I find really cool about this game is its thematic involving the natural world and insects, because you control a princess named Reco using as "craft" a large golden beetle called Kiniro in the fight against insects, just remember that most often in the shmups the environment is set to futuristic times with high-tech ships, so Mushihimesama has a differential. Okay so I finally decided to write a review on this game, keep in mind that I have about 8 hours of game-time but wasn't recorded due to me being offline.
I will make the review as short as possible since I was not impressed at all and was so frustrated.
Paranautical Activity is an FPS Rogue game that copies the style of binding of isaac, from the character voices, to the weapon description, the level progression and more, which I think is great but sadly they screwed up something so bad.
Fast-paced action, nice controls, easy to understand weapons and items.
Nice enemies, good level progressions, replay-ability, a lot of secrets.
There are some levels that just throws the game for me and sadly you have to go through some of them "random luck" to finish a run, they're the dark room levels, your vision is dead, the rooms are TOO DARK
I get it they tried to add a horror factor and maybe copied the idea of the shadow curse of binding of isaac but they did it so bad, this is FPS you cant make it impossible to see the floor around me and the enemies thats so dumb.
So many times I had an op run I was killing bosses so easily, but then I encounter the dark levels and I die from normal enemies because I cant see them.
All you can do is keep on jumping and shooting around like a maniac hoping you might see the red glowy small light that some enemies have, but eventually die because its almost impossible to see them coming, this really REALLY threw the game for me, reached the point where its not even funny anymore I just barely finish those levels by jumping constantly, then next floor ? Same level ...
There are a lot of bugs in the game, I keep getting glitches every time I start a new run that brings up the menu and doesn't go away "I think they tried to force pause the game so you cant move while the level starts but screwed up"
The music is REALLY good but even at my best headsets they do sound a bit ...static I guess ? or maybe thats how they meant to do them, I don't know.
The game could have so much more but it ruined all of that with the shadow levels it just threw the entire game out of concept, ruined my experience, made the game unbelievably frustrating and I just had to alt+f4 when I got 3 dark levels in a row.
If you're ok with playing this game with the dark levels that will frustrate the hell out of you, get this game on the current 1.99$ price sales, dont get it full price.

Let me begin by saying that Myst, to this day, is one of my favorite games. I played it the year it came out and it defined me almost as much as it defined the genre of gaming it created. In the following years I played every Myst sequel, read all the books, and bought all the remakes and soundtracks. I preface with this to say, RealMyst: Masterpiece is terrible.
I understand that the first neophyte steps I took onto Myst Island, shrouded in mystery and its share of bewildering puzzles, can never be replicated. Nor has the aesthetic ever been so beautiful as it is in my age-gilded memory. But the graphics in this ‘masterpiece’ are indeed terrible. It’s distractingly terrible. But not nearly so distracting as the nauseating movement, unpredictable controls, and constant crashing (you could blame my computer).
If you have never played the Myst series, then it’s hard to say if you will enjoy this game or not because it really is dated. I’m not sure anyone can have that sense of abandonment that the very first strangers to Myst had because we have now become so used to games dropping us into a situation we have no idea how to handle. But the story behind it all is, even now, unique and beautiful, especially if you continue into the sequels.
I have always enjoyed the puzzles of the Myst series because they feel as though they were built by engineers. They feel practical and organic. They build on the experiences you play through. They make reading the stories and carrying your ‘Myst Notebook’ around with you exciting because you feel like you are studying a new culture and journaling your own progress through a world. In fact, if there was one thing that I think makes the Myst games unique, it is their exploration of culture.
If you could go back in time and play the game in its original form, I would suggest doing that exactly. And then I would give this Masterpiece Edition a huge thumbs down and say, don’t even look at it. But since this ‘Masterpiece’ is the only version you are likely to find, I would still say that the game is worth it. It’s challenging and touching and in truth a (poorly aging) masterpiece.

First played Myst as a child.  My father bought the game for me because the box cover looked cool. What I found was an intensely immersive and compelling game unlike anything I had experienced prior. I recently installed realMyst: Masterpiece Edition and overall I would say it is a worthwhile, if somewhat brisk, gaming experience - if you go into it understanding its limitations.
The updated graphics and 3D engine, along with new video settings that are now available, serve to enhance the overall experience and gameplay.  The sound and music, as well as the day/night cycle, give an aura of surrealism/realism beyond what I initially expected.  The game is still intriguing, with a simple, engaging story that is revealed to the player in pieces, adding to allure.  The puzzles are challenging, yet solvable and you shouldn't need to consult the in-game hints or Internet walk-throughs to progress. Flashlight feature is helpful and the water/lava textures look great. But that is not to say it is not without its flaws.
Some of the pain points:
- While free-form mode is cool in that it allows you to navigate your environment in 3D, it often clashes with the point and click elements of the original game, sometime resulting in making the operation of solving puzzles way more frustrating than need be. (You can revert to classic mode to avoid this)
-Only 5 save slots
-Only being able to carry one red/blue page at a time, which results in having to retrace your steps from Myst to an Age and then back again
-Addition of the Age of Rime provides some context to the sequel Riven, but overall from a puzzle/gameplay perspective it seems short and pointless
-Preserves the original outdated video encoding which can be somewhat jarring and detrimental to the well-crafted immersion of the rest of the game
-Not well-optimized.  You will more likely than not experience FPS drops in certain areas if you max out all settings
-Achievements are meh - you get them through natural game progression, obvious interactions with the environment or in some cases by just wildly random actions.  In any case I never really felt I achieved much of anything by earning them.
-Without the nostalgia factor, younger gamers may feel unfilled by the shortness of the game, lack of sophistication by today's standards, or familiar gaming tropes that newer games have borrowed from Myst over the years/decades.

I remember this game from my childhood. Always intrigued me, but for whatever reason, the puzzles felt like they were beyond my reach. I tried restarting a few times using the CD version, but never figured out up from down. Recently, I thought I'd try installing it again, but there are compatibility issues with Windows 10, so I put this game on my wishlist and waited till there was a good deal on it. For about $5, this is definitely a steal.
Coming back to it, remembering how my dad played, I had a certain nostalgia for the island and its ages. But then I realized it was not so confusing once you figure out the switches and tower rotations in the beginning. After that point, things come into place. I don't actually recall exactly how the game used to look, but the updated graphics and night/day cycles are great. I also don't recall being able to just hold down the left mouse button in order to let you move at a pace that is much closer to your average fps than what I remember from Myst. Either way, it felt smooth.
There is definitely room for more improved graphics, but what was done for this version is quite good and well worth what I paid for it. Although it's definitely not as hard as I thought it may be, coming into it and trying to really solve the puzzles on my own for the first time, it does require some basic mapping that isn't immediately obvious to a first-time player or someone like me who only has a passing recollection of the ages and puzzles. That being said, even if this game were easier, I find that the island and its ages have a certain charm and mystique that is unique, and exploring these places is enjoyable.
Would recommend to anyone interested in puzzles, maybe looking for a nostalgia trip to the 90s and those who like point and click adventures.

It's easy to forget (or not realize if you're younger) just how much of an impact Myst had when it was first released. It was the first modern first-person adventure game and the best selling game of all time for a decade. EVERY SINGLE first-person adventure game released since then has been influenced by it in some way.
Also, you know, it's a pretty good game, even after all these years.
For these reasons, everyone should play Myst at least once. So, if you have not played a Myst, or want to play it again, realMyst: Masterpiece Edition is the one to get.
The full-3D environment looks nice (definitely nicer than the original realMyst) and makes it feel more cinematic and less like a glorified slideshow. The mouselook + WASD makes it somewhat easier to play for FPS gamers as well as allowing players to look around the environment more and explore. The additional content and the small details that tie-in to the books and additional games are nice touches.
That said, while this version is the best, it's not perfect. There are a lot of little bugs that are incredibly annoying if you trigger them; they are especially pernicious when trying to 100% the achievements. Also the day/night cycle goes from being somewhat visually nice to being increbibly annoying real quick and the flashlight that is supposed to help you with this is practically useless.

The atmosphere, story and mystery still hold up today but the puzzles feel totally unremarkable by modern game stardards. I found most of them pretty easy, aside from the stupid piano engine and the number gears. I enjoyed it, but it didn't blow me away like a lot of reviews said it would.

Ben There, Dan That! and Time Gentlemen, Please! are a couple of rip-roaring point-and-click adventure games . With tongue firmly in cheek, sit back, relax, and put your mind to work solving puzzles, and reading some very funny dialogue. It's like a book, only good!
From an horrific and untimely death in deep, dark Peru, via preposterous-and-suspect alien invasions, to whipping back-and-forth in time to stop Hitler and his army of robot Nazi dinosaur clones, this is one set of adventures you're unlikely to forget.

Fun and relaxing adventure with enjoyable protagonists. Lots of text, sharp lines and meta-jokes - the characters make fun of their own pixel-ish ugliness and game behavior, there are references to other oldschool adventures and genre traditions. A noteable amount of foul language, and characters some may not like to see (Hitler), but it all remains parody. Some interesting puzzles, especially when the time travel comes into play requiring you to think in the fourth dimension. You get to combine a few dozen items too - just like the old times.

Still, for some reason.. I like this game for some reason.  Maybe it feels like the developer wasn't just looking for an easy buck and they put some heart into this little horror adventure game, I dunno.
