SKIP TO THE BOTTOM FOR TL;DR/PROS AND CONS
Before we begin, I'd just lke to say that I'm fully aware of the drama surrounding this game, and I don't care. Drama doesn't affect the game at all. Now, you might say the fact that the developers lied about multiplayer is something worth noting, but I would say it's not. Don't buy games based on the imaginary multiplayer mode that's not even in the game, this is grade school logic. Alright, without further ado, lets jump into this one.
GAMEPLAY:
So if you buy a rougelike, you're buying it for the gameplay, and Paranautical Activity has a decent ammount of it. Sure, a lot of the rooms and enemies feel very samey, but it's got this addictive trait to it. You basically go room to room shooting various enemy's, whilst collecting items and weapons to bolster your arsenal and defeating bosses. However, this game has absolutely God awful balancing, as if it was barely playtested. At the end of the day, I had a ton of fun with this game, but all that fun will be gone in an instant because of some absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
To start, there are certain classes that you cannot pick certain items up with. If you play as the Tank class, you CANNOT pick up ANY items that slow you down at all,  or you will be boned.  The enemies that just relentlessley follow you will be faster than you, and then you'll die, and there's no possible way to avoid this in certain rooms. In fact, for any class, any item that slows you down is a death trap. And some are comically underbalanced, "Nine Armor and you get a speed reduction" is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. So since you  can't pick up any items that make you go slower, you might think this means you should only pick up items that make you go faster, but you can't. I had one playthrough where I was going so fast, I litterally broke the game. Like legit, I was so fast time in game would stop, but this just means the froze. The game refused to get better FPS and stop freezing, until I died, which is some ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. I don't understand how the devs would let this slip through, one of the first things you should do is to  test what happens when you get all the items in the game.
Another thing that's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, is what I think is the final boss, Dhalia. This might spoil some things for you if you're one of those people who want's to be blind to everything, but I don't care. She litterally spawns in two or three of other bosses every thirty seconds, effectively flooding the room with bosses. And after you kill her spawned in bosses, there are no drops  from them, meaning you can't undo any damage they did to you. And as if this wasn't bad enough, Dhalia has many more hit points than any boss before her ever has. I would beat the other bosses in about 30 seconds flat, but I barely chipped Dhalia's health in that time. You're probably thinking "Oh, look at this kid whine about how the game is too hard! Boo ♥♥♥♥in hoo!" but I'm not whining about how it's hard, I'm whining about how it's unfair. It's like the devs knew that the player would be OP as hell by this point, so they just said "♥♥♥♥ it, lets do all the bosses." so the difficulty goes from a 5 to an 11. It's rediculous.
STORY:
I really have no clue on this one. You're on a boat, and there are demons and nazis for some reason??? I haven't beat the game yet, but nothing really follows the nautical theme. It's like the game wanted to be DOOM the rougelike, so it started doing that, then occasionally it remembers, "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ I'm supposed to be nautical! Like sailors and such!" And then it'll throw in a sea themed boss.
GRAPHICS:
Meh. There's nothing to make them stand out, and it doesn't really feel artsy or like the game needed to be blocky. I mean I kind've like the style, but there are parts when the walls and floor will have high def looking textures that completely stand out from the blocky theme and it just kills it. I mean the models are all pretty good with the blocky style, but there's just not enough color to make everything pop, and even though it's cubes and such, it feels flat.
SOUND:
I don't know how to judge dubstep because I don't listen to it, but the sound isn't nautically themed that's for damn sure. I try to push it to the back of my mind, but there's maybe 5 soundtracks at max, so they just wind up being grating and annoying as hell.

The operative word for these games is crude. The sketchy artstyle matches the humor: gross, awkward, unpredictable. One moment you're digging through dinosaur boogers, the next you're collecting samples from Hitler's toilet. Your reaction to those two examples will probably give you a good sense of whether you will find the jokes appealing.
What's underneath the crudity is a lovingly rendered, shockingly well-executed pastiche of the best LucasArts adventures. The comedic timing in these games was carefully studied at the foot of Monkey Island, and the inventory puzzles call back to the most infuriating moments of Day of the Tentacle. The puzzles in both games can be extremely challenging, but none of the solutions go into cat-mustache territory -- every puzzle makes sense within the world's twisted logic, and most seem obvious in retrospect once you tease out the solution. The size of your inventory helps push you towards reasoning out solutions instead of trying everything on everything else (though the volume of funny responses will maybe push you to do that anyway.) Finishing each game gives you that deep feeling of smug satisfaction, which is really the highest recommendation for a point & click.
Also, these games are probably way underpriced because each would have individually stood as a full-price, 6+ hour adventure game back in the 90s and you get both for one low, low price.

Time Gentlemen, Please! and Ben There, Dan That! are two separate games in that follow our heroes Dan and Ben as they attempt to simply watch a marathon of their favorite TV show Magnum P.I. While rigging up a makeshift television antenna, our heroes transported to an alien ship, to different eras and to different dimensions. As they try to solve their way back to their own home and return to a much needed television break. (Alice in Wonderland type traveling)
Gameplay is like standard point and clicks. You interact with objects, sometimes bring them along or use them on other objects or NPCs. There are puzzles but not too difficult to solve which jokes and riddles. Some may be a bit tough, but in hindsight it's "why didn't i see that or get that joke". The story is easy to follow and easy to pick up.
These games are filled with humor and quick quips about the events around them. Dan Marshall and Ben Ward do a marvelous job integrating humor into their game. The game may not be for everyone but for people who like jokes and like point and click adventures, this game is worth buying and worth your time trying. It's light on your wallet and can give you a few laugh in the few hours you play through this game.
Only issue may be if you don't really get the humor that can be off-putting. Some humor may be seen more mature. But simply you will recognize in time, it is a lot Dan and Ben taking shots at the environment, npcs, and each other.
Definite must play. Especially at the price.
Also, there is a rumored third game coming soon. - You can follow Dan Marshall @danthat - and see what he has in store for the future adventures of Dan and Ben.

I have reached these games by complete chance. The depth of them and the similarity I felt to a game type I almost forgot surprised me, and left me wanting to come back to play every time off I took a time off. Hell, I got bored with other games after having another taste of a real quest game!

Ben There, Dan That! and Time Gentlemen Please! IMO are unappreciated gems.
While these games are kinda short, they have enough novel concepts and interesting events to keep the player entertained; there was almost never a dull moment.
The humour in these games is absolutely fantastic, and there were so many times when I found myself laughing out loud while playing.
Storyline:
You Play as Ben and Dan, two british best friends and roommates, who embark on an epic quest to create a makeshift TV antenna so they can watch their favourite show, Magnum, P. I. and you follow their adventures which somehow lead them to alien encounters, time travel and more.
Gameplay:
You switch between playing as Ben or Dan at a time, each having unique actions that the other doesn't, and throughout both games you will find yourself enjoying the hilarious dialogue sequences between the two, and the conversations they have with the other characters in the game.
Like most games of the genre, these games have an inventory system, and puzzles that require the use of certain items that you pick up on your adventures and their combinations, but the puzzles are most of the time hilarious and intuitive, not the frustrating kind that requires a  ridiculous amount of guess work.
Graphics:
The games' graphics are in 2D, but they feature a unique and pleasant art style that I found quite nice and a refreshing change from the usual murky graphics in modern games, and while the first game's visuals are considered outdated by today's standards, the second games' are definitely an improvement.
Overall, these games were a tremendous amount of fun, I have thoroughly enjoyed both of them, and at their price (often on sale for $0.5, yes that's 50 cents) they are certainly worth a try.
I fully recommend them to anyone looking for some relaxing fun that doesn't require a huge time investment.

It's a neat game for 3$. As a person who put in nearly 1000 hours into mount and blade I had fun with this game. Once you got going and hiring lords to back you up it got pretty crazy. Based on my Hours of Record when writing this I beat the game is roughly 7 hours with the last hours being a sort of slong due to some issues.
cons:
1: Not many things to put your money into late game.
2: You have to issue orders to each of your knights which in the late game you can easily have 15-20+ which ordering them through takes more time then it needs to. I personally see two ideas to fix this. Let there be a muti select  so you can quickly rush through and pick the knights you want before choosing where you want them to attack or hang around. Another change is to let you tell your knights to "Roam" Where they will move to lands that near by and being attacked. If they are not being attacked they will move in to attack and raid lands. This would cut down on micro in the mid to late game.
3:As of writing this, there is no mouse support when in combat you may not really need it. The Menus and map really needs it.
4:There is only one mode that I can tell. So if you want the game to be easier or harder you can't tell it such things.
5:Real issues of slow down in the late game as the AI of every knight and roamer moves around the map when in combat. When you have a few 200s of men on both sides and with the map AI running in the back ground and even joining in mid combat when being awesome. Slows down the game and lead to frame rate issues.
6:There is no real punishment for the most part of missing a hit and getting it blocked. I feel there should be a gold and xp bonus based on hits made/hits blocked to make smaller battles more useful to the player.
7: There is no auto battle for cleaning up small roaming squads.
8: You can't get personal bodyguards aka weaker knights to help you out on harder fights.
pros:
1: It has what I personally like about Mount and blade warband and what I like about one finger death punch.
2: The early game is vary strong and seems to work well for what the game seems to aim for.
I can't come up with many pros since it's a fast and weirdly addictive game with most fights not lasting to vary long and when you die you don't out right lose the battle. If you've never played Myst before, and love puzzle games, this is a classic. For longtime fans, especially those who never played the later releases; this is the definitive version to pick up. There is an additional Age to explore after beating the game, and while short, it adds a lot of depth to the characters that are here. Some of which I now feel should have been in the original game, considering how it connects to Riven.
There is also a loving nod to Ti'ana, which if you've read the books, this is just such an awesome easter egg, and if you haven't read the books, I suggest you do if you love this series, as it is canon and written by the creators. Of course, you don't have to read those until after playing the game, as it will spoil some of the fun of discovering the island's mysteries on your own. Which brings me to the only real gripe I have....
I've already played this game several times in my life, and I wish I could somehow forget all the solutions, and the game itself, only so I can experience it all again in the same way as I had many years ago. However, with the addition of Free Roam, it does feel fresh as I was able to explore the island a lot more freely than I ever have. Though, the free roam was a bit more clunky than I would have liked, it was still a nice touch.
Those are my closing thoughts. Now I can only hope Riven gets a treatment like this at some point.

Rating 8/10
==Campaign== This game is really good, I really enjoyed it. I played trough the whole campaign SOLO and CO-OP with 4 others. The Co-op campaign can support a max number of 4 players which makes it a absolutely fantastic for a group of friends to play. I never knew killing zombies could be so much fun. The campaign is quite long in my opinion. The Campaign uses maps and locations from "Sniper Elite V2" and adds a few others, even though it uses them again it's a total makeover and if you played Sniper Elite V2 you would have a nostalgia trip from time to time and you'll love that feeling. What makes me love this game even more is that fact that there are Easter Eggs characters, by that i mean the guys from l4d2 and l4d1. All the characters from those Valve games are inside and can be played in the CAMPAIGN AND HORDE MODE !
==Horde== This would be survival mode of this game. Unfortunately the max number of maps is 6. From the number of locations you discover troughout the campaign only a few or just 1 or 2 new ones are added into the horde mode. The maps are really really small especially the one called "Dead End" which it's just an alley where you can't go anywhere. The only thing you can do in that alley is survive as long as you can and fight zombies that spawn from 2 sides and sometimes crawl out of sewers / windows or fall from rooftops (usually they die from falling but some survive). Horde is completely different from the campaign, you;re supposed to stay in an area and survive as long as possible no new zones, no nothing. You choose a zone, you must survive in it. Use the spots/vaults/jumps/climbs/drops etc etc. to your advantage when playing. There are infinite ammo piles for your primary, secondary and pistol for you to use so you don't to worry about your bullets that much. Looting the zombie corpses when you run out of special equipment to use (grenades, mines etc) is a great way to get a chance of finding ammo for your main weapons or find special equipment
==Multiplayer & Co-op== This was a problem for me and some of my friends while playing Horde and Campaign. We would often chose the best player with the best connection for us as our Host because if chose the wrong one we would have to lean our shots much farther from the zombie's head or shoot a zombie in the head and wait 2-3 seconds for it to die which is a long time and get you killed. The Host doesn't have any problems only the players playing with him. Fortunate for us, the lag was quite good and the delay to kill a zombie with a headshot was around 0.5-1 second or lean forward just a bit with the sniper rifle to get a headshot. Of course that makes it harder if you play on different difficulties cause difficulty affects bullet drop.
A second note is that even if there is an option for quick match and finding servers, I managed to find a server in less than 15 seconds with a very good ping for me. I did this multiple times and I got servers with good ping
==Side Note== As a side note, there are 2 special weapons in this game that can be found troughout the Campaign or in Horde mode, those are special weapons. The "Preacher" being of them is a really good shotgun, excellent for close-medium range that only has 15 ammo in total and 2 in the barrel. It can 1 shot most of the zombies, except the really powerfull ones. (one of them is the machinegunner zombie). The ammo is hard to find and can only be found in safe rooms, on zombie corpses or randomly on the map near ammo stashes and such.
"Panzerfaust" is the last special weapon you can find. Everything i said about the preacher applies to this weapons as well. This is a rocket launcher. The ammo is somewhat scarce and has a very big radius. It even has a knockback animation when you fire it to show you how powerful it is. As I said, the ammo is scarce and be mindful with it. I have no what's the max ammo on this thing because i never reached the ammo limit. The most i got was 1 rocket on me, and 6 others as spare ammo, i dont know if you can go any higher than that
==Performance==  The specs are on my profile and it's public, so go take a look. High+ i had over 60+ fps while maintaining a Discord server of 10+ people in chat

The premise of this game is delivering a "near-realistic" real-time strategy experience, which they delivers quite nicely.
The graphics of the game, and the sound are not astonishing, but they are great.
What the meat of the game is the gameplay.
First, the game have large map when playing. People playing this game for the first time will be confused with the sheer size of the map, and with the so much action going on. With so much units in play, it's quite impossible to micro-manage every units, though it's expected also to do a lot of micro-managing.
Second, there are a lot of unit varieties in this game. There are two factions, NATO and Warsawa PACT, but there are a lot of nations who make up the NATO and the Warsaw PACT. There are United States, Canadian, United Kingdom, French, West German, Danish, Norwegian, and Swedian units for NATO, and there are Czech, Uni Soviet, Poland, and East German units for PACT. Each countries have different unit types (though some countries have same units), depends on their nation tactics. Each nation have their own flavor, and most units are unique to a particular nation.
Third, this game requires actual tactics to be used. And if we discuss tactics, there are so much things to think about in this game. Some players may be set back by the difficulty curve, so bear that in mind.
For example, in this game it is the upmost important to know the location and composition of the opposing force. For this task, you will need to send a recon. You can send a recon vehicle, send a recon helicopter, or a recon infantry to be dropped behind enemy lines. Recon vehicle are great, helicopters are better at spotting but easily shot down by SAM, while recon infantry are quite good at being hidden, but hard to be dropped behind enemy lines.
Want to advance with your tanks? The metal beasts can be cut down easily by :
- Anti-tank guided missiles launched by infantry in those buildings
- Anti-tank guided missiles launched by that IFV
- Hellicopters with ATGM
- Aircrafts with bombs or ATGM.
Want to advance? Make sure you got :
- Logistic vehicle supporting your troops with fuel, ammunition, and spare parts,
- Anti-air umbrella covering your advance,
- Recon troops in front to know the enemy location, and recon troops behind your advance to prevent getting flanked,
- Decent artillery to counter-artillery or to blast enemy strongholds,
- Etc.
In summary, there are so much things to do. You need to think about the logistic, reinforcement, air corridors, recon, etc. This game is about tactics, not about which unit is the strongest. The strongest tank from the Soviet Union can be stopped by a guided missile from a lowly NATO infantry, The best aircraft from NATO can be cut down by a cheap but hidden AA battery. The best AA tank with radar guidance can be blasted by ECM aircraft. The best tank can be cut down by a helicopter gunship. The best gunship can be cut down by AA. The best tank can be cut down by infantry in the buildings. The best infantry formation can be destroyed by long range artillery. The best artillery can be destroyed by aircraft. So much variables, so much tactics, so much way to lose and win.
This game also involves building "decks" of "unit cards". So you enter battle with the units you choose, on the quantity you choose. You can focus on heavy tank units, or focus on helicopter/plane units, though these decks are discouraged to be used in multiplayer games, because balance is the key.
Fourth, this game has great multiplayer. You can play up to 10 vs 10, but take care to read the forums first to know decent tactics. A lot of players here (like all MP games) think they are the "god of gaming" and can't take gaming as a game.
The primary bad thing of this game is you can't fought against a custom enemy AI. All enemy AI in Skirmish have preset deck, which you can't change. The other bad thing is the AI, they are not very good, it makes the game less realistic, but the AI is still acceptable, in my opinion.
I fully recommend this game.

Amazing game. Original mode is an intense shooter (more about fast, sparse bullet patterns than what most people would think of as "bullet hell") that's actually fairly accessible for people new to the genre - once they acclimate to its speed, at least. Maniac mode (a more traditional bullet hell-style mode) is excellent as well, and then there's the for-experts-only Ultra. On top of that, there's also the Novice modes (enjoyable for newcomers) and the 1.5 DLC (a great thorough rebalancing that changes up the scoring system and adds new enemy placements, as well as the exciting MAX modifier that gives both you and your enemies drastic powerups). At this point, it goes without saying that one of this game's biggest strengths is its wide variety in modes - it really does cater to players of all skill levels.
Mushihimesama is aesthetically brilliant, too. The soundtrack is great, the giant bug theme makes for a lot of really cool enemy types (how many other shmups have you fighting gigantic antlions, pitcher plants, or water striders?), and the colorful environments are lush with gorgeous details - the art is fantastic all around.
This game is easily recommendable to anyone with interest in shmups.

TL:DR - Hmm, did I make the wrong move getting this? I guess I'll just play for as long as the return policy allows me... wait, how am I at five hours already?!
Full - This game is a great example on how to do difficult platform games correctly. Minimalistic graphics and electronic music aside, this game excels in two key things: controls and level design. The controls are the more interesting of the two aspects. At first I found them to be both stiff and slippery at the same time, and I thought that gameplay would suffer massively because of it. Thankfully, I was proven wrong, as the controls are optimized for accurate air control, which you will be doing a lot of. This brings us nicely to the level design, which while difficult [naturally], accompanies the controls amazingly. Any deaths that occur are on you and any inaccuracies on your input, instead of insanely BS level design (even if it seems like that); the way it should be.
The game may be overtly difficult, but, lucky for you, you have unlimited lives. This allows you to run through the stages again and again to fine-tune your accuracy and speed, and maybe, just maybe, make it into the top 500 in the global scoreboards. Because of this, the game is extremely addictive: Be warned if you try to play this game within the return policy's limits [not that you'll need to use it here. :) ], you may run over if you really like it!
Overall, I absolutely recommend this game if you need a break from the more complicated games available today, and just want to relax/rage/what-have-you with a simple to learn, but hard to master platformer.
On a last (but unrelated) note, this game won an award in 2015 for the best Canadian-made Game. Even if you didn't know that, if you died on the tutorial stages, your first achievement is "You Suck, but that's Okay". This game truly is a Canadian's vision of a difficult platformer.

Battleborn is a game that I bought hoping for a reflection of Borderlands.  Honestly it falls short in the humor department. The gameplay for the most part is pretty smooth. However, body blocking feels incredibly wonky.  What I mean is the character collision boxes feel much larger than the characters themselves.  Multiple times I have been running from a melee hero as a ranged hero, if I hit a wall, there is limited sliding and the second the melee hero touches me, I am pinned and slashed to death. Intentional or not, it makes for a very hopeless feeling during the encounter. (I guess you could attribute this to me not being very good at the game yet as well.)
In hindsight, I would not have bought this game at the current price.  I see the appeal for multiplayer, but I'll continue my search for a driving storyline that doesn't have forced humor.

Honestly I had alot of fun with this game. I find the game very charming and pretty to look at and I especially like the humor in it. I'm a fan of the Borderlands series so I didn't see a way how I couldn't like it.
Every character has their own unique personality and skills. I find the characters to be pretty solid. You may not like them or find them generic at first, but I found that people warm up to them over time.
Some people would compare this to another game such as Overwatch, but this isn't the case at all. As I've played both I can safely say that they are VERY different games with their own thing going for them. There's no need to compare them.
Campaign is basically like Borderlands without the loot and way more characters. The Helix upgrade system is pretty nice especially for multiple playthroughs of levels. Also not to mention that every time you start up a mission again, there's different voice lines to hear, which is one of my favorite things about the campaign.
Some people might find the campaign weird or not fun for various reasons. I find it pretty fun. I love the characters and bosses during the campaign and definitely ask people to give it a try.
Moving on, Multiplayer has;
Capture: Your basic Capture Point/Domination type game mode.
Incursion: A game mode where you and your team push to destroy 2 objectives which are giant sentries with shields on them. Generally needing minions to bring down the shield while the players kill it with focus fire to win.
And Meltdown: A game mode where you escort minions into the enemy's base to be sacrificed for points.
I enjoy playing every game mode but by far my favorite has to be Incursion mode as I find it to have the most replayability.
Multiplayer is the general MOBA setup of 5 VS 5 set ups going at eachother with varying teams of characters. You need a bit of team coordination or you're going to end up getting your♥♥♥♥♥kicked. But for the most part it has a familiar play to your average MOBA game such as League of Legends or DOTA. Outplay opponents with your use of skill synergies and farm up XP for pushes and engagements.
I find every character excels in some way at doing certain things, and with that I find that there isn't too much that's severely imbalanced, at the time of this review, the only one I can really say is too strong would be Galilea for various reasons. I haven't felt that anybody is broken otherwise.
There's supposed to be an update soon to fix imbalances and such. The game is still pretty fresh, give them some time fix it up a bit. I know nowadays people aren't a fan of rough releases and such, but have some patience. Stuff will be fixed if enough people point it out. Even giant companies who release games on much larger scales have day 1 problems due to unforseen circumstances.
If there's any cons to put about the game, it'd definitely lie with the strange gear system and the character unlocks.
I don't find the gear system to be terrible, I just find it's strange to have your gear rely on RNG boxes you buy or pick up during campaign.
I'm usually not too opposed to unlocking things in-game as it has something to work towards, but characters shouldn't have such high requirements in some cases. Being a game you have to buy for 60 dollars, it's strange to see a game with nearly every character locked right away. I'm not too picky, but easier ways to obtain characters you WANT to play early on would definitely benefit it.
I have to say, the game is definitely hit or miss with people. I find the game very fun though and give it my full support and hope to see the game shine through eventually. As I said before, people should just have a bit of patience when it comes to new releases.

I didn't make it terribly far in this game before realizing that the $6.99 price tag is a bit high - at least in my experience. It's kind of a standard top down shooter. Except where you'd normally have something like a space ship or a tank, you have a cockroach with a laser strapped to it. The laser can be upgraded using your score - which resets each level. The upgrades are also only temporary.
The overall gameplay is pretty basic - shoot everything you can. Utilize the binoculars to help see enemies further out that may kill you quickly if you come upon them too quickly. Find a few healthpacks here and there if necessary. And don't fall off stuff - you'll die. However, I will say it at least runs relatively smoothly. It's not the prettiest game but it's quick and everything seems pretty snappy to me. Be warned that if you move your crosshairs to the edge of the screen (in fullscreen), your mouse may go off screen and you'll lose control of the crosshairs. Simply moving your mouse back in screen will fix this - but it's still a minor annoyance.
While the game isn't necessarily bad, has it's quirks such as the mouse issue or overly loud music (or option of completely muting everything), it's still just too much for me. This game feels more like something worth a dollar or two, if that. Not seven.

All in all, I really like this game. And while I will recommend, I must say that it's not perfect. That's understandable though, because this game is early access. This is good to know because that means the devs can still iron off the rough spots. And since I've noticed that they are reading their game's reviews, I decided that I'd list off a few rough spots that have been getting on my nerves in case they ever read this review.
1st up is a controls issue for the keyboard. Every time I try to dash northwest or southeast, no dashing occurs. I can dash in all other directions, but not in the 2 I previously mentioned.
Up next is an issue with the knights. When I order a knight to defend a region, I expect that knight keep to that region and eradicate any traitors that set foot inside that region's boundaries. But rather than doing that, the knight in question charges headlong into the neighboring traitor territories, calls down a retaliation force too large for him to handle, and comes back broken, battered, and looking for more men to start the cycle all over again. Which brings me to my next problem.
When your knight comes back from their aforementioned beating in the traitor territories, they immediately seek out a fresh army. The trouble with that is that when you have many knights, it is very difficult for the castles and villages and other troop producing locations to keep up with the demand even when fully upgraded. This leads to the knights sucking the region dry and leaving it open for the traitors to swoop in and take over again.
And there is 1 final problem that really bothers me. And this problem is that while you can strike down foe after foe on the battle field without using a single power, your ordinary attacks do absolutely nothing to buildings. In my opinion that make absolutely no sense what so ever. Seriously, if your minions' normal attacks can do it, then why can't your normal attacks do so to?
In short: Great game, Endless Loop. But the keyboard controls need a little fixing, the knights need to learn how to follow orders, the troops need to be trained faster, and the player character needs to be able to deal at least a small amount of damage to buildings with their normal attacks.

Laundry Bear Studios took a low-poly approach and succeeded. Removing gruesome details helped the player get past fears and explore death in a different light. Using various shades of violet gave the funeral home a gloomy yet personable feeling and the use of yellow on objects to gently guide players to their goal was a great choice.
What makes the game truly notable is that it makes an interesting statement about what gaming can be. This game had the potential to educate and enlighten the player with information about funerals, coping with death, and funeral homes. There's a great Adam Ruins Everything episode about funerals.
However, I watched that video six months ago and had forgotten most of it by the time I played the game. I probably forgot the majority of the video by the next day, honestly. However, A Mortician's Tale was not a video. It was an experience that I was living. I personally had to clean many corpses with a sponge, shave their body, put their eye caps in, sew their eyes shut, put their mouth full of cotton balls, massage them to reduce rigor mortis, and pump them full of formaldehyde while draining their blood. By having a personal experience with it, I can remember the steps vividly.
This game isn't the first to inspire its players to change their world view about something, but the way that it was done felt very unique. It wasn't layered in some 40-hour story about saving the world and it was just a side quest you had the option of doing, it was its own thing. It was upfront about the quest the player would go on and taught the player something they probably didn't know much about.
I'm reminded of the controversy about Gone Home which was branded a walking simulator. Since there were no puzzles, it was not considered a real game (despite having gating mechanisms, a start, and a goal). At its core, a game is an experience. It's supposed to be something personal that a person can interact with. Video games are a medium of art that should be used for so much more than what it currently is doing, and A Mortician's Tale is one of the first games to step in that direction.

Such a shame Battleborn is misinterpreted as Overwatch's younger brother. It's a continuation of Gearbox's trademark humour, but in an FPS MOBA style. Without the mass advertising that Blizzard can afford to pump into their IPs, I fear this gem will be forgotten

I feel compelled to make a review of some kind for this gem of a game that's being buried under the unfair comparison to overwatch. They're both great games that approach the first person shooter genre in completly different and awsome ways, I have no problem reccomending both.
But for battleborn specifically...it's so varied it's hard to make any sort of comparison, think first person moba but with the catch of collectible currency used to upgrade some of the towers/minions so even noobs like me can contribute meaningfully for some of it's pvp, borderlands co-op modes and an incredible aesthetic with fun characters to choose from.
It's fun and importantly in the genre really unique. It'd be a damn shame if it was overlooked because of the timing of it's release.

When it comes to Battleborn, I think of it as a great game. There are many features that make it a nearly perfect FPS MOBA game, one of the first of it's kind.
Gameplay: Battleborn's gameplay is superb when it comes to the campaign, but the PVP section of the game has a slightly steep learning curve in order to understand a character when swapping from PVE to PVP. However, the gameplay is still simplistic and easily understandable to most gamers. However I still wish that the cross over from PVE mechanics to PVP mechanics was smoother than it is currently.
Graphics: For being a game made in the Unity Engine, lag is at a minimal and the quality is above average. Though the design is cartoony, it happens to fit the story in a nice neat bow. The game is visual pornography in many ways due to it's colorful and bombastic nature.
Story: The Story is slightly Unoriginal but the way they drew out the story and how they tell it makes it seem as though it is it's own new thing. Though the story jumps around quite a bit and the build up to the final boss doesn't make much sense, it does appear to be drawn out in a way that seems, appealing.
Lore and Characters: The Characters have insane personality and hardly any of them would be considered a first person genre character but they fit in their universe so well that it is nearly impossible to whine about it. Their humor and insanity adds a personnal connection that isn't seen in FPS games such as Call of Duty, it doesn't force you to relate to someone, because no one in this game is considerably "human," but it makes you want to connect to them because their personnality is so insane and unbelieveable that you just want to be that expressive. As for the lore, though it may be short, it brings out the darkest and brightest halves of the characters without being lengthy and concerningly boring. The lore is done in the right way that you want to read the character's stories
Humor: The Humor, though it may be Vulgor, is original and always brings a laugh along once in a while, adds some character to the game. Granted, this is Geabox, what do we expect of their games? Serious gameplay with no humor and nothing but dark twisted stories? If that were the case, I wouldn't play Battleborn.

Mushihimesama is a brilliant CAVE shooter that is a direct port of the 360 version, available for people on PC for the first time. Mushihimesama sets a standard in terms of modern STGs and cave games in general that we can get a taste for and is absolutely worth your time.
Vertical shooter, you control 1 ship called Reco and you have a choice of 3 different shot types they are :
M-Power (best all round shot type)
W-Power (wide shot type for clearing large groups of enemies in stages, low mobility)
S-Power (powerful concentrated attack good for taking out bosses and single targets, fastest)
In game certain enemies drop the icon which gives you the power ups, there is a timer that counts down if you don't collect the power up within the time it switches to a different shot type which could be good if you need it for a specific boss enemy,or you are looking to clear specific enemies meaning it helps you plan more strategic.
There are 3 bombs given to you at the start but not like the classic screen clear bombs you get given a bomb that affects a certain area, you are still invincible during its active frames but you have to aim where you want it to go.It is also used in advanced techniques such as misdirection allowing you to have a better chance of surviving challenging patterns.
You start with 2 lives, and the first 1-up is available with a score of 10000000, there are a total of 5 stages and every stage has a mini boss and under certain conditions during the 5th stage you can get the true last boss.
During original mode the scoring mechanics are quite simple and to get good scoring you have to master surviving to gain the 1cc. Basically to get good scores you need to achieve NMNB (No miss No Bomb) The enemies drop gems and there are small and large diamond gems, small gems are worth 100 points, large ones 1000 which are dropped by airborne enemies. There are also gems for grounded enemies with small grounded gems worth 825 points and 2000points respectively.
The number of gems collected during the current life on the current stage with a bonus from no missing is added together as a score bonus at the end of each stage, and at the end of the final stage the number of lives remaining and bombs are multiplied resulting in the final score.
In the maniac and ultra mode, there is a counter called the parent counter and it increases when Reco is shooting enemies on the screen with her shot and decreases whenever she is not hitting an enemy, each enemy has their own counter that is similar to the parent counter and decreases if Reco is not shooting at it until it dies, and the higher the mulitiplier the more score you will recieve.You can gain an option powerup, a new counter called the child counter,the child counter will only increase if the options laser is hitting an enemy using her main shot, an advanced technique called counter banking allows you to use the C shot for example, if a player has 4 child counters with a vaulue of 500 each, everytime you counter bank, you will add 2000 to the parent counter causing your multiplier to skyrocket, mastering the technique and keeping track of your score and chaning will allow your parent counter to improve your score dramatically.
Overall Mushihimesama is an amazing game and in HD from its original 2004 arcade release, it looks amazing and worthy of being released on PC in 2015, its challenging with different modes for every skill level and you can spend months and years playing this game.

Time Gentlemen, Please is the sort of point-and-click adventure throwback that gives you a bunch of ridiculous items and asks you to find practical uses for them. Unlike a lot of the classics I thought the solutions to puzzles were genuinely clear and the few times I got stuck I felt like it was my own fault for not trying something obvious.  There are enough puzzles that need you to find out a specific way to use an item rather that just using it in the right spot so it doesn't feel like a case of just using everything on eveything else until you stumble on the solution. On the whole it's on the easier side as far as these games go.
The writing in the game is more the star of the game than anything else. It's a pleasant change of pace if you get sick of adventure games that simply repeat "I can't do that" for everything that isn't solution related.  Attempting to combine most items or use them with most things in the world will give you unique dialogues for each action. Often with little hints towards solutions hidden in them. The humor alternates between referencing classic adventure games and toilet humor. At first it's pretty funny to examine random items and get rewarded with♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes, but it wears a little thin by the end and if you're new to adventure games all the references will probably fly over your head. It's definitely has an intended audience that will find it hilarious and the rest will probably scratch their heads. Overall I thought the jokes and one-liners were funny way more often than not, just by the sheer volume of them it's a little tiring by the end.
Also I'm not a fan of having to click through the different look/talk/use/move options, I'd rather be able to select the one I want, but it's not horrible by adventure game standards, just frustrating after a while.
Ben There, Dan That is also included in the package. It was a freebie game that was the blueprint for Time Gentlemen, Please. It's much shorter, but it still has the same mechanics and clever writing. The puzzles are pretty one-dimensional though though.

"Time Gentlemen, Please!" and "Ben There, Dan That!" are linear PnC adventure games that were written and designed by fans of most of the classics of the genre.  This is probably the ultimate fan tribute at the time of their release.  That all being said though, these games really don't constitute a real cash value.  Sorry fellas.  The graphics are incredibly simple.  The interactivity is minimal.  The humor is pretty flat.  The challenge lies only within pixel hunting.  If you are a real diehard fan of all PnC games, buy the pack for under a dollar, and be warned that your time will probably be wasted.  Thankfully they are pretty short in length.  Everybody else, just simply don't bother.  You can download much more entertaining PnC games for free elsewhere.

With the revitalization of P.O.C. adventure games, we are given a game that harks back to the oldschool style. How does it hold out?
Story- Ben and Dan are two programmers (both real people who put themselves in their own games) who must go on an epic quest in order to catch reruns of Magnum P.I. On the way, they are kidnapped by aliens bent on world domination and so Our intrepid heroes must travel through the very fabric of space and reality in a race against time to save the world and catch old 80's sicoms. In the sequel, a week has past since the end of the world so Dan and Ben now find themselves traveling through time to fix everything (making things worse actually) and try to stop Hittler and his unstoppable robo-dino army from ruling the world. As you can see, the story is as rediculous as can be but then again, it is a commedy. The humor of the game and its story may not be for everyone but any fan of Monty Python-style humor will get a kick out of this game. C+
Graphics- The graphics have a rather charming appeal that grows on you, and what I mean by that is that it looks like the microsoft paint doodle of a 15 year old kid when he is board. The animation of the characters are almost non-exsistent. But the enviroments are varied and do draw you in wanting to know what you will see next. Like I said, it does grow on you. D+
Sound- There is vertually no sound effects in the game and music is sparse but what music there is is quite fun to listen to and reminicient of the old 8-bit days. C
Gameplay- The game follows a simple P.O.C. format and you can interact with nearly anything with anything for humorous effect. It does kinda get annoying when you have to scroll your mouse through a number of command points (look, talk, touch, etc.) and if you accidentally past the command you want, you have to scroll through everything again so it would have been nice for a reverse scroll to be available. The challege of the game itself is actually very fair, as in not too easy (via Telltale) and not too hard (via Lucas Arts), and is quite fun to explore the different resposes to different actions and very rewarding even if you don't get it right.B+
Overall- This game is obviously not for everyone. But it is an absolute blast to play and one of the funniest games to play. Highly recommended. C

This game is special.
Original developer and publisher: Code Avarice
Current developer and publisher: Digerati Distribution
Initially the game was placed on Steam Greenlight on Aug 31, 2012
Then they had a successful Kickstarter campaign that collected $12,540 USD. (August 4, 2013 - September 3, 2013)
There were issues with the greenlight campaign:
"Code Avarice already set up a placeholder Steam Greenlight page and Steam 'didn't want to send the message that indies can seek out publishers to bypass Steam Greenlight.'"
But Officially, the title got Greenlit by 8/28/2013.
Subsequently, in October 2014 the developer threatened Gabe Newell's life over a Steam listing issue associated with the title.
"harsh lesson Paranautical Activity developer Mike Maulbeck learned today when after a Steam snafu erroneously advertised his game as an Early Access title he crossed a line and tweeted a death threat to Gabe Newell. Following this outrage, the game was pulled from Valve's distribution service."
Needless to say, the developer didnt handle the situation and associated fallout well:
This caused the game to be removed from the Steam store, the offending dev to resign from the studio ("Code Avarice"), the "Paranautical Activity" IP to be sold to another company ("Digerati Distribution & Marketing"), followed by the offending dev rejoining his original studio.
On the Early Access Steam store page, they claimed "We're planning to add multiplayer co-op in the very near future, as well as a ton more content, and of course some bug fixes and polish."
They also claimed that:
"Paranautical Activity multiplayer is definitely a thing that is happening...We’ve been really busy trying to get MP working...The multiplayer patch will be going live before the year anniversary of the game (february 14th)[2014]"
Subsquently, the devs disclosed that they would not add a multiplayer mode.
"Sorry to those who purchased this game under the guise of the fact it will be multiplayer. We just couldn’t rebuild the entire game to make this happen, there is only two of us.”
Allegedly, the devs were asking for good reviews of the game and doing some "heavy moderating" ie. censoring of negative critique, on their forums.
The offending dev claimed he was "quitting the video game industry."
However, he is already working on 2 new games:
"Arkshot and Timefight Zone" as of 4/2016.

Rating: 8/10
Overview: First Person Adventure
The Good:
+ Great Graphics being very faithful to the original Myst. Day and Night cycle added for immersion.
+ Very distinct ‘levels’ that feel very different from one another and fun to explore.
+ Puzzles that are creative and compliment the atmosphere of the world
+ Fantastic soundtrack
The Average:
+/- Though I love the puzzles there are a few that can be difficult to figure out.
+/- This is not a well optimized game, even with a system that should be able to easily play it, maintaining 60fps was very difficult, often hitting 30 fps.
Conclusion:
This game brings back childhood memories. I feel that if you ever played the original Myst you would enjoy and appreciate this game so much more, however even if you didn’t, this is still a great game to play if you love exploration and puzzle solving.

Finally, my childhood demons are quelled.
The ultimate frustrations of never getting off the island, of desperately flicking switches and pressing buttons with no success have been sated.
realMyst includes some nice tweaks, but wisely has kept the game intact, even including the option to play with the original control scheme. Both the original and free roam can be a little clunky, but the game moves much more quickly.
Now that I've finally beaten this game, I can safely say MYST remains probably one of the best adventure games ever made. The style, sound design, acting and puzzle integration are something you would think every adventure game designer would have picked up on. While Myst has a reputation for being cryptic and difficult, I contend that's nostalgia talking. Lack of inventory eliminates tedious item-hunting and the frustration of throwing things at the wall until something sticks. The structure of the game immerses the player in the puzzles/realms rewarding them by revealing more and more story, rather than having a linear plot be bottlenecked by puzzles as obstacles.
I would also like to give the developers of realMyst on making the in game walkthroughs spoiler-preventative, though I rarely had to consult them, given the quality of game/puzzle design. Still a classic, still worth playing.

For an EA game, this feels pretty complete. There are some issues, mostly to do with balancing and game length, as well as some bugs.
First things first, the positives:
1. Easy to learn (controller is a good idea as someone who prefers keyboard/mouse). All the buttons do simple things and it's really not hard to get into the mechanics. The trick is learning to use your B and your combo metre effectively.
2. Pretty meaty for EA. 6 hours isn't bad, and I imagine the game will get longer. As it stands, the gameplay remains pretty much the same start to finish, but that's not a bad thing.
3. For the most part, the game is responsive and if you play well, you will be rewarded.
4. Finally, the game isn't ugly. Models are repeated but they don't look bat at all.
There are a few negatives:
1. Very prone to dominant strategy. You never want to expend all your combo meter because there's never a better reason to spend your last combo meter than to heal.  A lot of the combos are redunant because some of them are simply better. There's no real reason to use the YYYY combo because the XXXX combo does the same thing but is easier to judge.
2. Some instances stunlock you for an unfair amount of time and damage, and very rarely do you feel like you deserved the amount of damage you took as a result of being stunlocked. Thankfully, your AAAA heals you from pretty much the start of the game, so health isn't a huge issue.
3. The rules aren't equal for you and your opponent. Your opponent can respawn even if he is out of soldiers and can often win just because he could hold out long enough to bring in replacements, but you lose the moment you lose your last soldier, even if you are still fine - you aren't given a chance to hold out for reinforcement.
4. Often, it's not worth trying to fight the bosses properly, just slamming the XYXY until they're dead is more effective. They just don't take enough damage from you hitting them normally to make it worthwhile.
5. Last thing, and just a bit of a nitpick, (they added a button to skip these events, but I would've just liked to be able to turn them off) but every time a hero comes into your camera view, you're forced to sit through a little intro ditty. It wouldn't be so bad, but it interrupts play and can often mean you take damage as it interrupts a keystroke that would've seen you dodge a rock or arrow that ends up stunlocking you.
For an early access, I wholeheartedly recommend this game. I had fun and I never really truly felt like the game was being unfun, and I could always come back from sticky situations if I played it right. To put a number to my score, let's say 4/5 EA status noted.

I've enjoyed two playthroughs now and can see a few cracks, towards the late game you'll be fighting many battles small and large with multiple enemy knights and for everyone of these knights it will stop the game play whilst they throw some dialogue at you, this does disrupt play and if you're going up against 3+ knights all of them telling you how "you won't best them today" it gets real old real fast.
However there's some solid foundations too, massive battles, friendly knights work like enemy knights, which is rare to find in any game let alone a small indie game. The Ai is good enough a good blend of aggression and resupply, there isn't a defence only rushing to aid those being attacked.
I'd point out even if you focus on upgrading your soldiers and put no points into speed health or anything else, you will still not be able to get all the upgrades before the aggressing barbarians are supermen with special abilities decimating your hero making the whole affair arbitrarily difficult.
A few good features might include:
Garrisoning castles and villages, I don't see a point to outposts as they don't offer a bonus and just make an area less valuable rather than more defended.
Perhaps an ability or command to make friendly knights follow you directly so either side can lead co-ordinated attacks on armies etc.
You could expand on the rpg elements, by unlocking mercenary camps who spawn patrols and can have men added to the army (different archers and units), healers if that was a route you would like to take.
Sieges could feel more siege like, archers on the walls firing down this could be achieved by adding a hit or damage penalty to besieging archers when targeting defending archers on the walls.
Knights have shields, it may make the combat more frantic if a block function was included where they raised the shield to negate some or all of the damage at a cost of movement and attack or the dash meter.
Overall I rate the game highly, there are a few areas for improvement that I believe the devs will correct natrually or add to, so there isn't much point to going over them in this review.

you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I normally don't review games, but after playing this game I felt like I had to say something.
I've played league of legends for a bit, not amazing at it or anything but I know how it works.
Granted, maybe I haven't put enough time into the game - I haven't played much of the story at all. But this game is just super confusing. This is going to be all over the place but to start, the matchmaking is terrible. You get matched with people 50 levels higher than you (and it doesn't matter which side they are on, they shouldn't be there at all!) Apparently there is an elo type matchmaking system, but it doesn't account for the fact that you gain levels from story mode. So someone could have played each character to the max on story and know how to play each character super well, then get matched up against someone who just bought the game. The story mode level system should be kept separate from the multiplayer leveling system. They might have the same experience as a new player in the multiplayer mode, but they have access to all kinds of gear loadouts that the new player does not. Speaking of the gear loadout system, how the hell does it work? Does the game give you any sort of useful information? No. Sure the stats that each gear piece gives you is shown to you, but how do I know how much it affects the character I'm going to use? It doesn't tell you the stats of each character anywhere, so what use is it to know what percentage attack damage you are increasing, if you don't know the base stats of the character? Again, maybe I missed all this stuff, but after 27 hours if I couldn't find it, maybe it should be clearer.
If your computer is the slight bit outdated, forget about this game. The animations are cool, but there's so many that if you get close to any enemy, good luck telling what the hell is going on.

TL;DR: Nice and challenging minimalistic puzzle game of dynamic sort with occasionally frustrating hitbox issues.
has a simple premise: place spheres to move along predefined paths so that they won't hit each other. All spheres have to complete one full cycle to complete a level. The simple mechanics works to build increasingly challenging dynamic puzzles.
The puzzles start really simple: shapes are just two circles to place spheres on. Ported from a mobile game, you get three stars ("a perfect level") if no spheres are destroyed during a level. It's worth noting that the game is really generous with achievements, serving one for each 3-starred level.
As you get further, the puzzles get more complicated. For instance, you might need to place two spheres on a each shape. Not all shapes are circles either: there are also rectangles, triangles and ellipses, often mingled up together.
Moving shapes are usually the trickiest ones. Additionally, there are (sometimes moving) spiky walls that destroy spheres on contact. Sometimes a time restraint is imposed through the spheres being destroyed automatically after a set number of cycles, but this was never a problem for me.
A trick is that you can also press on a single sphere to make it stay still, for instance to avoid collision or fine-tune its pace. In case of moving shapes this will also stop the shape from moving. However, if there are several spheres on a single shape, it will only stop one of the spheres from moving so you have to be careful.
is not without frustration. While part of the puzzles is creating perfect cycles, you also have to make sure the spheres do not get too close to each other.
For whatever reason, the spheres might make several happy cycles together but if they have been close together, they might rather randomly just collide with each other despite their previously peaceful cycles. To me in these cases it usually does not look plausible that they could have hit each other. An example is in order:
Take for instance two spheres, moving along a perfect circle very close to each other at a steady pace. It's theoretically impossible for them to hit each other, right? But in
it does happen, probably because of numerical imprecision in the collision detection. It's frustrating when you are just about to complete a level and then this ruins it.
Then again the levels are usually rather short. One try lasts from a few seconds to a minute so not a lot of time is lost due to a failure.
Another issue occurs with moving shapes and to a lesser extent with fast moving spheres: it can be tricky to hit them with the cursor, especially since you need precision to avoid collisions. The spawn spots, i.e. the buttons that create spheres, are small so the issue is worse with moving shapes. Fortunately these levels are rare.
Though I played it with mouse, one could use a touchscreen device. I wouldn't know whether this is difficult on those as well.
While I encountered a couple of bugs along the way, the developers have been kind enough to fix them as they have been reported, albeit at a slower pace than preferred. It took several weeks to fix the bug with the last achievement but everything seems to be working correctly now.
I completed the game 3-starring every level in about 9 hours but I think the completion time would vary a lot between players and their pattern recognition and hands & eye coordination skills. On mobile the base game is free-to-play with ads and in-app purchases of some kind, so the current price on Steam seems good to me, given that there are no ads or other remnants from mobile to be seen. I recommend
especially to casual puzzle game fans.

If you have the patience to put up with a gameplay made out of sheer trial and error, then Sydney’s World can offer you one of the cutest, most charming tales ever put on Steam.
On the surface, Sydney’s World seems like a clichéd fantasy story about a brave little girl trying to save her dad from an evil wizard. However, upon closer inspection, we see a tale full of imagination, a large cast of fun characters (although we rotate them out a bit too fast), exciting adventure, adorable voice acting, wonderful music, some morals about the world, and everything else you need for what this game really is: the perfect bedtime story.
If Sydney’s World only had those ingredients, it could have been a perfect visual novel. Alas, it had the urge to include standard RPG Maker gameplay, only with terrible design choices: trial-and-error mazes and death traps, puzzles where the solutions are more like blind guesses, and one of the most unpredictable and random combat systems I ever met.
It will take a special kind of patience to face these challenges, but those who persist through the game’s many levels can find an enchantingly cute journey that will leave them all warm and fuzzy inside.

WHO SHOULD BUY THIS?
- Fathers of young daughters
- old school JRPG fans
- People who use RPG Maker and want to support their community
- People who want to see what you can do with RPG Maker VX ACE - It's cheaper than buying the full RPG Maker software, and quicker than learning how to use the RPG Maker demo.
WHO SHOULDN'T BUY THIS?
- People expecting an RPG like Skyrim. This is an old school RPG, not an action game with skill trees.
- People who are unforgiving of new devs.
- People who hate cuteness, specifically puppies.
REVIEW
This is the first time I've ever written a review before I have finished the game. Well, I should say 'we' - I'm playing through with my youngest daughter.
One of the things that I really like about this game is that the dev is approachable and very friendly. Call me old-fashioned, but that goes a long way in this day and age. He posts gametips in the Steam forums. Contrast and compare to AAA companies, who often don't even come here.
Some people say that this game has mismatching art styles: These people have missed the point. According to my daughter - who might I point out, is actually in the target demographic - the art is PERFECT, and explains everything you need to know about the characters before they even speak.
That's another thing, this has voice acting. And it's pretty damn good when compared to AAA titles. And the vocal direction is spot on, seriously some of the best I've ever seen.
As for the game itself? It was clearly a labour of love for the dev, and I suspect that he would not have released it were he not a father.
It's a cute little RPG Maker game. The dev doesn't always use the graphics in the way that we are accustomed to seeing them used, but he is clearly a very creative person. He is not afraid to turn convention on its head, and he doesn't hold your hand throughout the puzzles.
CONLCUSION.
I 100% think that you should buy this game because it's worth the money and the time, and I would be very proud of myself if I had made and released a game for my daughter: without being morbid, I think the dev has achieved a kind of immortality here, if you take my meaning.
(As I play through the game, I will adjust my review accordingly, adding more specific information.)

The game *looks* beautiful and I don't hate it by any means. But on balance, I just don't enjoy it enough to recommend buying.
The biggest issue for me is that the conversations typically feel rail-roaded. The partner (regardless of whether you are playing male or female) is always leading the conversation, and asks questions that feel leading. It wouldn't stand up in court. Trying to disagree or to influence the conversation's direction ends up with responses that typically feel like being punished. It's natural that in a game like this the developers won't be able to recreate an actual conversation, but I feel like it wouldn't have been too hard to allow the computer to recognise some core story threads that, if brought up by the player, it would then be able to pick up and continue, e.g. having an open relationship; wanting to talk about the future instead of the past etc. This would give the player some sense of agency. Admittedly, I did not put much time in this, so maybe that content is there, somewhere. But if it is... I just didn't enjoy the game enough to discover it.
I was also REALLY unimpressed when at least one of my conversation attempts received the reply "TODO", which I assume means "to do", i.e. there is just unfinished code in here. The game is being sold as finished so this seems lazy. Surely they have some kind of file with all the text in the game and should have at least been able to hit CTRL + F for all instances of "TODO" before publishing?
I love the concept behind this game, and the visual production is great, so I hope the developers continue their work - but I think some re-thinking and re-working is required for this form to really shine.

Two Mantis. (Manti?)
One passion.
Will love overcome all, or will you lose your head?
First Impression Gameplay:
Anyways, the game's plot (no spoilers) is about a praying mantis couple contemplating the idea of taking their relationship to the next level.
The only problem is that in the world of the mantis, the act of mating is typically fatal for the male (at the jaws of the female!)
Game play is mostly text based, with a few emoticon type clicky responses as well.
The AI seems to respond appropriately to what you say, and you actually have to type out your responses.
Simple one word answers don't suffice for long, as the AI will catch on and become "bored."
You're able to play as either the female or the male, with the decisions you make influencing the end of the game.
Everything takes place in one setting, and the entire game is going back and forth in a conversation between the two lovers.
Now as far as my opinion on this game, I feel a bit in the middle.
Gameplay was interesting for a while, but I got bored within half an hour.  There is only so much back and forth conversation between the AI I can take.  It would have been nice to have something to break up the monotony.
Sometimes conversation felt circular, arriving back to where the conversation originated.  (though to be fair, many serious conversation in real life do as well)
I like the concept of this game, and I think it will appeal to a large amount of people.  Which is why I will recommend it.  But personally, this kind of game gets boring for me quickly.  I went and played to two endings, and that was more than enough for me.  Last thought is that I think the price is a bit steep at $7.00.
I think this game is worth getting, but I would advise to wait until it is on sale for 50% or more.

This is a bullet hell shoot'em up that, like most good games of its genre, possesses a lot of depth and challenge, especially when you start focusing on scoring. Replaying each stage and constantly learning new things and improving your survivability/score is a lot of fun!
Aside from Normal mode, this game provides a Novice mode (less/slower enemy bullets) and Arrange mode (different bullet patterns). If you own the DLC, you get access to the V1.5 mode (different enemy placements and bullet patterns). Normal and Novice modes provide 3 difficulty challenges each, with more complicated bullet patterns and scoring systems in higher difficulties.
I find the soundtrack awesome and quite catchy overall. Arrange and V1.5 modes have their own sets of remixed soundtracks, which you can also assign to other modes to keep the background music fresh.
The game came out with a few bugs but, as of this review, most of them, as far as my experience goes, have been resolved. I also find the more complicated scoring systems, present in higher difficulties or in certain modes, a bit convoluted at first, while the game doesn't do enough to explain them, which will require checking a guide or two.
If you like bullet hell shoot'em up games, this is is a very well-crafted and gorgeous one. If you don't like them, this might still be worth checking out, but will likely not change your mind. If you haven't tried any and you're curious about the genre, this is a good place to start, with its Novice mode serving as a nice starting point.

While it is great to see Cave release their games on the PC platform, their first release leaves a little bit be desired when it comes to options.
I'll get it out of the way right away, this is a port of the XBOX 360 version and not much was really changed from that port. That means no graphic options and the game is stuck at 1280x720 and the game suffers from some vertical tearing due to lack of V-Sync. Other than that, the controls can be fully rebound on Keyboard an controllers.
Now, the game itself its pretty fun. If you do not know, Mushihimesama is what people would call a ''bullet hell'' due to amount of bullets on the screen at once. You play through 5 stages and face the final (and a secret-final boss if you meet the requirements) and that's it... Or is it?!
Actually, no! Mushihimesama does offer enough content for both beginners and experts of the genre in order to provide them the most out of the game.
First of all, you have several modes of play which includes a novice modes for newcomers, the original game with the three main difficulty settings, an arrange mode focused on high scoring and lastly a DLC 1.5 revision of the game which changes the way some of mechanics of the game work out too. If you think you need to practice a stage or a boss, you can always chose your mode (Except novice for some reasons) then play the section you want until you master.
At its core, the gameplay of Mushihimesama consist of shooting down enemies and bosses while avoiding a big amount of bullets on-screen as mentioned previously. While it may seem overwhelming at first, you'll notice that your player's hitbox is a very small blue dot that appears when doing a ''focused'' attack. The scoring sysem does vary depending on the mode you chose and if you are interested in learning more about it, I suggest looking up scoring guides on steam. They are very helpful and teach you how it all works.
Now do I have some issues with the game other than the poor PC options and screen tearing? Yes, I do.
One thing the game could do it better label the prompts in the menues and what the button imputs do on the option screen when rebinding them. It took me some time before finding out that the two fire buttons it gives you do different things, since it was never labeled. No instruction manual is provided with the game either as far as I know.
A second problem is the arcade emulation. To a veteran, this is going to sound like a weird complaint because that's usually a good thing if the game is true to the arcade original. The problem with Cave's games is the slowdown when the screen is cluttered. The game constantly speeds down and speeds up when it gets hectic and I've personally never liked that in a game as it usually becomes incredibly distracting and tends to get me killed during the phases due to the controls slowing up and down all the time. I enjoy games that never slow down and I can't get for the life of me why an option to remove them was not added. Some arcade ports (Like the fantastic Gradius Collections on the PSP system) added a way to remove hardware slow down and the overall experience is, in my opinion, better.
Though the game's biggest issue is hat it has to save CONSTANTLY.
Here's how often it does it; It saves when you chose a game mode. It saves when you quit training mode to get back into the training settings. It saves when you change the options (fair enough). It saves when the game is over. It saves when you go back to the main menu.
It gets irritating really quickly because you just want to get back to the previous menu without interuptions, and those 5 seconds it takes to save  every single time you do something adds up. I don't have any other games that saves as often as this one and it again shows this is a rather poor PC port in terms of technical fidelity.
Overall, is Mushihimesama worth its asking price. Personally, I think 20$ is a bit much considering there are cheaper offerings that are as good as this game and I find releasing the V1.5 mode as DLC on day 1 to be of poor taste considering this game is old, very old in fact. If it was 20$ for the whole package (including the soundtrack) this would be an absolute positive recommendation from me. As of now, I can recommend this game to people who don't mind the retail price and would like to either get into the genre or for veterans who never played this game. It's a pretty fun game.
Or you can always wait for a sale, but that's up to you.

N+ was great, but this is even better.  For people who like dying hundreds of times in Dark Souls, this is your game.

Imagine a game with sharp design - both visually and mechanically - and then give (generally) two people ten years to temper and sharpen that game until it could slip through twelve feet of marble when dropped at shoulder-height.
That's n++.
Do you like platforming? Do you like fancy, minimalist design? Do you like games that you can spend fifteen minutes in, and then set aside for later? Do you like games that gently ramp up the difficulty until you realize that you're (successfully) climbing an inverted-angle cliff? You could be a fan of just one of those four things, and I am almost certain that it would be enough to make n++ worth your time and money.
As of writing this review I only have half an hour or so in-game, but I've been playing n for much longer than that (and have briefly played n++'s PS4 iteration). I can already tell that this is a continuation of the more-or-less perfected design principle that placed n in my heart nearly a decade ago.
I may update this review as I progress further into the game - but I don't play games I hate, so you can just watch my hour count go up instead, if you wish.
