I first played the original N (The Way of the Ninja) game when I was a kid and I remember it being incredibly difficult and could never beat the harder levels. A few years later N+ was released which I played on DS. I managed to beat every level in that one but it was far easier or perhaps I just had more patience due to the chill nature that comes with a handheld device.
N++ is defiantly the most difficult of the lot. There are a few different game modes, solo which I managed to beat all the new levels in but gave up on the expert levels, I completed about half of them but the other half were to rage inducing for me to want to put another 50 hours into grinding out. There is a Co-op mode with is Local Co-op only so if you’re like me and have no friends ;_; then your basically locked out of atleast 2 achievements. I tried going through the co-op levels playing as 2 players myself but some levels require coordinated moves which is too confusing for me to want to learn.
Lastly there is a race mode which is also local co-op only but you can just play that solo easily.
Every 5 or so levels you beat you unlock a new color theme which changes all the colors of the game and gives it a fresh look and interesting method to play. Some themes work better for visually seeing what you need to do, what you need to avoid or what you need to dodge
When you complete a level death ragdoll is disabled which I really liked about the original games so that is something that I think they should have kept for fun.

"If you are interested in making a complete Stand-Alone game with unique characters, models, assets and game play mechanics not provided in AGFPRO and commercialize it for sale, you will need AGFPRO Premium and either Unity Free or Pro software."
It's a fun little toy but it's just that- a toy. As the buried quote from thier Steam page states, you can not actually make a game with Axis "Game Factory."
Axis "Game Factory" is a gloified Unity tool that was seemingly made into a stand-alone program to make people think it can actually do something on it's on.
The most you are likely to do if you do make the mistake of buying this is have a little fun messing around building a couple of maps. And while that can indeed be fun it comes now where close justifing the $100+ cost for the program, DLC, and premium.
If you want to have fun building something buy MineCraft or the Sims.
If you want to make a game use an actual game engine. Unity, CryEngine, Unreal.
There are few shortcuts. You'll have to learn a little.
If you buy Axis the only thing you are likely learn is to do more research before buying something.

This is my first FMV game, and I had a blast with it.
You take control of Inspector Jenks who is called out to discover what happened in the death of a young woman named Kate.
The game's map is fairly small, and there's a quick travel option so you don't have to click too much.
As you progress through the game, you'll meet new people, question them, find new evidence and try to figure out the mystery.
The main point of the game involved you finding contradictions (hence the title) that each character may or may not say. This requires you to match up one clue with another that contradicts it, leading to their admitting of a lie.
The acting is quite good, a bit cheesy at time but in a fun way. There's a nice ambience and interesting enough story to keep you going as well.
The FMV never brings down the game, and I always felt like I was the one in control. It's a very cool title, and even not on sale, $10 is still a great price! I spent almost 8 hours playing through once, and for that much you would see a movie for 2 hours, so why not put that towards this?
If you get stuck, there are guides online, but I definitely encourage players to figure as much out as they can on their own, it's much more rewarding.
Anyway, if any of that sounds interesting, give this little gem a try, you'll love it if you enjoy murder mysteries!

While I found the story to be well written, and quite well acted, near the end of the game it did come a bit off of the rails on both counts. However, the story did wrap itself up nicely, and even left itself enough in the way of story to provide a possible sequel, which I will certainly play should it come to fruition.

Myst is pretty much the definition of a classic point-and-click game, and to an extent not much really needs to be said about it. It's the sort of game that just drops you into a strange new world without any explanation, and lets you figure out how its various mechanisms work on your own. This version is an enhanced version of the original realMyst, which itself was a 3D remake of the original Myst, allowing you to walk around like a standard first-person game instead of being locked into the usual 360 swivel-cam. The Masterpiece edition greatly improves the graphics, but at the expense of having pretty strange performance; despite my GTX 970 and overclocked i5, I barely managed 30 fps when the preset was set to Very High, but when setting the preset to Medium High (turning it to anything lower than that decreases the mouse speed, for some reason) and turning on all of the settings in the Advanced options it ran at around 70 to 100+ depending on the area. The ability to move freely increases immersion, but also makes the puzzles a bit more difficult in my opinion by making it less obvious what you can and can't interact with, which is further increased by the better graphics of this version, but I consider that to be more of a plus. realMyst might not be the version of the game that the original developer prefers, but it's the one I'd rather play.

It's a mesmerizing, alien world, I was absolutely enthralled while playing.
It can be annoying that the player can only hold one page at a time though.  An annoying synthetic limitation.
Regarding performance, it actually does run better if you first set it to minimum settings and then to maximum or whatever it is you want to run.  It is indeed poorly optimized, but it makes you forget that quickly.

In summary, I really wanted to like this game, and I was intrigued by the game´s visuals, subject matter and mood, but I was very dissapointed to find the game experience so completely void of life (quite a coincidence, no?). It´s  a shame they didn´t make an actual game, it had so much promise.

The art is nice, the music is fantastic, it's quite educational, and there are some poignant moments but ultimately it's a 40 minute narrative with no actual player input, no drama (despite plenty of opportunity in the later half of the story) and no chance of failure.
I feel this game would be very much improved if its potential were realised.
The game gives you lots of advice on how to talk with and comfort grieving family members appropriately and you are also encouraged to make friends or become a point of contact for clients, this led me to believe there would be opportunities to engage in actual dialogue at the funerals and respond in a multiple-choice manner but there is no such opportunity.
The only interaction is a repetition of clicking on people and getting very short dialogues before clicking on the deceased to show respect, I am not even sure if clicking on people and reading their dialogue is required but it wouldn't surprise me if it weren't.
There was plenty of missed opportunity for small storylines and different endings here.
Your character also has a number of friends who correspond with you via email throughout the story but only one of them turns out to even be relevant to the actual story. You cannot respond to anything they say, which is a shame as one of them was actually annoying to me and I wondered if the outcome would change if I had the opportunity to respond. Nope.
I enjoyed the story for what it is, but unfortunately what it is does not justify the price tag of £9.11 (reduced from  £11.39 when I bought it). If it were more appropriately priced at around one third of that value then I would almost certainly have given it a positive recommendation, but unfortunately I'm wishing I spent that money on something else instead.

I was so excited to play this game but have been left feeling disappointed and a little ripped off. The game is incredibly short. I finished it in about forty minutes (I actually thought I had just finished the tutorial before realising I'd finished the entire game). Asking for €14.99 for forty minutes worth of gaming is ludicrous.
That said, it is a genuinely charming game. It has an interesting, thought-provoking premise, the art style is lovely, and the music is excellent, but the gameplay is sadly lacking. You cannot interact with the families or organise anything. You cannot fail. You are guided through every single procedure, and even if you try to go off script, nothing happens.
I love both traditional games and interactive/visual novels and I think AMT has fallen somewhere between the two. Unfortunately, there's not enough elements of either to make this game a satisfying experience.
Sadly, I cannot recommend A Mortician's Tale at the current price.

I first played the original N (The Way of the Ninja) game when I was a kid and I remember it being incredibly difficult and could never beat the harder levels. A few years later N+ was released which I played on DS. I managed to beat every level in that one but it was far easier or perhaps I just had more patience due to the chill nature that comes with a handheld device.
N++ is defiantly the most difficult of the lot. There are a few different game modes, solo which I managed to beat all the new levels in but gave up on the expert levels, I completed about half of them but the other half were to rage inducing for me to want to put another 50 hours into grinding out. There is a Co-op mode with is Local Co-op only so if you’re like me and have no friends ;_; then your basically locked out of atleast 2 achievements. I tried going through the co-op levels playing as 2 players myself but some levels require coordinated moves which is too confusing for me to want to learn.
Lastly there is a race mode which is also local co-op only but you can just play that solo easily.
Every 5 or so levels you beat you unlock a new color theme which changes all the colors of the game and gives it a fresh look and interesting method to play. Some themes work better for visually seeing what you need to do, what you need to avoid or what you need to dodge
When you complete a level death ragdoll is disabled which I really liked about the original games so that is something that I think they should have kept for fun.
More of the same from N+ but improved and expanded upon.

A well deserved Thank-You to Mare & Raigan and their programmer(s) for creating this amazing game!
In early 2001, N initially started off as a free and very fun downloadable flash game created ground up by two people
Fast forward more than a decade to find N++ as one of the great hidden gems in the platform genre. And to this day, the devs continue to add content while aiding with bug fixing when necessary.
It's also worth mentioning N++ was released for console as well. So no matter if you rather play on console or PC, It's a Win-Win for anyone who enjoys those difficult & rewarding platformer experiences!

It's a small but decent rogue-like.
Tl;dr
It's a fine small indie game (5-7h core gameplay length), but I'd only recommend getting it if it's 30% off or less.
You start with one hero, and as you progress through the rather small maps, you will get the option to hire one extra hero at the start of each new map.
You gain XP, advance the heroes' stats, equip them with gear and mod the gear with crystals.
I failed a handful of times, before I managed to beat the game (too slowly for the achievement); This took me roughly 5 hours.
I then did it again a couple of times before I managed to beat it well within the time for the achievement.
The game gets progressively easier each time you restart, which both works and feels fine, but it's still annoying to think that your first time is the hardest possible scenario.
On my first couple of attempts, I could only hire 3/5 heroes.
When I beat the game the first time, I had 4 heroes.
After the next retry, I was given the option to fill all 5 available hero slots... and the mods I found were also getting progressively more powerful with each new game I started...
I think what annoys me the most, is that the game is build like a rogue-like, but it gets easier each time you play it. It's as if they made the game as a single-playthrough experience which lowers the difficulty automatically each time you fail (which would be a fine small game IMO), but then they added the replayability unlocks to it...
There are unlockable heroes, which are limited to unlock only one new hero per playthrough, as well as hero-variations if you have used each hero well enough (i.e. kill 30 enemies with Hero A1 to get A2. Get Hero A to 10 strength to unlock Hero A3)
If you "just" want to complete the game fast enough to get the achievement, this took me 7 hours.
If you want to try all the different heroes as well as each of the 3 variations of the heroes, then I'm guessing it might take 20-30 hours.
I suspect it will start to get rather repetitive if you're trying to unlock all the heroes though, but I was not bored during this first win.
Conclusion:
I'd say this game has 5-7 hours of effective gameplay, followed by an optional grind of roughly 10 hours to unlock everything (maybe less).
I bought the game on sale, so I'm quite happy with the amount of entertainment I got for it.
I'm not sure if I would want to pay 15 EUR for it (normal price for my country), so I recommend getting it on sale (30% off or less).

Short, nice-looking turn based game.    Maps, item drops, and combat starting positions are all random to drive the challenge.  Good run-thoughs can turn bad pretty quickly.  Replayability is good because you can mix the four helper mercenaries from a group of about 10.  Two game modes- first keeps hero and merc experience [rogue] and  second always starts them green.   Most interesting thing about this game is that it achieves a sliding degree of difficulty without just wrenching the enemy health/number.  If you play easy with fully leveled up heroes and take your time you should succeed about 90% of the time and get a weak ending to the story.  If you blitz through to get the fast ending using unleveled crew that success rate will drop to around 5%.
King's Bounty meets with rogue genre! Although variety (item/enemy/etc) is a little lacking for a rogue game, the art style is pleasant enough to make this light-hearted game very enjoyable.
It's just so boring.  Combat is boring.  Exploring the map is boring.  The random events are boring.  There's just nothing about this game that gives me a reason to want to play it.

A fun and challenging strategy RPG.  Crowntakers takes me back to Vandal Hearts and Shining Force.  These types of games have been left behind, but I could play them over and over again. I've been playing Awesomenauts since the Starstorm Days, back when damage was measured in Single Digits and Everyone's Biggest Fear was Ashley Burch as a Psychotic Child & a Cheese Eating Surrender Lizard. And seeing all the Changes such as Damage Multiplication, a Snowballing Level System and Two Whole Groups of Expansion Characters I can  happily say I enjoyed every patch I've seen.
Awesomenauts is what happens when you strip down the MOBA Formula to it base level of Turrets, Cores and purchasable Items and then apply them to a 2-D Platform Shooter. And in Normal Circumstances, it would just get washed away amidst the sea of MOBA's, but where it shines like a beacon is it's aesthetics...
The games main Style is that it takes itself after the ideaforms of kids shows from the 80's and 90's, effectively even having their opening cutscene like the opening to a kids show, and the characters reflect that greatly if not in their design then definitely in their themes.
Outstanding characters of such include a Gangsta Frog(Straight Outta Frogspawn!) A Paladin made of Ice Cream, A Genetically Cloned Space Marine... who isn't wearing any Trousers.., A Rogue Bird Cop who is wielding probably the coolest weapon ever! A Love Letter to Quentin Tarantino's Movies, with a Lisp. And most recently a strangely interesting rendition of A Famous Soldiers-of-Fortune Team.
It's Fanbase may be Small, and it's Future ever-Uncertain; but it's direction to go F2P might be the decision to improve it's numbers and make the future of this Game Bright, provided the content is consistent...

Honestly a 10/10!

I can't believe this game is from 2014, it has probably the best graphics I have ever seen.
All animations are extremely lifelike and when characters talk the audio is *perfectly* synced to the the lips (and I play it in German btw). It feels like watching a CGI movie, while it isn't.
Here are a few screenshots I made (in 1080p)
The game design is well done too. You have a normal attack and a "break block" attack with various animations. Both can be charged for heavy attacks. You have a timed block and a dodge. And a special ability (slow time, but maybe more can be unlocked). And that's it. Combos are not executed by pressing long and complicated sequences of buttons, but by pressing the right button at the right time, which can be tricky in a 1v4 situation.
When an enemy is low on life, you can decide to execute them. This starts an automatic sequence where you have to press buttons that correspond to the current strike animation. There are a lot of different sequences, which even consider the environment sometimes, like smashing an opponents face on a wall. The coolest thing is executing two enemies at the same time.
As you are a leader, sometimes you get the ability to command your troops on the battlefield, for example to create a turtle formation (with you inside).
Level design is very linear, but that seems like the right thing for this game, as it is focused on telling a specific story with specific moments that are embedded in the scenery. Though sometimes you will encounter invisible walls or things that feel like it (a pile of trash you can't walk over). A tad too static.
I find the character progression a bit pointless, because it seems you can only improve modifiers like maximum hp, focus gain, etc. Unlocking attack "skills" etc wouldn't make much sense either because of how the fighting system works, but it feels a bit like someone decided to latch on a progression system just for the sake of it. It's not like it hurts the game, it's just the weakest point I have discovered so far in this overall amazingly executed game.

Games like Ryse: Son of Rome are probably the reason why Steam should have a "Recommended on sale" review option. Let's start with the positives though, the game has an interesting and unique storyline, with great acting, animations and graphics. You get the chance to play as a Roman soldier, slaying your way through barbarian enemies, executing them in a spectacular way that probably never felt so satisfying and gruesome in any PC game before. (Emphasis on "PC game", so you can't come up with God of War.) Besides, it's always refreshing to play with a new title in the world of sequels and prequels. However, after finishing the first few missions, the fighting and executions become extremely boring due to them having no variety, you basically kill the same few types of enemies with the same few types of moves all the way through the game. There are some boss fights, and you can purchase new executions, even lead Romans into battle in shield walls or shoot enemies with ballistic arrows, but that's still not enough, they don't add too much variety to the game, and they're still not complex enough to keep your attention for long, leaving the gameplay to drown into repetitive boredom once again. Personally my biggest problem with the game was the poor optimization though. In many missions I experienced stuttering and frame-rate drops for seemingly no reason, my PC highly exceeds the system requirements. I read about the issue online and it looks like I wasn't the only one having this problem, but after trying to fix it through what people said might reduce the stuttering the problem was still present. During some missions the game was stuttering, during some other missions it didn't. Perhaps others will be more lucky with this technical issue of the game, but I'd still only recommend buying it on a sale, as it's not worth to pay the full price for a game that might constantly stutter on your computer because of the developer's bad optimization and refusal to release a patch/fix.

Here is some information that I haven't seen widely reported.  I recorded footage from the game with a 120 fps camera, and found that my inputs were responding around the the 13th frame.  This is 6 frames of lag at 60fps.  To put this in perspective, I tested Crimzon Clover with vsync and it had 5 frames.  I hope they can bring the lag down to that level.
My final thoughts are that this is Cave's first Steam release, so hopefully they can get better at dealing with PC related issues going forward.  I really urge people to purchase this game, so that we may get many more ports and maybe a new release.

This is a really good port of one of CAVES best shooters.  It's one of the more approachable bullet hell games they've made so it makes sense this would be the first one they bring over to get people interested over the arguably more difficult Dodonpachi Series.  Unlike other bullethell shooters, CAVE games don't rely on rote memorization to do well; They have a nice blend of freeform movement and tight bullet dodging which doesn't feel gimmicky or cheap.  If you're experienced in the genre or have good reflexes then even you can make it far on your first playthrough.
*The controls are as tight as they always were and every death will be your fault (no blaming th controls here :P)
*The game comes with 3 game modes (4 if you get the 1.5 DLC) each with 3 difficulty levels to control exactly how hard you want your experience to be.  You have Novice, Original, Arranged, and 1.5 (aka Matsuri).  Each has their own soundtrack which you can mix and match with other modes in the game in the options.  It's really customizable.
*The visuals are really crisp and good looking.  It's only in 720p, but it doesn't take away from the art direction and the cleaness of everything presented.  The menu is very slick and easy to navigate.  You won't be entering and exiting a lot of menues to switch modes or play with options for each game.
*The framerate is great at least for me.  It switches between 59-60 fps during gameplay but I've never visually noticed or felt it. The main menu where you select which mode you want to play is 30fps but once you choose a mode it changes to 60.  There is slowdown during the game but IT'S 100% INTENTIONAL.  Cave's games have what's known as "earned" slowdown.  The game will LOOK like it's slowing down but if you look at your FPS counter it should still be +/-1 fps from 60 at all times during gameplay.  This is written 2 days after launch of the game but there have been framerate complaints from some people saying the game goes as low as 54fps for them.  I have a pretty basic non-gaming laptop and it runs fine for me.  I suspect it's some graphics card issue or they're running other programs in the background which might cause it to slow down.
All in all, if you are a veteran or a newbie trying to get into the genre then you can't go wrong with this quality title.

On balence one of the best multiplayer games out at the moment in my view.  The free DLC's and constant updates and patches from the developers is a welcome change from the lackluster support most games seem to get these days.  Its not an easy game to play, the learning curve is steep and while Singleplayer will teach you the basics it has little replayability and is dull compared to the vibrant multiplayer.
What at first seems simple and even one dimentional (Pact vs NATO, everyone gets planes, tanks, infantry etc) gets ever more complex the longer you play until you find yourself building "Decks" (Military formations assembled before a battle) in ever more obscure and challenging combinations or swapping out units one at a time to find the "perfect" balence.  Want to field a balenced Pan-Nato army? Not a problem! Want to limit your force to only Pre 1975 units? and only of a certain kind? thats fine! From a certain country? No worries! and so you find you have made a 1975 Norweigan Motorised Deck with no anti air units, practically no tanks and a virtually non-existent airforce.... but you have ALOT of men with guns... and so the sillyness commences.
The real joy of the game is combining the hours of fun that can be had building decks with playing with a freind.  This allows each of you to take wildly lop-sided decks that would usually get slaughtered in a 1vs1 but mean you can cover each others weaknessess in thousands of differant deck combinations.
Overall its not a perfect game, the single player is lack luster, and some units need tweaking.  On the other hand the multiplayer experaince is, while complex and harsh to those getting into the game. A huge ammount of fun espechially if played with teamspeak etc 9/10.

A solid almost-modern warfage RTS which breaks free of so many conventional RTS mechanics that it is noteworthy sheerly for its originality in design. Rather than stapling you to a set list of units for a specific side and following a metagame written out by some MLG koreans who can twitch click "Flight of the Bumblebees" zerglings in their sleep, this game lets you BUILD a faction from anywhere between 100-400 units per "deck". Not only that, but the pacing of the game is in this insanely good sweetspot between being slow enough to make the game feel more about macromanagement and being fast enough that the feeling of intensity and engagement never dies. Expect medium difficulty learning how to play multiplayer well with a long climb to mastery.
I would not recommend ranked, the games there are just awful and usually just consist of exploits in unit balancing. The singleplayer is somewhat fun, but has a lot less to keep your attention. The real fun is in playing with friends, or players you synergize with well in-game. Pulling off a good ambush or attack never gets old.

A Mortician's Tale is less a game and more of an interactive story of some aspects of life in the funeral industry.
What I liked:  humanizes the funeral directors and tears the veil a bit on the care they show your departed loved ones.  The graphics are charming.
What I didn't like: considering the game begins in a small, family-owned funeral home, it was odd that the director, Charlie, isn't responsible for more than just cleaning, embalming, and cremating.  Most directors in this setting are responsible for a whole lot more of the process.  I also didn't like that the tutorial-ish explanations of what to do are displayed on every preparation.  The firs time it makes sense, show me what to do, but to hold my hand through the entire process tells me this isn't a game, but rather an interactive story.  *spoiler alert*  The narrative sees the small, family-owned funeral home be acquired by a larger corporation.  I feel like this paints a picture of inevitability that family-owned can't survive in the industry, which is false.  It also portrays a "this or that" idea that larger funeral home operations only care about money, which is also not necessarily true.  There are "mom and pop" operations that are just as guilty of that.  It's a pretty short story.  Short enough that they really ought to charge less for it, ironically enough.

After several attempts over the years at replaying this mainstream cult classic RPG, I've managed to finish it at last. Once upon a time, when the game hitted the shelves, I enjoyed it greatly. There weren't much RPGs released back then, especially games with lengthy and well written stories. And the game still shines today in that department, with memorable parts scattered unevenly along the journey through completion.
This game is mostly a social commentary, it's themes are war, social strata, slavery, corporation abuses, and at its core the dilemma of using or withholding the use of power. Companions are rather unconventional (especially at the time of release), have entertaining backstories, legitimate motivations and idiosyncracies. They are a definite strong point of the game, as is the story. The pace is another strength, lasting roughly a 30ish hours, you will troddle through varied setpieces, quests that can be solve in several ways (with different consequences and possible rewards for each), hostile environments that can be navigated through by different means, and finally well placed diversions (mini games, quirky dialogs and interactions with the environment).
But the game suffers from a clear lack of polish, which at the time of release were rendered irrelevant due to its strengths, but is now a huge obstacle to the enjoyment of the overall experience. The combat is the most glaring flaw as it makes a sizable part of the game. While it is still entertaining enough due to the nice animations and "D&Desque" system in place, the overreliance on trash enemies wears your patience slowly but surely down. There is no meaningful character progression in a mechanical sense either, as skills and feats are underwhelming at best and trivial at worst. While there is variety in how you deal with enemies, and cross dangerous locations, some are broken, and while the game is forgiving for the most part when it comes to difficulty, there are definitely some hefty spikes here and there. Quests and dialog trees can be clunky, pathfinding and AI is atrocious, copy-paste NPCs make it hard at times to recognize quest givers and break immersion all together. And the list goes on.
While despite all those flaws the game could still be entertaining as a linear story driven experience with light RPG elements, the complete disregard of the player's choices in the narrative earns it a thumbs down. The game always presents you with multiple choices, some good, bad or in between, when it comes to important decisions and companions they don't matter at all. In some key points of the plot it becomes farcical, has you say/do things and the characters and the world purely ignore your actions. To me this is the straw that breaks the camels back.
It sure would be nice if this received a resolution update like KOTOR II....

Contradiction is a game as charming as it is hilarious.
An FMV murder mystery, you follow Detective Frederic Jenks who has traveled to the small English village known as Edenton to investigate the death of a young student.
The meat of the game consists of moving from location to location in this small village and interviewing its residents about the death. When you someone tells you new information or you find some new piece of evidence, these are added as topics that you can ask the other residents about. Eventually, someone will give you an answer which contradicts something they've said previously and it's up to you to catch them doing it.
The writing and performances in this game elicited more than a few laughs out of me, while still providing a interesting mystery to solve. It toes that line pretty well. I really look forward to any potential follow ups to this.

N++ is - at its core - a completely fundamentalist platformer. You can kiss your sorry concepts of fully voiced characters, combat and plot goodbye, squire. There's just you, a whole bunch of obstacles, and the end of the level.
The highly momentum-based platforming in the N series was perfected back in the original 2004 flash game and nothing has changed since. This may sound like a bad idea in today's age of gaming innovation (where sequels have your standard new ideas and updated mechanics) but it completely works out in N++'s favour. Why fix what isn't broken?
Although seeming sluggish and clunky to a newcomer, with each clutch victory and hazardous jump you can really feel your mastery over the game increase. And with 2,360 total levels to get through, you'll have plenty of time to practise.

I actually remembered the first N being a flash game back in 2005, I used to play the hell out of that game before I discovered Steam or even had a game console in general; beated all the levels and episodes. Then my brother and I got a Xbox 360 (we "shared" it with each other) and found out there was a sequal called N+, once again, I played it to death and completed all episodes.
7 years later, I just saw N++ and instantly, all the memories I had with N and N+ just came flooding back.
I feel like my snarky, 3rd grade self again!

Where most adventure games have charm and silly object interactions, TGP! has it non-stop. How could you say no to that?!
This game does something amazingly right that I've never seen any other adventure game do - it continues to be funny and interesting even when you're stuck. There is dialog for almost every object and item interaction; the normally annoying job of trying to use every object with every other object is actually RECOMMENDED in this game. It really is no exaggeration when I say it has literally 10x more dialog than even the most verbose adventure games.
Do start with Ben There, Dan That! though. It is simple and short (~2 hrs), and you'll quickly see the humor this series employs.

I was really pleasantly surprised by this game.  It's got a lot of charm, everything is really well polished, and it's decently challenging without being too punishing.  I'm a big fan of rogue-lites and tactical strategy games and this does both portions justice, although with only a moderate amount of depth.  Think of it as a really well-done, casual-minded rogue-lite.  8/10
Starting off can be a bit rough, but once you unlock some of the 'good' characters, like the scout, the game becomes much, much easier.  Also 'easy' mode is the way to go while you're getting a hang of the game and still unlocking.  A lot of the problems I had in the beginning were from rushing and not exploring, thinking the time pressure element was more important than it actually is.  Unfortunately, once you get the hang of it, it's a bit too easy.  And if you get the DLC, the game is also substantially easier, but does have more 'fun' content.
Combat is the major portion of the game and I'm glad to say it does it quite well.  Certain mercs synergize quite nicely.  The map is never 'too big' and almost always fits entirely on the screen.  You always start first, but don't get to choose positioning, which is a fair enough tradeoff.  Most battles will be over in a few rounds.  Only the bigger boss battles stretch out and try your resources and resourcefulness.  Stun is a bit overpowered, which makes the barbarian maps a bit of a pain, but there are multiple options for avoiding fights, so it's by no means a gamebreaker.
There's a good number of 'fun things' like unlocks and achievements to keep you playing after you've won once.  A single run can last a few hours if you explore all the nooks and crannies.  I'm hoping they release some more DLC with an extended challenge.  Overall, it's a really fun game that I'd totally recommend for a weekend romp.  That said, $15 is a bit much, but during seasonal sales, it goes for much, much less making it an insta-buy.

[Spoiler-Free Review]
Crowntakers aims to usurp your playtime with accessible, character-based, combat on a grid. While certain elements leave something to be desired, ultimately, it's a game better than the sum of its parts.
You start out with a single hero, and gradually recruit mercenaries you meet in your travels (up to four extras per run). The mercenaries come with skills unique to them, and part of the fun is figuring out their strengths/weaknesses. In addition, each character comes with additional unlockable archetypes (i.e. skillsets), something I really appreciated. It made for fun rewards, a reason to use characters you wouldn’t naturally be inclined to, and gave everyone the potential to become useful where their default skills might be lacking.
I get that the game is more about proper resource management, the challenges you overcome, and the people you meet along your adventure, but a narrative consisting of two basic strings of storyline text (intro and finale), doesn't leave a whole lot of room for extrapolation. The story doesn't incentivize the player or encourage you to replay the adventure, it doesn't even help develop character.  It’s, summarily, placeholder text for a better story not yet conceived. Thankfully it’s also skippable (for the most part). Even the bits that come up when you investigate a new location are easily ignored, as the choices are basically, 'You wanna fight, or not?' (the answer is yes btw, always yes, and you don’t need to read through a snippet about an old woman begging for food to know it).
A typical run takes about an hour or so to complete (once you understand how everything works), and you will be required to run through the game more than once to unlock achievements and mercenaries. Where the story was lacking, the achievements are not, and provide ample reason to go back and play through the game over and over again.
Start with Easy Mode if you want to give yourself the best chance at enjoying this game. It’s a welcome entry point to the game mechanics and world. You play through the story the same way you would in Normal Mode, but with the added advantage that you don't lose experience and levels gained in each run. Failure never feels quite so devastating when you know your characters are going to retain their stats (for the most part) in subsequent attempts. By the time you’ve completed your Easy run, you’ll be more than ready for Normal. In either mode, the only thing poking and prodding you to go forward is that enemies grow stronger by the in-game day.
Collecting items and equipment, and taking on enemy mobs are rewarding experiences. The danger in a game so focused though, is that the game can become monotonous if the formula isn’t changed all that much from start to finish. Having special elements based around each area helps remedy this to a point, instead of fighting soldiers and thieves at every turn, some areas house natural threats/inhabitants and mysterious landmarks.
Exploring the map is enjoyable. Areas (in and out of battle) are vibrant and interesting. Each area has a unique look to it, and the contrast between them helps keep the game feeling fresh.
In a game you're likely to spend a considerable amount of time playing and replaying, 2-3 songs isn't really going to suffice. The tracks are good, and melt into the backdrop as you play, but even the best song is going to feel repetitive if it's the sole musical leg on which a game stands. The sound effects are satisfying though, my favourite being the sucking sound your cursor makes when hovering over items in your inventory.
I can't tell whether the maps are randomized. I've played through the game 4 or 5 times across each of the difficulties and each time, the maps kind of mesh together in my mind. It's not that it's overly samey, it’s just not immediately clear to me how the maps are differentiated. It could just be a by-product of the fog-of-war and the small scope of each area. However, it might be saying something that the random world doesn’t feel very random.
If I was to sum this game up in a word, it'd be barebones. Crowntakers is entertaining however, and I don't feel bad in recommending it to anyone. I just hope the devs continue to expand the offering. This game really deserves it.

is an indie game developed by Laundry Bear that follows the day-to-day work of… well, a mortician. You play Charlie, fresh out of mortuary school and recently employed by a mom-and-pop funeral home, Rose & Daughters. It’s inspired by Caitlin Doughty and The Order of the Good Death, and it includes many of the concepts surrounding the death acceptance movement. The game is brief — I finished it in an hour — and the mechanics are not strenuous at all. I thought I would have to memorize the embalming and cremation processes, but each time you tend to a corpse, the game walks you through what to do. I thought I’d have to navigate social situations surrounding grieving family members, but the game doesn’t require it.
Instead, the game introduces players to death acceptance concepts — home funerals, green burials, etc. — and allows players to acknowledge the dark and unaddressed feelings they may have surrounding death and dying
being heavy-handed about it. In fact, a lot of the daily work that’s often considered gruesome becomes rather routine with every new body to embalm or cremate. But the plot of the game, as short as it is, is a reminder of how disassociated much of Western society, in particular American society, is with its dead. And it is a gentle introduction to the notion that death does not have to be scary or “other.”
As a death worker, I’m already familiar with the concepts introduced by A Mortician’s Tale. I have already read Doughty’s first book, and I know what embalming and cremation entail. There’s always more for me to learn, but I recognized Charlie’s story and already knew its happy ending. But what I didn’t expect was how strongly some comments made by the grieving relatives moved me. At one point, I had to pause because I was actually crying. And when I reached the end of the game, when Charlie’s morals and beliefs manifested physically, I felt inspired by her devotion to the dead. “Me too, Charlie,” I thought. “Me too.”
Needless to say, I absolutely recommend this game. It’s only an hour long, so it won’t take much time out of a person’s day. It’s easy to play, and its brevity prevents the average person from getting bored of the rote tasks involved with cremation and embalming. It teaches players about death positivity and death acceptance. It ends in hope.

This is a weird franchise. I've played since I was young at the first and second game, however then a few years later they got a needless sequel that forgot what stuff needed fixing in the previous games and also pretty much killed the franchise. However, what about the first and second game? As usual I'm gonna start warning you about what the game fails, then move into it's strong points.
First and foremost, the biggest problem this game has is being around 20 hours long and having a story that you'll hardly care about. Remember Sacred? Similar games, however there the story hardly got in the way. Here however the story is all over the place, it's redundant, predictable and overall kinda worthless. After a while you might just end up skipping every dialogue. And it's sad because the first game wasn't so heavy on the story and made it more enjoyable. It also doesn't help much that the game is long but it honestly felt easy. It rarely got too hard, though I did grind up a bit at certain points to look for those damn set items, which might have something to do with it.
The second bad part it has are some of the changes from the previous game. On it, you could have a ton of companions from the beginning and it was up to you to choose what they equip, who to take and sh#t. Well, you don't get as much freedom in quantities here anymore as from the start you'll be forced to a VERY small amount of possible characters that can follow you, and you'll have to buy more character slots, with the final slots being locked for higher difficulties. Excuse me, but wasn't the most fun part of the first game to f#ck around with a party of 6 dumb#ss guys with sh#tty loadouts into dumb dungeons and getting killed half-way? Why the hell would this game hold 4 character slots to ransom? That's a pretty clear case of fixing what wasn't broken. Thankfully there's mods that fix that♥♥♥♥♥♥ and I highly suggest you use them.
Third is that for some reason this game tried to be more edgy. You know how it goes, back then most sequels went with the edgy tones and this game was no exception. For some reason there's way more blood, there's NPCs EXPLODING IN BLODDY CHUNKS OF MEAT when killed with hard hitting attacks, but it looks really silly and out of place in my opinion, after having played the first one. It does kinda show that they were running out of ideas or had their ideas mixed up.
There's also how the devs didn't fix a common issue with the first game, how linear the game is and that there's not that much rooms to explore. Sure there's hidden areas and all but with a game called DUNGEON Siege you'd expect a bit more freedom, more caves where to explore for a reasonable longer time for some mini-boss that'll drop a weapon you'll instantly use once and forget or something. As it is it's usually just a hidden cave with 2 or 3 rooms and some monsters/loot or secret rooms with better loot inside but reasonable smaller. Kinda lackluster on that regard
Lastly is that the game wasn't made for modern computers, so you should expect some compability issues and weird resolutions. Some of those are fixable by f#cking around the game files or by modding, though.
But what does the game do right, you might ask? Well...
The combat system is satisfying enough. Though the story might get boring and the game is linear as all hell, the combat doesn't get too boring. You get full freedom on building your small number of characters as you please, including having weird but cool pets instead of humans or even a FeCKING DONKEY WITH INSANE CARRYING SPACE. A F#CKING DONKEY. THAT is cool.
The game's lenght is also really good for it's price. Specially since it offers replayability and♥♥♥♥♥♥
The game also had a really cool multiplayer mode which is really cool... But it's patched out here. However, you can mod it back into it, and playing the game with a friend is quite fun!
And there's also completely randomized and it kinda adds to the experience. You can also upgrade items which adds to making your characters more customizable. Finally, there's also set items, which means that if you get multiple items from that one set, you get higher and higher special stats, which I REALLY LIKE! It's kinda hard to get those set items and you might end up farming up a bit, but it's worth it.
Overall, I would recommend the game, HOWEVER I would seriously recommend you to try the first game instead, and also to just avoid the third game like the f#cking plague. In a sale, it's a decent amount of fun and a really good lenghty game for a cheap price.
TL;DR Edition: It's average. The first game was better, here sh#t went edgier and gorier for no reason while the exploration stood the same and the story became a sour mess. But still kinda fun to go through, specially if you mod the multiplayer back in, as for SOME UNHOLY GODFORSAKEN F#CKING REASON THE STEAM VERSION HAS IT PATCHED OUT.

Pros - fast pased, rarely unsure where to go, no bugs as of yet, no crashes as of yet (last two are HUGE pluses)
Cons - many heroes are not suited for solo play, Dialogue gets tiresome and almost every npc has the same personality (21 year old suburbanite college student), lack of depth in items and character progression, cutscenes look like they were done by the cheapest animation studio china had, character animations and stances seem to be designed by a 21 year old suburbanite (lack of depth, substance and more interested in making references than anything else).
If Battleborn had been presented to some of my college character and game design teachers as a final project, they would have failed Gearbox purely on principle. Would it be wrong of them to fail the project out right? Yes, but at the same time I would kind of understand why they would fail it.
While there is a solid game at the core of Battleborn, the story, the dialogue and the character designs seem to be a mess.
Taunt animations seem to be more interested with making a reference (stupid birdman dance) than match up with the character and the dialogue for those taunts seem to have been the first thing that plobed into the writers head. But I do admit, there are a far good number that still work and are entertaining.
The designs seem to be all over the place, even within each of the character factions. Some of the characters poses seem to hint some of the modelers or animators have watched too much jo jos bizare adventure. (I don't care if she is a Pirate queen, no one would actually stand like). It almost seems like they cut the design time for this game in half and rushed it.
As for the item system, the most benefit you are ever going to get out of a single item seems to be around a 10% bonus to 2 stats. The balancing of the items does not seem very well thought out either. There is no real reason to have legendaries that cost over twice the resources each mission when you can have a free item that nearly does the same thing but reduces a stat, maybe even a stat that your character does not use.
I was really hopping for more from the items than just very shallow and minor stat increases.
To wrap this up, I have some harsh criticism for this game, but I will continue playing. But I can't say it was worth the price of admission. So for now I am saying no on my recommendation.
EDIT: I actually have not played the game at all since I wrote this and attempted to get a refund, looking back I was being really nice to the game . . . and people said I was being a jerk to it. Whatever I guess.

I don't understand why this game received so much positive ratings... I mean, it's not bad, but not as good as other said. There's lot of things that doesn't work.
1) Acting is really bad.
Some of the actors act quite well but the others are so bad, especially the main character who over-act each sentence. You can't believe in him one second...
2) You can't talk about everything
If someone said something about another person, you can't ask her/him if she/he doesn't speak about it first. That's the basis of an investigation and make nonsense to me.
3) All contradictions are not recognized
I don't want to spoil but, when someone says "I've never heard of him before he died" and later "I sold him some stuff", there is a contradiction here, but the game doesn't want it. Why ?
4) The story is so cliché
Think about an investigation that take place in a lost small village with a sect-like institute, what do you imagine ? Yes, secret society with some black magic, that kind of stuff. And we're not that far here. So predictable...
5) The investigation is not even legal...
The detective enters back doors, pick up some stuff without a warrant and noone cares about it. He's not a PI, he's a policeman. He can't do that...
But, the game is not that bad neither. The filmmaking is good, the logic behind subjects and evidences works well (most of the time) and, even if it's cliché, the story is well driven.
This is clearly a game with small budget, made by thriller fans, with a good atmosphere. And it deserves to be encouraged. But... it's not the AMAZING game others said here. It is a small, honnest, amateur game with its imperfection and it should be taken as it. That's why I don't recommend it, to warn you about its true value (but buy it still, Baggy Cat deserves to be known and a sequel deserves to exist ;) )

This is a game with a lot of struggles. It was originally denied access to Greenlight, then it was allowed and greenlit and released, then it was pulled from Steam and then it was put back on Steam. I originally got the game at launch. But let's put that aside and talk about what the game IS and not its troubled release history.
Paranautical Activity is a first person roguelike. From a gameplay perspective it borrows a lot from The Binding of Isaac, notably the room grid approach where the player needs to defeat all enemies in a room to progress instead of moving freely in a continuous level like in other roguelikes. And like Binding of Isaac, each floor has a boss at the end as well as optional minibosses. The first first person perspective alone and the three-dimensional design of rooms makes the game very action oriented and keeps you on your toes. There are also multiple "characters" to choose from, each with radically different weapons, so there is variety in gameplay. The presentation of the game is pretty neat, making use of voxels to render everything. And I can honestly say I had a lot of fun playing this game. If you want a very action oriented roguelike with FPS control, then I say give this game a try.

This game is an RTS in the sense that it is a strategy game in real-time. That said, you cannot come into this game with typical RTS conventions in mind. If anything, you should think of it as a computerized miniatures game, down to the 'deployment zone' at the beginning of each match on your 'table edge.'
For starters, you don't base build. There is an economy that allows you to call in more units from presumably off map locations, but to gain an edge you have to capture sectors (depending on your game mode). The amount of control you have over these units when you get them assures that if they are to die, it's your fault. Most engagements in this game aren't a matter of who has the bigger cannon or sometimes even more units (all of which are extremely detailed and astonishingly true to their real world counterparts), it's about manuvering them into good flanking and defensive positions so they don't end up destroyed by the enemy. It seems simple on paper, but it's more than that, as made clear by the addition of airplanes performing strikes and dogfights above an already chaotic battlefield. You'll start figuring out the importance of taking the right units to the right situation or you'll get to watch them turn into smoking wrecks.
This game is probably one of the best of any sort I've ever played, let alone strategy games. The only limit is a player's own capabilities, not an artificial 'level' or standard campaign mode. The game is a little daunting to get into at first, but paying close attention to the game's tutorials and your own experimentation should have you leading armies and creating your own decks (personalized unit lists assembled from unit 'cards,' all of which are unlocked from the word go) in no time. I've highly enjoyed the previous Wargame, this game and highly anticipate the release of the next installment, Red Dragon. I feel Eugen has quickly cemented themselves as essentials to the RTS genre and strategy games as a whole with this amazing series.
Also, 10 player vs 10 player battles and easy to pick up multiplayer? Heck yes.

There are a few rough edges here and there, of course, but everything I once listed on this paragraph has been patched eventually and I just gave up on updating this.
Also worth of note is that the stages are crafted well enough to keep things interesting, and the upgrades for skills, while not as detailed as the splash arts, are probably one of the most endearing features of the game. Some icons might even get a giggle out of you, be it due to the joke on their names or descriptions, or through a visual gag on the icon.
Visuals: 9/10
The sprite art is handled with care and pretty much everything on screen is easily readable. Some older nauts do deserve more care, though.
The gameplay videos did sell me the game, but what really captivated me was this.
The voice acting is solid, diverse, fun, quirky and unique... It started with the characters donning the voices of the developers themselves (and they actually did a great job with them), and evolved to professional voice actors and Youtube sensations (And they did a great job, too, specially Jesse Cox as Genji and Simon Lane - from Yogcast fame - as Skølldir). Although not all of them are all that appealing to me, personally, I have to admit that all of them suit their characters to a tee.
And the soundtrack is an even greater treat, it's amazing. Each character has a theme song, and a remixed version for Killing Sprees (that plays whenever you score 3 kills without dying). The theme songs, in conjunction with the character designs, instantly conveys what that character is about (Be it a Space Cowboy or anthropomorphic assassin or whatever). The Killing Spree remix gives you that thrilling boost when you're doing your part well. Of course, since the OST is so diverse, there probably are music from styles and genres which you may love, and some that, although it suits the character perfectly, isn't something you will enjoy listening all the time.
I just can't highlight my favorites anymore, there are too many.
Also worth of note are the announcers. The default is OK, even if a little bland, but the ones sold or unlocked are interesting and well acted, and contributes to the overall humor of the game. I leave them on random to provide variety.
Sound Design: 10/10
Solid voice acting by a spot-on ensemble, superb Soundtrack brought to us by Sonic Picnic.
MOBA is usually a genre that is hard to get into. Although there does have a skill gap between an expert team working cohesively towards their goals and a bunch of friends who just started now, there's one thing that is different about AN: You don't have to follow guides and trends to have fun. Your choice of character should be more tailored to your personal preferences more than on how viable they are for tournaments.
This kind of thing kills traditional MOBA's for me, meanwhile AN is a lot easier to get into and introduce to people you know, be them MOBA veterans, casual gamers, people who enjoy 2D games, or even my ten year old sister.
With that out of the way, let's talk about the core gameplay.
On the main modes of play, you and two other players pick characters to play against a team of 3 players or bots.
Each character has access to a main attack and two skills. There's a shop where you can buy upgrades for each of these, plus passive upgrades, organized in rows (One for each skill, one for the basic attack, and one general). You're limited to three items per row, and the choices you make influence attributes such as damage, range, and other effects. You and your teammates try to destroy your enemies turrets and base, while defending your own. Both teams are accompanied by droids that march on towards the enemy automatically. You know, in typical MOBA fashion. Except that in no other MOBA you'd control a small space ship dropping from a flying base onto the spawn area while collecting in-match money to make up for your losses on death...
The 2D perspective, and team dynamic ensued from the small team and really varied roster help differentiate the experience from other games in the genre.
Each character is unique, with varied skills and even mobility (Some jump higher, some some glide or even fly, etc) and deal damage. There's at least a few Nauts you will enjoy, no matter your preferences.
From Thursday to Sunday, a Brawl mode is available. These have varied sets of rules, such as Team Deathmatches, removed limits on the upgrades shop, etc. These are mostly fun, even if the queues for them do take a while.
There's also custom game modes and Steam Workshop integration for custom maps on a separate room-based structure.
New players initially only have access to four characters, that change every week. You can easily unlock a few characters permanently through free skins available in a myriad of methods, and for the others you have to play the game and acquire a currency called AwesomePoints.
In my experience, you get enough AP to unlock Nauts every few times you level up your account or each individual Naut, while unlocking features such as medals for your profile and access to more columns for each Naut's upgrade shop. So you try out different characters while playing or in a training area accessible via the shop and unlock the ones you like the most.
The in-game purchases with real money are cosmetic, changing aesthetics, voices or even sometimes the theme music of particular Nauts with skins and the voices and lines of the announcer through voice packs, among other items available such as avatars and drop pods.
These are standard MOBA/Online game fare, and do not affect gameplay.
These items available for real money can all be added to your Steam Wishlist (for your friends to gift you or to keep up with price drops during sales), and in my opinion are all fairly priced.
You can occasionally experience lag whil playing (that may happen more or less often depending on the playerbase in your country). Also, in my experience, the AN Community attracts less toxic players than other games.
AwesomeNauts is a superbly fun game, developed with care and love poured on all of its features, from gameplay to visuals to sound design. It's even more fun with friends, as usual with online games, and my recommendation for anyone who read this far is: Give it a try! It's fun, and it's totally free!

I like a lot of things about this game.

3) The focus on environmentally-friendly mourning practices. Was really not expecting this, and was pleasantly surprised.
4) An inclusive approach to mourning that, though its "action" focuses on basically Christian practices, acknowledges cultural differences.
5) What little gameplay there is could have gradually gotten more difficult and "plate-spinning", a la Papers, Please. It doesn't. This is a clearly intentional choice as doing otherwise would distract from the narrative and themes of the piece. There was probably an earlier version of this game that followed more typical gameplay "rules", and they probably decided at some point that that would only alienate the people who wanted what the game was actually offering. About the other reviews I'm seeing; there are a lot of people who think a game's length should determine its price point. I heartily disagree with that. The developers deserve to be paid.
Now, about the game: I quite enjoyed this one. Like a good short story, it was brief, but potent -- and I learned a good few things too over the course of it. I would've preferred that the tutorials went away after the first couple, or at least that you could toggle them. But the narrative has a very good heart; it's death-positive, of course, but more than that, it points out that our relationship with the dead can be as varied as with any living person. How you handle your living relationships matters. How you say goodbye does, too.
The gameplay isn't the main draw, though I did find a nice, meditative feeling to it -- the audio design does excellent work in this regard, as are the visuals. (That "diorama" style really suits!) As others have said, it IS short, and it does feel like it could have had at least a few more things to take care of before it wrapped up; but, that said...
If you take your time, read through the emails, and approach this game on a mellow night -- maybe with a glass of wine -- you're going to get a lot out of it. I sure did.

Caitlyn Doughty does seem to be a consultant on this game, but the information is bare bones. My best feedback to the devs would be to make the game longer and if you were going to put an emphasis on the business and upselling, include that mechanic in the game. This game helped. It's the first thing that's really helped since then. This game gets it. This game is important. And it's helped me walk through the pain a bit more, and recognize that we aren't alone in suffering and death. We all die, and we're joined by that. It doesn't have to be so terrifying.
P.S. - My husband is doing much better. Surgery went well, and he hasn't had to get any chemo/radiation yet. Things are looking up, but once your mind realizes you're mortal, you stay mortal.

Brilliant little strategy game!
Crowntakers is a stylish light roguelike tactical strategy. It combines RPG elements with hex-based combat and randomly generated events, items and battles. It offers nice variety of characters that you can recruit, train and equip with items.
The game doesn't hold your hand - it lets the player just play and figure out the rules for himself. My first few runs were kind of tough and I didn't do great, but when I discovered some cool strategies the game was a breeze. This is a warning for the hardcore players - once you understand how everything works, the game becomes too easy. However, it is a really great relaxing game that sucks you in with it's charm, beautiful art style and rock-solid gameplay.
The paid DLC offers a new level, one new character and some new items. I enjoy it, but it is by no means neccessary - treat it as something little extra you can get on the side. I sure hope they put out more content, as I really love this game.
Highly recommended!

The Bad
Just like the statement I opened with, Crowntakers reminded me a lot of FTL, but it lacked all the things that made FTL a fun game.
Character customization is practically nonexistent. There are no other weapons or armor to swap out on your characters (which could have really helped fight some of the monotony that is rife in this game); what you see is what you get until you upgrade to a marginally less lame version of the equipment.
The music is repetitive. Very repetitive.
The main character that you are stuck with looks like some backwoods halfwit and it is almost insulting that you are forced to play as him.
The Meh
The most Meh thing about Crowntakers is that they want to charge you money to get the game.
Verdict: Nay
If you have been wanting to play Crowntakers, don’t bother. It is a waste of time and you could better spend your time and money on a far more entertaining game. As always, thanks for reading.

I can recommend Crowntakers on sale. It just doesn't have the longevity to justify the full price.
Pros:
- Turn-based combat on a hex grid. It functions as you'd expect and is largely entertaining.
- Good aesthetic. Roguelites aren't always colorful or easy on the eyes, but this one certainly is.
- Strong upgrade system. You can find some really cool stuff that has a huge impact on how you approach battles. This ties into a con below, unfortunately.
Cons:
- Not balanced. Drops and store items are randomized, but not remotely equal. What you get and when has a *huge* impact on the difficulty of the game. One item (the book of bluffing) allows you to skip almost all of the combat in the game and gets you out of nearly every negative random event.
- No need to rush. The game claims enemies get stronger depending on how long you take, but after a deliberately slow playthrough, I am unconvinced. It does not seem to have a counter for taking your time and grinding powerful items. The attempt is giving you a "bad" victory if you take more than 18 days, but considering I won easily at 20 days making absolutely no effort to hit the deadline, I don't think it would be terribly difficult to reach the "true" ending with a similarly laid back approach.
- Enemy AI is moronic. It targets your units without regard to the damage incurred from doing so, for which units are likely to die if attacked, or for setting up its own counterattacks. Enemies love to set up overwatch in areas you'll never enter or guard on their second turn for no reason at all.
- Huge repetition of enemies. Ignoring bosses, there are all of 4 units in the royal army (of which I only saw 3 multiple times), 5 animals (3 recolors), and 2 alternate factions, both of which appear to only have one unit with minor variations. It's not enough to stay interesting over 7 areas.
- Few interesting random events. Crowntakers is clearly inspired by FTL, but where that game had different events at nearly every stop, this game instead offers you the same choices at nearly all stops, and Search (2h) is almost always the right one. What events there are have often entirely unpredictable consequences and lead to fights or damage for no reason at all. The characters and items required for special choices are often unclear and are never shown unless you have them.
Crowntakers is a great idea that unfortunately did not translate into a great game. My three hours played were enough to beat the game once and see *many* of the random events multiple times in spite of how rare it is to get one.

I mostly enjoyed Myst (realMyst: Masterpiece Edition). It has a lot of interesting puzzles (some much more difficult than others), and doesn't explicitly tell you how to solve any of them (or even really give you hints unless you consult an ingame advice book). This is both a good thing and a bad thing, in my opinion. It allows the player to feel a sense of accomplishment when they make progress, but can occasionally cause the player to feel frustrated and lost - then again, I imagine that's the sense the developers wanted to portray at points in the game. Despite this being the remastered version of Myst, I still feel like parts of the game haven't really aged well. For example, many of the clicking mechanics feel off, some of the cutscenes are extremely low-quality, and the free-roam mode doesn't always control well (but is still much better than the point-and-click mode). Overall, there were some parts of the story that I didn't like, but the different worlds and puzzles made the game pretty interesting.

An old, but not dated puzzle game that really holds its own despite the test of time. It still lives up to today's standards, and the lore of this whole series is incredibly deep and rich. Especially nowadays, where games aren't meant to be difficult, MYST is a welcome challenge, as it will keep you thinking and struggling, and the struggle only makes solving the puzzles even more gratifying. Rarely will you find the solution to something simply written down, and if you're playing through it for the first time, you could spend months just exploring the beautiful worlds in MYST. The only thing I can say is keep a journal while playing, you'll want to write down what you're doing and planning on doing so you don't lose your train of thought, and sometimes simply writing down what you've done will spark a thought on what to do next you wouldn't have thought of otherwise. Plus, there are plenty of things you'll want to have recorded for later, such as number sequences and such. Believe me, this game is difficult, if I hadn't kept a journal while playing, I wouldn't have completed it, but that difficulty could hardly be called a con. If you like puzzle games, good story, or are simply tired of multiplayer and simple games, you should definitely give MYST a try. The updated graphics in this version are worth the extra money (plus there's some extra content that I won't spoil here), trust me.

I had to look it up after assuming the game was bugged. Speaking of original-flavor realMyst, I also miss the day-night cycle in Selentic. The new skybox is cool, but I'm not sure it's worth losing that beautiful red-to-purple-to-black twilight.
All that said, this is an absolutely beautiful game, superior to the original realMyst in pretty much every way not mentioned above, and should now be considered the definitive version of the game.

is essentially a Quake clone. But it's a bad one.
The performance is rather abysmal. At first it felt like I was navigating through quickly drying mud. I have a variable 3 switch 1600DPI max mouse and I turned the sensitivity up all the way and it did become what I would consider somewhat “playable” however the game randomly and for little reason seems to go into slow motion.
Now, the steam overlay wasn't working and I wasn't about to use FRAPS to get an accurate reading for frame rate but ostensibly at least from what I could tell no frames were lost it just seemed to slow them all down. It did not seem contingent on number of enemies on screen or particle effects either. It seemed more affected by the player location on the map. It became basically unplayable despite fixing the relatively still noticeable input lag from increasing the sensitivity and DPI.
There is just no reason for a game that appears like it was made in the early 90's to perform so poorly and at such high temps. Before anyone decides to berate me thinking my system is not powerful enough or some other such.
I have run Dying Light at 1080p @ 60Hz on medium at temps 10°C lower than what this game was running at.
Regarding the game itself aside from performance there is not much to say. It's single player Quake-esk map design. There doesn't seem to be any indication of what weapons you have so you end up sort of haphazardly blundering your way through the cycle. It seems like it would be a very standard nostalgic/throwback to classic FPS games if it did run well. But it doesn't.
It has this very 80's heavy metal soundtrack that sounds like it'd fit well in a Top Gun movie. It's definitely attempting to give a certain vibe but all the other issues vastly outweigh any sort of enjoyment you might have convinced yourself of having.

Deactivate DOF and "Ambient Obscurance", and the game will only occasionally run slow.
Monument is a old-school fps in the vein of Quake that contains quite a lot of verticality - there even is a kind of double-jump/climb mechanic in there to further facilitate this. Navigation around the sprawiling, mazelike levels is it's very own skill mechanic, and it's yellow-brownish temple ruins contain a lot of secret areas, reachable by the more complicated movement mechanics.
If you like simple, oldschooled FPS with quite some platforming in it, Monument is a real treat.
Of course it's weapons' kinaesthetic leave a lot to be desired, and you shouldn't expect gunplay that's anywhere near Doom or Quake. At least they sound decent.
All in all - for a good 90s flashback it's most definitively worth it's asking price.

-The game is locked to horizontal 720p.
-This means vertical mode (TATE) must be used in a horizontal resolution.
-Movement is hard-bound to the arrow keys. (This will be addressed in an upcoming patch)
-Keybindings are thankfully available, however, half of my keyboard doesn't seem to be recognized.
-There are crashes upon pressing Start at the title screen, entering/exiting a game mode, and quitting the game. (Pressing Alt+Tab or waiting a few beats before doing the action might help you, but there are some gamers who can't get around these crashes at all. This will be addressed in an upcoming patch too.)
-I'm not sure if it's just me, but sometimes I find Reco continue moving in a direction a split second after I stopped pressing into that direction.
-Sometimes, the main menu items disappear upon returning from a game mode.
To fix some of these issues, particularly the crashes and locked resolution and even frame rate ones, look up GeDoSaTo and set it up.
Past these flaws, the game itself seems to run beautifully. The new HD visuals are more pleasing on the eyes compared to their blurry arcade originals. I can't comment on the accuracy of slowdown compared to the Xbox 360 version or the arcade PCB, but Degica did get members of the shmup community who own either versions to playtest.
If you're new to shmups, then this game might seem too overpriced for what seems like a quick half-hour affair, but that's ignoring the brilliance of arcade gameplay that truly shines when you aim to complete the game in only one credit (1CC, one credit clear) without any continues. Probably the best analogy for this post-arcade and post-NES age is speedrunning. As you play through the stages over and learn from your mistakes, you start learning the stages and developing all sorts of strategies and techniques to carry you over to the final goal of surviving the entire game. That alone will give you hours upon hours of gameplay. If you enjoy the game and want even more hours of gameplay, then you can kick up the difficulty and this game offers in addition to Original, Maniac and Ultra. Or you can start getting into scoring and aim for the global high scores. Or you can check out the other modes that come with this game.
The new modes give a great shakeup with Arrange being a full-powered big numbers scoring affair (with autobombs) and 1.5 injecting more excitement into the base game with a stronger shot, more pronounced slowdowns, and an emphasis on point-blanking along with some tweaking to the stages. Personally, 1.5 is a must-have and it really makes this port so grab that too.
While Mushihimesama isn't my favorite Cave game, I could see why this would be their first released title. This game (Xbox 360 version) never got a region-free release. It also has an emphasis on styilized slowdowns as if you're dodging in bullet time, which is a nice introduction for newcomers to the bullet hell genre. Another newbie-friendly mechanic is the consistent use of bullet-canceling. Throughout the stages, there are huge enemies that spit out massive bullet patterns and if they are defeated, then all the bullets on the screen disappear into gems, giving you a breather and encouraging you to gather as many bullets as possible. There is also a focus on the basic manuvering skill of going from one side of the screen to another as opposed to the more complex approaches of other Cave games.
The scoring mechanics are also fairly simple too. Original focuses on doing chip damage, destruction of boss parts, and surviving. Maniac/Ultra are about boosting up the multiplier by controlling your shot rate against certain enemies from certain positions on the screen to milk them for points before destroying them, and then chaining from one enemy to another to maintain the multiplier and prevent it from decreasing. Arrange/1.5 modes introduce point-blanking for gems. On top of all this are other minor mechanics such as the aforementioned bullet-canceling or "no-missing" (never dying within a stage for bonus points). Personally, the base game scoring mechanics aren't my cup of tea because the multiplier mechanic is very particular, but I do like point-blanking.
Cave is making a huge entry on Steam with this game, and if you buy this game, then you're telling them that there is a future for their shmups, because they are planning to make new ones on Steam beyond ports of their prior titles.
I'm going to end this review with a tip. Did you know? Reco doesn't wear panties.
