I say I'd recommend this game, but truthfully.... I'd recommend it only if it was going through some sort of sale. I waited and bought this game on its release because I was very excited about the concept and style. While it was beautiful and had an interesting story on the surface, it felt... kind of empty...
I'm looking at the game's Key Features written in the description and I read "Talk to the deceased's loved ones, discover their stories, and learn how each of them mourns in different ways" and... maybe I didn't do this right but, I didn't really discover anyone's story? Everything is always on the surface.
We know very little about anyone, in my opinion. I can't connect to any characters, not even the protagonist, because I've only gotten some kind of brief information about them.
I can agree it was informative and taught me things about the funeral industry and processus, and I consider those parts interesting and quite an original topic to make a game about. I appreciate that.
But like other reviews I've read, I felt like I was playing a tutorial the whole time. I honestly thought that the 'real game' would happen once Charlotte gets her own business, so when I realized it was actually the ENDING that was... disappointing to say the least.
You can't interact with anyone, can't make your own decisions (except for that one suicide case - I assume it was to prevent triggering people who are sensitive to this kind of things, so that was nice to add if that's the case?), can't get invested in the story much.
Actually, I felt like it's more like one of these educational game you play online to teach stuff to kids, with the educating part, the game's constant assistance, the limited story and characters, etc. I personally wouldn't pay almost 20$ for this kind of things, but I'm aware that may just be in my case.
TLDR:
Cute, beautiful game with a good concept and great potential, but it's so short and limited that one can't help but feel somewhat robbed and disappointed.
I would like to see this as a longer, more solid game with more options, or at least more story.
Great job, still!

I don't get this at all.
Edit: Okay, that was pretty useless. I deserved those downvotes. Let me elaborate.
This isn't a game.
Your actions in MT are very limited. You are basically railroaded through each scenario, with no chance of failing. Given enough time, you could complete MT with the monitor turned off by clicking randomly until you achieved whatever you were expected to do. "Game" implies that there is some kind of challenge , but there is none.
This isn't a simulation.
Or at least it's so basic that it barely can be described as one. As seen in the trailer, the "simulation" aspect involves preparing the dead for whatever ceremony you are assigned to prepare them for, but other than teaching you a few trivia you may not have known about the process, you learn very little. You don't manage any business aspect, or make any kind of choices except for one optional scenario. There's a few "top 10 tips for not being a jerk at a funeral" emails here and there, so I guess you could marginally call it educational.
This isn't a Visual Novel.
Arguably, you could call it one. There's  couple of storylines inferred from the emails you have access to, but none of it is required reading to progress in the game. You don't interact with anyone though. In fact, I only recall seeing one single character acknowledging your presence at all.
I don't understand the purpose of MT other than to entertain some morbid fascination with death. It certainly doesn't involve me to the point that I become invested in what's going on, or feel more comfortable or at ease about the subject it deals with.
The price is way above what value I feel that I got out of this experience, even at a discount.

So I spent 75 minutes in-game, and I have completed it - including reading all the e-mails and playing minesweeper.  I could go back and try out the one alternate case, but probably won't.  There are two hyper-linear mini-"games" that make up the prep work, and the tutorial remains on no matter how many times you've prepped, and you can only click in a way that's constructive to the step you're on.  There are no choices except one, but aside from the sensitive topic, which is already talked about more in introducing that option than it is in the case itself, there seems to be no meaningful distinction between it and its alternative.  This is essentially an hour to an hour-and-a-half visual novel, so if that's what you're looking for, go for it.  There is some good information about the funeral service industry, but it's inserted pretty hamhandedly.

Wow.
As someone who works at a funeral home, I was really interested to see what Laundry Bear had up their sleeves. The answer: barely anything.
To play through the game, it took me all of 40 minutes from start to finish. FORTY MINUTES. And in those 40 minutes, I did literally EVERYTHING you could do. I read all the emails. I talked to every family member. I prepped every body whether it be for a traditional service or a cremation. All of this while having my hand held like a rambuctious 2 year walking through a parking lot with his overprotective helicopter parent.
You can't make any mistakes during prep. The game literally has a giant bar at the top telling you what to do EVERY SINGLE TIME. And if you try to go off book? Nothing happens. You literally can't fail.
Oh, and the entire message of the "story"? Corporations are EVIL! Like that hasn't been rehashed in about 1,000 new games every year.
All in all, you play a very tiny part in each of these funeral services. You don't take a hearse and go pick up any of these bodies. You don't help guide these digital families through the arrangement process. You don't work with cemeteries or churches or local florists or anything. You just do a quick embalm/cremation and wander around at the visitation, listening to people vaguely talk about their loved one before moving on to the next one.
I can't recommend this game even a little bit, even if it's free. It has no gameplay value, much less replayability value. And I'm sorry if this review seems a bit longer than the game itself. I had quite a bit of extra time to kill...

A fun turnbased roguelike where you are a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of a king, racing against time to free him from being deposed and become recognised as a legitimate heir. Combat is quite fun with zomes of control, lots of different characters/skills/item variety and lots of replayability. Crowntakers has far too many encounters/mechanisms that are simply poorly explained, visualized or simply far too brutal. You will rapidly find yourself facing enemies that the game says are far too tough for you if you ever make the mistake of clicking the 9H option, so why add it? The rewards for clicking 9H are laughable (+1 str that you can buy for 1 gold). Add in the random start locations taking any semblance of strategy out of the battles and you've got a game that just feels annoying rather than hard. 1 minute you're facing 5 health minions, the next you're suddenly facing 3 armor/13 health minions who can inexplicably counter attack. And the bosses who can teleport or can't take damage from melee, inexplicably, without any reason, without any warning.
Obviously you're supposed to play it again and again, but other games the pressure is gradual, the challenge ever growing. This one it's, easy, easy, easy, STUPIDLY STRONG. Having played 4 games, the difficuly ramp up just isn't there, even on 'easy'. There's no balance, no finesse, no satisfaction. You simply feel like you wasted an hour of your time to get rofl-stomped against an enemy that doesn't obey the same rules and makes any sort of strategy completely pointless.
I've played and loved FTL/Dungeons of the Endless/Rogue Legacy but this simply doesn't work.

Let's see...how does the game go? Die, die, die, die, die, die, die. The end.
No, I'm not very good at this game and that's the rub.
I understand what Crowntakers is trying to do. It's trying to be a cute, short, rogue-like game. I just think it doesn't pull it off very well. I've played many rogue-likes and either this game is obtuse or the difficulty needs to be adjusted because it seems to be the same old thing. I get through the first map OK. I died probably 10+ times on the second until I cleared the Wolf boss. The third map? Not a chance nor do I see how it's even possible. The map is filled with enemies that literally just appear on the battlefield and stab you for a couple of points of damage before you can act. That might not sound like much but when you only have 7 HP to start, a couple of hits like that and the game is over because I almost NEVER find anything to heal with. So where's the fun? I don't even see how it's possible to win and that's where the game breaks for me. A good roguelike holds out hope of winning next time if things just go your way a little bit better. After an hour and a half, I don't see any opportunity to progress.
Ok, I realize that sounds whiny. And I asked for help on the forums. The general responses were (from a very limited group of fans) along the lines of "suck more noob" and no developer response. That certainly didn't help my impressions of the product.
That's too bad too. I find the art style cute and the music ok. I want to play in this world. But I'm not able to figure out the "puzzle" and repeatedly dying doesn't make for a good roguelike, it makes for a boring one. The real trick in crafting a game of this type is balance and I don't see it as being well balanced. Moreover, with very little variability from start to start the game quickly becomes tired and tedious. That's a fairly fatal flaw. In most roguelikes your next game is very different from the last one. In this one it's just another go at a very similar map. This isn't a recipe for fun. Given the large number of roguelikes out there, this one can be safely avoided. I paid about a buck fifty for the game and I didn't even get that much enjoyment out of it. YMMV.

Dungeon Siege 2 is an awesome game. Simple to play, and rich in story and lore, this game is an all around enjoyable waste of time, having improved in all the right ways on it's predecessor and somehow still remain relevant nowadays.
Graphics (vs. todays standards) = 6.5/10
- This is by no means a bad thing. The game can play very smoothly for pretty much any PC. I add the .5 for the beautiful scenery, the cool effects on the more advanced weapons and status effects, and the visuals of the actual combat. This game was well on par when it was released.
Gameplay = 9/10
- Everything is so intuative and simple. You will find yourself repeating many actions, but they will feel new each time (sorting through the loot to see what you equip and what you sell or store, changing abailities according to foes you encouner, etc.) A few pathing mechanics can be annoying at times, and automated action priorities may conflict whith what you want to do at the moment, but it will be refreshed with every click fixing the issue at that moment and causing it to be but a minor setback in a very smooth play. The gameplay is rather linear, but you find yourself branching off the paths to discover hidden secrets, or returning to places visited to find something new or missed.
Story and World = 9/10
- It's no "The Last of Us", but you do feel immersed in this world. The main story is rather simple, bad guy wants to take over the world and in turn make it an awful place, and only you got the guts to stop him (together with a few followers), but the world is very rich in it's own lore. Usually I would skip through chit-chat from the NPCs, but in Dungeon Siege 2 the voice acting and actual story call your attention. Amazing voice acting by the way. So many NPCs feel so unique, and having certain members in your party will cause different conversations between them. The world it's self is diverse and scenery changes throughout revealing an enormous continent with a vast range of environments each with unique flora and enemies.
Replayability = 8/10

I highly recommend anyone into the "RPG/lvl-up charachters and abilities" genre to give this a go. The current price is more than welcoming vs. the time you will spend on it and the enjoyment it provides.

Another con: you can only save in one slot by pressing CTRL+S so no older saves possible but not needed. You just need to save while you are in town or before boss fights. Bugs: enemies sometimes get stuck in the wall so they do not attack but your heroes barely attack them too and it is hard to get their loot if you do not stand close enough. Sometimes enemies, especially last remaining of the horde assault will stop attacking you until you strike them (it may be intended as losing morale over dead allies), but to me it looks like bug. Some enemies and even your melee characters tend to circle over their opponents to strike them from another angle, which has no special effect on damage. Ranged attackers tend to shoot walls and ground if below or behind the terrain and you have to manually move your selected one deeper to enemy lines to move whole party. But still these bugs do not destroy whole game experience, it is not disaster.

This is the pinnacle of achievement for BioWare. I will try not to be bias as BioWare began in my hometown, but if you're a fan of Star Wars or even just rpgs, this is a must play. Even 10 years since its release it still matches up to the recent SWTOR, perhaps even topping it. An excellent story and combat system, this is truly a masterpiece. There is a major spoiler that would even make M. Night Shamalamadingdong proud.

Even today, KOTOR I stands as an excellent example of what an RPG can be, and strongly breaks the assertion that all movie-licensed video games are terrible and cash-grabs. It isn't just a great RPG or a great entry of the Star Wars universe, but is also and quite simply a great video game that can be enjoyed by a wider audience than just RPG and Star Wars fans.
Story is an EXTREMLY important part of this game, and a highlight to that as well. You are a Republic soldier on a ship called the Endar Spire, and your goal is to escape before the Sith destroy it. You crash land on the planet Taris, and your adventure unfolds through exploration, character-development, and revelation. Choice is present in this game as well, adding replay-value as well. I cannot give away much about the story without spoiling the game, and it is best to experience it for yourself. Personally, I had no qualms with it, and the game stays true to the Star Wars universe while adding flavours of its own. The setting of 4000 years prior to the movies also makes it so you can appreciate the story without any past knowledge of Star Wars. I would even dare to say that this game easily triumphs over the stories of the movies.
How about gameplay? It is a turn-based game with many different weapons (from ranged to melee), powers and abilities that can be disposed against the enemy, and thankfully this game has a lot of different foes to defeat. The layers of strategy are quite endless, as you always have two squad-mates present at any time. Do you charge into battle while they cover you with gun-fire? Do you all throw grenades to make quick work of your foes? Difficulty options are also present, which are nice as some weapon configurations can allow you to be a god while others will leave you crying for mercy. Luckily with squad-mates, this is really a non-issue. There are also side activities, called swoop racing and pazzak, which are fun side games that provide replayability.
Also a side note, but combat can be paused to issue commands, and you watch the action unfold. Modifiers can allow you to deal more/less damage, and you can even miss, as the game has a dice-roll mechanic in its turn-based formula.
As for graphics, the game is clearly dated by today's standards. In terms of art style, this game is spot on. It retains Star Wars' signature look and style, and developer BioWare has added their own flair and style to it, making the game stand out in this department, and being memorable to that. This can also be said for the sound, which is indentical to what you would expect from the franchise. Lasers to lightsabers all sound spot-on, and both the soundtrack and voice work are fantastic as well.
In terms of replayability, the great story and presence of choice already make it a game that you can put multiple playthroughs into. There are also many side quests and lore that you can delve into, and maybe you'll see something that you didn't see before on a second or third playthrough. Even the gameplay can offer up different experiences depending on how you play. My run of the game was about 31 hours, and this was ignoring most side-quests, so you will find your money's worth at $10.99, especially if this game goes on sale.
Honestly, this is one of few games I can say I didn't have any personal issues with. Others may differ in opinion, but to me KOTOR was flawless. If you're a Star Wars or RPG fan, this game is a MUST BUY. I'd strongly reccomend it to anyone, however the combat mechanics may turn some off, especially if you loathe RNG. However, in this particular game it comes off as natural and is perfectly fine, unlike the TES III Morrwind combat system, as it is turn-based. If I had to rate this game out of 10, it would definitely be a 10/10, but like every game it does have mechanics that have the potential to be even better.

reasons I like [this]older games:
1)Dev's were hungry.  They made great games because the industry wasnt fat with mediocrity and advertising was limited to a niche market: the gamers playing the game.  This forced studios to care about the title and make absolutely sure they got it right.
2)There were uncharted areas in gaming and boundaries were constantly being pushed back.  Voice acting, dynamic story affected by the gamers choices, challenging rewarding exploration were just a few.   Bioware constantly pushed the limit with these aspects of gaming and more.  Another oldie but rarely talked about goodie in the annals of gaming history is Jade Empire.  It was a playtest of sorts for exceptional storytelling, expanded good vs evil story dynamic, and an exceptional combat mechanic.
3)It's not a sequel.  New stories, or in this case, a familiar setting used to spin a new canon excite me.  Granted, sequels have their place (KOTOR2, Fallout 3, ES IV,V) but, as in hollywood a lot of retreads and remakes have been hitting the market recently.  We need new blood(as much as i am looking forward to FFVII remake, i am apprehensive about it as well).
What this game got right is almost too much to put into review.  The graphical fidelity is still pretty good.  Character models are obviously dated and animations are clumsy but the scenes and backgrounds are very good.  The storytelling is beyond excellent.  This and KOTOR 2 are the gold standard that all other games should try and achieve.  Difficulty is challenging without being impossible.  It is a pleaseure to see the DC stats on items and get a sort of 'in between' perspective of mechanics up front and behind the screen.  Voice acting is exciting and it holds one of my favorite pseudo-villians of all time in it.  No spoiler, you have to play it to discover who/what i am refering to.
If this game released before your time, i challenge you to discover the roots of some truly great games today.  It's like listening to the group that inspired your favourite band, provided its not some s**t pop flavour of the week, which i can assure you THIS IS NOT.

Two absolute bare bones point-and-click adventures. If you aren't into British humor, it is probably going to be painful to read through the game dialog. Although separate games, they really should be treated and played as one single long adventure since Time Gentlemen, Please! is an immediate sequel to the much shorter Ben There, Dan That! Combined, these two games hold overwhelming entertainment value for their wild and crazy adventures, completed by truly bizarre and humorous inventory item uses. In comparison Ben There, Dan That! is simply a prototype for the much more refined Time Gentlemen, Please!, but together they complete a highly enjoyable adventure game. They take me back to simpler times when games like Space Quest and Leisure Suit Larry were king.

realMyst is a very simple yet sometimes complex puzzle game that was made back when home computers were just starting to find their way into households. In other words, don't expect there to be a huge amount amount of gameplay here. If you buckle down, you can beat this game in one sitting. That's not to say that there's no challenge to it as there certainly can be at times.
For the most part, you're playing to find out about the unfolding story. This game used to be a point and click adventure. It seems to have upgraded to being a free roam First-Person which can ultimately betray any new comers to the game leading you to believe there's more to the puzzle than what there really is. You can now roam in unchecked corners and behind bookshelves which you could never do in the first place so if you're stumped on a puzzle, it's best not to start checking every nook and cranny. To be safe, they've added a feature so that you can use the point and click system which at times can be pretty difficult to use since there's multiple things to click on so you have to be pretty precise about what you want to inspect.
The puzzles themselves aren't terribly difficult although a couple of times I will admit I was so stumped I had to use the hint system and in those cases, I feel that you have to have had accidentally stumbled upon the answer rather than using your own intellect as there is no clue to how that could've been solved. Also there seems to be a number of objects you can interact with that add no value to the gameplay or story itself. I have to imagine these were added in simply for the novelty back then but today, they're unnecessary and merely serve to distract.
The story tries its best to layout a path for you to follow, but it doesn't seem to matter in the end which order you decide to do the levels in just so long as you bring back something important from each level. In the end, the story sort of leaves you hanging. It has a resolve, but leaves you with "come back for the sequel if you want the whole story." Not to mention a lot of the writing within the game details a lot more history to the Island, yet none of those elements are anywhere to be found or mentioned ever again and it's hard to imagine everything that's being described happening in such a small place since the levels themselves are fairly small with not a lot of scenery to back up the writings.
This game definitely has it's own charm though and I would recommend it. It's pretty unique and as long as you can get past the first couple puzzles, you'll probably have no problem finishing the game. Except the tram part. That part sucks.

Being a console gamer, I was mostly oblivious to PC games. Most of the computer games I've played were board games, Solitaire, "push-the-block" puzzle games, and Space Cadet Pinball. It wasn't until recent years, where I found out about the world of early PC games, particularly LucasArts point n' click adventures, such as the Monkey Island series, but chose to stick with my N64 and PS2. As I continued gaming, I became more and more accustomed to the newer generations, but as gaming morphed into a soulless machine spewing out nothing but meatheads in power-armor teabagging endless n00bs, boring brown enviroments, gun and ragdoll physics, etc, I started exploring the realms the more cerebral games of yore just to keep my interest in the hobby alive. One of the games in particular that peaked my interest in the adventure genre is, Myst.
Myst is a graphic adventure game from 1993. The game thrived on the PC back then and was remade and ported several times on many systems, including the Playstation, Sega Saturn, the Jaguar CD of all things, and Nintendo DS & 3DS (Both are regarded as the worst ports of the game) I did prior research in the game and checked out a bunch of reviews. Almost all of them kept yapping about how they loved this game as a kid, all this nostalgia-gushing, how the reviewers kept kissing the game's♥♥♥♥♥ I kept thinking, "Is there ANY reviewer sees this game for what it is, other than from childhood significance?" I decided to give the game a shot on my PS3, via PSOne Classics. I played it and I hated it...at first
In the game, you take the role of the stranger. Some random stumble-♥♥♥♥ who happens upon a book that transports him/her to the island of Myst. The Stranger is left with no choice, but to explore the island. The island holds a library, a rocket, an observatory, a cabin, and a power room. All of which contain puzzles for the Stranger to solve. These puzzles reveal four different books that transport the Stranger to different worlds, called "Ages". Upon entering the library, the Stranger finds two standalone books, the red and blue book. Both contain a message shrouded in static as both books have missing pages. The pages have been scattered through the different Ages located on Myst Island. The Stranger is now tasked to piece together why he/she is there by putting together the books and deciphering the messages.
The main detractor of the game is the whole graphic adventure aspect. As soon as you start the game, it places you on a picture of the island, and a cursor. You start clicking around and realize your means of locomotion are through pointing and clicking, suffering screen-by-screen. I've been spoiled by 3D-games like Mario 64, Banjo-Kazooie, even first-person games like Perfect Dark. The screen-by-screen felt really strange and slow. It took time to get used to it and I eventually stopped noticing. As soon as I got used to it, I was in for a cerebral, and sometimes obtuse ride.
The game averts several gaming mechanics. There is no combat system, no enemies to fight, no risk of dying, no time limit, and no hands to hold. Myst Island is your oyster! Also, be prepared to take notes. Seriously, you're going to have to write a whole bunch of stuff down. Many of the puzzles involve memorizing numbers, symbols, safe combinations, some of them are visual puzzles, some are auditory (One involves deciphering sounds to distinguish between north, south, east, and west) This isn't a game that you play, but one that you experience. It's solely about piecing together the story of how you got there and how you're supposed to leave.
Myst is quite a unique experience. I'd liken it to those "escape the Room" puzzles, but on a much bigger scale. The puzzles are challenging, if not a bit obtuse, the settings look nice, given the old graphics (I'd recommend the Masterpiece Edition, an HD remastering) and story seems interesting, (Though, I'll have to play the other 4 to get the whole story). If you're tired of teabagging n00bs and wish to experience a game that involves your grey matter, rather than an itchy trigger finger, then step up and see what you've been missing.
I missed out on Myst back in the day so was very excited to find this version. I liked it a lot and didn't run into technical glitches. Definitely recommend if you like puzzle games.

What I appreciated is that they put hints/clues that did not give you direct answers unless you really wanted them. They gave you clues or thoughts to help trigger solutions to problems you might be facing.
You start off this game by entering this Age called Myst and you just have to explore since you don't know how or why you got there. If you liked Amnesia, which starts the same way and also requires you to explore to find clues and requires reading, this is a great game. However, it is NOT as dark as Amnesia. It is more Sci-Fy then Horror and there are no monsters jumping out at you. But this game can be very eerie, simply because you are alone. There's no other physical beings around you, just their stories that have been left behind. It also requires you to figure out who and what to trust based on your judgment. There's 4 possible endings to the game.
If you like strategy or findings clues and putting one and two together, get this game. Some of the visuals changed from the original PC, but it was still satisfying for me. There's so much thought and logic put into the puzzles in this game, which can make it VERY challenging.
Will forever recommend.

The primitive polygon graphics work well enough to present this 3rd person adventure game.    Graphics look simplistic but the game runs smoothly in 4K.
Unfortunately two key problems make the game difficult to recommend.
Firstly, the adventure guidance isn't very clear - this used to be fine back in the old days of adventure games where you couldn't just pull up a web page telling you where to go.   But now, being deliberately "abstract" and just hiding information from the player in an attempt to make the game more difficult is just annoying.
Secondly, while you can zoom in and out, you can't change the camera angle.  Considering your first task is to climb a tall building, preventing the user from actually looking around for a tall building is just asinine.    What could have made quite a fun adventure game is sadly marred by technical and gameplay faults that could have been picked up within less than 10 minutes of gameplay testing.

Catmouth Island might be ok in its basic concept for all I know, but the camera angle used in the game was a major turn off.
You have to look for items, but the camera is set at a really weird angle behind the character that makes it impossible to see more than a few body lengths ahead.
At the very start of the game you are instructed to look for a massively high tower, but the camera angle has you looking down at the ground all the time, whereas it would have been the most logical thing in the world to be able to look up, so that you could see this high tower in the distance.
The poorly-made camera angle was really hard on my eyes (I suspect that they were impossibly trying to look ahead, instead of down at the ground at a 45 degree angle), so I gave the game the flick after a few minutes of playing it.
It was a shame, because the artwork looked quite good.
However, in the short time I played it, I found the dialogue boxes to be a bit annoying (the dialogue boxes pop up when you click on some objects).
Also, it was rather poor that the developers didn't allow the option of changing the controls for the game.
The game could have been ok to play, if it was made differently.
But, as it stands, I cannot recommend it.
This is a good game and could be finished fast, but some puzzle could take some time, mainly at beginning.

I recommend this game even though I can't bare to play it, the camera is simply super annoying! I hope the developers try to fix it someday, since there is a very interesting game behind that stupid camera. They should also change Mya's apparel.

As a person who has played his share of action games, and utterly enjoyed it at that, here goes: don't buy this game.
If you love the classic action games, if you're reminiscing of the days when
franchise wasn't about flashy fatalities and
wasn't associated with something relic and old-school, just download Quake 1, play it, and move along with your life.
This game tries to be Quake way too hard, and I can't say that it succeeds at it. Weapons are way too similar, monsters are way too ugly (not because it's an artistic impression, but because artist was too lazy to model it better), levels are way too brown and look-alike.
Overall, there's nothing unique in the whole game to recommend. Controls are laggy, graphics and physics are outdated, sounds and music are annoying, level design is clumsy. Like I said, if you like old-school FPS games, just play Quake 1 one more time.

Do you like Quake?  Do you love old school first person shooters from the mid to late 1990's?  Do you love fast-paced action?   Then I reccomend going back and replaying Quake, or Quake II or Unreal, because Monument will leave you unsatisfied on all levels.   To be fair, this game might actually be decent if you could convince it to run at the proper speed,  but even on a high-end machine, it runs as if you were attempting to play Quake... on a 286.    I played through a level and a half, stopping mid-way through the second level as I could not get beyond a wall due to the game's loose grasp of physics.
In the "about" section for the Store Page, they describe each level as being unique..  which is true in that each level is not set up in the same manner.. but from what I've played, there isn't a heck of a lot of diference visually.   Lots of browns to give it that Quake vibe.  I've mentioned Quake a lot here, and with good reason as that is the closest as I can figure to what Monument is attempting to be.   Right down to the use of the "jump" sound the big Q's protagonist makes.
Other gripes are minor, but still worth noting.  The developers intended to give Monument a retro look and feel, but the desings for the game's weapons and pickups are more unimaginative than retro.  The Shorgun Shells look like an 8-pack of Fruit-by-the-foot rolls.  The starting pistol looks out of place and is, frankly, dull.   Nothing has the originality and creativity of the weapons from the games this one tries to emulate.
Hitboxes and collision detection are also ridiculous.   Often it takes several tries to grab a pick-up.  and enemies may shrug off the first few rounds you put into them, or die mysteriously on the first hit.
The game is -not- without it's merits, however.
There are sections where you must push a block up against a wall to jump over.  Points for that,  I actually happen to enjoy platforming in my FPS games and this coupled with some interesting environmental platforming sections are kind of neat.    But.. your jump hight may not be enough to get you where you need togo, and in some spots, you can actually jump up a wall without needing the block.  This is OK, however, because the block does not obey the same rules as other objects in the game.   I pushed a block off of a ledge in the second level and actually had a good laugh as it floated down towards where I pushed it, as iff under the effects of the moon's gravity.   This changed to frustration, however as getting the block to stay where I wanted it was a Sisyphean task.  I eventually got onto the block, but was unable to achieve the height I needed to get to the next area.
Boo.
In conclusion,  Monument has a few good ideas, all of which are executed poorly.  The game moves at a snales pace and the only thing speedy about it is it's soundtrack, which is admittedly pretty decent.  But not decent enough to save this game from getting a negative score.
If you want to check it out for yourself, I reccomend waiting until it is on sale.

After reading the reviews, I tried to go into CI not expecting much but I couldn't help but hope.
The graphics while being low poly actually made a refreshing change. Not since Jak & Daxter have I been impressed at the depth of field in a game. Also interesting graphically are the puffs of smoke from the cursor and the way walls of entered buildings drop comically from the sky upon leaving.
There is a *lot* of walking in this game. While it does make the world seem actually big and possibly more realistic, it gets tedious very quickly. You are given a teleport option between sites but that takes little away from it. Coupled with the unusual camera angles that can only be rotated left and right and not up and down, it makes a short snacky game into a multiple visit affair. You can at least click on things far away and the pathfinding will take over for you, making treks down mountain paths a chance for a player break.
As a side note, I like how when you run for a long time, Mya gets out of breath.
The humour while not awful is mostly forgetable. It's like a family or PG movie in that there's quite a few adult humour bits that should fly over younglings heads. Plus, toilet humour (literally too)!
[The store page said "There's occasional swearing and coarse language...Therefore it is not suitable for younger players" but I honestly can't remember anything that bad.]
The puzzle solving is a little odd. Most puzzles are solved for you if you have the correct item. So it's mostly just a bit of back-and-forth running about. Which does hurt you once you've forgotten where things are. There was one story puzzle that (AFAIK) involved trail-and-error.
There also seems to be a lot of things missing or at least alluded to. My guess is it's either teasers for the next episode but it could just be bad design.
My complaints:
The 2 mousebutton thing to see interactive objects is really annoying. Can't we have a keyboard shortcut?
There are no audio/volume controls.
Only one save slot available
You had to use the toilet twice to get the book?!?
The game is relatively short and there's a promise of sequels but I doubt any will exist anytime soon.
The ending took WAAAY too long that I missed the top of the house. I had to play a game on my phone to suffer thru it. I thought at the time it would have been perfect to play the credits over, so when the credits played straight afterwards, I was utterly disappointed.
To reiterate, if it gets down to 24c and you have the patience, pick this game up. For anyone else, I can't say you'd be missing much.

To keep it short; it's Quake except not good.
If you want a longer explanation, allow me to explain:
Monument is an FPS that is trying really hard to be Quake. It's got a hard-rock/metal soundtrack, a grimy and hellish colour palette, and a crap-load of GUNS AND BLOOD. However this game sure as hell ain't Quake.
The game-speed of Monument is incredibly slow; like, REALLY SLOW. Everything moves like molasses running on molasses. I wouldn't call this slow for the sake of strategy, stealth, or tension either; because if that was the case the enemies wouldn't be so easy to deal with.
The difficulty of Monument is non-existant. I never died from an enemy once. From falling into an instant-death pit, sure; but never from the enemies. The enemies are all nearly brain-dead. They'll get lost trying to turn a corner and get stuck on a wall's edge for ten minutes before catching up to you because they move. so. slowly.
Even if an enemy does land an attack, it rarely does that much damage; and when you do get damaged you can heal up that sliver of missing health with the plethora of health pick-ups the game tosses around.
I haven't even mentioned the weapons; oh boy the weapons. None of them feel fun or satisfying to use; and they aren't well-balanced either. There are two guns you get later-ish in the game; the rifle and the plasma gun. Those two weapons hold so much ammo and do so much damage, that they turn Monument into a game of hunting mosquitoes with tactical-nukes. So if the game wasn't easy enough; there you go.
Despite all of these problems the game at least feels like some heart was put into it. It isn't a shameless asset-flip or a meme-clutching, youtube-bait game. I could definitely notice the flickering of some fun, imaginative ideas that were sadly muddled by a lackluster execution. I hope that the developer isn't discouraged by the negative reviews, but instead uses the critique to motivate themselves to make something fun and revisitable. There is potential, but in its current state Monument isn't living up to it.
PROS:
- Levels are creative and interesting at parts.
- Soundtrack was okay?
CONS:
- Terrible and buggy collision physics (prepare to get stuck in walls).
- Slow and plodding gameplay.
- Unsatisfying weapon feedback.
- Muddy and lumpy visuals.
- Little to no difficulty.
SCORE: 4/10

What they say:
Slow-paced
Laggy
Terrible controls.
What I say:
While the game is mostly fast paced by movement, it does get a bit slow-paced due to the monsters coming at you and animating slowly. I honestly never experienced any lag and I have it on high settings. Terrible controls? The controls were simple enough for me. Maybe because I'm used to Half-Life.
Anyways, Monument is a game that brings you back to the old-school shooter age such as DOOM and Quake.
Graphics:
The graphics do not meet the expectations of today's high end gaming, but looking from going from the old-school shooter to going to these 3d graphics, it gives a good nostalgia feel.
Gameplay:
The movement is fast-paced. However, when it comes to monsters, things become a bit slow. Unlike DOOM, you can't just crash in and nuke the monster with bullets. It requires thinking and moving around the monster in this game.
The puzzles presented here reminds me of the usual puzzles I see in the DOOM games. Also, what is great is it comes with a save feature, so before you screw up your moment, at least you don't have to worry to run through the whole level again.
Level design is a combination of "straight-forward" and "hidden path" type.
Music:
If I was listening track by track, I would enjoy the music. Depending on how long you spend on the levels, it can get annoying. It's mostly a metal/hard rock type of music here. Really suits the atmosphere.
Conclusion:
Monument may not catch up to today's look-a-likes of DOOM and Quake. However, it reaches just enough to give an enjoyable and nostalgic experience for old-school shooter players.

Save feature.

Atmosphere that brings back DOOM and Quake memories.

Graphics and animations of monsters could be improved.

This game.... Ooof, what should I say? I've played this game a loooot and there's so many things I'm still finding about it. I mean, yeah,  it's a free game and there's no set story line or anything to complete but something about this game keeps me still playing it.
I find the combat to be relatively simple but at the same time, it can be much more complex when you take it a step further. It's a standard 2D platformer shooting game involving many different weapons that could be utilized to kill your foes. However, that isn't all. Some weapons are used to get around easier, where if you know proper tricks and practice enough, you can essentially fly across from one side of the map to the other, sneaking past enemies.
And that's not all! In addition to the classic Deathmatch and Team Deathmatch, there are other game modes you can select including Capture the Flag, Survival, Zombrains and (if anyone decides to host it) Climb. And yes, you CAN host your own servers! Granted, you'll have to portforward in able to do so but don't let that deter you! Spasman, our ever..... trusty and hardworking developer (Hehehe, jokes. Spasman really is great.) typed up an entire little comprehensive guide on how to portforward, easy enough to follow that even
would be able to understand. Heh, now if only I actually could access the proper locations..... Ah, I digress.
As mentioned before, the combat is relatively simple but can get complex due to some of the wide variety of weapons available. Damage and mechanics are different among all of them and how you best use them is up to you. Now, you may hear about some people salting about certain guns and that's totally fine! It's kinda normal that there are some certain guns that are stronger when in the hands of certain people.
Speaking of salting, the community in Bman is also pretty nice. You'll find a wiiiide variety of people here, some of which you may regret meeting but also many others who are great to just play with and chat casually while shooting each other to death! And don't be afraid about being a newbie, everyone has to start somewhere. I mean, I wasn't too much until I was taken under the wing of several pros in Team Deathmatch where I really began to flourish (or fail to) and show my true colours (they aren't pretty. They're dazzling.)
Would I recommend this game? Definitely to give it a spin.
Would I say it's the best game? Probably not, if I were to be honest. There ARE some irks here and there but I still find this to be a great game I keep coming back to.
Is it easy? There's always room for improvement.

Cave has finally come to Steam! An excellent game to start with, Mushihimesama is one of Cave's finest.

================
Quick Review
================
Control [5/5]
With some of the sharpest control around, even with an analog stick, Mushihimesma's control is simply amazing.  Any controller at all will have you playing like a pro in no time.
Challenge [5/5]
Some of the most difficult Bullet Hell gameplay is yours to challenge in Mushihimesama...If you want to. Novice modes allow for newbies to get in on the fun too.
Length [5/5]
There are so many modes available to play even without the DLC Version 1.5 that bullet hell fans are sure to get solid weeks of gameplay out of Mushihimesama. Players will definitely spend a decent amount of time finding the best mode for them. Our picks go to Novice and Arrange.
Visuals[4.75/5]
Mushihimesama has some really cool looking visuals, but they are definitely not as polished at Muhihimesama Futari would later be.  Regardless amazing anmiation and awesome design oozes - sometimes almost literally - from this game.
Sound [4/5]
One of the better OSTs to come from Cave, Mushihimesama narrowly beats Futari in terms of composition...so it's kind of a shame that the bitrate for many of the tunes here, especially in Version 1.5 make for a very washed out sounding audio presentation. Ouch.
Ingenuity [4.25/5]
There's no denying that Mushihimesama paved the way for great things in the future. While not as polished as its obviously superior successor, Mushihimesama has features that still make it worth playing regardless.

Zombie Army Trilogy (ZAT) is a 3rd person over-the-shoulder Zombie Shooter game using the Sniper Elite engine. With features like the bullet-cam that was introduced in the main Sniper Elite series as well as up to 4 player co-op the game will have you troucing through Nazi Germany shooting zombies to save the world.
+ Really fun and satisfying gameplay.
+ Lots of different types of primary and secondary weapon choices.
+ The dark and brooding aesthetic is visually pleasing.
+ The game sounds great.
+ Up to 4 person co-op (game can be tailored for solo players too).
+ Bullet physics such as wind and gravity affects the trajectory of your shot on the higher difficulties.
- While the aesthetic is nice to look at, it doesn't vary at all throughout the 3 chapters.
- The music and soundtrack leaves little to be desired. Play your own music.
- While the bullet-cams are really cool, it does get a bit annoying.
- Most of the secondaries feel useless except one or two.
- The score system ruins the immersion of the game.
I had never touched a Sniper Elite game before playing this; having played this for 24 hours at the time of writing I will probably pick one up when it goes on sale. I had a really fun time blasting through Nazi Germany solo and convinced some friends and family to pick it up after they tried it on my PC. It runs really well on my PC with almost 0 frame drops throughout the whole experience, even with 4 person co-op on maximum zombie spawns on max difficulty.
That being said the game does has its flaws. It gets really repetitive in its zombies. Start off a level, kill a few zombies straggling about, survive a zombie siege, move on, rinse, repeat. If you care about narrative stories then you'll be disappointed as the game doesn't really offer any. The story is told through your exploration of the environment and the very limited cutscenes before and after a level. Zombies also do not do well with stairs or elevated platforms since they tend to get bobble up and down rather than go up them smoothly making headshots a pain. Because of this a lot of levels are really flat with almost no elevation to deal with this issue.
To sum up, Zombie Army Trilogy was a lot of fun for me to play. I have cleared this game solo on Marksman difficulty with spawns set for 4 players and had a blast trying to deal with that challenge. I'm looking forward for my friends and I to clear the game on Sniper Elite difficulty when they get their hands on the title. It does have it flaws that a lot of zombie games do have, such as repetitiveness and map tropes but it doesn't deter away the fun that the player enjoys. If you like shooting zombies, you'll like this game.
7.5/10

Paranautical Activity was obviously intended to be some mixture of a 3D Binding of Isaac clone with Painkiller, and for the most part it succeeds in that. Player movement is fast and fluid, there's an interesting variety of weapons, and it offers a nice challenge and degree of skill-based gameplay. It lacks enough enemy and room randomization to have huge staying power as a roguelike, but what content there is definitely justifies the sale or bundle price if you're into the roguelike FPS subgenre. It's not as good as Ziggurat but better than heavy bullets. Voxel graphics look decent, soundtrack is pretty crappy but easy to ignore or mute, I haven't encountered any major bugs, overall I'm pretty pleased with it. Paranautical Activity may not be a great indie game, but it's a solid one, and for the reasonable price of admission I think that's enough.

Crowntakers is a a casual, colorful tactical turn based game.  I thought I would give it a try...and was really surprised by how many great game design choices the developers made!

Examples of great game design:
+ Every map is randomized - not only the map layout, but also your units' positions!
+ The fight is not going well and you're in a bind.  Do you use potions now or save them for a later fight?
+ Mercenaries have different abilities, and choosing which mercs to use (and their variant skills) and building combos make it fun and replayable
+ Normal is quite difficult, so the ability to carry over experience after defeat in Easy mode is a great option.  (I was able to beat the game in my 2nd easy playthrough, but it was close!)
+ Runes for your fighters have good variety - enough to make choosing which merc gets which runes important for battles.
+ A new merc can be unlocked with each playthrough, which incentivizes playing it again and again, even if you've won already (winning one time through might only take 3-4 hours)
+ Your hero and each merc have unlockable skills. To unlock them you have to do perform various feats with each hero, which incentivizes you to change your tactics each playthrough.
+ On the main map, at each cave/house/roundtower/etc, you can only choose to perform one action out of 2-5 options. Once you've done the action, you have to live with your choice!  On the next playthrough, you can choose differently...
+ There is a trade-off between spending time searching all the houses, caves, etc, and progressing through the map.  Every night it says "another night has past, your enemies have gotten stronger".  It's another design element to force the user to choose a strategy.
+ The user interface, menus and buttons have a good layout and are pretty intuitive.
+ The encounter stories are entertaining.  They are short vignettes, entirely appropriate for the casual theme.
Overall, very impressed with the design elements, as well as the bright colorful art.  I already want to play this developer's next game, too!

I've been following this game since it’s early stages. I was in touch with the game’s creator, Gabby DaRienzo, to help clarify different aspects of working in a mortuary that she had questions about. It was fun to see it come together and Gabby has a great interest in the death positive movement, making the game a really progressive example of the day-to-day experiences of a funeral director.
I review games as often as I play them (not at all!) so I appreciated A Mortician's Tale for being simplistic in its game theory and using careful pacing to walk me through each scene. The muted purples and pinks combined with a dreamy soundtrack create a calming atmosphere that still looks vibrant and feels just a touch lonely as well, all of which is to say it’s similar to the way planning a funeral feels to the uninitiated.
You character is a female mortician (Charlie), fresh out of mortuary school who gets a job with the female-owned firm Rose and Daughters Funeral Home. Charlie's daily email is where you find out what your next funeral task will be, which requires you to prepare a body for an embalming, cremation, or burial while also learning about industry topics like corporate vs. independent funeral homes, indigent burials and green funerals. It aims for education and sparks thought-provoking conversation, as evidenced between my partner and I when I got to scenes like the cremation (“you can be cremated with your clothes on?”)
True to life, the story is largely told through email and the overheard conversations at the funerals. Charlie’s inbox is where we find out information about the company (they get bought out by corporate), her personal life (she’s queer friendly) and the larger industry issues happening (the alternative death movement is gaining speed). Everything feels very timely about the game, which is a refreshing change if you struggle (like me) to find cultural examples of funeral service that does not uphold antiquated stereotypes, ie. old white men in suits.
There is an impressive amount of death industry information packed into this fairly short game which took me about an hour to complete, even with my exceptional embalming tools knowledge. I was charmed by the details in the email exchanges that referred to current industry trends like mushroom burial suits and eco pods and felt surprisingly moved at many of the mourners observations at the funerals. When Rose and Daughters has to sell out to a corporation to stay in business, we learn it via a remorseful email from the owner, a very real experience that is now all too common.

First of all, unless you've literally never played any version of this game before, the puzzles are not going to surprise you because THEY ARE STILL EXACTLY THE SAME. You can literally dig out your old notes from twenty years ago and use them to get through to the endgame.  This is probably my only real complaint with the re-releases of Myst, at least as far as the gameplay is concerned; would it have been so hard to add a random element to the puzzles?  Or maybe change a couple of them a little?  (Well, okay, there's a new Rime age and all, but even that one has been recycled from the original RealMyst.)
So I guess nostalgia rules in the realm of Myst... but the main appeal of this game has always been its appearance, and I'm happy to say that has improved.  This version updates the original RealMyst to bring it in line with what modern hardware can produce, and the full 3D movement makes navigating the islands much easier (Channelwood treetops, I'm loking at you).
The Steam version brings Myst up to date with Achievements, because that's what the kids are into these days (okay, I had fun trying to get them all too).
If you're into the quiet, cerebral and immersive type of game, why not go for the one that made itself a landmark and give this game a try?  If you're an old fan of the game, there won't be too much in the way of new content to bring you back, but you'll have already made up your mind on this game by now anyway!

The game does not work on Windows 7 64 bit systems. The lighting makes the game impossible to play by throwing completely opaque shadows that cover the puzzles in total darkness. Really glad I bought the game after the refund policy was created.

Third, this game lacks a cover system and in this day and age that is inexcusable.
Fourth, this game claims to be an adventure game, when really it is an adventure LAME. Or something. Don't ask me, I'm not a word person. I'm an ACTION MAN.
Fifth, this game is very cheap, which probably means it's bad.

After nearly 18 years, I have finally managed to complete one of the first Windows-based games I ever played.
When I began the original Myst as a kid, I was clearly stumped by the (then) challenging puzzles, and never made it past the Mechanical age, let alone completed the game.
Being not only to complete the game, but be able to move around in a (now) normal fashion satisfied a need I wasn't aware I carried for two decades.
For those that still wish to complete what they never finished as a child, this is the game for you. Otherwise, this is a hit-or-miss depending on how much you enjoyed things like Ether One or similar slow-pace puzzle games.

I know this game has been around for a long time, but I only just heard about it.
It's very hard to convey the feel of the game by watching videos - you just have to experience it for yourself. It's pure platforming joy - and pain as you're stuck... and then euphoria when you finally get through a crazy level....
The brutally hard levels remind me of old school games like Miner 2049er on ColecoVision, where I recall being brought near the point of tears trying to beat the later levels.
But it really is the feel of controlling the ninja character - very unique. And the vast amount of levels are all expertly designed.
I love how you can just get through a level without getting all the gold - and sometimes that's hard enough - but that leaves open the future challenge of having a perfect run through the level. You can choose how far you want to go each time.
Absolutely one of the most impressive games I have played in a long time. In a way, it's so good that it almost feels like a game you'd play in a dream, and then when you wake up you wish it was real... but in this case it is real!

I spent hours and hours back in the day playing N, the free Flash game that preceded N+ and N++.  For that alone I would have passed some money the developer's way, but N++ is definitely worth it by itself.  It's a tough, unforgiving platformer in the mould of Super Meat Boy (or vice versa, given how old N is).  It has a peculiar momentum-based approach to platformer (screw physics!).  Once you get the hang of it, you'll be performing incredible walljumps and near-flying around levels.  There's a huge amount of levels to play; 9 hours in and I've barely completed half of them.
If I have one complaint, it's the adjustment in approach from N.  In N and N++ you have gold which you can collect to extend your forever-reducing timer.  In N, you had to go out of your way to collect gold to give yourself enough time to complete episodes (sets of 5 levels).  The only question was on which level you were going to divert to make sure you had enough time for later levels.  In N++, you can complete every episode (that I've played so far -- including several in E, the toughest category) without worrying about the timer.  You collect lots of gold easily on your way round, and you never have to worry about the time.  The gold is just if you want to get a high-score.  I can understand that this is a new approach: always completable but you can go back for high scores, but it means an episode is just an independent set of 5 levels. I miss the tension that the timer added in N.
Still, recommended if you like games that kill you brutally every 2.3 seconds, but after one button press you're up and running again.  This time, you can avoid that mine. This time, you can jump over the missile.  This time, you got killed by a machine gun. But next time, next time was the mine. Then past the mine, but killed by the missile. Then the mine again. Then the machine gun once more.  Next time though, next time...
A beautifully updated engine for a timeless game with secret horrors and puzzles that are almost difficult but end up being just right.

Fantastic. This game is a 10/10. It's by far the most comfortable game I've played in a while between the customizable color schemes (lots to choose from but my favorite is Evening, especially at night time which would make sense), the relaxing music which is a sort of slow and relaxing type of EDM/techno mix (musically illiterate I apologize) and the overall tone of the game. It's just what a game is supposed to be: fun. It makes me happy to play this game. Competitive shooters are great and they let me be tactical and appreciate tension, but sometimes that can get a bit frustrating, especially with how bad my internet is. Most other games are great too, but usually there is something about it that just annoys you. This game has none of that. It's just pure, wholehearted fun and it's very relaxing. You can be quiet and relaxed or you can be loud and hectic. It's what you want it to be, even the colors and the music to some degree.
Pros:
+Very fluent. Masterfully executed 2D ninja platforming.
+Doesn't take much to run it. Older hardware shouldn't have a problem.
+The most comfortable game I've played in a while. Don't like the colors? Feel free to change them. Change the music too if you don't like it.
+You have 3 controls: Move left, move right and jump. It's very easy to pick up. Yet it is hard to master.
+Rough estimate: 1300-1500 levels. Plus a level editor. Don't worry about not having enough content.
+Music is great and fits the game well in addition to creating a calm tone.
+Cheap. $15 isn't gonna hurt.
+It can get funny sometimes. Especially when you die. The lasers in particular create some funny ragdolls.
+A variable experience. It is what you want it to be: Fast, slow, intense, mindless fun, anything.
Cons:
-Refuses to cooperate with most recording software. I have tried NVIDIA ShadowPlay and OBS on both game recording and desktop recording modes. (I believe this has something to do with OpenGL)
-The mouse is useless for the game anyway so this hardly matters but if you're in the steam overlay, the top left 25% of the screen is where your mouse is limited to. It's weird but hardly an issue because the game doesn't use the mouse anyway. Could make the Steam Overlay annoying though.
-There is one level (out of the 500-700 I've played so far) that I am convinced is impossible due to the time limit it gives you. I'm not sure though. Fortunately you don't have to beat it to play the next one.

They reduced the price on this game so I'm not really sure if I can recommend it or not, but I will go over what I saw.
While others did not like it, I saw some potential in this game. But I also saw a wide variety of graphical errors, poor and clunky controls, and a weak enemy AI. In addition, the game was short and beatable. Yes, I actually did go through it in 2.3 hours.
The graphics were merely okay in parts. In other parts there was flickering, misaligned textures and so forth. Even in Doom I didn't see any graphical errors that bad. The guns themselves were okay graphically, but obtuse and awkward. Some of them didn't make any sense either. Some were totally overpowered and others were completely underpowered.
The level design was very linear and predictable. There were no jump out of your seat moments in this game. One level after another of predictability. That is what made it so easy to complete in such little time. The final boss was a bit of a joke... and was way too easy. Even Doom and Quake were more difficult than this game.
The music... now this was one of the weakest points of this game. The constant 80s guitar metal shredding was annoying! And it was just looping over and over again. There was no reality variety in the music. This is something Doom and Quake excelled at.
If you paid $10 for this game, I pity you. I think I bought it for $2 (but don't recall). It's $3.99. Do I recommend it for that price? No. Wait until it goes on a bigger sale. Perhaps it'll be a $.99 bargain bin game soon enough. So this game will get a thumbs down from me.

There are alot of reasons you can come up with against KOTOR.  Its age,  glitches, bugs, having to install restoration and/or mods to get it to work, etc.  But that shouldnt hold you back if they aren't game breakers to you personally.
Underneath the 10 year + old asthetic is a good, and enjoyable experience.  Not you're typical on rails bioware game.  In fact, I'm someone that couldnt get past the initial corridor-on rails-experience that is Mass Effect.  The battle here is done in "pause and choose your action" style. I went into this game with low expectations, and its been slowly turning my head.  It's a rich Universe, that of Star Wars and the game does well on its own feet establishing a story within that Universe.
Companion characters that all have their own motives and personalities.
Good or Evil?  I can't tell yet which of them might turn on me, help me, hurt me, judge my actions, leave me, or just plain stop caring.
Multiple  "mini games" within KOTOR that are pretty fun in and of themselves from Pod Racing, to Panzaak.
There seems to be different ways of doing many of the missions/quests which is always welcome and can help to produce a narrative that is personal to each player and each playthrough.
Flying through the galaxy can be dangerous, but the Ebon Hawk can handle anything thrown at it(as long as I don't miss my shots while I'm in the seat of the Ebon Hawks Turret blasters).
Spectacular isnt a world I'd use, but Very Good is how I'd describe it.

Monument makes a noble attempt at imitating the style of the classics Quake and Quake 2, and at least in that much it is somewhat successful. While nothing visually in it is anywhere near as good, it definitely captures an unmistakable feel of those games. Unfortunately it fails on almost every other level. Awful levels, boring shooting, bland weapons, abysmal weapon designs, poor testing and polish. The soundtrack is alright, the visuals - while they could definitely use some refinement - are alright, but the gameplay has too many problems to make this a worthwhile experience.
The enemy models look ridiculous and the way that they spawn in your field of view rather than just existing in the levels is annoying and pulls you out of the experience, as well as killing any potential strategy in approaching a fight. The guns aren't fun to use, they don't have punch, the gunplay is unsatisfying, even the aiming feels a little bit wonky. With a lot of fixes and a dedicated level designer, this could be turned into something good, but what has been released isn't there. Not even close. You can grab dozens of Quake mods for free which will give you a more enjoyable experience than this.

Star Wars KOTOR is way better than I expected. As a Star Wars fan, I had heard about this game for years, but hadn't gotten around to it. Then it hit as part of a Humble Bundle and I scooped it up, chose it for the first game in the bundle to play, and burned through 50+ hours without even noticing. The graphics are very old-school polygonal, but have a nice Star Wars feel to the universe they build. The story is a fine Star Wars adventure, and the production is the right level of quality - good, but not over-the-top so to distract. There's a good array of characters and individual arcs, and although I'm not an RPG guy I did enjoy equipping certain characters and building them up, although it would have been nice to have a slightly larger party at times. A karma system determines the storyline, and I plan on playing again as the opposite run, as well as changing up the team as I relied heavily in my first pass on Jedi and their Force powers to the point of overwhelming all else.
The character work deserves its own paragraph, there's a lot of great personalities with their own unique ways of doing things. I started out stealthy before finally succumbing to brute force, and each time that affected the team loadout. Droids, aliens, gunmen, and Jedi all end up in your crew and each one has a nice story arc. I ended up chasing down every single story element I could find regardless of how it helped my experience points, they were simple tales but interesting.
As for play, most of it is straightforward action-RPG and you can set your secondary characters' basic action behavior (dubious though that is at times, so always pause and pre-set their actions as far ahead as you can). There are a few pure action elements, speeder track races and random space battles, both of these are pretty terrible so make sure you save before you get in the ship because you may end up dying and ruining a lot of gameplay otherwise - learn with the keyboard to move in these rather than the mouse, the swoop races are pretty easy once you get down the very simple keyboard movements, the space battles will require more finesse and the only way to move the turret at the speeds you need is with the keyboard.
Overall, this game has great story, good production, a good in-universe feel, and aside from a few small minigames it's fun to play.

Fantastic Game! A triumph of a game! Bioware has delivered an unbelievable game!
5 out of 5 stars:
I rewarded its first star for the story. Wonderfully immersive and expansive on Star Wars Lore and Canon.  I insatiablly sought further and further into the SW universe as one hour turned to two turned to three hours of gameplay in one sitting (I"m not proud of it, but it was worth every moment!). Great narrative structure introducing premises and antagonists in an easy to digest matter.
A second star goes towards the gameplay.  Don't quote me on what version of Dungeons and Dragons rules KOTOR employs, but my familiarity with their character and combat system from playing other Bioware classics such as Neverwinter Nights meant easy sailing for me and a low learner's curve.
A third star goes towards the music, which I consider a fundamental aesthetic to visual and audible medium such as movies and high quality video games. Bioware kept the classic SW theme by John Williams, but what Jeremy Soule's music added to the atmosphere was sublime. Music is a crucial cosmetic to a game like this as it influences the mood and tone and how I react and connect with scenes emotionally. Very critical; nailed by Jeremy Soule. His soundtrack at times is as memorable as Williams's, which is saying something.
A fourth star goes towards the combination of voice acting, graphics (very charming, and well aged!), and scenery. The worlds constructed visually are immersive, and I got lost myself exploring the vast deserts of Tattoine, forests of Kasshyyk, the meadows of Dantoinne. I was convinced by the stories told by the voice actors of each character, and I felt an honesty in the voice performances, that is, no one overperformed.
Which leads to the final star I gave this game:
The fifth star goes to how well each previous aspect was woven together. Everything was sublime. I will not say too much plotwise, but the final stretch of this game was so emotionally draining for me (as my avatar tried to be a strong leader in a really troubled time!) that I was exhausted by the time it was over. This final star goes to this game for successfully draining me and for raising the bar for how I expect a video game to emotionally deliver.
I hungrily wait for the next time I play this game.

The game has a lot of unnecessarily long chats and walks, the camera movement is terribly limited and there are no meaningful directions of what should be done (Yes, you've got the scrapbook, but then what? Spend 5 minute talking to a single NPC?). It has an interesting visual, though.

The first episode of Catmouth Island is a different pointy-clicky with loads of silliness packed in! I find the low poly, cel shaded style graphics quite appealing, and it fits the game perfectly. Good use of music as well.
If there's one aspect pulling this game down, it's the camera, and the controls for it. You are able to zoom in and out, but only between two very different ranges. And while you could rotate the camera around Mya, the main character, there was no way to change the angle. These two things made the adventuring aspect of this game feel a bit cramped. It also would not have hurt being able to rotate the camera without the use of a keyboard, and going to the map should probably not have been the second step of zooming out.
But while the camera controls could have been a bit better, the game itself is well worth playing through. It's walking a fine line between hilariously strange and playfully serious; It doesn't take itself at all seriously, yet it doesn't try to shove jokes down your throat either. Instead you are led through surreal dialogues and strange choices of action as if they were completely normal. In many ways it makes me think of Suda51's "Flower, Sun and Rain" for the DS, but much more adventurous and fun!
If anything, I wish the game was longer. But as long as there will be sequel episodes, I will be playing them. Well worth it!

As a light-hearted adventure it's the kind of game that appeals to me, but ultimately it fails to reach me because of a single technical flaw. The. Camera. If it had a view from the back of the PC (or even a first-person view), it would be much more enjoyable. The author commented that it would impact performance, but maybe leave it to users to determine whether they mind it..? I mean, in ten years time, will it still have a performance impact? What about today's users with good machines? It's sad when a project built with love is also lacking in long-term sight.

If you're a Mushihime veteran just looking to know if this is a good port or not, the answer is yes.  It doesn't have a lot of uber PC master race settings like resolutions above 720p, but the gameplay is intact and then some, and it beats the heck out of paying out the butt for the PS2 or 360 versions.
If you're otherwise wondering if this game is for you... that depends.
If you want old-school, masochistic, NES era Gradius style challenge, you won't find it here... unless you try for the True Final Boss (hereafter referred to as "TFB").  To get to him, you must beat the game on Maniac or Ultra without continuing.  ...Or just play through Arrange mode, which is a special mode with it's own rules, which happen to include giving you access to the TFB.  Everything else in the game however is easily accessible as the game gives you unlimited continues, and as of this review, there's no way to turn them off.  You can not use them, but eh...
But if that's what you're looking for, get something like Gundemonium Recollection or Jigoku Kisetsukan: Sense of the Seasons instead (the latter of which is free).
What you will find here however is still quite an amazingly well designed shooter with gorgeous art, a lovely soundtrack, and tons of replay value, especially if you're competitive (there's online leaderboards in this version), love to focus on personal improvement, want to get all the Steam achievements, and/or actually ARE going for the TFB.
And to be fair, the unlimited continues aspect also gives the game a certain flexibility... you can get good at the game at your own pace, or just play it to veg out at your computer without worrying about death, or get a better idea of how all the levels and modes differ without looking at a guide, etc.
I just want to be transparent and helpful about this feature, as it's a bit of a controversial one in shmups that can make or break a game for many people.  Myself included in some cases.  Yes, this game has unlimited continues on all modes and difficulties, and there's no way to disable it.  Whether that's a good or bad thing, I leave up to you.  Both approaches have different things to offer with their own advantages and disadvantages.
On the merits of the game's overall design however, I do absolutely recommend it.  Just know what you're getting into.  It's a game you'll finish in 45 minutes if you just play through it... or a game that'll take countless hours of your time if you wanna go deeper.
