(I got this game for free from a friend)
: back in 2004 a simple free flash game was released under the name of N (which means "The Way of the Ninja"). Over the years N went on to receive several updates, won 2 audience choice awards and managed to capture people's attention due to its simple game mechanics, addictive quality and unforgiving nature. Surprisingly it managed to capture the attention of a Microsoft employee and from there the second game, N+, was born. N+ came onto the Xbox 360 in 2008 boasting new levels, refined visuals, tweaked sounds, an actual soundtrack, customisation and local as well as online co-op. I loved it, and so did many others I imagine, but even with a later Nintendo DS and PSP release... the developers still didn't have enough money for a proper PC or PS3 port. Thankfully the developers heard our pleas, and after a deal with Sony was accepted, N++ for PS4 (and later PC) was given full approval.
N++ is a solid platformer through and through. The aim of the game is to navigate the agile ninja to a switch and then to the accompanying exit in each level. This sounds simple, and it is, but you’ve also got a rather short lifespan (represented by a timer ticking down to 0 at the top of your screen) which can be extended by optionally picking up gold. As you go through the 25 “Intro” episodes: new enemies are introduced and the levels become harder too. Knowing how long to press the “Z” button (which determines how long/high you jump), when to wall-jump and how much momentum you need is absolutely vital to succeeding in this game. And that’s what I love about this game. The controls are slick, and everything feels responsive, so the only thing you can blame when everything goes wrong is yourself and tear what remaining hair you have left on your head.
Don’t get me wrong – the game’s accessible to everyone. Extra challenge however comes from players attempting to collect all the gold in each level or getting the fastest time. Heck, I spent a good quarter of my playtime just trying to compete with my Steam friends for the best leaderboard position and global rank. What's neat is that you can actually watch your friend's replays to see how they beat a certain level. If replaying levels is not your thing though, N++ has got you covered. Remember when I said that the “Intro” section had 25 episodes? Each episode actually contains 5 levels and there’s 100 more episodes in the “N++” section. If you finish that, there’s another 100 episodes (which are all old maps from previous N games) in the “Legacy” section. So altogether that’s 1125 levels and this is just the “Solo” mode. That’s right! There’s also the “Co-op” (only local co-op in this game) and “Race” modes to look forward to, so you won’t be finishing any time soon.
Outside of all of this there’s a level editor for you to play around with which is amazing. What’s even better is you can play levels made with this on the PS4 version and vice versa. The icing the on the cake is “Funlocks” though, which are little bonuses you can unlock (they’re mostly extra colours which change the look of the menus and the levels themselves). Other things worth mentioning include the soundtrack – it’s not overpowering and fits the game’s aesthetic perfectly – and the excellent port. While some PC gamers may be annoyed about the fact that the game’s locked to 60 FPS, it’s more than playable for me and I assure you that everything is super smooth. I personally would like an option to unlock the framerate but apparently this was done so everyone's replays would be the same.
That's all I can really say about this game, and I'm actually surprised this didn't end up being a longer review, but all I'll say is this: N++ is absolutely worth it. It's a 9.5/10 for me. Pick it up when you can... you will not be disappointed.

N++ (NPLUSPLUS)
Indie Platformer
Metanet Software Inc.
Metanet Software Inc.
is an indie platformer developed and published by Metanet Software Inc. This is a very simple game to review, since seeing some gameplay explains everything.
The minimalist graphics, powered by OpenGL 3.3, are polished and smoothly animated. The performance is quite solid, and there are plenty of options to play around with.
The game is a straight-forward platformer. There are multiple blocks that contain 5 levels where your goal is to get to the exit. It starts off pretty simple, but the more you play, more traps, enemies and challenges are introduced, keeping the experience always fresh.
There are also two overlooked game modes that are worth buying the game for alone: Co-op and Race. In Co-op, you and other three players must cooperate to get at least one of you to the end of the level, and the sacrifice of at least one of them is necessary. In Race, you and other three players try to reach the end of the level as fast as possible while also capturing the yellow dots to increase your final score.
The game is very damn hard, and sometimes quite frustrating. Some traps are very overpowered, and trying to pick up every yellow dot to increase your score is going to require a lot of patience and focus.
The electronic soundtrack is very good, with a couple of memorable tracks that improve the experience.
2360 levels. Level Editor. Co-op. 26 Steam Achievements. There is plenty of content that will keep you coming back for more.
Overall, this is a solid, challenging and content-rich puzzle platformer that, while not fully enjoyable, is still highly recommended for the quality of its platforming and the great co-op mode and level editor.

Contradiction is a special FMV game that has come out during a time when many games aim for graphical perfection, long epic stories, and interesting combat rather than a shorter more concise story with puzzle based game play. The story is great always keeping the player interested as the story unravels before them as the characters keep telling them well placed lies that can be difficult at times to spot. Detective Inspector Jenks is intriguing and has an aptitude for making me laugh; his interactions with Paul Rand are by far the best part of the whole game. The in game help system is fantastic helping give the player enough information to continue with the game without giving too much away. The cinimatography was professional making it feel natural when viewing the character interations and the movement of Jenks from place to place. The music was subtle creating the right atmosphere for the game.
In all the game was thoughly enjoyable and highly recommended.

So I have about 15 hours logged in this game. I've unlocked all of the characters, and all of their seperate loadouts. I did all of this on easy, which is the only game mode available to you until you beat the game once.
This game is actually a lot of fun. I really enjoy a lot of aspects of it.  It does a good job of blending the resource managment that you find necessary in roguelikes with the meaningful strategic choices that are present in any good tactical RPG. The engine works pretty well, I've only had one freeze, and one sound bug. But it autosaves before every fight, so no crash is every too big of a deal.
My biggest problem with this game is that it feels, mechanically and systemically, unbalanced. It seems to work at first glance, but the more you play it the more you find yourself consistently frustrated by stupid things.
A perfect example of this is their equiptment upgrade paths. In the game, you upgrade your character's equptment by using upgrade materials (Iron->Steel->Gold for Weapons;Cloth->Leather->Gold for Armor). The upgrade itself doesn't add any stats to the equiptment, but rather adds a slot to it. That slot can be filled with a rune to grant various bonuses. The important thing to note here is that any upgrade is, by itself, useless. Without a rune, there is no reason to upgrade, These materials can be found in the world, or bought from the blacksmith. Now here's the thing: Each character you recruit into your party needs to start with iron before moving onto steel, but iron stop showing up in shops or the world around zone 3 of 8.  So unless you horde enough iron to upgrade all of your future recruits by the time you leave the third zone, you can never upgrade them. And this directly goes against what a good roguelike player would do. They wouldn't waste money (which is used to do pretty much everything in the game) on materials that they can't use for another 50% of the campaign. Its locking away valuble gold in useless assets.
This is an EASY problem to fix. Just have certain events have an option to drop iron/cloth in later zones. Boom. Done. But this level of imbalance persists throughout the game across a lot of little mechanics.
My other big concern is that the difference between 'easy' and 'norma' is the difference between night and day. The difficult jump is so large in fact, that it qualifies as a design flaw in my opinion. Not necessarily how hard it is, but the fact that you force the player to play easy mode, a lot, before unlocking normal, and then expose them, with no transition, to the insanely more difficult normal mode just seems silly. Not only that, but the differences between the two modes isn't actually explained. They mention that your characters will all start from level 1, and you are foced to fight the bosses at the end of each level, but that's just a small part of what makes it so different.
The differences I've noticed are:
Characters start from level 1
Fewer rewards from battles
Significantly faster enemy growth
Must fight bosses
Majority of objects in the world are now locked, and require a lockpick
Lockpicks no longer sold in stores
Res scrolls no longer sold in stores
Mercenary selected is restricted to 2 ranom mercs selected from the roster of 9 at each tavern (biggest and most significant change after the level honestly)
I am going to keep playing normal, but as of right now (especially considering how luck dependant the combat can feel sometimes) I fail to see how it's beatable.
TL;DR REVIEW:
Good game. Needs a few patches. Don't get excited about Normal mode though, just play and enjoy the mandatory Easy mode when its still beatable and fun.

If you’ve paid even the slightest attention to games in the past few years, you’re now very aware of what a roguelike is. Even games that have little to anything to do with the traditions of the genre have introduced randomness as a mechanic in order to take advantage of the buzz the term now generations. However, as ubiquitous as roguelikes have become in the last few years on PC, there have been few to try it in an FPS, and fewer still that succeed when they try. Paranautical Activity was actually one of the first as it went through Early Access, but controversy stemming from the game’s original developer delayed its full release to just recently, when a new publisher bought the rights to the title. It’s a good thing too, because Paranautical Activity feels like Doom made in a different age, and certainly deserves recognition for setting the standard of what a procedurally generated shooter should be.

Well, I've made it about a fifth of the way through the game or so, and I'm not sure whether or not I really want to put in the necessary effort to finish playing through. Going from what I've played so far (Selenitic Age and part of Channelwood Age) a large proportion of the puzzle solving simply seems to be the grunt work of walking around to get to levers and switches that need turning off/on with the actual working out of the puzzles taking less of the effort. So, having walked around a lot and been unavoidably beeped at by one puzzle over thirty times (urgh!) I don't really know that I want to go on.
The controls aren't anything to write home about either. For moving around you have the choice of either Classic Myst or Free Roam modes. Classic Myst just means moving around on rails and clicking to either move forward or turn, and it just felt clunky and restrictive and didn't always go where I wanted it to. As for Free Roam, well, as on the tin it's a lot more freeing and you can move around a lot more smoothly, but it's also a bit harder to interact with the environment and I'd often find myself trying to flick a switch from just a little too far away and having to readjust my distance and try again.
Never mind that I've already had the game glitch on me once already switching between the two modes!
...
And now I have a great nostalgic urge to find a copy of Zork: Grand Inquisitor (which I would recommend playing instead) so I can wash the taste of this clunky game and it's clunky interface out of my brain, but that might just be the boredom and exasperation talking.
EDIT: Well, I managed to finish it... and I guess I'm mostly ambivalent. It does probably have a nice feel in places, but I found the controls a bit lacking; the puzzles solving to be about 90% drudgery and about 10% thinking (some of them you can even solve almost by accident); some of the sound effects to be a little grating; and the hammed up poor quality FMV acting to be a bit underwhelming and jarring.
As a puzzle game (and I guess as a game in general) I'd probably fail it, and I don't know that it's worth the asking price, but maybe you can just enjoy wandering around the levels? If not there are plenty of free 'room escape' type games online or you could pick up a copy of 'Zork: Grand Inquisitor' or 'The Room' instead and get better value for money.

The learning curve isn't terrible, but it is there. This is a real time tactical game that feels like one of the best turn based games. The real fun is the multiplayer, but i would recommend playing at least an hour or two of the single player first. The A.I. is fairly aggresive, and can be diffucult, but it does seem to know where you are when it shouldn't. The campaign is not worth completeing, but the experience will help you inthe move to the awesome....best I've played in years..... multiplayer. I would start with the 10v10 games, these games are big, so a few players being newbs doesn't kill the team. If you ever played the close combat series back in the day, this is similar, though very different. It "feels" realistic, though units are warped to fit the battlefield size they roam (for instance, there are artillery pieces in the game that could fire rounds for miles upon miles in real life... that in the game can fire most of the length of the battlefield, still an awesome range...if unrealistic technically) But leopard 2A4s fare against a rush of T-72s the way they you would expect (they murder them), and die to T-80Us (The soviet monsters of the field). Luck plays a factor (units have a percentage chance to hit a target for instance, and all of the stats are modified by factors like veterancy, range, terrain, etc etc) I highly recommend this to anyone who enjoys strategy, and especially if you run towards a realistic streak (even though its just a feel). If you do decide to pick up this game (a steal at its full price, I've logged over 900 hours on this game) I highly recommend the guide by Sandygunfox, but only after you are at least a few multiplayer battles deep. The things he talks about are not for the true newb, just use the tutorials and some campaign for that, but his guide is awesome (one warning is that its one true flaw is that some few units stats are adjusted in almost every update in a continus strive for the sake of balance, something welcomed by the community, but it makes sandies suggested units something one should take care with....though they mostly still stand the test of time).

N has been available for a long time (since 2004 I believe) for free on the internet. It's a fantastic game and if it's your type of game you can easily sync hundreds of hours into the title. It is not for everyone though. Most platformers have a sense of progression, a going from point A to B if you will. You are trying to rescue the princess or defeat an evil presence. This game however is much more....Arcadey in its approach. There is just a crapload of levels and aiming for highscores is encouraged. It's not so much about beating the game but doing as well as you possibly can. The backbone that makes N such a joy to play however is its movement system. It's really built around building up momentum and maintaining it in order to make improbable jumps and landings. It takes a little while to get a hang of but once you do it's the best feeling platformer of all time in my humble opinion.
So that's N. If you have your doubts about it its free to play in your browser right now! Just Google N the Ninja and you are good to go.
But if N is free is it worth paying money to play N++? Absolutely!
Think about it this way. Imagine you are  in class and Prom is coming up. There's a nerdy chick in the class who is kinda cute and has a great personality but she wears glasses and her hair is always up in an unattractive bun she has braces, wears a frumpy jumper etc. But she invites you to the Prom and you are like, yeah sure fine. It won't be too bad you guess. And then you show up and your jaw hits the flaw. This girl looks absolutely stunning in her dress, her hair is long and shiny, her braces are gone, she looks like a supermodel now! You just can't believe the transformation! You just can't stop pinching yourself about how lucky you are to be at Prom with her!
That is what the difference  between N and N++ is. N++ is just a more polished experience than N in every way imaginable. The game looks beautiful in its minimization. The music fits the game amazingly well. The levels are more refined and there are more of them.
Which isn't to say that it's a perfect game. Most of the problems stem from the reality that it's a PS4 port. So for example the game won't run faster than 60fps for those of you with high refresh monitors. Or the built in level editor is more built around a controller rather a keyboard and mouse. But just like when you get this girl home from Prom and strip her naked you find a small pimple on her bottom are these small blemishes really going to stop you from enjoying yourself? Are you really going to regret your decision? I really, really don't think so.
So if you enjoy the game N do yourself a favour and take it to the damn Prom already. You really won't regret your decision. Just buy it!

Zombie Army Trilogy is a third person shooter that support both single and co-op gameplay.
The story takes place in alternative timeline of World War II era where German's final plan is to unleash an ancient power, but something goes wrong and overruned by undead army.
---------------------------------------------------------
The gameplay is straightforward; the goal is to proceed from point A to B along with some objectives. Each level serves variety of world setting and captures the sense of hopeless. They are massive, detailed, and have some memorable moment even though the gore stuffs are bit exceed and unnecessary to create the atmosphere in cheap way. Horde mode is optional survival mode, but encourages your strategy and teamwork as well.
The gunplay is by far the strongest point and satisfied. Each sniper rifle has different fire rate, magazine size, velocity (which affect on higher difficulty), and zoom level. The game borrows most mechanics from Sniper Elite and execute very well, because sniping zombie requires more steady aim and prediction. It also offers a great challenge on higher difficulty as you have to make every headshot and less secondary ammo to emphasize the usage of sniper rifle. Keep it mind that your bullet works as projectiles and can accidently hit the wall if you aim near the corner.
You will encounter most of common zombie and skeleton. There are some elites and specials which force you to prioritize and change position, although most of spawn point are pretty much static as you can predict where they come including items and explosives.
---------------------------------------------------------
However, random elements are low and cause no replayability unless you need to collect all achievements on higher difficulty which replaces more Elite spawn points. Collectable are fun to hunt, but it doesn't reward anything besides achievements. There are some rare bugs / glitches where the enemies could be stuck in level and prevent player to proceed or the game won't allow you to collect more explosives.
Overall, Zombie Army Trilogy is very entertaining, challenge, and well-optimized. Single player could be very terrified and intense while co-op is fairly messy and hilarious with your friends.

Crowntakers is a pretty damn good game. It’s quite difficult, even for a rogue-like, and will definitely challenge you. Even playing through on easy can be fairly tough depending on your luck.
The art style is really nice, and definitely suits the game itself, which is always a good thing. The gameplay is certainly interesting - it’s a fair bit of fun and does take some learning. There is no tutorial so you have to learn the game for yourself, which personally, in a game like this, I think was a good thing, particularly since it’s not overly complicated and I did enjoy working things out.
The combat system is well thought out and quite easy to understand, but does have some little intricacies to it, such as the opportunity mechanic. Also, it’s clear what you’re doing before you do it, so you can’t really blame the game if you screw up, particularly when it comes to combat, which is certainly important in any rogue-like. (for example, the game displays whether you are at risk of taking damage from opportunity strikes, while also clearly displaying things like directions units can hit, where you need to be to backstab etc. It also shows if a ranged unit will be able to attack a certain unit from a new position before you move it – something not enough games get right).
The levelling up and equipment systems complement each other nicely and would allow for a variety of possible builds for a character. The rune system is a really cool idea – when you upgrade equipment instead of getting just a flat bonus you get spots for runes which give things like crit or dodge chance, lower cooldowns or armor. It combos nicely with the stats you can pick when you level up, giving you a degree of freedom when it comes to
So, while normal mode will certainly be the favourite of all of the hardcore rogue-like fans, I think the easy difficulty is a welcome addition, since this game is very hard, and letting you keep that little bit of progress really does give you that motivation to keep trying, because you get a little bit closer to winning every time. It also means newer players who may not be particularly experience with rogue-likes aren’t just thrown into the deep end and scared off by the difficulty.

This is a poorly balanced mashup of FTL-like exploration with HOMM-style turn-based combat.  It hides its incredibly unforgiving randomness behind the disclaimer of "Roguelike," yet it provides little sense of progression or accomplishment.
Grinding is the name of the game here.  You'll spend the first several hours fighting the same 3 enemy types - wolves, guardsmen and thieves - over and over as you run through the same scripted scenario over and over.  The environment becomes tiresome and repetitive very quickly.  The points of interests that you'll come across aren't interesting at all.  Most of them provide some a generic text description before presenting a single "Search" option.  They'll either provide loot or do damage to your party.
The mechanics of combat are simple, and there is very little depth to the tactical nature of the combat.  This makes each run-through (and eventual death) flat and uninspiring.  I do not feel as though I have learned anything from that run-through which will aid me in the next.  I am left with the feeling that I merely ground out a little bit more xp to become numerically stronger, to get a little bit further when I play the same series of events and combats over again.
The made-for-mobile interface is reasonably polished and makes this experience less painful than it could have been.
The idea of FTL with turn-based party combat is a good one.  Unfortunately, this is not the game to do it justice.

The full review:
The help files suck and I still dont know what all those symbols with the hand and arrow on the right hand side does (Hold in inventory, give to someone, drop?)Theres not to much in the way of deep tactics, but its entertaining.
Basically, you move around a hex board. You choose the direction you go, and then you walk to the next crossroads. Sometimes theres a place you can interact with (search a cottage, visit a merchant or blacksmith, an inn, cave , a fight ect). Random events happen at these places. Usually searching for small items, but other things such as HP or gold gain/loss, or nothing at all
The blacksmith and inn are used to improve your weapon/armor, buy things, rest and buy food, hire mercenaries. To improve your weapons you need to buy or loot a certain item shown in your inventory screen then take that item to the blacksmith and pay a fee. The item is upgraded. Then you take armor/weapon runes and put them in the slots you get from upgrading. The runes have different effects, and are swappable but only armor runes work with armor and vice versa.
Mercenaries are the people you hire at the inn to help you fight. They can gain XP and some of their their XP is persistant even after you die. So they get better and better as you go. Every mercenary is slightly different. I have found an archer and a fighter. Each character has 2 special skills they can use to help them in battle, and they are all different for each mercenary that Ive found so far.
There is a day/night cycle and after every 24 hours (shown in the lower left corner) the enemies get stronger a bit. So you have to balance searching everything and getting to the end of the map. The maps are random for each playthrough, so you dont know where everythings going to be.
Fighting is done on a turn based hex grid. Its simple. Move, attack, and choose facing. The arrow that is yellow instead of red is the chars back. Backstabbing does extra damage so facing matters. There is permadeath, so when the hero dies, you have to start again. Your mercenaries keep their XP (depending on gameplay mode), though, so its not like everythings completely lost.
Seems like itd be really fun on a phone if I was stuck waiting for something. I dont do the phone-as-gaming-device thing though.

I'm going to write down a bunch of tips, I of course love playing this game and finished it.
-Hk-47 is in my opinion the best companion, which is why most of my games have me starting out as a Scout class(for the repair skill).
-Darkside force powers are better for a jedi relying on force(high wisdom) and lightside powers are better for a jedi who are mostly melee focused(Str and Dex)
-Make sure to pause before battles and see the enemies weapons(activating the right shield based on the enemy's weapons) , you can then take control of each of your party members and give them buff actions(force powers, stims, and/or shields).
-Allies don't use their stronger attacks on their own.
-Don't upgrade blasters(I would ignore heavy and rifles since two-handed or dueling doesn't effect them) or melee weapons(Lightsabers have their own skill), unless you are planning on sticking buy those weapons for the whole run.
-Make sure to get the implants skill(level one min), if you're a scout you get this automaticly
-Your starting class levels, don't effect you're jedi class level. A lot of players stop leveling the starting class to get more jedi level ups, I stop at level 5 most of the time, but the min is 2.

Amazing game.  It's FMV, but it's well done.  The puzzles are almost all conversation based, and involve paying attention to what people are saying. More importantly, the puzzles almost all make sense.  Only maybe one of them, I think, was kind of out there.  For a game like this, only one is a pretty big achievement.
I absolutely loved the acting, as well.  The main character is goofy in the best possible way.  The character himself is serious, but the acting is just . . . perfectly goofy.  I don't know how to describe it.  Watch the intro sequence and you'll see what I mean.
Overall for a game developed on a budget, it's extremely well done.  Probably the best FMV game I've played outside of the Tex Murphy series, and a lot of the reason I'd put them above this one is just because there's more to them.  This is an 8-10 hour experience at most, probably, and it left me wanting a lot more at the end.  If this were the first chapter in a series of games, I'd buy the rest in a second.
Highly recommended.

It's the rare case of a good modern FMV game. Takes between 5-10 hours to complete and see everything (depends if you are stuck or not and if your are compulsive enough to talk to every characters about every clues). Charming and memorable characters with good acting, mostly serious but there is some hamming to it. A good balance I would say. The main character, the detective Jenks, is like a cross between the 10th Doctor and Columbo. You need to find clues and interrogate people to find contradictions (lies) in their statements, because of course it's a murder case and you have until the end of the day to find the culprit(s)! Would rate this a 7.5/10 (consider it a 6.5/10 if you can't stand FMVs and a 8/10 if you are a massive fan of the genre).
Cons:
- the interface is a little bit clunky with some bugs that are not game-breaking (if you can't click on a statement or exit an interview, you need to view again any video, it will debug your cursor). I recommend the mouse interface and not the keyboard one. Don't bother with a controller.
- the save function is not well implemented (no auto-save and when you save it is not always apparent that it worked, but for me it worked 100% of the time). Don't forget to save manually. You only have 2 slots to save though.
- the game windows launch offscreen and you don't have settings about it, but the fullscreen works, so it's more of a nitpick really.
For a very small budget title, these flaws are understandable.
Pros:
- No moon logic. For the most part, it's easy to advance in the game and it's probably impossible to get permanently stuck. The game is generous with the tips.
- the main gameplay element, finding the contradictions, is really satisfying. You will feel like a badass when you will find the less obvious ones. There is a way to "cheat" if you are stuck or, well, you could always check a guide on the Internet but it's really not necessary.
- the intrigue is good enough, you won't get bore.
- gorgeous and real visuals (it's full FMV, no distracting computer rendered backgrounds and effects)
- the acting is definitively top notch for an FMV game, just don't expect any Oscar-worthy performances.
- my computer is old and it runs very smoothly on it. Loading time is minimal and transitions between locations are shorts and realistic (it's a rare occurence in FMV). The map system is also a great way to navigate more quickly between locations.
Neutrals:
- the ending. It feels rushed but at the same time it's a great setting for a sequel. A lot of red herrings and loose ends could be explored, but the lore is interesting enough on its own even for a sequel  with minimal ties with the first game.
- we have a good chance to get a sequel (neutral because expectations will be way higher for the sequel)
- the music: it is good enough but lacks variety and it is a tad too loud compare to the voice acting for my taste.
- there is no cross-examination between multiple characters' statements, only between two statements of the same character. It makes for a simple and focused game, but a lot of waste potential too. Should definitively be a part of a sequel.
- the game don't overstay its welcome but at the same time can feel a bit too short especially because of the ending. IMO, it feels like the production runs out of time/money to make the ending they wanted to initially. It's still great though.

Myst.....ah yes, Myst. the great grand daddy of just about all point and click adventure games. one of the first games for PC that I played back in the day. and let me say, after seeing and playing the new and improved version I am impressed! I almost did not buy this version, after reading about problems that others here seem to have had. but I downloaded version 2.0, and to be honest I found it to be bug free on my PC's. I installed it on 2 desktops running Win XP, and 3 newer laptops all running Win 7. the desktops, although aging, ran the game flawlessly. and I was pleased to see that on the 3 laptops, the game automatically went to widescreen, to match the displays on those sytems. they are all Dell inspiron 1545's, 2 with the onboard intel graphics and 1 with the ATI radeon onboard. the ATI ran the game with the max setting chosen in the setup menu. the 2 intel's ran it just fine set on high in that same menu, with the game set to classic mode and the movement slider at three fourths. to be honest, I used the classic mode on all these systems, because I don't like using the keyboard a lot when playing. you can still admire all the new beauty by holding the right mouse button as you look around. toggling the F key turns the flashlight on and off, a feature I was very happy to see added. as I said, the game ran flawlessly for me, and thats saying something on the standard laptops. granted, my 2 desktops (both pushing 10 years old) are running the Nvidia Geforce 5200 with 1 gigabyte video ram (itself an aging card) and pentium 4 CPU's, but still the game runs and looks beautifully. I suggest to others that you make sure your system meets at least the minimum requirements stated to have the most fun. but as I said the laptops ran the game just fine (with a little tweaking in the setup menu) with the standard Dell intel graphics. all 3 are running the P9700 core 2 duo cpu at 2.8Ghz. but even these laptops are pushing 7 years old at this time, so again I was very impressed with what Cyan has done with this newest release of Myst. the grass waving in the breeze....the water lapping gently at the shore...and birds flitting overhead as the sun set in real time. I have over 150 old PC games I've collected over the years, and have a 14 yr old HP pavilion running win ME that I play them on when nostalgia hits me. but I can honestly say it was a real moment for me when my 15 year old daughter put away her Nintendo Wii controller and came in to play Myst with me when she saw what was going on. and we played it all the way through together. and she was just as impressed as I was. I only hope Cyan gets to work on Riven and the other myst games as well. I would certainly buy them, and I suggest this game for all those old gamers like me who want to show thier own kids that these old gems can still have tremendouse play value in the high tech world of today.

I'm so disappointed in this rework that I could cry. I am super sad about this.
The textures are flat, the lighting is stark. The original sounds are pumped jarringly straight into your ears with no remastering, mixing, or accounting for environmental effects. The pages on the books you read are razor-edged polygons, when these books are supposed to be old and weathered and dog-eared. The models are low-poly and the bump-maps are just the original textures made black and white. The screws on the marker switches are warped and shiny blobs. Textures collide and intersect as they hit seams. The pillars in the library are models with repeating textures on them—with no wear on the corners, no dust, no visible seam! They are sterile and stock-photo perfect. Not a single moment has been spent trying to make the environment textures match the models they're on.
I don't know what to think. This is heartbreaking.
Please, if anyone from the realMyst team reads this, I'm a highly competent artist, as well as an amateur sound designer. Please let me help you.

I can't handle playing first-person games without an inverted mouse option, so I had been hoping that an update would fix the initial release's lack of such an option. I was elated to learn that the 2.0 patch added just such an option, so I eagerly booted up the game, only to discover that the newly-added "invert mouse" option inverts not just the vertical axis but also the horizontal! The traditional WSAD-style controls have also been altered so that left and right are pan controls rather than strafe options. This makes the game pretty much unplayable.
I honestly cannot understand how such monumental design errors can make it out into the public's hands without someone somewhere in the process saying "hang on a minute here, this is now a totally different control scheme from just about every single first-person game on PC that's ever been released, maybe we should stick to the norm?". If you want to introduce a dearly-loved classic such as Myst to a new generation of gamers who've grown up with mouselook and WSAD controls, this isn't the way to do it.

If you've NEVER played this game, but enjoy first-person puzzles, I recommend giving it a try.

Wow. When I was younger I was given this game. New to the RPG genre at the time, I played about 5 minutes and basically hated it. About a month later I decided to pick it back up.

I'm going to write down a bunch of tips, I of course love playing this game and finished it.
-Hk-47 is in my opinion the best companion, which is why most of my games have me starting out as a Scout class(for the repair skill).
-Darkside force powers are better for a jedi relying on force(high wisdom) and lightside powers are better for a jedi who are mostly melee focused(Str and Dex)
-Make sure to pause before battles and see the enemies weapons(activating the right shield based on the enemy's weapons) , you can then take control of each of your party members and give them buff actions(force powers, stims, and/or shields).
-Allies don't use their stronger attacks on their own.
-Don't upgrade blasters(I would ignore heavy and rifles since two-handed or dueling doesn't effect them) or melee weapons(Lightsabers have their own skill), unless you are planning on sticking buy those weapons for the whole run.
-Make sure to get the implants skill(level one min), if you're a scout you get this automaticly
-Your starting class levels, don't effect you're jedi class level. A lot of players stop leveling the starting class to get more jedi level ups, I stop at level 5 most of the time, but the min is 2.
-A downside to this game is you have to chose a side and stick to it, once you get max in the darkside or lightside you get a buff the lessens the cost of darkside or lightside force powers, but increases the cost of the forces powers on the other end. It really encourages your character to be an evil overlord or a saint. If you are going pure lightside there is a questline that you'll end up skipping, although you could find a way to earn the lightside points back.
-The game's combat is a 20d type system so saving throws are your chance to evade, take reduced damage, or resist force powers if your "roll" is high enough.
-Two-handed only effects double-sideds lightsabers, staffs/double-edged blades, dual wielding lightsabers, swords, or blasters.
-Make sure to pick out Two-handed or dueling when picking out skills for your character.
Well I should have written a guide, but I have to recommend this game(even though it probably is popular enough).

I should probably have seen the Early Access reviews before purchasing it, but this is where you get a bit more savvy about positive reviews than negative ones.
And frankly, this game isn't too bad. It's just not... fun and doesn't feel too interesting. Think Doom and Binding Of Isaac, but with a worse Health system, weapons that feel powerless at times, and surprisingly bad frame drops at times.
Paranautical Activity (Deluxe Atonement, for its re-release after the minor controversy), is a rogue-lite FPS game, that seems to take notes from Doom and Binding Of Isaac. Yet, it seems to do it in ways that work against the game. While it does use some of the things (fast paced shooting, randomized rooms and floors, varying stats on each character), it doesn't use it well.
Weapons feel quite good to use, although some of them feel rather weak. The shotgun, from my point of view, felt like the biggest let-down of all the weapons, with the bow being powerful and one or two-hitting enemies, with no problem.
Power-ups feel nice too but with next to no proper explination as to what they do, when you pick them up, leave you to guess what they do, for whatever situation you're about to plummet into, with said power-up.
Enemies are... alright. Mostly tedious to deal with, since some range from simple "fire a bolt, wait for a while, rinse and repeat" to "'bullet hell'-like spam". Surprisingly, the most annoying enemy I faced was the floor sharks. Why? Tank-y characters can't dodge well, and with the floor sharks, I've ended up being juggled by them, shooting them with a shotgun that did abysmal damage, until I either died or completed the room that way.
Levels are pretty much the same square box, with randomised preset props, and enemies are dumped in when you enter. Nothing to write home about, except for what could amount to some problem with moving under staircases. Ended up getting stuck there, which has broken the flow of gameplay, quite a lot. There also seems to be some odd dissonance with the enemies that spawn in some rooms? Sometimes you get enemies who spawn in there, who get stuck in parts of the level geometry and just kinda... sits there.
The characters have different spawn weapons, health and speed, meaning that you have some variety in what you can do and can't do. And by variety, it boils down to how far you can get with the fast characters. I mentioned above that the tank-y characters are slow, and even the extra health they have, just makes them a sitting duck until they die. Along with some of them getting weapons which would be ideal for fast characters, since they promote "attack-retreat" tactics, they work against the character, requiring them risk taking hits, which they most likely will, to pump in shots that don't feel like they do much. Compared to the bow or the sicle, the shotgun feels like the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ pistol you throw out the window, as soon as you see anything remotely non-pistol like.
The bosses are... okay. They look interesting, but their design and looks are pretty much meaningless, since most of them just fire shots are you, non-stop until they spawn enemies or do some third thing that makes them slightly different from each other. And, honestly, they could be interesting if most of them didn't feel like the same boss. They just move around the area and shot, not really doing anything else, than the animation their set. Which sucks, cause the bosses I fought, looked really interesting.
The game itself, is it worth it, even after all that I complained about? For some people, if you've run out of rogue-lite games, akin to Ziggurat, it could be. If there's some more tweaks to the game, such as a revamped health system, characters and weapons being buffed, as well as some changes to make bosses less dependent on luck or power-ups, it can be a very fun game. Also the font is pretty damn ugly to look at, in the menu. And the menu looks really amateurish, which is kinda sad, considering a lot of indie games do a lot to make the menus look presentable.
Was I satisfied with the product? No. I felt like I bought a game that could've benefitted from more time in Early Access, especially now that we have a new dev team who works on the game. Hopefully, some future patches can make them game more fun to play and less annoying to deal with.
Do I recommend it? As you saw above, I don't. If you want to jump into the genre of rogue-like or rogue-lite or whatever the cool kids call it, look for a game like The Binding Of Isaac, Ziggurat, or look up some games within that genre on your own. If you really want it, prepare for a game that you may dislike or find too tedious to keep playing.

After the credits, the game's developers write that it was an "experiment".  And it clearly shows.  Some aspects of this game (writing, acting, atmosphere, the mystery until the very end where it just falls apart) are superb.  However, other aspects are very poor.  Setting aside some technical matters with the game (I view this game more as an interactive movie than a game per se so I give it a pass on the simplistic interface), I feel that this game had severe problems in the development of the plot.  The writers often seem to have trouble in finding ways to move the plot forward naturally - often the inspector just something on the ground (I can recall three keychains or fobs that people just seem to drop for no reason for the inspector to find).  Then are moments that pull you out of the game, when the main character's behavior is simply bizarre and unnatural.  This was particularly the case in matters involving police investigation methods (he frequently behaves more like a burgler than an investigator) or in how he responds to threats of violence to himself or others (shrugging and acting exasperated instead of calling in armed backup to arrest everyone in sight). And the conclusion was very disappointing.  It might have been meant as a twist, but you spend 90% of the game investigating strands in direction X and it turns out in the last interview that actually it was direction Y and the guilty party just confesses for no apparent reason.  Still, for the price I enjoyed my time with the game and have no regrets in purchasing it.  The acting and writing were frequently very good.  I hope the developers try again and that their next experiment goes better.  I would definitely like to see what they can do with a bit more experience!

I will admit before I start that this game plucks a couple of nostalgia strings for me. First. I really loved the old point and click adventure games and Contradiction has some elements of them in its mechanics. Second, I have a soft spot for FMV games, as flawed as they can be.
Pros:
-The cast of Contradiction is really fascinating to watch. Even though Inspector Jenks (played by Rupert Booth) gives off weird reactions and skirts the edge of acting hammy, I couldn't help but laugh and enjoy him. The Rands were so sinister in their own ways that I couldn't wait for the next moment I had to talk to them. Heck, even some of the side characters had their own moments that made me laugh. Sure most of these performances are wacky, but they're done in a way that let's you know they know what they're doing and they're not breaking your immersion like a bad FMV game would've done.
- The main mechanic, going through interviews and spotting contradictions (well, most are, but a few aren't really contradictions by definition), does something I really appreciate: it makes you think. Some of these contradictions can be hard to pick out, you'll have alot of clues and pieces of conversation to go through, so there's more work you'll have to do before you reach your conclusion. However, once you do you feel good about yourself and say "ha, got you you lying SOB!"
- The narrative as well is interesting. There are multiple threads that come up that could lead you think you know what's really going on and they all are legit. Even when I got to the ending I still enjoyed how it transpired and how the game's creators played with your expectations.
Cons:
-This doesn't bother me as much, but this is a short game. If you're perceptive and/or using the tip system, you could probably beat this game within 3-4 hours. If you're hoping for a long game, this isn't for you.
-Not replayable; there isn't no new game plus or extra material after you beat the game. Again, this does not bother me as much, but this will be a turn-off for some.
-I will not get into spoilers, but...there are going to be alot of open plot threads that it might irritate you when you reach the end. I'll admit, I thought they'd close some of these plot threads in the end. Unfortunately, that is not so. It is true most of this was because the developer hit their budget limits and that they want to return to this story in the future to jump from those plot points. However, that is just an explanation, not an excuse.
Nevertheless, I think most that enjoy narrative focused mystery games will enjoy this one. There's enough elements in here to keep you engaged in solving the mystery and chuckle while you're doing it. It's not a comedy game, but it's a game that knows what it is and plays with some of the sillier elements in service of it's story.

You get what you pay for. It's basically Binding of Isaac in first person. It's only a notch above mindless fun, though. Even so, you'll get a few hours of play time into it if you really like it.
Get it on sale or in a bundle.

Contradiction is an FMV adventure/murder mystery game that originally released on the iPad in January 2015 before launching on PC six months later. Thankfully, the interface for the PC version was changed to acknowledge the different input schemes between the two; while it's not the most visually appealing interface, it's functional.
You play as Detective Inspector Frederick Jenks, tasked with looking into the supposed suicide of one Kate Vine, a PhD student found by the lake in the small village of Edenton, having drowned. You go about this task by exploring Edenton looking for clues, bumping into people, and asking people questions about evidence found or given by others. The people you interview aren't always telling the truth, however, meaning you have to pick out when characters make two statements that are at odds with each other—these namesake contradictions—and Detective Jenks will give them a chance to explain themselves. These mechanics work decently well, although it can be frustrating when statements that logically should be at odds with each other aren't considered contradictions, and having to explore all of the areas of the village to find the one area that has a scene that will advance the plot can be annoying, especially due to the fact that the transitions between areas are completely unskippable.
The entire game is shot rather well, but has a few spots of less-than-stellar audio quality—excusable, given the rather tight budget constraints the game was made on. It's never bad enough to be an actual problem.
Speaking of audio, the soundtrack (and indeed, most (all?) of the game) was made by Tim Follin, well known for pushing the hardware of '80s and '90s consoles and computers to the limit to produce some amazing soundtracks. While Contradiction's soundtrack isn't as recognizable as much of Tim Follin's earlier work, it manages to set the mood perfectly.
The acting and writing is fantastic. Jenks is goofy and exaggerated, which can feel a bit at odds with the more naturalistic tone of the rest of the actors, but I find the contrast between Jenks and the others amusing, especially when up against some of the "obvious bad guys" of the cast. My only real complaint with regards to the writing is that the mystery is solved before many of the other questionable things you find along the way are resolved, setting up for a sequel that might not happen, unfortunately.
It's not perfect, but I have no doubt in my mind that it
worth your time, if you're interested in it. Just cross your fingers that a sequel gets announced at some point. I want to know how the rest of the story ends.

From Studio 48, the same publisher/developer responsible for Locked-In Syndrome, comes their second horror title, Judas. About 95% of the gameplay takes place inside of a small apartment location, where the player is tasked with solving puzzles in order to both escape, and figure out the horrific events that unfolded within.
There is little guidance to help the player along the way, which may cause some to feel frustrated at the difficulty of the enigmas. It's a stark contrast to their previous title, where the puzzle solutions were too easy to find. However, since most of the game takes place in a small room, it's not too hard to figure out what to do next. Rather than opting for creepy background music, the developer has used a series of sound effects such as screams, doors opening and slamming shut, and other eerie sounds to try to create a tense atmosphere. It doesn't really work too well, but the effort is there to some degree.
The story, although sub-par, has rather grim subject matter. If you were a victim of child abuse, then Judas may not be the game for you. It centers around a father who drastically hurt his daughter, and his wife. I won't go in to anymore detail here, as doing so would spoil the remainder of the game, and the plot itself is paper thin to begin with. The graphics aren't terrible, but they're not high quality; it's easy to tell that this is a very low budget title.
Though it's not a strong recommendation, Judas isn't necessarily a terrible game, it's just low budget. The developer did put in some moderate effort to the game, and did end up releasing a patch to fix the crashing issues that it suffered from in the beginning; although their presence is absent from the forums. There are some pretty cool horror effects, but don't expect to be scared out of your pants while playing Judas. Lasting just over half an hour, the game isn't worth the $3.29 asking price, but if you can catch it on sale it's worth picking up if you're short on horror games to play.

Another great game from Nihon Falcom.
This game is an Action-RPG similar to the Ys series, but is way more focused on Dungeon Crawling gameplay, while taking a few inspirations from western art and gameplay design. The great interconnected structure of the dungeons make exploring the world fun, and just like in the Ys series leveling up actually means that you get much stronger. Treasures in this game are varied enough: Aside from your typical loot stuff like potions and equipment you also get various guardian cards and nice spells throughout the game so that it never really gets boring. It also helps that every single weapon has additional spells that can the equipped, making even weaker weapons useful at times.
Like it is expected from Falcom, the graphics are fairly crisp, especially for a game from 2005 and the soundtrack is really well done. While the game is rather focused on fighting, you get some nice, clever block puzzles, especially in the later dungeons. While game progression is fairly linear, the dungeons and mazes itself allow for some neat exploration, and finding key items that give you new abilities encourage you to revisit older dungeons.
It doesn't come without some flaws, though. The game is not that well done for controller, the inventory has to be used by mouse. The story is fairly cliche and a little bit more variety surely wouldn't hurt. But  all in all this still adds up to a fun ride that lasts a good 12 to 15 hours.

Let me start this off by saying I am a fan of Falcom's games as a whole and that all of their games are created with a high standard of quality. That being said, I did not enjoy this game. Not every idea that Falcom has tried over the years has worked out all that way. Xanadu Next is one of those ideas that, to me, fails.
The biggest issues I have with this game stem from it's lack of content. There's very little to this game and I can't help but wonder why they released it with so little substance. In order to reach a somewhat passable gameplay time length, they really had to stretch things out in this game through excessive grinding, recolored/reused enemies, and the awful key system. I don't want to go into too much detail but I'll breifly break those down.
The grinding isn't always necessary as combat is simple, easy and you will get very familiar with the enemies very quickly anyway. However, the bosses deal a huge amount of damage and have high defense so you will need to grind for exp to increase your stats so that your character meets the stat requirements for the better gear. This mechanic, even on paper, was just asking to be abused. They definitely could've gotten worse with it but even on Normal, it takes a considerable amount of time fighting the same enemies over and over just to get the exp and gold required to gain the gear needed to fight the bosses.
And I didn't even mention the skill get system, which requires using a weapon for a certain amount of hits to gain the skill the weapon has permanently. Another pointless system that just wastes time. It's really odd too, the proficiency goes up as you use it to a max of 200, all the while the attack for the weapon goes up too, so often you will get a stronger weapon in terms of it's base power but with it's proficiency at 0, it'll deal much less damage for a significant amount of time once you first wield it. Not smart. It forces the player to take a decrease in damage just so they can later do more damage with the same weapon, and the cycle repeats through out the whole game. You kinda need to do it too for the necessary skills some of the weapons have.
Anyway, onto the reused enemies. There really are a fairly short amount of enemy types in this game. Most of the enemies are recolored at least 3 times, with others appearing less often than that. It gets pretty boring to reach a new area only to be greeted by the same enemies you fought in a previous area. And since they behave almost exactly the same, fighting them is just as easy. Most regular enemies are quite easy, just thrust and get behind them, attack their back and they die. Alternatively, just walk around them as they are attacking to get a few hits in. I assume the developers realized this, so they compensated for that by adding rooms full of the same enemy. It's not uncommon to walk into a small room packed with 8 or 9 of the same enemy. In large numbers like that, you are gauranteed to take damage. Some of the trap rooms like that usually require chuggin potions and just tanking through it.
Combat in general isn't very fun. It's a bit too simple, I see it as the popular hybrid between action and turn-based that is rarely any good. It lacks the complexity and fun of a deeper action combat system yet also lacks the strategic party system of turn-based games. So in the end, you are left with one button mashing combat. no block, no dodge, no combos, just some skills you can occasionally fire off a limited amount of times (unless you use skill potions). As stated several times already, enemies don't pose a threat unless they come in large numbers. Bosses however are pretty tough and not exactly in a good way. I didn't have fun fighting any of the bosses (haven't fought the last boss yet) but some of them are cheap as hell. Huge fast attacks that deal massive damage and small chance to actually deal any damage to the boss, either that or they bombared you with tons of smaller projectiles and objects that's gauranteed incoming damage. Bring potions and you can tank through them easily though. Without any potions and you will die quickly.
Finally, I bring up the key system. Unlike the clever dungeon design of a game like Legend of Zelda, where the keys are found in the dungeons that they belong to and help guide the player through a natural path, Xanadu Next goes in a different direction. Keys are bought in the shop, and each time you buy one the price increases up to a max of 500. Doesn't sound too bad at first, until you realize that many areas of the game require a ridiculous number of keys. Almost every single door is locked and requires burning a key. So you mine as well grind for money and buy a few dozen keys before going to a new area, otherwise you have to stop your exploration, go back to town and buy more keys. This is flat out bad game design that does nothing more than hinder the pacing of the game. It doesn't help that areas/dungeons can be a bit confusing with so many copy paste rooms that look the same and a mini-map that leaves a lot to be desired.
One last thing to mention, while the controls are pretty tight and map out well on a controller, for some dumb reason the menu can only be interacted with the mouse. It's really cumbersome to swap out accessories/skills frequently and you have to keep taking your hand off the controller to the mouse, and you cannot move while the menu is open but the game is not paused. So during fights, this is a huge problem if you need to swap in some heals or switch a skill. This is one of the reasons I hardly used most of the skills in the game, since you can only equip 4 and it's too cumbersome to change them out, I stuck with the same two for most of the game. (the most useful ones anyway)
Now it may sound like I'm being pretty negative about this game but I wouldn't say I hate it. It's a competently made game with solid visuals, a decent soundtrack, good dialogue (although lacking any characters worth carring about) and acceptable controls. It's really just the lack of content and various design decisions that hold this game back from being great. For me, it's in the middle, a 5/10. It has a lot of very old-school design that don't exactly fit the modern jrpg traditions that are more popular/common. That being said, if you enjoy really classic dungeon crawlers where grinding for exp and gold doesn't bother, this might be a decent game to try out. For everyone else, there's many better Falcom games you can play instead. (Go get Ys Origin, it's fantastic.)

Knowing how much I loved the Ys games, a friend of mine bought a copy of this back with them from a trip to Japan in 2006. At the time, I had absolutely no idea how to read even the tiniest bit of Japanese, but I somehow managed to complete the game though sheer brute force (for the most part the main problem was figuring out what the multiple guardians and passive skills did). Since then, I’ve played through the game many times and was extremely happy to see that the game would finally be getting an official English localization.
Xanadu NEXT was first released in 2005, so don’t expect mind-blowing graphics. That’s said areas look nice, from freezing mountains and damp caverns to humid jungles and sprawling castles that always keep the player interested as they explore the world. Combat and area effects are nice and clear, never getting in the way of combat or making things difficult to deal with. Despite its age, there are still some really nice effects to be seen, such as the reflections on the water and boiling lava pits.The story is good fun, but nothing too ground-breaking. Without spoiling anything, the story takes place in in the ruins of Harlech Island, and after a short time there the player’s character is mortally wounded, resulting in them gaining the power of the guardians, powerful beings that sustain the character’s life. You can see some of the twists coming from a mile away, but overall I would describe the whole thing as “Neat”. Whilst not a direct sequel to previous entries in the series (Xanadu/Xanadu II/Faxanadu), there is some similar terminology and themes thrown around that link it back to Dragon Slayer (from which the series’ first spawned) to keep long-term fans happy.
Xanadu NEXT is often described as JRPG/Anime Diablo and for the most part that’s pretty fair. If you’ve ever played games like Diablo, you’ll be able to jump right into Xanadu without too much difficulty, though as mentioned by others that controls and the configuration thereof can be a little clunky.  If you’re just going to do a causal run, I would recommend taking the time to set up a controller configuration that works for you (Xbox/PS4 Pads etc), as when you play through the first time it can be very easy to lose your cursor onscreen when attaching large groups of enemies, which can often result in you accidentally attacking and exploding pot or moving your character into a nice big pool of lava.
The main chunk of Xanadu Next involves having to navigate your way through sprawling dungeons, room-by-room, filled to the brim with a range fantasy monsters. From your typical bats and skeleton enemies to larger chimera with snakes for arms and giant Vega-claw-wielding Lizard men, the range of Enemies in Xanadu will keep you busy.  Unlike other diablo-esq games, you can’t really get away with running head first into battle, hacking away and blobs of enemies until they go down. In Xanadu there are certain ways you should approach each enemy, for example; attack griffons whilst they’re on the ground and either back off and wait until they land, or shoot off some magic spells if you have the charges to spare. When fighting the aforementioned lizard men it’s a good idea to dodge their initial attack before getting behind them to deal out some massive damage. Because of all this, the player is always engaged in the combat, and is never simply mindlessly tearing through big mobs.
There are a range of spells and skills that can be used to defeat enemies. The former can be purchased from shops or found hidden throughout the world, whilst the latter can be learned by gaining proficiency in the many available weapons.  Essentially every weapon has a proficiency level which goes up by attacking and killing enemies with it. Once the player becomes proficient in a weapon they can switch to another whilst still being able to use that weapons skill. The earned skills include powerful attack skills, stat boosts and even additional passive abilities such as being able to see enemy information or gain more gold. However, the player can only actually equip 4 of these skills (and spells) at any given time, so it’s important to switch them out as the situation dictates (stat boosts for boss fights and more gold for general exploration). This whole system encourages the player to try a range of different weapons to gain useful skills and abilities.
As well as Spells and Skills, the player is able to switch between a numbers of different Guardians found throughout the game. The player can equip one Guardian at a time that can be levelled up by defeating set numbers of enemies. Each Guardian grants powerful boosts to help the player along in their quest and much like the skills, it’s important to switch Guardians out depending on the situation the player is about to face. Heading out to explore? Equip the Guardian that boosts the amount of EXP received. Selling items? Equip the Guardian that boosts charisma, letting the player sell and buy for more. Going into a Boss fight? How about the Guardian that gives the player more charges of their Spells?
Speaking of bosses, there aren’t too many in the game, but when you run into them they are huge set pieces that are sure to initially catch you off-guard. Most of the boss fights are a good gateway, not just for ensuring that you are at the required level, but also to put you to test and see if you have gotten to grips with newly acquired skills and spells. Even more-so than the regular enemies, it’s incredibly important to watch the bosses attack patterns and use the appropriate tactics to succeed. Yes you can go into some of the battles guns blazing, but you’ll take a whole heap of damage and burn through those precious potions (which affects your final end-game rank).
Finally, as with all Falcom games, the soundtrack is simply amazing. With remixed versions of the original Xanadu theme and pumping boss music, there’s something for everyone here. Even if you decide not to get the game, go and check out “Evildoer” and “The Eternal Maze” for a seriously good listen (for the former, check out the Sword of Justice version).
Overall, Xanadu can be a little on the clunky side, but is a very different and fun experience.

tl;dr version: Highly recommended if you like adventure games and/or puzzles, and if you don't rage on non-major technical issues.
--------------------------------
Since I'm mostly used to point-and-click or modern adventure games, Myst was a new experience for me. It's a great concept- the player has to rely on visual and auditory observations to solve some large-scale puzzles, which are all completely logical and range in difficulty from easy to medium-hard (but I've played quite a lot of adventure games and am used to them; newcomers to adventure gaming may find the puzzles harder, but still doable). There is no pixel-hunting and no inventory system, which automatically dispenses with inventory item combination puzzles found in most adventure games.
The developers suggest playing the game as if the players were actually present in the Myst universe, for a fully immersive experience and to better appreciate the story. Therefore I recommend playing Myst when you have quite a bit of spare time and are mentally relaxed. This is not the sort of game you'd want to play to take a break from your hectic activities or in the midst of a busy time to relieve stress. I made that mistake and my general attitude was just to plough through all the puzzles. Nevertheless, even though I didn't pay much attention to the story (or the environmental story-related clues), I found it fairly intriguing.
The environments are simultaneously strange and beautiful, and have certain mystic feel to them (probably why the game is called Myst?). There are not a whole lot of things to interact with, which I think is very good, because that means there's very little noise in terms of puzzle-solving; most of the things the player can interact with are related to some puzzle or the other. The music and soundscapes are soothing and appropriate to the environments, especially in Rime age.
Now for some technical issues- first of all, realMyst: Masterpiece Edition is a remastered edition (graphics/interface overhaul) of realMyst, which itself was a remastered edition of Myst. The masterpiece edition also has a free roam feature. In the previous versions, the player had to click on a place the go there and the field of view was quite limited, which may have been restrictive but was not necessarily a bad thing. However, mouse movement in free roam view is very clunky. There are no subtitles, which makes it hard to listen to the characters' monologues, and there are no options to adjust the music level. The graphics aren't -that- good and the game suffers from poor optimization.
Still, I highly recommend it for adventure gaming or puzzle aficionados who don't mind the above-mentioned issues (plus RMME supports achievements and trading cards, and has additional puzzles to Myst or realMyst).
Could not ask for a better remake of such a great game...   Maybe FFVII but even that is a bold statement.

realMyst: Masterpiece Edition is a complete overhaul of the original Myst game from 1993, porting it to a modern 3D engine that allows for free-exploration as opposed to clicking on still, 2D images. It's actually done suprisingly well and stays true to the original through-out, even including the original scenes that had used real actors. I did find the performance a little choppy in some sections but never to a point where the game was unplayable. The new graphics engine brings a new life to Myst, while my elitist self prefers the original, this looks absolutely amazing and they pretty much nailed the aesthetics of the original re-imagined in 3D.
Myst is the first entry into the series and gave birth to one of the most incredible puzzle/adventure games of all time, it has some really clever puzzles that will tap into parts of your brain that are covered with cobwebs and will force you to think not 'outside the box' but 'without the box'. The plot is one extremely immersive trip that you have to uncover yourself and there are a few Myst novels that go into it with a lot more detail.
Myst starts you off glaring at a book with a moving image of an island which sends you to the island, Myst, upon interaction with it and thats where this mind numbingly fascinating adventure begins. You soon discover that there are two books placed in a library and with exploration and interactions you discover that there are two people trapped inside them, one within each book. You'll need to collect pages of the two books to free them, which are scattered around the 'Ages' (different worlds within the game) and you'll need to solve a series of complicated, yet extremely logical puzzles to progress through these diverse and unique worlds in order to find the pages and uncover more of the plot.
Myst features some amazingly designed puzzles, you'll need to write down notes, memorize figures, find clues and memorize sounds to solve them, the levels are abstract and beautiful, each completely different from the last and you'll be able to explore and solve puzzles in which ever order of world you please. This is trully an amazing adventure which has been brought back from obscurity by Cyan and would recommend anyone interested in puzzle games or interested in trying something different to invest in it.

If you like adventure games and classic "who-dun-it's", then Contradiction is up your alley. You are Inspector Jenks and have seven hours to solve a murder in a secluded English village. As you may suspect, there is more to the town and its inhabitants than it seems.
Simular to LA Noire, you interview various people in town and try to spot the liar. How? By finding the contradictions. The more they talk, the more likely they will slip up and contradict themselves. Challenge their contradictions to learn more and progress the story. The game starts you off easy, but ramps up the difficulty gradually throughout the game as you collect more conversations and more information about a wide variety of inquiry.
Don't worry. If you ever get stuck, you can always phone the chief to hash out what you've learned so far. I did this several times. By listening to him and Jenks talk it out in a new way, it was always enough to put a new perspective on what I had learned and push me in the right direction. This is different than a "cheat" which actually gives you the answer. Try not to use those. There are several achievements to be won by not using them. There is something else...
It's live action!
FMV games of old, like Wing Commander 3 & 4, used FMV for part of the game play, but Contradiction does so 100% of the time. Navigating the town and knowing what to ineract with are made obvious through text and picture overlays on screen. Remember, the "game" is solving contradictions, not a pixel hunt. And to this games credit, the narrative never felt "jumpy", like in other story driven games, like Telltale's Walking Dead. In that game, there are obvious jumps in the script depending on the choices you have made with odd camera cuts and disjointed dialogue. That was not so here.
Clean, crisp and enjoyable. Time to get moving Jenks. The game is afoot.

Have a hard time getting into stat-heavy games, but love the way leveling up feels?  Me too!  Luckily, Nihon Falcom has our backs, specializing in blazing-fast ARPGs that combine the satisfaction of power accumulation, the real-time thrill of the arcade, and the exploration of Zelda.
is another great example of what they do.  If you've played
, this is similar, except that instead of charging enemies head-on, you always try to get behind them; it's a game about being a backstabbing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, whatever the characters blather about knighthood and so on.  There's no dodge button, so I suppose you could think of this mechanic as an abstraction of flipping around and missing evil's poisoned blades by the hair of your chinny-chin-chin.  It works well, and it actually feels
to have combat stripped down to NES simplicity.
Only one minus:  the localization.  The story was a secondary consideration for me, going in, and I think it's a given that the narrative isn't supposed to be as strong as that in an Ys game.  However, it's just intriguing enough that by game's end, I began to get invested, but was constantly frustrated by the game's awkward English script.  There are too many archaisms, pseudo-archaisms, and extra little wedged-in words that only serve to muddy meaning.  Remember, XSEED: there is power in prose that is lean and mean!  I can recommend some great 1950s crime fiction if you're interested!

I bought this game because Falcom can do no wrong, and it looked similar to Ys.  It certainly turned out to be a fantastic game, but nothing like what I expected.  It's an action RPG, but that's about where the similarities to Ys ends.  Xanadu Next focuses much more on dungeon crawling and exploration, and the atmosphere is relatively dark.  Much of the story and world history is revealed through texts you find hidden in treasure chests throughout the game, some hidden quite well.  I found it incredibly addictive to search every corner of every dungeon looking for secrets, hidden treasures, and discovering more of the game's lore.  The level-up system is very open ended, giving 6 points to allocate to your stats however you please for each level you gain.  The game guides you with equipment stat requirements, so it's pretty hard to mess up your stats, but there is also a level-down option in the case that you want to level up again and redistribute your stats.  The game uses mouse controls, which I'm generally not too fond of, but it functions well and even adds a bit to the feel of the game, so it's not so bad as I expected it would be.  This game was a great surprise for me and is a really amazing experience.  I highly recommend it.

A beautiful recreation of a timeless classic, realMyst: Masterpiece Edition brings a piece of gaming history to modern times.  While the graphics and sounds are completely revamped to match modern-day standards, the gameplay stays true to its original and does not fail to deliver the nostalgic Myst-feeling.
It is, admittingly, a rather peculiar game, a slow paced and thoughtful puzzler in a surrealistic setting. Its puzzles can be overwhelming at times, especially for those unfamiliar with the genre, but they always have a logical (sometimes surprisingly straightforward) solution that makes you feel really smart if you solve them on your own. But even for those non-hardcore adventure gamers among you, the game offers a built in (optional) hint system that gives you little advices without spoiling too much.
There are only few negative points that should be mentioned; The controls and movement feel a bit wonky at times and you might occasionally get stuck on objects on the ground (nothing game-breaking though), however Cyan is working on a fix for that at the point of this review. The in-game cinematics still have the low resolution from previous renditions of Myst, which seems a bit out of place considering the otherwise beautiful graphics. And the missing inventory (you can only pick up and carry one item at a time) is a rather annoying remnant from the original Myst game, often requiring an unnecessary amount of backtracking.
In summary, realMyst: Masterpiece Edition is a game that wants you to immerse yourself, absorb the scenery and use your logical thinking. If you are a fan of the Myst series to begin with, this is almost a must-have, but any other adventure fan might take a look at this as well, to get a chance to enjoy a game that wrote history in a new and stunning visual design.
