It isn't your run of the mill arena battler/shooter that gives you a class/character/hero to play and says "have fun", it gives you said character, lets your modify your abilites on the fly, lets you create custom loadouts to enhance your play style, encourages you to create your own challenges all the while rewarding you with choices of customization and heroes.
There's an issue with being locked out of content such as instant access to heroes and every skin in the game, however, if you were given everything out of the gates wouldn't you pick the most popular choice and stick with it? Put some time into each loadout, helix tree and build your locker of skins and you'll find yourself choosing a variety every time you play. The lore challenges add extra difficulty and fun to your games with your favourite character or try each at random, they all offer funny and fleshed out background to the well seasoned world (or star) created in battleborn.
The single player portion of the game is well paced if a little hectic (you may find yourself zoning out of the audio dialogue) and depending on your sense of humor, can be quite entertaining from a narrative standpoint. If you'd rather focus on the gameplay, you can progress in both single player and multi player in any form you choose. Trying out a new hero in single player can give you the confidence you need to take it into a match of incursion or meltdown and do well, rather than forcing you to risk the wrath of potential bad apples in multiplayer.
If you enjoy a solid FPS, customization elements and in your face action Battleborn might be a good investment. With some refinement along the way, Battleborn could be amazing.

Well what can I say? A game that takes MOBA style elements in one of its PVP modes that I find it hard to dislike. A satisfying PVE that, while not for everyone, is fun to explore every so often just for a change of pace. They considered a lot of stuff... Though that doesn't mean the game's without flaws.
There are some... ALMOST crippling balance issues. I say almost because the characters that are unbalanced have their counters. Galilea is one such example - far too much damage for her defence, or so I hear, but as an Orendi main I seem to have no problem showing her what for. Your mileage may vary, and I'd pay heed to those words. Devs have said they're gonna nerf the hell out of her.
Pay no heed to those that compare this to Overwatch. They are vastly different games. Battleborn boasts more MOBA-oriented gamemodes in a decidedly PvE-centric manner, with high kill times on player characters and longer, more involved strategies. Overwatch is a quicker game that requires strategy and thinking beforehand, with much more PVP-centric gamemodes and a more modern feature set for the FPS genre.
This game brings FPS and MOBAs together in a pretty great way, and if anyone's scared off by that, I welcome you to really give it a go. In the game's early stages, it's quite easy to get to grips with what a character's capable of and develop your playstyle.

On first glance it might seem that Gearbox has gone flat out insane by deciding to challenge Blizzard's Overwatch with their own team-based FPS, but the truth of the matter is that the games have very little in common once you get past the cartoony graphics and ability-based gunplay.
Whereas Overwatch is a pure team-based FPS most similar to Team Fortress 2, Battleborn draws its inspiration from both Borderlands and Super Monday Night Combat, with the end result being a MOBA that plays like a fast-paced FPS, rather than the opposite. Another key difference is that Battleborn actually features a fairly lengthy campaign that can be played in either singleplayer or co-op, though the overall focus is quite clearly on the competitive multiplayer.
In total the campaign will take you around 7-8 hours to beat if you're simply going for story progression, but if you're looking to complete all of the challenges and the optional hard mode, you can easily double that amount. For the most part I would say I had a great deal of fun with it, especially in multiplayer where you have a whole bunch of people roaming around and cleaning out hordes upon hordes of robots and demons. In many ways these campaign missions feel like dungeons you might find in an MMO, with simple layouts, clear objectives, and tons of 'trash' enemies you need to wipe out before proceeding to a big bad boss. Sadly there is one gigantic issue that I still can't wrap my head around - you're unable to chose which mission you want to do when playing the campaign in multiplayer!
In other words, you might run in to repeat missions while just trying to progress through the story, and hunting down a specific challenge in multiplayer is next to impossible unless you feel like constantly rolling the dice and hoping the correct map appears. I will fully admit I could be missing something here, because none of this makes any sense, but despite trying my damnest I haven't been able to figure out how. This was especially aggravating when my team wiped out on a particularly difficult, and obnoxiously bullet-spongy boss, and then simply dispersed rather than attempting to fight him for another 10 minutes. Since I didn't feel like doing all of it myself, I returned to the matchmaking queue and desperately tried to get the same map again, but to no avail as the system kept tossing me wherever it felt like, which naturally meant anywhere besides the one map I wanted to see.
That puzzling issue aside, its also worth mentioning that you should not be going into Battleborn's campaign with the hope for a good story, because the barely connected shambles of one certainly don't impress. If you're looking for a ton of enemies to explode, power-ups to collect, and bosses to stab in the kneecaps then Battleborn is the game for you, but if you're after a compelling narrative, or characters that are capable of conversing in anything other than puns, then I would suggest you run far, far away and never look back.
As I've mentioned before, Battleborn is at its core a MOBA game that just so happens to involve a whole lot of shooting, rather than an FPS with a bunch of NPCs running about. I don't mean this in a derogatory way, however, as the gunplay and overall movement in Battleborn is far more satisfying than what I've experienced in the recent Doom beta, but the long time-to-kill and the need for good ability usage in order to bring down enemy heroes is something that people looking for a pure team-orientated shooter might not appreciate, so its well worth repeating again.
To explain all of it in detail would take forever, so allow me to simply say it like this: the action is fun, the pace is refreshingly fast, and every single one of the heroes I've tried out played uniquely enough to keep me entertained throughout my dozen hours with the game. There might have been some balance issues here and there, but nothing I couldn't overcome through gratuitous use of explosions, so as far as the core gameplay goes, I have few complaints.
, while Battleborn has the potential to be one of the most interesting MOBA/FPS hybrids out there, it has one gigantic issue that it needs to overcome before it ends up getting anywhere near to that lofty goal. That issue is the fact that Battleborn does next to nothing to discourage players from leaving the game, which means that almost no match actually ends properly!
The most infuriating example of this is when players quit a match before it even begins, and then instead of searching for a new player or just cancelling the match Battleborn starts it anyway, balance be damned! It might not seem like that big of a deal right now as you read this from the comfort of your toilet seat, but after you invest 20 minutes fighting tooth and nail in an insanely close match, the last thing you want to see is "PLAYER X HAS LEFT THE GAME". The moment that message appears you know the pendulum has started swinging, and that no matter how much you struggle, you're going to lose anyway!
I initially had slightly mixed feelings about Battleborn, but after spending a couple of days getting to know its mechanics, heroes, and the overall gameplay style, it began to grow on me. Rather than settling down into a couple of heroes as one might usually do in a new MOBA, I found myself constantly switching around as each hero brought in a new and fresh way of playing that always managed to remain fun.
With all of that said, however, I don't think I'm going to be playing more Battleborn until the matchmaking gets fixed, because there is no worse feeling in a competitive game than doing your very best, and then losing due to factors completely out of your control. Though I will for now leave the rating as a recommendation because I did genuinely enjoy my time with Battleborn, and the issues mostly come from other people being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, but I would still recommend you check the patch notes before deciding on your purchase, just in case.

Ryse: Son of Rome is a simple hack and slash game. In the game, you play as Marius, a Roman general manipulated into killing Nero and his family for peculiar reasons. The story is muddled with no real plot but it's a simple fighting game that can give you a few kicks. I just played on Beginner as I realised the game was basically this standard formula. Go to zone, spawn enemies, kill and execute enemies, rinse and repeat. However, you will find that the graphics engine, Crytek, is pretty decent.
Gameplay-wise, you hack and slash along a linear model, moving from one point of the story to another. The game emulates a similar style to games like Rocksteady's Batman where you attack enemies and auto-block attacks with a specially timed button (Spacebar). There is nothing exciting. This is meant to be a game, not an art project.
Conclusion, I believe you will not get a great degree of excitement and wonder from Ryse. The game could be greatly improved as I've seen the works that have been created in the Multiplayer Arena. The levels there have much more interesting content and I believe that content should have been included into the single player campaign. The reason why I've given a negative review is that the Yerlis were not able to bring out the fullest potential of a game. It felt like there was more marketing involved instead of game design and the game was not up to par. While there are no major issues, I think it's not a good idea to approve of games that are not wonderful. The list below will further breakdown my thoughts.
1. Simple to Play
Shift to Dodge, Left Click to Attack, Right Click to Shield Bash, Spacebar to Block. Executions are colour-coded, blue for left click and yellow for right click
2. Multiplayer Arena
It's so much more interesting than the single player campaign.
3. Scorpio Shooting
At least there was a time when you could shoot barbarians and war elephants.
4. Graphics
Ooh, Crytek makes the game look pretty good. It's not perfect as you can't interact with all the objects but they look nice.
5. Formation Attacks
Simple concept. Form up and block with the Spacebar and hold left click to fire pileums. It's even auto aim.
1.  Boring Repetitive Campaign Fights
Basically, you just go into a zone, fight barbarians like the Rocksteady Batman games and that's it. Do it over and over again.
2. Too Many Quicktime Requirements
Honestly, I have to press E then match the left click(blue) and right click(yellow) so much that it got boring.
3. Dull & Bad Storytelling
Summer vs Winter? Huh? Those are really lame characters. Where's Spring and Autumn? Why does Winter want Rome to be destroyed? Why are you overlapping 2 different impetus in the game? Marius wants to take revenge for his family and Winter wants to destroy Rome. It's like you are trying to tell 2 different stories in one game but are unable to complete either. You have characters like Nemesis, the goddess of revenge appear for 5 seconds while explaining Damocles betrayal and then that's it. WTF!
4. Marius's Reasons
Yes, you want to kill the Emperor Nero because his policies caused a great war but you have to kill Winter too. That's kind of really hard and you are missing a method to do it. Without this method, you have an incomplete story of revenge.
1. Put the Gladiator Modes into the Campaign
The Arenas had god powers, sandstorms, spinning traps, etc. It provided so much more interesting levels. Your campaign is just a linear clickfest.

I thought this was just going to be a generic fighting game but I decided to give it a shot anyway.
Pros:
Beauitiful game :I know its a few years old but on my 1060 I still thought it was really pretty.
The executions are fun to watch:  Seriously a blast to watch your centurion smash people with his shield and stab them. I wish I had known you could unlock more executions earlier, I think I would of enjoyed it a little bit more.
Challenging boss fights: A lot of the the boss fights require good timing to get the perfect dodge or deflect. Not nearly as challenging as Dark Souls 3 but still a lot of fun.
You get to control formations of Romans: Marching with a group of other Romans and ordering them to raise their shields or throw spears is a welcome change of pace. You also get to control balistias and archers.
Cons:
Weak story: The story is basically divided up between Britain and Rome and focuses centerally on Nero and the barbarians. None of the characters are memorable except for your commanding officer. The second half of the game feels very rushed. I would of liked to have seen more of Rome and of had the more of the 2nd act fleshed out.
Gameplay gets a little repetitive: This isn't too horrible because the enemies you encounter do get more numorous and challenging. It's fun pulling off huge combos, especially when you are surrounded and can do double executions. I just think that some people could get pretty bored of stun, slash slash, block stun execute constantly. I didn't really care though.
Overall I would give this game a solid 7.5 out of 10. It's a very fun pretty mindless fighting game thats very pretty. The story is weak and its a little bit repetitive but I highly recommend it for anyone that enjoys fighting games but isn't looking for that big of a challenge.

For those unfamiliar with the game, Myst is a classic first-person point-and-click puzzle game, originally released in 1993.
series is set in an interesting universe where different worlds can be visited through specially-written books, and this is exactly what you'll be doing throughout the game. Each world has a unique theme and a set of puzzles to solve, but rather than puzzles being your typical logic minigames - they rely observation. Pulling random levers, pushing buttons and trying to figure out what they do is what Myst puzzles are all about. The game itself is actually very short and can be beaten in under an hour if you know what you're doing.
.
is a faithful remake of the game. Not without flaws, but certainly worthy of a recommendation. Its new modern features and visual effects make the experience even more immersive, while doing a great job preserving the charm and aesthetic of the original game. Free-roam controls add complete freedom of movement, while classic control scheme can also be enabled at any time.
The game doesn't always run well, and compared to some of the modern games of the same genre its visuals certainly lack consistency and polish. However compared to original Myst it looks and plays much better.
-----------
I previously criticized realMyst:ME for somewhat awkward controls, crashes, poor performance and visuals while better than the original - still not good enough to justify the low framerates even on a high-end machine. Thankfully, the 2.0 update brought improvements to all of those areas.

- Model and texture quality is very inconsistent throughout the game. In some areas the game looks better than even modern AAA games, while in others the model and texture quality looks 15 years out of date. Prior to the patch though, the latter was a much more common occurence.

Pick this up if you're feeling nostalgic, or if you've never played MYST it's still a great game. The graphics are fairly good, but still look dated and of course the live action parts are still in their original low resolution. The free roam control scheme is a little clunky but it lets you get around a lot faster than the classic point and click. You can use WASD and shift to sprint, but if you're standing still you have to right click and drag to look around. You'll have to do a lot of running back and forth so you'll appreciate it. The flashlight is great to have because it gets REALLY dark at night.
The clues for the puzzles are fairly out in the open but some of them take some really out of the box thinking. There is a really great help library, it starts off giving vague hints but you can dig deeper if you're really stumped until it eventually outright tells you what to do, so you'll never get stuck (unless you refuse to use it). It tries very hard to minimize spoilers. You will also have to obsessively screenshot every clue and keep a pad and paper nearby. Read all of the books, there's important stuff in them. One of the ages you'll have to rely on your auditory memory a lot so WARNING if you're tone deaf you will not have fun with this one.
The funny thing about the puzzles is they all seem pretty obvious in hindsight. There is never anything that's completely unfair or left to guessing or chance, though some of the logic is a little convoluted. Overall if you're good at these types of games or you're not ashamed to take a hint here and there this will be a fairly fast playthrough. I'd say pick this up when it's on sale.

You find a clue. You talk to everyone about it. With a certain person you'll discover a contradiction and get another clue. Rinse and repeat. Most of the time is spent running around town talking to everyone about everything, even if it will most probably lead to nothing. Except when it does.
Even if the gameplay is repetitive I absolutely encourage everyone to buy and play this game for its interesting story so the creators decide to produce more.

Dungeon Siege 2 picks off where the previous one left off, but greatly improves on a nubmer of mechanics.  It is a longer, but still very enjoyable game, with some quality of life changes to streamline the story and gameplay.  Overall I enjoyed it, and would recommend to gamers who enjoy old-school top-down RPGs.  It's very enjoyable in that regard.  The story was also improved, in my opinion.
Personal Cons
Click system change:  The changes to the original click system felt weird to me, making it feel more like Diablo, but I eventually accepted it and enjoyed it.
Talent System:  The talent system was an interesting addition, and gave more depth, but it was rough because you couldn't ever change them.  Without playing you weren't sure what would be benefical later, which led to some talent points being wasted.
Party size reduced to 4.  Part of what made the original Dungeon Siege fun was the party size, but I understand why they wanted to make the change, especially for balance reasons.  Some of the itemization was strange to me
Boss Fights: Some of the boss fights, especially the last one, felt so clunky and obnoxious, which shows the games age.
Pros
Long, and decent story, was fun to explore.  It was a little annoying that it did not connect with DS1, but was very great. Great exploration feeling, lots of fun areas.  Some of the backtracking was annoying, but overall it was great.
Buy it if it's on sale, and you wanna kill 30-40 hours on an RPG.

This game is a classic ARPG that differs from a lot of third-person or One-Man ARPG, where you can control up to 6 characters in your party. This feature keeps the game interesting throughout as you spec up your main starter character and have the ability to improve your other party members and try out their skill sets. The voice acting is pretty decent, and the storyline is interesting. There's a heap of side quests to do as well, and some are pretty challenging and have puzzles that you have to solve to move forward in the main quest or open a chest to find epic loot.
My only concern was toward the end-game it gets a bit grindy to reach the final boss, and replayability is good but would be better with friends as you play through game again on a harder difficulty (similar to Diablo II's difficulty levels). Boss fights are at first challenging but once you get the jist of their mechanics they are pretty easy. With the resolution configure making it 1920x1080 with v-sync, the game looks pretty decent for it's age (2005 I believe).
Overall it's a classic Action RPG with interesting combat system, able to control up to 6 party members and fairly decent choices to focus your character on i.e. a Mage can focus on Fire, Lightning or Death Magic, or Summoning Skills.

A fun enough game in the genere of "builder" where you take on the role of a manager of a high rise. The building part is basically not to challenging - you have to think what goes together, but distances seem not to matter. So while an office do not want to be close to a noisy venue like a restaurant - they dont mind to much hauling their way all the way up or down to get lunch etc.
However.... What WILL drive you absolutely bonkers is how devestatingly unforgiving it is when it comes to finances. About the worst game I have ever played in that regard - and I have played a lot of builders. Typically - IF you come out a bit unlucky or wrong from the start, you can scrap the game and restart as there IS NO WAY to "get back into it". How so?
Typically tenants give you cash, but cost you something to wire phone, electricity and water etc. So it is all about balance. But unless you love playing with a calculator and fiddeling with numbers to project the outcome - you can get "locked" into a downward spiral you just can not get out of. A typical example will be that you expand a new office, but forget to put electricity to it. Basically you will be moving on such a shoestring budget in the beginning that if you mess up the order of first getting a tenant (which you pay for) but forget to hook up - say - water: They might move out again before you can even hook up the darn thing the VERY NEXT DAY.
Ok - so that is all part of the game you say. "Go play sandbox if you want it easy". Fine. How about the fact that your $3000 a day powergrid suddenly goes bust. No problem you think - you got a maintenence guy right on it. But hey. Before he fixes it - you have 6 tenants moving out. And he went STRAIGHT TO WORK. And with the 6 tenants gone you lost vital rent to stay afloat. And suddenly you can not afford to put new tenants in. And.. then it unravels and goes to♥♥♥♥♥♥ (I seen this happen several times).
Basically the game is fun if you like the genera, and like it "punishing". Meaning you need a lot of skill, and a bit of luck to get going. Once you DO get going - it is more about space management.
I would give it 6/10 right now. It is fun if you like the genere, and i would say worth the cash for a good few hours of fun. But it becomes very repetitive after a while

This is simply the finest RTS I have ever played. The number of units (800+!!!) and attention to detail in modeling the look and capabilities of those units is second to none. The focus on realistic warfare (w/in reason) makes it one of the few RTS's that feels every bit as tactical as the best turn based strategy games. In fact, I would say it is the most tactical wargame I have ever played.
The game is very easy to control in terms of moving units around the map, but is incredibly deep when it comes to truly learning how to play the game well. I have over 150 hours in the game and am still learning the nuances.
The game looks like a dream, with excellently represented units from NATO and the Warsaw Pact. Great unit detail and great special effects with the smoke and fire and explosions. Only the infantry modeling leaves a little to be desired. The scaling is also incredible. A spin of the mouse wheel will zoom you in so that a single unit fills your entire screen in wonderful detail. A spin of the wheel in the opposite direction will zoom out to the point that the entire map is visible on your screen.
My only negative is that the SP campaign is absolutely byzantine and unsatisfying. Good luck figuring out how to play it. But the real value of this game is in the SP skirmish mode and MP. MP is brutal, but extremely rewarding after you learn the ropes. You will lose often, but it will never feel cheap. When you lose it is because you screwed up, when you win it is because you were the better player.
Deep, user friendly, and pretty to look at, this is the best RTS on the market.

This game was really fun for the first few hours. I really liked the art style and the interface - the whole aesthetic is pretty charming. It reminded me of what I
I remember SimTower being like. But it didn't take long before the whole thing started to unravel, and its two fatal flaws became abundantly clear.
First, for having such breadth of tenants and services, this game is surprisingly linear. It basically requires you to have significant mixed use in your building to progress, eventually tasking you with meeting more and more of the tenants' needs, starting with mid and high level commercial and dining spaces, and escalating into increasingly specialized and unusual building services. Advanced rooms from the residential tree are locked until you build enough restaurants and stores, and so on.
"All right game," you'll say. "I'd like to build a luxury residential highrise today."
"No," Project Highrise replies. "In order to unlock that luxury apartment type, you must have at least 3 medium restaurants, and at least 2 large category B stores. And you must prepare all your tenants' taxes."
Taken aback, you reply with a simple "WTF?" WTF, indeed.
It's at least plausible that a residential landlord might pay for pet care, laundry services, or other common amenities to entice new wealthy tenants. And it's not inconceivable that office building landlords would offer bottled water, office supply, and courier/mail room services to their tenants directly, instead of contracting them out. But wealth advising? Auditing? Temporary staffing? These are simply not services that a commercial landlord would need or want to provide in the real world. Those services can be provided so much more competently and cheaply by outside companies or individuals that specialize in these kinds of things. You know, like an auditor, a wealth adviser, or a temp agency.
So, in addition to having a restrictive, linear structure, Project Highrise's other major flaw is that it takes place in an artificial vacuum. Outside the building's walls, there are no delis, coffee shops, laundromats, office supply stores, or other things you might expect in your average downtown. Each and every one of your tenants' needs must be met by the building owner, no matter how specific that need is, or how much expertise is required to fulfill it. Even the office workers who commute to the building (presumably from somewhere) and leave at the end of the day must have all their office support needs met by their landlord, and by no one else. If you don't meet enough of their needs, they're liable to just up and move out. Truly, in Project Highrise, it is a Tenant's market. And it's mind boggling.
TLDR: The game looks like SimTower from 1000 feet up, but when you get right down to it its a cute, but linear and weirdly insular tower management game that insists there is only one right way to build a tower in modern society: like a completely self-sufficient city within a city that does everything for everyone.

Well what can I say? A game that takes MOBA style elements in one of its PVP modes that I find it hard to dislike. A satisfying PVE that, while not for everyone, is fun to explore every so often just for a change of pace. They considered a lot of stuff... Though that doesn't mean the game's without flaws.
There are some... ALMOST crippling balance issues. I say almost because the characters that are unbalanced have their counters. Galilea is one such example - far too much damage for her defence, or so I hear, but as an Orendi main I seem to have no problem showing her what for. Your mileage may vary, and I'd pay heed to those words. Devs have said they're gonna nerf the hell out of her.
Pay no heed to those that compare this to Overwatch. They are vastly different games. Battleborn boasts more MOBA-oriented gamemodes in a decidedly PvE-centric manner, with high kill times on player characters and longer, more involved strategies. Overwatch is a quicker game that requires strategy and thinking beforehand, with much more PVP-centric gamemodes and a more modern feature set for the FPS genre.
This game brings FPS and MOBAs together in a pretty great way, and if anyone's scared off by that, I welcome you to really give it a go. In the game's early stages, it's quite easy to get to grips with what a character's capable of and develop your playstyle.

On first glance it might seem that Gearbox has gone flat out insane by deciding to challenge Blizzard's Overwatch with their own team-based FPS, but the truth of the matter is that the games have very little in common once you get past the cartoony graphics and ability-based gunplay.
Whereas Overwatch is a pure team-based FPS most similar to Team Fortress 2, Battleborn draws its inspiration from both Borderlands and Super Monday Night Combat, with the end result being a MOBA that plays like a fast-paced FPS, rather than the opposite. Another key difference is that Battleborn actually features a fairly lengthy campaign that can be played in either singleplayer or co-op, though the overall focus is quite clearly on the competitive multiplayer.
In total the campaign will take you around 7-8 hours to beat if you're simply going for story progression, but if you're looking to complete all of the challenges and the optional hard mode, you can easily double that amount. For the most part I would say I had a great deal of fun with it, especially in multiplayer where you have a whole bunch of people roaming around and cleaning out hordes upon hordes of robots and demons. In many ways these campaign missions feel like dungeons you might find in an MMO, with simple layouts, clear objectives, and tons of 'trash' enemies you need to wipe out before proceeding to a big bad boss. Sadly there is one gigantic issue that I still can't wrap my head around - you're unable to chose which mission you want to do when playing the campaign in multiplayer!
In other words, you might run in to repeat missions while just trying to progress through the story, and hunting down a specific challenge in multiplayer is next to impossible unless you feel like constantly rolling the dice and hoping the correct map appears. I will fully admit I could be missing something here, because none of this makes any sense, but despite trying my damnest I haven't been able to figure out how. This was especially aggravating when my team wiped out on a particularly difficult, and obnoxiously bullet-spongy boss, and then simply dispersed rather than attempting to fight him for another 10 minutes. Since I didn't feel like doing all of it myself, I returned to the matchmaking queue and desperately tried to get the same map again, but to no avail as the system kept tossing me wherever it felt like, which naturally meant anywhere besides the one map I wanted to see.
That puzzling issue aside, its also worth mentioning that you should not be going into Battleborn's campaign with the hope for a good story, because the barely connected shambles of one certainly don't impress. If you're looking for a ton of enemies to explode, power-ups to collect, and bosses to stab in the kneecaps then Battleborn is the game for you, but if you're after a compelling narrative, or characters that are capable of conversing in anything other than puns, then I would suggest you run far, far away and never look back.
As I've mentioned before, Battleborn is at its core a MOBA game that just so happens to involve a whole lot of shooting, rather than an FPS with a bunch of NPCs running about. I don't mean this in a derogatory way, however, as the gunplay and overall movement in Battleborn is far more satisfying than what I've experienced in the recent Doom beta, but the long time-to-kill and the need for good ability usage in order to bring down enemy heroes is something that people looking for a pure team-orientated shooter might not appreciate, so its well worth repeating again.
To explain all of it in detail would take forever, so allow me to simply say it like this: the action is fun, the pace is refreshingly fast, and every single one of the heroes I've tried out played uniquely enough to keep me entertained throughout my dozen hours with the game. There might have been some balance issues here and there, but nothing I couldn't overcome through gratuitous use of explosions, so as far as the core gameplay goes, I have few complaints.
, while Battleborn has the potential to be one of the most interesting MOBA/FPS hybrids out there, it has one gigantic issue that it needs to overcome before it ends up getting anywhere near to that lofty goal. That issue is the fact that Battleborn does next to nothing to discourage players from leaving the game, which means that almost no match actually ends properly!
The most infuriating example of this is when players quit a match before it even begins, and then instead of searching for a new player or just cancelling the match Battleborn starts it anyway, balance be damned! It might not seem like that big of a deal right now as you read this from the comfort of your toilet seat, but after you invest 20 minutes fighting tooth and nail in an insanely close match, the last thing you want to see is "PLAYER X HAS LEFT THE GAME". The moment that message appears you know the pendulum has started swinging, and that no matter how much you struggle, you're going to lose anyway!
I initially had slightly mixed feelings about Battleborn, but after spending a couple of days getting to know its mechanics, heroes, and the overall gameplay style, it began to grow on me. Rather than settling down into a couple of heroes as one might usually do in a new MOBA, I found myself constantly switching around as each hero brought in a new and fresh way of playing that always managed to remain fun.
With all of that said, however, I don't think I'm going to be playing more Battleborn until the matchmaking gets fixed, because there is no worse feeling in a competitive game than doing your very best, and then losing due to factors completely out of your control. Though I will for now leave the rating as a recommendation because I did genuinely enjoy my time with Battleborn, and the issues mostly come from other people being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, but I would still recommend you check the patch notes before deciding on your purchase, just in case.

So here's a ravioli recipe
You will need the following ingredients:
KEY: RAVIOLI, STUFFED PASTA, PASTA + NOODLES
INGREDIENTS
2 cups all-purpose flour
1/2 teaspoon fine sea salt
Pinch of freshly grated nutmeg
1 tablespoon semolina flour, plus more for dusting
3 extra-large eggs
1 tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil
Filling
Now let's get into the fun stuff in just 4 easy steps
Step 1: In a food processor, pulse the flour with the salt, nutmeg and the 1 tablespoon of semolina. Add the eggs and pulse until incorporated. With the machine on, add the olive oil in a thin stream and process just until moistened crumbs form. Turn the crumbs out onto a semolina-dusted work surface and knead just until a smooth dough forms. Wrap the dough in plastic and let stand at room temperature for 30 minutes.
Step 2: Cut the dough into 4 equal pieces and cover with plastic wrap. Work with 1 piece at a time: Flatten the dough into a 5-by-4-inch oval, about 1/2 inch thick. Dust lightly with semolina. Roll the dough through a hand-cranked pasta machine at the widest setting. Fold the dough in thirds (like a letter), then run it through the machine at the same setting, folded edge first. Repeat the folding and rolling once more. Roll the dough through at successively narrower settings, two times per setting, until it is thin enough for you to see the outline of your hand through it. Lay the dough out on a work surface lightly dusted with semolina.
Step 3: Brush any semolina off the dough. Select a shape from the three options below. Fill and cut the ravioli according to the instructions; transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet lightly dusted with semolina. Repeat with the remaining pasta dough and filling.
Step 4: In a large pot of boiling salted water, cook half of the ravioli over high heat until al dente, about 3 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer the ravioli to a platter. Repeat with the remaining ravioli and serve.
Here are 2 helpful suggestions on how to make your ravioli experience a lot better.
1: The uncooked ravioli can be frozen for up to 1 month. Freeze on a large baking sheet in a single layer, then transfer the ravioli to resealable plastic bags.
2: Serve with warmed tomato sauce or freshly grated Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese and melted butter.

And that is how you make the best damn ravioli.

I'll start off this review with a TL:DR; Battleborn is awesome.
It IS NOT OVERWATCH! They are only similar skin deep. Do NOT think this is the same kind of game. This has a campaign, longer TTK and different playstyle. It's a team oriented game first and foremost.
With that out of the way I'll go into more depth. The game has a fun story mode (with dialogue that changes each time you replay the mission for a couple of times.) Lots of fun characters, 25 at the moment if I am not mistaken. So you can certainly find someone to fit your playstyle. On the topic of the characters, their humor is great. Some are rather bland but most are highly entertaining in both playstyle, artstyle and commentary.
Onto the multiplayer (that doesn't have to be!) You can have bots, play co-op against bots, or play true PvP. There's 3 different modes with 2 maps per mode (NOT ENOUGH MAPS but they are all colorful and fun, save for one)
You have Capture which is essentially hold points. Incursion which is closer to a traditional MOBA, get into the enemy base and destroy their sentries while farming and recruiting mercs by beating them at their camps and finally Meltdown which is hilarious and fun. In Meltdown you essentially escort your minions into giant grinders to appease a hilarious God and try to prevent the enemy from doing the same. Destroy, destroy, destroy.
Onto the negatives of the game, every game has them...
The matchmaking is basic as it can be, it does not take into account skill or level and you will often have imbalanced matches. If you can get over this and just play to have fun that's great but a lot of people could be turned off by this lack of any kind of ranking or skill based matchmaking.
The maps do not offer enough variety, as I said it's 2 per mode. What if you dislike a mode? Now you're down 2 maps out of 6.
Finally the game does have some FPS issues. Friends have confirmed it with me.
All in all the game DOES have lots of replayability and lots and lots of fun to be had in the MP if you can simply get over the imbalance and enjoy the humor and crazy action. It has something for everyone with the heroes. Hop in and just have a blast.
I've enjoyed this game so far. Although I would recommend waiting until a sale, because at the time I personally don't think there's enough in the game for the 60 dosh price tag.

Xanadu Next is a distant cousin of FaXanadu, and twice removed from another NES favorite of mine Legacy of the Wizard.
This game is from the golden years of 3d jRPGs, before advancing technology required tens of millions of dollars to appeal to the mass market. Its far from pretty, its controls are finicky, and you might just miss how to advance to the next area in spots due to a sparse (though effective) script. That's how games worked at the turn of the century.
If you like Falcom's other work, XSEED's other localizations, or some of the "off-Broadway" jRPGs of yore, you'll probably enjoy Xanadu next. Think Vagrant Story, Shadow Hearts, King's Field, and maybe just a hint of Quintet (Soulblazer / Illusion of Gaia).

I would definitely recommend this game to a casual gamer who likes murder mystery. It was a surprise when I started playing, not exactly what I had expected.
Purposefully avoiding reading reviews, summaries and clips of the game I dove right in without knowing a single thing about it. It's kind of like playing along with a Murder, She Wrote episode.
The filming is surprisingly crisp quality, so detailed you can see facial hair pores and dandruff on shirts. The acting was good too - my favorite characters were probably James and Ryan. James just because he reminds me of a friend and seems cool (though quirky odd), Ryan because he was a very entertaining, mysterious character - the actor did a really good job interpreting the personality of Ryan. Over all, the characters had a very real feel and as this was filmed in an actual place in actual locations, the scenery of course has a real feel as well. Which really helps to bring it together.
If you are expecting a super interactive game, where you control the walk down the paths, have 360 degree views and such, you will be disappointed. This is a very linear, static game, which is understandable since you are actually playing a movie more so than a game. To put it simply, imagine you are watching a movie and it can't continue until YOU make the next decision (where to go, who to see, what question to ask), the detective in the movie can't piece things together until YOU point out the 'contradictions' in suspects' stories.
Overall, a very simple idea when you break it down to the bare bones, but the execution and presentation of the idea is what matters. And the team at Pneuma Films did a very good job. I hope to see a sequel at some point.
Now all of that being said, the game does have some negative points. Already the linear/static quality of the gameplay will turn off a large portion of people, but I still implore anyone looking for a VERY casual, yet interesting, game to play in between their rounds of CSGO or Fruit Ninja to try it out. It's a short game, only about 6-8 hours if you keep good track of things along with the game system.
The saving system is very frustrating. As far as I can tell, the only time you can save is when you are planning on quitting the whole game (Save and Exit in the Menu). From personal experience, this is a very, very hindersome quality. I... accidentally knocked my tower over while I was playing and that of course caused my computer to shut down. Well, when I got  back into the game, I went from 48% completion to 4%, because I never saved between those two points.
Granted this is my own fault, but I really didn't want to keep quitting the game just to save.
When you are selecting contradictions in peoples' stories, you can't unselect. So, if you accidentally picked the wrong option, you HAVE to pick a second option to get it to clear the first so you can select the appropriate one. Since this doesn't affect the events in game, it really isn't that bad. Just a personal frustration.
This is the first game of it's style that I have played and I highly enjoyed it.
One 'disappointment' I did have is that I thought it would be more like a Choose Your Own Adventure book than a static mystery. It didn't detract from my enjoyment of the game, but it was a thought that popped up a few times while playing. It would be fun to have multiple endings where you could arrest the wrong person or something.
The second disappointment is a bittersweet one. It was the ending. So as not to spoil it for everyone else, to put it simply I was expecting one thing but got the other. While it really wasn't a bad ending, it just was in comparison to what I was expecting. Which I suppose is something real detectives sometimes suffer in their line of work, lol. But still, it felt good to solve the problem no matter what the out come!
Anyway - if you get the chance to play this game, I recommend it.
Also - You can get all achievements on one play through so long as you don't cheat. I looked up the cheating method just because I was curious how you could even cheat in this game. It probably would make more sense if I tried it, but after reading how to do it, I don't see the point as it would completely ruin the game and the whole point of even playing.

I spent 5 hours on this game, and got 47% of the way through (to 9pm).  I found the super linear aspect of this game to be quite frustrating.  While the story is good, and the acting is fun, the gameplay killed it for me.  It boils down to:
Foreach Hour
Systematically visit every location, and ask each suspect every question available.
Each time that this reveals some new information, repeat this process, until the hour advances.
While some smart gameplay can cause you to skip perhaps 20-30% of suspects, I really don't see advancing much faster with better game play.
The gameplay also stalls out sometimes when trying to find a contradiction.  That requires quite a bit more thinking / searching through already seen dialog.
Ultimately, I chose to abandon this game, not because of how hard it was, but simply based on how linear the gameplay was.  Might as well just watch a play-through on youtube, which is exactly what I did.
I would like to see more interactive fiction like this, but please, improve the gameplay to be much less linear, and reward smart gameplay, versus requiring a brute force to find the solution that the developers wanted.  I think the game designers could have acomplished a 2x or 4x better game, with about the same investment of their time and art assets, just by being smart about the actual gameplay.
Ultimately, I can NOT recommend this game.

This game takes everything that was good about the original flash game, and turns it into a package of platforming bliss. The objectives are simple, the controls are a combination of responsive and weighty, the enemies are intuitive, yet deadly. All of this put together in the developers' hand-crafted level designs creates some incredibly satisfying gameplay. For perfectionists, levels attain that Hotline Miami-like rhythm: run, jump, die, restart, do it a little better each time, iterate, iterate, succeed. For the more difficult levels, it can feel like an accomplishment to just figure out how to complete the level, let alone actually performing those actions.
On top of thousands of these levels, there's much more content that's better left untalked about (check all those secret options in the options menu, it's a rabbit-hole of content if you are persistant enough). Additionally, the game contains a level creator and browser, so you can make and discover tons more creative and challenging maps. This is all backed by six hours of trance-inducing electronic music, the repetition being appropriate for this type of gameplay.
To me, this game isn't just a game, but a way to present an example of a perfect platforming system. There's nothing I'd want changed about the mechanics, nothing that I feel another game could do better in this genre. I heartily recommend trying it out.

Star wars Knights of the Old Republic (abbreviated KOTOR) was published by Bioware in July 2003 and is nowadays considered an old school rpg cause it follows a linear gameplay style ( which will be discussed in detail later on) and the typical bioware fighting system in a raw state.

The story in KOTOR is really well written and I would like to give a brief introduction to it without major spoilers. However no introduction can be done without tiny spoiler.

no it doesnt lol.)

1)Find your KOTOR executable (The path is usually: C:"Program files or Program files 86 (depending if you have 32 or a 64 bit operating System) > steam > steamapps > common > swkotor > kotor.exe) You can do so by opening the windows explorer!

~~~~~~~Gameplay~~~~~~~
Typical Bioware stuff is to be expected in this one:
1) You got 3 (Translators note: ? ) of companions which follow and fight with you while also taking to your character and each other.
2) Very long and detailed dialogues with many options to choose.
3) The tactical pause system, which allows you to stop a fight at any moment in order to assign orders to your companions/character

I still own the physical Deluxe Edition of this DSI & DSII and was very excited to see them reach steam so that I can access and install it no matter where I might be in the world. I have probably put roughly 3k hours or more into this game alone.
I still consider this game to be one of the best action RPG's ever created. Rich story and lore, not the greatest but decent voice acting for it's time. In some ways this DSII still puts some of the newer RPG's to shame, and it is easy to see where some of todays RPG's draws it's roots from here.
At first glance the graphics look outdated, since this is not a remake of DSII, one should expect the graphics not to be top notch in comparison to today's titles. But once you zoom in to take a more detailed look at the characters, enemies, weapons, armors, & spells, it is still quite amazing. Far from the majority of cookie cutter RPG's of today DSII still stands out from the rest.
DSII is full of sidequests along with it's main storyline. But best of all true individual party member customization. A choice not truly given in a lot of today's titles. When a character joins your party you are given a "suggestive" path, based on the character's background in the story. But, every character & party member has all the ability trees available to them. You are not forced to build into that characters suggested tree. You want to turn your warrior into a a dual wielding assassin but also have healing, ranged, or combat magic abilites? You can do that. Or a fire wielding combat mage with a bow? You can build that too. A party of all mages? Sure. Picked up a bowman you want to turn into a healing mage? No problem. True freedom to make the party you want. Or even go solo if you want to.
There are still many mods available for DSII out on the net, some of them giving minor changes to complete overhauls or new maps and in a few cases a whole new story and storyline. Want to beat down your enemies with an overpowered pillow? How about pots, pans, spoons & forks? Want to play as one of the enemies in the game? Grab the mods. With all the mods available out there it gives the game a very high replay value.
Since the closing of gamespy, there has been no full internet accessibility. But creating a virtual LAN over the net using a 3rd party program like Hamachi or Tunngle can easily overcome this issue. And the Steam version user can connect to a retail disk user provided they are playing both the same version, example: DSII to DSII, or DSII BW to DSII BW, and same patch version (Since I own a retail copy disk I have been able to test this). If not, then you will not see each other in the LAN lobby. I would like to see cloud support in the future. (It is easiest to add the BW expansion Killa has provided in "guides" to get LAN working as it comes with the original DSII:BW launcher.)
In this review I would also like to thank Killa and everyone else that have done all the work to get the DSI & DSII expansions for steam working and making all the necessary files available. So that all who have purchased it can enjoy the complete classic Dungeon Siege experience. Since DS3 lacks everything that made DSI & DS2 such great games. Also if you enjoy the Dungeon Siege series of games give Space Siege a try, which is a spinoff of the Dungeon Siege series of games set in a fictional future. Unlike Dungeon Siege, however, items are limited much like Shadowgrounds (No relation). Also Space Siege lacks the party play style of Dungeon Siege, and I have not had a chance to test multiplayer on it (unlike DSI & II, Space Siege used GPGNet, & I have not yet had a chance to see if the service still works). But still nonetheless another great game in the Dungeon Siege realm.

is a skyscraper management sim. You'll design a building and attempt to attract businesses as tenants as well as others to live in apartments. You can try to specialize in order to optimize space and upkeep costs; or to mitigate noise/smell complaints between retail and living/office spaces.
As a general rule of thumb, these management games typically have a 3 step cycle.

The problem with this game is there isn't really ever a 3rd step. Not one that is required anyways. The only thing, at least early on, that you need to manage is manually telling workers to renovate offices to avoid grime buildup. Other than that, you'll be spending time allocating office space and making sure things like copy services aren't overburdened. As well as making sure you stay ahead of the utilities demand. Each type of potential tenant has specific things that they'll require to be attracted to your space as a place to conduct business or live. But those thing's are more of a place and forget. Making managing them not really something that ever needs to be looked at aside from clicking on the maintenance office occasionally and informing them what to renovate.
The beginning cycle is rather slow and was the only time I ever needed to be concerned with money. Once I had expanded to 4 floors or so of insurance/finance/creative offices with some places to buy some bagels and coffee along the way and have my services and utilities set in a way that was low upkeep for the number of tenants I was set. I never once went anywhere near the red. Even when city events would happen and people went on strike or the subway went down. It never made a dent. Even when things broke down. Some tenants might leave while it was fixed but were easily replaced by placing an ad or two.
Early on, insurance offices are easy, low rent, not terribly fussy and usually only require copy and/or courier services and an electric line. Maybe a phone line for finance or creative offices but they offer much higher rent. Easily worth more then the small amount it costs to get a phone-line up and running. You can sort of turtle a bunch of them up, place a shop in the entrance or high traffic area and “make them dollar bills y'all”. From there you can expand with relatively low stress. Furthermore, once you place an operations office and earn enough influence, you can automate renovations removing the need for
even sooner. Eventually, you'll build more floors. Replace lower offices with fine dining and large retail stores and build penthouse suites and rooftop cafes among larger offices higher up the tower where more civilized, quiet folk reign.
There is a very rudimentary tech/research tree. Operations, optimizing cost of maintenance and construction. Politics, allows you to expand plot size with a lobbyist for the city. And finally, aesthetics, attracting artists and making the prestige rise faster allowing you to attract larger more fancy businesses in a more expedient nature. But these requirements can be maxed relatively quickly with an even nominally profitable tower.
There are some scenario challenges that are okay but personally I find these type of games sandbox modes to be much more engaging.

Project Highrise is to SimTower, what Stardew valley is to Harvest Moon.
IOW, it takes a formula loved by many, fixes it, improves it, makes it current and then gives it back to the people that have desperately wanted it for ages. Even with that said, I'm happy to consider this game one that can stand on its own in its genre; it doesn't need the Sim Tower comparison, it just helps. It's well made, well thought out and clearly a passion project for its makers.
Some people seem to suggest it's boring, too easy to turn a profit.
I see what they're saying but to me, it really only amounts to 'I perfected playing the game, now it's boring for me because I consider 'winning' to be the only source of enjoyment and keep repeating the same method to achieve it.'
If I were to expand on that though, then I'd offer that, yeah, if you're an experienced management sim player you're likely going to find the sweet spots in this game pretty easily. Even on hard it's not difficult to turn a profit once you know the right type of buildings to get you started and once the profit starts ticking over, you're pretty much on easy street regardless of difficulty. Tenant number fluctuation can add a bit of variety, as can random events but these are still quickly overcome once money stops being a huge issue.
That said, that's not really the point and I don't feel it's a reason to dislike the game. The point here is to make an impressive tower, something nice to look at AND functional, and to enjoy the variety that comes with the initial trial-and-error and ongoing restarts to try new ideas.
There's many areas in this game to scratch various itches, e.g. I spend my time these days pushing new limits and trying new ideas, trying to make buildings that are only one type - the expansion content helps with this, I love making giant hotels - or spacing them out, having individual buildings for apartments, shops, offices, etc. It's also worth mentioning that in most play throughs, if you're not really pushing it, it's still going to take a handful of hours (at least) to get any initial loans paid off, start turning a profit and get your star rating up, which is when you really start being able to expand and build creatively.
This is nothing new though, Sim Tower was the same, as were pretty much all the Sim-games, so also was any of the RCT games, TTDLX, any tycoon game... the list goes on. Anyone with a decent amount of experience can easy smash early game in this genre and be laughing within a fairly short order. That's not really why you play it... well, not what I believe it's about, at least. If that's not your thing, hey, maybe avoid it.
Is there enough content? Ok, well, I have 30 hours currently and I don't think I've built everything. There's also a bunch of cheap content packs that expand on mechanics as well as decoration... so... yeah... not sure what more people expect from a $20 game.
Ha, SimTower cost me $90 when I bought it back in the day, think about that one.
Does Project Highrise get frustrating, or fiddly? Yeah, sometimes... I think generally though, it's pretty good and about as streamlined as it can get. If you're building 10 floors at a time, then sure, laying all the wiring, cabinets, etc, is going to be a pain. I'm not sure what ways around that exist to be honest, someone smarter than me will have to answer that one.
To give it some context, when I first played the game you had to run wiring, etc, along each floor manually. Now, you can auto-fill a whole floor, so obviously this was a common complaint that's now been addressed. Just food for thought there...
Overall, I stand by my initial statement, this is the game that the younger me wished Sim Tower could have been when he played it so many years ago.

I won't say the same for solo play however. I played the game by my lonesome a few times and its by far the worst experience I've ever had. Without the communication that was present with the group I started with I found myself in games where players would not follow through. Players who in many cases just stood behind the turret and never made any effort to advance against the enemy. You have the free hero rotation like that of LoL along with the nauts (champions in LoL) being purchasable with awesome points. Heres where I have to give props to how the F2P aspect was handled. Awesome points are actually fairly easy to obtain and I never feel as though I am being forced into a situation where I can't play at least one naut I enjoy. Since I started playing I've already bought 2 nauts, with 10k saved up as I'm split on who to purchase next. I love how the points are handled, as I said I never feel as though I am being forced into nauts I don't want to play.
Overall:
If you have a group to play with definitely go for it, it's free afterall and as I said the free aspect is handled well.
If you have to play alone I'd find something else frankly, I don't think it's worth the effort.

Myst is an old, classic adventure game from 1993 that casts you on the mysterious island of Myst. You will have to visit different worlds (or,better said, ages) on the behalf of two brothers, Sirrus and Achenar, who are trapped inside their own books and need your help to be released. To this end, you must collect magic pages that are scattered around the various ages.
Myst is a pretty non-linear game: you can access every level from Myst in any order you choose (provided you found the way in) and can decide to return to areas you've already explored later. Myst's puzzles remain fair from the most part, with only some rare exceptions. One could argue that the game could have used an inventory system for the pages: you can carry only one page at a time and, should you find another one and pick it up, the previous one will be returned to its own location. The level's design was Myst's strongest suit at the time of its release and is still noticeable to this day. It's worth mentioning however that the tile is rather short, clocking about five or six hours.
This updated release introduces full 3D navigation for the whole game's world, updated graphics and a bonus (albeit short) age, Rime. The new controls are comfortable enough, although a little unresponsive during some transictions, and the new models give Myst much more life

[First of all, let me just admit that I know the programmer of the game personally. I talk to him online all the time, and I've hung out with him. This does not affect my opinion of the game in the slightest. If I thought the game was bad, I wouldn't be writing this.]
Paranautical Activity is a first-person shooter roguelike set on a nazi U-Boat. If you like shooters there is plenty here to enjoy, if you like roguelikes there's even more, and no two runs will likely ever be the same. Being a roguelike, each of the eight stages is filled with procedurally generated rooms. These rooms are filled with an increasingly difficult selection of enemies, along with a boss, a sub boss, a shop, and bonus rooms with various bonuses and challenges. Each floor is also a race against the clock to beat the the boss and progress before an unkillable phantom comes to hurry you along under threat of murder.
There are several playable characters, each with unique play styles. Some, such as Gorton, require precision but do crazy amounts of damage; and others, such as Dy-No-Mite, allow for a more loose play style at the cost of self-destructive splash damage. There is a selection of super weapons that range from a ninja sword that wrecks shop up close, a cannon that demolishes most things, and a gun that uses its ammunition to create more health, bombs, and armor.
There is a wide selection of items that can help you along (and more than a few that will make your going much tougher). Some can make you immune to explosions. Some can basically remove the cap on your rate of fire. Some can give you much more health at the cost of your speed. Some can make all floors dark. Some can do nothing other than change your character's injured sound to a selection of girlish "Ooches" and "Ouches."
The varied enemy design ranges from rocket-propelled turtles that fire missiles, glowing monkeys that jump back and forth between the floor and ceiling, and sharks that hunger for your feet. Bosses range from a pair of flying eyeballs that divide themselves when they die, a battleship with kamikaze planes circling it, and a nazi scientist that can resurrect the dead.
Though the game doesn't officially release until around halloween, the final content patch just went live a few hours ago, so I feel comfortable finally officially recommending this game to anyone who enjoys the concepts behind it's design. If you like shooters, I recommend this game. If you like roguelikes, I definitely recommend this game. If you like games that marry the two concepts, then I can't imagine why you wouldn't love this game.

Visually the game looks and runs beautifully at a smooth 60 FPS on a 550Ti on maxed everything, there is no pop in and the texture swapping is seamless and unnoticable and textures of units and the environment also all hold up very well under very close scruitiny, allowing you pick out the details of the battlefield in glorious 1080p.

CS games just feel so tight, movement is weird and just doesn't flow or feel natural.
Either way I wanted to give this a go, thinking free game why not...can't be too bad... Well it's horrible... Graphics could easily be upgraded and improved on, pixels...pixels everywhere, just looks bad. Little tutorial help, unless you've never played a first person shooter, tutorial is almost no help. Explains nothing about crafting, items. Clicking through all these daily rewards which there is no info about. What are these items? Why do they matter? How do I use them? Says I unlocked all these guns and got them, but not access to them? Can't equip or use.
In 22 minutes of gameplay i'm already extremely overwhelmed with so many features and options with no tutorial. I have no interest in playing and spending hours going outside of the game to figure out what half of it is, how it works etc. Doesn't take a smart person to realize the game is centered around pay-to-win. Or at least, pay to have fun or get anything good. If this was a game like World Of Warcraft, that makes sense to have purchase options for mounts, its an MMO, you buy that to show it off and have something unique. In a first person shooter, I come to shoot things and have fun, not have to worry about crafting systems, pay-to-win setup or anything like that.
Overall, very clunky, doesn't look or feel good and way too much fluff and pay to win. After exiting, had to shutdown computer because the game was still running even though in task manager, no game was running. I simply cannot fathom how there is any enjoyment or fun in any type of game like this and this is why I cannot recommend it. Like Star Wars, RPG games, and old school game mechanics.
This old title shows us how games should be made.
$10.99
I have over a thousand hours on Dota 2, 700+ on Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, and more than enough on Garry's Mod. So why would I play this game if I have plenty of hours on my other games? There's a simple reason for this.
Bioware. Yes, the timely company turned EA division, makes this game great.
While this game will prove a challenge for people who want non-stop action, this classic title has to be one of the most solid RPG games, if not PC titles ever made. Before I got a Steam account, I played this game with CDs (yes real CDs).
There's actual content to the story, and the plot is well thought out and executed. Your actions will have consequences, and will either lead you down to the light or dark side of the force. Beyond just simple dark vs. light, the game offers other ways of having a unique experience.
Using your repair and computer skills, you can clear rooms filled with enemies, or fix up and alter a robot to fight for you. Want to avoid enemies? There's a stealth skill for that. Want to avoid fights in a bar? The persuasion skill is your go to skill. Maybe you even want to have the most powerful force powers available to you? There's a way to go about that as well. The only limiting part of the game is base story, which should be entertaining and engaging. It can be a little dry, as there is a lack of humor, but this title does very well considering its ESRB rating (Mass Effect isn't in the same boat).
As always, it wouldn't be a Bioware game without companions. Each offers something unique, and will progress your back story which isn't mandatory.
Downsides? Well every game has some which isn't surprising. For being an old title, the graphics are very simple. If you failed to notice the processor requirement of an Intel Pentium 3, then I'm not sure what to say. There's nothing you can really do to improve the graphics of the title, but there are certainly ways to modernize them. By default the game is only compatible with a 4:3 ratio monitor. By using third-party utilities, you can resolve this and get a better experience with a now standard 16:9 monitor.
Being an old school game, it does have all the “attributes” available. Yes, you will have to micro manage things like points in “wisdom” and “dexterity”. If you want to avoid all of that, play with the “auto upgrade” button. The game does also have a “dice roll” system, where there are chances to miss/hit and not do complete damage. Mass Effect 1 carried on from this, in case you were wondering where that game got its mechanic from.
All in all, this title should impress you for being so old, yet being so solid. Why games aren't being made like this anymore, who knows...

It's clear to see why Lovers in a Dangerous Spacetime is universally acclaimed. Besides the pun, it's an imaginative game that is designed for couch co-op with up to 4 players. It's got a loveably charming visual style, great music and mostly fun setpieces. But in my opinion, it is flawed. The first 2 worlds are fun, fast-paced and chaotic even with only 1 other player. The 3rd world starts to become slow, tedious and meandering. Lots of enemies you can't kill, or even can't hit unless you bring them close to a sun.
The 3rd world boss uses all these new, frustrating mechanics and throws them at you while you TRY to hit him within a very short timeframe while also trying to dodge a bunch of stuff. This is super frustrating when you only have 2 people and you want to be moving the ship to have a good angle to line up shots, you want to then shoot him in the short vulnerability frames, while also using the shield to deflect the 2 or 3 cardinal directions from which the sun, icicles, his legs and body are all coming at you from. With 4 people I could see this being a breeze because you can cover most ground while also taking advantage and doing the most amount of damage after making the boss vulnerable. With 2 people there's about 5 seconds for every minute where you get to do anything other than fly around and dodge. You're also waiting for him to throw out a sun this whole time because otherwise you literally can't do anything to him.
Anyway, that's so far the worst part of the game and it's one that only seems relevant with 1 or 2 players. Everything before that ranges from enjoyable to amazing. If all you want to do is play a pleasant co-op experience with a friend or partner... I think there's better games out there. If you have 3 other people then you will probably love this wholeheartedly throughout Lovers runtime. Me? I liked it. It's good but imperfect. So I recommend it with that warning of difficulty spikes and exercises in tedium.

I find this game very fun to play. It's fast paced, the characters are actually interesting and the game looks nice.
There are a few balancing issues in the game, but it was just released; that's to be expected (not nearly as bad as some of the balancing problems in Overwatch right now; looking at you, Zenyatta. You're so weak you're almost unplayable...). Mostly just 1 character in all honesty, you see her every game. Galilea for those who haven't played yet.
Not enough supports in my opinion right now, but the ones we do have are actually nice. Though Miko is the best one in general, sadly. Would be nice to get more, which we probably will.
Character personalities are very well done, I personally find myself playing Shayne and Aurox constantly. Great fun to be had there.
Story missions can be very long and grindy, but that's after you've beaten them and simply wish to get silver or gold. First time going through? Very fun, long, fleshed out, and it tends to be funny. You can see allot of Borderlands style in the game.
While there are downsides in the game, they are very forgivable when you look at the big picture. The game is worth it in my opinion, I don't regret buying it at full price. If you're looking for a fun multiplayer game to play, this one's a great one to look into.

Xanadu Next is a 2005 PC game from Falcom which has been recently ported over to Steam with some minor tweaks and updates.
It's an action RPG that pits you in the role of a Knight and his companion (and Sister), Char. They are in search of a mythical castle known as Castle Strangerock. This journey brings them to a town which ends up being the main hub of the game. Around the town lie ruins, forests, mountains and much more for you to explore.
If you like Action RPGs, you need to play Xanadu Next! I've never heard of it myself until it was released on steam and I simply picked it up out of curiousity. It blew me away and I've been addicted to it since.
There was some issues on itial release but around 5 patches got released within minutes of the game releasing on steam. The team were actively searching for issues that users were encountering with the game and hot patching them instantly. It was amazing to see such a swift response in this day and age.
I mainly used an Xbox 360 controller to play the game. It works nicely but has an issue with the Inventory (all controllers do). The original Xanadu Next from 2005 had no controller support at all, so this was esentially patched onto the the game. The inventory still looks for a mouse control which is something the team haven't been able to overcome yet. Thankfully they implemented a way around this. There is a button on the 360 controller you can hold to begin emulating a mouse, it's a bit awkward but it gets the job done. Honestly, it works perfectly with a Steam Controller and I highly recommend using a Steam Controller if at all possible.
The graphics are date now in 2016 but there are methods to sharpen them. A quick google search of "Xanadu Next Nvidia Inspector" should bring you to a Neogaf thread where users are attempting to gain the best visuals possible from the game.
All in all, I HIGHLY recommend Xanadu Next to users who love Action RPGs.
Here is a short list of games I would compare it to:
- Dark Souls Series (especially in terms of difficulty)
- Baldurs Gate: Dark Alliance Series
- Vagrant Story
- Diablo Series (without the massive amount of loot and less enemies)

Firstly, I'd like to point out that this game is still getting more content added to it gradually. So this review is to reflect -current- gameplay and content.
I have greatly enjoyed Paranautival Activity, and it has probably frustrated me about as much as Binding of Isaac has with regards to finding hard bosses, picking up bad items for my build, etc.
If you like games similar to Binding of Isaac or Tower of Guns, this one is a great middle ground. The weapons all have their own advantages (Personally, the sickle is the best weapon in the game hands down) and each item is useful in its own right and can add interesting or frustrating abilities. For example, one item gives you the same jumping mechanic as VVVVVV has, that is, switching gravity and standing on the ceiling instead of jumping. It's cool, but can be a huge pain sometimes.
The enemies are all interesting and difficult in their own right, and certain builds will find some enemies easier than others. I'd give the graphics, gameplay and amount of current content a good 8/10. I'm extremely excited about more stuff being released when the time comes, as I'm sure I'll come back to this game more.

I really want to like this game, I really do, but in it's current state and at it's current price, I can't. Paranautical is a rouge-like first person shooter, think Binding of Issac, mixed with Bioshock, which is a beautiful idea, and the 3D pixelated graphics give it a lot of charm, but that's about where charm ends, being a first person shooter, Paranautical Activity is very unforgiving, to put it in perspective I have beat The Binding of Issac multiple times, with multiple charcters, but with Paranautical Activity I'm lucky if I can make it passed the first floor. A lot of the trobule is you are constantly surrounded by enemies, which normally is'nt so bad, but like most FPS when you take damage there is usually a damage indicator, so you know which direction to turn and shoot, not with Paranautical Activity, so you figure that you'll use explosives to handle everything, well that's where another game breaking flaw shows it's ugly head, when you kill an enemy it burst into red pixels that skatter onto the floor and stay there for a few seconds, not bad right? Well every explosion also has a particle effect to the same degree, just orange pixels, so if you kill a group of enemies with an explosion you're in for a lot of particles, and unfourtately the game can't take all the pixels on screen, so it starts to lag real bad, and I know it's not my computer, because I can run games like Skyrim, and Dark Souls with no problems. So there is a lot of good in this game, it's got a great idea, all it needs to do is fix some bugs, but it seems like the developers don't want to fix anything, and until they do, or until they lower the price, I can't reccomend this game, however, if you can find the game for cheap, and you wanna kill a hour or two, pick it up.
