This Character Creator pack's review will be very similar to that which I wrote for the main Indie Bundle Graphics pack, which I backed on Kickstarter in the middle of 2012.
Like sound tracks on Steam, you are not buying an application. You're buying a bunch of content that downloads to your system and will be accessed directly.
This bundle comes with a large amount of content (often broken into pieces, so you can assemble them for a much larger variety of funished pieces) that can be used in prototyping your games, finished games, websites, and just about anything else. Personally, I use it for prototyping my projects (and possibly hiring an artist for custom work, when all is said and done).
At the time of writing, there are almost 1,300 images in this pack. For someone with no pixel-art talent, the character creator bundle is particularly useful for me. I no longer just copy and paste in ridiculous clip art from the web as placeholders or use big grey blobs to represent characters - I refer to the art pack and pull out *actual* artwork to make *actual* characters.
Anyone who would scoff at the price either doesn't actually need artwork or has not dealt with commissioning or licensing actual artwork for games or other projects. I have. You'll usually wind up with a lot more strings limiting your use of the content and you'll pay more than this entire pack costs just for one piece of art work - whether commissioned specifically for you or just licensed from an existing royalty-free clearing house.
If you don't know if you need or want this art bundle, then you probably don't. But you
if you do. And for the price, it's hard to pass up.

I've just bought this and taken a quick look at it and I like what I see so far. This graphics pack is a valuable asset for those making (pixel art) RPG games and could easily be used with the RPG Maker series (though you do have some work to make it compatible). But aside from RPG Maker you can also use the characters for any other 2D engine.
Characters you create will be around 125px high and 50px wide and you have about 6 base bodies to build upon. With the body, head and facials being all seperate elements the sky is the limit when making your characters. Add one of the few dozen clohing items (also seperate elements) to the character and you're close to an infinite number of characters you can make.
With the PLUS, there's also a CON to the system. With these models being made with RPG Maker in mind (though too big for that), there's not much room for animation in other engines aside from the 'fixed' RPG Maker animations. I want to incorporate these models into my Unity RPG game I'll be making and animate them with Spine (awesome skeleton animation tool,  not on Steam) and that'll mean that I have a lot of work to do and I'm not sure how it'll come out from the pixel art style the pack has.
An other CON is the clothing for your character, there are also a lot of 'loose items' in there that don't seem to match with anything and there's a lot of 'fixed' sets as well, where you somewhat *MUST* match them, lowering your freedom of choice in sets.
In all, I think this pack is certainly worth to grab if you want to make a fantasy RPG and are in need of a flexible character creation system...

So...I gave this a "yes" vote mainly because there isn't a "maybe".  The orignal Myst was one of the all-time greats, but it has to be taken in the context of the time when it appeared.  21 years have passed since then and it certainly wouldn't do so well today, when people expect full 3D accelerated graphics, full motion video, etc.  realMyst is an attempt to remake the game with these expectations in mind, perhaps to introduce the game to a new audience, to draw back folks like me who played it when it was new, and of course, to make a few bucks.  By the way, this is the third time they've updated the game and re-released it (not counting ports of the original game to many platforms).
So how well does it work?  Well, it's not great - pretty good maybe.  The 3D engine seems poorly optimized.  Even on decent hardware it runs slowly, especially with the graphics cranked up.  The controls are clumsy, especially the mouse-look functions.  For some reason the game is very dark - they added day/night cycles and it seems to be perpetually night, and indoor locations are often so dark as to be unplayable.  For this reason, a flashlight has been added to the game, which is a necessity most of the time, but it really takes away from the game's visuals to only be able to see well in the spotlight.
On the other hand, everything from the original game is here, you can move around somewhat unrestricted compared to the static screens in the original game, and when the lights are on it looks pretty nice.  The story is somewhat timeless and still "plays" well today.
Here are a few notes on what I had to do to make the game playable (on a system with a 3.4 Ghz core i7 processor, 16 gigs of ram and a Radeon HD 6970M graphics chipset with another gig of ram).
1. Turn down the resolution
2. Turn down some of the effects
3. Learn to ALWAYS mouse-look with the right mouse button - you don't have to do this while walking, but you do have to do this while standing still, and switching back and forth between methods is too confusing
4. Keep the flashlight on at all times except when the glare obscures something on the screen
5. Press shift while walking to speed up - otherwise movement is very slow
A couple of other notes - there are a ton of hint guides for this game.  Try not to use them.  It's not a long game, the puzzles are meant to be challenging, and if you buzz through it with a lot of hints it will definitely not be worth $18.  Some of the hint guides may even be wrong in some particulars (correction, ARE wrong in some particulars).  Look at everything.  READ everything.  Take notes.  Relax and play at an easy pace.  Despite being 21 years old, Myst still has a great story, some neat moments, some fun puzzles - it CAN be worth the $18.

This is the best remake of Myst out there at the moment, and the definitive playable rendition of the game by my reckoning.  Myst is one of the most accessible classics in the point-and-click adventure genre, emphasizing with its sheer simplicity the joy of the exploration and puzzle-solving without ever coming off as overly contrived or campy.  The visuals are striking, the worlds are rich with lore and characterization, the central murder mystery is compelling and subtle, and the puzzles are never so abstruse as to be unsolvable (as Riven, Myst's sequel, sometimes errs).  For those familiar with the Myst games, realMyst: Masterpiece combines the HD graphic quality of Myst: Masterpiece edition with the full 3D world offered by realMyst (including Rime, the extra age, and day/night progression in all the ages), and does so quite successfully.  The game gives you the option whether to play in full 3D (which is pretty well-executed, though it can be glitchy in places), or according to the game's original advance-by-clicking controls, offering hard-core Myst fans an experience more true to the original game.  The visuals are updated across the board, and many nice touches have been included in this edition that enhance (in my opinion) the Myst experience.  In short, this is the new Gold Standard for Myst, and I highly recommend the game to everyone: gamers, non-gamers, and Myst fans alike.

Vanilla Myst had two major issues, and with this game one of them has been fixed.
The first issue is the nature of the puzzles themselves. Although they are deliciously challenging at times, there is quite a bit of 'find solution, write down solution, walk across map, apply solution'. This will never be fixed, but it certainly doesn't make the game anything less than spectacular.
The other issue, and by far the most severe issue, was how old the damn game was. Assuming you could even get it to start, you had to find a legacy version of Quicktime and were playing the game in 320x240 which some monitors don't even support anymore. A side effect of it's age was the graphics quality being garbage. Usually I can overlook graphics in a well-crafted game, but when a game relies so heavily on immersion and observation, and is prerendered with zero fluidity of movement, having visuals as poor as Myst's simply detracts from the overall experience.
It is for these two reasons that I had trouble getting people into the Myst series. Riven, which is quite possibly the greatest game of all time, relies on players having experienced Myst's universe and story. So you were left with two choices: Wrestle Myst into submission and persuade yourself to beat it, where the only redeeming factor at this point is it's imperfect puzzles, or play the also-ugly and also-buggy realMyst.
With the release of realMyst Masterpiece, I can finally say that Myst is fixed. While the graphics aren't quite perfect, and there are still a few cosmetic bugs, and the puzzles are the same puzzles as ever, I feel like this game actually deserves to be Riven's prequel.
In short, there is no longer any reason why you should not play through realMyst Masterpiece and then play Riven.

I specifically remember playing Myst back when I was 5 or 6, didn't realize what I was doing at the time, but I thought it was really cool how the game looked and played. This was basically the game that made me really like computer games.

For the first time, you are able to walk around the island and the Ages, able to take in every detal. The only things that were kept from the original Myst were the sound files and the original actor videos. I'm very happy to finally play Myst the way I believe it was meant to be. Not only has this pretty much been a nostalgia trip for me, it also brings Myst to the modern age where high graphics and the "first person" dominates so today's generation can appreciate the game.

I highly recommend anyone get this, whether you traveled to Myst 20 years ago, or are looking to get into the series now, this is the perfect way to bring yourself into the world of Myst.

I'm a fan of the Myst series going back to the original release and am even a proud backer of Obduction, the recent successful Kickstarter by Cyan, but I must confess I'm rather disappointed by this latest remastered version of their original blockbuster. Sure, the game replicates the fundamental details of Myst, but the new graphics are quite shoddy in my opinion. When the first edition of realMyst arrived many years ago, it genuinely pushed the limits of the 3D hardware available at the time. Initially it was heavily criticized for poor optimization, yet paired with the right hardware and with subsequent patches, looked quite excellent for its day. The presentation with realMyst: Masterpiece Edition, however, might have been passable 5 years ago, but it's distinctly behind the pack for what's acceptable today, even factoring in that Cyan is a sort of indie developer lately. Textures and other details are soft, while the lighting is harsh and unrealistic. Perhaps this approach was taken to make the title easily adaptable for portable devices and low-end systems. In any case, the dated and simple graphics don't warrant the cost on PC if you've already played any of the previous versions. It's also a shame in my opinion that Cyan continues to use their one mega-hit as a crutch, when perhaps their time might have been better spent creating a real-time 3D version of Riven or possibly remastering one or more of the other sequels. Given these results it might have been better still if they'd simply remastered the original game using pre-rendered graphics, but possibly at 2k or 4k resolution. It surely would be more impressive visually than what we have here. If nothing else it was lush graphics that consistently defined the Myst series. This rendition sadly fails to live up to that legacy.

Great game. A delicious mix of Agatha Christie, Midsommer Murders, and contemporary thrillers. You play the part of Jenks, a policeman investigating the death of Kate Vine. As Jenks investigates the case in a quaint little English village, he learns that it may not be quite so quaint and cute after all. Secrets, lies, hidden agendas abound as Jenks learns that there was more to Kate’s demise than meets the eye.
Harkening back to the golden years of FMV adventure gaming, Contradiction goes some way to recapturing the highlights of that time. FMV adventure games went the way of the dodo in the late ‘90s, due to the rising costs involved and the twilight of the adventure game genre. So, it’s great to see it’s emergence here.
Now that is not to say that Contradiction has the same level of sophistication of the old favourites of the genre, such as The Pandora Directive or Phantasmagoria, as Baggy Cat was working within a very tight budget. The mechanic is therefore much simplified, but this does add some degree to nuance to the game’s primary mechanic. As the title suggests, the main method of progressing the plot is to spot contradictions and inconsistences in the responses of the people Jenks questions. Catching a character in a lie will usually prompt them to give Jenks a new piece of information to further the case. Some of these contradictions are easy to spot; others call for you to have been paying close attention to cut scenes and the story. As I say, this is a deceptively simple game mechanic, and it gets you to look deep into the story and nut-out who has been telling ‘porky-pies.’
The acting is quite good, overall. One of the old beefs with FMV games was horrendous actors, but Contradiction—while hammy at certain points—comprises believable and relatable acting. You come to feel like you know the characters, how they think, and what they might be concealing from you. Filmed on location in an English town, the overall atmosphere is great. The music is another high point and perfectly suited to the mystery setting.
I have few gripes with the game, most of which can be attributed to its limited budget. The games UI can glitch out from time to time, but this can usually be solved by performing an action to reset the UI—replaying an answer or moving to a new location. The character of Jenks is also somewhat incongruous. A cop with a sort of wing-bat demeanour, a stickler for the rules and yet he performs several searches without a warrant. Also, he is investigating the murder all by himself. Aside from being able to the call the police chief, there are no supporting officers…in a murder investigation! This is probably a budget issue, to keep the cast list low, but it still strikes one as ‘off.’ It may have been easier to swallow if he were a PI, rather than a cop? My last niggle is that there were occasions where it does seem that characters make contradictions, but the game does not recognize them as such. In the interests of keeping this review spoiler free, I will not go into details. It only happened a handful of times, but it can be quite vexing.
On the whole, I loved the game. The engaging story and nicely developed atmosphere made for a highly immersive experience. If you like a good mystery, I would recommend you try Contradiction.

I didn't know what to expect of Xanadu Next, the only thing I knew were:
- ~10 Years old
- Plays Like a mix of Diablo/Nox/etc and Metroidvania

Verdict:
Really enjoyable experience! Finished the game yesterday. They really made the mixture work. It doesn't even resemble Diablo to 100%. The combat system is a hybrid of Ys & Diablo I'd say. Through clever positioning you can get a lot of mileage in this game.
The skill & stat system is also different. Through leveling of weapons you unlock their given skills. That means you have to switch weapons a lot, if you want to have a lot of selectable skills! Only the unlocking of spells resembles Diablo 1, which is done by reading Books you can find or buy in shops. The Stats are also negligible most of the time. Your weapons and armor are the only things which dictate your character development. Not much variation on that end.
But there's no need for that to be honest. Xanadu Next is a story driven game, as usual with games made by Falcom, with interesting puzzles, dungeons and boss fights. So if you want to explore a world, with backtracking through new unlocked items, give Xanadu Next a shot! Really fun Game!

Having finished the game last night, and planning to play it through multiple times, given that there's a ranking system in place that rates your performance on things like speed, damage dealt, damage received and character level when you killed the final boss
(it's 100% spoiler-free), I decided to chime my review in.
First, to clear some common misconceptions. The first is the that people believe that Xanadu Next is like an Ys game. Ys games barely have any puzzles, Xanadu Next does and the puzzles are close to what Alundra had, where you push boxes around, you destroy the environment and use your items creatively.
It's a lot more stat-focused than Ys, but not entirely stat/loot-focused like Diablo. It has less action focus than Ys, and has a lot of puzzles instead. The combat is more about positioning your character, flanking and attacking from behind while avoiding attacks than just tanking and attacking, and most of the skills assist with that sort of thing (pushing enemies away and such). If it sounds like a mouse cursored Dark Souls, it kinda plays like it, but instead of rolling you move your character around with no invisibility frames whatsoever. Sure, you can try to face-attack your enemies, but expect to see "DODGE" written a lot while you're hammering potions and go back and forth to town to replenish. And forget about grinding levels instead of trying to get good, since Falcom games are notorious for having anti-grinding mechanics. If you're dying, it's your fault, unless you do 5-10 damage in a 500 hp monster. Actually, I beated a boss like that, but the fight lasted a while, I'm good at dodging though. All attacks can be evaded, theoretically speaking you can zero damage the entire game WHEN THEY'LL FIX THE FRICKING FIRE OOZE EXPLOSION RANGE BUG *throws tandrum afk*.
To expand on the "git gud" instead of "git grinding" claim: Because there's a "level down" system in the game (you need to ask a certain NPC to level you down), with the right items you can achieve perfect level ranking by killing the final boss as level 1. While you cannot avoid leveling and gear matters (it's an RPG, OBVIOUSLY!), it's not the end of everything.
Yeah, the game has bugs and bugs, like your mouse and skill dragging misbehave if you play on any resolution that isn't your desktop resolution, flickering, and like the fire oozes I cannot tell the difference between bugs and features. So, while I hesitate to recommend this game in its current state, because the time I'm writing this the game was out for 3-4 days so it's buggy.
But evaluating the core game, I got what I expected: Zelda marrying Dark Souls with Diablo mouse and keyboard movement, a skill system that lets you learn abilities from weapons the more you use them, hair-pulling puzzles, and "git gud" traits that forces you to grind only if you're really bad. But seriously I'm more fan of the "Dark Souls"-esque methodical combat system of Xanadu Next or "Dynasty Warriors"-esque combat system of Diablo.
If you clicked the screenshot I linked at the beginning, you'll also see my play time. Subtract a few hours because I suck at solving puzzles and because I was wandering at times not knowing where to go and you'll get 14-15 hours. But again, it has some replay value in that you can play the game again for higher ranking or do the optional dungeon (it requires an event to trigger the entrance opening which happens a bit before the final boss fight), which is supposedly random-generated room placement, but I don't expect to have my mind blown, since this isn't a loot-grinding game like Diablo.

‘Cinematic’ is probably the best word to describe this game, as everything about it seems designed to be absolutely gorgeous to watch – from the stunning graphics and excellent in-game set pieces, even to the gameplay mechanics. But that visual excellence comes at a price in gameplay. Ryse is one of those titles that makes me wish there was a neutral ground for recommend, as I don’t really want to recommend the game in the traditional sense – but it isn’t a bad game, and I don’t want to give it a ‘negative’ review.
The gameplay is fairly simple QuickTime based. You block, and attack, taking cues for when to do what from the animation of the enemy. If you are fast enough, you do more damage or whatever. The most annoying aspect of the game is that it isn’t possible to choose who to attack – and sometimes I’ll block or attack based on the animation of one enemy, only to have my character go careering across the screen to attack another, and mistime it.
When enemies reach low enough health, you can ‘execute’ them – a pre-animated, often brutal, cinematic kill with slow-motion and shifting camera angles. At first they were disorientating, but after a few they meld seamlessly into the rest of the game, adding to its cinematic excellence. As you level up, you unlock more execution animations, but I don’t think they affect gameplay in any way.
Aside from the standard combat, there are set events where you command a legion, move forwards and backwards, raise shields and throw pilum. Mechanically, it’s simple, but again this is all about the cinematic touch and these events are, if not fun in a gameplay sense, definitely enjoyable. Other times you make tactical choices – do you want your legion to cover the left or the right flank, while you do the other? Do you want your archers to focus on the enemy foot soldiers running up to face you, or the enemy archers keeping back?  It often feels arbitrary which choice to make, as there is usually no obvious pros and cons to either decision. At the end of the day whichever choice you make, the rest of the battle plays out the same, just on the left or the right flank.
So gameplay-wise the game is meh, but the cinematic focus combined with some stunning levels make Ryse genuinely enjoyable to play-through, and it feels a bit strange to be recommending a game based entirely on that – but here we are. If you are a fan of quick-time based combat games, you probably can’t go wrong with Ryse, and if you are not – like me – you can set it to easy and play through for the thoroughly decent story and fantastic visuals, and still have a good time. Although I wouldn’t call the game fun, it is definitely enjoyable.

The most important thing to know about Battleborn is that it's not Borderlands. It shares some ideas that Borderlands has pioneered and popularised, such as the 'shoot-and-loot' gameplay, and a distinct, cartoon-like art style that helps blend punchy, rewarding action with occasional bursts of light-hearted humour, but it's not a spiritual successor to Borderlands in any way.
In essense, I believe Gearbox has taken the many concepts behind the mechanics and setup of Aliens: Colonial Marines and improved them greatly. This comparison is not a smear, but rather a sign of hope - the same developers who developed the egregious insult to the franchise that A:CO was have been able to pull off an incredibly fun, captivating new IP without recycling too much from previous games.
Above all, this game is fun. It's designed to be fun, be it played solo or with friends, and the gear progression will keep those who obsess over stats and RPG elements interested for many playthroughs after the relatively short and superficial campaign has finished.

The leader of an arguably evil empire has struck a deal with otherworldly monster aliens to serve them rather than die at their hands and now the rest of his empire along with four other factions are forced to work together on a last stand at the last surviving star in the universe before it too goes out against their former ruler. Who wasn't even a real ruler, he just usurped the throne from a beloved Empress, the dastard.
Like Borderlands, Battleborn takes every thinkable (and several unthinkable) reference and trope in sci-fi and fantasy and throws them into the blender to create its world - so you have more lunky awkward robots to laugh at and pound away, walking shout-outs and awesome walk-away-from-explosion scenes to enjoy. The visual side is seriously informed by saturday morning cartoons as evidenced by the badassful animated introduction that replaced the pre-rendered 3D animations of the Beta.
Unlike Borderlands, Battleborn is built to focus on multiplayer. You can still do stuff solo - but it won't be "real" solo, as you'd be essentially playing co-op mode alone. Yes, it's always-online, but the retail version is yet to fail me even once on connection issues, whether in solo, co-op or competitive play.
So...
Competitive modes are variations on MOBA themes: there's a traditional "help minions (creeps, whatevs) traverse the landscape, reach objective, hurt objective", a variational "escort minions through the landscape so they can sacrifice themselves at an altar" and a "hmm, how about we actually CAPTURE some objectives?" mode, each with their own maps  (initial release comes with two maps for each mode).
Story mode is eight-and-a-prologue huge Borderlands-ish levels offering 20 to 40 minutes of play (on average, depends on difficulty mode and the skill level of everyone involved) with lots of quippy dialogue some of which actively varies depending on party composition which should help a bit with replay value as you unlock more heroes.
MOBA-style, there's gear that's sort of persistent between characters, which you obtain through an in-game store (only in-game currency, no MTs here!) or random drops in story missions, which you arrange into sets of three items and activate mid-game when you have enough energy shards (normally used to pay for in-mission things such as buildables, summonable allies and so on) -- providing balancing in the fact that awesomer gear is exponentially more expensive to activate.
Another balancing thing, you start each level - story or battle - at Lv1, and can progress up to Lv10, unlocking dual either-or upgrades at each level. As you play more as a single character, you may unlock extra either/or/or options for some levels, adding new build possibilities which may drastically change the way a character plays.
It's an entertaining after-work time-burner that has enough capacity and variety to survive binge play, but its overall longevity will be highly dependant on whether the DLC packs will bring enough new content (aside from new characters, the plans are only to add five more) to make the game last long enough until Borderlands 3.
Mandatory disclaimer for people who cannot differentiate between Battleborn and Overwatch: Overwatch is the one with the worse hype-to-game-content ratio. Battleborn is the one that isn't a reskin of Team Fortress 2. Overwatch is the one that advertises inclusivity but doesn't bother confirming it. Battleborn is the one that demonstrates it. Overwatch is the one with the Pixar-style animated scenes. Battleborn is the one with the 2D-animated ones. Overwatch isn't on Steam. Battleborn is. Overwatch is from the guys that failed to bring you Warcraft Lord of the Clans. Battleborn is from the guys that brought you Duke Nukem Forev-- okay, I probably should've skipped that one.

Balance in MOBAs is a thing that should always be centered, however with this game, there's always stronger characters than others, and playing meta characters always gives you an edge, especially in the dreaded solo queue. With the addition of the XP system, carrying a team when you have been matched with poor teammates due to the matchmaking system not functioning anywhere near up to par is extremely difficult and near impossible because their poor playing affects the entire team strength.
In terms of community, the one present in this game is typical cancerous toxic MOBA community. Nobody is wrong, everything is always everybody else's fault, and no advice is taken critically and without return flaming. Servers, or lack thereof, has and will always be a huge detrimental factor in this game alongside the poor netcode. The year was 1993. The CD-ROM format was expected to fail by analysts. There was no reason for most consumers to even purchase a CD-ROM Drive. Nearly every computer game was still being published and sold on floppy discs. Consumers NEVER had any files large than a few megabytes to store. Video on computers weren't really a thing. Nobody had digital camers or camcorders. There were no vast amounts of photos to store. Heck, the average hard drive at the time was smaller than a CD-ROM's 700 MB. Usually half that size. There were virtualy no reasons at all why a consumer would ever need a CD reader in their computer, unless they wanted to play music over their PC speakers. And who would want to do that? Most experts expected the CD-ROM to die as a format.
And then Myst was released.
Looking back at the original game, it looks primitive. It's barely anything more than a bunch of pictures you click through and interact with to solve puzzles. There were a few videos and the audio was ever present, but that was it.
However, at the time, this was amazing. There weren't many games that offered a beautiful first person view like this. Even though the game consisted entirely of pre-rendered pictures, the game really made you feel like you were there. The developers were forced to create wonderful ambient sounds and a deep enthralling theme and story to really suck you in. The game was met by critical reception and acclaim.
And it saved the CD-ROM format. After Myst, EVERYONE was releasing their game on CD. It was a truly successful game, even netting it it's own parody game in the form of Pyst, developed by Parrotty Interactive, starring John Goodman.
The year was 1997.
I was eight years old and my dad had purchase our first computer. I can still remember watching him play. He LOVED the game. I think he spent hours reading the in-game books, pouring over puzzles, and making notes in his little Myst notebook. I grew up playing the original Myst and all of it's remakes. However, it's been around 14 years since I last played the game.
realMyst: Masterpiece Edition is an excellent modern interpretation of the original realMyst that was an excellent then-modern interpretation of the original Myst. Unfortunately the original realMyst lags horribly on Windows 7 and the other Myst remakes crash a lot, so this is your only bet.
It's a beautiful game, with all of the original depth, originality, and puzzly goodness of the original Myst and realMyst. Except this games has Anisotropy! And grass!
Truly, the graphics are stunningly beautiful, I can't say that enough. And the day/night cycle really makes the island feel more alive than it did before. Now, if they'd just patch in some weather effects.
However, the optimization of the graphics and performance is a bit poor. My laptop is by no means a powerhorse, however I have no problem running Skyrim or GTA IV at medium graphics. realMyst ME doesn't do so well on my computer. Anything mid-range or higher causes my FPS to drop pretty quickly. However, the game is still beautiful and an improvement at the lower settings.
The story to this game is basic, as it is a product of it's time. There was only so much room on CD-ROMs! Speaking of which, the game is also a bit short. Your hour will vary depending on how clever you are or if you've played Myst before. I, surprisingly, remembered a lot more than I thought I would and I finished the game shortly under ten hours. But your mileage really may vary. It takes a while to really learn what to do when starting out. You have to read the in-game books and really get inside your head a bit to figure it out. Don't rush in and give up on each puzzle after a minute if the solution isn't apparent. Think about what you've seen or read and see where it might fit into the world or on each level.
This game is a classic and monstrously fun. If you enjoy it, make sure to look out for the Starry Expanse Project who are currently making realRiven, the sequel to Myst. Also, the original Riven is on Steam and doesn't seem to share the compatibility issues the other Myst titles do.
Really, it's not a bad deal for the price, especially if you own the original realMyst, giving you the 33 % discount. Enjoy the game!

realMyst-Masterpiece is the game Myst wanted to be 20 years ago, but runs happily on Windows 8!  I'm happy there's a point-and-click mode (in addition to the free-walk mode), and that the point-and-click fully animates transitions.  I'm ecstatic that the world now has solar cycles, and that you get a flashlight, and that the puzzles are unchanged.
I'm less excited that the graphics are not as eye-popping as the original graphics appeared to be 20 years ago.  Granted, the original graphics by today's standards are crap; still, realMyst uses rendered textures in a typical 3D engine, so it looks "good" but not "great".  (Though, I'm a bit of graphics nerd, so I notice things like the lack of volume rendering and specular highlights.  It's still good though.)
Curiously, the added age (Rime) has no actual point.  It has three puzzles (a stove, an elevator, and some crystals).  It has places you can go to, things you can look at, and switches to flip that have nothing to do with any puzzle.  It feels like they stopped halfway developing it.  But, getting to it was a very well-done extension to the classical Myst game.

A year or so ago I was feeling nostalgic, and I attempted to load up my old copy of the original realMyst (from disc). Sadly, the game simply won't run on a modern machine without constantly crashing, and I gave up hope of experiencing the game again. So I was all the more delighted when I found out about realMyst: Masterpiece Edition, which I picked up the day it was quietly released on Steam. I'm glad to say that this game has all the greatness of the original, with the added bonus of better graphics and the inclusion of the original game's artwork.
For the uninitiated, realMyst is the 3D recreation of the original Myst game, which was released all the way back in 1993. Once an adventure created through still images and small inset videos, the world is fully eplorable and features all the neat things one expects to see in modern 3D game worlds, thanks to the Unity game engine. Added ambient effects include a day/night cycle and weather on Myst and many of the Ages, motion blur, depth of field, and a toggleable flashlight. It's also possible to set the game to jump between all the camera angles from the original game, but transition in 3D between clicks. It's a little bit bumpy at times, but helps strike a good balance between the new graphics and the underlying game of the past.
All the familiar sound effects and music from the original game are here as well, only in higher fidelity.
I have only minor complaints with realMyst: ME - mostly surrounding disparities between the control mechanics of certain puzzles, but none of which are really worth mentioning here. I also feel like some of the textures and 3D models could have been created at a higher resolution in places, but overall, things look pretty good.
I definitely recommend realMyst: Masterpiece Edition. It's a mostly faithful remake of Myst, and a great way to see the game realized on modern hardware, for fans of the series and newcomers alike.

I hadn't heard of the N series before discovering this game (so no comparisons will be made between N++ and the originals), and I'm in love. After 100%ing Super Meat Boy, I've been itching for a pure platformer for a long time. N++ has filled that void.
If you're looking for a game with:
story
a short experience
high-def, ultra realistic graphics
DLC
difficulty settings
then N++ is not the game for you. However, if you're like me, you don't care about any of these things and just want pure platforming, this game is a must add to your collection.
So far, I have no complaints with this game. The controls feel smooth and heavy, and platforming is less dependent on twitchy reflexes and more planning your jumps appropriately to conserve momentum. The levels (2500+ official levels!) are varied and well designed - from open arenas based on dodging rockets to linear pathways filled with mines, each level is designed to challenge but always fair. The game runs at a smooth 60fps, and although an option to increase the fps cap would be nice, it is perfectly playable at 60. The soundtrack is perfectly fits the minimalist style and is over six hours of music.
Not to mention the user generated maps, the local co-op (or competition), and plans for online multiplayer in the future. This game is a masterpiece and I will be playing it for a very long time to come. Solid platformers are few and far between, and N++ sets a very high standard.

This game rocks! I bought and played through all three chapters a while back, and due to a back injury, found myself looking for something to fill the time. This second playthrough has been even better than the first! Being able to play through as any of the 8 Left 4 Dead characters has added a whole new feel to the game!
First and foremost, this is a sniper game, so if you don't like sniper rifles do not buy it! Most of the pistols are ok but most of the secondary weapons like SMG's are complete garbage and actually hurt your score more than they help. As you play the game, your score is greatly increased by modifiers based on how many consecutive kills you have without any bullets missing their target. Even a short, concentrated burst from a secondary weapon is likely to reset your score streak back to zero. Its not a huge deal, but it feels like it was done on purpose to force you into using the sniper rifles if you want a decent score. While this makes sense, (given that the game is based on Sniper Elite gameplay), it fails horribly when you get stuck in a tight hallway. Most of the time I run low on sniper ammo I end up needing to kite enemies for long distances in the hopes of finding some more ammo. Again, this is only because I'm trying to maximize my score in this second playthrough on Sniper Elite difficulty.
I like that they add various pickups around the maps so you have something to hunt down if you want more out of the game. Like the issue above, this really only affects you if you're trying to maximize your score or if your a completionist and they can be ignored if you want.
The bullet cam is one of the best parts of the game. Being able to watch a bullet tumble through three different zombies that were on the other side of the map is a super fun addition to a zombie killing game. Only a few times throughout the whole game did I feel overwhelmed. Most of the time you can reposition yourself and keep going. The times this didn't work, it was very satisfying finally figuring out what path I needed to take and who to kill first.
I would definitely recommend this game to anyone that enjoys laying waste to the hordes of the undead!

Zombie Army Trilogy (ZAT), is a very well made zombie shooter game that combines two previous games, into one with an additional chapter added to make up the entire story.  While there are plenty of shooter games our there, and even more zombie shooting games, few can compare to the atmosphere that ZAT brings.
The story involves 4 characters who are sent into nazi germany to determine what is going on.  Upon arrival, they find out that there are zombies running around and it is concluded that something is turning the nazi soldiers into zombies.  You push further into the country and reach the inner section of Berlin and attempt to find the source of these zombies, only to find that its beyond your ability to do anything about it.  After narrowly escaping, you are told about an artifact that when completly put together, can some how counter the effects of the zombies or destroy them some how.  Armed with only the first of three pieces, you go back inside Germany and find the second part of the artifact.   Just like before, you push through hordes of zombies while going from place to place, and eventually you defeat an Occultist leader who then leaves behind  a piece of the artifact.  After that, you escape yet again with new found hope.
And then in the final chapter, you find out the location of a the third piece.  Early on, you find that the person who owns this final piece is the one and only Hitler, but due to be transformed into a zombie, he has unique powers that allows him to rule over the zombies.  So once again you push your way through Germany to find where Hitler is hiding inorder to acquire the third and finaly piece, and then hopefully putting an end to Hitler himself.
With that said, the story is pretty simple overall since you are going from place to place, looking for artifacts and looking for a way to take down the leader himself.  Its not a very complex or emotional story and non of the playable characters talk, but its a good-enough story to make it have a purpose.
This is one of the key parts of the game that makes it shine.  The game has a third-person camera angle most of the time, but you can go into first-person if you want to scope a shot.   Considering how the game relie son you having three firearms at a time, one of which is a sniper rifle, you will spend most time shooting in first-person, and running in third-person.   As stated before, you have three firearms from the start:  A sniper rifle, a secondary (AR, shotgun, rocket launcher) and a pistol.  Sniper rifle is for all around use, secondary is for backup or specialty kills, and pistols are for when ammmo is low or if you are knocked down and want to bring a few enemies down with you.  There are about 8-10 different weapons for each firearm type with secondary weapons having more unique options.  On top of that, you have 4 explosive weapons to use as well: dynamite, landmind, tripmine and grenade.  Each serve a purpose and are ery effective at serving it.
The mechanics of the sniper rifles in particular, are really amazing.  They all have pros and cons that can vary from firing speed, bullets per clip/mag., bullet velocity, reload speed/type, and level of zooming.   In my opinion, they are very balanced in what they do since some can fire fast and have little sway, but reload longer and have a small clip, or fires moderate and has a small clip but reloads fast and has very little bullet drop.   The secondary rifles are similar but are less significant since they are usually your fallback weapon of choice.
Another game mechanic, are the enemies and boy will this take a while to explain.  Over the three chapters, new enemies will appear and they will have unique features to them.  The first type are the fodder troops.  These are your average footsoldiers who have nothing special to them.  Some may have helmets which can protect them from certain headshots, while others have a firearm and will randomly shoot it every now and then.  They are slow, can have very wonky body movement which helps to make it a challenge to headshot them, and are common to be in large numbers.  Then there is the suicide bomber.  Name says it all but he has a distinct voice that can be heard and they run fast.  You either shoot the explosive on him, kill him the old fashion way, or let him approach you and then run away at the last second.  They are weak in healt but their explosion can pack a punch.
From there, we have the sniper.  Word of warning, that anyone who faces them in the first chapter, knows that these guys are a pain in the a** to deal with.  They deal high damage and jump from place to place before taking a quick shot and jumping away.  In the higher difficulty, facing two or three at once, will certainly result in you being Knocked Down.  In the next two chapters, they have a unique cloud haze that makes them a bit easier to spot, but still they are a pain.  Next we have the tank semi-boss zombie.  These guys have high health, move slow but have a machine gun that even at a distance, can hit pretty hard.   Typically spawn during a horde wave near the end to make it feel like a boss.  Next there are skeletons.  Pretty simple enemies that you can either stomp on or kill them by hitting their heart.   After that, there are the 'summoners' who are enemies that summon zombies that are on fire.  While the fire zombies take one bullet to take out, they can be summoned in large numbers and the summoner himself can't be instantly killed.  He is slow and his damage is really high if he directly hits you but he rarely attacks.   And that after that, there are other enemies that do things such as prevent zombies from dying until they themselves are killed first, and there are the bosses which I wont spoil.
Are they ultra 4k HD hyper realistic quality?  Nope, but they look great and give off that feel of a dark and glumy setting that just feels right.  In ZAT, they have improved the fraemrate when compared to the individual games, and aside from a minor dip in performance when enemies spawn based on if there are 4 players, the performance is solid.  Those with lower rigs can easily run this although the fog will cause a drop in the first chapter.  Aside from that, the game looks simply great for what its meant to be.
The sounds of the weapons are good.  The zombie's sounds are great and some of them use a deep and satanic sounding voice which is fitting.  However, its the music that really sets the mood and is another key part of what makes this game great.  While the music is chapter 2 and 3 are good, the music in chapter 1, is perfect, simply perfect.  It starts off kind of simple, but as you progress in the chapter, it slightly changes itself and feels so gloomy and hopeless, but the piano makes it sound like there is still hope in all of this, even when the odds are against you.  You just have to experience to understand what I mean.  And lastly, the ambience sounds are fitting and creepy.
Personally, I love it.  The first time playig it, is the best time.  I played it with my best friend and she and I always have a blast playing it, even if she constantly has the higher score.  Some people might get bored of the  lack of more maps and chapters since there are 3 chapters with 5 sub-chapters, each subchapter lasts about a half hour or so, depending on how fast you play or how fast you complete objectives.  Its enjoyable if played with a friend or two and even more so if you do the Endless game mode.
ZAT is a very well made zombie shooting game that is perfect for people who like to be snipers or like to play shooters with friends.  Its unique feel is enough to get peoeple interested with it and keep them playing.  There are still other things to talk about but Im out of space to write it.  So in short, just buy it and have a friend join you.

First of all this FMV game is made by this company
They claim that this was a low budget production, but how can it be when it has someone famous in it like Paul Darrow? For those that don't know Paul Darrow was Avon in the classic Scifi series known as 'Blakes 7'. Blakes 7 on the other hand was definitely low budget. So with that in mind where is the esky in the game? The cardboard computers with flashing lights? The paper Mache houses? Seriously if this was low budget then they spent every penny the best way they knew how. Sound, music, effects and acting was all pretty much top notch and quickly teleports the gamer into the world of murder.
The biggest appeal to this game is its use of storytelling. You take control of a private investigator known as 'Jenks' who appears to be more a wannabe detective than a real one with his over the top acting, catch phrases like 'Have you seen THIS!' and his careless sloppy police work like handling forensic items instead of using evidence bags. Whatever evidence he does discover would be thrown out of court in the real world because of this. ANYWAY...
As you stroll around the sleepy town of Edenton questioning the members of the town regarding the death of a local girl known as Kate Vine, your task is to interrogate everyone you come across, gain more and more snippets of information and look for contradictions in the statements of each person you interview. Only then can you progress the story further by accusing the aforementioned of a contradiction and watching them squirm out of trouble by revealing more.
Why the death of Kate Vine is even warranted for further investigation in the beginning is beyond me as the questionable evidence regarding her drowning involving narcotics and alcohol seems highly plausible, but what seems to be only as a unwarranted gut hunch is enough for Jenks to knock on everyones door bothering them every single millisecond like he is some type of Jehovah's Witness hyped up on speed.
Seriously! Every time you find an item, you have to go back and knock on everyone’s door again asking them, 'have you seen this!' Stranger than that, is the fact that everyone seems okay with this and none of them try to take out a restraining order on you. You start knocking on everyone's door at 5pm and you continue to do so every hour until you get to 12pm and the murderer confesses.
While the game has a great use of gradual story telling in a superb delivery deserving of a standing ovation at the Oscars, there are a number of things I thought could have been improved. For one thing there are a lot of loose ends which go nowhere, but only hints towards maybe a future sequel if donations are ever acquired. Secondly the murderer simply only tells you what really happened in the end instead of the gamer getting treated to a cinematic flashback. This seemed disappointing in comparison to many other movie treats you get rewarded with as you progress through the secret society known as 'Atlas'. Thirdly there seemed to be a rather low use of Easter eggs in the background, this surprised me since there were so many opportunities of placement that any crime/gumshoe/sci-fi fans with a keen eye could have been rewarded with. Fourthly there is nowhere i can see where one can buy merchandise from this game like T-shirts, coffee mugs, masks and freedom necklaces which so many have hinted their pleasure towards and finally there is no multiple endings or choice decisions which change outcomes as the game plays out entirely the same way for everybody making the whole journey more play out like a visual novel than an adventure game.
With the above grunts placed aside I would highly recommend this game for everyone, especially if you are looking for a game which you can play with a few around the lounge as it was intentionally designed for that purpose. Regardless of the ending provided in the game I am still personally convinced that Servalan was behind it all, with her new mind control weapon. What really happened well you will just have to buy it for yourself to find out aren't you? As Jenks would say,

It's been a while since I played a point and click FMV game. These things were huge back when Myst came out and popularized the genre. This was a nice throw-back to those games, with an interesting mystery to explore.
The premise is simple, you are a detective tasked with investigating a questionable suicide in a small town. Your job is to talk to the victims friends and piece together what happened by finding contradictions within their statements. Without spoiling too much, you soon uncover a deeper mystery, and its up to you to get to the bottom of it all.
The gameplay is pretty straightforward, talk to everyone you can about any evidence you've found, then find out who's lying by catching them in a contradiction. Unlike with most point and click games, you don't have to scan enviornments with your mouse, instead you're given a magnifying glass icon when something relevant is on screen. Another staple of the genre is using items on objects to advance, and again this is made simple. Objects will have a fairly obvious use outside of dialogue, you will never get to the point of trying every item on every thing to try and advance.
If I have one complaint about the game, its that it's a little too easy. With the exception of contradictions, the tip menu directs your investigation very obviously if you ever get stuck. If you have people to talk to, or evidence to find, the tip menu will tell you exactly where to go. Another thing, is there is no way to lose. With no branching story paths, there is no way you can dead end your investigation or get it wrong in the end. As long as you can find evidence and contradictions, you will advance the plot.
All in all I enjoyed the game, though it is more a visual novel than a game. There are no puzzles, no way to lose, and no branching story paths. I will say I thoroughly enjoyed the story, but I do wish there were more paths to take story wise. When the game ends, you feel like theres a ton more to investigate, and it leaves you feeling like the ending was a bit rushed.
In conclusion, its a point and click throwback, with a pretty interesting story to explore, but there is room for a lot of improvement if the game ever gets a sequel.

Balance elevates and limits this game. More than any of Falcom's projects from their late Windows PC period, systems, aesthetics, and non-linearity counterbalance to create a sprawling action adventure that, even with its shortcomings and missed opportunities, seems fully conceived and replete with potential. If anything, this game rewards you for experiencing as much of it as possible, and of Falcom games and outside influences it took from.
I'm already near the end of my third Xanadu Next playthrough, storming my way through Castle Strangerock with every skill, technique, and trick in my book. Every time I know I'm playing one of the easier, often more accessible Falcom games from this period, but it never gets old. Even Gurumin has difficulty options this game sorely could use, not that it's bad or merely good w/o them. Ys: The Oath in Felghana, released the same year as Xananext, has that and more detailed NPCs to entertain you, not to forget Ys VI: The Ark of Napishtim which is heavy on both world-building and character. The soundtrack, as textured, baroque and diverse in genre (including hard rock for two tracks later on), isn't as large and full as Gurumin's or Trails in the Sky FC's. And you don't get interesting mechanics those games feature, like rhythmic critical hits or attack/experience multipliers based on how many monsters you rend and how quickly. After some thinking I get how unusual Xanadu Next seems to fans of the company's games, mostly because it blends bits and pieces and then provides a number of seemingly less significant but unique systems.
Here's the thing. Xananext doesn't outright need those qualities to immerse you and keep players entranced. From the start it has a strong story hook, quick pacing, and challenge (from enemies, puzzles, and equipment pre-requisites) to demand attention. Then it gives you multiple ways to build your character as you travel through dungeons dwarfing anything from contemporary Falcom titles, with meaningful statistical/resource management and combat just as punchy. Xananext bridges the gap between the company's games from this period, but also calls back to a time when hand-holding was limited, and when Falcom's storytelling and game progression carried players forward in a more subtle way. You start as a disgraced, then nearly deceased knight seeking redemption at the edge of the country, but eventually become a hero of legend through hard work and the luck to be on Harlech at just the right time. Plenty of story threads connect and foreshadow each other at just the right time, propelling you through caves, heights, forests and the netherworld looking for someone or something. The game rarely lets up, with a gentle but firm difficulty curve; your skill selection and choice of weapons/armor change radically over the course of a playthrough, with myriad options for your character and play style. And Xananext doesn't skimp on features Falcom's games are known for, like multi-phase bosses, a user interface that services the game perfectly, and surprising ways to replay faster and better than before.
The variety of rooms, puzzles, group mini-bosses, vistas, and funny conversations with Harlech villagers still impress me. Mechanics like back-attacking for added damage—encouraging you to use better tactics in battle for offense and defense—defeating undead immediately using magic (enchantments), slicing up environmental objects for loot and more weapon proficiency, and leveling down to alter your build (while using stat-buffing skills) all keep me interested. But they're interesting also because the level and enemy design intertwine to make you master and treasure your skills and strategies. Some key items end up in storage, but others are essential for searching every nook and cranny of Harlech Island, which remains a treat on repeat playthroughs. Guardians allow you to customize your character that much more, and are generously easy to maximize levels for should you conserve Guardian statues for later. Meanwhile hints in the environment, as well as foreshadowing in the game's lore and NPC dialogue, let you piece together most if not all mysteries surrounding Xanadu, perhaps even what's happened to the world around. If I had to play one sequel made for any recent Falcom game, Xanadu Next Scenario II would be it just because of the sequel hook(s) this story leaves.
XSEED's release of Xanadu Next, while still suffering from conditional bugs and mistakes not caught in testing, adds true widescreen support, a revised English script, and compatibility fixes letting you play this decade-old game on modern Windows. It runs great on PCs you wouldn't expect could handle a polygonal dungeon crawler with as much detail and effects as this (par for the course with Falcom PC games, but still), And while gamepad support takes some time to configure to your liking, the result of Falcom patching it in later because the game didn't launch with any way to use gamepad, I'm fine occasionally holding "Use Mouse" for cursor movement to access inventory before getting back to the adventure. Xananext thrives on fluidity and giving you many ways to beat it but also master it; the post-game letter ranking's there to encourage this after all. If you want a modern Falcom classic with a straightforward but subtle story, pushing forth an involved and interconnected world that only gives you a break when you really need it, then Xanadu Next should be your next sword-and-sorcery exploit. The Dragon Slayer and that magnificent castle ain't gonna find themselves, much less an ancient royal conspiracy mirroring the one your character's been running from for too long.

It's a very cool action-RPG thus far. The story actually starts out surprisingly decent (though it seems like it has fallen off a bit now that I'm in the first real dungeon, but one event actually caught me off guard), and the combat is quite good. It feels satisfying AND forces you to make a lot of strategic choices. For example, one enemy explodes and hits every creature in the room, including yourself, when you kill it. Another enemy goes down far easier with magic, but can be killed with melee attacks if you're low. And magic reliably damages enemies that you're too weak to defeat in melee, but is VERY limited (i.e. you have to recharge in town or use MP restoratives, which aren't sold in shops, to get more spell charges).
And related to that, stats make a HUGE difference in this game... I went from only doing 1 damage against certain enemies and the first real boss to 1 - 3 shotting the enemies and having an actual chance against the boss simply by allocating all my level up points for one level into attack.
Death hurts in this game, and the difficulty is no joke. You lose every unimportant item you were carrying plus 50% of your gold. The only save point I've seen thus far is in town, but after you get a certain item, you can warp back to town any time you like, plus there's moderately expensive Diablo style portals you can buy on top of that that'll take you back to where you stopped, so there's quite the risk vs. reward system going on.
People who like lore in their games will love this. You collect tablets and journals, your companion translates them for you, and once translated, you get to read up on some of Xanadu's history.
...Oh and, oddly enough, the game seems designed with keyboard and mouse in mind. You click and your character (who's default name is Falcom, so I can only assume they REALLY want you to name him either after yourself, or with a fancy name of your own making) goes there like in a PC hack and slash game. I think you can use controllers, though the store's page says "partial controller support," and given what that often means, I haven't brought myself to try it yet.
So yeah. Even if the rest of the game sucks, and I don't think it will, I'm glad Falcom, XSeed, and Marvelous brought this game over. I'd love to see more older RPGs like this that we didn't get back in their heyday.
UPDATE: Tried the controller.  Actually worked mostly fine for me using an Xbox 360 controller.  Only issue is, by default, you have to hold down the start button to use the mouse for navigating your equipment menu.  The game still feels like it was designed purely with a keyboard and mouse in mind when it came out back in 2005, but a controller does have certain advantages, like having a single button for using items instead of four, and not having to "aim" the cursor at enemies.
I also have run into some mild bugs, but nothing gamebreaking like some people are saying, just minor text bugs (seemed to happen when I used the default name of "Falcom" for some reason, restarting and using an original name seemed to fix it), and a weird graphical glitch in one room that quickly went away.
I've heard of more serious things happening, but haven't run into them myself, so I cannot comment on them.  I'll just say, be aware that there might be issues.
I still highly recommend the game though.  The gameplay is incredibly satisfying.  The combat just feels great, and the way you explore in this game is extremely well done, unlocking bits of the island and its dungeons piece by piece.

If you want Strength, Endurance, Magic, etc.

Sad to say you are missing out on a gem. If you like old school RPG's with dungeon crawling and randomly smacking down enemies? Buy it.

Some. More thoughts:
Ryse: son of Rome is the hack and slash equivalent of a third person corridor shooter. It's combat is fun to play and gratifying to watch. But there is no real depth beyond what you get at the start. Ryse basically does combat-cutscene cycles, with no other variety such as puzzles etc. Levelling is basically useless as you get more xp than you know what to do with. The real reason to play ryse is the visuals and it's story. It's sad crytek couldn't make a sequel. Am sure a sequel could have gone toe to toe with the likes of God of war. Battleborn, a FPS-MOBA by Gearbox, the makers of the Borderlands Series. Thereby it presents you with the same fun humor we came to love from Borderlands.
The Game has so far been an amazing experience. I've bought the €64.99 Digital Deluxe (Game+Season Pass) edition
and it was definitely worth my money.
The game is set in a universe that slowly gets swallowed by "The Void", an unknown force which is not really explained. With only one star remaining 5 faction gather around this star to fight of the Void.
But, one of these factions, The Jennerit, sides with the Void to secure their own survival. This faction will be our main enemy troughout the campaign.
That said, the game comes with a story mode and multiplayer.
Let's begin with the story mode. Of course we should not expect some Telltale story telling, neither should you expect a linear story. The missions are all separate, independent missions accompagnied by some back story.
You could better describe it as a dungeon raid from MMO's, where you enter as a party of five (or less), complete some objectives and fight a final boss.
In my opinion this was the best way to go, as it makes it much more fun to replay the missions and try them on another difficulty level. And I suggest you replay them, because just like in dungeons in MMO's they drop loot, which can be used in the multiplayer. They also give you credits, an ingame currency (don't worry, there is no cash shop), and you can  complete challenges to unlock more Battleborn.
My overall score for Story Mode: 7.5/10
That brings us to multiplayer, the real selling point of the game.
Currently (08-05-2016, DD-MM-YYYY) there a 3 game modes in the game (not including multiplayer story mode): Incursion, Capture and Meltdown (you can read what they are in the game's description).
Each mode has currently 2 different maps to chose from. I wish there where more maps, but I expect some to come out as dlc and included in the season pass.
There are also 25 characters to chose from (and 5 more announced). Most of them are locked via challenges, unlock them with relative ease.
As for the gameplay, I greatly enjoy it. The Characters are very well done, all very unique with really satisfying skills. When you start a match, your character starts at level 1. Throughout the match you level him to level 10 and each level you can choose an extra passive skill. When you play a character you also level it outside of the match, you go can up to level 15 and it unlocks skins, taunts and up to 5 extra passive skills you can choose from during a match. (It may seem it will give other players a benefit, but in the end you can only have up to 10 passive active skills and they don't have that much of an impact.)
The game also has a loadout system. It allows creating a loadout with 3 pieces of gear (collected through missions, or bought by credits), these gear pieces give little bonuses like movement speed, crit, healing etc. in story missions and multiplayer matches. Again it may seem like it will give people with better gear a benefit, but again, they don't have much impact. On top of that, during a match you need to buy your gear pieces with shards (something like gold in Dota) and of course the best pieces of gear cost the most.
So overall the multiplayer is amazing. There is only one problem, some battleborn (only 2) are a little unbalanced
and are significant stronger than other, I expect it will be fixed in the upcoming patch, but it still is a error that
should not have been made.
My overall score for Multiplayer: 8.5/10
I really recommend this game, and suggest if you pick it up, to get the season pass as well in order the benefit from all the dlc's.

I'm not going to lie. This game has a very Borderlands/Anthony Burch-tier humor style in its writing, and at some points it can be grating. And yet at other points, it can be fun and fitting. I consider it its lowest point in terms of story, which is sad considering the amount of effort Gearbox goes to force its humor in your face.
There, now that my one major quirk with the game is taken care of; lets get on with the good parts.
Hero Selection:
Pretty damned amazing. You start off with a sizeable roster that is pretty varied in roles. Almost feels moba-ish, in which there's support, tanks, and DPS. Many of the characters in the game need to be unlocked, not from a paywall but from an achievement/challenge perspective. Usually it's pretty simple: Level your account to hit the rank needed to play the character, or do various secondary challenges (Kill 50 players, get Silver medals on all story missions, play five times as one faction) in order to unlock them.
PVE:
Story writing aside, I have quite a few complaints with how the mission roulette is set. You either have to play with a band of four people you know in order to select a mission you need to complete (Saboteur or Heliophage come to mind), or you need to solo queue and hope one of the three randomized missions that pops up is one of the few you need.
Thankfully Gearbox countered this by letting you play a private session where you're able to select which story mission to progress from, where you're gated to the highest level mission you've completed. As of this review, I have still yet to complete Saboteur and Heliophage because I have no friends (kill me fam).
PVP:
What an absolute cluster♥♥♥♥. This is where class balance is shown to not have been a major consideration in Gearbox's head. Many heros perform underwhelmingly in PVP, while others can pretty much solo every class without a challenge.
And what PVP modes they do have, they don't have a really intrinsic guide on what the bloody Hell you're supposed to be doing. Sure they give that mini-tutorial at the start of the match, but all the intricacies of the map are just left to the players best guess.
Of all the PVP matches I've played, it's usually been either an hour long standoff in the middle of the map because their healers are just blatantly keeping everyone topped up forever, or its an absolute stomp because one team is missing a healer or tank.
Solution: Buff everyone.
TL;DR: The game has a wide selection of heroes to play, a decent loot system, a subpar PVE storyline, and absolutely craptastic PVP. Still a lot of persistent bugs and glitches that need to be ironed out as well as a major rebalancing of PVP. It is indeed still one of Gearbox's better releases if compared to Borderlands or (god's sake) Aliens: Colonial Marines.
A good note is that it's less 'meme-y' than Borderlands, if that kind of humor makes you cringe.

My son and I played the original Myst game last night for about 4 hours. The last time he played this game was 20 years ago when he was only 13 years old. We both got hooked on the game and have played every subsequent game. I am really glad that Cyan is coming out with a new game next year (Obduction).
The reason I am writing is to inform players of built-in controls that are not listed in the contol menus for "Free Roam" mode that will help make the game play much smoother. In general we found that free roam mode is much smoother and more pleasurable to watch than "Classic Myst" mode.
* If you hold down the left mouse button when you move the mouse, only the hand cursor moves and not the player.
* If you hold down the right mouse button when you move the mouse, then the player moves with it.
* If you hold down the shift key when you move side to side or forward and backwards, then you will travel much faster and get to your destination much sooner (like the difference between walking and running).
*If you have trouble maneuvering to a particular spot like we did last night when we tried to go down a ladder, switch to "Classic Myst" mode and let the automatic locator do it for you.
We are running the game in the "Max Quality" setting and have very few lag problems. I do however have a beefy computer that I built for video editing:
* Intel 6 core running at 4.6GHz
* 32 GB Ram
* EVGA 560GTX video card
* Combination SSD and Hard drives

Project Highrise, released in 2016 by Chicago-based SomaSim games, is a spiritual successor to SimTower (1994). The game allows you, the intrepid developer, to construct a building from ground up. Similar to SimTower, you view the building in cross section -- laying out floors, building elevators, and deciding whether you want to go focus on hotels, apartments, or offices.
Managing you services and your budget is a big part of the early game for Project Highrise. As the level of each tenant you have access to increases, they will require more intense utilities and ancillary uses. You'll find that while you could get away with just electrical lines at first, you'll now need to provide water, gas, phones and cable. You'll also need copy services, couriers, restaurants, cafes, and much more.
While the early game can be challenging and interesting, things really slow down by the mid game. If you've reached this point, you have a basic grasp of how to balance a budget and have expansion plans that are working. Unfortunately, the challenge is really gone at this point and you are striving to... fill up the rest of the buildable area? Your options for customization are also rather limited and only helped somewhat by the purchasable dlc.
If you are nostalgic about SimTower and can't get it to run anymore, Project Highrise might scratch that itch. The basic game has hardly evolved since it's predecessor from decades past, but that might not be such a bad thing.

3 Stars out of 5 from me. Just finished the game and thought I'd comment.
Contradiction has you playing the role of a police inspector (not a very good one who doesn't carry around evidence bags, but hey). The game consists of you questioning people about a death to determine whether it was suicide or murder. The game part comes with trying to find areas where a witness contradicts *themselves.*
First, I love that the old FMV style has been updated. The acting was pretty good (a little over the top with some, but not horrible). It's nice to see what can be done with modern day technology.
The story wasn't bad. I read a ton of mysteries and am always very critical when it comes to them. There are two cardinal rules: 1) Checkov's smoking gun and 2) you play fair with your reader.
I found it frustrating that I couldn't learn something from one witness, discover it contradicted what another witness said and then go back and re-question the original witness. (i.e., like you could do if it were a real investigation). You can only find descrepancies in individual statements. I think the game could have been greatly improved had the player been allowed to better simulate an actual investigation.
#2 is the reason why I cannot give this game full marks. In the very first hour you come across something you should be able to question a couple people about. However, even if you select the questionable statements, the game does not indicate the contradiction.
that contradiction exists. The game just won't allow you to do anything about it until the end. That's ridiculous. I have watched two let-s plays on this game. Both times the players also picked up on this clue.
So basically, the developers decided they were going to hinge their entire mystery on something people will probably notice right off but
to follow-through with it. This is not how you should write a mystery. If they need to rely on not playing fair with their readers/players then they need to rewrite until the story works. Make it a red herring. Give them a plausible reason that you only discredit as you continue to investigate.
I found that last big incredibly disappointing in an otherwise fun game. And it was fun. I would consider purchasing a sequel. I just hope they learn how to write mysteries properly by then.

Cold War gone Hot? or Not?
Luke Warm maybe.
This RTS does everything wrong according to popular design these days including massive learning curves, complex designs and controls, 850+ units and massive scale. These are all things that in typical RTSs? Would be the wrong thing to do. As many would say "Gameplay over Realism". Wargame does the opposite in an attempt to prove that even simulations can be fun but unfortunately? It misses just by a hair.
GFX - IRIS Zoom v4 is amazing. It can truely render a lot of detail at any range, making every land scape so wonderous that it's FPS worthy close up, and Hi-Res Sat image worthy from far away. It lacks in the partical department and animations, (which on infantry is down right BAD) but for a game of this scale? It still shines well on max settings.
SFX - Language specific factions and realistic sounding weapons seemingly ripped right from the military recordings. Does well on accuracy but lacks in variety. Units say the same things over and over, just in diferent tounges and explosions all blend together since there is little sound emulation going on; just raw sound being queued on events.
Interface - Needs some work. Once you get the hang of it, it's no big deal but little things like having the Hot Key letter listed some where on the buttons would be great. Also, the Info tabs for each unit would do well to add descriptions of that units militarial role. As it sits right now, massive amounts of research needs to be spent before one plays their first skirmish because unless you're well versed in Cold War era military hard ware and patient enough to read through the Key Binding tabs, you're more or less S.O.L.
Game Play - Simulative, powerul yet lacking. It's a bueatiful game that fudges up very little however; eventually? The lack of "design" begins to show. So much detail seems to be spent on replicating the Cold War era units and maps that little attention has been given to the over all design of the game flow. In short, the polish is lack luster in one major area - Pacing. It's rock solid everywhere else from Soft Counters to Hard Counters to powerful deck building options to rewarding great tream work! But in the end? It's the pacing that I had problems with. The scale of the maps are misleading since the units are designed to be close to realistic; thus having effective ranges that in some cases? can = several miles on their own. When you take that into context, maps are no longer that huge, it's just the units are that small. Battles erupt very easily with little room to actually move since everything is so small that the time it takes to relocate is punishing. Couple this with Air Power and other forms of CAS and bullrushes of powerful air strikes or chopper raids punishes any newer player to dust; and becomes maintstream equivilents of the Starcraft Zerg 6pool builds in higher levels. After studying this strange flaw right after I at least picked up the basics, I concluded that pacing was the oddest ball in the court. You start each battle with a set amount of points to spawn your initial force. After words, it's up to capturing "sectors" to see a trickle of points come in. The issue here is that in large point battle, your first force will be brissling and wonderous; ready to wreack havoc. However once combat starts the slow trickle cannot replace either sides forces at a pace that justifies the start. If points are set low, then the force remains small period since the economic rate never changes; and often these small starting pulls leads to lame rushes anyway. If there was some player control over the rate of income and the ammount of income recieved, games could be set to be more diverse than they are now, all because the pacing is off.
Verdict - Its grande, it's bueatiful and it's accurate. But a gold star game? It's not. It's damned close though. It needs better pacing options and greater player control over game play types for diversity. Add these and this would be my replacement for all things RTS. With that said? I'd recommend this game to any all hard core RTS gamers. It is like World In Conflic mixed with Total War in terms of mechanics. Just know that its better as a Sim than it is an Arcade game.
