Every so often the fine folks at Crytek feel compelled to put out a video game which seemingly intends to show the entire industry how high the bar can be set, so far a graphics are concerned.
The visuals in this game are stunning, achieving near-photorealism with every aspect except faces, and those are not bad.  Backdrops are epic, armor gleaming like authentic roman plate, for the colosseum to the Briton woods, the scenes are superb. Also have to thank crytek for the use of some otherworldly breast physics...  SJW's have stripped away femininity from so many games, so thanks for the physics, guys and gals.
The treatment of history is loose and liberal creative license is taken, but it works.  The scale more epic fantasy than documentary, it sets the mood for an engaging story.
With a total playtime of just under ten hours, i found myself wishing for more.  I am greedy, I suppose...  However, now that I better understand the games Mechanics, I am certain I will revist the campaign soon, and see if I can elevate Marius a bit closer to the epic god of battle he almost was my first playthrough.
There are some collectibles and codex unlocks hidden on side paths throughout the campaign, I didn't really chase them too hard as I think they were only for achievements sake...  No xp.  No big deal.
The characters could have done with a bit more development, but you get the point and understand the motivations.
Oh... yeah... THE COMBAT.  This was the entire point here folks.  Brutal, third person, block and dodge, hack and slash, counter and execution MURDER.  Detailed and directional, with some rpg upgrade mechanics, every encounter rewards the player with the potential of absolutely nasty executions, which are the highlight of the game.  QTE's that aren't a bad thing in this context, rewarding XP for proficiency.  You will love it.
Full price or sale, this game is worth it.

For anyone in debate over Battleborn VS Overwatch. Now for the review!
I have played both and I personally prefer Battleborn. I love the quirky characters and the way they interact with one another. The characters are easy to fall in love with as far as personality and gameplay and offer much in the way of lore, comedy and story.
Gameplay is much liek a FPS MOBA, minus the intense stress of FPSs like CS:GO, and the boring, grueling nature of DOTA. This game somewhat resembles Smite, with a heaping dash of it's own uniqueness that you can only tuly experience with purchase.

The lore is fun to achieve, even though it can be tasking and difficult at times to accomplish, but you get to learn about each character, sometimes weapons and you get have a sound dialogue unlocked for each which can either be humorous or, developmental in-depth character insights. The lore also often fills in those gaps in the story that are understandable due to the way the story modes are played.
Story mode and the story in general, while fun, lacks adequate substance. But as I said, the lore provides some much needed cement for gap filling. The story chapters as they stand, are meant ot be played at random and only partially in order, which makes it easy to just ready up with randoms, and not really misso ut on any of the story.
Listen, watch the video if you're in debate about Overwatch VS Battleborn. It will help you to purchase one, or the other or both. I plan on both eventually but for now, Battleborn is my first love and has been since Pax Prime. I've been a loyal fan since and have ventured through their closed technicals and betas. I met N+ on 360 years ago and I still have fond memories of playing multiplayer with my family and friends.
I was very excited to see N++ was a thing, and coming to PC (because I'm mostly a PC gamer and my family and friends that have moved away are still available to play with on PC)
Let's start with cons >>
Multiplayer is local only. Its nice that they have multiplayer, but I was really hoping to get to play online. I was pretty disappointed when I found this out, and for most people this is situation specific. If you still play multiplayer locally then no worries!
Character color. We can't figure out how to change our character's colors like we could in N+. I googled it and found some forums saying that you can't, although I'm not ruling it out, maybe it does exist. However if it doesn't I'm sad about that too. I liked the colors and their corresponding names. I was always Cherry bomb, and we still yell "BANANA" when my little brother dies in any game.
So, those two things are pretty miniscule, and specific to my personal taste.
Pro's. >>
You can color swap the whole game. They have themes that don't just change the look of menus, but the whole game itself. This is pretty rad.
Racing. Multiplayer has coop like in N+ but they added in racing and this was the most fun we have had so far with it.
Assasins. The lazers and missles you remember are back for another go. But, they are small fry compared to the new enemy assasins that spawn and kick yo♥♥♥♥♥
So many levels. With the level creator and being able to share online there are more levels than you can ever hope to play. Now personally I have attempted to play additional levels in games like trackmania, and the majority are garbage, so this may have some gems but I bet it will take some digging. This is speculation though I have not really adventured outside of the base game levels yet.
Conclusion >>
I loved N+. And I think what is bugging me has to do with the multiplayer. I just sort of feel let down. Its still fun, it looks sharp, controls are still crispy like bacon. But to be honest after about half an hour we end up switching to Overcooked instead.

I never played an FMV game before, but this one just sparked my interest.  My wife and I had a great time working our way through the puzzles, and actually finished the whole thing (a rarity for both of us to stay interested to the end!)

FMV games got a bum rap during the 90s, with the advent of CD media, but they have kind of made a resurgence lately, with games like Her Story, the Tex Murphy revival, and now Contradiction.
In Contradiction, you play the part of a police detective investigating the mysterious circumstances behind the death of a young girl in a nondescript English village. Contradiction plays more or less like a point and click adventure game of old, you move about a location, talking to people, solving puzzles, figuring things out, and advancing the storyline. However, in this case, the puzzles are about finding 'contradictions' in the stories of the characters you question. The main game loop is questioning suspects and finding cracks in what they're feeding to you.
Everything each character says is aggregated into your trusty little notebook, and you have to figure out which pieces of information contradict with each other.
Once you find a contradiction, you put together the two bits of information that are odds with each other and present it to the suspect. It feels extremely natural and engaging. As the game progresses, you get more and more information, making it harder to figure out exactly where the contradictions lie. Instead of the brainless pixel crawling of old, trying to randomly mixing up items in your inventory to what comes out, or using every item on everything, I believe this game's system actually requires more thought than other games in the genre, and it doesn't fall into the usual pitfalls of "cheapness" of the genre. Even if you're stumped, the game uses a supremely clever "tips" system, in which you call your police department chief, who after being appraised of the current situation will more or less point you in the right direction without giving you the answer.
The game uses entirely real locations, and is professionally, beautifully shot.
An FMV game pretty much lives and dies by its cast, and I think the people here are fantastic. Inspector Jenks (you) brings about the perfect amount of slightly over the top acting, with at times a tinge of modest self-awareness, such as when you ask something entirely ridiculous that your subject would obviously know nothing about. The tone is just right for the game, it doesn't take itself 100% seriously and yet doesn't feel like outright cheese either.
As an aside, Contradiction was developed by famed 8bit/16bit composer Tim Follin, known for Silver Surfer, Plok and Solstice, among others. He has been working in the advertising/film industry for several years, so he knows what he's doing. Like I said, everything is shot professionally and looks very classy. It's almost like an interactive TV show.
Anyway, to any fans of old PC adventure games, I can't recommend this game enough. It has charm to last for days.

We play a lot of adventure games as a family (e.g. Telltale Games, Double Fine, etc...) and this is a great throwback game. The contradiction investigation mechanic works well, but wish there'd have been a way to take contradictory interview points between the suspects. That said, it was really enjoyable and hope they are able to get the support they need to do a sequel.

The team who made the game have studied up on the roman soldier and the shortsword gladius that they used, slash horizontal and vertical is possible, stabbing and heavy jump stab/slash as well, shield is able to heavy attack with a jump and slam or a light breaking block push with the shield, lastly if combos are performed well you can kick as well.

Being able to command troops and yell out tetsudo as i cover from burning arrows and slowly advance to command my soldiers to throw spears, to see them die around me if they get hit by the arrows, to command the soldiers to hold a line and having them have a life bar as it drains away, telling archers when to fire volleys, immersion they have nailed it good.
Due to the low amount of combos of the hack and slash once you figure out the attacks of the boss fights it does become easy enough to complete them.
The executions are one of the finest i have seen and so realistic yet quite entertaining as they are horrific, to mention those i can rememeber.
1. Slash of the arm see the bone, hit with the shield as he kneels and then a stab in the neck from above.
2. Slash of the arm and then the leg and then finish of with a downward stab.
3 knee to face.
4. Foot to the face.
5. Double executions kill one follow up the killing with the second one each get a hit.
When i think i have seen them all i see a new executions that i had not seen before all depending on landscape, see a wall of spikes execute near them and and push the enemy on to them, or throw them into the fire and get an achievement.

1.Kill an elephant with a ballista.

The way I see it, there are two types of people looking to buy this game: 1).You were an old fan of the game and wanted to masturbate to some nostalgia (a noble goal), or 2). you've heard the gushy ♥♥♥♥-songs of the fans swooning about how hunky Carth is or how the twist puts M. Night Shamalamadingaringdingdong to shame (before he did it himself of course), and want to see what the fuss is.

Gameplay can be generously described as adequate, but makes little effort to advance beyond that, with many abilities either incredibly overpowered or completely♥♥♥♥♥♥weak, and many enemies sharing the same problem.

The graphics aren't great, even for someone like me who doesn't much care about all that anti-aliasing and post-processing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but if you go into the game with the mind-set of "for the time" you'll generally find them be sufficient.

If you know anything about Bioware, however, you'll be unsurprised to find that the story is KotoR's bright spot. The characters are interesting, though they can come across as flat and generic at times, but that sort of fits with the themes of the game's story. See, KotoR is something of a return to formula for Star Wars, dropping the angst and comically bad writing of the prequels for the same style of base-archetypal Joseph Campbell narrative as seen in the original trilogy, using generic personality types and a basic good-versus-evil conflict in an innovative setting to re-master the concepts.

Then, just when you've gotten complacent with the story and the back-to-basics formula, the game throws a twist that totally shifts the narrative in a way I will not spoil here, suffice to say that it demolishes the established themes for a more complex device continued in the equally-good sequel that shakes up the morality and ethics of the universe (though I have my quibbles with the quasi-narrative disconnect between this aspect of the mechanics and story).

In summary, KotoR can be described with the standard Bioware mnemonic: "Gameplay lacking, story packing," and while I recommend this game, I can see why a more gameplay-oriented spod would be discouraged.

Definitely intended to be a modern day SimTower. Unfortunately, it misses the mark on a number of important things. Unlike SimTower, you need to wait on construction crews to build up floors, then build the units themselves, then basic necesscities, etc. Waiting on the construction crews to hurry up and get things in place so you can keep playing slows the game down to a tedious and annoying grind.
The game forces you to paint yourself into a corner with how your building is laid out, only to need to destroy it and start again. The problem is that, before you can rebuild anything, you have to wait for your construction crews to clear the debris of what you destroyed, first. While you wait for this to happen, things spiral out of control as the units you just destroyed and hope to rebuild are missed.
Further, the end-game units have such a ridiculously long list of demands before they'll even consider moving in. Once they do, they have even more requirements you didn't know about in advance. They'll promptly move out, forcing you to learn by trial and error.
Worst of all, that list of requirements does a poor job of communicating to the player what, exactly, that units needs are. They'll simply say "A better variety of ____", instead of "Six different kinds of ____".
The game makes intentional decisions to slow you down, frustrate you and force you to rebuild. But the tedious nature of how construction and deconstruction works make the whole process extremely frustrating.
Overall, a good attempt at a new SimTower. But not quite good enough.

The biggest drawback was with the construction crew, there are only five people that build one thing at a time, in the order that you build it.  This became a big problem later as the building got larger.  There is a way to increase the number of construction and maintenance workers, you have to go into a config file and find the proper entry to change. This is tough because I really wanted to like this game. I love sim tower and many other creative management games but this one has too little going on for it to be considered worth it.
- Aesthetically it's alright but still feels like it leaves more to be desired.
- This game has way too much downtime. I found myself with many moments of just "Fast forwarding through whole days just to get a paycheck" for a huge chunk of my playtime. The game has a few too many money sinks which makes progressing a huge grind to start off with.
- Even though the game has you unlocking things as you go, you hardly feel like the progression had any impact or worth.
- You can't get too creative with your decorations. You're limited to one prop per tile and you can only place them on empty spaces. You can't add furniture to houses, stores, anything... Just vacant lobby spaces~
- Mod support is pretty lacking. It's definitely there and I was keen to start making mods for this like I have for cities skylines but it's very restricted in what you can make.
- The way this game handles micromanagement could of been handled better. I don't have any immediate ideas on how to improve it but it feels off and slightly unenjoyable.
- For larger maps, services would become next to useless/broken since they are either limited in number, or had to run all the way to the left side of the screen to perform their service and then run all the way back. I found myself having to build everything that needed a service on the far left hand side of the map and have a non-demanding city slum on the right hand side...
I could probably think of other points but I'm just gonna leave it at this. The game had promise but I feel it's a bit too late for me to get my hopes up for that to change.

This review was negative when the game launched, due to several issues with game optimization.  A patch on February 27 corrected most of these errors, and the game behind them is the same MYST as always.
Now that this game is far more likely to run on your system, the question left is whether or not you should buy this instead of the first RealMYST. I believe it is a matter of preference. RealMYST runs almost perfectly fluid and costs less than half the price of the masterpiece edition.  On the other hand, this modern update boasts new textures, lighting effects and post processing effects that can make the gameworld seem more alive. Despite these improvements, the masterpiece edition's textures are still noticeably bad by modern standards (particularly the leaves on trees). The game still appears to require more resources than one might think necessary to run smoothly.
Ultimately I think whether these improvements are worth the cost is a question best left to you. The game is playable now, and I will honor my original statement and recommend it.

I'm playing this right now and I'm very impressed.
The Myst games are still to this day very unique games. These games have always been about discovery, exploring very well crafted and believable alien worlds, and figuring out how the environments, natural and man-made structures in these worlds work. Learning the backstory and lore of each world also adds a lot to the experience (in the games this is usually done by reading journals). For me, they are a great and relaxing experience of discovery, and I wish there were more games like this.
So far I've explored Channelwood, Stoneship age and Myst Island, and I believe this game is to date the best representation of the worlds of Myst 1. The game has greatly enhanced textures, lighting, shadows and water compared to the original Real Myst, and the fact that you can move freely and that the worlds are much more dynamic compared to the original Myst adds a lot to the experience. The worlds are now more believable than ever, with great attention to detail: the day/night cycles are amazing to watch, the sky, moon, clouds, lighting, water, dense vegetation, and several nice touches like different elements appearing at night... the flashlight is also a nice touch.
The main negative aspect of the game for me has already been pointed out by others, and that is the bad performance. The game indeed seems to be poorly optimized, and sometimes it stutters briefly. But it is not so bad as I have everything maxed out at 1920x1200 and in general it runs fairly well on my computer. I seem to get an average of 30fps, which is perfectly playable for this kind of game. I have an i7-2600k@4.4GHz and a GTX 560Ti (I don't know if the game is more cpu bound or gpu bound, and from what I've read others seem to be getting a worse experience). I haven't experienced any bugs or crashes.
All in all, I think this game is well worth it for any fan of Myst.

Although they are not our typical style of game, my partner and I occasionally enjoy playing point and clicks together. I saw Contradiction and managed to convince her, with a bit of hesitation, that we should give it a shot. We had a lot of fun and laughs with it.
Contradiction: Spot the Liar, is a point and click murder mystery game that revolves around finding clues, spotting lies and contradictions in the characters responses, ringing the Chief, and, most importantly, watching loads of FMV scenes where the characters are portrayed by flesh and blood actors. The story revolves around a the death of Kate Vine, a student of a pretty dodgy libertarian Ayn Rand style business school set in a small English hamlet.
What really makes the game is the acting. In particular, Rupert Booth brilliantly plays Jenks up to 11 in terms of his mannerisms, and comes across as a mashup of Richard 0'Brien and David Tennant. Every sign of the horns he pulls was a source of hilarity, and although it was a little cheesy, it is also incredibly endearing. Another special mention has to go to Paul Darrow, who does a wonderfully sinister and creepy portrayal as Paul Ryan. All the other actors do a great job with their respective characters but it's these two that, for me, stand out the most.
The gameplay of finding clues and spotting contradictions, for the most part, is very solid. There are a few times where both of us felt like the contradictions were a bit of stretch, but for the most part they sit in the virtuous mean of not being too obvious and requiring some thought, while also not being a complete stretch of the meaning of the term. It's difficult to get these things right, and the few times where the game was a bit obnoxious in this regard is totally forgivable and forgettable.
POTENTIAL SPOILER BELOW
Overall, we loved the game, and would highly recommend it, although I do feel like this is probably the kind of game where you get the most out of it playing with other people. I would also love to play a sequel should it ever come to pass, and would be happy to donate to any kickstarter should the need arise.

Contradiction is one of the best FMV games I've played in years and a very good game in it's own right.
The FMV format does have limitations but it's big strength is having real actors and real locations. That's why contradictions format of a detective trying to piece together a mystery works well. The actors can give away subtle clues, they may be lying or feeling uncomfortable that only LA Noire with it's advance facial capture comes close to recreating.
The characters are all pretty interesting from the very quirky Inspector Jenks, the reserved and frosty Rebecca Rand and of course the excellent Paul Darrow as Paul Rand sneering his way through dialogue.
The mystery has lots of red herrings and false threads so unlike a lot of mystery games not every clue matters and must be used and sometime the most innocuous thing leads to a big revelation.
That's not to say there are not flaws. Although the video is great quality the sound is a little tinny in some scenes.
Being an FMV game there is a low level of interaction but it suits the format. It can get a little frustrating having to sit through the transition scenes (though they do get shortened)
The interviewing is a bit stop and start as you will find out a bit of information from person A that allows another conversation stream with everyone else. So you have to go round asking each person that one extra question. I swear I knocked on one characters door 30 times and mostly with only 1 extra question to ask.
The menus are simplistic but functional. The clue system generally is good, but can sometimes get stuck on suggestion (you have 5 questions for person A, when that person isn't available to answer them), but overall keeps you from becoming too frustrated. The cheat system will spell out for you pretty much what you need to ask next, as sometimes the contradication can be stretching the term.
Overall very enjoyable, it's different to the usual fare and shows the potential FMV games still have.
Similar games would be the Sherlock Holmes Consulting Detective series.

Can't see anything so you're stuck spraying and praying because of it all too. Best part is? There's no particle effects options so there's no way to reduce them or turn them off. Unless they give us more performance options to tweak those particle effects I can't recommend the game and have opted for the refund in Steam.
Take every competitive game you love into a blender, mix them up, inject some roids and you have Battleborn...

This game is absolutely fantastic. I spent this week testing all the upcoming games, Overwatch, Paladins, and Paragon. Every single one of them was an OK game, but each was missing something. Battleborn hit the mark perfectly. It's a fast paced FPS-MOBA with individual character progression, skins, achievements and titles, and an interesting PvE gameplay.
The combat and playstyle is very smooth and organic, and each character (currently 25 available) has a unique play style that makes each play-through refreshing and interesting, combined with a levelling system that lets you customize each ability every time you play.
The majority of downvotes are either complaints about 'repetitive' story (this is primarily a MOBA, and the missions are still fun even after multiple play throughs) and the fact that people somehow missed the fact that this is a MOBA and not Borderlands 3.
As for the multiplayer, it consists of three gamemodes a capture point, Meltdown (minion push), and a standard MOBA type, but with a twist. I will not cover the capture point gamemode here as that is as you can imagine. Meltdown consists of two teams attempting to push waves of minions into the opposing team's portals in order to sacrifice them to appease a god. Their standard MOBA match consists of two giant siege-spider-tank things that must be destroyed in order to win, throughout the course of the match you can hire stronger minions by defeating them around the map, and purchase various towers such as a speed-boost and a health regen.
The overall playstyle is very unique and cannot easily be compared to any game that is currently out. On the whole it is leagues above the other games I mentioned, although that is of course somewhat subjective.
TL;DR
Buy it, Try it, Refund it if you don't like it.

As to whether or not it's worth the full $60 - I cannot say. But so far I've had a blast. Tons of characters, achievements, and unlocks. Three different PVP modes, all of which are a lot of fun. The story mode could maybe use a little work in terms of bugs/balance (no retry on mission failure during normal mode? No regroup option with a good party for story/pvp?) but is otherwise very solid.
The solo missions can be real grind if you don't have a pre-made group selected, but when you do they're great, and as usual gearbox's writing is both hilarious and engaging.
All in all I foresee that a lot of the issues (non of which are major) facing this game are easily resolved and I anticipate that they will be. I definitely recommend it so far.

I love this game, You might have heard some comparisons to Overwatch and such but the game is NOT like overwatch at all. It reminds me quite a bit of a Hybrid MOBA and thats not necessarily a bad thing at all. Your character will level up and choose skills for each and every new battle they do, with each battle earning you some sweet new things like Player level EXP, Character EXP for further skins and of course Credits. Credits can be used to purchase loot packs that contain new gear and possibly new skins. There are also in game shards, this goes hand in hand with building and Gear, I'll make an attempt to explain rather quickly -
So Gear are items that are usually obtained from Loot packs but can also be optained from PVE.. Gear offers stat boosts, kind of like shop items in DOTA 2 but you can only have 3. Gear is not automatically equipped at the start of a battle, Instead you'll have to unlock a piece by its shard cost, it can be any piece in any order of the 3 you equipped into your loadout, so long as you have the required amount of shards. This is where you'll have to make decisions about what you want to do, Because your base defenses that are available to be built by anyone also require shards, usually 200-400 shards.
Can you see how I might want to call it a hybrid moba? There are different game modes but I mostly only play Capture so thats all I can really comment on in length.. Capture is sort of like Double Domination from Unreal Tournament. You'll need to capture and hold points to gain team score. Kills don't give you score in this game mode so team work is a must.
You'll find Shard clusters and shard pickups around the map, so always keep an eye for them. You'll also find Varelsi Mobs around the map, killing them grants you a level - they're important. Kill them, they're a bit hard to miss - they look like Metroid Prime's Space Pirates.
As for Incursion which I've yet to play at all - Incursion is a game mode in which you push through Enemy lines and destroy their Sentries/towers.
Lastly, there is Meltdown . Meltdown is sort of like  a MOBA at this point, but instead what you'll be doing is feeding your Minions into their ...Teleporters? Cores? Well, you'll be feeding them into a firey pit that they will always make an attempt to push for. your enemy will be doing the same and you'll need to push through your enemy and their minions as well to achieve this sadistic victory.

I wasn't expecting much going in. It looked like a basic mobile pinball port.
But, no, actually, this is a serious effort. A very well made pinball game overall, with maybe a few rough spots.
:
* Clever table designs (some
clever like the baseball themed Fastball)
* Good, deep, mostly balanced, fun and challenging rulesets (check them all out here:
.
* Good atmosphere - art, sound, music
* Mod system adds a fun layer of complexity to the game (if you don't mind having to unlock them)
* Well designed global cross-platform tournament system!
* Lots of well designed achievements!
* Quite good physics
* Very low system requirements
* Fun daily challenge system
* Ability to zoom camera
* Optional live leaderboard system (though currently it only uses local scores except for the daily event table)
* Responsive developer
:
* Fixed top-down camera view (it's a 2D game, and otherwise the art looks pretty good, though I wouldn't call it "wow graphics" like the store page, except maybe ironically)
* Camera zoom is a global setting but tables have different heights. In particular, there is one very, very tall table that even on the lowest zoom level does not fit and will require scrolling. It's clever, but I don't really want to play a scrolling table these days.
* Sound effects are delayed for me (but it's tolerable, and I don't have input delay with vsync off)
* No mouse launching, unlike in mobile version (this is especially problematic for the bagatelle table)
* I don't think I like the powerball system (a special ball you can launch that costs tickets (scarce game currency) that doubles your points but also moves faster. But I might change my mind on it. At least it's an interesting concept. It just doesn't seem like something I want to worry about when playing for score. It may not actually be a good idea to use though for advanced players because the loss of control may outweigh the point bonus. EDIT: after playing more, these don't seem to be worth the risk anyway
The physics are "somewhat" basic (e.g. it's 2D and ball seems to have no spin - although the ball will sometimes slide down flippers instead of bouncing), but what's there works very well. Most of the stuff I would expect to work, works. I feel like I generally have very good ball control. It's quite pleasant. It's very good for a 2D game.
* Carnival: currently this is my favorite. Strong multiball element (several mb modes, stacks with other things). Good ruleset in general. Fun DMD video mode. Mirrored lower playfield.
* Brix: this is Breakout. You go through 50 levels. I've only gotten through about 10 so far. You can buy checkpoints and start at a later level that you've unlocked. Pretty clever and fun overall.
* Fastball: super clever ruleset (incorporates baseball rules very well). Baseball fans will love this, I think. Mini-game that emulates those little tabletop baseball pinball devices.
* Treasure Hunter: super tall layout (mandatory scrolling). Lots of flippers. Decent mode oriented ruleset. The higher you go up the table, the harder it is to control the ball / keep it up there.
* Wild West: Hard to get into with some difficult shots. Certain mods are particularly powerful on this table. The theme is fun, and the ruleset is interesting once you learn it.
* Space Frontier: Another table that's hard to figure out at first, but quite fun with a deep ruleset, interesting shots, and interesting mods.
* Bagaball: this is a decent bagatelle design where you want to match the ball color to the appropriate part of the playfield. But the lack of mouse launch control makes perhaps more difficult than it should be.

Just hanging out on MSN and playing CS 1.6 & KZ with a friend.. those were some good times.
I was introduced to KZ around 11 years ago by an expert KZer who guided me and played through various maps together with me. We'd try out jumps in every de_, cs_, as_ and es_ maps while playing through kz/duck maps without much any longjumps or bhopping (my best LJ was probably 240 or less). As I started playing KZ I would only use space to do the jumps, but still found the climbing to be fun. Later on I bound the jump key to mwheel and was able to bhop quite a lot better. I remember actively playing KZ for around 3 months and then continuing to play it every now and then for 9 more months before stopping to play both CS 1.6 and KZ.
Ever since playing KZ and being introduced to level editors or full quest/map editors in games that I've played, KZ has been a big influence in making maps for them. I've found it fun to make reasonably challenging KZ inspired "jump puzzles" in Neverwinter for example. Guild Wars 2 also has these, which is cool.
I've only rarely played Kreedz on my steam copy of CS 1.6 since stopping to play the game mode long time ago, but after seeing a post mentioning the standalone release of KZ I thought I should give this game (mode) a chance once more.
I think the standalone game is just as fun as the game mode back then. The game requires a good amount of patience and in my opinion a lot of time to learn, too. You might spend a good half an hour on one jump when you are new to the game, but it can be rewarding to get through the climbing course faster and faster each time. I like the Paint Tool addition (for those boring moments) and how you can play certain maps in co-op just like before.
I suggest giving it a try.

I discovered N in 2006. It was familiar. Move, jump. Oh, look, you can wall-jump... and control your velocity in the air. Nothing alien. But then, after powering through a dozen episodes, I hit a wall. It wasn't easy. I kept running into these drones. I took a step back. Watched the whole level, which fit so nicely in a single screen. The gameplay is smooth. Only three keys. Minimalistic design, without distractions. Cool music. Awesome colors. Plenty of levels. N++ hits all the right buttons. Your main challenge isn't to go fast: it's to finish the level, and get all the gold. Speed is secondary to timing. That's why N (now plus plus!) is my absolute favorite platformer.

This review is for Project Highrise plus the available DLC (Las Vegas, Miami Malls and Tokyo Towers). I purchased this game as a bundle on a Steam sale which included the available DLC
INITIAL OBSERVATIONS
Project Highrise in my opinion is not much like the old 1990’s Sim Tower.  You can build a tall building with offices, hotels, restaurants and apartments but for me that is as close as those two games get.  I consider Project Highrise more in line with a city builder such as Cities Skylines
In Project Highrise you get to choose the direction you want to take your building beside just up, whether it be by adding hotels, apartments, stores, businesses or a combination of all of these (must have the DLC).
POSSIBLE LEARNING CURVE
For me there has been a slight learning curve to discovering the game’s mechanics and the tutorials only helped a little to get started.  Playing with unlimited resources I found helps a lot (besides it's fun) in learning the game as well.
DLC ADDS VARIETY
As of this review, I have not played Project Highrise (PH) without the DLC (Las Vegas, Miami Malls, and Tokyo Towers)  These DLC give the game depth and variety with its added hotel building expansion which includes casinos, stores, art galleries, event venues, in addition to apartments, office and multi-level lobbies.
GRAPHICS AND SOUND
Both the graphics and sound of PH are decent but are nothing earth shattering. The game could do more with additional animations and sound effects which would add a little more vibrancy to the game.
UNLIMITED MONEY AND RESOURCE OPTION
In the main menu, there is an unlimited money feature which allows for more creative and faster building from the start.  However, it’s important to note that even with the unlimited money and resources option enabled, not all in-game building options will be available at the start (although plenty will be) because tenants have requirements that must be met in order to place them in your building.
OPTIONAL CONTRACTS
Project Highrise features optional contracts which are basically a checklist of goals and achievements you can obtain depending on the particular deal or contract you sign.
Note: Fulfilling contracts help build your wealth faster especially if you are not playing with unlimited resources
YOUR TENANTS ARE NEEDY PEOPLE
Tenants who you might wish to occupy a space in your tower will have needs or requirements that must be met before they can be placed in your building. Some have few needs like electricity and water while others might have more such as cleaning services, prestige, more restaurants placed in your building or trash-pick up services.
Prestige (stars) reflect the level of the good in your building and the happiness (or sadness) of your tenants and visitors. You gain and lose prestige stars by forming various actions in game or allocating space for specific tenants.
ELEVATORS
Unlike in Sim Tower, elevators in PH do not need to be monitored for capacity and usage times.  However, their location does matter depending on what type of tenant you choose to locate nearby.  Some businesses or apartments for example may not be happy if placed next to the elevators.
In addition, smells, noise levels etc, must be monitored to keep your tower dwellers happy.
MODDING
This game has mods.  Always a good thing.
LOTS OF SPACE
One awesome thing I love about Project Highrise is the amount of space you have available to build your tower or towers.  The player is actually given a few options in the main menu. There is Standard, Narrow, Short and Wide or Extra Large.
ROOM FOR IMPROVEMENT
While the game can provide hours of fun, it has room for improvement.  I list a few things here.
PH lacks music options during game-play. In fact there is only one soundtrack available and IMO was a poor choice for this game. Unless you enjoy repetitive elevator music, you may agree.  The game would do well with music mod of some sort.  Fortunately, the music can be turned off completely.
The current animations and sound effects in the game are fine but having additional animations, visuals and sound effects would further enhance the game’s overall quality, likeability and charm.
A faster third speed would be nice
Waiting for things to develop can be a looonnng wait.  The current speeds available are normal and fast.  Sometimes fast isn’t quite fast enough.
Escalators and Parking Spaces
Wish there were escalators and parking spaces.
MY RATING OF PROJECT HIGHRISE
Overall, I would highly recommend this game especially if you enjoy city builders and any Sim Tower style game.  My nine-year-old daughter can also attest to the fun factor this game provides.
Get the game plus DLC in a bundle on a Steam sale for $10-$15 and it’s a great deal.

Over a year has passed since my initial review, which in hindsight I realize was pretty harsh. As a 3D artist who was inspired by Myst to work in the games industry, I have high expectations of Cyan. I purchased the new realMyst on Steam for the sole purpose of having a copy of Myst that will actually run on modern hardware. Revisiting Myst is a tradition for me. The feeling of "standing" on Myst Island is akin to building a warm fire in my brain. It is a deep, nostalgic trip to my childhood; dreamlike, mesmerizing, and incredibly familiar. I return to Myst to remind myself of who I was when I was younger, and reflect on the person I am now. I was optimistic when purchasing the new Unity-based realMyst, despite some disappointing pre-release screenshots. Unfortunately, my fears were well-founded.
realMyst: Masterpiece Edition (RMME) suffers from dramatic inconsistency. It is often sloppy and unoptimized, but can be, at times, staggeringly beautiful.
I feel the consistency in art direction which made the original realMyst [which also suffered from poor optimization] look good for its time was lost to accommodate for shaders and surface normals in the Unity engine. I suspect most of the normal maps from the game were generated from the original diffuse textures in CrazyBump, and not much care was put into the nooks and crannies to make things look right. The original Myst gave attention to every detail, with every bolt and screw painstakingly rendered. RMME is plagued with glaring texture seams and poor texel density distribution across the various Ages. Things are not made to look lived in, but are clean with poorly tiled textures. Comparing the foliage on Myst Island to Channelwood, I can't help but think how some level-of-detail work could have really paid off while showcasing some of Unity's best features, or would have at least made these choices less apparent.
When the game gets dark, it gets
dark. I imagine the flashlight was included to combat this, but it only serves as a painful reminder that the artists neglected to put proper spec maps on models. Everything I shine the flashlight on turns a blinding white, even with bloom disabled.*
The control scheme has also taken a misstep from the original realMyst. In Free-Roam mode, you are unable to stand in one place and look around without holding right-click, and the cursor reacts awkwardly as you look around. Moving up and down ladders is a chore, and having to rely on my meta-game first-person camera instincts to navigate breaks all immersion the game tries to render. Classic Mode completely locks your camera view, disabling the ability to appreciate various angles in realtime without accessing the menu again to disable it. I believe while trying to simplify the control scheme that the designers have in fact created a more cumbersome system that alienates and punishes users who are already familiar with playing first person games on the PC.
I hold out hope that Cyan plans to release future updates to refine RMME, for I would really appreciate having it be my go-to Myst game in the future. The fact that Myst, Myst: ME, and realMyst cannot be made to work on modern hardware without breaking your computer is tragic.

I bought this game more out of curiosity, as I've read a lot of negative reviews for it and I wanted to check for myself if all the negativity is justified. In some cases it is and this is why I'm going to start out with the Cons:
- Extra repetitive combat, at some points the game even became a click-to-kill simulator. Too many scenes of fighting where the gameplay could've been different. Maybe some mazes, some puzzles instead of brain-dead clicking. I know that it is supposed to be this way, but it gets kinda boring after a while. And while the combat was repetitive, so were the enemies, being represented by few models and animations.
- If you have a degree in History, you might get an epilepsy crisis at some points, due to historical innacuracy. Though, the heroic soldiers of the Roman Empire, the military strategies, some landscapes of Rome are spot on and all those little things made me love the game more than I hated it for mistaken the story of Damocles (which was Greek, btw), misplacing Nero in the wrong era and so forth. I am not that upset for the historical innacuracy as I see this game as a possible introduction to the Roman Empire to people who want to learn more and can do so on their own.
- Some scenes made me want to hang myself in the bathroom in frustration. I can't say that the boss fights were not fun, but killing a boss just to find out you didn't and have to kill him again, or fighting a group of barbarians just to fight another group of barbarians so you can fight the barbarian elite after that gets really frustrating.
Why have I given this game a positive review though? Because I really enjoyed the following pros more than I enjoyed the cons:
- Executions are fun, even though they also get repetitive. I really enjoyed seeing in a video game this elementary, barbarian skills of men back in the day, while I equally enjoyed leading a Roman Legion in tactical warfare, something new and revolutionary for the barbaric tribes of the era. The combat (that repetitive combat) was done well and in a realistic way.
- The story was great. As I said, do not expect historical accuracy, but for a video game I felt like I was reading a good book, or watching a great movie. Plot twists, different scenarios, various locations and so forth. I will not spoil anything though. I found it quite short - maybe because I wanted it to go on - but as it was, it was enough and amazing.
- I really found the graphics of this game awesome. The textures are amazing, the faces are well done, the battlefields look good and so forth.
- The cutscenes were breathtaking. I sometimes in games tend to skip them, but in this game I didn't want them to end. They were so immersive in the story.
- Most of all, it was a fun game. You get to do some scavanger hunt in order to find the collectibles, you get to play as a Roman soldier (which is kinda rare) and if you enjoy games like God of War, you probably will like this game too.
In conclusion, it is a great heroic, fantasy game set in a historical time that can keep you intrigued and entertained.

I generally do not write a review for a game that I have not played at least five hours, but I made this an exception due to how easy it is to experience all there is within the first thirty minutes.
I purchased
out of curiosity during one of the Steam sales event.
I obtained the game under the impression that it could be a nice pass time game allowing me to go on a rampage;
the game definitely delivered in that aspect, I was given an environment and monsters to shoot at.
The problem with this game, however, is the fact that the entire game seems to be just a showcase of an idea.
Due to this very fact, I was no longer able to endure this game past the 25th minute mark.
I do realize that this game is still in early development, but I would in no manner consider this a game.
The definition of providing early access is to allow people to purchase the game and test it for the developers,
with the fundemental qualification for an early access game being having most, if not all, of the core mechanics present.
This was not the case.
This game feels like it is showcasing the classes and the monsters, with overly simplistic menus with very lacking choices.
This game delivered a functioning showcase, as I have yet to encounter a debilitating glitch,
but other than the above point, there are several other problems I would like to point out:
1) The game does not receive updates frequently enough.
Out of the some eight months of owning this game, the game has yet to receive major function and mechanics update.
The update frequency can easily rank just below the notorious
.
2) The classes are extremely unbalanced, for future update reference.
I have been playing tanks most of the petty amount of time I have endured this game,
as I was shown time and time again in the game that tanks somehow have amazing advantage in both offensive and defensive capabilities compared to many others. I could mow down all mobs regardless of the distance with just the shotgun.
3) The game still does not have multiplayer functionality.
The developer's blog did mention encountering problems on December of last year with creating the multiplayer function, but that was seven months ago.
4) Despite randomized, the game has a very limited amount of mobs, rooms, bosses, and items.
As such, the game was not very engaging, as within twenty minutes, the player may have already encountered every single possible instance. Hence why I could not hold my attention onto the game for even 30 minutes.
Until the game performs a major update with multiplayer capability, and also have far more variety in its instances,
I do not recommend purchasing this game.
TL;DR:
Ranging from instance variety and mechanics, the game is too lacking in too many manners.
Until this game has a multiplayer function and an expanded library of instances, this game is not recommended.

Pinball Deluxe Reloaded is a port of an Android/Iphone pinball. It's an awesome little pinball game, which is really worth a try.
I like the retro feeling you get from having 2D tables instead of all the modern tables on Arcade or FX. Two tables really stand out for me: The Brix table, which is like Arkanoid with different levels and with its changing play field reminds me of Enigma from Epic Pinball. The other one is Baga Ball which dives deep into the history of Pinball tables without flippers.
But all tables have heart and are really individual. There is an extra long table and the Baseball table feels like a real game.
A key point which sets Pinball Deluxe Reloaded apart from other pinball simulations is the ability to change the gameplay experience for each table with "mods", which you can earn and level-up. You can increase your chance for an Extra Ball with a mod or score more points from bumpers. Each table has 10 individual mods. Also, you can double your score with power balls.
Daily Events and challenges keep drawing me in. On some ends, you will notice that the game was ported from a mobile game like when you view the table how little of the screen is actually used.
Overall it is a welcome distraction from the modern pinball games on Steam.
The only thing I'm really missing at the time of release is a local hot seat mode, but lets see what the future brings.

Battleborn is an excellent mix of a MOBA and a shooter. While its controls aren't as tight as those of Overwatch (I hate that comparison, but it seems to be what the general public is comparing it to) it definitely is a competent shooter in itself while also sporting a lot of charm due to its vast array of characters.
While the game definitely is better with friends, it's still a fantastic game if you're playing it by yourself, just be sure to play the story mode through the matchmaking system, as it's much better to actually play the co-op campaign co-op instead of solo. As for the versus multiplayer aspect, it's guaranteed to hold your attention for a good while with 25 different characters and 3 game modes. There are only 6 different maps to speak of as of right now, 2 for each game mode, but the maps feel different enough to warrant there not being more right now. Unfortunately 2 of the maps are poorly optimized (Echelon and Coldsnap, the latter being the worse of the two when it comes to optimization), but with more maps (as well as characters) coming down the line, hopefully Gearbox can iron that issue out.
In this short review I just wanted to briefly brush over the major offerings of Battleborn and hopefully provide you with information that will help you decide whether or not it's worth a purchase for you. There are a lot of stuff I haven't covered, like loot, progression, lore challenges, boss battles etc., but for me, this is the kind of game I've been waiting for for ages without knowing it. Battleborn definitely has a few issues, but I am hopeful that Battleborn does well and that Gearbox is able to turn it into a longlasting franchise.

I've played a lot of action RPG's over the years, MMO's included. In terms of the action RPG category I honestly have to say Dungeon Siege 2 takes the cake as the best game ever released. The speed of play and game mechanics are perfect, especially for their time. Unlike the Diablo series, Dungeon Siege 2 takes a less of a "run and gun" approach to the game. What I mean by this is when your fighting adversaries you actually have to stop and put up a fight. Those who have played Diablo know that if you're playing in a big party you pretty much never stop running while mowing down enemies in the process. I prefer the Dungeon Siege approach because it feels more like a role playing adventure, which is what I am looking for. As for the mechanics, they nailed it. The loot is always great, there are tons of different items, magical, unique etc. There isn't really any one thing about the game that I can honestly pick apart and say "I really wish they had done that". Every good aspect of action RPG's is contained in this game and the bad left out. And the storytelling? Second to none.
Graphically this game is 10 years old now from me writing this review. That said, in the year 2005 3d graphics were certainly nothing new. If graphics factor heavily into your purchasing of a game, this game will probably never live up. But it still looks pretty good. The environments are very beautiful, and the team who made this game definitely took their time putting work into every little detail.
The last thing I will say is when you buy this game.. it comes with glitches. If you have a windows 7/8 computer you have to download some direct x patches (from the microsoft website), setup some commands to enable widescreen, and also I had to do something to get the mouse to appear. If you want to play multiplayer it is disabled, but there is a workaround possible, and you can play with friends from around the world by setting up a virtual server. If you can figure out all these things you can get the game to work as it was originally intended in all it's glory.
My rating of this game 9/10 :)

Myst was first released to critical acclaim in 1993, 21 years ago! Seven years later, in 2000, RealMyst was released. A game that took the slideshow world of Myst and turned it into a living, breathing real 3D game world. Now, 14 years later, in 2014, comes RealMyst Masterpiece Edition! Some say that this is just a cheap port, others say it's a money grab. The truth of the matter is that it is an entirely new engine, built from the ground up, to give us the greatest version of Myst ever created. Not only does this game include graphical updates, but the control system is much better as well. No, it's not the most graphically advanced came of the decade, but it's advanced enough that old fans will appreciate it, and new fans will be born from it.
If you have been a fan of the Myst series for the last 20 years, this is a great platform to revisit the world from. If you are new to the Myst world, be aware, this game is probably unlike anything else you have seen. There are no tutorials, and the storyline is a mystery for most of the game. The visuals are exciting and the puzzles are mystifying. This game is entirely about the journey, not the end. So enjoy it while it lasts.
This video is for those of you like me, who loved the original RealMyst, but want to see how it really stacks up to the newest version of the game.
Here is another video that compares the original 1993 Myst to RealMyst Masterpiece. The photo's are available in-game when you use the classic control mode, and press the shift key.

Ok. Where to start. I'm going to approach this in chronological order of my
thorough dissapointment with this title. My first wave of frustration eminated
from the lack of an options menu right at the beginning. I like to set my
resolution at least before starting a new game, so I had to watch the nice intro in
an eye wrenching 1280x720, which was a little annoying but overall not a huge
deal. After spawning in the world a menu comes up and tells you that you have a
choice between free roam and and classic mode, awesome. Naturally, I pick free
roam, because nostalgia's great and everything but classic mode really defeats the
purpose of playing a real time version of Myst. Walking around in free roam was
terribly confusing at first and didnt seem to make any sense, but what I figured
out is that if you're standing still you have to hold down the right mouse button
to look. But you can look freely without doing that while moving. This is a
terribly unintuitive control mechanic that makes free roam into a kind of mental
gymnastic constantly trying to remember to hold down the mouse button every
time you stop for half a second. It is the most pointlessy alien and baffling first
person mechanic I've ever played. It's like Cyan has been sealed away in a glass
dome for the last 20 years and essentially invented their own control mechanic
based on what they knew from developing the orginal Myst and didnt bother at all
to take an example from literally any other well designed first person game. It's
also worth noting that when holding down the right mouse button, not only is it
uncomfortable to hold it down while moving the mouse, the sensitivity is
inexplicably lower which adds a new variable of unnessecary awkwardness into
this madman's equation. In line with my frustration with the controls is the fact
that there seems to be mouse acceleration that cant be disabled. I personally view
mouse acceleration with the same burning hostility that I would normally reserve
for someone who had just burned my house down and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥on my dog. And I
can't be the only one who feels this way so it would be nice to have a little
checkbox or something like all of the FPS's ever that have a mouse-acceleration
feature. You know, just a thought. Now, that that's out of the way let's talk about
the engine. I've never been overly impressed with the Unity engine, and personally
would not choose to develop in it myself, but I really want to believe it can be
used more efficiently than this. The fan for my decent graphics card that can run
Crysis 2 with no real problems was screaming at full speed after about 2 minutes.
I don't know if Cyan develops their real time titles in house but theyve never
seemed to reflect a firm grasp on how to develop assets for a games engine.
Theyve always seemed to approach it with the same technique you would use for
production rendering, in the 90's no less, going completely off the chain with
texel density and poly count for example, yet making no use of masking or
layering or anything of the sort that a modern node based shader editor can do to
hide atrociously tiling textures. Foliage density is unneseccarily higher than a
crack head fresh out of rehab, and I noticed a couple instances of vertex normals
being softened when they clearly didnt need to be which is just plain sloppy. I also
have a sneaking suspicion that they took some of the textures from the 2000
version of realmyst and hastily ran them through crazy bump. I love the original
Myst. It is a masterpiece, but this just seems like a sloppy insult to the original,
which is exactly what I thought of the original realMyst from 2000. I hate to say
this, because Myst is so close to my heart, but I cannot reccomend dropping 17
dollars on this mess of a game. If you're going to remake a classic for a 20th
anniversary, have the decency to do it right.

This is a cautious recommendation from someone who grew up with Myst. A lot of this will be similar to a review for realMyst's original release.
This is just as awkward to control as realMyst was, and having to move the mouse to slide a Marker Switch up and down or move the flow controls in Channelwood from side to side is not an easy experience if you are using free movement.
This game uses the same movie files from realMyst (the brothers' library videos are the same as the original release, other videos are newer and less-well-acted). Myst: Masterpiece Edition runs like garbage on modern systems--if it runs at all--but at least when you play that you believe that Atrus believes what he's saying and isn't just reciting old dialogue.
Having the original gameplay images for Myst pop up when you press Shift (while not using free movement) is a nice touch, though if you are running this on a modern resolution you'll barely be able to see the images in the center of your screen.
The sound is as great as it ever was, although just like with realMyst, this version of the game does not completely mute the music at appropriate times (as in the fore-chamber).The music itself is not changed from classic Myst and that's a huge point in this release's favor.
I guess there's a flashlight now but having just finished the game I never used it. Not sure what the point of it is unless you're too lazy to turn the crank on the battery in Stoneship. I can't think of any other locations that are very dark and also have something worth seeing. I don't even know what button it is bound to. Probably F.
At the end of the day, this is still Myst, and one of the first games to tell a deep story purely by observations of one's environment (Gone Home also does this very well). Modern systems don't have many other ways to play other releases of Myst without jumping through compatibility hoops so having this on Steam is cool---BUT the original release is on iOS in untouched, fully compatible glory.
If you own realMyst, this game is 12 bucks instead of 18. Maybe that will help sway you.

I grew up playing the original and the ability to walk around myst island with improved graphics is just amazing.  Cyan did a fantastic job with this remake of the realmyst game from 2001 or so. If you love myst then you should fall in love with this version.
Summary:
In Myst you play an unknown traveller that finds a book somewhere (you don't find this out until you read the Myst novel's.)  Once you open its cover, you are transported to Myst Island.  Once there, the player discovers the lore of the D'ni and how they created links to worlds that already existed in other dimensions through the use of "The Art."
The Art is a way of creating linking books to other worlds.  You, the player, are in one of those worlds.  Myst Island is a refuge for Atrus and his family.  Through reading the books in the Myst library, you discover everything about Atrus' sons and gain some insight into his travels in other worlds.
in Myst, you must solve a way to get back to your world.  From reading certain notes spread thoughout the island and in other worlds, you discover a plot to imprison Atrus and leave him for dead by his wicked sons, Sirrus and Achenar.
Conclusion:
For its day, Myst was an amazing game and truly the first of its kind on CD-ROM.  Each indidual screen was created on a mac and each time the player clicked forward, they would move to the next pre-rendered screen.  Now, you can move all around freely.  realMyst ME is the definitive edition for the original Myst game.
Keep an eye out for the starry expanse project too.  It's a small dev team remaking RIven in Unreal 4.  Riven is the sequel to Myst.  If you've never tried it, at least play the original Riven.  You will feel immersed in both games because there is just so much lore to be found in both.

Pretty true to the classic Myst as best as I can remember, though it has been long enough I had to resolve much of the puzzles.  The 3D work in the 'common' areas is really nice, but in other areas it feels very crude.  For example the ending of the maze, you can see the textures tiling as you go by.  Same on the fortress.  They also did not remake the videos, especially the 'bad' endings.
A bit choppy on max settings with a very strong gaming machine.  Definitely not warranted for the quality being rendered, but it didn't really affect the gameplay.  Effects that seem to be from the engine (ie. water/lava) look really good.
I played it through and only had a single crash while alt tabbing to check e-mail.
The 3D controls were pretty good, if a bit awkward at first.  Going up and down a spiral staircase in a certain realm was actually rather odd.  Moving around in 3D does, imho, make the game easier as things are much easier to find and figure out than in the traditional navigation.
I also found a typo in one of the journals.  The journals are worth reading, as a kid playing the game I didn't really read for the story, just the clues and missed the whole plot and meaning of the red/blue books.
The 'final' realm is also a bit dependent on your audible skills.  I am a bit tone deaf, which made that realm a challenge.  *You definitely need sound to finish that portion of the game.*
Overall, having had played the original Myst many years (decades?) ago, this was an enjoyable second play through.

This is a wonderful game. This was my first game I ever owned back when I was a child, so I have a nostalgic bias. To the review; this game from the get-go is aesthetically 200% better. It looks like any indie FPS you can buy nowadays minus a tutorial and immediate plot. I put countless hours into this game as a child and never beat it. I recommend this game to anyone who wants an relaxing, in-depth story told to them through puzzles, journal entries, and a non-hostile environment.
Good things to say about this game:
-Beautiful
-Flashlight feature is helpful
-Easy conversion from classic point-'n'-click to real-time first person.
-Story remains intact if not more immerse
-More brainpower and problem-solving required than any game on the modern market
Bad things to say about this game:
-Suffers from massive framerate drops in real time first person. I drop from 60+ FPS to around 15-20 frequently; it's not a hardware issue either, it's a frame cap.
-First person controls are different and take some getting use to (Letting off WASD brings up a cursor)
-Not a casual adventure game; requires hours upon hours to reveal the entire story, get through each puzzle (if you're new to the game), and navigate each area.
This is a time-consuming masterpiece. Mozart is to the Classical genre of music, as Myst is to Adventure games. Very few games deserve such artistic praise, this ranks number 1 on my list.

"I wish there were some elevators"
This game is pretty neat. It is a lot like SimTower from back in the day, but with some extra neat features like gaining the ability to gain additional perks through hiring consultants and spending "influence points" or, by conducting marketing campaigns where you spend "buzz". There are also a number of contracts which allow you to gain a little extra cash by meeting city goals. For instance, you might get a contract for increased urban densification where you're rewarded for building a number of apartments. I went after this contract and over-leveraged myself, taking out a loan to complete the project only to fall short of the cash I needed to finish, leading to a rough few days where I thought I might go bankrupt. But when I finally managed to collect enough money to finish building and opening some of them, alongside a media campaign which dropped the price of building them and increased the rate at which they filled, I managed to scrape by and claimed my reward from the contract (plus the large increase in daily revenues I experienced after that). That was fun.
Now for the bad. The pathfinding on the people living, working, and visiting your tower is horrendous. They will wander back and forth across floors, alternating constantly between stairs and elevators while complaining that your building has no elevators. I think the best way to handle this is probably to remove the stairs, but it makes no sense why this should occur. In the picture I linked above, that worker was literally standing in front of the elevator complaining that my building doesn't have elevators - and people will move out based on this complaint (except for your service workers - they're stuck there like indentured servants, mwuhaha). This quickly gets frustrating. Also, this seems to be a disregarded issue that the devs likely won't fix seeing as the game already has 3 expansions.
The services you add to your building are kind of neat, but also kind of jarring. In what world does a building manager build and pay for a copy center, a parcel delivery office (FedEx?), a water delivery service, etc etc. Especially with the ability to rent to different and unique tenants who move in, it seems like a better option would have been to attract businesses that perform these services, leading to awesome synergies within the same building (e.g. having a parcel delivery company that benefits from other offices in the building, plus increases their happiness in kind). The game already kind of has that synergy building element between businesses in other ways (e.g. creatives and lawyers often want cafes they can frequent) - that approach would have been much more interesting. On top of that, my janitorial services seem to do very little except satisfy the couple of office types which expect them, with offices rapidly getting dirty and requiring repairs from my maintenance office.
Another jarring thing is how the market can suddenly start booming in your city... for a day. So rents will go up and people will move in faster for that day only... because apparently that's how markets work. It's kind of a neat idea, but it really detracts from the world-building (tower-building?) aspect that is part of the core of this game.
It is also quickly starting to get dull for me. It is hard to explain why exactly. I love these kinds of games usually. I sunk tons of time into SimTower back in the day, and when I can find time I occasionally spend long hours on city builders like Cities Skylines.

The best way I can describe my reaction to this game is 'mixed but likely to improve.' I'll try to explain why.
In my opinion the 'Simulation' genre, is a genre that is almost more Sandbox than the Wide Open Sandbox games. The Simulation genre of games like Tropico, Project Highrise, or a huge amount of Kalypso's library are literal sandboxes, where you decide what kind of game you're going to play this time.
"I'm going to build a huge hotel with zero offices and the best Casinos and Concert Halls on the block."
"I'm going to build a mall with no offices or apartments, and literally nothing but stores and restaurants."
"I'm going to build a Dystopian Style Office complex with nothing but Plebs making me money."
And so on. Think of them like terms and conditions for your playthrough of that Sandbox mode.
And well....the more DLC that comes out for a game, the more tools you have in the sandbox. The more options for roleplaying with your imagination and building your tower come out. The DLC is pretty cheap, and the game goes down to around $5 for the base game during sales (It's 5.49 Canadian as of this review), and the bundle gives you a good 10% discount on all DLC if you get it as it comes out.
Ultimately although my reaction to this game isn't that it's the most stellar thing ever. I seriously have to look at something like say Tropico 4, or Fallout 4, or the Sims 3 and ask myself. "How fun would those games be if you had JUST the base game and literaly no extra content?" No cement factory or plantation in Tropico 4, no farm plots, robots, or vault stuff in Fallout 4, and literally none of the wacky stuff that makes Sims 3 into the equivalent of living in a Midsummer's night dream with Witches, Fairies, and Robots.
So yeah, this game might seem like a 7/10 right now, but I have no question that when the last DLC is out and we have every tool available to us, it'll be an amazing piece of tower fun. I mean it's not like the game will get worse with more options.
So I'll give it a recommendation, it's certainly worth the money if you get it on sale, and it's a simulation game, so you're likely going to spend enough hours in it just getting through the first few scenarios to make it worth it.

It's a platformer, but there isn't really any jumping, and definitely no running. What you do is simply shoot yourself from platform to platform, either straight ahead (which is faster, but be careful of untimely death to mines) or in a direction of choice (which is slower). That's all there is to it.
When it works, it works really well. The game sends you almost into a trance of high-speed hops and techno chiptunes. Understanding when you can safely jump straight will make it even faster, but even the directional hop has a fairly generous level of aim correction (which is a good thing in this case, believe me) so it won't slow down the rhythm that much. Some other choices are a bit more baffling though. Having to complete 5 levels at a time... sure, the average stage is about 2-3 seconds, but dying at the 5th stage and having to speed through the previous 4 again, eventually wears a bit thin.
Too bad, because every other trick in the book  has been used. You can skip every intermediate sequence, you can get back into a stage you have already beaten to collect the bonus trinket without losing your previous record... if it weren't for the 5 stages requirement, the game would be a lot less stressful. Even so, it's still worth playing for those who live off twitch platformers.

The fundamental motion in Hopiko is the hop. More specifically, it is a straight line. The gameplay is as simple as it gets. You hop from place to place. That’s it. You can’t stay on platforms too long, as they expire and kill you after a few seconds. The screen is littered with obstacles. It’s reminiscent of the Donkey Kong Country games’ barrel obstacle courses. Like some other modern indie games, it has a very short and intense gameplay loop: you die, you die, you die, but eventually you succeed. Success happens after dozens of death, but it is always a satisfactory feeling. This is due to Hopiko’s design choice for a death to set you back to the beginning of a set of five levels. The levels can be pretty tough, asking of you precise timing. This isn’t as annoying as it sounds, because a level in Hopiko can take less than a second to complete, and rarely lasts longer than maybe eight seconds. It is a blisteringly fast and frantic game, snapping from platform to platform, dying, then doing the same over and over. Because of that death system, the tension ramps up every recursion through the stage, until it is finally relieved at success. It’s a great dynamic.
The story is something about viruses in a video game console. It’s silly and irrelevant. The visuals are basic, simple and direct pixelart. The sound effects are the same. The music can drone a bit, as the track only changes for every game instance & World (I think), though the music itself is good. With all this, the simplicity of the game might seem like it would peter out the excitement, but somehow, Hopiko constantly finds ingenious ways to twist it. The game is genuinely engaging throughout. Every few stages, a new mechanic is introduced, and all of them are clever. Hopiko constantly surprises and elates. Every mechanic added lines up with the core mechanics of the game, and each level is like a satisfying ludic haiku.
Hopiko is a game meant to be completed 100%. It fits in with obstacle course games like Flywrench and Dustforce. There are three things: just finishing the stage, finishing each level in a set time period, and collecting an item in one of the five levels. It can be surprisingly difficult, but due to the fast reset times and the fast gameplay speed, shuttling back through the levels never feels to arduous to redo. For 100%, you unlock several gameplay modes for the World, and new audio tracks (this part is a bit silly). You get bonus levels, which function as a kind of no-brakes cart track of sorts. You also get Speedrun modes, which challenge you to beat the entire World as fast as possible, with checkpoints every five levels, and Hardcore modes, which ask you to beat the entire world without dying once. These are good incentives for completion, but nothing is as enticing for the completion as just the general thrill of success you get from the actual feat. The difficulty curve (both regarding this completionism, and regarding the general curve of the game) is so fluid that the you don’t even notice it’s getting harder.
Hopiko is a fantastic little game with a deceivingly simple structure that consistently deepens in creative and engaging ways. Currently, my only real complaint is that there isn’t a level editor; this game would fit perfectly in the Steam Workshop, Zipping back and forth between platforms in these levels is addictive and satisfying. This is a perfect game for completionists and those who love skill-challenges.

It's got a pretty great idea that's been executed pretty well. The problem is that it doesn't do much else to stand out other than its gimmick of being 'the 2D Moba'.
, and rarely do you ever feel like you're making plays or doing anything special. Some characters grant more satisfaction than others, but overall there's still an empty feeling to the gameplay that doesn't get filled.
A possible reason for this is that the abilities are limited and generally lack flair. You're also limited to using only a basic attack, 2 abilities, and a jump. There's very little depth to character play because you're so limited in your skill rotations. You can't even call them a rotation in Awesomenauts. As an attacker type of character, you usually have one ability that helps you land the other one, or chains with the other one. After you use both of them, you're left to use left click.
Then you do that for the whole match, when it comes to the actual PVP fighting part of it. There's no ultimate or a third ability to make situation skill rotations possible. Every character, with pun completely intended, is extremely 2-dimensional.
It's sad, because it has a really good idea and great characters, and overall decent execution. The problem is that it just lacks depth, and it's kind of a messed up level of funny given that the game is 2D and not 3D, while lacking depth.
If you're looking for a game that puts a spin on the MOBA genre, with a heavy emphasis on skillshots- give Smite a spin. Awesomenauts, due to its design, is very team-play oriented. If you're looking for a team-play oriented MOBA, you should try your hand at Heroes of the Storm.
